question: A 20-year-old man presents with hearing loss and pain in his right ear after an air- plane flight. The otoscopic examination reveals a perforated right tympanic mem- brane. What are the appropriate discharge instructions?

options.text: Discharge with ENT follow-up in 2 to 3 weeks
Urgent ENT follow-up for surgical repair
Water irrigation of ear canal daily

correctAnswer: Discharge with ENT follow-up in 2 to 3 weeks
englishExplanation: Barotrauma can result in a perforated tympanic membrane, which tends to heal without intervention within a few weeks; perforations from blunt or noise trauma also tend to heal without intervention. Antibiotics are generally unnec- essary unless there is a suspicion for foreign material remaining in the ear. Patients should follow-up in 2 to 3 weeks with an ENT specialist to evaluate for healing and ongoing hearing loss. If the tympanic membrane has not healed in 3 to 6 months, surgical repair may be needed. As long as the perforation exists, exposure to water in the auditory canal should be limited. Patients with tympanic membrane perforations will typically complain of sudden pain and hearing loss. Transient vertigo and tinnitus may also accompany this di- agnosis. On examination, blood and debris may be found and should be cleared. Incorrect Answer Explanations Systemic antibiotics are generally not indicated for a tympanic membrane rup- tured by barotrauma. Perforated tympanic membranes should be kept dry and tend to heal on their own within a few weeks. Antibiotics are only indicated in cases where foreign debris may be present in the canal or inner ear. Surgical repair should be considered if the tympanic membrane has not healed in 3 to 6 months, but an urgent ENT evaluation is unwarranted if the injury is due to barotrauma. Tympanic membrane perforation due to penetrating trauma is more likely to require surgical intervention, and patients should be instructed to see the ENT specialist within 24 hours. Warm water irrigation is a home remedy for cerumen removal. Perforated tympanic membranes should be kept dry and tend to heal on their own within a few weeks.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 16-year-old girl presents with swelling, marked erythema, and pus drainage of the upper helix of her right ear following a piercing; the earlobe is spared. Intravenous antibiotics are started to treat a Staphylococcus aureus infection. Which organism should also be targeted with pharmacotherapy?
englishExplanation: Auricular perichondritis is an unusual infection that can be caused by trauma, ear surgery, or high ear piercing in the upper cartilage. Mild infections can be treated with oral antibiotics with activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Although generally avoided in children, fluoroquinolones may be used in this set- ting regardless of the patient's age. More serious infections, like the one affecting this patient, require intravenous antibiotic therapy to cover both Staphylococcus aureus and P. aeruginosa. Admission to the hospital and consultation with an otolaryngolo- gist are also appropriate to prevent permanent damage and deformity. Surgical drainage of an abscess might be indicated; consultation with an otolaryngologist is indicated to make this determination. Perichondritis is an infection of the cartilage; since there is no cartilage in the earlobe, the earlobe is typically spared. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acinetobacter baumannii is an opportunistic organism that typically infects hospi- talized immunocompromised patients. Pneumonia, meningitis, and necrotiz- ing fasciitis are conditions associated with A. baumannii infections. Eikenella corrodens normally inhabits the human mouth and upper airway. Clinically important infections occur in human bites, in patients with cancers of the head and neck, and in intravenous drug users who lick their needles. Moraxella catarrhalis is known to cause otitis media, bronchitis, and sinusitis. Unlike P. aeruginosa, M. catarrhalis is not associated with otitis externa or perichondritis.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the most common bacterial cause of suppurative perichondritis?
englishExplanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most commonly isolated bacteria in sup- purative perichondritis. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of nonsuppurative perichondritis. Pseudomonas should be suspected in perichondritis due to an ear piercing within the first 30 days. Incorrect Answer Explanations Moraxella catarrhalis is not a common cause of perichondritis. It is a common cause of otitis media. Staphylococcus aureus is not the most commonly isolated organism in suppurative perichondritis. However, it is the most commonly isolated organism in nonsuppu- rative or non–abscess-forming perichondritis. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common cause of perichondritis, but it is not the most common cause of abscess-forming perichondritis. Pseudomonas aerugi- nosa is the most commonly isolated bacteria in suppurative perichondritis.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which antibiotic would provide appropriate coverage for a patient with suspected suppurative perichondritis of the ear?
englishExplanation: Of the antibiotics listed, ciprofloxacin is the best choice for treating suppura- tive perichondritis. When treating abscess-forming or suppurative perichondritis, coverage needs to be expanded to include treatment of Pseudomonas aerugi- nosa. P. aeruginosa is the most commonly isolated bacteria in suppurative perichondritis, and it should be suspected in perichondritis due to an ear pierc- ing within the first 30 days. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amoxicillin gives adequate gram-positive coverage and is appropriate in cases of non- suppurative perichondritis. However, it does not cover for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is a likely cause infection in suppurative perichondritis. Cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin and would give adequate gram-posi- tive and gram-negative coverage. However, cephalexin does not cover for infec- tions caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which must be covered because the infection is suppurative. Vancomycin is inadequate for coverage of suppurative perichondritis. In cases of sup- purative perichondritis, antibiotic coverage should be expanded to include coverage for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Intravenous vancomycin is not a common treat- ment for perichondritis, but in severe cases, such as those requiring hospital admis- sion, it may be used in conjunction with intravenous antibiotics covering Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the most common cause of perichondritis?
englishExplanation: Ear piercing is a well-established cause of perichondritis. Perichondritis in this setting is highly linked to infections by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. If a pa- tient presents with the piercing still in place, it should be removed. Incorrect Answer Explanations Minor trauma (ie, a superficial abrasion or scratch) is not the most common cause of perichondritis. Minor trauma could possibly lead to perichondritis in an immunocompromised individual, but it is otherwise uncommon. Otitis externa is not the most common cause of perichondritis. However, severe otitis externa can cause perichondritis. In cases of perichondritis complicated by otitis externa, the patient should be treated with oral and otic drop antibiotics to cover Pseudomonas. Otitis media is an uncommon cause of perichondritis. Severe or untreated otitis media has been known to rarely cause perichondritis. However, severe or un- treated otitis media can cause inflammation and infection in the mastoid air cells, re- sulting in acute mastoiditis. Mastoiditis occurs more commonly in children than adults. Symptoms may include fever, mastoid tenderness, and overlying erythema. CT imaging should be performed in cases suggestive of acute mastoiditis. Antibiotic coverage should be broad to cover for Pseudomonas as well as gram-positive and gram-negative species.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient presents with suppurative perichondritis 1 week after getting an ear piercing. The patient is afebrile with a nontoxic appearance and normal vital signs. Which action is most appropriate?
englishExplanation: All patients who have perichondritis in the setting of a foreign body should have it removed. In this case, the foreign body is a retained earring. Oral antibiotics are typically sufficient for treatment. Antibiotics coverage should include gram-positive species. When perichondritis is caused by a piercing or other for- eign body, coverage should be expanded to include Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Incorrect Answer Explanations Most patients with perichondritis can be managed on an outpatient basis with oral antibiotics. Antibiotic coverage should include gram-positive coverage. In the setting of a piercing, suppurative perichondritis, or a severe case, coverage should be ex- panded to include Pseudomonas. Although most cases of perichondritis can be managed on an outpatient basis, some severe cases may require admission for intra- venous antibiotics or surgical management in the setting of abscess and necrosis. In this case, the patient does not meet any clear criteria for admission. Although follow-up with otolaryngology is always recommended, emergent consulta- tion is likely not required for most acute cases of perichondritis. Exceptions to this rule include severe cases, associated severe injuries, and abscess with necrosis. Oral antibiotics are typically sufficient for the treatment of perichondri- tis. At minimum, antibiotics should provide good gram-positive coverage because common culprits of infection are Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species. Antibiotic coverage should be expanded to include Pseudomonas aeruginosa in se- vere cases, suppurative cases, and cases associated with piercings.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the most recognized complication of severe perichondritis?
englishExplanation: Cartilage necrosis is the primary complication of perichondritis. Untreated abscesses due to perichondritis can lead to cartilage necrosis. Concern for an abscess-causing cartilage necrosis should prompt broad antibiotic coverage (to in- clude Pseudomonas aeruginosa), incision and drainage, consultation for special- ist evaluation, and possibly hospital admission. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute otitis media is rarely associated with perichondritis. Simple cases of suspected bacterial acute otitis media can be managed with outpatient antibiotics if the patient is stable and without associated complications. Auricular hematoma is not a complication of severe perichondritis. However, auric- ular hematomas due to trauma are one of the most common causes of perichondritis. Mastoiditis is not commonly linked to perichondritis. However, all examina- tions of acute ear pain should include palpation over the mastoid process with a con- sideration of mastoiditis in the differential diagnosis. If there is clinical suspicion for mastoiditis, intravenous antibiotics should be ordered, followed by imaging, consul- tation with otolaryngology, and admission to the hospital.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 6-year-old boy presents with severe eye pain and blurred vision after acciden- tally getting plaster in his eyes. What is the best initial step in management?

options.text: Measure the pH level of the eye

englishExplanation: After chemical exposure to the eye, patients typically present with eye pain, decreased visual acuity, photophobia, and difficulty opening the eyelids. A chemical injury to the eye is a true emergency, as time is paramount in salvaging vision. Therefore, it is inappropriate to delay irrigation, even to assess visual acuity; irrigation should always be the first step in treating chemical exposure to the eye so that the offending agent is removed. Irrigation should preferably begin at the place of exposure, using any drinkable fluid if water is unavailable. Ideally, the patient's eye should then be irrigated again on ar- rival (bypassing triage, registration, and initial examination) with at least 1 L to 2 L of normal saline, using intravenous tubing or a polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) scleral lens (eg, Morgan Lens) if possible. Irrigation should con- tinue until a neutral pH is measured in the eye, which often takes 30 to 60 minutes. A Morgan Lens may be preferred for prolonged irrigation over 60 minutes. Importantly, alkaline substances are more dangerous to the eye than acidic sub- stances. Moreover, wet alkaline substances, such as plaster or cement, can collect in the fornices, so irrigation should aim to actively clear debris from the fornices to avoid continuous alkaline injury. If concern for globe rupture exists, a Morgan Lens should not be used. After initial irrigation, the pH level of the inferior cul-de-sac can be tested with litmus or pH paper, and irrigation should continue until the pH is between 7 and 7.5. If the pH level does not normalize after initial irrigation, check for retained debris in the fornices and remove it with a cotton-tipped ap- plicator. Once a neutral pH is obtained, test it again 20 to 30 minutes later because corrosive material can be released from the cornea for several hours. If the pH subse- quently changes, further irrigation is warranted. A physical examination often reveals conjunctival injection, but in severe alkaline burns, the conjunctiva can appear white due to conjunctival ischemia. Any patient with corneal clouding or an epithe- lial defect after irrigation must undergo an ophthalmologic evaluation. Incorrect Answer Explanations It is imperative to begin irrigation as soon as possible unless there is concern for globe rupture. Visual acuity should be assessed once the eye is properly ir- rigated and reaches a neutral pH level. The pH in the inferior cul-de-sac can be tested with litmus or pH paper, but this task should be delayed until after initial irrigation if there is concern for significant corneal injury, such as in chemical ocular burns. The pH level should be tested until the pH normalizes. Then, it should be tested again about 30 minutes later to ensure the pH remains neutral. Examination of the interior of the eye using a slit lamp should be one of the last stages of management for chemical ocular burns. Prior to a slit- lamp examination, the patient's eye should be irrigated, have a neutral pH, and be ex- amined to determine visual acuity. Delaying these management steps increases the risk of vision loss due to continuous alkaline or acidic burns to the eye.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 25-year-old man presents with bilateral eye redness and a watery discharge over the past few days, as shown. He denies trauma, vision problems, and fever. He says that the redness started in one eye then spread to the other. He also says he had a dry cough 1 week earlier that has resolved. Fluorescein examination of both eyes is negative for any uptake. What is the appropriate treatment? Credit: Copyright 2016 American Academy of Ophthalmology.

options.text: Cool compresses to the eyes and diligent handwashing
Intravenous antibiotic treatment and immediate ophthalmology consultation
Oral acyclovir and topical trifluridine with ophthalmology follow-up in 48 hours
Polymyxin B-trimethoprim ophthalmic solution for 7 days

correctAnswer: Cool compresses to the eyes and diligent handwashing
englishExplanation: This patient has viral conjunctivitis, the most common cause of acute red eye. The image shows the characteristic diffuse hyperemia and mild discharge. Adenovirus is the most likely cause; it is highly contagious, and antibiotic treatment is of no use. Viral conjunctivitis is self-limited; it typically lasts 1 to 3 weeks and requires supportive therapy only, such as cool compresses, and dili- gent hand hygiene to minimize the risk of spread. It is most contagious when discharge is present; patients should stay away from work, school, and daycare dur- ing that time. Many infections start in one eye then quickly spread to the other. The clinical presentation of viral conjunctivitis includes fullness, tightness, warmth, or a scratchy sensation, but not pain, in the affected eye; diffuse hyperemia on the con- junctiva; watery or mucoid discharge; and a tender, swollen preauricular node. Symptoms commonly develop after (or while) the patient has had a URI. One or both eyes can be affected. Some patients also have keratitis, characterized by slight vision defect, light sensitivity, and a foreign body sensation. If keratitis is suspected, follow- up with an ophthalmologist within 48 hours is recommended. The same is true if the condition worsens after 3 days or does not improve after 7 days. Incorrect Answer Explanations If there are concerns for a more aggressive infection like endophthalmitis, then intra- venous antibiotic medications and immediate ophthalmology involvement are war- ranted. Since the patient has no vision deficits and an otherwise normal eye examina- tion, this more aggressive type of infection is unlikely. This patient has viral con- junctivitis, the most common cause of acute red eye. The patient has no signs of dendritic lesions on fluorescein exam, so it is unlikely that a herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis is present. Thus, oral acyclovir is not the cor- rect pharmacotherapy. This patient has viral conjunctivitis, the most com- mon cause of acute red eye. Antibiotic drops are indicated when treating bacterial conjunctivitis. Since this patient's symptoms are bilateral and the discharge is watery rather than mucopuru- lent, a bacterial infection is unlikely, so antibiotics are not warranted. This patient has viral conjunctivitis, the most common cause of acute red eye.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 22-year-old woman presents with right eye pain that started 2 days ago. When asked, she says she occasionally leaves her contacts in when she sleeps but denies feeling any foreign bodies. After the contact lens is removed and a numbing drop is put in her eye, a fluorescein examination is performed and shown below. The pa- tient says her eye "feels better already." What medication should the patient be discharged on? Credit: Copyright 2016 American Academy of Ophthalmology.
englishExplanation: This patient has a corneal abrasion/ulcer, most likely as a result of wearing her con- tacts too long. The contact lens should be discarded, and an ophthalmic antibiotic solution should be instilled once all other foreign bodies have been ruled out. As a result of the contact lens use, Pseudomonas should be covered by an antibiotic such as ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, or tobramycin. Since the abrasion is covering the central visual axis and the contact lens use, the patient needs to follow up with an ophthalmologist in 24 hours. It is important to differentiate abrasions from corneal ulcers, which have a more cavitary appearance and require very close ophthalmologic follow-up and management. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cycloplegics like cyclopentolate 1% or homatropine 5% can help with the discomfort of a corneal abrasion theoretically by decreasing the associated ciliary spasm. However, atropine can last up to 2 weeks, which is too long for ongoing outpatient management of the corneal abrasion by an ophthalmologist. A fluoroquinolone or tobramycin antibiotic drop should be used to cover Pseudomonas in abrasions due to contact lenses. Erythromycin ointment would have been an appropriate antibiotic selection if the pa- tient did not wear contact lenses. However, it has inadequate Pseudomonas coverage, so a fluoroquinolone or tobramycin should be used. However, it has inadequate Pseudomonas coverage, so a fluoroquinolone or tobramycin should be used. Proparacaine helps make examination of the eye possible and provides immediate pain relief, but it should not be used beyond the initial encounter. Prolonged use of topical anesthetics can blunt the normal protective mechanism of the cornea and de- lay healing. A fluoroquinolone or tobramycin antibiotic drop should be used to cover Pseudomonas in abrasions due to contact lenses.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 14-year-old boy with no medical history presents with right eye pain that started while mowing the lawn. On examination, his visual acuity is 20/25 in the right eye with injected conjunctiva. Wood lamp examination shows no visible foreign body to the anterior cornea, and fluorescein staining shows a small corneal abrasion with a negative Seidel test. What is the most important next step in evaluation?
englishExplanation: Given this patient's history and examination findings, an ocular foreign body is the most likely diagnosis. Corneal examination does not reveal a foreign body. However, fluorescein staining reveals a corneal abrasion, suggesting that trauma did occur. It is important to examine underneath the eyelids to ensure a foreign body is not present. If a foreign body is missed under the eyelids, it may con- tinue to cause corneal abrasions when the patient blinks. The lower eyelid is easily everted by grasping the eyelashes and eyelid and gently pulling down while having the patient look up. The upper eyelid is more challenging to evert. It is best to use a cotton-tipped swab placed over the upper eyelid and gently pull the upper eye- lid up and over the cotton swab. This allows for exposure of the eyelid mucosa for for- eign bodies. Foreign bodies found under the eyelids should be gently re- moved, often best with a moistened cotton-tipped swab. For this patient, once the evaluation for foreign bodies is complete, prophylactic topi- cal antibiotics should be given for treatment of the corneal abrasion. Ciprofloxacin should be used if the patient wears contacts, due to increased risk of Pseudomonas infection. Tetanus prophylaxis should be updated as well as indi- cated. Follow-up with ophthalmology should be given to ensure healing of the abra- sion and to assess for any potential complications. Incorrect Answer Explanations A dilated eye examination is infrequently performed in the emergency de- partment. This is typically reserved for eye specialists and is especially useful for retinal and optic nerve evaluation. In the case of a foreign body, a dilated eye exami- nation would be of little utility. Intraocular pressure measurement is used to diagnose acute angle-closure glaucoma or an evolving retrobulbar hematoma. Both of these diagnoses are unlikely in this current scenario. Acute glaucoma is highly unlikely in an otherwise healthy 14-year-old child with a normal visual acuity. Retrobulbar hematoma should be suspected in the setting of significant facial or orbital trauma that would predis- pose to bleeding behind the eye, particularly in a patient on blood thinners. This is highly unlikely to occur from relatively minor eye trauma, as in this case. Slit-lamp examination of an injured eye is helpful to diagnose an anterior cham- ber injury or posterior chamber disease. It is often useful when assessing for iritis, uveitis, or other anterior chamber pathologies. It is unlikely to help further in this case since a magnified examination of the anterior chamber has not revealed a visible foreign body. Key Points Ocular foreign bodies can end up under a patient's eyelids and can cause repeated corneal abrasions when blinking. Evaluation for foreign bodies under the lower eyelid can be done by gently pulling the eyelashes and eyelid down and out, revealing the undersurface of the eyelid. Evaluation for foreign bodies under the upper eyelid can be best done by placing a cotton-tipped swab over the outside of the upper eyelid and gently rolling the eyelid up and over the swab to reveal the underlying mucosa.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 33-year-old woman presents with a lump on her eyelid, as shown. She denies vi- sion changes, pain with extraocular movement, or drainage. What is the appropri- ate treatment? Credit: Copyright 2016 American Academy of Ophthalmology.
englishExplanation: Of the conditions that present with a red eye, two that can be clinically indistinguish- able are chalazion and hordeolum. This particular patient has a chalazion, which is a lump in the eyelid caused by blockage of a meibomian gland. To help promote resolu- tion, the patient should be instructed to apply warm compresses. A chalazion is usu- ally painless, but some patients experience mild tenderness. The chalazion is pre- ceded by the hordeolum, either external (stye) or internal. Both types of horde- olum are more painful than a chalazion and are associated with mild con- junctival hyperemia, but all three conditions are treated in the same way, with warm compresses and no antibiotics. Nonurgent referral (within 30 days) is recommended for both chalazia and hordeola if they continue to grow and do not resolve or if they begin to affect vision. If that happens, the ophthalmologist might perform a biopsy or excision. Incorrect Answer Explanations An over-the-counter topical vasoconstrictor-antihistamine medication may be effec- tive as a second-line treatment for allergic conjunctivitis if systemic antihistamines fail. However, this patient does not report itching, which is characteristic of allergic conjunctivitis. Other symptoms include binocular tearing, conjunctival hyperemia, swelling, and watery discharge. Warm compresses are the appropriate treat- ment for this patient's chalazion. This patient's vision is still intact, so excision of the chalazion in the emergency de- partment is not indicated. The patient should be instructed to follow up with an oph- thalmologist if the lump grows or starts to affect her vision. Warm compresses are the appropriate treatment for this patient's chalazion. Oral antibiotics are not indicated because the inflammation is localized and is not caused by a bacterial infection. If the patient had pain with extraocular movement, cellulitis would be a concern. In that case, intravenous antibiotic therapy and an emergent ophthalmologic consultation are indicated. Warm compresses are the appropriate treatment for this patient's chalazion.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: When treating a patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma, what is the next best step in management if administration of three doses of timolol drops does not de- crease the intraocular pressure?

options.text: Administer one dose of acetazolamide 500 mg IV or PO
Administer one drop of 1% pilocarpine solution and observe
Continue administering timolol drops until the pressure falls below 22
Discharge home on timolol and pilocarpine with close ophthalmology follow-up

correctAnswer: Administer one dose of acetazolamide 500 mg IV or PO
englishExplanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is a medical emergency. The goal of treat- ment is to quickly lower the intraocular pressure, and instillation of tim- olol is the correct initial action. The American Academy of Ophthalmology rec- ommends administering one dose of acetazolamide 500 mg IV or PO in ad- dition to the timolol. Intravenous administration of mannitol is one way to lower the pressure, but it must be carefully administered in patients with low blood pressure. Other appropriate treatments include apraclonidine 1% drops and pilocarpine 1% to 2% drops every 15 minutes. Pilocarpine is effective only after the intraocular pressure has decreased so that the pupil can constrict and pull the iris away from the angle to promote drainage of the aqueous humor. After the pressure has been lowered, the ophthalmologist might perform laser iridectomy. If administration of three doses of timolol drops does not decrease the intraocular pressure, emergent ophthalmology consultation is needed to provide definitive treatment and minimize the risk of permanent vision loss. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pilocarpine is part of the overall emergency management of acute angle-closure glau- coma, but it is effective only after the intraocular pressure has been lowered. The pa- tient needs to be treated with acetazolamide first to accomplish this. Continuing the timolol drops and waiting for the desired response without consulting ophthalmology delays definitive treatment. Medical treatment should be initiated by the emergency physician at the same time ophthalmology is consulted to evaluate the patient and provide definitive treatment. This patient needs to be treated with acetazolamide if timolol is ineffective. A patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma cannot be discharged before the pres- sure has been lowered given the risk of permanent vision loss. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is a time-sensitive emergency that requires quick evaluation by an ophthal- mologist. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is a time-sensitive emergency that requires quick evaluation by an ophthalmologist. The patient needs to be treated with acetazolamide if timolol is ineffective.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 23-year-old man with a history of sickle cell disease presents with blurred vision after a ball hit his eye. A physical examination reveals blood in the anterior cham- ber and an intraocular pressure of 30 mm Hg. Which medication is contraindicated?
englishExplanation: This patient has secondary glaucoma and increased intraocular pressure (IOP) as a result of traumatic hyphema. Patients with traumatic hyphema and associated increased IOP need medical management, typically with topical alpha-adrenergic agonists; topical beta-blockers; intravenous mannitol; and oral, topical, or intravenous carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. However, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are contraindicated in patients with sickle cell disease because they lower the aqueous pH in the anterior chamber, which can cause the RBCs to sickle and become less flexible. This can clog the outflow through the trabecular meshwork and further elevate IOP. Caution should also be used when giving mannitol to sickle cell disease patients because the resulting diuresis can lead to hypovolemia and sub- sequent changes in the morphology of RBCs. Hyphema can occur as a result of trauma or spontaneously as a result of an underly- ing condition, such as sickle cell disease. Hyphemas are graded by the amount of blood pooling in the anterior chamber: Grade 1 (<33%), Grade 2 (33%-50%), Grade 3 (>50%), and Grade 4 (100%). In the case of traumatic hyphema, check for other in- juries and then evaluate the eye carefully. Patients with hyphema usually present with eye pain, blurry vision, and light sensitivity. On physical examination, blood can be noted in the anterior chamber, and IOP may be elevated. Emergency de- partment management of any patient with hyphema requires evaluation for con- comitant injury (especially globe rupture or orbital compartment syndrome), re- duction of IOP, and a request for an ophthalmology consultation. Basic treatment includes placing an eye shield, limiting patient activity, elevating the head of the bed, controlling pain and nausea, and correcting coagu- lopathy, if present. It is important to note that rebleeding can occur in 30% of hy- phema cases and typically occurs 3 to 5 days after the injury. Incorrect Answer Explanations Topical alpha-adrenergic agents, such as brimonidine, decrease production of aqueous humor to reduce IOP. There are no contraindications to use topical al- pha-adrenergic agents in patients with sickle cell disease. Topical beta-blockers, such as timolol, are used to decrease the production of aqueous humor in the anterior chamber by directly acting on cyclic adenosine monophosphate on ciliary epithelial cells. Topical beta-blockers may be used in sickle cell patients. Cholinergic agonists, such as pilocarpine, are topical agents that result in miosis and increased outflow of aqueous humor. However, pilocarpine is usually in- effective when IOP is greater than 40 mm Hg due to pressure-induced ischemia of the sphincter pupillae muscle. Notably, pilocarpine is safe to use in patients with sickle cell disease.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which pupillary finding is characteristic of an acute angle-closure glaucoma attack when exposed to light?

options.text: Abnormally dilated pupil with sluggish response
Mid-sized pupil that is minimally reactive
Small pupils that do not react

correctAnswer: Mid-sized pupil that is minimally reactive
englishExplanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is caused by a rapid and sudden increase in intraocular pressure (IOP) above normal (10-21 mm Hg), causing is- chemia of the iris. This ischemia causes the pupil to be minimally reactive and mid-sized, around 4 to 6 mm. Patients present dramatically with a headache, vom- iting, blurry vision, and a painful red eye. Seeing halos around lights is also a characteristic finding in patients with angle-closure glaucoma. Patients who are at higher risk of acute angle-closure glaucoma include those patients over age 60 years, those who have a family history of this diagnosis, and those with hyperopia, or farsightedness. Whereas above 21 mm Hg is an elevated IOP, typically these patients have elevated IOPs above 40 mm Hg, which is an indication to start treatment. Recognition of this diagnosis is of utmost importance, as patients can lose their vision if treatment is delayed. Ophthalmology consultation is required emergently as, ultimately, these patients require an iridotomy, but treatment should be initiated in the emer- gency department until that procedure can be performed. Treatment aims to reduce IOP by administering drops of timolol, pilocarpine, and apraclonidine as well as intravenous acetazolamide. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute angle-closure glaucoma typically presents with a mid-sized, minimally reactive pupil, as opposed to an Adie tonic pupil, which is abnormally dilated and sluggishly responsive. Adie tonic pupils are caused by parasympathetic denervation of the affected pupil that results in abnormally dilated unilateral or bilat- eral pupils that react (constrict) sluggishly to bright light, but appropri- ately accommodate (reduce in size) on a close object. Damage to the parasym- pathetic ciliary ganglion may be idiopathic or caused by viral infection, trauma, mi- graine, or tumors. Argyll Robertson pupils are small bilateral pupils that do not react (con- strict) when exposed to bright light but appropriately accommodate (re- duce in size) on a close object, as opposed to acute angle-closure glaucoma pupils, which are mid-sized and do react, although minimally. Argyll Robertson pupils are highly specific for neurosyphilis and are found in other conditions like diabetic neuropathy. The pathophysiology is unclear but is thought to be damage to the midbrain. Management is to treat the underlying cause. A Marcus Gunn pupil demonstrates a relative afferent pupillary defect produced by decreased pupillary response to light in the affected eye. In the swinging flashlight test, the affected eye demonstrates poor constriction (and ap- pears to paradoxically dilate) with bright light. The most common cause of a Marcus Gunn pupil is a lesion of the optic nerve or of the contralateral optic tract. The pupil in acute angle-closure glaucoma does not paradoxically dilate. Key Points Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with a minimally reactive and mid-sized pupil due to ischemia of the iris. An Adie tonic pupil is an abnormally dilated pupil that constricts sluggishly to bright light but appropriately accommodates on a close object. Argyll Robertson pupils are small bilateral pupils that do not react when exposed to bright light but appropriately accommodate on a close object. They are highly specific for neurosyphilis. A Marcus Gunn pupil demonstrates a relative afferent pupillary defect in which the affected eye poorly constricts and appears to dilate with bright light.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 50-year-old woman developed sudden-onset right eye pain and blurry vision as- sociated with vomiting 1 hour prior to arrival. What is the most probable diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with acute painful vision loss. The rapid rise in intraocular pressure (IOP) often occurs in low light settings and in the evenings when mydriasis and the peripheral iris block a narrow angle. Symptoms in- clude severe eye pain, headache, decreased vision, halos around lights, nausea, and vomiting. Conjunctival injection, corneal edema, a shallow anterior chamber, and a mid-sized, poorly reactive pupil are characteristic of acute an- gle-closure glaucoma. Patients typically have an IOP greater than 40 mm Hg. Emergent ophthalmological consultation should be obtained, and treatment in the emergency department should be initiated to reduce IOP. Intravenous acetazolamide should be given as well as drops of timolol, pilocarpine, and apraclonidine. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amaurosis fugax is monocular, transient, and painless vision loss due to lack of blood flow and perfusion to the optic nerve and retina. Acute angle-clo- sure glaucoma, by contrast, is associated with pain. Symptoms of amaurosis fugax re- solve in seconds to minutes. It is described classically as a dark curtain or shade over the eye. Common causes are atherosclerotic and embolic disease, hypercoagula- ble states, and illicit drugs. At the time of examination, visual acuity has often re- turned to normal, given the short duration of this condition. Fundus examination typically shows signs of chronic ischemic disease, like cotton wool spots or reti- nal hemorrhages. Central retinal artery occlusion causes unilateral painless vision loss due to decreased retinal perfusion, as opposed to the painful nature of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Causes include artherosclerotic or embolic disease, thrombosis, inflamma- tion of the arteries, and collagen vascular disease. Examination commonly reveals an afferent pupillary defect, cherry red macula, and cholesterol emboli (Hollenhorst plaques). Retinal detachment presents with painless vision loss in the affected eye due to the separation of the retina from the underlying choroid. Floaters and flashes of light are also commonly reported. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is associated with pain, as opposed to being painless like retinal detachment.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 50-year-old woman developed right eye pain, blurry vision, and nausea 6 hours ago. She has diffuse redness of the conjunctiva with prominence around the cornea. The pupil is mid-sized and nonreactive to light. There is no exudate or photophobia. What is the most probable diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is caused by a rapid and sudden increase in intraocular pressure (IOP) above normal (10-21 mm Hg). Patients present dramatically with a headache, vomiting, blurry vision, halos around lights, and a unilateral painful red eye. Ischemia of the iris causes the pupil to be minimally reactive and mid-sized. Whereas above 21 mm Hg is an elevated IOP, these patients typically have elevated IOPs above 40 mm Hg, which is an indication to start treatment. Recognition of this diagnosis is of utmost importance, as patients can lose their vision if treatment is delayed. Ophthalmology consultation is required emer- gently; ultimately, patients require an iridotomy. However, emergency department treatment should be initiated until that procedure can be performed. Treatment aims to reduce IOP by administering drops of timolol, pilocarpine, and apracloni- dine as well as intravenous acetazolamide. Incorrect Answer Explanations Central retinal artery occlusion commonly presents with acute unilateral painless vision loss. Classically, a fundoscopic examination reveals a cherry red spot. A red eye and pain are usually not associated with central retinal artery occlu- sion. Ophthalmological consultation should be obtained emergently. Iritis commonly presents with a constricted pupil, deep eye pain that is worse on eye movement, and consensual photophobia. A slit-lamp examina- tion typically shows cells and flare; patients with iritis can also have red eye, nausea, and decreased vision, as described in this case. However, a mid-sized pupil without photophobia is more characteristic of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Orbital cellulitis commonly presents with chemosis, proptosis, painful extraocular movements, and visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect. The mid-sized pupil and lack of exudate instead point to acute angle-closure glaucoma.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient presents with the sudden onset of a painful red eye. What would be diag- nostic for an acute angle-closure glaucoma attack?
englishExplanation: An acute angle-closure glaucoma attack is triggered by pupillary dilation. When this happens, the angle closes between the peripheral iris, trabecular network, and cornea. This closure causes the intraocular pressure (IOP) to increase. Parasympatholytic agents, sympathomimetic agents, dim light settings, and emo- tional stress are known to cause pupillary dilation. IOP is measured with tonom- etry. Normal pressure is 10 to 20 mm Hg, but IOP may exceed 60 to 80 mm Hg in an acute attack. Above 40 mm Hg is typically an indication to start emergent treatment to lower IOP, and consultation with an ophthalmologist should be sought immediately. Incorrect Answer Explanations Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is an inflammatory disease of the large blood vessels. Patients may present with a temporal headache, double vi- sion, and jaw claudication. ESR, a marker of inflammation, is commonly greater than 60 mm/hr, while normal is 1 to 40 mm/hr. An elevated IOP, not an elevated ESR, is diagnostic for acute angle-closure glaucoma. Uveitis is inflammation of the uvea (iris, ciliary body, choroid). Slit-lamp examination reveals the presence of cells and flare in the anterior chamber, which are characteristic of this diagnosis. Cells and flare are not present in cases of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Anterior uveitis presents with a red painful eye with blurry vision and photophobia. The ciliary vessels are dilated, and the pupil is irregular. Optic nerve sheath diameters of less than 5 mm on ocular POCUS suggest a nor- mal intracranial pressure, while diameters more than 6 mm suggest an ele- vated intracranial pressure. While glaucoma causes optic neuropathy and vision loss, the measurement of optic nerve sheath diameters for the diagnosis of glaucoma is not established and is not the testing of choice when determining the presence of acute angle-closure glaucoma. An elevated IOP, not intracranial pressure, is present in acute angle-closure glaucoma.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the appropriate treatment for acute angle-closure glaucoma?

options.text: Copious irrigation, pH testing, and topical antibiotics
Lidocaine and then lateral canthotomy and cantholysis
Topical nonsteroidal medications and a topical antipseudomonal antibiotic

englishExplanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma is caused by a rapid and sudden increase in intraocular pressure (IOP) above normal. Appropriate treatment is targeted toward lowering the IOP by: (1) reducing the production of aqueous humor with beta-blockers (eg, timolol), alpha-adrenergic agonists (eg, apraclonidine), and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (eg, acetazolamide); (2) facilitating the outflow of aqueous humor with parasympathomimetic miotic agents (eg, pilocarpine); and (3) reducing the volume of aqueous humor (eg, mannitol). Definitive treatment is laser iridotomy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Copious irrigation with isotonic solution (normal saline) is the appropriate treatment for chemical burns to the eye due to acid or alkaline injuries. Repeated test- ing of the pH guides the need for continued irrigation. After normalization of the pH, topical cycloplegic agents (eg, tropicamide) and topical antibiotics (eg, erythromycin) are recommended. Administration of lidocaine, followed by a lateral canthotomy and cantholy- sis, is the appropriate treatment for orbital compartment syndrome, pos- sibly caused by a retrobulbar hematoma, abscess, or emphysema. This treatment is a rapid temporizing measure to preserve vision when the IOP is more than 40 mm Hg. Antipseudomonal coverage (eg, ciprofloxacin) and cessation of contact lens use are appropriate for a corneal abrasion in a contact lens user. Topical NSAIDs reduce corneal abrasion pain, and oral analgesics may also be re- quired. Eye patching is not indicated, and administration of undiluted topical anes- thetics for more than 24 hours is untested and may be dangerous. Tetanus prophy- laxis is unnecessary unless there is corneal perforation or contamination with organic material. Reevaluation in 24 hours is recommended.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the most common complication of untreated traumatic hyphema?
englishExplanation: Traumatic hyphema can result after blunt injury to the eye and is characterized by blood or blood clots within the anterior chamber caused by damage to iris root vessels. The most common complications of untreated traumatic hyphema are in- creased intraocular pressure and rebleeding. Rebleeding can occur 3 to 5 days after the original insult in up to 30% of cases. The blood within the anterior chamber settles toward dependent portions of the eye based on patient position. Thus, a hy- phema may not be visible in a supine patient or a patient with a hyphema that has not had adequate time to layer toward the inferior portion of the anterior chamber after changing position from supine to upright. Hyphema treatment focuses on lowering the risk of rebleeding and increased intraocular pressure using medications such as topical beta-blockers, intravenous mannitol, topical alpha-adrenergic agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and topical steroids. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bacterial keratitis is a corneal infection that may or may not be associated with a corneal ulcer, is and not associated with traumatic hyphemas. The most common risk factors for bacterial keratitis include contact lens use and ocular injury. Physical examination findings of bacterial keratitis include lid and conjunctival edema, reduced vision, conjunctival and scleral injection, and corneal ulcer. Endophthalmitis is caused by inflammation of the vitreous humor and is usually the result of infection following ocular surgery, not hyphemas. Other etiologies include penetrating globe injury as well as hematogenous spread. Clinical findings of endophthalmitis tend to be apparent on physical examination and include eyelid ery- thema and swelling, conjunctival and scleral injection, chemosis, and hypopyon. Symptoms of retinal detachment or tear include a decrease in visual acuity on ex- amination and seeing flashes of light, floaters, or a veil or curtain in the visual field. Retinal detachments are not associated with hyphemas. The diagnosis of a reti- nal detachment requires an indirect dilated examination by an ophthalmologist be- cause most tears occur in the peripheral retina, which is not visualized on direct fun- doscopic examination.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 32-year-old woman with a history of sickle cell disease presents with eye pain. A focused physical examination reveals the findings shown below. Which medication is most likely to harm the patient? Credit: ARZTSAMUI/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: Acetazolamide is an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that can reduce in- traocular pressure in most patients with hyphema, but it can worsen in- traocular pressure in hyphema patients with sickle cell disease. Patients with sickle cell disease can develop spontaneous hyphemas and are more likely to de- velop complications, such as vision loss, rebleeding, and increased intraocular pres- sure. Acetazolamide can reduce aqueous pH in the anterior chamber of the eye and result in increased sickling of RBCs, which can subsequently clog the trabecular meshwork and increase intraocular pressure. Thus, acetazolamide is contraindicated in the setting of sickle cell disease in patients with hy- phema. Other agents that can be used to lower intraocular pressure in hyphema in- clude topical beta adrenergic blockers, such as timolol. Positioning the head of the bed upright at 45 degrees is also beneficial. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cyclopentolate can be administered safely to patients with sickle cell dis- ease. In the setting of hyphema, cyclopentolate can decrease “pupillary play” (ie, constriction and dilation of the iris that can worsen bleeding in the anterior cham- ber). Cyclopentolate is an anticholinergic medication that blocks the responses of the iridic sphincter muscle and stimulation of the ciliary body muscle. It should be avoided in patients with narrow anterior chamber glaucoma and should be adminis- tered in consultation with an ophthalmologist. Homatropine can be administered safely to patients with sickle cell dis- ease. In the setting of hyphema, homatropine can decrease “pupillary play” (ie, con- striction and dilation of the iris that can worsen bleeding in the anterior chamber). Homatropine is an anticholinergic medication that blocks the responses of the iridic sphincter muscle and the stimulation of the ciliary body muscle. Homatropine should be avoided in patients with narrow anterior chamber glaucoma and should be admin- istered in consultation with an ophthalmologist. Timolol is a topical beta adrenergic blocker that can be used to decrease intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor production. Timolol can be administered to patients with sickle cell disease with elevated intraocular pressure.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: In the setting of a hyphema, which condition is most likely to require additional medication to aid in clotting to decrease the risk of developing increased intraocu- lar pressure?
englishExplanation: Hemophilia A is characterized by a lack factor VIII, which is required for clotting, and bleeding events in these patients are directly related to deficiency of plasma factor levels. Treatment of bleeding events in hemophilia A requires adminis- tration of factor VIII based on the severity of bleeding and the desired increase of fac- tor level. Patients with hemophilia A are at significant risk for hyphema. Ocular bleeding is considered to be severe and can lead to vision loss, so factor VIII should be administered to attain a desired factor level increase of 100% in hemo- philia A patients with hyphema. A typical initial dose is 50 units/kg, which will likely require repeat dosing every 8 to 24 hours. Incorrect Answer Explanations Factor V Leiden is a mutation of factor V of the clotting cascade which leads to clotting events. Hyphema in the setting of Factor V Leiden does not require specific reversal to avoid complications associated with hyphema, such as increased intraocular pressure. Increased intraocular pressure due to hyphema in a patient with Factor V Leiden should be treated in the same way as in other patients: with topical beta-blockers and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Patients with systemic hypertension and hyphema do not require specific administration of medication to decrease risk of increased intraocular pressure related to their systemic hypertension. They would require treatment of the hyphema with the same medications as in other patients, including topical cycloplegics, anti- cholinergics, and glucocorticoids as well as oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and topical beta-blockers in the setting of increased intraocular pressure. Patients with sickle cell disease are at increased risk for spontaneous hy- phema. Additional medication is not needed for these patients to assist in clotting, but the approach to these patients may differ if they have sickle cell disease or sickle cell trait. Hyphema in a patient with sickle cell that does not involve increased intraocular pressure should be treated in the same way as in other patients: with cycloplegics and topical glucocorticoids. Sickle cell patients with elevated intraocular pressure in the setting of hyphema should not receive carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or mannitol due to the risk for increased sickling. Furthermore, it is important to note that this population is at risk of rebleeding, so the sickle cell status of the patient should be known.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 54-year-old man presents with eye pain. A focused physical examination is per- formed, and the following finding is noted. What is the best next step in management? Credit: Yoko Okunuki, Junichi Sakai, Takeshi Kezuka, and Hiroshi Goto (CC BY 4.0; via Wikimedia Commons)

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees

correctAnswer: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees
englishExplanation: Hyphema is an accumulation of blood in the anterior chamber of the eye. Once hyphema is identified, it is important to raise the head of the bed as soon as possible; raising the head of the bed to 45 degrees can prevent occlusion of the trabecular meshwork by promoting layering of suspended RBCs inferiorly by gravity. Trauma is the most common cause of hyphema, but it can also occur sponta- neously in conditions such as hemophilia and sickle cell disease and in patients on anticoagulation therapy. One of the most common complications of hyphema is in- creased intraocular pressure. Incorrect Answer Explanations The treatment of hyphema in the emergency department consists of interventions de- signed to prevent rebleeding and intraocular hypertension. Treatments used to achieve these aims include cycloplegics, miotics, corticosteroids, and an- tifibrinolytic agents. Interventions should be directed by an ophthalmologist who is able to closely follow-up with the patient for serial examinations to ensure no re- bleeding, infection, or corneal perforation occurs in the setting of topical steroids. Although consultation with an ophthalmologist is crucial, elevation of the head of the bed is a simple intervention that should precede contact with an ophthalmologist. Measuring intraocular pressure is a component of a routine ophthalmic workup, but an open globe must be excluded prior to measuring intraocular pres- sure with tonometry in the setting of trauma. Intraocular hypertension (defined as pressure >21 mm Hg) occurs in more than 30% of cases after a hyphema but may not occur for several days after the injury, necessitating close follow-up during the first week. Although intraocular pressure measurement is crucial, elevation of the head of the bed is a simple intervention that should precede a focused physical exam- ination with tonometry. Hyphema is most commonly encountered as a consequence of blunt trauma. Associated findings can include orbital wall fractures, globe rupture, eyelid laceration, corneal abrasion, lens dislocation or subluxation, and corneal foreign bod- ies. In addition to a slit-lamp examination, a focused ophthalmic examination should evaluate for the presence of globe rupture; inspect the eyelids, lashes, lacrimal ducts, and cornea; and assess pupillary response, visual acuity, extraocular movements, and visual fields. Restricted upgaze or lateral gaze can suggest a blow-out fracture with entrapment. Diagnosis requires CT of the facial bones. Although CT of the facial bones may be required to rule out concomitant injuries, elevating the head of the bed in the presence of hyphema is a simple intervention that should occur prior to obtain- ing facial bone CT.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the most common sequelae of untreated hyphema that may be seen in the emergency department?
englishExplanation: Hyphema is an accumulation of blood in the anterior chamber of the eye. One of the most common complications of hyphema is increased intraoc- ular pressure. Increased intraocular pressure can occur in one-third of all hy- phema patients and can be elevated due to occlusion of the trabecular meshwork. The larger the hyphema, the greater the likelihood of increased intraocular pressure. Trauma is the most common cause of hyphema, but hyphema can also occur sponta- neously in conditions such as hemophilia and sickle cell disease and in patients on anticoagulation therapy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Corneal blood staining associated with hyphema can vary in incidence between 2% to 11%, but it generally occurs in the setting of larger hyphe- mas. Corneal blood staining is the result of hemosiderin deposition into the corneal stroma and results in decreased visual acuity. Corneal blood staining is associated with increased intraocular pressure >25 mm Hg for ≥6 days' duration of hyphema, so it is recommended that such eyes be treated surgically by day 6 if hyphema does not resolve below 50%. Optic nerve atrophy in the setting of hyphema can occur as a result of in- creased intraocular pressure or due to optic nerve contusion and occurs in roughly 12% of patients. The risk is greater if elevated intraocular pressure is allowed to remain at 50 mm Hg or more for 5 days or 35 mm Hg or more for 7 days. Peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) are characterized by adhesions of the peripheral iris to structures in the anterior chamber. In one study, PAS occurred in 5 eyes in which the hyphema remained longer than 8 days. Formation of PAS is associated with persistence of the hyphema for more than 8 days, and inci- dence is higher with larger hyphemas. PAS formation is the result of inflammation or clot organization. However, PAS is a less common complication of hyphema than in- creased intraocular pressure.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 67-year-old woman presents with left eye pain and blurry vision over the past day. She denies trauma to the eye and exposure to foreign bodies. Examination re- veals injected conjunctiva in the left eye and photophobia. Visual acuity is 20/30 in her right eye and 20/100 in her left with normal intraocular pressures bilater- ally. No visual field cuts are noted, and the fluorescein examination is normal. Slit- lamp examination reveals a significant number of cells in the anterior chamber. After discussion with ophthalmology, what is the correct treatment and disposition?

options.text: Discharge with instructions to use prescription ophthalmic antibiotic drops for 1 week
Explain the cause of the symptoms, assure the patient they are temporary, and discharge
Prescribe cycloplegic eye drops, and arrange ophthalmology follow-up within 24 hours
Request an emergent ophthalmology assessment in the emergency department

correctAnswer: Prescribe cycloplegic eye drops, and arrange ophthalmology follow-up within 24 hours
englishExplanation: This patient has iritis or anterior uveitis, which is inflammation of the ante- rior segment of the uvea and the ciliary muscle. The key finding is cells seen on slit-lamp examination. The photophobia is caused by ciliary spasm, so a cycloplegic agent (cyclopentolate, tropicamide) should be given to help with pain relief. Complications can include vision loss, so patients with iritis should follow up with an ophthalmologist in 24 to 48 hours for reassessment. Prednisolone drops should be started only after consultation with oph- thalmology. The clinical presentation of anterior uveitis includes periocular pain, photophobia, blurred vision, ciliary flush, and a small or irregularly shaped pupil. Slit-lamp examination findings include floating particles in the anterior chamber and turbidity in the aqueous humor. Anterior uveitis is an autoimmune response that can be isolated or develop in association with seronegative spondyloarthropathies (her- pes simplex, herpes zoster, sarcoidosis, Bechet disease). It also has been associated with malignancy and ulcerative colitis. Before making the diagnosis of iritis, it is im- portant to rule out trauma and other foreign bodies on initial evaluation. Incorrect Answer Explanations A 1-week course of ophthalmic antibiotics would be the appropriate treat- ment for a corneal abrasion. In this case, a corneal abrasion is unlikely given the negative fluorescein examination. However, it is important to do the fluorescein examination to rule out an abrasion since the patient complains of eye pain. Reassurance and discharge would be appropriate if the diagnosis were subconjunctival hemorrhage. Although the patient has injection of the conjunc- tiva, no signs of frank hemorrhage are noted. Patients with subconjunctival hemor- rhage have no symptoms other than the hemorrhage itself, which usually is caused by a sudden increase in venous pressure due to a Valsalva maneuver. Emergent ophthalmology consultation is the right action for patients with conditions such as acute angle-closure glaucoma, open globe, or retinal detachment, who require immediate treatment. Although this patient has blurry vision and af- fected visual acuity, no visual field cuts were found on examination. Additionally, retinal detachments do not typically cause pain.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 50-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis presents with an atraumatic red and painful right eye associated with blurred vision, watery discharge, and photophobia that began 2 days earlier. His visual acuity is slightly decreased in the right eye but normal in the left eye. Pain with a consensual light reflex is present. Flare and ciliary flush are noted on slit-lamp examination, but the intraocular pressure is within normal limits. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: ARZTSAMUI/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: A painful consensual light reflex in the presence of a red eye is highly sug- gestive of iritis (anterior uveitis). The uvea consists of the middle layer of the eye (iris, ciliary body, and choroid); when the anterior portion of the uvea is inflamed, it involves the iris and ciliary body — a condition commonly called iritis. Inflammation of the anterior uvea and spasm of the ciliary body result in the patient's symptoms, including eye pain, blurred vision, tearing, and con- sensual photophobia. Minor trauma and chronic inflammatory condi- tions, such as ulcerative colitis and systemic infections, are often associ- ated with iritis. Visual inspection often reveals circumcorneal redness of the eye, particularly at the limbus (junction of the cornea and the sclera), which is known as “ciliary flush.” Slit-lamp examination reveals cells (leuko- cytes in the anterior chamber giving the appearance of dust in a beam of light) and flare (hazy appearance to the anterior chamber due to protein accumulation) and of- ten shows synechiae (adhesions between the lens and the papillary margin of the iris). In some cases, decreased intraocular pressure (IOP) may also be present. Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist is recommended in cases of suspected iritis be- cause patients need a full, dilated eye examination within 24 hours to ascertain if the inflammation involves the posterior uvea. Causes of iritis include infections (eg, herpes, cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, syphilis), systemic inflammatory conditions (eg, ulcerative colitis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, sarcoidosis, multiple sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus), drugs (eg, bisphosphonates, fluoroquinolones), or other causes such as lym- phoma. Treatment of noninfectious iritis involves anticholinergic dilating prepara- tions (which help prevent synechiae formation but are contraindicated if acute nar- row-angle glaucoma is suspected), topical steroids (which reduce the inflammatory response), and oral analgesics (which help reduce ocular pain). Infectious cases of iri- tis should be treated with the appropriate agent (eg, antiviral medication for herpes or cytomegalovirus infections) with the help of an ophthalmology consultation. Incorrect Answer Explanations The hallmark of glaucoma is elevated IOP, which this patient does not have. Patients with acute narrow-angle glaucoma experience ocular redness, blurry vi- sion, mild-to-moderate pain, nausea, vomiting, and the perception of “halos” forming around objects. Corneal clouding is often present, IOP is elevated, and the affected pupil is mid-dilated. Acute narrow-angle glau- coma should be managed with pilocarpine, timolol, and hyperosmotic agents. Definitive treatment is surgical iridotomy. Patients with corneal abrasions often complain of acute discomfort, pho- tophobia, watery discharge, and foreign body sensation. Ciliary injection is usually present, and fluorescein staining reveals an epithelial defect. Simple corneal abrasions should not present with cells and flare on slit-lamp exami- nation, which rather suggests the anterior chamber inflammation of iritis. Additionally, a painful consensual light reflex should not be seen with corneal abrasions. Patients with scleritis present with severe orbital discomfort that is often bilateral. Redness is most apparent at the sclera, not the limbus. Nodular patches of the sclera and scleral edema are usually present, as are tearing and photophobia. Scleritis is often associated with systemic disease or infection. Treatment can involve oral analgesics and high-dose steroids, but emergent ophthal- mologic consultation is imperative.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which topical medication should be avoided in patients with iritis?
englishExplanation: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic cholinergic agonist used to induce miosis. Miotics should be avoided in iritis because they may increase inflammation and the risk of posterior synechiae formation. Iritis is caused by inflammation of the iris and surrounding structures found along the anterior portion of the uvea. It is also known as anterior uveitis, which can include inflammation of the nearby ciliary body (iridocyclitis) in addition to the iris. Inflammation of the vitreous humor is known as intermediate uveitis; inflammation of structures posterior to the lens, such as the choroid and retina, is termed posterior uveitis. Iritis is the most common form of uveitis. Patients present with photophobia, ciliary flush or diffuse conjunc- tival injection, and decreased vision. Incorrect Answer Explanations Atropine is a long-acting cycloplegic agent that is in the same family of medications as homatropine, scopolamine, and cyclopentolate. Cycloplegic agents are frequently used to treat anterior uveitis by decreasing ciliary muscle spasm in order to relieve pain, keeping the pupils mobile in order to prevent synechiae formation, and preventing further protein leakage (flare). Cyclopentolate is a short-acting cycloplegic agent that is in the same family of medications as homatropine, scopolamine, and atropine. Cycloplegic agents are fre- quently used to treat anterior uveitis by decreasing ciliary muscle spasm to re- lieve pain, keeping the pupils mobile in order to prevent synechiae formation, and preventing further protein leakage (flare). Prednisolone is a topical corticosteroid that is used to treat anterior uveitis. Topical corticosteroids are the drugs of choice in the treatment of noninfec- tious iritis. Ophthalmic corticosteroids decrease inflammation in the anterior chamber.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which finding is required to diagnose iritis?

options.text: Cells and flare on slit-lamp examination

correctAnswer: Cells and flare on slit-lamp examination
englishExplanation: A hallmark finding of iritis is cells and flare on slit-lamp examination, which is caused by inflammatory cell infiltration within the anterior chamber. Flare is hazi- ness of the anterior chamber fluid, which is normally clear, and is caused by an in- flux of proteins reflecting breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier. Cells and flare may be seen under high magnification using a high-intensity 1 mm x 1 mm slit beam of light at a 45- to 60-degree angle, following dark adaptation. Other exami- nation findings indicative of iritis include plethoric perilimbal vessels causing con- junctival injection concentrated around the iris or diffuse conjunctival injection, hy- popyon caused by the settling of inflammatory cells to the inferior portion of the an- terior chamber, and keratic precipitates (ie, inflammatory cell deposits on the corneal endothelium). Iritis is caused by inflammation of the iris and surrounding structures found along the anterior portion of the uvea. Iritis is also known as anterior uveitis and includes inflammation of the nearby ciliary body (iridocyclitis) in addition to the iris. Inflammation of the vitreous humor is known as intermediate uveitis, and inflamma- tion of structures posterior to the lens (eg, the choroid and retina) is known as poste- rior uveitis. Iritis is the most common form of uveitis, and affected patients can present with decreased vision, photophobia, ciliary flush, or diffuse conjunctival injection. Incorrect Answer Explanations Intraocular pressure can be either elevated or decreased in iritis. Decreased in- traocular pressure results from a decrease in aqueous production due to ciliary body inflammation. Alternatively, certain etiologies of iritis, such as disease associated with HSV, can result in significantly increased intraocular pressure due to blockage of aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork by inflammatory cells. Iritis tends to produce miosis of the pupil of the affected eye. This occurs due to ciliary muscle spasm related to inflammatory mediators acting directly on the pupillary sphincter muscle. Mydriasis is often seen with toxicologic ingestions, cra- nial nerve neuropathy, brain injury, and eye trauma. Iritis can be unilateral or bilateral depending on the etiology. Etiologies such as reactive arthritis, HSV, and toxoplasmosis result in acute and unilateral disease, whereas syphilitic uveitis can be unilateral or bilateral. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, sarcoidosis-associated iritis, and any iritis that is chronic in nature is typically bilateral.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: An otherwise healthy 22-year-old man presents with redness, pain, blurred vision, and photophobia of the left eye with minimal tearing that has worsened over the past 2 weeks. He also endorses a 1-month history of low back pain and hip pain that is worse at night and improves with exercise. On examination, his left pupil appears constricted, and conjunctival injection is concentrated around the limbus. What is the most likely cause of his ophthalmic complaints?
englishExplanation: Anterior uveitis (or iritis) is associated with systemic inflammatory diseases such as seronegative spondyloarthropathies (eg, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, Behçet's disease, and psoriatic arthritis). Patients with ankylosing spondylitis have a frequency of uveitis of approximately 25% to 30%. Uveitis may be the first presentation of an underlying spondyloarthropathy and should prompt consideration for follow-up and further testing. Although activity and severity of uveitis is not associated with spondyloarthropathy, 50% of patients with recurrent iri- tis have spondyloarthropathy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with acute angle-closure glaucoma have conjunctival injection, ocular pain, blurred vision, and photophobia. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically unilat- eral, and discharge is minimal. Although it may appear similar to uveitis due to the preceding similarities, pain with acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically severe and can be associated with a headache and vomiting, unlike uveitis. Additionally, the pupil in acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically fixed and mid- dilated; in iritis, the pupil is constricted and poorly responsive to light. Infectious conjunctivitis can be viral or bacterial and is a common cause of red eye. Although conjunctivitis can be unilateral, it is not uncommon for the disease to spread bilaterally due to the transmission that results from patients rubbing their eyes. Conjunctivitis produces mild discomfort, and vision is unaffected. Although conjunctivitis causes a red eye similar to iritis, conjunctivitis is usually painless. Infectious keratitis causes inflammation of the cornea and is typically associated with viruses, but keratitis can also be caused by bacteria, fungi, and parasites. Keratitis can be associated with conjunctivitis, but it is more painful and causes blurred vision. If keratitis is associated with a secondary anterior uveitis, a con- stricted pupil will be observed, but keratitis alone is associated with a normal pupillary size and response.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the mainstay of treatment for noninfectious iritis?
englishExplanation: Treatment of acute iritis (or anterior uveitis) depends on the underlying cause. For noninfectious iritis, anti-inflammatory measures such as topical steroids (eg, prednisolone 1% or dexamethasone 0.1%) are used at different frequencies based on the degree of inflammation. It is important to note, however, that steroids must be administered in consultation with an ophthalmologist. Cycloplegic agents are also used in acute iritis to prevent the formation of poste- rior synechiae and relieve ciliary spasm; commonly used medications include cy- clopentolate and homatropine. The treatment of infectious uveitis depends on the or- ganism causing the disease. Topical and oral antivirals are used for iritis from HSV and varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Topical steroids follow the initiation of the antivirals. Iritis is caused by inflammation of the iris and surrounding structures found along the anterior portion of the uvea. Iritis is also known as anterior uveitis and in- cludes inflammation of the nearby ciliary body (iridocyclitis) in addition to the iris. Inflammation of the vitreous humor is known as intermediate uveitis, and inflamma- tion of structures posterior to the lens (eg, the choroid and retina) is known as poste- rior uveitis. Iritis is the most common form of uveitis, and affected patients can present with decreased vision, photophobia, ciliary flush, or diffuse con- junctival injection. Incorrect Answer Explanations Antivirals are not used to treat noninfectious uveitis. Systemic antivirals such as acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir are used to treat HSV and VZV iritis. HSV is the most common infectious agent to cause the disease. Concomitant treat- ment with a topical steroid and a cycloplegic is necessary. Immunosuppressants such as antimetabolites, calcineurin antagonists, or cyto- toxic medications may be needed in patients with iritis who fail to respond to top- ical steroids and cycloplegics. Indications for use include bilateral disease, fail- ure to respond to steroid therapy, or severe disease that interferes with daily living. Examples of antimetabolites include methotrexate, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil. Calcineurin inhibitors include cyclosporine or tacrolimus. Systemic steroids are usually unnecessary in acute anterior uveitis. They may be used when the response to topical steroids is inadequate, but they have ad- verse effects when used for prolonged periods of time.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 32-year-old woman presents with the following finding. She reports eye pain, photophobia, and blurred vision but denies tearing, discharge, and headache. On examination, she has a constricted pupil that is poorly reactive to light. Intraocular pressure in both eyes is 12 mm Hg. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: ARZTSAMUI/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: Anterior uveitis, also known as iritis, is caused by inflammation of the iris and the surrounding structures found along the anterior portion of the uvea. Iritis may involve inflammation of the nearby ciliary body (iridocyclitis) in addition to the iris. Inflammation of the vitreous humor is known as intermediate uveitis, and in- flammation of structures posterior to the lens (eg, the choroid and retina) is known as posterior uveitis. Iritis is the most common form of uveitis, and affected patients present with decreased vision, photophobia, ciliary flush, or diffuse con- junctival injection. Noninfectious iritis may be treated with topical steroids and cycloplegics. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with acute angle-closure glaucoma have conjunctival injection, ocular pain, blurred vision, and photophobia. Although acute angle-closure glaucoma may appear similar to uveitis, pain is typically severe and can be associated with a headache and vomiting, unlike uveitis. Additionally, the pupil in acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically fixed and mid-dilated; in iritis, the pupil is constricted and poorly re- sponsive to light. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is typically unilateral and discharge is minimal. Intraocular pressure is increased in acute angle-closure glaucoma. Infectious conjunctivitis can be viral or bacterial and is a common cause of red eye. Although conjunctivitis can be unilateral, it is not uncommon for the disease to spread bilaterally due to eye rubbing, which can transmit infection to the unaffected eye. Conjunctivitis produces mild discomfort and vision is unaffected. Although conjunctivitis causes a red eye, it is usually painless, unlike iritis. Infectious keratitis causes inflammation of the cornea and is typically associated with viruses, but keratitis can also be caused by bacteria, fungi, and parasites. Keratitis can be associated with conjunctivitis but is more painful and causes blurred vision. If keratitis is associated with a secondary anterior uveitis, a constricted pupil will be observed, but keratitis alone presents with a normal pupillary size and response.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 32-year-old woman presents with a 24-hr history of blurred left eye vision that is associated with flashes of light. She also reports a lightening of red colors when viewed with the left eye compared to the right. Her extraocular movements are in- tact, but they worsen her retro-orbital headache. Visual acuity in the left eye is de- creased compared to the right. When a light is shined into the left eye, both pupils appear to dilate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve that causes monocular vi- sion loss. The most common etiology of optic neuritis is demyelination, but oth- ers include parainfectious causes associated with viral syndromes (eg, measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox, whooping cough, and following vaccination); infectious causes (eg, cat-scratch disease, Lyme disease, syphilis, cryptococcal meningitis, and varicella-zoster virus); and noninfectious causes (eg, sarcoidosis or other autoim- mune disorders).
