Symptoms of optic neuritis due to dysfunction of the optic nerve vary by cause but generally include reduced visual acuity of the affected eye; relative afferent pupillary defect; dyschromatopsia, with impairment of red-green color vision being the most frequent; diminished light brightness and contrast sensitivity; and visual field defects, such as scotomas. In demyelinating optic neuritis, which comprises the majority of cases, 90% of patients experience pain in or around the eye that is exacerbated by extraocular movements. Two-thirds of demyelinating optic neuritis cases occur in women ranging in age from 20 to 40 years. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is a cause of acute monocular vision loss, it is painless and complete. Headaches are atypical. CRAO can be associ- ated with amaurosis fugax (ie, transient vision loss), and physical examination can show a relative or complete afferent pupillary defect, a pale optic disc, or a cherry-red spot on the fovea. Giant cell arteritis symptoms include a unilateral throbbing headache (usually located over the temple of the affected temporal artery) and transient monocular vision loss, but giant cell arteritis rarely occurs in patients younger than 50 years old. Symptoms can be brought on by actions such as brushing the hair or teeth or by chewing (jaw claudication) secondary to vascular insufficiency of the mas- seter and temporalis muscles. Symptoms can be systemic, such as fatigue, fevers, and weight loss. Retinal detachment is a cause of painless acute monocular vision loss due to sepa- ration of the retina from the underlying choroid in the affected eye. Associated headaches are uncommon. Symptoms include flashes of light, floaters, and a de- crease in peripheral or central vision.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What approach is contraindicated for a first-time presentation of demyelinating optic neuritis?
englishExplanation: Oral steroids have been found to have a higher 2-year and 10-year recurrence risk of optic neuritis in either eye when compared to intravenous corticosteroid use; therefore, oral steroids are contraindicated as a treatment for demyelinat- ing optic neuritis without prior intravenous steroid therapy. Intravenous steroids have been found to accelerate the recovery of visual function in selected pa- tients with demyelinating optic neuritis; however, long-term visual outcomes are similar in patients who receive no intravenous corticosteroids. Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve that causes monocu- lar vision loss. The most common etiology is demyelination, but others include parainfectious causes associated with viral syndromes (eg, measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox, whooping cough; and following vaccination); infectious causes (eg, cat- scratch disease, Lyme disease, syphilis, cryptococcal meningitis, and varicella-zoster virus); and noninfectious causes (eg, sarcoidosis and autoimmune disorders). Incorrect Answer Explanations Interferon beta is a cytokine administered weekly via intramuscular injection. It has immunomodulatory effects on the progression of multiple sclerosis. Patients with a diagnosis of optic neuritis and evidence of white-matter lesions on brain MRI with first attack — which is suggestive of multiple sclerosis — can benefit from treatment with interferon beta. Intravenous methylprednisolone is strongly recommended in patients with optic neuritis and abnormal brain MRI that is suggestive of underlying multiple scle- rosis. Intravenous corticosteroids have been found to relieve pain, increase the rate of visual recovery (but not long-term outcome), and decrease the risk of developing multiple sclerosis within 2 years after symptom onset. Without treatment, the prognosis of optic neuritis is excellent, with vision im- proving within a few weeks. Improvement continues over months, with 90% of pa- tients achieving 20/40 visual acuity or better at 1 year. Subtle changes to color vision and a mild relative afferent pupillary defect may persist. Observation can be a valid route in patients without white-matter lesions on MRI, and it can be decided based on the patient's degree of pain and desire for more rapid visual recovery when weighed against the side-effect profile of high-dose steroid therapy.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient who presents with decreased vision and pain with right eye movement is diagnosed with optic neuritis. Brain MRI shows contrast enhancement in the or- bital portion of the optic nerve as well as four cerebral white-matter lesions. What disease is this patient most at risk for developing within the next 10 years?
englishExplanation: Optic neuritis has been found to be associated with multiple sclerosis. In patients with normal MRI, 22% develop multiple sclerosis 10 years after optic neuritis onset. However, those with MRI showing one or more white-matter lesions have a greater chance of developing multiple sclerosis (56%) at 10 years. Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve which causes monocular vision loss. The most common etiology of optic neuritis is demyelination, but oth- ers include parainfectious causes associated with viral syndromes (eg, measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox, whooping cough, and following vaccination); infectious causes (eg, cat-scratch disease, Lyme disease, syphilis, cryptococcal meningitis, and varicella-zoster virus); and noninfectious causes (eg, sarcoidosis and autoimmune disorders). Incorrect Answer Explanations Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an immune-mediated acute peripheral de- myelinating polyneuropathy that results in symmetric paralysis, usually beginning in the legs. Optic neuritis is rarely associated with GBS. Sarcoidosis is a widespread, immune-mediated granulomatous disease that can af- fect many body systems. Optic neuritis is rarely associated with sarcoidosis, but it is much more commonly associated with multiple sclerosis. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an immune-mediated inflammatory disease that affects multiple body systems. SLE-associated optic neuritis is un- common and occurs in approximately 1% of lupus patients.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which study is the most reasonable choice to confirm a diagnosis of optic neuritis?
englishExplanation: Optic neuritis is a clinical diagnosis made in the setting of acute unilateral vi- sion loss. Patients will typically be 20 to 40 years old and will have pain on eye movement, with a normal fundoscopic examination and a relative affer- ent pupillary defect. Although MRI of the brain and orbits is not required to make a diagnosis, it can provide valuable prognostic information and guide treatment deci- sions, especially since optic neuritis is a possible initial manifestation of multiple sclerosis. When the presentation of optic neuritis is atypical, MRI of the orbits with gadolinium can provide confirmation of the diagnosis with evidence of optic nerve enhancement, while MRI of the brain can show evidence of cerebral white-matter lesions. After finding cerebral white-matter lesions on brain MRI in a patient with optic neuritis, treatment with intravenous corticosteroids can decrease the risk of developing multiple sclerosis during the following 2 years. Incorrect Answer Explanations Orbital CT has a very limited role in the diagnosis of optic neuritis. CT can detect size differences of the optic nerve and can help exclude other orbital pathology, but MRI is superior, with better soft-tissue contrast resolution. Typical cases of optic neuritis do not require CSF analysis, although this can be helpful in atypical cases (eg, age <15 years, bilateral presentation, or signs of infec- tion). CSF analysis can show oligoclonal bands and can assist in the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis in patients with lesions disseminated in space but not time. CSF analysis can also assist when other etiologies of optic neuritis are suspected, such as tuberculosis, Lyme disease, or syphilis. A tissue biopsy is rarely necessary for a diagnosis of optic neuritis. An op- tic nerve biopsy can be considered in cases refractory to empiric therapy or if pro- gressive optic neuropathy persists despite treatment.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient diagnosed with optic neuritis has questions about the likelihood that their vision will return to normal. What is the best counsel to offer?

options.text: Expect excellent recovery with some deficits
Expect permanent vision changes without treatment
Expect resolution without recurrence following treatment

correctAnswer: Expect excellent recovery with some deficits
englishExplanation: This patient should be counseled to expect excellent recovery with some visual deficits. The prognosis of optic neuritis is excellent, with vision improving within 3 to 5 weeks without treatment. Improvement continues during the next few months, with 90% of patients achieving 20/40 visual acuity or better at 1 year. Subtle changes to color vision and a mild relative afferent pupillary defect may persist. Counseling regarding the chance of developing multiple sclerosis and the re- currence of optic neuritis is crucial. Also, there should be communication with oph- thalmology, neurology, or neuro-ophthalmology regarding brain MRI for the assess- ment of cerebral white-matter lesions. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although recovery of visual acuity is excellent several weeks to 1 year following onset of optic neuritis, patients typically retain some mild deficits. These include possible changes to color vision, contrast and motion perception, and sensation of brightness. Patients may also retain a mild relative afferent pupillary defect. Without treatment, the majority of optic neuritis patients experience re- covery of their vision within 1 year. A minority of patients (3%) do develop per- manent mild (20/30) to severe (20/200) visual acuity loss and scotomas that may impair driving. Treatment with intravenous corticosteroids has been found to hasten recovery of vis- ual acuity 4 to 6 weeks after onset. However, 6-month outcomes are unchanged between those who receive steroids and those who do not. Recurrence of optic neuritis is common (occurring at 35% within 10 years) and can involve the orig- inal or the contralateral eye. Patients with recurrent optic neuritis have an increased risk of developing multiple sclerosis.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 57-year-old man presents with difficulty seeing out of his right eye over the past 3 hours. He denies ocular trauma, eye pain, and headaches. He states that he saw some floaters at first but now has some blind spots when he looks in certain direc- tions. On direct ophthalmoscopic examination without dilation of the eye, the eye appears normal. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU with pinpoint correction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: With floaters and visual field cuts, the patient must be evaluated by an ophthalmologist within 24 hours for concerns of a retinal detachment. Even with a direct ophthalmoscopic examination of the retina, most of the retinal tears seen in a detachment are in the periphery of the retina and might not be seen. Only large retinal detachments are seen on direct ophthalmoscopic examination as pale areas. To visualize smaller detachments, a dilated indirect and direct retinal ex- amination must be done by an ophthalmologist. Emergency physicians are now also using ultrasonography of the eyeball to make this diagnosis. From the perspective of an emergency physician, the diagnosis is made primarily on symptoms and clinical history. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute angle-closure glaucoma is usually painful and sudden in onset with loss of visual acuity. Patients sometimes have a headache associated with the find- ings. The pupil is classically fixed and midpoint with a hazy cornea. The in- traocular pressures must be quickly lowered using medications like timolol, and emergent ophthalmology consultation is required to avoid permanent vision loss. This presentation is more consistent with retinal detachment. A central retinal vein occlusion presents with a monocular vision loss that is typically painless. On ophthalmoscopic examination, the classic finding is a “blood-and-thunder” fundus. These patients require further evaluation by ophthal- mology. This presentation is more consistent with retinal detachment. Giant cell arteritis, commonly called temporal arteritis, presents in patients in this age range but typically involves a headache. The patient frequently has other systemic symptoms as well, including fatigue, anorexia, fever, myalgias, and tenderness to palpation over the temporal artery. The diag- nosis is made with an elevated ESR and temporal artery biopsy. The treatment is in- travenous steroids, followed by oral steroids. This presentation is more consis- tent with retinal detachment. Key Points Retinal detachments are diagnosed based on history and cannot be ruled out solely based on a normal direct ophthalmoscopic examination. Visual field cuts can be positionally dependent in the setting of retinal detachment. Otherwise, patients still usually have baseline visual acuity. There is typically no pain in the eye or headache associated with a retinal detachment.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 55-year-old woman presents with painless loss of vision in her right eye that oc- curred suddenly. A physical examination reveals a pale edematous retina with a visible red macula. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
englishExplanation: This patient has central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO), which typically presents as sudden, painless, and profound monocular vision loss. CRAO is caused by an occlusion of the central retinal artery that can stem from many different etiologies, including embolus (carotid or cardiac), thrombosis, vasculitis, giant cell arteritis, sickle cell disease, and trauma. The most common cause overall is carotid artery atherosclerosis followed by cardiogenic embolism. Classically, the retina appears pale, whitish, transparent, and edematous in CRAO pa- tients. The characteristic “cherry red spot” in the macula can be seen due to the choroidal circulation in the macula, which is the thinnest portion of the retina. Emergency treatment is aimed at rapidly moving the clot from the central artery to a branch, thereby reducing the size of the infarct. CRAO is a true ocular emer- gency. In some centers, interarterial thrombolysis can be attempted by a neurovascular specialist, so neurology should be consulted immediately. Ophthalmology should also be consulted to determine the necessity of ur- gently reducing intraocular pressure (IOP). In consultation with specialists, other treatments can be attempted, such as ocular massage, vasodilators, and hyper- baric oxygen therapy. The retina will suffer permanent damage within 90 minutes, so treatment must begin immediately. If a traumatic etiology is suspected, a careful assessment for other injuries should be completed as well. If an inflamma- tory condition like giant cell arteritis is suspected, systemic glucocorticoids should be given. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bell palsy, a painless dysfunction of cranial nerve VII, may cause de- creased vision due to weakness of the facial muscles; the eye itself is not involved. Patients with Bell palsy may complain of dry eye due to an inability to close the eyelid, which may cause discomfort. Retinal examination, however, should be normal in Bell palsy. Glaucoma is generally a slow-developing, nonpainful cause of vision loss due to chronically high IOP on the optic nerve. Acute angle-closure glaucoma can present with monocular pain and associated vision loss, but it is more commonly associated with elevated IOP, a mid-fixed pupil, and a hazy edematous cornea; there is no retinal pallor associated with acute glaucoma. Optic neuritis, which is associated with multiple sclerosis, presents with painful loss of vision. Many patients experience decreased color saturation sensitivity — often specifically describing reds as appearing less vibrant. Eye exami- nation often reveals a swollen, edematous optic disc while the retina ap- pears normal.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the most likely fundoscopic examination finding for a patient with central retinal artery occlusion?

options.text: Asymmetric cupping of the optic nerve
Blurred disc margin with tortuous veins
Retinal pallor with cherry red macula

correctAnswer: Retinal pallor with cherry red macula
englishExplanation: Central retinal artery occlusion causes painless, usually monocular, acute vision loss. The central retinal artery supplies the inner retina. When the central retinal artery becomes occluded, the blood supply to the inner retina can be dimin- ished or completely obstructed, causing the retina to become pale on fundoscopy. The macula is the thinnest portion of the retina. The underlying outer retina is supplied by the choroidal circulation from the ciliary arteries, which branch off the ophthalmic artery separately from the central retinal artery. The thin macula then appears as a “cherry red spot” because it is translucent and shows the underlying choroidal circulation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Asymmetric cupping of the optic disc is suggestive of glaucoma. Other exami- nation findings may include disc hemorrhages and notching of the optic nerve. These findings are due to the increased ocular pressure leading to optic neu- ropathy, which causes the optic cup to enlarge compared to the optic disc. Increased intraocular pressure is also typically noted. Billowing elevation of the retina is suggestive of retinal detachment. An ele- vated retina appears lighter in color or gray. However, if the retinal detachment oc- curs peripherally, the fundoscopic examination may appear normal. An indirect oph- thalmoscopic evaluation by an ophthalmologist is necessary. A blurred disc margin with dilated and tortuous veins and retinal hemor- rhages are consistent with central retinal vein occlusion. As the central retinal vein is occluded, venous stasis and edema occur, which can be seen as dilated and tortuous veins with a blurred disc margin and hemorrhages on fundoscopic examina- tion. This finding is known as “blood and thunder.”

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: From which artery does an embolus originate that leads to central retinal artery occlusion?
englishExplanation: The internal carotid artery (ICA) branches include the ophthalmic artery, which supplies the central retinal artery. Therefore, plaque rupture from the in- ternal carotid artery can lead to thrombosis of the central retinal artery, which is a terminal artery. The ICA also branches into other intracranial vasculature, including the anterior cerebral artery and middle cerebral artery. An embolus from the ICA can occlude any of these vessels, causing a cerebrovascular accident (CVA). In a patient who presents with a central retinal artery occlusion or CVA, it is important to evalu- ate the ICA and carotids with additional imaging studies, such as carotid Dopplers, MRI, or CT angiography of the head and neck. This imaging assesses vessel narrowing and extracranial carotid atherosclerosis for possible endarterectomy or stenting to prevent further CVAs. Incorrect Answer Explanations The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) originates from the internal carotid artery. The branches of the ACA do not supply the ophthalmic artery; therefore, an embolus from this vessel cannot occlude the central retinal artery. The basilar artery originates from the vertebral arteries. Its branches include the anterior inferior cerebellar artery, pontine arteries, and superior cerebellar artery. It does not supply the central retinal artery. The middle cerebral artery originates from the internal carotid artery. Its branches include the lenticulostriate arteries and superior and inferior trunks. These branches do not supply the ophthalmic artery; therefore, an embolus from this vessel cannot occlude the central retinal artery.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: In a stand-alone emergency department, a patient presents with monocular, pain- less vision loss, and central retinal artery occlusion is suspected. What is the ap- propriate disposition for this patient?

options.text: Refer to neurology in the next 24 to 48 hours
Refer to ophthalmology in the next 24 to 48 hours
Transfer to a nearby hospital for ophthalmology evaluation
Transfer to a stroke center with both neurology and ophthalmology

correctAnswer: Transfer to a stroke center with both neurology and ophthalmology
englishExplanation: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is an ischemic event of the eye. Patients should be emergently seen by both an ophthalmologist and a neurolo- gist for evaluation of possible treatment modalities such as intra-arterial thromboly- sis. Early treatment may prevent permanent vision loss. While definitive manage- ment of CRAO is controversial, possible therapies include ocular massage, intra-arte- rial thrombolytics, and anterior chamber paracentesis. Incorrect Answer Explanations CRAO is an emergency that can result in permanent vision loss in as little as 4 hours. Thus, referral to neurology in 24 to 48 hours is inappropriate. CRAO is considered an ischemic event of the eye and should be emergently evaluated by both a neurologist and an ophthalmologist. CRAO is a vision-threatening emergency that can cause vision loss in as little as 4 hours. Thus, referral to ophthalmology in 24 to 48 hours is inappropriate. CRAO is best managed emergently at a stroke center with concomitant ophthalmology consultation. Transfer to a nearby hospital for ophthalmology evaluation alone is inappropriate. CRAO is an ischemic event that also needs to be evaluated by a neurologist, most appropriately at a specialized stroke center.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient presents with painless vision loss. A fundoscopic examination shows monocular blurred disc margins with dilated and tortuous veins and diffuse retinal hemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) causes painless, monocular, acute vision disturbance ranging from blurred vision to complete vision loss. Due to the occluded vein, venous stasis occurs, causing edema and dilated, tortu- ous veins with a blurred disc margin. The congestion can also cause diffuse retinal hemorrhages. This finding on fundoscopic examination is known as “blood and thunder.” Because this condition is usually monocular, the contralateral fun- doscopic examination is generally normal. Risk factors include hypertension, dia- betes, hypercoagulable states, hyperlipidemia, glaucoma, cardiovascular disease, smoking, and increased age. Incorrect Answer Explanations Central retinal artery occlusion also causes monocular, painless, acute vi- sion loss. However, because the artery is occluded, the fundoscopic examination shows retinal pallor due to the lack of blood supply. Because the macula is the thinnest part of the retina, the underlying outer retina blood supply is seen as a “cherry red spot.” Optic neuritis can cause painful or painless vision loss. It is most commonly monocular, but it can be bilateral. On fundoscopic examination, edema with blurred disc margins and hemorrhages may be seen at the optic disc, but the outer retina should not be affected. Therefore, diffuse retinal hemorrhages on fundo- scopic examination should not be found. This difference separates it from central retinal vein occlusion. While the fundoscopic findings of papilledema are similar to those of CRVO, pa- pilledema findings are bilateral, which distinguishes them from CRVO. Papilledema is due to increased intracranial pressure that obstructs the vasculature of the optic nerve, which causes vascular congestion that can be seen on fundoscopic examination as blurred disc margins and edema. Another finding that may also dif- ferentiate papilledema from CRVO is that most people with papilledema have pre- served visual acuity.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: An elderly patient presents with suspected central retinal artery occlusion and jaw claudication and is found to also have an elevated ESR. What therapy should be started?
englishExplanation: Giant cell arteritis (GCA), otherwise known as temporal arteritis, is a rare cause of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). GCA is an inflammatory dis- ease of medium- and large-size vessels that causes vasculitis. The disease usually presents in patients older than 50 years. Symptoms include jaw claudication and headache as well as other systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and myalgias. Laboratory work can be significant for an elevated sedimentation rate. If there is con- cern for GCA, treatment should include the immediate start of steroids (methylpred- nisolone IV if there is threatened vision loss), even before a biopsy can be performed for confirmation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Heparin has been used for patients with CRAO; however, like most other conserva- tive therapies for CRAO, it has not proven efficacious. In patients with concomi- tant GCA, steroids have been shown to improve vision and therefore are the most ap- propriate therapy. Intraocular pressure–reducing drops such as timolol are used to treat glaucoma. Glaucoma causes acute painful vision loss with increased intraocular pres- sure, differentiating it from the painless vision loss in CRAO. With GCA, the intraoc- ular pressures are not elevated; therefore, intraocular pressure–reducing drops are not indicated. tPA may be appropriate in the setting of a cerebrovascular accident, such as a large vessel occlusion. Some studies have evaluated the utility of systemic intravenous tPA in CRAO. The risk of intracerebral hemorrhage as a result of systemic tPA, how- ever, may outweigh the possible benefits, especially in cases where the likely cause is GCA, which should be treated with steroids.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which diagnostic test distinguishes postseptal (orbital) cellulitis from preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the orbits

correctAnswer: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the orbits
englishExplanation: Although different symptoms suggest that a patient has postseptal (or- bital) cellulitis rather than preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis, a CT scan of the orbits is required to make the diagnosis, preferably performed with IV contrast. Obtaining an MRI is also an option. In general, preseptal cellulitis is seen in patients younger than 10 years and usually originates with URIs in the si- nuses or eyelids. However, similar symptoms can be seen in postseptal cellulitis, which is classically characterized by pain with extraocular movement and proptosis in significant infections. Patients with mild preseptal cellulitis can be treated as outpatients with oral antibiotics. In contrast, patients with postseptal cel- lulitis require admission for intravenous antibiotic therapy and management by an ophthalmologist. CT scan is unnecessary for uncomplicated preseptal cellulitis, but if signs or symp- toms such as pain with extraocular motions, proptosis, or decreased ocular mobility are present, CT is recommended to evaluate for diagnosis as well as complications. Incorrect Answer Explanations Blood cultures do not definitively rule in one disease process over the other. Preseptal cellulitis is ultimately distinguished from orbital (postseptal) cellulitis by contrast-enhanced CT scan. ESR is not a specific test to differentiate between the two types of infection. Preseptal cellulitis is ultimately distinguished from orbital (postseptal) cellulitis by contrast-enhanced CT scan. Although some studies suggest that ocular ultrasonography can help diagnose orbital cellulitis, CT is still the definitive imaging modality. Preseptal cellulitis is ulti- mately distinguished from orbital (postseptal) cellulitis by contrast-en- hanced CT scan.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What physical examination finding most strongly indicates that an eye infection is the result of orbital cellulitis?
englishExplanation: Orbital cellulitis is a serious infection of the orbital fat and muscles that can threaten one's vision and even one's life. It must be differentiated from preseptal cellulitis, which is an infection of the anterior eye structures. Both can cause ocular pain, eyelid swelling, and erythema, but only orbital cellulitis typi- cally leads to pain with extraocular movements, ophthalmoplegia, prop- tosis, diplopia, and decreased visual acuity. Orbital cellulitis is a much more serious entity and can lead to vision loss in up to 11% of cases. Complications in- clude subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess (most common), cavernous sinus thrombosis, and brain abscess. CT of the orbits can confirm this di- agnosis. Treatment is always admission with intravenous antibiotics (van- comycin and ceftriaxone or cefotaxime). Cellulitis involving the structures around the eye can be differentiated by the tissue planes involved in the infection: preseptal (ie, periorbital cellulitis) or postseptal (ie, orbital cellulitis). Preseptal cellulitis is considered a less serious condition, generally caused by a Staphylococcus aureus infection from local trauma (such as an eyelid abrasion) or, rarely, by hematologic spread of an Haemophilus influenzae infection from the ear or lung. Both conditions are more common in children. A patient with preseptal cellulitis may present with eyelid swelling, ocular pain, and possibly fever. Preseptal cellulitis is considered a benign condition that can be treated with oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid in the outpatient set- ting for most cases. Children younger than 1 are at greater risk of pro- gression to orbital cellulitis, so admission for treatment with intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone and vancomycin) is still recommended in this age group until orbital cellulitis is ruled out. Incorrect Answer Explanations Eye erythema can be seen in both preseptal cellulitis and orbital celluli- tis, so it does not differentiate the worse etiology. Additionally, some cases of orbital cellulitis actually do not present with eye erythema because the infection is deeper in the orbital structures (fat and extraocular muscles). Preseptal cellulitis is limited to the periorbital tissues and does not involve the orbit directly. Visual acuity, ex- traocular motility, and pupillary reaction should be unaffected in pa- tients with preseptal cellulitis. A patient with either orbital or preseptal cellulitis can have eyelid swelling. A distinguishing clinical examination finding in the patient with orbital cellulitis is pain with limitation of extraocular muscle movements. Other later find- ings of orbital cellulitis can include proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and a decrease in vis- ual acuity, but these are not findings associated with preseptal cellulitis. Ocular pain can be present in both orbital and preseptal cellulitis, so ocu- lar pain cannot reliably distinguish between either type of cellulitis. Pain with ex- traocular movements, ophthalmoplegia, or changes in vision can indicate orbital cel- lulitis, which involves the deeper structures such as the extraocular muscles.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A child presents with painful swelling and redness to the left eyelid with associated ophthalmoplegia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Orbital cellulitis is a severe infection that involves the fat and muscles within the orbit, posterior to the orbital septum. Patients present with red- ness and swelling to the eyelid, proptosis, and painful limitation of ex- traocular movements. Commonly caused by a bacterial rhinosinusitis, orbital cel- lulitis is more commonly seen in pediatric patients than in adults. Orbital cellulitis is treated with prompt administration of intravenous antibiotics, which can be transitioned to oral antibiotics once the patient has demonstrated clinical improve- ment. Affected patients may develop orbital and subperiosteal abscesses. Vision loss and cavernous sinus thrombosis are rare but are also potential complications. Incorrect Answer Explanations Allergic reactions involving the eyelid can cause redness, swelling, and pruritus. Allergic conjunctivitis is also associated with watery discharge. Neither allergic reac- tions nor allergic conjunctivitis are associated with ophthalmoplegia. Patients usually experience symptoms in both eyes and may describe a burning sensation, but typi- cally not pain. Triggering allergens can be environmental or topical irritants. Management of allergic conjunctivitis includes allergen avoidance and topical application of antihistamines with mast cell stabilizing properties. A chalazion is a localized nodular swelling of the eyelid that is not tender or painful. Chalazion is caused by obstruction of the meibomian gland and has min- imal erythema. A hordeolum has a similar appearance of localized swelling; however, it is infectious and often causes pain and redness. Both chalazia and hordeola generally resolve spontaneously. Warm compresses can be applied to encourage drainage. Preseptal cellulitis is often challenging to differentiate from orbital cellulitis; how- ever, preseptal cellulitis is not associated with ophthalmoplegia or propto- sis. Both conditions occur primarily in children, and neither involve the globe itself. Preseptal cellulitis is an infection of structures anterior to the orbital septum of the eye, and it can develop after sinusitis, trauma to the face or eyelid, or insect bites. Patients experience pain as well as redness and swelling of the eyelid. In younger children, it can be difficult to obtain a full ophthalmic examination, so a CT scan may be required to differentiate between the two diagnoses. Preseptal celluli- tis can be treated effectively with oral antibiotics.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which diagnostic test would best distinguish preseptal cellulitis from orbital cellulitis?
englishExplanation: Preseptal cellulitis can be difficult to differentiate from orbital cellulitis, especially in younger children whose ability to cooperate with the full physical examination may be limited by their developmental stage. CT scan with contrast of the orbits and sinuses is the most useful diagnostic tool to distinguish between the two conditions. Patients with orbital cellulitis will demonstrate fat stranding of the orbital contents, proptosis, and extraocular muscle edema. These findings will not be present in pa- tients with preseptal cellulitis. Additionally, if a patient has developed complications of orbital cellulitis, such as orbital or subperiosteal abscesses, these can also be visu- alized on a contrast-enhanced CT. Incorrect Answer Explanations Blood cultures are unhelpful in distinguishing preseptal from orbital cellulitis. Blood cultures are often negative in preseptal cellulitis and are not routinely recom- mended. The exception to this would be a very young infant who presents with fever. It is also recommended that blood cultures be obtained prior to starting intravenous antibiotics in patients with presumed or confirmed orbital cellulitis. It is difficult to obtain fluid from the eyelid to send for culture unless there is a drain- ing abscess or wound. Even if a sample can be obtained, the results will not differ- entiate between preseptal and orbital cellulitis. The most common microbial pathogens presumed to cause both infections are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Fluorescein staining of the eye is helpful in identifying injuries to the cornea, but it will not differentiate between preseptal and orbital cellulitis. After applying a drop of sterile saline to the fluorescein strip, the eyelid is gently pulled down and the tip of the strip is placed on the conjunctiva. A cobalt blue light can then be used to vi- sualize any corneal epithelial defects. Corneal ulcers, abrasions, lacerations, and den- dritic lesions consistent with herpes keratoconjunctivitis can also be visualized on flu- orescein staining of the eye.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which medication regimen is the correct treatment for mild preseptal cellulitis without evidence of skin trauma?
englishExplanation: Oral antibiotics can effectively treat mild preseptal cellulitis in adults and children who are old enough to reliably cooperate with the examination. The antibi- otics administered should provide antimicrobial coverage for Staphylococcus au- reus, Streptococcus pneumonia, and anaerobes since these are the most common causative organisms. Current recommendations include monotherapy with oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid for patients without signs of perior- bital trauma (no need for empiric MRSA coverage) or dual therapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus either amoxicillin, amoxicillin- clavulate, cefpodoxime, cefuroxime, or cefdinir. Younger infants or any indi- viduals who appear to have a more severe illness should be admitted to a hospital set- ting and given intravenous antibiotics to treat presumed orbital cellulitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient with mild preseptal cellulitis can be treated as an outpatient, so intravenous antibiotics are unnecessary. Additionally, monotherapy with clindamycin would be an ineffective treatment for preseptal cellulitis be- cause it does not provide adequate microbial coverage against nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHi), and clindamycin has increasing resistance for MSSA and MRSA. Ophthalmic erythromycin is an ineffective treatment for preseptal cel- lulitis. Preseptal cellulitis is often caused by sinusitis or local trauma to the eyelids and face. Although erythromycin treats Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, and Haemophilus, topical application will not penetrate the commonly affected soft tis- sues to provide adequate treatment. Ophthalmic erythromycin is indicated to treat bacterial conjunctivitis and is also applied prophylactically in the eyes of newborns to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum, which is primarily caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin and would be an inappropriate treat- ment for preseptal cellulitis. In patients with an allergy who are unable to take a penicillin, then a second- or third-generation cephalosporin is in- dicated. Cefdinir, cefpodoxime, or cefuroxime would be appropriate cephalosporins to use. If the allergy is life threatening, or the patient is unable to take cephalosporins, then levofloxacin should be started.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which finding can develop as a complication of orbital cellulitis?
englishExplanation: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a rare but dangerous complication of in- adequately treated orbital cellulitis. Contiguous spread of infection from or- bital cellulitis can cause a septic thrombus to form and obstruct the cavernous sinus, reducing venous drainage. In addition to the clinical presentation consistent with or- bital cellulitis, patients may experience severe headaches and demonstrate pa- pilledema on examination. In severe cases, patients may experience hemiparesis, seizures, and altered mental status. The diagnosis of cavernous sinus thrombosis can be confirmed by imaging, which may demonstrate a thrombus in the affected cav- ernous sinus and an associated filling defect. Treatment includes prompt administra- tion of intravenous antibiotics and antithrombotic agents. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ciliary flush is an examination finding in which the vessels adjacent to and surrounding the limbus are dilated and have a red-violet appear- ance. Ciliary flush indicates inflammation of the cornea, iris, or ciliary body and is not seen in patients with periorbital cellulitis or conjunctivitis. Ciliary flush can be best seen by the examiner in daylight or natural light. Ciliary flush is associated with serious eye conditions, such as acute angle-closure glaucoma, iritis, and uveitis. The presence of this physical examination finding warrants ophthalmologic consultation for further evaluation and treatment. Dendritic corneal lesions are a characteristic finding of herpes keratitis and are unrelated to periorbital cellulitis. These lesions, which can be visualized on fluorescein staining, have a linear branching appearance with terminal bulbs. Primary herpes conjunctivitis is usually self-limiting and nonspecific. Patients with recurrent infection or keratitis present with a painful red eye; increased tearing; and blurred vision. Treatment includes oral or topical antivirals and prompt ophthal- mology follow-up. Topical steroids should not be administered without first consult- ing with an ophthalmologist. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative intracellular diplococcus bacterium that can cause conjunctivitis, but is not a complication of periorbital cellulitis. Gonococcal conjunctivitis (GC) occurs when the eye comes in contact with infected genital secre- tions. In neonates, it is referred to as gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum and results from maternal transmission. GC is prevented by the topical administra- tion of prophylactic ophthalmic antibiotics immediately after birth in all newborns. Symptomatic patients will present with mucopurulent discharge, con- junctival injection, and eyelid edema. The diagnosis can be confirmed via Gram stain, culture, or PCR. GC can be treated with a single dose of ceftriaxone and saline lavage. Alternatively, cefotaxime should be used in infants with significant hyperbilirubinemia.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: For which nasal foreign body is a topical vasoconstricting agent such as oxymeta- zoline contraindicated in toddlers?
englishExplanation: Removal of a button battery from a toddler's nose is an emergent procedure (within 4-8 hours) because the battery can cause alkaline necrosis of the nasal septum. However, the use of a topical nasal vasoconstricting agent such as oxymetazoline to make removal easier is contraindicated; the presence of an ion charge from the nasal drops can cause electrolysis and result in a severe alkaline burn. Otherwise, vaso- constricting agents are recommended for the management of many nasal foreign bodies. Vasoconstriction has the advantage of potentially minimizing bleeding during or after the removal procedure and of decreasing local edema around the foreign body to ease removal. Incorrect Answer Explanations Even if the sponge absorbs some of the vasoconstricting agent when it is applied, a vasoconstricting agent can still reduce the nasal mucosal swelling and de- crease the bleeding and trauma associated with removal of the foreign body. Hard plastic toy beads are often difficult to grasp, and using a vasoconstricting agent can decrease local edema to make removal easier. Magnets, particularly those across the nasal septum, can be quite destructive. Removal can be accomplished by using the handle of bayonet forceps to attract one of the magnets away from the septum. A topical nasal vasoconstricting agent is often useful, not contraindicated, in this setting. Key Points Topical nasal vasoconstricting agents are helpful for the removal of most nasal for- eign bodies. Topical nasal vasoconstricting agents or any other electrolyte liquid should not be used when the foreign body is a button battery.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 2-year-old boy presents with a 2-week history of purulent discharge from the right nostril that has not responded to a 7-day course of amoxicillin. Which course of action is most appropriate?
englishExplanation: It is prudent to consider unilateral nasal discharge in very young children to be a nasal foreign body until proven otherwise. Thus, examining inside the nose to look for the foreign body would be the best course of action. Although a “double barrel” runny nose is a very common nonspecific finding, unilateral, purulent nasal dis- charge is much less common and can indicate a nasal foreign body. A his- tory of nasal foreign body insertion is unknown by the parents up to 25% in children. Preferably, the possibility of nasal foreign bodies should be ruled out before antibi- otics are prescribed. Diagnosis is typically through direct visualization of the for- eign body on examination. Most of the time, x-rays are unnecessary, as they will not reveal radiopaque foreign bodies (exception for button batteries and magnets). Other presenting features include foul odor; nasal pain; and rarely, epistaxis, nasal obstruction, or mouth breathing. Nasal foreign bodies are most common in toddlers and preschool-aged chil- dren. They are more commonly encountered in the right nare, simply due to the predominance of right-handedness. There are a myriad of foreign bodies that may be found in the nose, but the most dangerous are button batteries and paired magnets. These need to be removed in a timely fashion because button batteries can cause tissue necrosis within 4 hours, and paired magnets spanning the septum can cause necrosis of the septum over a period of weeks. Emergent ENT referral is war- ranted for these two foreign bodies. Most other foreign bodies can be removed in the emergency department using a variety of techniques. Incorrect Answer Explanations Given the failure of amoxicillin therapy, the source of the purulent, unilateral dis- charge in this case could likely be a nasal foreign body. If the discharge is the result of a foreign body, it will need to be removed right away to resolve symptoms. Antibiotics and antihistamines would likely be ineffective until the foreign body is removed. Antihistamines are first-line agents for treatment of moderate symptoms in allergic rhinitis. However, this patient's source of nasal discharge may be sec- ondary to a retained foreign body rather than an IgE–mediated allergic response. Furthermore, purulent discharge does not indicate an allergic cause, but rather, an infectious case. Thus, the best course of treatment in this case would be to examine the nose for the possibility of a foreign body. Nasal suctioning has importance in disease processes such as bronchiolitis for young babies. Although it has also been described to potentially remove a nasal foreign body, it is unlikely to remove a foreign body that the physician is unaware of. Always perform a thorough examination of the nares before attempting to suction or remove any foreign body. Although nasal saline irri- gation can provide relief of nasal congestion from URIs or allergies, performing nasal irrigation without first looking to see if there is a foreign body is unadvised. If per- formed on the side of the foreign body, it might worsen the obstruction. Notably, a method has been described for using saline irrigation from the opposite nare to try and force the nasal foreign body out, but again, this should not be at- tempted until after a thorough examination.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 38-year-old woman with a history of asthma and eczema presents with nasal congestion of 1 week's duration. Over the past few days, she has had persistent sneezing, rhinorrhea, and nasal stuffiness. Examination reveals inflamed nasal turbinates and slight erythema in the oropharynx. There is no tenderness to palpa- tion of her sinuses and no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with symptoms consistent with allergic rhinitis, a diag- nosis that is primarily clinical. Patients with allergic rhinitis tend to have other atopic medical conditions, such as asthma and eczema. Treatment involves remov- ing any precipitating allergens, such as pollen or pets. Allergic rhinitis is treated with nasal inhaled steroid sprays, saline nasal rinses, and oral antihistamine. For more severe cases, inhaled or systemic steroids might be indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient has no sinus tenderness, facial pain, or fever and has not had symptoms for more than 10 days, so bacterial sinusitis is unlikely. The use of antibiotics in sinusitis is controversial, as there is mixed evidence that it improves outcomes. Nasal foreign body is unlikely since the patient is an adult. With a nasal foreign body, symptoms are more likely to be unilateral. Treatment for nasal foreign body is removal, either emergently if there are signs of airway compromise or electively in the emergency department or by an ENT specialist. Button batteries in the nose must be removed immediately. This patient has no fever, cough, sore throat, or myalgias, so a URI is unlikely at this time. Most URIs are viral and require only supportive therapy.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 30-year-old woman presents with headache, fever, and decreased vision in her right eye over the past 24 hours. Examination reveals exophthalmos of the right eye, no pupillary reflex, and a clear anterior chamber. When asked, she denies weakness and numbness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a known complication after infections of the head and neck, including dental infections and sinusitis. Since cranial nerves III, IV, V1, and V2 run along the wall of the cavernous sinus, they can be af- fected as a result of an infection. Most infectious etiologies in cavernous sinus throm- bosis are from Staphylococcus or Streptococcus species. Cavernous sinus throm- bosis must be considered in a patient with fever, headache, and vision changes, although chills, lethargy, nausea, or vomiting may also be present. Blood cultures, CBC, and coagulation studies (PT and PTT) should be or- dered, as well as CT of the head and orbits with contrast. Parenteral antibiotic treatment should be started with gram-positive coverage (nafcillin plus a third- generation cephalosporin or vancomycin if concerned for MRSA). The patient should be admitted with neurology and ophthalmology consultations. A classic rare finding is weakness of cranial nerve VI — known as abducens palsy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute angle-closure glaucoma typically presents with findings of a hazy cornea with a fixed pupil. This patient's cornea is clear on examination. The constellation of symptoms is more consistent with cavernous sinus thrombosis given this patient's fever, headache, and vision changes. Temporal (giant cell) arteritis can present with unilateral headache and vision changes, but it is not seen in patients younger than 50. In fact, the criteria for diagno- sis by the American College or Rheumatology include age >50. An ESR >50 and tem- poral artery biopsy confirm the diagnosis of temporal arteritis. The constellation of symptoms is more consistent with cavernous sinus thrombosis given this patient's fever, headache, and vision changes. A transient ischemic attack is unlikely given the patient's age, sex, and lack of history of other neurologic presentations. The constellation of symptoms is more con- sistent with cavernous sinus thrombosis given this patient's fever, headache, and vision changes.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient presents with 5 days of acute nasal congestion, purulent nasal discharge, and facial pain that worsens with leaning forward. What is the best initial treatment?
englishExplanation: This patient has acute rhinosinusitis (ARS), which is a common disease process seen in the emergency department. Most of the cases of ARS are actually acute viral rhinosinusitis (AVRS), whereas only about 2% of these infections represent acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS). AVRS and many cases of ABRS are self limited, and the initial focus of treatment should be symptomatic care, which includes nasal saline irrigation, over-the-counter analgesics and antipyretics, and intranasal steroids. Other symptomatic treatments with less evidence include in- tranasal ipratropium, intranasal saline spray, oral decongestants, oral antihis- tamines, and nasal oxymetazoline. The diagnosis is typically clinical, with patients presenting with two or more of the following: nasal congestion, facial pain or pressure, anosmia, or purulent nasal discharge. Additionally, fever, tooth pain, maxillary pain, and increase in symptoms with leaning forward may be reported. Complications of ABRS include pe- riorbital sinusitis, orbital sinusitis, Potts puffy tumor (osteomyelitis of the frontal bone), intracranial abscess, or meningitis. Physicians should make sure to do a thor- ough history and physical examination to make sure none of these complications, al- though rare, exist. ABRS can be initially treated symptomatically in an immunocompetent host. Recommendations vary, but one recommendation is to provide symptomatic treatment as above for 7 days; if the patient is not improving, then start antibi- otics. Others argue for a wait-and-see antibiotic prescription. A general thought is to reserve antibiotics for patients with purulent nasal discharge and symp- toms for more than 7 to 10 days. The antibiotics of choice are amoxicillin, amox- icillin-clavulanate, or doxycycline if the patient is allergic to penicillin. If the patient is at high risk for Pseudomonas, then high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate is recommended. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although nasal oxymetazoline can provide symptomatic relief of nasal congestion due to ARS, it is not the first-line treatment recommended — nasal saline irrigation is. Nasal oxymetazoline is also not recommended for use beyond 3 days as it can lead to rebound congestion or dependence. First-line therapy for ARS includes nasal saline irrigation, analgesics, antipyretics, and nasal steroids. Patients can also use oral decongestants, nasal decongestants, and oral antihistamines. Although oral amoxicillin is the correct treatment for a patient who has prolonged ABRS requiring antibiotic therapy, most patients with ARS do not need antibi- otics, as ARS is most often viral in nature or self limiting. Oral antibiotics are not the correct treatment for someone who has only had symptoms for 5 days. Most recom- mendations state to initially treat ARS patients with symptomatic therapy as above, and if symptoms persist for more than 7 to 10 days, then treat with antibiotics. Macrolides, such as azithromycin, are not a recommended treatment for ABRS anymore due to the high resistance against Streptococcus pneumoniae. If one were to treat with antibiotics, the first-line therapy would be amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What clinical finding distinguishes an aphthous ulcer from herpes labialis?

options.text: Aphthous ulcers are >1 cm, while the lesions from herpes labialis tend to be <0.3 cm
Aphthous ulcers are frequently associated with signs of systemic illness
Aphthous ulcers are painless, while herpes labialis lesions are painful
Aphthous ulcers generally occur on the nonkeratinized mucosa inside the mouth

correctAnswer: Aphthous ulcers generally occur on the nonkeratinized mucosa inside the mouth
englishExplanation: Aphthous ulcers, commonly called “canker sores,” are multifactorial, noninfectious, inflammatory lesions that generally form on nonkera- tinized oral tissue. Typical locations include the buccal mucosa, soft palate, and floor of the mouth, including underneath the tongue. By contrast, herpes labialis le- sions — caused by HSV-1 and commonly called “cold sores” — occur predominantly on the keratinized oral tissue outside of the lips and around the mouth. When they do occur intraorally, these lesions generally appear on keratinized tissue, primarily the hard palate and tightly bound oral gingiva. Both types of lesion are recurrent and of- ten provoked by stress, illness, or trauma. However, the early disease progression is distinct. Aphthous ulcers first appear as erythematous, painful macules that evolve into ulcers, whereas herpes labialis is characterized by small painful vesicles that eventually rupture and coalesce into larger ulcers. In terms of appearance, both lesions are characterized by an exudative, yellowish ulcera- tion surrounded by an erythematous border, but their shape tends to differ. Because herpetic lesions are often formed by several vesicles, the outline tends to be irregular. Aphthous ulcers are generally oval-shaped and stand-alone in appearance. Both lesions tend to self-resolve in 1 to 2 weeks. Treatment is supportive and in- cludes general oral hygiene and pain control using 2% viscous lidocaine or an over- the-counter, swish-and-spit anesthetic. Topical steroids such as dexamethasone oint- ment can expedite healing for aphthous ulcers, whereas treatment for herpes labialis can include antiviral medication such as acyclovir or valacyclovir. Incorrect Answer Explanations Lesion size is an unreliable way to differentiate between these common oral afflic- tions. Aphthous ulcers tend to be between 3 and 5 mm, and although complex aphthous ulcers can be larger, they are comparatively rare. The individual vesicles of herpes labialis tend to be small, but they commonly coalesce into one large irregular ulceration. Aphthous ulcers generally occur on the nonkeratinized mu- cosa inside the mouth, while herpes labialis lesions occur predominantly on the kera- tinized oral tissue outside of the lips and around the mouth. Aphthous ulcers are rarely associated with signs of systemic illness. In fact, symptoms such as fever, malaise, and arthralgias should prompt further investigation for the presence of an autoimmune or systemic disease. Aphthous ulcers generally oc- cur on the nonkeratinized mucosa inside the mouth, while herpes labialis lesions oc- cur predominantly on the keratinized oral tissue outside of the lips and around the mouth. Both aphthous ulcers and herpes labialis lesions are quite painful. Therefore, pain is an unreliable way to differentiate between the two oral afflictions. Aphthous ulcers generally occur on the nonkeratinized mucosa inside the mouth, while herpes labialis lesions occur predominantly on the keratinized oral tissue out- side of the lips and around the mouth. Key Points Aphthous ulcers and herpes labialis can be differentiated based on location: Aphthous ulcers are intraoral and found on nonkeratinized mucosal surfaces, while herpes labialis predominantly occurs periorally on keratinized surfaces. When found intraorally, herpes labialis typically occurs on the keratinized tissue of the hard palate and oral gingiva. Aphthous ulcers tend to be round or oval-shaped and are well circumscribed, while the ulcerations of herpes labialis are irregularly shaped and formed by multiple vesicles. Aphthous ulcers are treated with oral hygiene, topical anesthetics, and topical steroid ointments.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 4-year-old boy presents with a mass on the right side of his neck located just an- terior to the border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The mother says she first noticed it 3 days earlier. The patient has not complained of any pain and has had no difficulties breathing or swallowing. There is no erythema appreciated over the area. Ultrasonography demonstrates a cystic structure. What is the most likely cause of the neck mass?
englishExplanation: Branchial cysts, sinuses, and fistulas are produced by abnormal develop- ment of the branchial arches and clefts, and this patient's presentation is con- sistent with a branchial cleft cyst. Most children who present with these neck masses are younger than 5, and the masses can occur spontaneously. Patients are usually well appearing with no difficulties with breathing or swallowing. The sec- ond branchial cleft is the most common site of origin (95%). If there are no signs of an underlying infection, outpatient excision by an otolaryngologist is the de- finitive treatment. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient has no signs of an underlying infection, so an abscess is unlikely. If he had signs of an infection, ENT consultation would be suggested. Given the location, if there were an infection, incision and drainage might be indicated. This presenta- tion is more consistent with a branchial cleft cyst. Hemangiomas typically present in the first 2 to 4 weeks of life and last until 9 to 10 months of age. After this, they tend to get smaller. They are usually mobile and soft and have a blue tint. Given the patient's age and no signs of discoloration, a heman- gioma is unlikely. This presentation is more consistent with a branchial cleft cyst. Because the mass is not midline, a thyroid mass is unlikely. Additionally, the patient does not demonstrate any signs of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. This pre- sentation is more consistent with a branchial cleft cyst. Key Points In children, branchial cleft cysts can show up suddenly as a neck mass and prompt a visit to the emergency department. Branchial cleft cysts can look troubling, but they're usually benign; outpatient referral to an ENT is appropriate disposition.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 22-year-old man presents with significant pain at the site of the extraction 3 days after having his left upper wisdom tooth extracted. He has no problems breathing or swallowing. An examination reveals no significant swelling, and his temperature is normal. What is the best next step in treatment?

options.text: Close the site of the extraction with absorbable suture
Discharge the patient with a prescription for oral antibiotics
Instruct the patient to see his dentist then discharge him
Irrigate the site with saline and refer the patient for dental follow-up

correctAnswer: Irrigate the site with saline and refer the patient for dental follow-up
englishExplanation: Postextraction alveolar osteitis, also known as dry socket, occurs in about 30% of im- pacted third molar (wisdom teeth) extractions. The etiology is a displacement of the clot from the socket that exposes the alveolar bone and results in a lo- cal osteomyelitis. In most cases, all that is needed is irrigation of the socket with chlorhexidine 0.12% oral rinse or warmed normal saline. Patients often need analgesia, either with an NSAID, an opiate, or regional anesthe- sia. If there are signs of infection, antibiotics are warranted, either penicillin VK or clindamycin for penicillin-allergic patients. All patients should be referred back to the dentist who performed the procedure for follow-up. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient's presentation is consistent with dry socket (postextraction alveolar os- teitis). Closing the dry socket with sutures is not the right course of action. It does not treat the underlying osteomyelitis, and it increases the risk of an abscess formation. This patient's presentation is consistent with dry socket (postextraction alveolar os- teitis). Discharging this patient on oral antibiotics alone is not correct treatment, es- pecially since he does not have any signs of local or systemic infection. This patient's presentation is consistent with dry socket (postextraction alveolar os- teitis). Care should be initiated in the emergency department before the patient is re- ferred back to the dentist. If the socket is not irrigated, the risk of worsening infection may increase in the days prior to follow-up.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 5-year-old girl presents after a fall. An examination reveals tenderness but no movement of the upper left central incisor. Minimal blood is noted around the su- perior aspect of the tooth, but no other oral lacerations are noted and the tooth is otherwise intact. What is part of the appropriate management for this injury?

options.text: Dental resin bridging of affected tooth to another stable tooth
Emergent dental consultation in the emergency department
Extraction of the tooth in the emergency department
Soft diet and follow-up with a pediatric dentist in 48 to 72 hours

correctAnswer: Soft diet and follow-up with a pediatric dentist in 48 to 72 hours
englishExplanation: Most pediatric dental injuries are minor and rarely require significant intervention. In this case, there is tenderness but no movement of an intact tooth and some bleeding to the sulcus, which is consistent with a dental concussion. No emergent evaluation is needed, and a soft diet with follow-up is the best approach. The peri- odontal ligament is the soft tissue that maintains the tooth in position, and it can be easily injured with trauma. Thus, it is important for emergency physicians to be fa- miliar with the different traumatic injuries that can occur to the periodontal liga- ment. Concussion refers to injury without increased mobility or displacement of the tooth but with pain to percussion. Subluxation occurs with injury to the periodontal ligament or other supportive tissues, with increased movement of the tooth but with no displacement. Intrusion indicates dentition that is displaced into the bony socket; there can be associated bony injury to the socket. Lateral luxation occurs with dental displacement from the socket in a lateral direction. Extrusion indicates dentition that is partially displaced out of the bony socket. Avulsion occurs with den- tition that is completely displaced out of its socket. When managing pediatric dental trauma, it is also important to determine primary versus secondary teeth. Most chil- dren don't start losing primary teeth until age 6 or 7, then they have a mix of primary and permanent teeth until about age 13. Incorrect Answer Explanations A dental resin bridge is used to anchor a subluxed tooth into position, but its use is reserved for affixing a permanent tooth. Since this child is 5, all of her teeth are primary teeth. Additionally, this tooth is not mobile and does not necessitate a bridge, even if it was a permanent tooth. Emergent dental consultation is not required for this case due to the nature of the in- jury. The tooth is in position without significant luxation and is a primary tooth. Although an emergent consultation is not needed, urgent dental follow-up is advised. Extraction should only be considered in the setting of dental trauma with a primary tooth that is severely luxated but not avulsed. Extraction may be per- formed by a dental specialist if warranted, but this is rarely performed in the emer- gency department. Key Points Pediatric dental concussion warrants dental follow-up but not an emergency consultation. When treating a pediatric patient who has a dental concussion, tell the parents to put the child on a soft diet and follow up with a dentist.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 50-year-old man presents with fever and odynophagia. A physical examination reveals throat swelling, tongue elevation and swelling, and trismus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Ludwig angina is a severe inflammation caused by infection of both sides of the floor of the mouth. It results in massive swelling of the tongue, which can lead to airway obstruction and difficulty swallowing. The cheek can also be swollen and firm because this disease may be an extension of a dental abscess, poor dental care, or recent lower-molar extraction. Classic signs include fever, malaise, and drooling. Physical examination will reveal tender and “woody'' induration in the sub- mandibular space, which results in tongue elevation. Trismus is typically ab- sent initially, but it will be present as the disease progresses to the parapharyngeal re- gions. The patient should be positioned upright; if indicated, fiberoptic intubation should be used to manage the airway, and care should be taken to avoid induc- ing laryngospasm or complete airway obstruction with the airway manipulation. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics should be given to cover polymicro- bial and anaerobic bacteria. A CT scan may confirm the diagnosis in stable patients. All patients should be admitted for intravenous antibiotics, surgical source control, and consultation with ENT. Incorrect Answer Explanations Epiglottitis occurs more often in adults than children because childhood im- munization against Haemophilus influenzae type B is becoming more widespread. Adults with epiglottitis usually present with 2 to 3 days of worsening throat pain, fever, and pain on swallowing. However, the swelling from epiglottitis occurs lower in the airway than with Ludwig angina, making tongue swelling a distinguish- ing factor favoring Ludwig angina. The presentation of exudative pharyngitis includes fever, sore throat, pharyngeal exu- dates, and tender cervical adenopathy. However, the tongue's swelling and elevation in this case differentiates Ludwig angina from pharyngitis. Peritonsillar abscess presents with sore throat, fever, and a “hot potato” voice. Distinguishing features include asymmetry of the tonsillar pillars, uvular deviation, and trismus. Although trismus can be present with peritonsillar abscess and Ludwig angina, peritonsillar abscesses are not commonly associated with tongue swelling or elevation. Trismus is also present late in the course of Ludwig angina.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the best antibiotic choice for an immunocompetent patient with Ludwig angina who has developed anaphylaxis from penicillin use in the past?
englishExplanation: Since this patient has anaphylaxis to penicillins, levofloxacin plus metronidazole is the best combination. Levfloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic with broad coverage against gram-positive bacteria, such as MSSA, as well as gram-negative bacteria, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Levofloxacin, however, has low activity against anaero- bic organisms and needs to be paired with an antibiotic (eg, metronidazole) that can provide such coverage when treating infections such as Ludwig angina. If the patient is also younger than 18 or has high risk for MRSA, then vancomycin or linezolid can also be added. If the patient is not allergic to penicillin, then the first-line treatment would be ampicillin-sulbactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole. Ludwig angina is a polymicrobial infection of the submental, sublingual, and submandibular spaces. Implicated organisms commonly include viridans streptococci and oral anaerobes in immunocompetent patients; however, immuno- compromised patients can also have contributing gram-negative organisms and MRSA. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ampicillin-sulbactam is indicated for the treatment of Ludwig angina in immuno- competent patients without penicillin allergies. While ampicillin-sulfbactam provides coverage against gram-positive organisms and anaerobes as well as gram-negative bacilli such as Escherichia coli and Klebsiella, it cannot be used for patients with previous anaphylactic reactions to penicillin. While the combination of vancomycin and aztreonam provides coverage against gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, it does not provide coverage against anaerobes. Ludwig angina is typically polymicrobial, and coverage must include both oral flora and anaerobic organisms. While the combination of vancomycin and cefepime provides coverage against gram-positive and gram-negative organisms, including Pseudomonas, it does not provide coverage against anaerobes. In addition, cefepime is a fourth-genera- tion cephalosporin. While the cross-reactivity between penicillins and fourth-genera- tion cephalosporins is very low, there are safer options for patients with anaphylactic reactions to penicillin.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 32-year-old man presents with fever, sore throat, and neck pain. His vital signs are BP 107/60, P 130, R 25, and T 38°C (100.4°F); SpO is 94% on room air. On examination, tense edema and erythema overlying the patient's neck and edema to the floor of the mouth are noted. The patient is spitting secretions into a basin. What is the most important next step?

options.text: Obtain a CT scan of the neck

englishExplanation: Ludwig angina is a polymicrobial infection of the submental, sublingual, and sub- mandibular spaces. Infection can progress rapidly and cause airway compro- mise by posterior displacement of the tongue. Late signs of airway compromise in- clude stridor, an inability to manage secretions, and cyanosis; therefore, early de- finitive airway management is key. As these intubations can be difficult, con- sider alternatives to traditional rapid sequence intubation, such as awake fiberoptic intubation. A tracheostomy may be necessary if intubation fails. 2 Incorrect Answer Explanations Antibiotic administration for patients with Ludwig angina is a critical component in care; however, definitive airway management should take precedence be- cause it may take over 1 week for resolution of edema with antibiotic therapy. Additionally, antibiotics should be given intravenously. Although most cases may be managed with close observation and intravenous antibiotics, the patient in this scenario has signs of a compromised airway with an inability to tolerate secretions. Although airway management, including adequate preoxygenation, is critical in pa- tients with Ludwig angina, BiPAP is unlikely to be beneficial. In these patients, airway compromise is likely due to posterior displacement of the tongue, ren- dering BiPAP ineffective. Obtaining a CT scan of the neck can be helpful in situations where the diagnosis of Ludwig angina is equivocal; however, patients can have difficulty breathing when supine. Definitive airway management should take precedence in patients with a clinical diagnosis of Ludwig angina.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 38-year-old man presents with neck pain and difficulty swallowing. He is in res- piratory distress, stridulous, and sitting upright on the edge of the stretcher. He has a muffled voice, trismus, and brawny edema to the neck. What is the safest way to secure this patient's airway?
englishExplanation: Ludwig angina is a polymicrobial infection of the submental, sublingual, and sub- mandibular spaces. Patients with Ludwig angina frequently require emergent definitive airway management due to the risk of rapid progression of the infection, which causes posterior tongue displacement and airway com- promise. Nasotracheal intubation with the use of a flexible fiberoptic laryngoscope while the patient is awake and upright can facilitate visualization and access to an air- way with anatomic limitations such as trismus, including in cases of an- gioedema, epiglottitis, and cervical spine immobility. Awake fiberoptic intu- bation usually requires light sedation and no paralysis. Flexible fiberoptic laryn- goscopy requires proper equipment and training. Emergency physicians should prac- tice this skill prior to use in critically ill patients. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with Ludwig angina may require a surgical airway if attempts at intubation are unsuccessful. At some institutions, it is not uncommon to attempt to secure the airway in the operating room, where unsuccessful intubation can be fol- lowed by a formal surgical tracheostomy. Cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy should not be the first attempt at definitive airway management and should be reserved for when attempts at nasotracheal or endotracheal intubation are unsuccessful. Patients with Ludwig angina typically have trismus; therefore, direct laryn- goscopy via oral endotracheal intubation can be challenging. Direct laryn- goscopy requires supine positioning of the patient as well as sedation and paralytic administration. Patients with Ludwig angina can have airways that are difficult to vi- sualize when supine due to the elevation and posterior displacement of the tongue. Thus, direct laryngoscopy is not the safest way to secure this patient's airway. Video laryngoscopy can aid in visualization of difficult airways. However, patients with Ludwig angina often have trismus, which can limit opening of the mouth for orotracheal intubation. In addition, video laryngoscopy requires full sedation and paralytic administration, which can lead to loss of the patient's airway if intuba- tion is unsuccessful.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 54-year-old man presents with fever, sore throat, and neck pain. His vital signs include BP 120/80, P 110, R 27, and T 39°C (102.2°F). A physical examination is performed (see image). What is the most common etiology of this condition? Credit: Laura Duggan, MD.
englishExplanation: Ludwig angina is a polymicrobial infection of the submental, sublingual, and sub- mandibular spaces that can progress rapidly and lead to death through sudden as- phyxia secondary to loss of the patient's airway. More than two-thirds of cases of Ludwig angina are caused by a periapical abscess of the mandibular mo- lars, which can break through the cortical plate of the mandible and spread into the aforementioned spaces. Other etiologies of Ludwig angina include spread from a peritonsillar abscess and suppurative parotitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ludwig angina is not a complication of otitis media. Complications of otitis me- dia include conductive hearing loss, mastoiditis, and meningitis as well as epidural, subdural, and brain abscesses. Ludwig angina is not a common complication of streptococcal pharyngitis. Streptococcal pharyngitis can result in suppurative and nonsuppurative complica- tions. Suppurative complications include peritonsillar and retropharyngeal ab- scesses, otitis media, sinusitis, necrotizing fasciitis, meningitis or brain ab- scess, and, rarely, jugular vein septic thrombophlebitis. Ludwig angina is not a complication of traumatic intubation. Traumatic intubation can result in dental injury, soft tissue injury, vocal cord and larynx injury, temporomandibular joint dislocation, and cervical spine injury.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 54-year-old man presents with neck pain and swelling that has been worsening over the past day. His vital signs include BP 122/60, P 90, and T 39°C (102.2°F); SpO is 94% on room air. He is able to speak clearly in full sentences and handle his own secretions, but he is sitting upright in the stretcher. His anterior neck is erythematous, tender to palpation, and indurated. The floor of his mouth is raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Ludwig angina is a polymicrobial infection of the submental, sublingual, and sub- mandibular spaces that can progress rapidly and threaten a patient's airway via posterior displacement of the tongue. The infection is typically preceded by an odontogenic abscess that breaks through the cortical plate of the mandible. Definitive management includes intravenous fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergent intubation in patients with a threatened airway. An emergent otorhino- laryngology consultation is necessary for drainage of any infectious fluid collections.
