Incorrect Answer Explanations 2 Patients with epiglottitis may present with neck pain, sore throat, odynophagia, and difficulty swallowing; however, they do not have physical examination findings of anterior neck erythema, induration, and elevation of the floor of the mouth. Epiglottitis is an inflammation of the epiglottis and adjacent structures that can progress to a compromised airway. Physical examination findings may differ be- tween children and adults. Children may be febrile or stridulous, or they may have respiratory distress with a muffled or hoarse voice, pharyngitis, or tenderness of the anterior neck. Adults often have odynophagia, a sore throat, fever, or a muf- fled voice, but they rarely present with stridor (~33%) or hoarseness (20%-40%). Patients with a retropharyngeal abscess often present with fever, a sore throat, and neck pain or stiffness, but they do not usually have induration or elevation of the floor of the mouth. Typically, pediatric patients under age 6 years are the pop- ulation affected by retropharyngeal abscesses. However, they can also be seen as a complication of untreated odontogenic infection that has spread to the retropharyn- geal space. Patients with sialadenitis may present with facial swelling and tenderness as well as purulent drainage from the duct of the infected gland; however, they do not have anterior neck swelling, induration, or elevation of the floor of the mouth. Sialadenitis is the inflammation of a salivary gland and can be acute or chronic. A sialolith (salivary gland stone) can sometimes be seen at the ductal opening of the affected salivary gland.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent, painful, ulcerative lesions in her mouth and on her vulva. She was seen by her ophthalmologist last month for uveitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: The triad of recurrent stomatitis combined with uveitis and genital lesions is highly suggestive of Behçet syndrome, as illustrated in this case. Stomatitis (in- flammation or sores on the inside of the mouth) is the most common manifestation of Behçet syndrome, and stomatitis itself can be caused by multiple other etiologies such as recurrent aphthous ulcerations, HIV infection, herpes infections, autoimmune conditions, and medications. Behçet syndrome may also cause GI, neurologic, joint, or vascular problems. It is believed to be a vasculitis in etiology. Recurrent oral ulcerations must be present to diagnose Behçet syndrome, as they are present in almost 100% of cases. Other manifestations that are present with oral ulcerations, indicating the consideration of Behçet syndrome, include genital lesions (~75% of cases), ocular lesions (uveitis, retinal vasculitis), skin lesions (such as erythema nodosum or pseudofolliculitis), and a positive pathergy test. Oral lesions are often the pre- senting symptom. Treatment options for Behçet syndrome include colchicine, topical symptomatic medications, and topical or systemic glucocorticoids. Incorrect Answer Explanations Methotrexate use, even at standard doses, may cause oral lesions, in- creased liver function tests, thrombocytopenia, and rashes such as toxic epidermal necrolysis. Methotrexate is sometimes used to treat uveitis but does not cause it. If stomatitis occurs with methotrexate use, it can be alleviated with dose reduction and increasing concurrent folic acid dosing, which can be monitored by the patient's rheumatologist. Mouth ulcers are most commonly caused by recurrent aphthous stomati- tis, also known as canker sores. Seen alone orally, they are known as simple aph- thosis; with genital ulcers, they are known as complex, as long as no other criteria for Behçet syndrome is present. In this case, the patient also has uveitis, which war- rants the consideration of Behçet syndrome. Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause oral lesions in up to 50% of pa- tients. These lesions, however, are typically described as painless, not painful as in this case. Other common clinical features of systemic lupus erythematosus include a malar rash, arthralgias, pericarditis, glomerulonephritis, and retinal vasculopathy.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 45-year-old man presents with right submandibular swelling over the past week. He denies trauma and says the pain is worse when he eats. There are no signs of overlying erythema, and he has no other symptoms. The physical examination re- veals a firm submandibular gland with no drainage; attempts to milk the gland do not remove the mass. What is the appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge the patient on oral antibiotics
Instruct him to use analgesics and sialogogues
Obtain a CT scan of the face
Perform incision and drainage of the mass

correctAnswer: Instruct him to use analgesics and sialogogues
englishExplanation: This patient has symptoms consistent with sialolithiasis, which occurs when a sali- vary gland stone gets stuck in the salivary duct. The obstruction most commonly oc- curs in the submandibular gland (80%), followed by the parotid gland. Salivary gland stones are almost always unilateral in presentation and usually consist of calcium carbonate or calcium phosphate. They are most likely to be symptomatic in middle- aged men. Sometimes, the stone can be milked out of the duct, which resolves the symptoms. If not, as long as the patient does not have any signs of an underlying in- fection with the obstruction, the only therapy needed in the emergency department is analgesia and sialogogues (like lemon drops) to help promote passage of the stone. If the stone does not pass, the patient should follow up with an ENT specialist. Incorrect Answer Explanations Without any signs of infection, antibiotics are not indicated. Passage of the stone will resolve the symptoms. Analgesia and sialogogues are the most appropriate emer- gency department therapy. The diagnosis is made based primarily on clinical examination. CT of the face, along with emergent ENT consultation, is needed only if there is suspicion for an abscess. This patient is afebrile and has no other clinical signs of an overlying infection. Analgesia and sialogogues are the most appropriate emergency department therapy. Since there are no signs of an abscess, incision and drainage is not indicated. If a pa- tient with salivary gland stones does have an abscess, ENT consultation is prudent to determine the next treatment steps. Analgesia and sialogogues are the most appropri- ate emergency department therapy. Key Points Sialolithiasis most commonly presents in middle-aged men in the submandibular gland. Assuming no other signs of infection, initial treatment is to promote passage of the obstructing stone using sialogogues. If there are signs of overlying infection, antibiotics and close ENT follow-up are indicated.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 52-year-old woman presents with unilateral facial swelling that has been present for the past week without fever or systemic symptoms. She says she has had a "bad tooth" for about a month but has been unable to see a dentist. She is immunocom- petent, and she has no trismus. What is the next step in treatment?

options.text: Perform local aspiration of the swelling

englishExplanation: This patient has a periodontal infection that has extended into the buccal space without evidence of systemic infection. The initial treatment is oral an- tibiotics. Penicillin VK, amoxicillin/clavulanate, clindamycin, and doxy- cycline may be appropriate antibiotic choices. Chlorhexidine gluconate 0.12% rinse is an alternative, but it is expensive and not always covered by insurance. The underlying etiology of the patient's symptoms is usually dental caries and poor dental hygiene, so a follow-up appointment with a dentist is indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although this patient may eventually require a tooth extraction, this rarely needs to be performed in the emergency department. Most dentists prefer that the patient start a course of antibiotics before extraction. There is rarely a discrete fluid collection in a periodontal infection, so inci- sion and drainage is unlikely to enhance management. If this is suspected, an ultrasound examination can be performed to look for a hypoechoic area. For the same reason that incision and drainage is unlikely to be successful, aspira- tion is unlikely to result in an improved outcome for this patient. Instead, this patient should be started on a course of oral antibiotics and referred to a dentist.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 25-year-old man presents with mouth pain and bleeding gums. He smokes ciga- rettes but does not have any other significant medical history. He is currently homeless and has not had access to good medical or dental care for a long time. In addition to encouraging a proper diet and dental referral, what is an effective treatment? Credit: Courtesy of Robert B. Blankenship, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: This patient has acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (ANUG), also known as trench mouth or Vincent angina. Treatment includes debridement, antibiotic oral rinses (chlorhexidine twice daily for 2 weeks), and systemic antibi- otics. Although penicillin is used for many dental infections, it is not recommended for ANUG. Oral antibiotic recommendations for ANUG include metronidazole, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or clindamycin. Anaerobic bacteria are generally re- sponsible for ANUG. ANUG is a rapidly progressive, severe form of gingivitis. Risk factors include mal- nutrition, smoking, poor oral hygiene, and impaired host immunity. Patients typically present with foul breath, severe mouth pain, bleeding gums, and sloughing of the gingiva. Some patients have fever, lymphadenopathy and malaise. The ulcerations look like they were “punched out” in between the teeth. Most patients present in their 20s. If untreated, the disease can spread rapidly to neighboring tis- sues and bone. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acyclovir is an antiviral used to treat herpes gingivostomatitis. This patient has ANUG, which is treated with debridement, chlorhexidine rinses, and oral antibi- otics. Herpes gingivostomatitis would look different than ANUG. Herpes gingivos- tomatitis is characterized by vesicular lesions, whereas ANUG has interdental lesions with a “punched out” appearance as well as sloughing and bleeding of the gums. Nystatin swish and spit is the treatment for oral thrush, which is a candidal infection which occurs in infants, immunocompromised individuals, and those on in- haled steroids. Nystatin is an antifungal that would be ineffective or ANUG, which is polymicrobial and mostly from anaerobic bacteria. Although penicillin is a common medication used for uncomplicated dental infections and gingivitis, it is not the antibiotic of choice for ANUG. ANUG is usually a polymicrobial infection that requires debridement, oral chlorhexidine rinses, and systemic antibiotics. First-line antibiotics of choice for treatment of ANUG are metronidazole, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or clindamycin.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 50-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of dyspnea, fever, and odynopha- gia. He has difficulty providing a history; his wife says he gets more short of breath when he lies back. On examination, he is sitting upright and has mild stridor. His vital signs include BP 140/95 and P 127; SpO is 97% on room air. Which condi- tion indicates an increased likelihood that he will need airway intervention?
englishExplanation: This patient's symptoms are suggestive of acute epiglottitis. The appropriate next steps are to determine how tenuous the airway is and then identify modifying factors that might indicate an airway more at risk. Several studies have shown that pa- tients who are more likely to be intubated are those who present with stridor, muffled voice, drooling, or a rapid onset of symptoms and those who have a history of diabetes. In an era of widespread childhood vaccination for Haemophilus influenzae type b, epiglottitis is rarely seen in children and is now more of an adult disease, with a mean age at presentation of 46 years. The triad of “the three Ds” (drooling, dysphagia, distress) occurs less frequently than it did in the prevaccination era. Patients with significant disease present with inspira- 2 tory stridor and the classic self-positioning to lean forward. Lateral x-rays of the neck might show the classic thumb sign of an enlarged epiglottis. Patients also have fever, cervical adenopathy, tachycardia, and pain on palpation of the larynx. After manag- ing the airway, intravenous antibiotics covering the predominant causes of Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species (cefuroxime or ceftizoxime) should be started, along with a steroid such as dexamethasone, before admission. Incorrect Answer Explanations A fever is classically associated with epiglottitis, but no specifics about fever (whether high or low) have been found to be related to risk for acute airway obstruction. History of diabetes is associated with higher risk of intubation in epiglottitis. Studies indicate that patients with a more rapid onset of symptoms, some within hours, are at greater risk and more likely to need intubation. Most patients have URI symptoms for a few days before diagnosis, although there are re- ports of patients who have had symptoms for more than a week before developing epiglottitis. History of diabetes is associated with higher risk of intubation in epiglottitis. Patients with epiglottitis do complain of pain with palpation of the neck over the area of the trachea near the cricoid. Although this one symptom has not been found to be predictive of the need for intubation, the amount of swelling seen with laryn- goscopy around the epiglottis (blocking more than 50% of the posterior vocal cords) and swelling extending to the arytenoids are predictive of more airway difficulty. History of diabetes is associated with higher risk of intubation in epiglottitis.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient presents with an abrupt onset of fever, sore throat, agitation, stridor, and drooling. A portable lateral neck x-ray is suspicious for epiglottitis. What is the next best step in management?
englishExplanation: Epiglottitis can present acutely, with rapidly progressive symptoms. It typically presents with fever, sore throat, and drooling. It can progress to sig- nificant airway compromise and obstruction within hours. Signs and symptoms of impending complete airway obstruction are stridor, tripod or sniffing posture, agi- tation, restlessness, or marked respiratory distress (eg, retractions). If these clinical features are present, emergency assistance should be called, with securing the airway (ie, intubation) as the priority. This procedure should ideally be performed by the most experienced operator in a controlled setting (ie, the operating room), with the most advanced airway equipment available. Preparations should be made for an emergency surgical airway. If clinical signs of impending com- plete obstruction are present, direct visualization by laryngoscopy should not be at- tempted unless attempting to secure the airway, and imaging should be deferred. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), Streptococcus pneumoniae, group A Streptococcus, and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common organ- isms that can cause epiglottitis. With the development of the vaccination for Hib, epiglottitis is now more commonly seen in adults than in children. Antibiotic cover- age should include an anti-staphylococcal agent and a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin. Steroids may be given to mitigate airway edema. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT imaging can exacerbate symptoms of epiglottitis. Because the patient must lie supine, it may precipitate respiratory distress and airway obstruction. The diagnosis of epiglottitis is typically confirmed by lateral x-rays or by the gold stan- dard, direct laryngoscopy. Lateral neck x-rays can show an enlarged epiglottis (usu- ally >8 mm in adults), or thickened aryepiglottic folds. If there are clinical signs of impending airway obstruction, imaging should be deferred. Diagnostic laryngoscopy is the gold standard for diagnosing epiglottitis. However, in patients with impending respiratory obstruction, the focus should be on securing a definitive airway. Fiberoptic intubation is often used for definitive airway management; however, operators should use intubation equipment that they are comfortable with, and which gives them the best chance at a successful first-pass intubation. Supraglottic airways, such as laryngeal mask airways, should never be placed in patients with epiglottitis. These devices are ineffective because the air- way obstruction is below the level of the supraglottic airway. Fiberoptic intubation is preferred, if available. Preparations should be made for a surgical airway.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: An adult patient presents with a slowly progressive sore throat and a fever over the course of 1 week. He has no evidence of stridor or severe respiratory distress. Direct visualization of the epiglottis is concerning for infectious epiglottitis with airway narrowing of less than 50%. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Observe for 4 hours and discharge if stable
Transfer to the operating room for emergent airway management

englishExplanation: Adults with epiglottitis with no signs of severe respiratory distress and with less than 50% supraglottic narrowing on laryngoscopy can be man- aged without airway intervention. However, these patients should be closely monitored in the ICU. Rapid worsening and airway compromise can occur at any point in the course of epiglottitis, regardless of the initial severity of the illness. Monitoring should include a repeat laryngoscopy at 6 or 12 hours to confirm improvement. If the clinical features of impending airway obstruction are present, emergency assistance should be called and definitive airway manage- ment should be the top priority. This procedure should ideally be performed by the most experienced operator in a controlled setting (ie, the operating room) with the most advanced airway equipment available. Preparations should be made for an emergency surgical airway. If clinical signs of impending complete ob- struction are present, direct visualization by laryngoscopy should not be attempted, unless attempting to secure the airway, and imaging should be deferred. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), Streptococcus pneumoniae, group A Streptococcus, and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common or- ganisms that can cause epiglottitis. With the development of the vaccination for Hib, epiglottitis is now more commonly seen in adults than in children. Antibiotic coverage should include an anti-staphylococcal agent and a third- or fourth-genera- tion cephalosporin. Steroids may be given to mitigate airway edema. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with confirmed epiglottitis need to be monitored closely for worsening airway compromise. Monitoring in the emergency department or in the telemetry unit is problematic because airway compromise may occur with little warning. Admission to the ICU is preferred, and experienced airway specialists should be available at all times. Studies suggest that 3% to 8% of patients who are ini- tially managed without artificial airway placement need airway intervention during their hospital course. Emergency department observation units may be appropriate in certain situations for monitoring patients with epiglottitis if airway specialists are present and close moni- toring can occur. However, patients need to be monitored for a minimum of 6 to 12 hours to ensure improvement. A repeat laryngoscopy should also be performed at this interval to document objective improvement and determine the disposition. Patients with less than 50% supraglottic narrowing on laryngoscopy and an absence of severe respiratory distress can be managed without imme- diate airway intervention. However, if respiratory distress occurs, airway inter- vention is best managed in the controlled setting of the operating room.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which pharmacologic option is the most appropriate antimicrobial coverage for acute infectious epiglottitis in an immunocompromised patient?
englishExplanation: Epiglottitis is classically caused by bacterial pathogens. Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) remains an important bacterial cause of infectious epiglottitis, despite a rapid decline in cases among vaccinated children. Other important bacteria include Staphylococcus aureus (including methicillin-resistant strains), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus pyogenes, and group A Streptococcus. In the immuno- compromised patient, it is important to provide coverage with broad-spectrum an- tibiotics tailored to cover Pseudomonas, and antifungals for Candida spp. should be considered as well. It is suggested that all immunocompromised patients with in- fectious epiglottitis receive a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin and an anti-staphylococcal agent (eg, vancomycin). Antibiotic treatment for infectious epiglottitis is typically continued for 7 to 10 days but can be extended in immunocompromised patients. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ampicillin-sulbactam is a beta-lactam antibiotic. It covers both gram-negative and gram-positive organisms, but does not cover MRSA and should not be the sole antibiotic of choice in immunocompromised patients with epiglottitis. The combination of cefazolin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is typi- cally used to treat cellulitis and soft tissue infections, not epiglottitis. Cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin, so it should not be used in immuno- compromised patients with epiglottitis. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is a folate synthesis inhibitor that has antimicrobial activity against MRSA. Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic that is typically used in skin and soft tissue infections. It provides antimicrobial coverage against S. aureus and MRSA. However, it should not be used as the sole antibiotic treatment in immunocompro- mised patients with epiglottitis.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Which procedure is contraindicated when managing a critical airway in a patient with epiglottitis?
englishExplanation: Supraglottic airways, such as laryngeal mask airways, are ineffective in epiglottitis because the airway obstruction is below the level of the supra- glottic airway. These devices should never be placed in patients with epiglottitis. Epiglottitis is characterized by swelling of the epiglottis and the supraglottic struc- tures. Immediate airway management is the mainstay of treatment in patients with severe respiratory distress or impending airway compromise. The airway should be managed with BVM ventilation prior to attempting intubation. Fiberoptic intubation is preferred, if available. If intubation fails, surgical or needle cricothyrotomy should be performed immediately. Incorrect Answer Explanations BVM is an important airway management adjunct in epiglottitis. In most patients, oxygenation can be maintained by BVM. If unable to oxygenate with BVM, intubation should be attempted by the most experienced operator with preparation for a surgical airway, if needed. In children younger than 12 years, needle cricothyrotomy is preferred if endotracheal intubation is unsuccessful. Needle cricothyrotomy is preferred over surgical cricothyrotomy in younger patients because it causes less damage to the larynx and surrounding structures. If attempts at endotracheal intubation fail, surgical cricothyrotomy should be performed immediately. In a controlled setting, preferably in an op- erating room, patients can be prepped for a surgical airway while endotracheal intu- bation or fiberoptic intubation is attempted. Surgical cricothyrotomy should not be performed in patients younger than 12 years.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: In adults with epiglottitis, which condition is associated with a higher incidence of requiring airway intervention?
englishExplanation: Epiglottitis is known to occur more frequently in patients with diabetes mellitus, substance use disorder, end-stage renal disease, and immune deficiency. Diabetes mellitus is a known risk factor for more severe cases of epiglottitis, and diabetic patients require airway intervention more frequently. Other factors associated with more severe presentations of epiglottitis include obesity, head and neck cancers, the presence of an epiglottic cyst or abscess, and pneumonia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Asthma is not known to put a patient at risk of developing severe epiglot- titis. However, in these patients, epiglottitis can present with atypical symptoms, such as dyspnea, cough, or tachypnea. Cirrhosis is not known to be a risk factor for more severe presentations of epiglottitis. Substance use disorders are associated with higher rates of epiglotti- tis, but not with a higher incidence of airway intervention. In studied cohorts of patients presenting with acute epiglottitis, COPD was not as- sociated with a more severe disease requiring airway intervention. However, patients with COPD may present with dyspnea and cough, which can make the clinical diagnosis of epiglottitis more difficult.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 6-year-old boy is brought in with a 3-day history of URI symptoms, including congestion, a fever that had been low grade, and a nonproductive cough. The mother says his temperature was 40.5°C (104.9°F) today. On examination, the boy is lethargic but arousable, and stridor is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: The most likely diagnosis in this case is bacterial tracheitis, a secondary bacterial infection following a viral URI; high fever and a toxic appear- ance are commonly associated with the airway symptoms. Other names for this disease process are membranous laryngotracheobronchitis, pseudomembranous croup, and bacterial croup. It is relatively uncommon (4-8/1,000,000 children), and the average patient age is between 5 and 8 years. The most common pathogen in bac- terial tracheitis is Staphylococcus aureus, followed by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus pyogenes, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. If bacterial tracheitis is suspected, emergent ENT consultation is warranted because mortality rates can be as high as 20%. Bronchoscopy is the diagnostic method of choice, and intubation under controlled circumstances might be needed to control a tenuous airway. Given the narrowing of the airway, a smaller-than-anticipated endotracheal tube might be needed. Given the copious drainage from the larynx, intubation might require advanced airway techniques and tried-and-true classics like looking for air bubbles. Emergency department man- agement also includes initiation of antibiotic therapy. The initial antibiotic choice is ampicillin-sulbactam combined with clindamycin and a third-generation cephalosporin. Vancomycin should be added if MRSA is a concern. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bronchiolitis is a lower respiratory tract infection that is usually caused by RSV and is most commonly seen in children younger than 2 years. Children with bronchiolitis do not usually present with stridor or lethargy, but they do tend to have more nasal con- gestion, cough, and wheezing. Bacterial tracheitis is suggested by the high fever and a toxic appearance with associated airway symptoms. Pneumonia does not tend to present with stridor. If in doubt, a chest x-ray can differ- entiate between the two since air-space disease on radiography and the absence of stridor suggest pneumonia. Bacterial tracheitis is suggested by the high fever and a toxic appearance with associated airway symptoms. Viral laryngotracheobronchitis, or croup, tends to present in slightly younger patients (6 months to 3 years), whereas bacterial tracheitis can present across a broader age range. Patients with croup also tend to have a less toxic appearance than with bacte- rial tracheitis. A barky or brassy cough is the classic sign of croup. Bacterial tra- cheitis is suggested by the high fever and a toxic appearance with associ- ated airway symptoms.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 73-year-old man is transferred from a skilled nursing facility because he sud- denly began having difficulty breathing. He underwent tracheostomy and gastric tube placement after a stroke 8 months ago. His vital signs are BP 165/90, P 110, R 30, and T 37.4°C (99.3°F); SpO is 85% on room air. Pulmonary auscultation re- veals decreased breath sounds and bilateral wheezing. What is the first step in this patient's treatment?
englishExplanation: Studies have estimated that 30% of emergency department visits for res- piratory distress associated with a tracheostomy are caused by obstruc- tion of the cannula. Obstruction of a tracheostomy tube secondary to a mucus plug, aspiration, blood, or granulation tissue can present as tachypnea, retractions, nasal flaring, hypoxia, cyanosis, reduced oxygen saturation, or increased secretions. Immediate treatment is best performed with preoxygenation, removal of the inner cannula, and suctioning of the stoma. The thick mucus tracheal secretions can cause a ball-valve mechanism, resulting in air trapping and hypoxia. If symptoms do not 2 resolve after two or three attempts at suctioning, then removal of the en- tire cannula might be required, with repeat suctioning to clear the mucus plug. A red rubber catheter may be used as a guide to exchange the tracheostomy tube. If the appropriately sized tracheostomy tube is not available for reinsertion, then an endotracheal tube can be a temporary substitution. In older children and adults, a double-cannula tracheostomy tube with an inflatable cuff is used to prevent movement of the tube or surrounding air leak. The inner tube can be removed for cleaning and pulmonary toilet. Common indications for tracheostomy tube place- ment include prolonged mechanical ventilation, anatomical or traumatic obstruction of the upper airway, and difficulty controlling airway secretions. Aside from underly- ing secretory disorders or myopathy, the tracheostomy procedure causes a weakness in the trachea that directly dampens the cough, so patients require pulmonary ther- apy, chest percussion, and cough assist to routinely clear secretions. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although chest percussion is often indicated for routine secretion clearance, it is un- likely to be helpful in a patient with obstruction of the tracheostomy secondary to mucus plugging, which requires direct suctioning. The patient's acute symptoms indi- cate a likely mucus plug. Patients with a tracheostomy tube can be prone to pulmonary infections or infection at the stoma; however, this patient is afebrile, making these etiologies less likely. When treating infection of a tracheostomy stoma it is important to use broad-spec- trum antibiotics to include coverage for the most common infections, such as Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas, and Candida. This patient, however, has an obstruction of the tracheostomy secondary to mucus plugging, which requires direct suctioning. Patients with a tracheostomy tube in place may present with exacerbation of an un- derlying cardiopulmonary disease process. However, these patients typically have a progressive course, whereas this patient had acute onset of symptoms; this is consis- tent with an obstruction of the tracheostomy secondary to mucus plugging, which re- quires direct suctioning.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 63-year-old woman presents with bleeding from a tracheostomy site. She under- went the procedure 10 days ago as part of her treatment for esophageal cancer. She is acutely short of breath, appears in extremis, and has significant hemoptysis. What is the most likely source of the bleeding?
englishExplanation: Erosion into the tracheoinnominate artery can cause life-threatening hemor- rhage. This is a rare complication after tracheostomy, but when it does occur, it is most common 1 to 3 weeks after the procedure. Immediate treatment should in- clude direct pressure and hyperinflation of the tracheostomy tube cuff with gentle tube traction, which provides direct internal pressure to the bleeding artery. An urgent consultation from ENT or thoracic surgery is necessary to ar- range definitive treatment. If bleeding is not controlled with the actions described, then an endotracheal tube should be placed below the bleeding innominate artery with the assistance of a flexi- ble nasopharyngoscope or bronchoscopy and advanced past the tracheostomy tube while withdrawing the tracheostomy tube. An endotracheal tube placed in this man- ner can be used to ventilate the patient, reduce aspiration of blood, and allow the physician to apply internal digital pressure to the artery while the patient is trans- ferred to the operating room for arterial repair by an ENT or thoracic surgeon. Non– life-threatening bleeding after a tracheostomy can be treated by removing the tube and applying silver nitrate or pressure with moist gauze. Incorrect Answer Explanations Portal hypertension resulting in dilation of the esophageal veins can cause life-threatening bleeding if they rupture, but it is not associated with a re- cent tracheostomy tube placement. Bleeding secondary to esophageal varices can be fatal and requires aggressive airway management, emergent GI consultation, and temporizing measures that might include placement of Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota tubes for balloon tamponade. This patient's malignancy does increase her risk for a pulmonary embolism, and the hypoxia is a worrisome sign. However, her recent tracheostomy increases her risk for tracheoinnominate artery fistula formation, which can present with hemoptysis (a seemingly minor sentinel bleed) or severe hemorrhage. A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is a communication between the tra- chea and esophagus that can be the result of a congenital malformation. It also can be an acquired condition, such as in the case of a tracheostomy-associated TEF. Secondary to a tracheostomy tube placement, TEF can be caused by erosion from an overinflated cuff or direct trauma from the procedure itself. It is best diag- nosed with bronchoscopy.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 57-year-old man is transferred from a skilled nursing facility because his tra- cheostomy tube cuff is not inflating. The tracheostomy was done 5 days ago for re- peated pneumonia and is still in place. The patient has no active bleeding and is not in distress. What is the most likely complication of replacing the tube?
englishExplanation: During the first 7 to 10 days after placing a tracheostomy tube, the open- ing is not considered mature or well developed. As a result, if the tube is ma- nipulated or a replacement is attempted, the tube could create a false passage in the neck's soft tissues. The likelihood of changing a tracheostomy tube safely depends on the length of time postsurgery and on the anatomy of the patient. Obese patients or those with neck masses are at a higher risk of tract collapse. If the tube must be replaced or adjusted during the first 7 to 10 days after the initial proce- dure, an otolaryngologist (ENT) or surgeon should perform the procedure. If the time since the procedure is greater than this time window, then it is thought that the tract has matured and the tube can be safely manipulated. Other complications after tracheostomy that occur early (<7 days) in- clude bleeding, infection, obstruction (with secretions or blood), or tube dislodgement. Late complications (>7-10 days) include tracheal stenosis, tracheo- malacia, tracheal arterial fistula, aspiration pneumonia, and tracheoesophageal fistulas. Incorrect Answer Explanations Aspiration pneumonia is a known complication of patients who have a tra- cheostomy. However, this complication is considered to be a late complication, generally more than 7 to 10 days after the procedure. Studies show that aspiration risk does not significantly change if the stoma is occluded with a finger or cap or if the trach tube balloon is inflated or deflated. Aspiration should be treated with antibi- otics if there is evidence of bacterial infection. Although the site is considered fresh, only minimal bleeding from changing the tube is expected. However, if there is granulation tissue present or there is erosion through thyroid vessels, tracheal wall, or the innominate artery, more significant bleeding may result. Tracheoarterial fistulas are a devastating complication of tra- cheostomy placement, but it is fortunately a rare complication. It most commonly occurs around 3 to 4 weeks postprocedure. This patient's tracheostomy tube is currently in place, so closure of the stoma is unlikely to occur during a tube exchange in the emergency department. Stoma closure is more likely to occur when the tube has been removed for several hours. Since this tracheostomy site is fresh, it is not considered mature and should be replaced by an ENT. If stoma closure has occurred in a mature tract, dilation may be completed by using pediatric-sized tubes and gradually increasing the size. The tube is directed downward (caudad) when replacing it. An obturator may also be placed in the tracheostomy tube, making the tube solid and less likely to be directed the wrong way.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: What is the most common early complication after tracheostomy?
englishExplanation: Tracheostomy complications are divided into early (less than 7 days) and late complications (more than 7 days) after the procedure. Approximately 90% of catastrophic complications occur within the first 7 days after placement. Hemorrhage is the most common early complica- tion and occurs in approximately 5% of tracheostomies. Bleeding can range from mild to life-threatening. Most bleeding complications within the first 48 hours after tracheostomy are directly related to the operation, usually from injury to superficial veins. After 48 hours, bleeding around the tracheostomy site or within the stoma needs to be investigated for tracheoarterial fistula. Tracheoinnominate artery fistula is the most emergent of bleeding complications and occurs in 0.7% of tra- cheostomies but has a mortality of 90%. Roughly 50% of these complications have a sentinel bleed, and most will occur within 3 weeks after the initial procedure. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pneumothorax and subcutaneous emphysema are early complications of tracheostomy tube placement. These occur in approximately 2% of procedures and are most commonly due to a posterior wall perforation during the procedure or an injury to the soft tissue tract anterior to the trachea from positive pressure ventila- tion. These complications are usually self-limiting and are treated conservatively. Tracheal stenosis is a late complication of tracheostomy and most com- monly presents 2 months after decannulation. It is caused by granulation tissue and fibrosis of the trachea, and patients are typically asymptomatic until the diameter of the trachea decreases by 50%. Tracheal stenosis is an important complication for emergency practitioners because it can cause difficulty for endotracheal intubation. Tracheoesophageal fistula is a rare, late complication of tracheostomy. It is usually associated with prolonged endotracheal intubation and is more commonly seen in patients with concomitant nasogastric tubes in place. Treatment usually re- quires surgical correction.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: Replacing a dislodged tracheostomy tube within the first week after cannulation carries the greatest risk of what complication?
englishExplanation: Dislodgement of a tracheostomy tube within the first week after place- ment is a medical emergency. The stoma is still considered immature within 1 week after cannulation, and manipulation carries the risk of creating a false lu- men. Replacement of a dislodged tracheostomy tube within the first week after can- nulation should be performed under direct visualization with fiber optics. Replacement should not be delayed, as the stoma can narrow within hours. If endo- scopic placement is unavailable, endotracheal intubation may be indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hemorrhage is a significant complication after tracheostomy placement. Even minor bleeding can indicate a sentinel bleed, and tracheoinnominate artery fis- tula needs to be ruled out. However, this is not a significant risk after early dislodge- ment of a tracheostomy tube. Obstruction is a common early and late complication with tracheostomy. It is com- monly caused by increased mucus production, granulation tissue, dried secretions, or blood. However, the greatest risk of replacing a dislodged tracheostomy tube with an immature stoma remains the creation of a false lumen. Pneumothorax is a complication after initial tracheostomy placement that occurs in approximately 2% of procedures. When a tracheostomy tube with an immature stoma is dislodged, the greatest risk of replacement is creating a false lumen, so the procedure should be performed with fiber optics.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient with a history of tracheostomy 3 weeks ago presents with acute-onset massive hemorrhage from the tracheostomy site. Which artery is most commonly involved?
englishExplanation: Tracheoarterial fistula (TAF) is a life-threatening complication of tra- cheostomy. The most common form is a tracheoinnominate artery fistula (TIAF). It is caused by erosion of the trachea's anterior wall by the tip of the tra- cheostomy tube cuff, resulting in a communicating fistula where the innominate artery passes under the sternum. TIAF commonly presents with acute massive hemorrhage and hemoptysis, although approximately 50% are known to have smaller sentinel bleeding episodes. TIAF most commonly occurs about 3 weeks af- ter cannulation and has a mortality rate of approximately 90%. It is important for emergency physicians to understand the innominate artery implication in tra- cheostomies in order to manage this life-threatening complication. Incorrect Answer Explanations The common carotid artery is associated with tracheoarterial fistulas. However, it is much less commonly implicated than the innominate artery. The inferior thyroid artery has been implicated in tracheoarterial fistulas but at a sig- nificantly lower rate than the innominate artery. The innominate artery remains the most common cause of this life-threatening complication. Injury to the inferior thyroid vein can be a cause of bleeding after tracheostomy. However, this is usually associated with trauma directly from the procedure, presents within 48 hours after cannulation, and is rarely life-threatening or a cause of massive hemorrhage. Key Points Tracheoarterial fistula is a life-threatening complication of tracheostomy, most com- monly involving the innominate artery. Tracheoinnominate artery fistulas are caused by erosion from the tip of the tra- cheostomy tube cuff into the anterior wall of the trachea, which results in a communi- cating fistula where the innominate artery passes under the sternum. Tracheoinnominate artery fistulas usually present with acute-onset massive hemor- rhage and hemoptysis, most commonly occuring about 3 weeks after cannulation, and have a mortality rate of approximately 90%.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A patient presents with massive hemorrhage from a tracheostomy, which is con- cerning for tracheoinnominate fistula. What is the best initial step in management?

options.text: Application of silver nitrate to stoma
Oral intubation with cuffed endotracheal tube

englishExplanation: Tracheoinnominate artery fistulas are life-threatening complications of tracheostomy. They can occur at any point after tracheostomy and are caused by erosion of the anterior trachea, causing a fistula with the innominate artery under the sternum. The initial approach to treatment includes hyperinflation of the tracheostomy tube cuff in order to tamponade bleeding while preparing for definitive treatment in the operating room. If this is unsuccessful, endo- tracheal intubation can be performed with inflation of the cuff distal to the tra- cheostomy site. Direct compression of the innominate artery can also be performed: insert a finger into the stoma positioned distally while apply- ing anterior pressure against the sternum to directly compress and tam- ponade the innominate artery. If this maneuver is performed, the airway should be maintained with endotracheal intubation or BVM ventilation while the patient is transported to the operating room for definitive intervention. Incorrect Answer Explanations Silver nitrate can be applied to the stoma for postprocedure bleeding, usually within the first 48 hours after the tracheostomy procedure. However, in the case of a tra- cheoinnominate artery fistula, specific maneuvers need to be performed to di- rectly compress and tamponade the innominate artery. Oral intubation can be performed in the case of a tracheoinnominate artery fistula, especially if respiratory compromise is present, but the initial maneuver should include hyperinflation of the cuffed tracheostomy tube to tamponade bleeding as quickly as possible. If endotracheal intubation is performed, the endo- tracheal tube balloon should be hyperinflated and passed distal to the stoma. Removal of the tracheostomy tube may be indicated if the tube is uncuffed, but re- moval should not be the first step in management with a cuffed tube. If a cuffed tube is present, hyperinflation of the existing tracheostomy tube should be performed. Key Points The initial approach to treating a tracheoinnominate artery fistula includes hyperin- flation of the tracheostomy tube cuff in order to tamponade bleeding while preparing for definitive surgical treatment in the operating room. Secondary maneuvers to treat a tracheoinnominate artery fistula can include endo- tracheal intubation, with inflation of the cuff distal to the tracheostomy site, or direct compression of the innominate artery by inserting a finger into the stoma and apply- ing anterior pressure against the sternum.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 65-year-old woman with a history of tracheostomy 1 year ago presents with in- creased mucus production, dyspnea, and shortness of breath. She presents in res- piratory distress, and a suction catheter cannot pass through her uncuffed, single cannula tracheostomy tube. What is the next best step in management?
englishExplanation: Tracheal tube obstruction can be a life-threatening emergency. It can happen as a late or early complication with tracheostomy and is often caused by se- cretions, mucus, blood, or formation of granulation tissue. There is a step- wise approach to managing an obstruction, which includes removing the inner cannula in a double cannula tube, suctioning, and deflating the cuff. However, if a suction catheter is unable to be passed, a complete obstruction is present. In these cases, especially in uncuffed and single cannula tubes, the tra- cheostomy should be removed to attempt to relieve the obstruction. If a suc- tion catheter can be passed through the entire tube, then a complete ob- struction is not present, and positive pressure ventilation can be used. Incorrect Answer Explanations BVM ventilation can be used in patients with tracheostomy and respira- tory distress who do not have a complete obstruction present. However, if a suction catheter cannot be passed through the cannula, the next best step in manage- ment is to remove the tracheostomy tube to relieve the obstruction. A rigid instrument such as a tracheal tube inducer (commonly called a bougie) is not recommended to evaluate for or relieve obstructions in patients with tracheostomy tubes. These instruments carry the risk of creating false passages and are unable to remove secretions. Oral endotracheal intubation is rarely indicated in cases of tracheostomy obstruction. The first step in managing a patient with a completely occluded tube and mature stoma should be removal of the tracheostomy tube. If removal does not im- prove oxygenation or ventilation, endotracheal intubation may need to be performed, ensuring that the endotracheal tube is advanced beyond the stoma. In cases of a ma- ture stoma, intubation through the stoma can be attempted as well.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 26-month-old boy presents because he has a high fever and neck pain when he moves his head. There is no history of cough or respiratory concerns, and he is awake and alert with mild emotional distress. His vital signs include BP 82/64, P 132, R 36, and T 39°C (102.2°F). An examination reveals tenderness of the right- sided anterior cervical lymph nodes and decreased range of motion of his neck. The HEENT examination is notable for erythema of the posterior pharynx with mild rhinorrhea bilaterally. An x-ray is obtained and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Christopher Amato, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: The history combined with the inspiratory lateral x-ray shown reveals a retropharyn- geal abscess (RPA) with swelling of the retropharyngeal tissue, classically showing more than 7 mm at C2, which is concerning for an RPA. RPA is an infection of the paramedian lymph tissue that usually occurs in children younger than 4. The paramedian lymph tissue atrophies as children develop, but it is still present at this age; this is why RPA is less likely in an older child. Signs and symptoms of RPA often include fever and tender cervical lym- phadenopathy, usually unilateral. Sore throat and neck pain can also be present; a muffled voice, drooling, and stridor are more ominous signs and in- dicate increased edema within the airway. Most references recommend CT scanning for making a definitive diagnosis and determining whether the child needs surgery if there is an abscess or if treatment with intravenous antibiotics is appropriate. Incorrect Answer Explanations Croup is a viral illness (parainfluenza 1 most commonly, also RSV, adenovirus, in- fluenza A) that affects the supraglottic airway and typically occurs in children 6 months to 3 years old. Symptoms include an upper respiratory illness; fever; hoarse voice; and the classic barking, seal-like cough, which makes it less likely in this case. Stridor is an indication of airway edema, so it is imperative to en- sure that the child has an adequate airway. Epiglottitis, although markedly less common with the advent of the Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine, affects patients in a wide age range, from newborn to adult. The average age among pediatric patients ranges from 2 to 7 years. Until de- velopment of the Hib vaccine, H. influenzae type b was the most likely causative or- ganism, and it can still cause epiglottitis even in those who are fully immunized. There is currently no predominant causative organism, so the infection can be due to Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and beta-hemolytic streptococci (groups A and C). Epiglottitis typically presents acutely (within 12-24 hours of symp- tom onset) with several hours of fever and a toxic appearance. There is a history of progressive sore throat, drooling, and dysphagia; severe stridor is usually absent, but the patient might be positioned in the tripod or "sniffing" position, so caution should be used when trying to examine the pharynx. Epiglottitis is usually a clinical diagnosis; however, an elevated WBC count with a bandemia can be present, and 70% to 90% of blood cultures are positive. Peritonsillar abscess develops in older children, adolescents, and adults. It is often due to extension of a primary tonsillar infection, typically group A streptococci, but it can be polymicrobial. This can cause the classic findings of an asymmetric pharynx with the affected tonsil deviated medially due to the infection. Although a child might complain of neck pain, there is usually no limitation of move- ment with peritonsillar abscess, which makes this diagnosis less likely in this case. Key Points Retropharyngeal abscesses are typical in patients younger than 4 years, and periton- sillar abscesses are more likely in older pediatric patients and adults. Presentation of retropharyngeal abscess includes fever, tender lymph nodes unilater- ally, and sometimes torticollis. Be careful when evaluating the pharynx in a patient who may have upper airway edema, indicated by drooling, toxic appearance, tripod or sniffing position, muffled voice.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: An ill-appearing 3-year-old girl presents with a high fever and meningismus. Head CT and lumbar puncture are normal. She begins drooling and states that she can- not find a comfortable position for her neck. Which course of action is most likely to yield the correct diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Although ill appearance, fever, and meningismus are most commonly associated with meningitis, alternative etiologies must be considered when that diagnosis is ruled out by lumbar puncture. One condition that also presents with this triad is a retropha- ryngeal abscess, which is best identified with a CT scan of the neck because it has a near 100% sensitivity for these abscesses. Children with retropharyngeal abscesses are almost always younger than 6 years and often present as ill ap- pearing and febrile. Because of the location of the abscess, they often have meningismus, but they can also present with drooling, stridor, or a muffled voice. Children with small retropharyngeal abscesses can be managed with admis- sion for intravenous antibiotics, but larger or more complicated cases require surgical drainage. Incorrect Answer Explanations A bronchoscopy is only indicated if meningismus is caused by an aspi- rated foreign body, which does not appear to be the case in this patient. Thus, a bronchoscopy would be nondiagnostic of the underlying condition. Intravenous diazepam can be helpful in managing straightforward cases of torticollis, which is typically diagnosed with history and physical examination. Although this patient has neck pain, she is also ill appearing, drooling, and febrile, which is not indicative of torticollis. Administering diazepam is nondiagnostic and would not determine the etiology of this patient's presentation. With meningitis eliminated as a likely diagnosis after a normal lumbar puncture re- sult, the next likely etiology is a retropharyngeal abscess, given this patient's ill ap- pearance, fever, neck pain, and drooling. Unfortunately, plain x-rays of the neck lack sensitivity in identifying retropharyngeal abscesses. The patient's age and neck position at the time of the x-rays can markedly alter the interpretation of these films, making them unreliable.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 10-year-old boy presents with bleeding from the mouth 5 days post-tonsillec- tomy. On examination, there is a small amount of oozing blood from a distinct area on the right post-tonsillectomy site. After a period of observation, the bleed- ing persists. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Figure of 8 suture to the bleeding tissue

englishExplanation: Clinically significant post-tonsillectomy bleeding is estimated to occur in less than 3% of cases, and it typically presents on postoperative days 5 to 10. Although it is rela- tively uncommon, this complication can be life-threatening, particularly in the setting of severe, brisk hemorrhage. In the majority of cases, post-ton- sillectomy bleeding is minor and can be controlled with topical interventions, in- cluding cauterization with silver nitrate, ideally in conjunction with local lidocaine with epinephrine injection. Direct pressure with gauze packing can be used in the setting of significant brisk hemorrhage not controlled by other means. Nebulized epinephrine or tranexamic acid (TXA) can be used in more serious cases to temporize the hemorrhage, particularly if an airway intervention is antici- pated; severe bleeding can lead to airway compromise, and emergent intubation may be required. Intravenous TXA should be administered in severe cases of hemorrhage. ENT should be consulted for all patients with post-tonsillectomy hemor- rhage, even if it is minor. These patients are at increased risk of bleeding progres- sion. Admission for observation is recommended for these patients to ensure the bleeding is controlled. The bleeding tissue is friable and often has an overlying es- char. This can be prone to sudden significant hemorrhage and can make bleeding control difficult. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient has minor oozing of blood from the post-tonsillectomy bleeding that is persistent. It should be managed to try to control the bleeding. Based on his current state, endotracheal intubation is unwarranted. It is likely this bleeding can be controlled with topical medications. Figure of 8 suture should not be employed in this case. The tissue post-tonsillec- tomy is particularly friable. Sutures may make the bleeding worse if it causes tearing through the tissue and disruption of clot. Intravenous administration of TXA is recommended in severe cases of hemor- rhage. It is unnecessary based on the relatively minor amount of bleeding this pa- tient is experiencing. Nebulized TXA can be used as an adjunct in post-tonsillec- tomy bleeding.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 32-year-old man presents with a sore throat, muffled voice, and fever. He was diagnosed 1 week ago with streptococcal pharyngitis, but he did not fill the antibi- otics he was prescribed. Examination of the posterior oropharynx shows erythe- matous and enlarged tonsils with exudates and a right-sided fullness with uvular deviation to the left. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with a peritonsillar ab- scess (PTA). PTA typically presents with significant sore throat, fever, muf- fling of the voice, pain, increased difficulty swallowing, and peritonsillar fullness on examination, often with uvular deviation to the contralateral side. Patients may also have drooling and difficulty breathing depending on the ab- scess size. PTAs are often caused by mixed pathogens, with Group A Streptococcus being the most common organism. PTA is often considered a complication of un- treated streptococcal pharyngitis, although it can also develop even if treatment is initiated appropriately. Most often, diagnosis of PTA is clinical. Examination findings are particularly helpful, including peritonsillar region fullness with uvular deviation. Imaging is not usually required. Treatment of PTA involves draining the ab- scess and administration of antibiotics. This can be done in the emer- gency department, and emergency physicians should be comfortable per- forming this procedure. Drainage of the abscess is typically done using an 18G needle on a syringe into the ab- scess after topical anesthesia and drawing back. A guard should be used to cover the needle so that no more than 1 cm is exposed. This will help prevent inadvertent insertion of the needle into the carotid artery. There is also risk of bleeding and aspiration with this procedure. A scalpel can also be used to open the abscess with a guard in place. However, this is less often practiced by emergency physicians due to increased risk and less familiarity and is more likely to be employed by ENT. If the procedure cannot be done safely at the bedside (ie, uncooperative pediatric pa- tient needing sedation or impending airway compromise), ENT should be involved for potential operative management. Medication treatment of a PTA includes antibiotics active against Group A Streptococcus, such as amoxicillin- clavulanate or clindamycin. Steroids, such as a single dose of dexametha- sone, should be given, as they seem to improve symptoms in the setting of a PTA. Incorrect Answer Explanations Mononucleosis can often be confused with streptococcal pharyngitis. The posterior oropharynx examination will be similar. However, the findings on examination suggest an abscess has formed and this is inconsistent with typical mononucleosis. There can be secondary bacterial superinfection leading to devel- opment of a PTA, although this is not as common in mononucleosis as it is in strepto- coccal pharyngitis. Retropharyngeal abscess (RPA) should be considered in patients with fever, neck pain, and difficulty swallowing with voice changes. These symptoms will also often be seen with a PTA. However, unlike a PTA, an RPA will not usually present with peritonsillar swelling and uvular deviation. The abscess in an RPA is more posteriorly and inferiorly located. Uvular angioedema should be considered when there is swelling to the uvula and may or may not include other findings of angioedema, such as tongue and lip swelling. Uvular angioedema will not present with findings of tonsillitis, and the uvula will typically be midline and swollen.

chapterTitle: Head, Ear, Eye, Nose, and Throat Disorders
question: A 7-week-old boy is brought in for evaluation of a neck mass. His mother says it has gotten bigger over the past month, but she did not take him to the doctor be- cause she does not have insurance. She is worried because he has not gained much weight over the past month and feels like he has a fever. Palpation of the thyroid gland reveals a fluctuant, nonmobile 4-cm mass in the midline with mild ulcera- tion of the overlying skin. Which feature of the presentation might suggest an eti- ology other than a malignancy?

options.text: Fluctuance of the mass when palpated

correctAnswer: Fluctuance of the mass when palpated
englishExplanation: Overall, this patient's presentation is concerning for a malignancy, most likely of the thyroid. The only sign that makes a malignancy less likely is the fluctuant na- ture of the mass, which is more consistent with a cyst. There are five features considered concerning in the evaluation of a mass for malignancy. The five features are associated skin ulcer, onset when the patient is a neonate, fixation of the mass to skin or fascia, progressive enlargement, and size greater than 3 cm with a hard con- sistency. Superficial lumps with a lack of all five of these features are be- nign approximately 80% of the time. Other significant clinical features in this case are fever and possible weight loss reported by the mother. Further exami- nation is likely to reveal diffuse lymphadenopathy. Given these findings, and since the patient has no source of regular care, the emergency physician should get a con- sultation. If the patient's airway is intact, the best course of treatment is consultation and close follow-up with a pediatric oncologist for definitive diagnosis with fine nee- dle aspiration, biopsy, or imaging. Incorrect Answer Explanations The size of the mass is suggestive of a malignant lesion. An ultrasound examination of the mass might help delineate its size and consistency. Fluctuance of the mass is least consistent with malignancy in this patient. The mother says that the mass has grown over the past month, which means that it was likely present before the baby was 4 weeks old. Onset as a neonate is one of the indicators for a malignancy. Fluctuance of the mass is least consistent with malig- nancy in this patient. Ulceration of the skin is concerning for malignancy in neck masses. Fluctuance of the mass is least consistent with malignancy in this patient. Key Points If a neck mass can be moved around and compressed, it's less likely to be malignant — those features are more consistent with a cyst. Neonatal onset of neck masses is concerning for malignancy. Skin ulceration of neck masses is concerning for malignancy.

question: When evaluating an otherwise healthy patient who presents with "stomach flu," which finding should prompt consideration for ordering stool studies?
englishExplanation: Bacterial gastroenteritis is less common than viral gastroenteritis, but the symptoms are usually more severe. A fever of greater than 38.5°C (101.3°F) is more sug- gestive of a bacterial etiology, especially coupled with a more toxic patient pre- sentation, and it has been listed as an indication to send stool studies. Despite this in- creased severity, bacterial gastroenteritis is still typically self-limited. In uncompli- cated gastroenteritis, supportive care is the most appropriate therapy. Treatment is rehydration: If the patient can tolerate fluids by mouth, electrolyte re- placement beverages and chicken broth are recommended. If the patient cannot tol- erate fluids by mouth, parenteral hydration and antiemetics should be given. Admission should be considered for patients who still cannot tolerate fluids by mouth after parenteral antiemetics or who have severe dehydration, severe symp- toms, or significant comorbidities. Not all textbooks agree on the use of antibi- otics to treat bacterial gastroenteritis. Azithromycin or fluoroquinolones are effective agents in bacterial diarrhea but are reserved for treatment of severe illness. Incorrect Answer Explanations Foreign travel is linked to GI illnesses, including "travelers' diarrhea." Travel des- tination, and whether it is low, intermediate, or high risk, is the most important de- terminant of the causative organism and risk for disease. Poor hygiene practice in lo- cal restaurants is likely the largest contributor to the risk for travelers' diarrhea. Bacteria are the most common cause (80%-90%). The most common pathogen is en- terotoxigenic Escherichia coli, followed by Campylobacter jejuni, Shigella spp., and Salmonella spp. Although certain regions are more endemic to virulent bacteria and/or parasite species, foreign travel alone should not prompt a stool study in a patient presenting with simple gastroenteritis symptoms. If a patient presents with both foreign travel and an indication for a stool study, such as fever or bloody stools, the clinician should consider potential pathogens in the foreign area. Such knowledge can guide initial therapy, pending the results of additional studies. Most cases of viral and bacterial gastroenteritis are self-limited and resolve on their own in fewer than 72 hours. Although less common, some cases take longer to resolve, which is still not atypical of the expected natural history of the ill- ness. In a patient with symptom duration of less than 1 week, normal vital signs, and a nonfocal physical examination, supportive care is appropriate. If symptoms per- sist longer than 1 week, however, alternative diagnoses should be consid- ered and additional studies, including stool studies, should be ordered, as indicated. Vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort are the hallmark symp- toms of acute gastroenteritis. Acute gastroenteritis is most commonly self-lim- ited and best managed with supportive care. Antimotility agents such as loperamide can alleviate symptoms in acute diarrheal illnesses and can be used in cases that are uncomplicated without high fever or bloody stools. However, they should be used with caution because they can prolong illness and prevent excretion of the causative organism and also mask hypovolemic states secondary to stoll pooling in the bowel. Key Points Most cases of gastroenteritis are self-limited and only require supportive care. When antibiotics are indicated to treat gastroenteritis, azithromycin or a fluoro- quinolone are the right choice. Antimotility agents are rarely indicated for gastroenteritis and should be used with caution.

question: A 63-year-old woman presents with nausea and severe, frequent vomiting that started about 3 hours after she and a friend ate at a church picnic; her friend is ex- periencing similar symptoms. The patient ate barbecued chicken, spinach salad, potato salad, and some cookies. On examination, she appears weak and dehy- drated. She has no fever, and her hemoccult test result is negative. Which organ- ism most likely caused this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation: When two or more individuals present with the same illness and a common food ex- posure, a foodborne illness is likely. The patient in this case has upper GI symp- toms (nausea and vomiting, rather than cramps and diarrhea) that started soon af- ter she ate, which is most suggestive of a Staphylococcus aureus infection. Typical S. aureus “food poisoning” has a short incubation period (1-6 hours) and manifests primarily as severe, sudden vomiting. The organism produces a preformed enterotoxin and multiplies quickly at room temperature. The enterotoxin directly affects the brain's emesis center, in addition to producing its usual effects on the GI system. Common foods associated with this syndrome include unrefriger- ated meats, potato and egg salads, and cream pastries. Incorrect Answer Explanations A Bacillus cereus infection is unique, in that it can cause both emetic and diar- rheal illnesses at different stages. Because the emetic illness typically has a rapid onset, it could be the culprit; however, a distinguishing factor from the history is that the patient ate chicken and potato salad that had most likely been sitting out, rather than refrigerated, which is more consistent with S. aureus exposure. B. cereus is classically the culprit with rice, sauces, and soups that have been cooked and inappropriately refrigerated prior to being served, as on a buffet. The diarrheal illness resulting from B. cereus infection is typically delayed 8 to 24 hours and is clinically similar to Clostridium perfringens presentations. A C. perfringens infection also causes watery diarrhea, and symptoms can develop within 24 hours of ingestion. Allowing precooked foods, especially meat and poultry, to cool slowly before being eaten provides time for Clostridium spores to germinate and grow to sufficient numbers to cause infection. Clostridium infections are self-limited and require only symptomatic therapy. A Salmonella typhimurium infection causes a severe diarrheal illness 1 to 3 days after exposure and can cause dysentery (visible blood in the stool). The bacteria generate symptoms after being ingested and multiplying in the intestine, hence the more prolonged incubation period. Fecal leukocytes are typically, but not invariably, positive. Although infections in most hosts are self-limited, symp- toms can be mitigated by treatment with a fluoroquinolone and an antidiarrheal agent such as loperamide. Infections with S. typhimurium, Campylobacter jejuni, and Shigella flexneri are clinically indistinguishable from each other. Key Points When treating suspected food poisoning, finding out what the patient ate and when helps narrow down the possible sources and causes of illness. Staphylococcus aureus illness typically presents with severe vomiting soon after the consumption of unrefrigerated meats, potato or egg salads, and cream pastries. If the patient has vomiting one day and diarrhea the next, then Bacillus cereus is likely to blame, especially if a buffet was involved.

question: A prisoner presents with a 1-day history of blurry vision, voice changes, and diffi- culty swallowing after drinking “prison wine.” What is the most likely cause of their symptoms?
englishExplanation: Pruno (also known as prison wine or hooch) is made by fermenting foods such as fruit, potatoes, jellies, ketchup, and other sources of sugar. Potatoes, if used, may har- bor Clostridium botulinum spores, which have the potential to produce toxin in the warm, anaerobic fermentation environment. Individuals who consume pruno may develop botulism as a result. Onset of adult foodborne botulism is generally 1 to 2 days after an individual in- gests the culprit food. Neurologic symptoms are accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Initial symptoms may include blurred vision, diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, and facial weakness; nystagmus and ptosis may be observed on examina- tion. Weakness will progress, affecting the trunk and upper extremities first, followed by lower extremities. Urinary retention and constipation may result from smooth muscle paralysis. Diaphragmatic paralysis may result, and patients commonly present with some respiratory complaints. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cobalt toxicity has occurred after ingestion of contamination producing beer drinker's cardiomyopathy. However, it is not associated with pruno (or prison wine) consumption. A small amount of methanol may be produced by the fermentation process. However, distillation is required to concentrate methanol sufficiently to cause toxicity, and there is generally no distillation in pruno (ie, prison wine) production. Additionally, methanol would not be expected to cause bulbar weakness as described in this case. Plumbism (or chronic lead toxicity) is associated with GI upset and neuropsy- chiatric symptoms. The bulbar symptoms described in this case are not typically seen with chronic lead exposure.

question: A mother brings in her 5-month-old baby because he has been constipated for the past week. She says he has been eating less for the past 3 days and seems "sluggish and weak." He has had no fever, vomiting, rash, or other concerns. His vital signs are BP 107/74, P 111, R 22, and T 36.6°C (97.9°F); SpO is 100% on room air. The child is awake and interactive but lies still during the examination. Examination findings are otherwise negative except for diffuse decreased tone. Deep tendon re- flexes are normal. What pharmacotherapy should the treatment include?
englishExplanation: The classic presentation of infant botulism includes a history of constipation followed by altered neuromuscular examination findings, with cranial nerve issues noted ini- tially. This is sometimes described as “floppy baby” presentation. According to the CDC, any of the following symptoms can be observed: constipation, poor feeding, ptosis, sluggish pupils, flattened facial expression, diminished suck and gag reflexes, weak and altered cry, respiratory difficulty, and respiratory arrest. Infant botulism is caused by ingestion of Clostridium botulinum, which can be attributed to ingestion of honey or corn syrup. The mortality rate is 5% to 10%. It is more common in breastfed infants because breastfeeding can affect the gastric acid or bile acids that would oth- erwise minimize the growth of Clostridium. C. botulinum can also be ingested on a fomite when local construction has caused it to be mobilized from the soil. The primary concern in infant botulism is paralysis of musculature related to breath- ing; deep tendon reflexes are spared and remain normal. Treatment includes sup- portive care, frequent evaluation of the respiratory status, and empiric treatment with intravenous botulism immune globulin. The time it takes to get results from stool sample testing is often too long given how difficult it is to obtain the sample in a constipated infant. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dexamethasone is a steroid that is often used to treat croup, and there is evidence for its use in treating asthma in one or two doses (depending on the study). However, steroids have no role in the treatment of infant botulism. Normal saline is best used as a volume expander and is only dosed at 10 mL/kg when the normal 20 mL/kg could cause harm (ie, increased intracranial pressure, conges- tive heart failure, renal dysfunction). This child has normal mentation and vital signs and does not warrant a fluid bolus at this time. Vancomycin can be important in the treatment of wound botulism, but penicillin is still the preferred first-line agent. However, vancomycin has no role in the treatment of infant botulism. Key Points Botulism should be considered in an infant who presents with constipation followed by neuromuscular dysfunction. Monitoring the respiratory status is crucial in the care of infant botulism. Supportive care and botulism immune globulin are key components of treating infant botulism.

question: A 6-month-old boy presents with hypotonia, poor feeding, and constipation. His mother says he has recently started eating “table food,” but no other family mem- ber has similar symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Botulism is caused by the ingestion of Clostridium botulinum spores, which can be found in products like canned food, fermented fish, and honey. Of the listed options, infant botulism is the most likely condition to be asso- ciated with ingestion of shared “table foods” given the patient's symptoms. Infants have weaker immune systems than adults, which would also explain why no other family members exhibit similar symptoms. In the United States, a common source of C. botulinum spores are environmental dust particles, and there is an established as- sociation between the ingestion of honey contaminated with C. botulinum and the de- velopment of infant botulism. This diagnosis should be considered in all in- fants who present with constipation and poor feeding. Some of the most common symptoms of infant botulism include constipation, difficulty sucking, difficulty swallowing, and hypotonia. C. botulinum spores can also be found in wound infections from intravenous drug use or cosmetic injections. Treatment of botulism consists of supportive care with botulism immunoglobulin for infants less than 1 year and botulinum antitoxin for those older than 1 year. Antibiotics should not be given unless there is suspicion for a concurrent infec- tion; penicillin is only indicated in cases of wound botulism. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ciguatera poisoning develops after ingesting contaminated fish. The char- acteristic symptoms include circumoral tingling, headache, tremor, diffuse paresthesias, and the reversal of hot and cold sensations. Ciguatera poison- ing symptoms in younger children include discomfort, irritability, watery diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal cramping rather than the constipation noted with botulism. Listeriosis develops following infection with Listeria monocytogenes. Neonatal listeriosis typically arises from vertical transmission and presents as sepsis, with or without meningitis. In older children and adults, listeriosis is a foodborne ill- ness associated with the ingestion of raw or unprocessed food such as soft cheeses, delicatessen meats, and vegetable products. Two of the more com- mon presentations associated with listeriosis are bacteremia, meningitis, vomit- ing, and diarrhea rather than the constipation found in botulism. Scombroid poisoning develops after ingesting dark-meat fish that has be- gun bacterial decomposition. Typical symptoms of scombroid poisoning include erythema, pruritus, urticaria, dysphagia, headache, vomiting, and diar- rhea. Symptoms of scombroid poisoning typically last only a few hours but can last 1 to 2 days.
