On examination, the patient has positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Which element of this presentation is most suggestive of coccid- ioidal meningitis?

options.text: Recent travel to the Ohio River Valley

englishExplanation: Coccidioidal infection or “valley fever” (after the San Joaquin Valley) is caused by the dimorphous fungi Coccidioides. Patients often present with primary pulmonary in- fection, although many remain asymptomatic. Infection begins with inhalation of air- borne fungi particles after soil disturbance leading to pulmonary infection. These pa- tients may present as pneumonia that did not improve with standard antibiotic treat- ment. In some cases, the infection can spread to involve the nervous system, leading to meningitis. The progression is slow, but patients may present with signs of meningitis with initial pulmonary infection. The main symptoms at presentation in about 70% of patients is persistent or recurring headache, and they often are without fever. Physical examina- tion may be atypical for meningitis with negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs. A lum- bar puncture with CSF culture is required to diagnose this disease, but in early cases, it may only be positive in about 15% of patients. Serologic and PCR testing is often re- quired to make the diagnosis. Coccidiomyocosis is endemic to the southwestern United states and parts of Mexico. Symptoms from infection begin 1 to 3 weeks after exposure and persist for months to years. It is especially concerning in patients with HIV since they may develop severe disease. Other immunocompromised patients, pregnant patients, and those who work in vocations that expose them to dust are at higher risk for infection. The rec- ommended treatment is fluconazole. Patients with meningitis are required to con- tinue to receive treatment for years — potentially over the course of their lifetime. Incorrect Answer Explanations Coccidioidal meningitis has a slower onset with insidious, less severe symptoms, and it may occur months after initial infection. Patients may not have fevers. The most common presenting symptom is recurrent headache. Undiagnosed coccidioidal meningitis is fatal. Patients with coccidioidal meningitis often have negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs on examination and present atypically. The main symptoms at presentation in about 70% of patients is persistent headache, and they often do not have fever. Coccidioides is endemic to the southwestern United States, not the Ohio River Valley. The disease is caused by inhalation of airborne fungi after disturbance in the soil in desert areas. Patients who are involved in excavation or work with soil are at higher risk for infection.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with abdominal bloating, diarrhea, and flatulence for the past week. She recently returned from a hiking trip and, when asked, ad- mits to drinking water from a spring. Her vital signs include BP 110/68, P 82, R 18, and T 37.1°C (98.8°F). The physical examination is normal, and she is other- wise healthy. What is the best test to confirm the diagnosis of giardiasis?
englishExplanation: Giardiasis is caused by Giardia lamblia and is the most frequently diag- nosed parasitic infection in the United States. Stool antigen is the test of choice for confirming the pathogen because it is consistently present in stool, re- gardless of Giardia cyst shedding (which is more variable). Giardiasis commonly af- fects hikers and campers who drink contaminated water, adults and chil- dren who spend time in child care centers, and people who engage in oral-anal sexual contact. Transmission can be waterborne, foodborne, or fe- cal-oral. Symptoms of giardiasis vary but generally include diarrhea, excessive flatu- lence, and abdominal bloating. In severe cases, steatorrhea (ie, excess fat in feces) can develop because saturation of the small bowel with organisms causes malabsorp- tion. A patient experiencing fatty stools may describe them as greasy or sticky, pale, floating, or particularly bad smelling. Metronidazole, tinidazole, and nitazoxanide are among the appropriate therapies for giardiasis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Serum antibodies against Giardia lamblia can be detected. However, this test is generally unhelpful because it cannot differentiate between acute and prior infections. Giardia lamblia is a parasitic infection; thus, a stool bacterial culture will not be diagnostic. Stool microscopy can be used to detect cysts and trophozoites, but it is limited and time intensive. Giardia cysts are intermittently excreted in stool, leading to false-nega- tive results with microscopy, and organisms quickly break down and be- come unrecognizable when voided. The sensitivity of the test increases with each repetition; although the CDC recommends assessing at least three different samples, this can be cumbersome, and results are dependent on technician expertise. One advantage of stool cultures and ova and parasite studies is their abil- ity to rule out other potential infectious etiologies. However, if giardiasis is highly suspected, stool antigen remains the test of choice. Key Points Giardiasis is the most common protozoal infection in the United States. Suspect giardiasis in any high-risk patient with diarrhea and flatulence. The diagnostic test of choice for giardiasis is stool antigen. Hikers, campers, children who go to daycare, and persons who engage in oral-anal contact are at the highest risk for giardiasis.

question: Which helminth causes a fatal hyperinfestation in immunocompromised patients?
englishExplanation: Strongyloides stercoralis is a nematode (roundworm) that infests the small intestine. Strongyloidiasis is typically asymptomatic, but abdominal pain and diarrhea can be present and can progress to dysentery. Elderly and immunocom- promised patients are at risk of hyperinfestation, which can be fatal. These pa- tients become overwhelmingly infested, and large numbers of migrating larvae cause both direct and indirect damage (eg, septicemia, pneumonia, meningitis, ileus). S. stercoralis infestations are most commonly found in humid tropical re- gions but should be suspected in military personnel, persons stationed overseas, and in refugees and immigrants. Larvae migrate through the skin (larva currens), often resulting in local pruritus, allergic manifestations, and an erythematous rash. Passage through the lungs can result in a cough, dyspnea, and pneumonia. Pharmacotherapy for strongyloidiasis includes antiparasitic medications such as ivermectin and albendazole. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ascaris lumbricoides, a nematode, infests the intestines. Ascariasis usually presents with symptoms such as a dry cough or pneumonia, as the larvae migrate through the lungs to the esophagus and gut. Once the infestation settles in the in- testines, local effects such as obstruction of the biliary duct or small bowel can occur. Eosinophilic pneumonia (also called Löffler syndrome) is associated with larval pas- sage through the lungs. A large worm burden can cause malnutrition but not a fatal hyperinfestation. Treatment options include albendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin. Enterobius vermicularis, also known as pinworms, causes perianal pru- ritus. It is easily transmitted between members of a family or persons in a day care center, and it can propagate by autoinfection. It generally causes localized infestation, rather than fatal hyperinfestation, but it can sometimes migrate to the ovaries or ap- pendix and cause disease. It is diagnosed with the classic “scotch tape test,” which al- lows visualization of the worms via an anal swab. Treatment options include albenda- zole, mebendazole, and pyrantel pamoate. Necator americanus, or hookworm, requires a large worm burden for the host to become symptomatic. Classically, it can result in chronic anemia; iron-deficiency anemia is seen in children with large parasite loads and requires iron supplementation. Adult hookworms penetrate into the intestinal mucosa and feed, resulting in ongoing luminal blood loss. Eggs passed in the stool mature into larvae in the soil; they can enter hosts by penetrating the skin of people walking barefoot, which can present with cutaneous larva migrans. Treatment options include albenda- zole, mebendazole, and pyrantel pamoate.

question: A 44-year-old man presents with sudden-onset high fever and sharp right upper quadrant pain that worsens when he inhales or coughs. He has also had abdominal pain, cramps, and diarrhea with mucus and blood in it since returning from a year abroad in Mexico. CT abdomen shows a cystic liver abscess. What pharmacother- apy should resolve the underlying condition?
englishExplanation: Metronidazole is the correct treatment for the most likely diagnosis in this case: amebic dysentery and hepatic abscess caused by the protozoan parasite Entamoeba histolytica. The presentation of E. histolytica infection can range from that of an asymptomatic infection to dysentery, as in this case, which is distinguished from diarrhea by visible blood in the stool. Rarely, infections progress to fulminant colitis. If left untreated, the parasite can seed the liver and cause an amebic hepatic abscess, which can then present with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and hepatomegaly without jaundice. For symptomatic patients, metronidazole treats both the dysentery and hepatic abscess. For pregnant pa- tients, paromomycin is an alternative. Other options include tinidazole and nitazox- anide. Half of amebic liver abscess cases have transaminitis, and three-fourths have an elevated alkaline phosphatase level. Two-thirds of amebic liver abscess cases are initially misdiagnosed in the emergency department; thus, imaging with CT or ultra- sonography is key to making the correct diagnosis. E. histolytica infections are usu- ally established by serology. Stool examination for the parasite is possible, but an- tidiarrheal medications, rectal contrast, and antacids interfere with the study. Liver abscess formation occurs at a late stage in the infection, and patients often cease passing cysts in the stool, making it even more difficult to diagnose by stool studies alone. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ciprofloxacin or azithromycin can be used for the treatment of traveler's diar- rhea or dysentery caused by bacteria, but it is not indicated in parasitic protozoan infections, as in this case which is seen with the amebic liver abscess on CT. Traveler's diarrhea is most commonly caused by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (especially in Mexico and Central America) and Campylobacter sp. (especially in Southeast Asia). Its presentation consists of loose or watery stools ac- companied by cramping, nausea, fever, or blood. Most cases are self-limited, not lasting 4 weeks, and the primary treatment is based on rehydration. Empiric an- tibiotic treatment can be considered, given the debilitating nature of the disease; however, it is important to avoid antibiotics in cases of suspected E. coli O157:H7 due to an increased risk of developing hemolytic-uremic syndrome. Loperamide can reduce symptom severity in traveler's diarrhea during the course of the illness, but it does not provide curative therapy. Loperamide is not recommended in cases of dysentery or in traveler's diarrhea without curative therapy, as it can interfere with diagnostic studies. In addition, taking loperamide has been implicated in a rare complication of toxic megacolon for patients infected with E. histolytica. Loperamide should not be given to children ages 3 years and younger or to patients with signs of invasive bacterial infection (bloody stools or fever). Other antidiarrheal agents include bismuth subsalicylate and kaolin. Mebendazole is an anthelmintic agent used in the treatment of round- worms, pinworms, whipworms, and hookworms. Patients with evidence of worms in fecal matter can receive empiric therapy with mebendazole and then tar- geted therapy after stool studies are performed. Helminth infections are rarely asso- ciated with chronic diarrhea and are only seen in patients with large worm burdens.

question: Which diagnostic study confirms a diagnosis of malaria?
englishExplanation: The gold standard for confirming the diagnosis of malaria is microscopy with thick and thin blood smears. Thick smears can screen for the presence of malarial parasites, while thin smears are used to identify the species of Plasmodium. Malaria cannot be ruled out until there are three negative sets of thin and thick blood smears 12 hours apart. Rapid diagnostic tests have also been developed and provide qualitative information via the detection of parasite anti- gens or parasite LDH. Nonspecific laboratory findings in malaria include abnormal renal and liver functions, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Malaria is a life-threatening illness that should be considered for any individual re- turning from a tropical or subtropical location with an unexplained fever. Transmission most often occurs in areas along the equator, including sub-Saharan Africa, South America, India, and Southeast Asia. Malaria is caused by the parasite Plasmodium and spread via the bites of Anopheles mosqui- toes. Of the five species that can infect humans, P. falciparum is responsible for the largest number of malaria deaths. The variable incubation period from the time of infection to the development of symptoms can range from 1 week to months or even years. The clinical features of malaria occur when the infected erythrocytes lyse. Early manifestations of malaria are nonspecific and include fatigue, malaise, myalgias, arthralgias, headache, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diar- rhea. The disease can progress to the classic "malaria paroxysms" — chills followed by high fevers and, finally, profuse sweating. Physical examination features are also nonspecific and include ill appearance, fever, tachycardia, tachyp- nea, splenomegaly, and signs of anemia. Severe malaria can occur if a person is left untreated, particularly in the setting of P. falciparum infection. Signs and symptoms can include seizures, delirium, coma, shock, respiratory distress, and jaundice. Incorrect Answer Explanations A blood or stool culture is the appropriate diagnostic study to confirm the diagnosis of typhoid fever, another common etiology of febrile illness in returning travelers. Caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi, it is endemic to regions such as India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and Mexico. Clinical features of typhoid fever are often nonspecific (eg, fever, headache, myalgias, abdominal pain, constipation); clas- sic manifestations of typhoid fever include relative bradycardia and a pale, erythema- tous, macular rash on the trunk (rose spots). Performing a lumbar puncture to analyze CSF is the correct action to confirm the di- agnosis of meningitis. Malaria can present with high fever and a severe headache, but not the nuchal rigidity classically seen in meningitis. Additionally, malaria is not associated with a rash; bacterial meningitis secondary to Neisseria meningitidis causes purpura and petechiae. If a diagnosis of dengue fever were strongly suspected, serology or detection of viral nucleic acid by reverse transcriptase PCR would be the correct choice. Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that is also a common cause of fever in a traveler return- ing from a tropical or subtropical location. Uncomplicated cases of dengue manifest as high fever, retro-orbital pain, headache, arthralgias, myalgias, nausea, vomiting, rash, and mild bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding, petechiae, purpura). Dengue en- demic to Southeast Asia presents as hemorrhagic fever with signs of increased vascu- lar permeability (elevated Hct, ascites, pleural effusion) and can progress to fulmi- nant septic shock.

question: Which malarial Plasmodium species causes the greatest overall morbidity and mortality?
englishExplanation: Plasmodium falciparum is the most common cause of severe malaria and is responsible for the majority of the morbidity and mortality associ- ated with this disease. In 2018, over 90% of the estimated 228 million global malaria cases and 405,000 deaths occurred in Africa, a region with a preponderance of P. falciparum. P. falciparum is one of five major causes of malaria in humans, along with P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi. All types of malaria commonly present with a cyclic, undulating fever that oc- curs every 48 hours (tertian) or every 72 hours (quartan), depending on the timing of hemolysis and systemic parasite release. Tertian fever is classically associ- ated with P. falciparum, P. vivax, and P. ovale infection, and quartan fever is associ- ated with P. malariae. Other major signs and symptoms of malaria include chills, di- aphoresis, myalgias, headache, vomiting, abdominal pain, and severe fatigue. Anemia is a common laboratory finding. P. falciparum, in particular, is associated with progression to more severe manifesta- tions of malaria, including multiorgan failure, altered mental status (cere- bral malaria) caused by cerebral edema, dyspnea from pulmonary edema, and renal failure from hemolysis. Severe anemia, microangiopathy, and DIC due to widespread hemolysis and severe parasite burden are major contribu- tors to morbidity and mortality. The historic Blackwater fever — characterized by jaundice, fevers, vomiting, severe anemia, and red-black urine — pri- marily results from severe P. falciparum infection. P. vivax and P. knowlesi infection can also cause P. falciparum–like severe malaria but are much less com- mon. Risk factors for severe disease include HIV, age less than 5 years, malnutrition, pregnancy, limited access to medical care, and medical comorbidities. Incorrect Answer Explanations P. knowlesi primarily causes malaria in monkeys but can cross over to hu- mans via mosquito bites. Although it is a somewhat rarer form of malaria globally, it is more common in Southeast Asia. It usually causes a milder form of malaria but can have P. falciparum–like severity in approximately 10% of cases. Uniquely, P. knowlesi causes fevers every day on a roughly 24-hr cycle (quotidian) but otherwise presents similarly to the other forms of malaria. P. ovale is a minor cause of malaria in humans that is endemic to similar re- gions as P. falciparum but is responsible for far fewer infections. Unlike P. falci- parum, it rarely causes severe symptoms or death but can cause a dormant liver infection that allows for reactivation. Overall, P. vivax has the widest geographic dispersion of all causes of malaria in humans, including Southeast Asia, South America, and parts of Africa. Notably, it is responsible for the majority of malaria cases in South America. P. vivax infection can cause P. falciparum–like severe symptoms but generally does not due to its modest parasitemia. Consequently, malarial P. vivax infections account for only a small portion of the global morbidity and mortality despite its wide distribution.

question: What is the most common symptom in an acute malaria infection?
englishExplanation: Regardless of the causative Plasmodium species, malaria is most strongly associated with an undulating and cyclic fever. Classically, cyclic fevers from P. falciparum, P. vivax, and P. ovale occur every 48 hours (tertian); P. malariae cyclic fevers occur every 72 hours (quartan); and P. knowlesi uniquely has a roughly 24-hr fever cycle (quotidian). The undulating fever in malaria is associated with the timing of hemolysis and systemic parasite release, but this pattern is rarely seen clinically. As a result, any patient presenting with fever and recent travel from a malaria-endemic region should be screened for malaria regardless of fever pattern. The other major signs and symptoms of malaria are flu-like and include headache, chills, diaphoresis, myalgias, arthralgias, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and severe fatigue. Incorrect Answer Explanations Diarrhea is not generally associated with malaria, although other GI symptoms such as vomiting and abdominal pain are. Patients who present with fever, diarrhea, and travel from a region with endemic malaria should be evalu- ated with a broad differential of infectious causes, including nontyphoidal Salmonella and other infectious diarrheas. Increased appetite is not generally associated with malaria. However, anorexia is a prominent feature of both uncomplicated and severe forms of the disease, as part of an overall constellation of flu-like symptoms. Jaundice is generally considered a common manifestation of severe malaria due to extensive hemolysis. However, it is not a common finding over- all and is not considered a feature of uncomplicated malaria. Patients who present with jaundice and concern for malaria require evaluation for severe features of the disease, such as profound anemia, end-organ damage, coagulopathies, and electrolyte abnormalities.

question: What is the greatest risk factor for malaria mortality?
englishExplanation: Malaria is a major cause of pediatric mortality globally, accounting for approximately 8% of pediatric deaths in 2017. In particular, children younger than 5 years are dramatically affected, representing 57% of all malaria deaths in 2017. Children less than 14 years represent approximately 66% of malaria deaths. Unlike most infectious diseases, mortality from malaria decreases with advancing age; those older than 70 represented only 5% of malaria deaths in 2017. Repeated malarial infections over time produce immunity, providing protection to adults, which can be passed as maternal antibodies that temporarily protect babies. As a result of waning maternal antibodies and lack of de novo immunity, children less than 5 years represent the most vulnerable population. Due to targeted interventions such as insecticide-treated netting, global malaria deaths have been decreasing overall for the past 10 to 15 years. However, other major risk factors for severe disease still present challenges, such as HIV infection, mal- nutrition, multiple medical comorbidities, and poor access to prompt care. Incorrect Answer Explanations Female sex is not a known risk factor for mortality due to malaria. Although there is thought to be no particular bias relating to sex and the disease it- self, there may be cultural and socioeconomic disparities between men and women that contribute to mortality differences. Pregnant patients, however, are at a much higher risk for both maternal mortality and fetal complications; one study estimated that malaria is associated with up to 25% of maternal deaths in endemic areas and drives higher miscarriage and prematurity rates. Regardless, young age is a much greater driver of mortality. P. falciparum, rather than P. ovale, infection is a higher risk for mortal- ity. P. falciparum is associated with much higher rates of severe malaria and ac- counts for a vast majority of deaths. P. ovale is generally associated with milder disease. Recurrent infection is actually associated with improved immunity and lower mortality. It is thought that the lower mortality rates with age are due to re- current infection-associated immunity.

question: What is the most appropriate treatment for an uncomplicated, chloroquine-resis- tant Plasmodium falciparum infection?
englishExplanation: In the United States, uncomplicated, chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum infection can be treated with one of four options: atovaquone-proguanil; artemether-lumefantrine; quinine with doxycycline, tetracycline, or clin- damycin; or mefloquine as a second-line agent. Atovaquone-proguanil and artemether-lumefantrine are the preferred agents for both adult and pediatric pa- tients but should not be used for pregnant patients. The other malaria-causing Plasmodium species are generally sensitive to chloroquine, which should be used in these cases. Generally, P. falciparum infections should be considered chloroquine-re- sistant and treated accordingly, regardless of geographic location. P. vivax has shown some pockets of chloroquine resistance in Southeast Asia and South America; patients with malaria from these areas should be closely monitored for chloroquine failure. Incorrect Answer Explanations Doxycycline, as a single agent, is inadequate to treat uncomplicated malaria. Alone, it is mainly used as malaria prophylaxis. It can be combined with quinine, how- ever, as an alternative first-line treatment for uncomplicated, chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum infections. Mefloquine is a potential treatment for uncomplicated, chloroquine-resistant P. fal- ciparum infection, but it is a second-line agent after atovaquone-proguanil, artemether-lumefantrine, and quinine with doxycycline, tetracycline, or clindamycin. The utility of mefloquine is limited by two issues: First, there is evolving resistance to it as a single agent; second, it can cause significant neuropsychiatric side effects, in- cluding hallucinations, confusion, memory issues, paranoia, and odd dreams. Quinine alone is not a recommended treatment regimen for uncompli- cated, chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum infections. However, quinine in combination with doxycycline, tetracycline, or clindamycin is a first-line treatment option, along with atovaquone-proguanil and artemether-lumefantrine.

question: Which finding on a contrast enhanced CT of the brain is most consistent with neu- rotoxoplasmosis in a patient with HIV/AIDS?

options.text: Solitary mass lesion in the corpus callosum

englishExplanation: Neurotoxoplasmosis, also known as cerebral toxoplasmosis, is an oppor- tunistic infection caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii. It creates characteristic “ring-enhancing” lesions with associated edema with mass ef- fect — often in the parietal lobe, frontal lobe, or basal ganglia — on a contrast-en- hanced CT of the brain; noncontrast studies may show subcortical lesions. Neurotoxoplasmosis is an AIDS-defining illness in HIV-positive patients, usually associated with a CD4+ count of less than 100 cells/mm. Patients with neurotoxoplasmosis frequently present with fever, altered mental status, headache, and even seizures. If multiple lesions are noted on a contrast 3 enhanced CT of the brain, it is important to determine if there is a risk of herniation before performing a lumbar puncture. In patients with neurotoxoplasmosis, a lumbar puncture will likely show a pleocytosis with elevated protein. Patients with le- sions concerning for toxoplasmosis should be admitted for further evaluation and treatment, including possible advanced neuroimaging, toxoplasma antibody testing, steroids, brain biopsy, and antimicrobials, in addition to an infectious disease consultation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with a CD4+ count less than 50 cells/mm are also at risk for cryp- tococcal meningitis, which may produce hydrocephalus on CT imaging. Lumbar puncture will generally show an elevated opening pressure and lymphocytic predominance. However, cryptococcal meningitis does not demonstrate the ring-en- hancing lesions associated with neurotoxoplasmosis. A solitary mass lesion in the corpus callosum is more characteristic of primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL); a lesion larger than 4 cm indicates PCNSL. However, patients with PCNSL may also present with multiple ring-en- hancing lesions on CT that are difficult to distinguish from those seen in neuro- toxoplasmosis. Modalities such as advanced neuroimaging, CSF sampling, and biopsy are used to determine the underlying disease but are unavailable in the emergency department; patients presenting with new ring-enhancing lesions should be admitted for this evaluation. Patients with AIDS are also at risk for HIV-associated dementia, which can present with subcortical atrophy and ventricular enlargement; lumbar punc- ture may demonstrate elevated protein. The treatment of choice for HIV-associ- ated dementia is antiretroviral medications. Notably, HIV-associated dementia does not demonstrate ring-enhancing lesions.

question: What is an indication to treat toxoplasmosis in an immunocompetent host?
englishExplanation: Posterior uveitis is an indication to treat toxoplasmosis in an immunocompetent host. In immunocompetent hosts, toxoplasmosis is generally a self-limited infec- tion. Most commonly, patients present with constitutional symptoms such as fever, chills, myalgias, headaches, or sore throat. Lymphadenopathy may be dif- fuse in some patients. The majority of patients who are not immunocompromised or pregnant do not require treatment for infection. However, a subset of patients may develop more severe symptoms such as meningoencephalitis, myoperi- carditis, or posterior uveitis. In these cases, patients should be treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine. Posterior uveitis may result in chronic scarring and vision loss. Incorrect Answer Explanations Fever is a common manifestation of systemic toxoplasmosis in immunocompetent hosts. It is generally self-limited and does not require treatment unless the patient is immunocompromised or pregnant. Lymphadenopathy occurs in 20% to 30% of patients with primary toxoplasmosis in- fection. It may persist for several weeks. It is generally self-limited and does not require treatment unless the patient is immunocompromised or pregnant. Myalgias are common manifestations of systemic toxoplasmosis in immunocompe- tent hosts. They are generally self-limited and do not require treatment unless the patient is immunocompromised or pregnant.

question: What finding does this contrast-enhanced CT scan demonstrate? Credit: Copyright 2024 Assoc Prof Frank Gaillard. Image courtesy of Assoc Prof Frank Gaillard and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 76689. Used under license.

options.text: Acute epidural hematoma due to trauma
Hyperdense MCA sign representing acute cerebrovascular accident

englishExplanation: The posterior area on the right shows a ring-enhancing lesion. Ring-enhancing le- sions on contrast-enhanced CT of the brain are generally associated with toxoplas- mosis, CNS lymphoma, or brain abscess. It is difficult to distinguish these three processes on CT, and MRI is often required for diagnosis. Often, toxoplasmosis will have a predilection for basal ganglia or corticomedullary areas. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute epidural hematoma due to trauma generally appears as a hyperdense lentiform-shaped area extradural to brain tissue on noncontrast CT. It may be a space-occupying lesion and displace normal brain tissue depending on size of the hematoma. The above finding demonstrates a circular ring-enhancing lesion without lenticular hyperdensity. Hyperdense middle cerebral artery (MCA) sign representing acute cerebrovascular accident is an early finding in acute stroke on noncontrast CT scan. It represents vi- sualization of hyperdense thrombotic material in MCA and may appear within 90 minutes of an acute ischemic event. The above finding is not in the anatomical area of the MCA and does not appear linear as a hyperdense MCA sign would. Hypoattenuation representing encephalomalacia is generally found in the area of a prior insult, such as an intracranial hemorrhage or cerebrovascular accident. It may be seen on noncontrast or contrast-enhanced CT. It is the result of liquefactive necrosis after brain injury. It appears as a hypoattenuation of brain tissue with margins at the area of insult. The above finding demonstrates a circular ring-enhancing lesion without diffuse hypoattenuation.

question: Which tick-borne disease is caused by a spirochete organism?
englishExplanation: Tick-borne relapsing fever is caused by spirochete bacteria, most com- monly Borrelia hermsii. It is transmitted by Ornithodoros ticks found in the western mountain and Pacific states. Symptoms typically begin as a rash or eschar at the site of the tick bite. After a 3- to 10-day incubation period, the patient develops fever, chills, malaise, headaches, myalgias, arthralgias, abdominal pain, and jaundice. The disease derives its name from its characteristic alternating febrile and afebrile periods, which can each last 3 to 7 days and can have anywhere from 3 to 6 cycles. Laboratory findings include leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and an elevated ESR. The infecting spirochete can be visualized on Giemsa- stained peripheral blood smears, which are best when taken during the febrile period. Treatment consists of doxycycline or erythromycin for 10 days. Severely ill persons can have CNS involvement with mental status changes or meningoen- cephalitis, in which case ceftriaxone should be administered intravenously daily. Incorrect Answer Explanations Babesiosis is caused by a malaria-like protozoan parasite, transmitted by Ixodes ticks, that infects erythrocytes and produces a nonspecific influenza-like ill- ness with fever, chills, myalgia, headache, and hemolytic anemia. What dis- tinguishes babesiosis from malaria is the presence of parasites in a budding tetrad formation (the Maltese cross sign) on peripheral smears. Treatment includes clin- damycin plus quinine, or atovaquone plus azithromycin. Colorado tick fever, which is endemic to the mountain regions of the western United States, is a self-limited disease caused by an RNA virus transmitted by the wood tick Dermacentor andersoni. It presents with headache, back pain, a biphasic febrile course (saddleback fever curve), and leukopenia. Each fever phase lasts 2 to 4 days; the entire course of illness is usually 2 weeks but can be longer in older patients. Treatment is usually supportive. Ehrlichiosis is a tick-borne disease caused by a gram-negative, intracellu- lar, rickettsia-like coccobacilli of the Ehrlichia species; it is transmitted by "lone star" or Ixodes ticks. It can present with an abrupt-onset fever, chills, headaches, myalgias, and sometimes a rash, but it does not have the cyclical pattern characteris- tic of tick-borne relapsing fever. Treatment includes doxycycline or tetracycline.

question: Which laboratory abnormality is classically associated with ehrlichiosis?
englishExplanation: Ehrlichiosis, also known as human monocytic ehrlichiosis (HME), is most com- monly caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, a tick-borne bacterium associated with the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum). Ehrlichiosis is strongly associated with hematologic abnormalities, most commonly thrombocytopenia, but also commonly with leukopenia and transaminitis. Ehrlichiosis presents mainly with constitutional symptoms like fatigue, rigors, headaches, myalgias, and arthralgias. Occasionally, ehrlichiosis can cause neurologic abnormalities such as altered mental status, meningitis, and seizures. A nonspecific rash is a rare finding, and its presence should prompt evalu- ation for coinfection with other tick-borne illnesses, such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever and Lyme disease. Renal, pulmonary, and cardiac dysfunction have also been described. Diagnosis is based on indirect fluorescent antibody, enzyme- linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), or PCR testing. Peripheral blood smears can also demonstrate characteristic cytoplasmic inclusions. Evaluating CSF can be useful for patients presenting with neurologic symptoms and may show high CSF protein, along with a CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis. The first-line treatment for ehrlichiosis is 7 to 10 days of doxycycline. Research shows no tooth staining in pediatric patients who receive short courses (less than 10 days) of doxycycline, and the CDC now recommends doxycycline as the first- line treatment for ehrlichiosis for all age groups and most pregnant patients. Patients with doxycycline allergies and pregnant patients with very mild symptoms can try a 7- to 10-day course of rifampin, although there is limited clinical evidence for its effectiveness. Treatment should be initiated prior to diagnos- tic confirmation if the clinical concern is high. This is especially true for patients with severe symptoms or those who are at high risk of severe illness, such as immuno- compromised and cancer patients. The mortality rate for ehrlichiosis is generally considered to be low; however, the mortality rate increases with severe disease and opportunistic infections secondary to severe leukopenia. Incorrect Answer Explanations An elevated ESR is a common finding in early Lyme disease, rather than ehrlichiosis. Lyme disease is caused by tick-borne spirochetes of the genus Borrelia. Borrelia burgdorferi is the most common species seen in the United States, while other species are more common around the world. Early Lyme disease causes a characteristic bull's-eye rash. High CSF protein (rather than low CSF protein) and CSF lymphocytic pleocy- tosis are features of ehrlichiosis. One study found these findings in over 50% of CSF samples from patients with ehrlichiosis who presented with neurologic symptoms. Prolonged PT is more strongly associated with Rocky Mountain spotted fever, as opposed to ehrlichiosis. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by the tick-borne bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii. It is known for its prominent laboratory abnormalities (thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, transaminitis, and hy- ponatremia) and characteristic rash involving the ankles and wrist that spreads proximally. Since coagulopathy is not a well-described feature of ehrli- chiosis, its presence should prompt evaluation for R. rickettsii coinfection.

question: An 8-year-old girl presents with dizziness and one episode of fainting at school. Her medical history is significant for ventricular septal defect repair. The physical examination reveals no abnormalities; her vital signs include BP 97/50, P 126, R 20, and T 36.1°C (97°F). An ECG is obtained and shown below. What other test should be ordered to make the diagnosis? Credit: alfa md/iStock/Getty Images Plus.
englishExplanation: This ECG shows a first-degree heart block. In endemic areas, rickettsial dis- ease should be considered, especially when there is evidence of heart block; early disseminated disease can affect the heart and lead to the ECG changes as shown. First-degree heart block is the most common ECG finding in pediatric pa- tients with Lyme disease, and it can be asymptomatic or lead to symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue, and palpitations. If the PR is >300 ms, it can also lead to more se- rious symptoms, such as syncope. Lyme carditis is found in up to 10% of untreated patients with Lyme disease and can present with nonspecific findings, including syn- cope or palpitations. Syncope is a common presentation in emergency depart- ments, accounting for almost 1% of visits. A thorough history and physical examina- tion can often distinguish syncope from other confounding diagnoses (eg, breath- holding spells, orthostatic hypotension). In children, syncope is most commonly vasovagal and least commonly cardiac (as opposed to adults). Incorrect Answer Explanations Antineutrophil antibody (ANA) is used in the evaluation of rheumatologic dis- ease, which could lead to cardiac disease in time. However, this is unlikely in an oth- erwise healthy child. Rheumatic cardiac disease is among the most common causes for acquired cardiac issues in children but is evaluated using testing for streptococcal infection and not an ANA titer. Electrolyte abnormality is an important component of the evaluation of arrhythmia, and potassium levels can be inferred by the appearance of the T wave on the ECG. If there is a history of poor oral intake or increased losses due to vomiting or diar- rhea, electrolyte evaluation would be needed, but this is unwarranted for this other- wise well child and with no evidence of abnormal T waves on the ECG. Acute myocardial injury is rare in children, except those with a history of Kawasaki disease, sickle cell anemia, or cardiac surgery. Although this child has a history of cardiac surgery, the ECG shows no evidence of ischemic injury.

question: A 32-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of headaches and confusion. He has an erythematous targetoid rash on his arm that appeared after he returned from a camping trip in New England 1 month ago, but he is otherwise healthy. A lumbar puncture is performed, and the patient is admitted. What is the best next step in management?
englishExplanation: Erythematous targetoid lesions (classic for erythema migrans) with a concurrent history of outdoor exposure to endemic areas should raise suspicion for Lyme disease. This patient also exhibits neurologic symptoms (confusion) consistent with Lyme disease encephalitis, which should be evalu- ated with a lumbar puncture (after a negative head CT) and treated with ceftriax- one 2 g IV. Lyme disease, which is transmitted through the bite of an infected tick, is caused by the bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi. The deer tick, a well-known carrier of the disease, is most prominent in the northeastern and midwestern United States. Distribution of Lyme disease in these regions has expanded, and the number of cases has increased steadily over the past 25 years. Initial symptoms occur within the first 4 weeks of transmission and classically include a rash consistent with erythema migrans, followed by fever, chills, myalgia, headache, and polyarthralgia. If untreated, patients also can develop varying degrees of heart block, Bell palsy, or cognitive dysfunction. Notably, Bell palsy alone is not considered a significant neurologic sequela and is not an indication for treatment with ceftriaxone. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acyclovir is the correct pharmacotherapy for herpes simplex encephali- tis, which can present with painful vesicular rashes, classically located in the perioral or intraoral region. Symptoms of this disease include changes in mental status, seizures, and abnormalities within the temporal lobe on brain CT or MRI scans. Although oral doxycycline is a common treatment for acute or early disseminated Lyme disease, this patient shows signs of CNS involvement beyond isolated cranial nerve palsy. Some evidence suggests that Lyme meningitis responds to oral antibi- otics alone. It is difficult, however, to distinguish Lyme meningitis from Lyme en- cephalitis in the early acute phase of emergency department evaluation, and these diseases often occur concurrently. Suspected Lyme encephalitis should be treated with intravenous antibiotics. For a patient with possible meningitis, early administration of antibiotics and antivirals is the cornerstone of appropriate therapy. Only a brief deferment to obtain brain imaging and a lumbar puncture is reasonable; an extended delay mer- its reconsideration and expeditious medicine administration. Spinal fluid cultures can offer speciation and resistance patterns in the case of bacterial meningitis, but it can take hours to days to receive results. Thus, it is inappropriate to delay antibiotic administration and wait for culture results.

question: What is the most common cardiac manifestation of Lyme disease?
englishExplanation: Approximately 10% of patients with Lyme disease have cardiac manifes- tations, and among these, palpitations are most common. In a large surveil- lance study of patients with Lyme disease, 6.6% had palpitations. Other somewhat less common manifestations include myocarditis, pericarditis, conduction ab- normalities (such as atrioventricular block and new bundle-branch block), and left heart failure. Lyme disease is a tick-borne illness caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi that typically presents with erythema chronicum migrans and may cause cardiac manifestations. Patients who develop complete heart block most often present with syncope due to a slowed ventricular escape rhythm. Lyme disease patients who develop heart block may transiently require a cardiac pacemaker until the symptoms resolve. The cutaneous rash in Lyme disease is known as erythema migrans and is the first stage of the disease, occurring 2 to 30 days after exposure. Cardiac, neurologic, and joint complications do not occur until weeks to months after the original presentation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Chest pain and shortness of breath are not typical symptoms of Lyme dis- ease. Patients most commonly present with palpitations, syncope secondary to heart block, and other nonspecific complaints, such as generalized malaise, myalgias, and arthralgias. While pericarditis is a potential cardiac manifestation of Lyme disease, it is uncommon. It occurs in less than 1% of patients. Tachyarrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia, are uncommon in Lyme disease. While rare, cardiomegaly and congestive heart failure can be seen in some Lyme disease patients. Conduction delays are most likely, while premature ven- tricular contractions and tachyarrhythmia are unlikely. When young, otherwise healthy patients present with new-onset bundle-branch block or heart block, Lyme disease should be suspected, especially in areas where infection is common.

question: What is the treatment of choice for Rocky Mountain spotted fever in pediatric patients?
englishExplanation: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is a tick-borne illness caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for all age groups and should be ini- tiated within 5 days of symptom onset without waiting for confirmatory testing. Although tetracyclines are typically avoided in children younger than 8 years, new studies have shown a lack of permanent dental staining that was previously thought to occur with use in pediatric patients. Additionally, doxycycline has been shown to be superior to other antibiotics for the treatment of RMSF and should be given as soon as clinically suspected. Doxycycline should be given for at least 3 days after fever subsides, often 7 to 14 days. Contrary to its name, most cases (60%) are reported in the following five states: Arkansas, Missouri, North Carolina, Oklahoma, and Tennessee. Common symptoms of RMSF include fever, rash, headache, myalgias, ab- dominal pain, and vomiting. The rash is described as small macules starting on ex- tremities, including palms or soles (or both), and spreading to the torso and later be- coming petechial. In severe cases, the illness can cause a vasculitis, multi–organ sys- tem failure, and even death. Early treatment improves outcomes, especially in pedi- atric patients, who are five times more likely to die from RMSF than adults are. Incorrect Answer Explanations Chloramphenicol is sometimes used to treat RMSF in pregnant patients with a mild course of illness or in patients with life-threatening allergies to doxycycline. Chloramphenicol should not be given routinely, however, as there is an increased mortality rate compared to doxycycline. Additionally, there is no oral form available in the United States, and chloramphenicol has some severe side effects, including aplastic anemia and gray baby syndrome. Supportive care is encouraged in RMSF, especially for patients with severe illness and multi–organ system failure. However, supportive care alone is insufficient for the treatment of RMSF. Doxycycline must be given as soon as clinically suspected be- cause a delay in treatment leads to increased morbidity and mortality rates. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole should not be used to treatment RMSF because it is less effective than doxycycline. Furthermore, sulfa drugs can worsen infection. Key Points Symptoms of Rocky Mountain spotted fever include fever, myalgias, headache, ab- dominal pain, and a macular rash that starts on the extremities, spreads to the torso, and later becomes petechial. Don't wait for test results to come back — early diagnosis and treatment of Rocky Mountain spotted fever are required to prevent fatal outcomes. The treatment of choice for Rocky Mountain spotted fever is doxycycline, even in pe- diatric patients.

question: In the first week of illness, what is an early finding in diagnostic testing for Rocky Mountain spotted fever?
englishExplanation: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is the most commonly diagnosed and most severe rickettsial disease in the United States. Clinical manifesta- tions consist of the classic triad of fever, rash (absent in up to 20% of pa- tients), and severe headache, in addition to malaise, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. In most patients with RMSF who have a lumbar punc- ture, CSF pleocytosis is commonly seen and is indicative of aseptic meningitis. Late features include altered mental status, seizures, renal failure, myocarditis, and respiratory failure. RMSF was initially identified in Idaho and Montana (hence the name), but most cases are diagnosed in the southeastern United States, particularly in North and South Carolina and Tennessee. Doxycycline is the treat- ment of choice for RMSF for adults and children of all ages. The mortality rate ap- proaches 0.5%, and death is more likely in children. Serious illness and death are most effectively prevented when treatment is initiated within 5 days of symptom onset. Incorrect Answer Explanations Antibody testing is frequently negative within the first week of the illness, so physicians must maintain a high index of suspicion to make the diagnosis. Unfortunately, most other blood tests reveal only nonspecific abnormalities. CSF pleocytosis may be present within the first week of illness. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a tick-borne illness caused by Rickettsia rickettsii — a small, rod-shaped, gram-negative bacterium — therefore, spirochetes are not found in the blood. CSF pleocytosis, on the other hand, may be present within the first week of illness. Myocarditis can be a more severe manifestation of RMSF and can cause an elevated troponin level; however, myocarditis is a late and rare sequela, not an early finding in the RMSF disease course. CSF pleocytosis, on the other hand, may be present within the first week of illness.

question: A patient presents with fever and fatigue after being bitten by a tick in Connecticut. Laboratory studies detect malarial-like parasites on the patient's blood smear. There is no history of travel outside the United States in the patient's lifetime. What is the most likely infectious organism?
englishExplanation: Babesiosis is an infection caused by the parasitic organism Babesia microti. It is transmitted by the bite of the Ixodes scapularis (deer) tick and is mainly endemic to the northeast and upper midwest of the US. The most common symptoms are fever, myalgias, fatigue, and headache, and symptoms often occur within 1 to 4 weeks of the tick bite. In more severe cases, patients can become jaundiced and develop hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, DIC, and other end-organ damage (eg, renal failure; al- tered mental status; and hepatic, respiratory, and cardiac compromise). Laboratory studies may show hemolytic anemia; decreased haptoglobin; thrombocytopenia; and elevated LDH, creatinine, BUN, and transaminases. Babesiosis should be suspected in cases with typical exposure (tick bite in endemic area) and typical symptoms (fever, myalgias, fatigue, and headache) in the setting of typical laboratory studies (hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevation of aminotransferases). Some patients may not remember a tick, so endemic travel history is also important to obtain. In suspected cases, it is important to have the peripheral blood smear reviewed as it may show intraerythrocytic parasites that closely resemble malarial parasites. The di- agnosis can be confirmed with serologic and molecular tests specific to babesiosis. It is important to note that immunocompromised, asplenic and older patients are at higher risk for severe infection. Babesiosis can also be transmitted through organ transplant and blood donation. The US started screening the blood supply for B. mi- croti in 2019, but it is important to notify patients that they cannot donate blood. The treatment for babesiosis is atovaquone with azithromycin or alternatively clin- damycin with quinine. Incorrect Answer Explanations Borrelia burgdorferi is the bacteria that causes Lyme disease. Lyme disease is a tick- borne disease that is endemic to the northeast region of the United States, but it is not identified on peripheral blood smears. Lyme disease can present in many forms, including the classic erythema migrans (“bullseye rash”) as well as a third-degree heart block from carditis. Patients can have neurologic manifestations as well. Plasmodium falciparum is the parasitic organism that causes malaria. Malaria is en- demic to subtropical areas of the world and is a less likely cause of positive blood smear in this case. The ring-stage trophozoites of malaria can closely resemble babesiosis on RBC smear evaluation, so more specific testing should be done to rule out malaria in these cases. Patients can have dormant malaria infections for years af- ter initial exposure. Rickettsia rickettsii is the bacteria that causes rocky mountain spotted fever (RMSF). RMSF is a tick-borne illness that is most prevalent in the southeastern United States. RMSF is not identified on blood smear. Initial presentation is similar to babesiosis with fever and headache with myalgias. Most people develop a rash at some point, of- ten starting on the ankles and wrists as well as the palms and soles of feet.

question: A 20-year-old woman presents with malaise and a rash. Her vital signs include BP 110/70, P 90, and T 38.3°C (100.9°F). The physical examination reveals tonsillar swelling with exudates, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and a morbilliform rash. She says she has been taking antibiotics for a sore throat but is otherwise "never sick." What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Infectious mononucleosis is a viral syndrome most often caused by the EBV. The disease manifests as generalized fatigue, sore throat, and lym- phadenopathy, and it generally affects young, otherwise healthy people. Splenomegaly is present in up to 50% of cases. Blood analysis demonstrates reactive lymphocytosis and transaminitis. Treatment includes symptom relief; pa- tients should be instructed to abstain from activities such as contact sports to avoid the complication of splenic rupture. Pharyngitis associated with mononucleosis can be misdiagnosed as streptococcal pharyngitis. Antibiotics often trigger a rash in patients with mononucleosis, but the mechanism of this reaction is not well understood. Ampicillin and amoxicillin are the most common culprits, but rashes also can also be provoked by azithromycin, levofloxacin, and cephalexin. Incorrect Answer Explanations Rashes that develop after antibiotic use in patients with infectious mononucle- osis are commonly mistaken for drug-related or allergic reactions given the time of onset. However, these rashes are not considered true allergies because pa- tients can subsequently tolerate the same antibiotic without manifesting symptoms. Furthermore, this patient is not demonstrating signs of anaphylaxis, such as an- gioedema, shortness of breath, hypotension, or shock. This patient likely has in- fectious mononucleosis, a viral syndrome most often caused by the EBV. Coxsackievirus can present with a wide spectrum of clinical diseases, ranging from typical URIs to pericarditis or even aseptic meningitis. Rashes related to coxsack- ievirus typically manifest as red spots on the palms, soles, and oral mu- cosa (hand, foot, and mouth disease) and are unrelated to antibiotic use. This patient likely has infectious mononucleosis, a viral syndrome most often caused by the EBV. Pharyngitis associated with mononucleosis is commonly misinterpreted as strep- tococcal pharyngitis given its symptom of exudative tonsillitis with cervi- cal lymphadenopathy. However, splenomegaly is not seen with streptococcal pharyngitis. This patient likely has infectious mononucleosis, a viral syn- drome most often caused by the EBV.

question: A 20-year-old woman presents with a severe sore throat, fatigue, and fever that started 7 days ago. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F). On examination, exuda- tive pharyngitis is noted, and the cervical lymph nodes are enlarged. Rapid strep test is negative. What is the most likely laboratory finding?

options.text: Positive rapid antigen test for influenza A

englishExplanation: Infectious mononucleosis presents classically with fever, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy; this patient presents with all three signs. Although the diagnosis can usually be made clinically, laboratory testing can clarify the etiol- ogy. Results can include the presence of atypical lymphocytes, and 80% to 90% of patients have heterophile antibodies. Testing for these is less accurate early in the disease and in very young and older patients. Some recommend to test for EBV titers and not use the heterophile and antibody test since, in most cases, infectious mononucleosis is caused by the EBV. Serologic testing shows that 90% to 95% of the adult population has developed antibodies to EBV. It is spread by close contact; EBV does not survive outside the human host for any significant amount of time, so it is commonly spread by saliva exchange (as would happen with kissing or sharing food). A prodrome of fever, fatigue, and malaise is present for several days before the classic onset of symptoms, including severe bilateral exudative tonsil- litis or pharyngitis; tender bilateral cervical adenopathy; and in more than half of cases, a palpable spleen. Treatment is primarily supportive, with rest, hydration, analgesia, and antipyretics as needed. Patients should be instructed to avoid contact sports for at least 3 weeks to prevent injury to the spleen. Incorrect Answer Explanations Streptococcal pharyngitis is less likely given the negative rapid strep test. If the sus- pected diagnosis were streptococcal disease, consideration of an antistrep- tolysin O (ASO) titer would be reasonable. However, the ASO titer peaks 2 to 4 weeks after the patient has had streptococcal disease, so it is unlikely to be positive at the time of the acute symptoms, and is not commonly used in the emergency depart- ment. Streptococcal disease is treated with penicillin; if the patient is allergic, a macrolide can be given. Pharyngitis can be a sign of gonorrhea associated with oral sex. In this situa- tion, the pharyngitis is typically mild and is associated with a concurrent genital in- fection. Because the patient's presentation strongly suggests infectious mononucleosis — and because the incidence of gonococcal pharyngitis is signifi- cantly less common than that of infectious mononucleosis — a positive test result for N. gonorrhoeae infection is much less likely. Influenza A can present similarly to infectious mononucleosis — with fever, malaise, sore throat, and bilateral enlarged cervical adenopathy — but an exudative pharyngitis is unlikely. Other influenza A symptoms include chills and rigors, headache, and myalgias as well as a dry cough, ocular pain, and tearing. Rapid testing for the antigen is commercially available and can help direct antiviral therapy.

question: A 10-month-old girl presents with difficulty breathing and a 3-day history of cold symptoms. On examination, the patient is hypoxic and in respiratory distress. A chest x-ray reveals a lobar pneumonia, and laboratory testing is positive for in- fluenza A. Which statement describes the use of oseltamivir for this patient's treatment?

options.text: It has no benefit because she has been ill too long
It is contraindicated because she is critically ill
It is not approved for treatment in this age group
It should be administered as an oral liquid

correctAnswer: It should be administered as an oral liquid
englishExplanation: This patient is acutely ill with both influenza A and a concomitant pneumonia. Given the resistance of influenza to amantadine and rimantadine of up to 90%, os- eltamivir is the preferred medication in this situation. It is thought that the greatest advantage of treatment for influenza lies in starting pharmacotherapy soon after the onset of the illness, with the greatest effect within the first 24 to 48 hours. The CDC recommends all hospitalized infants and children be treated even if the diagnosis is made more than 48 hours after symptoms started. Oseltamivir is available in capsules or as a suspension; it is not currently available in an intravenous or an intramuscular form. Dosing is based on age and weight, and it is typically given for 5 days. In this case, for an infant younger than 12 months, the dose is 3 mg/kg twice a day. The clinician should also consider local epidemiology and, if appropriate, treat the child for a community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) infection. An association exists between influenza infec- tions in children and CA-MRSA pneumonias. For infants 12 months old and older, until a weight of 15 kg is reached (usually at about 3 years of age), dosing for oseltamivir is 30 mg twice a day. For children weighing between 15 kg and 23 kg, the dose is 45 mg twice a day. For children weighing between 23 kg and 40 kg, the dose is 60 mg twice a day. For children weighing more than 40 kg, teenagers, and adults, the dose is 75 mg twice a day. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although the greatest effect of antiviral treatment is achieved within the first 24 to 48 hours, the CDC recommends that all hospitalized infants and children be treated with antiviral medications such as oseltamivir, even if the diagnosis is made more than 48 hours after symptoms started. The presence of an acute illness requiring hospitalization for a young infant with a lo- bar pneumonia and hypoxia is an indication for pharmacologic treatment of in- fluenza, not a contraindication. This infant meets the criteria for treatment of influenza; oseltamivir is not contraindicated based on the available information. Treatment for actively ill individuals is indicated regardless of age, and treatment with oseltamivir is indicated for this patient. Oseltamivir is ap- proved by the FDA for use in infants 2 weeks old and older for acute infection, and the risk-benefit profile indicates that it should be used in seriously ill premature in- fants as well. However, oseltamivir is not approved for prophylaxis against influenza for children younger than 3 months. The difference between prophylaxis and acute treatment is important in this case. Key Points Oseltamivir is the treatment of choice for individuals of any age with an acute in- fluenza infection. Oseltamivir is available in oral formulations of capsules and a suspension.

question: The number of novel influenza A cases being diagnosed in a small geographic area starts to rise. Over the following weeks, the number of infections spreads rapidly across the United States, followed by multiple areas of infection reported across Europe. How is this infection pattern best described?
englishExplanation: Because the virus has spread to multiple countries and across continents, this infec- tion pattern is considered a “pandemic.” Novel infections will typically start in a lo- calized area, known as an “outbreak.” As the virus spreads relatively close to the original outbreak location, it is termed an “epidemic.” Once the epi- demic has spread to multiple countries or across continents, it is termed a “pandemic.” When considering viral infections, particularly influenza, it is im- portant to have an understanding of epidemiology and how disease propagates. Influenza is a common infection, particularly during “flu season” which tends to be from October to March each year. Seasonal flu strains will vary from year to year but are typically influenza A and B variants. Although this pattern is expected, viruses will periodically develop that are particularly contagious and virulent. This was re- cently seen in the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. Additional epidemiological terms that are used to describe a disease include “en- demic” (a persistent, constant, usually low level of the disease in a popula- tion) and “hyperendemic” (a constant, high level of disease across a popu- lation). The term “sporadic” is used to refer to a disease that occurs infre- quently and without any particular cadence. Examples of sporadic disease would be rabies and tetanus. Incorrect Answer Explanations The CDC definition of “endemic” is a disease that has a constant presence or an usual prevalence of a disease or infectious agent in a population within a geographic area. The disease in this question is a “pandemic,” as it is rapidly spreading across the world. According to the CDC, “epidemic” refers to an “increase, often sudden, in the number of cases of a disease above what is normally expected in that population in that area.” The disease in this case initially started out in a local- ized geographic area and would be epidemic at that point. However, since it has spread across the world, it is now a “pandemic.” An “outbreak” has a similar meaning to epidemic. However, the term “out- break” is usually used in the early stages of a disease's emergence when the cases are localized to a small geographic area. An example of an outbreak would be a sudden emergence of a group of cases within a neighborhood in a large city; it would become epidemic as the virus spreads throughout the city and beyond.

question: A 70-year-old patient with a history of hypertension presents to urgent care with cough, congestion, and fever. A point-of-care PCR test results as positive for in- fluenza B. Which finding should prompt a transfer to the emergency department for further evaluation?
englishExplanation: Influenza is a frequently diagnosed viral illness that has its highest prevalence from October to March, with an incubation period of 1 to 4 days after exposure. The pri- mary symptoms of influenza are fever, generalized malaise, myalgias, nonproductive cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea, and headache. Symptoms of more severe disease or influenza complications include severe range vital sign abnormalities, chest pain, difficulty breathing, leg swelling, syncope, and altered mental status. Risk of complications from influenza are significantly higher in the elderly as well as patients who are immunocompromised or have underlying chronic disease, such as diabetes, heart disease, and lung conditions. Complications that can occur from influenza include bacterial pneumo- nia, myositis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myocarditis, and heart failure. There are multiple influenza viral variants in the Orthomyxoviridae family. The most common are influenza A and influenza B. Influenza A viruses are de- scribed based on two surface proteins, being hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). There are 18 hemagglutinin protein variants and 11 neuraminidase variants. Influenza B variants are divided into Victoria and Yamagata lineages. Influenza is a significant disease that causes high levels of morbidity and mortality. For the 2023 to 2024 influenza season, the CDC estimates that there were an estimated 40 million influenza cases in the US, with 470,000 hospitalizations and 28,000 deaths. Incorrect Answer Explanations Fever is quite typical in influenza patients. A fever of 39.2°C (102.6°F) does not require transfer to the emergency department. This can be treated with over- the-counter antipyretics, such as ibuprofen or acetaminophen. Additionally, main- taining fluid hydration with cool or cold liquids will help with fever reduction as well. A heart rate of 110 would not be considered particularly concerning in the setting of acute influenza, particularly if the patient is febrile. If the patient otherwise lacks concerning findings on evaluation, this heart rate should not immedi- ately prompt an emergency department referral. If the urgent care clinician is con- cerned about discharge with an elevated heart rate, the patient can be given oral or intravenous hydration and antipyretics, and the heart rate can be reassessed. Nonproductive coughs are very common in influenza patients and do not require transfer to the emergency department. High fever with a productive cough, particularly 5 to 7 days after the first symptoms of influenza, may suggest the devel- opment of bacterial pneumonia and would prompt evaluation with a chest x-ray to assess for lung infiltrates.

question: What is the best estimate for average influenza vaccine efficacy over the past decade?
englishExplanation: Reviewing data from 2009 to 2025, the vaccine efficacy has ranged from 19% during the 2014 to 2015 season to 60% during the 2010 to 2011 sea- son. The majority of seasons fall between 30% to 50% efficacy, with the average being 43%. Development of the annual influenza vaccine is a complicated process that begins long before the vaccine is released. Data is shared and analyzed among numerous health organizations, including the United States CDC; WHO; The Francis Crick Institute in London; and health agencies in Japan, China, and Australia. Using laboratory reports and clinical studies, the best estimations for the most likely influenza strains are made and the vaccine is created to target those strains. Currently, seasonal influenza vaccines are trivalent, covering two in- fluenza A variants (H1N1 and H3N2) and one influenza B variant (Victoria lineage). As a result of this process, the vaccine efficacy for being on tar- get for the seasonal influenza strains is variable year to year. Despite its variable effi- cacy, when considered broadly, the influenza vaccine is quite effective in reducing hospitalizations, ICU admissions, and deaths across all populations — most notably in patients who are elderly or have comorbid conditions. A 2017 study by Rondy et al, shows that hospitalization rates among patients vaccinated against influenza were 40% lower than in patients not vaccinated. For the 2023 to 2024 influenza sea- son, the CDC estimates that there were an estimated 40 million influenza cases in the US with 470,000 of those being hospitalized and 28,000 deaths. Hence, receiving the influenza vaccine helps significantly reduce the burden of disease associated with influenza cases. Incorrect Answer Explanations In the past 15 years, there has only been one season that the influenza vaccine efficacy was <20%. That was during the 2014 to 2015 season when it was 19%. All other years have been significantly higher, with an average of 43% vaccine efficacy each year. Most years have not seen influenza vaccine efficacy in the 60% to 80% range. The highest in the recent past was 60% during the 2010 to 2011 season. Most other years have had efficacy in the 30% to 50% range, with an average of 43% efficacy over the past 15 years. Over the past 15 years, there has been no season that has seen influenza vaccine effi- cacy higher than 80%. The average has been 43%, with the vast majority of seasons being between 30% to 50% efficacious.

question: Which patient would likely benefit most from the use of oseltamivir in treating in- fluenza A?

options.text: 3-year-old girl with no medical history and 72 hours of flu-like symptoms
25-year-old man with no medical history and 24 hours of flu-like symptoms
60-year-old man with a history of hypertension and 6 days of flu-like symptoms
75-year-old woman with a history of diabetes and COPD and 36 hours of flu symptoms

correctAnswer: 75-year-old woman with a history of diabetes and COPD and 36 hours of flu symptoms
englishExplanation: The 75-year-old woman with a history of diabetes and COPD and 36 hours of flu symptoms would be most likely to benefit from oseltamivir. Oseltamivir is one of many antiviral medications that acts by inhibiting neuraminidase, a viral enzyme involved in helping release new virions from host cell surfaces. The Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) has level A recommendations to treat hospitalized patients and those with comorbidities with os- eltamivir or other neuraminidase inhibitor regardless of symptom onset. Particularly susceptible patient populations are those 2 years of age and younger, those 65 and older, patients who are pregnant or recently post- partum, immunocompromised patients, or those with significant comor- bidities (ie, diabetes, COPD, asthma, interstitial lung disease, cardiac dis- ease, and malignancy). Most studies are equivocal or show a reduction in symptom duration of no more than 12 to 24 hours. Despite wide-spread marketing, the overall efficacy of os- eltamivir is poor. A large systematic review and meta-analysis published in Lancet in 2024 suggests there is low certainty of evidence that oseltamivir “might reduce” duration of hospitalization in patients with influenza. For outpatients with mild dis- ease and no concerning comorbidities or risk factors, the IDSA has level C recom- mendations for treatment; if treatment is initiated, it should be done so within 48 hours of symptom onset. Dosing regimens are typically twice daily for 5 days in patients with confirmed in- fluenza. These doses will need adjustment in the setting of renal disease. Oseltamivir may also be used for prophylaxis after exposure in high-risk patients and is typically dosed once daily for a week. Nausea and vomiting are frequently reported side effects of oseltamivir. Although it is less common, there is also an associa- tion with the development of delirium and hallucination in patients taking oseltamivir. Incorrect Answer Explanations A 3-year-old patient with no medical history would be considered overall low risk for developing severe influenza. Additionally, it is not recommended to initiate os- eltamivir in this population after 48 hours, given an overall poor efficacy at that point. Although the 25-year-old man is within the 48 hour window of initiating oseltamivir, this patient is otherwise healthy and is overall low risk for significant influenza com- plications. As such, the 75-year-old woman with multiple comorbidities would benefit more from this medication than he would. A 60-year-old patient with only hypertension and no other risk factors is unlikely to benefit much from oseltamivir. Additionally, this patient has been symptomatic for 6 days. It is not recommended to initiate oseltamivir in otherwise low-risk patients af- ter 48 hours of symptom onset.

question: What is the sensitivity and specificity of point-of-care PCR flu swabs for testing influenza?
englishExplanation: Multiple tests are available to diagnose viral illnesses, including influenza. Point-of- care (POC) PCR tests for influenza have become highly sensitive and spe- cific, consistently >95% for both. Many of these tests (including influenza A and B, RSV, and COVID-19) have been developed as POC tests that are able to be performed in the clinic space, taking less than 30 minutes to run. This is particularly helpful when evaluating patients and determining what treatment should most appropriately be prescribed. Rapid influenza diagnostics tests (RIDTs) are also available. These tests tend to detect the presence of viral antigens. These tests are highly specific (>95%) but are much less sensitive, averaging around 40% to 70%. It is important to understand the sensitivity and specificity of the tests being used in your clinical environment, as this may significantly change the management of patients. If your clinic is using an RIDT, it is much more likely to have false-negative results. This should be considered when diagnosing and treating a patient with flu-like symptoms. Incorrect Answer Explanations POC PCR influenza tests are highly sensitive and specific, with most studies suggest- ing >95% for both. An influenza test with a low sensitivity and a high specificity would be more consistent with a RIDT or influenza antigen detection test. A test with 40% sensitivity and >98% specificity would more likely be a rapid antigen detection test. POC PCR influenza tests are highly sensitive and specific, with most studies suggesting >95% for both. An influenza test with a low sensitivity and a high specificity would be more consistent with a RIDT or influenza antigen detection test. A sensitivity of 50% and specificity of 80% is not consistent with either influenza POC PCR or antigen detection tests. PCR for influenza is >95% sensitive and specific, and antigen detection/RIDT tests are very specific (>95%) but have low sensitivity.

question: What is the primary strategy for preventing hantavirus infection and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS)?
englishExplanation: The Sin Nombre virus, a strain of hantavirus that causes hantavirus pul- monary syndrome (HPS), was first discovered in the southwestern United States in 1993. The most common host of this rodent-borne RNA virus is the deer mouse, but other kinds of mice and rats are known to spread disease. Thus, rodent control is the primary strategy for disease prevention. In places where carrier rodents are known to live, traps should be placed, holes or gaps should be sealed, and precau- tions should be taken when cleaning infested areas. Humans typically contract the pathogen by breathing aerosolized particles of rodent urine and feces, often while cleaning. Patients experience nonspecific viral symptoms for 3 to 5 days, fol- lowed by pulmonary edema and severe myocardial depression. Treatment is sup- portive care, usually in an ICU setting. Although the incidence is low, mortality rates are significant (30%-50%). Incorrect Answer Explanations There is currently no vaccination to prevent the Sin Nombre virus. Rodent control is the most effective strategy for preventing hantavirus infection. Ribavirin has been shown to decrease mortality rates in patients with hantavirus in- fections that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; however, the drug has no proven benefit in the treatment of HPS. No formal recommendation cur- rently exists regarding the use of ribavirin or other antiviral medications for prophy- laxis or early cases of HPS; further investigation is required to determine the poten- tial role of these agents. Although respiratory protection potentially could prevent exposure to airborne urine and feces particles, this approach to prophylaxis is impractical in daily life. Primary rodent control is preferred. Key Points Hantavirus spreads via aerosolized particles of rodent urine and feces. Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome starts out as a mild viral infection but is followed by severe pulmonary edema and myocardial depression. Rodent control is the best way to prevent the spread of hantavirus diseases.

question: What symptom in a patient's history best supports concern for severe dengue fever?
englishExplanation: Patients with severe dengue disease often exhibit hemorrhagic signs and end-organ damage. Dengue fever is an illness that often presents in stages. The WHO lists some symptoms that are potential warning signs the patient is developing severe dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome): severe ab- dominal pain, blood in the vomit or stool, persistent vomiting, hep- atomegaly, tachypnea, restlessness, fatigue, and bleeding from the gums or nose. Notably, patients who have previously been infected with dengue are con- sidered to be at higher risk of developing severe dengue. Dengue fever is caused by an arbovirus and is transmitted by mosquito vec- tors. It is most commonly found in Asian countries, the Americas (Caribbean and Mexico), and the western pacific. Patients can have milder viral symptoms or have se- vere dengue fever, which can be fatal. The typical febrile phase of dengue can consist of high fevers (>40°C [104°F]), severe headache, rash, pain behind eyes, lym- phadenopathy, myalgias, bone pain, nausea, and vomiting. Approximately 3 to 7 days after onset, patients may reach a critical point where the illness may progress to severe dengue.
