A tourniquet test can be performed on these patients to look for petechiae, which would be concerning for more severe disease. For this test, a blood pressure cuff is inflated on the arm to a point midway between the diastolic and systolic BP and remains in place for 5 minutes. The test is positive if there are more than 10 petechiae in one square in 2 minutes after deflating the cuff. Bedside POCUS may also be helpful to identify “plasma leakage” in these pa- tients who are experiencing severe dengue, such as pleural effusions and ascites. The diagnosis can be officially made with serologic testing or viral studies. There is no specific treatment for dengue fever other than supportive care. Aspirin and NSAIDs are not recommended for treatment in these patients because of their anticoagulant properties, so acetaminophen is recommended for pain and fever control. There is now also a vaccine available which is given to patients aged 9 to 45 who live in endemic areas and have had at least one case of dengue infection in the past. According to the WHO, unvaccinated patients who had not had previous infec- tion may have had better outcomes than those with no history who were vaccinated, thereby making vaccination most beneficial in those with previous infection. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bone pain is often attributed to severe myalgias and is a typical symptom that patients may experience with dengue fever, which is why it is often referred to as “break bone fever.” Dengue fever is also associated with muscle pain and joint pain, which is present in about 70% of patients. These symptoms, however, do not necessarily indicate transition to severe dengue. Fever is common in both dengue and severe dengue fever, and it is often high (>40°C [104°F]). When patients enter a critical phase of dengue between day 3 to 7 of symptoms, fever may begin to decrease. Signs of severe dengue may begin to manifest around this time as well. Thus, fever is not a helpful sign in differentiating severe dengue fever. Rash can be seen in about 50% of dengue fever cases. It is a maculopapular or macular rash that can occur on the face, trunk, or limbs, and it may also be pru- ritic. The rash alone does not predict a more severe form of dengue fever, but a pe- techial rash can develop in hemorrhagic dengue and can look similar to the rash in meningococcemia.

question: What is the recommended treatment for arboviral infections such as dengue fever or yellow fever?
englishExplanation: Unfortunately, there is no specific treatment recommended for arboviral in- fections. The mainstay of treatment is supportive care, of which acetaminophen is used to control pain and fever. In dengue or other hemorrhagic fevers, avoiding NSAIDs and aspirin as part of supportive care is recommended, as these may worsen bleeding. Monitoring, antiemetics, intravenous fluids (as necessary), and re- assessment are also important. Arboviral infections are a group of viruses that are transmitted through the bite of mosquitoes, ticks, and flies. Japanese encephalitis, yellow fever, dengue fever, West Nile virus, Zika virus, and Chikungunya are some of the more common forms of arboviruses. These viruses often present with more mild forms of illness, but patients can develop severe disease including encephalitis and hemorrhagic fevers which can be fa- tal. In cases of more severe arboviral infections patients tend to have four syndromes: hemorrhagic fever, arthritis and rash, fever and myalgia, and encephalitis. A few ar- boviral infections have preventative vaccinations available that may be recommended when traveling to endemic areas. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acyclovir is not a recommended treatment for arboviral infections. The main treatment in these infections is supportive care. In patients who have symptoms that are concerning for encephalitis or meningitis, acyclovir should initially be or- dered until HSV infection is ruled out, but it should not be continued once HSV en- cephalitis is ruled out. IVIG is not a recommended treatment for arboviral infections. The recom- mended treatment is supportive care. IVIG is sometimes used as postexposure pro- phylaxis in immunocompromised patients who are exposed to measles or infant bot- ulism. It provides passive transient immunity to help fight certain infections. Remdesivir is not recommended for treating arboviruses. Supportive care is the recommended approach for all arboviral infections. Remdesivir is a nucleotide analog RNA polymerase inhibitor medication that was created to target COVID-19 infection.

question: A 25-year-old woman presents with fever, altered mental status, vesicular sores on her lower lip, and new-onset seizures. Given the most likely diagnosis, what CSF analysis results are expected?

options.text: 4 WBCs with a glucose level 60% of serum glucose
360 WBCs with a high lymphocyte differential
2,450 WBCs with a high neutrophil differential

correctAnswer: 360 WBCs with a high lymphocyte differential
englishExplanation: Although the most common viral etiologies of meningoencephalitis are nonpolio en- teroviruses (85%), this patient's presentation is highly suspicious for HSV en- cephalitis, given the labial vesicular lesions and seizures. With that in mind, the CSF analysis is expected to be typical for viral encephalitis, with moder- ately elevated WBCs and a high lymphocyte differential. Also likely are a normal to elevated opening pressure, a glucose level of approximately 60% of serum glucose, and greater than 200 mg/dL of protein. Encephalitis is inflammation of the brain; myelitis is inflammation of the spinal cord. It is rare and unlikely to have encephalitis without concomitant meningitis. Even though most pa- tients with viral meningoencephalitis have a benign course, the mortality and mor- bidity rates for HSV encephalitis are high, and any suspicion for this diagnosis should prompt intravenous administration of acyclovir. Patients with suspected HSV en- cephalitis should be admitted to the hospital; a critical care setting also should be considered. Incorrect Answer Explanations A test result of 4 WBCs with a glucose level 60% of serum glucose would be expected from negative or normal CSF. Normal CSF contains very few WBCs (typically <5) with a variable neutrophil predominance, given the lower num- ber of total cells. Opening pressure would be normal; the CSF glucose level would be approximately 60% of serum glucose; and the level of CSF protein would be less than 200 mg/dL. Fungal meningoencephalitis is more common in immunocompromised patients, such as those with an HIV infection. The CSF in these patients has an elevated WBC count compared to normal, but not typically to the extremes of bacterial meningitis, and lacks a neutrophil predominance. The glucose level is mildly low, and the protein level is extremely elevated compared to normal. Bacterial meningitis classically presents with fever, nuchal rigidity, and photophobia. The CSF from a patient with bacterial meningitis contains markedly elevated WBCs with a neutrophil predominance, a low glucose level (lower than the normal value of 60% of serum glucose), and an ele- vated protein level. The most common bacterial causes of meningoencephalitis are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Listeria mono- cytogenes in the extremes of age. Early treatment with broad-spectrum antibi- otics remains the hallmark of therapy for bacterial meningitis, typically with ceftri- axone and vancomycin with the addition of ampicillin in patients with concern for Listeria. Antibiotics should never be delayed in order to obtain an "untainted" CSF culture. Key Points Bacterial results from CSF include significantly elevated WBCs with a neutrophil pre- dominance, a low glucose level, and a high protein level. Viral results from CSF include moderately elevated WBCs with a lymphocyte pre- dominance, a normal glucose level, and an elevated protein level. Treat patients with antiviral agents without delay if the clinical picture suggests HSV encephalitis.

question: Which clinical presentation of herpes zoster most suggests an underlying immuno- compromised state?

options.text: Lesions in three or more dermatomes
Vesicles on the tip of the nose

correctAnswer: Lesions in three or more dermatomes
englishExplanation: Herpes zoster is the reactivation of the dormant varicella-zoster virus that causes a painful vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution. The rash characteris- tically involves one dermatome and is unilateral. Involvement of three or more dermatomes, known as disseminated zoster, should raise suspicion for an underlying immunocompromised state, such as HIV/AIDS, lympho- proliferative disorder, chronic immunosuppressant therapy, or organ transplant. Healthy people can also have reactivation of herpes zoster, and one in every three persons has zoster at some point in life. Incidence increases with age and is most common in patients older than 60 years. If an immunocompromised state is not al- ready known, further investigation is warranted. Incorrect Answer Explanations Zoster lesions can become superinfected with bacterial pathogens in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts, often as a result of ex- coriation and skin breakage. Treatment should include appropriate antibiotic therapy in addition to antiviral therapy. Disseminated zoster, lesions in three or more der- matomes, should raise suspicion for immune compromise. Vesicles in the auditory canal suggest herpes zoster oticus, or Ramsay- Hunt syndrome, and can occur in an immunocompetent host. The characteristic triad includes vesicles in the auditory canal, unilateral facial paralysis, and ear pain. Treatment involves oral steroids in addition to antiviral medication. Disseminated zoster, lesions in three or more dermatomes, should raise suspicion for immune compromise. Zoster vesicles on the tip of the nose, also known as Hutchinson sign, repre- sent reactivation of the virus along the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve. The nasociliary branch also innervates the cornea and should prompt evaluation of the eye for herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Reactivation along any trigeminal distribution can occur in immunocompetent hosts. Treatment involves topical oph- thalmic steroids in addition to antiviral medication. Disseminated zoster, lesions in three or more dermatomes, should raise suspicion for immune compromise.

question: A 24-year-old woman who is 12 weeks pregnant presents with a widespread itchy rash, shortness of breath, and nonproductive cough. The physical examination re- veals a diffuse, vesicular rash in various stages of development. A chest x-ray demonstrates a bilateral interstitial pattern. What is the correct management? Credit: CDC/J.D. Millar, MD, MPH, DTPH.

options.text: Administer valacyclovir orally and discharge with follow-up in the morning
Administer varicella-zoster immune globulin and admit
Start cefazolin intravenously and discharge home on cephalexin

englishExplanation: This patient has varicella pneumonia, and all pregnant patients with vari- cella pneumonia should be admitted and treated with intravenous acy- clovir. Varicella can be a dangerous infection in adults, especially in those who are pregnant or immunocompromised or if pneumonitis develops. When associated with pregnancy, varicella pneumonia is the leading cause of varicella-re- lated illness and death in adults, with a reported maternal mortality rate of up to 44%. Varicella presents as a full-body rash that starts on the trunk and is characterized by asynchronous vesicular lesions. The rash shown here is a clas- sic example, with differing stages of scattered, vesiculopustular lesions with an ery- thematous base. Other complications of varicella pneumonia in pregnant patients in- clude development of congenital varicella syndrome in the baby and, if the mother develops varicella rash right before or after delivery, risk for neonatal varicella. Fortunately, reported mortality rates from varicella pneumonia have been significantly reduced since the introduction of intravenous acyclovir. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pregnancy is a risk factor for complications from varicella pneumonia, so discharging this patient with instructions for follow-up care is the incorrect management. Up to 40% of pregnant patients with varicella pneumonia require mechanical ventilation, necessitating admission for close monitoring. Additionally, oral valacyclovir is unlikely to be a sufficient treatment for the infection. Patients with se- vere varicella infection and those at risk for complications should be admitted and treated with intravenous acyclovir. Varicella-zoster immune globulin (VZIG) is indicated for prophylaxis in susceptible pregnant patients who have been exposed to the varicella- zoster virus. The primary purpose of VZIG prophylaxis is to prevent or attenuate maternal disease. Although VZIG has been used in combination with antiviral medi- cations in the treatment of acute varicella infections such as varicella pneumonia, the mainstay of treatment is intravenous acyclovir. Isolated varicella lesions, especially those with a superimposed cellulitis induced by manual trauma, can be confused with impetigo, which often responds to antibiotic therapy that covers both Streptococcus and Staphylococcus, such as cefazolin and cephalexin. To provide correct treatment, distinguishing between the two condi- tions is important. Impetigo frequently occurs on the face, neck, and extremities and can include blisters with yellowish liquid; varicella lesions often concentrate on the trunk and face and can include blisters with clear liquid. Given this patient's respira- tory symptoms and chest x-ray findings, the diagnosis of varicella pneumonia is clear, and the correct treatment is intravenous acyclovir.

question: Which finding most strongly suggests that a patient has chickenpox (varicella) and not smallpox (variola)?

options.text: Diffuse rash of vesicles in various stages of development
Greatest density of lesions on the face and neck
Patient with fever, myalgias, malaise, and headache

correctAnswer: Diffuse rash of vesicles in various stages of development
englishExplanation: The rash of varicella (chickenpox) has vesicles that appear in different stages of development and classically appear as “teardrops” on an erythe- matous base. The vesicles of chickenpox also tend to start on the trunk and then spread to the rest of the body. By contrast, the now-eradicated disease of variola (smallpox) usually features uniform vesicles in the same stage of devel- opment that begin on the head and face before spreading to the rest of the body. For both diseases, lesions progress from maculopapular to vesicular to pustular and then form crusts. Chickenpox has become drastically less common since the advent and routine use of the vaccine, but sporadic cases still occur. Smallpox was officially eradicated over 40 years ago, but there is still concern that smallpox could be revived as a biological weapon. Incorrect Answer Explanations Smallpox lesions begin on the face and neck, before spreading to the rest of the body. Notably, the face and neck also have the highest concentration of lesions in these patients. Chickenpox, on the other hand, usually starts on the trunk and spreads to the rest of the body, but the trunk is where the majority of vari- cella lesions are located. Both chickenpox and smallpox may cause oral lesions in the oropharynx, but these are not specific or diagnostic findings. By contrast, the oral lesions of measles (otherwise known as Koplik spots) are clustered white lesions on the buc- cal mucosa that are pathognomonic for the disease. Both smallpox and chickenpox can cause systemic symptoms, such as fever, myalgias, malaise, and headache. These criteria, however, do not differ- entiate the two diseases.

question: In a patient who has HIV/AIDS and suspected pneumocystis pneumonia, which finding is an indication to administer steroids?
englishExplanation: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is one of the most common opportunistic infections in persons who have HIV/AIDs. The disease, which is caused by the fun- gus Pneumocystis jirovecii, can be managed with trimethoprim-sul- famethoxazole for 21 days. Steroids are indicated for the management of severe PCP, as indicated by a PaO less than 70 mm Hg, an A-a gradient of 35 or more, or an SpO level less than 92% on room air. Common treatment regimens include prednisone (40 mg PO twice daily with a 3-week taper) or methyl- prednisolone (starting intravenous dose four times a day). Patients who require steroids should be admitted to the hospital because their conditions typically worsen in the days following the initiation of therapy. Symptoms of PCP often are insidious and include nonproductive cough, fatigue, malaise, fever, and dyspnea. In the emer- gency department, the diagnosis is made clinically; confirmatory testing requires di- 2 2 rect bronchoscopy and should not be delayed if suspicion is high (eg, patients who have CD4 counts <200 or previous opportunistic infections). Incorrect Answer Explanations Pneumocystis pneumonia is commonly distinguished on chest x-ray by diffuse inter- stitial opacities in a characteristic batwing distribution. These hazy opacities with preserved alveolar and vascular markings are often described as having a ground-glass appearance. However, x-ray findings are normal in up to 20% of pa- tients with PCP, so plain film imaging alone should not be used to rule out the dis- ease. Chest CT can be useful if clinical suspicion remains high despite normal x-ray findings. A low CD4 count should prompt consideration for an opportunistic infec- tion; however, this finding should not be used to guide any specific medi- cal therapy. A CD4 count below 500 is considered abnormal, but a count below 200 with a concomitant HIV infection is an AIDS-defining finding. Patients with CD4 counts below 200, who are deemed high risk for PCP, should receive antibiotic pro- phylaxis. Patients with CD4 counts below 100 have an increased susceptibility to tox- oplasmosis and Mycobacterium avium complex infections, and those with counts be- low 50 are at increased risk for cytomegalovirus infections. Serum LDH often is elevated in patients with PCP. Although this finding has a 90% sensitivity for detecting the disease, its specificity is poor. An el- evated LDH in the right clinical context should prompt the physician to consider a di- agnosis of PCP; however, it should not be used to guide medical management. Key Points Pneumocystis pneumonia is one of the most common opportunistic infections in pa- tients with HIV/AIDS. Treatment for pneumocystis pneumonia is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 21 days. Add steroids to treat severe pneumocystis pneumonia is defined by PaO less than 70 mm Hg, A-a gradient 35 or more, or SpO less than 92% on room air.

question: Which patient should be evaluated for a significant immunocompromising condition?

options.text: 17-year-old who has itchy, red, raised plaque on the inner thigh extending to the groin
22-year-old who has fever, cough, and night sweats following a recent trip to Arizona
32-year-old who has white plaques in the posterior pharynx with odynophagia and redness
38-year-old who has multiple well-demarcated spots of lighter skin on the chest and back

correctAnswer: 32-year-old who has white plaques in the posterior pharynx with odynophagia and redness
englishExplanation: White plaques in the posterior pharynx with associated odynophagia strongly suggest esophageal candidiasis, which is a fungal infection caused by Candida albicans. This pathology is typically found in significantly immunocompromised patients, including those with HIV/AIDS (in whom esophageal candidiasis is an AIDS-defining illness) or cancer with neutropenia. The presence of thrush or oral candidiasis is not unusual in patients using steroids for conditions such as asthma, but the presence of odynophagia suggests a more extensive involve- ment of the candidiasis. Clinical suspicion should arise in any immunocompromised patient with new odynophagia or oral thrush and concomitant odynophagia. Oral thrush without esophageal involvement should not cause discomfort with swallowing and can occur in immunocompetent patients who regularly use inhaled corticos- teroids without rinsing. The diagnosis can be confirmed with upper endoscopy. Esophageal candidiasis is typically treated with fluconazole for 14 to 21 days. Incorrect Answer Explanations Raised, red plaques in the inguinal crease suggest tinea cruris, or jock itch. Tinea cruris can certainly affect immunocompromised persons, but it is common among healthy persons. Thus, its presence alone is not a marker of serious underlying immunocompromise. Tinea cruris is a dermatophyte infection that usually in- volves the groin but can spread to the buttocks, thighs, and perineum while sparing the genitalia; notably, it is more common in men. The fungus is transmitted via per- son-to-person contact or autoinoculation from simultaneous tinea pedis or corporis. The lesions, which are similar to those of tinea corporis, classically appear as erythe- matous, annular plaques with central clearing and sharply demarcated borders that may contain vesicles. Tinea cruris should be treated with topical azoles, and the af- fected areas should be kept clean and dry to prevent recurrences. Recent travel to the Southwest with associated pulmonary and systemic symptoms should prompt consideration for coccidioidomycosis, or valley fever. Valley fever can afflict immunocompetent patients who have traveled to en- demic areas, including the southwestern United States, regions of Mexico, and South America. Valley fever is usually self-limited. Symptoms include fever, cough, night sweats, headache, and shortness of breath. Pregnant patients and those with se- vere disease, known immunosuppression, or underlying cardiopulmonary disorders should be treated with an oral azole antifungal agent, such as ketoconazole, flucona- zole, or itraconazole. Tinea versicolor, a common fungal rash caused by Malassezia furfur, is not suggestive of an immunocompromised state. The fungus requires oil to grow and is more common in teenagers. Although hyperpigmented or hypopig- mented, scaly truncal lesions are classic signs of the disease, the rash can be any color, hence the name. First-line treatment of tinea versicolor is the daily application of topical selenium sulfide shampoo for 1 week. Topical azoles also can be used. Patients should be aware that discoloration can last several months and is not a sign that treatment failed.

question: Which finding is most commonly associated with acute retroviral syndrome?
englishExplanation: Acute retroviral syndrome has a constellation of variable symptoms and is associated with early HIV infection, usually developing within 4 weeks of infection. It classically presents with fever, myalgias, fatigue, nonexuda- tive pharyngitis, diarrhea, headache, and diffuse adenopathy. Acute retro- viral syndrome also has distinct mucocutaneous findings, such as painful mucosal ul- cers and a generalized, erythematous, maculopapular rash that can affect the palms and soles. Patients with symptoms suggestive of acute retroviral syndrome should be tested for HIV immediately. Fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody tests can detect p24 antigens or HIV antibodies beginning 2 weeks after exposure. HIV RNA (viral load) testing is confirmatory and can detect infection after 1 week. Negative results on both an antigen/antibody test and an RNA test effectively rule out HIV infection. Patients presenting within 2 weeks of a high-risk exposure should undergo follow- up testing within the appropriate time frame. Local protocols may vary, so please check local protocols for appropriate HIV testing. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pharyngitis is a common symptom of acute retroviral syndrome, but it usually presents without exudates or tonsillitis. Exudative pharyngitis is more strongly associated with bacterial pharyngitis and mononucleosis. Acute retroviral syndrome is associated with decreased CD4 counts and results in significant lymphopenia, not lymphocytosis. Lymphopenia is often transient and makes patients vulnerable to early opportunistic infections. Lymphocytosis is not associated with acute retroviral syndrome and is more strongly associated with other viral illnesses, such as mononucleosis. Dry cough can be a symptom of acute retroviral infection. Productive cough, on the other hand, should raise concern for superimposed pneu- monia, given the risk of opportunistic infection in early HIV infection.

question: An HIV patient presents with altered mental status, severe headaches, and fever. Brain MRI is obtained and shown below. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient? Credit: Copyright 2022 Dr. Ian Bickle. Image courtesy of Dr. Ian Bickle and Radiopaedia.org. rID: 53993. Used under license.
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms of CNS toxoplasmosis. CNS toxoplasmosis is treated with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine. Leucovorin is administered with these drugs to prevent potential megaloblastic anemia and pancy- topenia that can result from pyrimethamine therapy. Patients with poorly con- trolled HIV are at risk for many infections, including toxoplasmosis. Typically, toxoplasmosis is seen in patients with a CD4 count less than 100 cells/mm. Brain CT with contrast or brain MRI will show multiple punctate or ring- enhancing lesions with surrounding edema, as seen in this patient's MRI image. Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular protozoan that is most commonly en- countered in cat feces or undercooked meat. Most immunocompetent people are able to clear the T. gondii oocysts when ingested. However, those that are im- munosuppressed, especially those with AIDS, are at high risk for developing a dis- seminated toxoplasmosis infection. In addition to encephalitis, toxoplasmosis can involve pneumonitis and chorioretinitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acyclovir is used to treat HSV. HSV can cause severe infections in both immuno- competent and immunosuppressed patients. HSV is known to cause meningitis and encephalitis, but it is unlikely to cause multiple intracranial lesions, as seen in this case. Clotrimazole and nystatin are used to treat thrush from candidiasis. These agents are ineffective against toxoplasmosis or other infections, such as cryptococcosis. Ethambutol and clarithromycin are used to treat Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC). MAC causes widespread infection and affects multiple organ sys- tems. Typically, this is seen in HIV patients with a CD4 count of less than 100 cells/mm. Although there are case reports of intracranial lesions caused by MAC, this is a rare finding overall, and this patient is most likely presenting with toxoplasmosis.

question: Below what CD4 count does cryptococcal meningitis become much more likely in a patient with AIDS?
englishExplanation: Patients with a CD4 count of less than 100 cells/mm are at a higher risk of developing cryptococcosis than patients with higher cell counts. Some sources suggest that the likelihood of cryptococcosis is considerably higher at less than 50 cells/mm. Even so, it is understood that this infection is much more likely to occur at lower CD4 counts and in cases of severe AIDS. Cryptococcosis is caused by invasive Cryptococcus fungi, which can cause severe infections in immunosuppressed patients. The infection most often causes meningitis, with fever, altered mental status, and neurologic deficits being the usual presenting symptoms. The diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis is made by testing CSF for cryptococcal antigens, culturing for fungus, or performing the classic India ink stain. Treatment includes intravenous amphotericin B and oral flucytosine for 2 weeks. Subsequently, patients are put on a long, 8- to 10-week course of fluconazole. Incorrect Answer Explanations A CD4 count of 150 cells/mm is the level at which patients start to be- come more susceptible to histoplasmosis. Histoplasmosis is caused by the fun- 3 3 3 gus Histoplasma capsulatum and is typically treated with antifungal medications, such as amphotericin, fluconazole, and itraconazole. A CD4 count of 200 cells/mm is the level at which patients with AIDS be- come more susceptible to Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). PCP is most often treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and prednisone. A CD4 count of 250 cells/mm is the level at which patients become more susceptible to coccidioidomycosis, another fungal infection. Coccidioidomycosis is treated with antifungals such as fluconazole.

question: A patient with HIV and a CD4 count of 100 cells/mm presents with symptoms of pneumonia. The following chest x-ray is obtained, and antibiotics are started. Under what circumstance should the physician also administer prednisone? 3 Credit: Tomatheart/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: This patient is showing signs of Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). Treatment for PCP includes either oral or intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), depending on the infection severity. Prednisone should be added for patients with an SaO of less than 70 mm Hg or an alveolar-arterial (A-a) oxygen gradient of greater than 35 mm Hg. Some sources also suggest starting 2 prednisone for patients with room-air SpO of less than 92%. Steroids have shown a decrease in mortality in such patients. This patient meets the criteria for AIDS (ie, HIV positive with a CD4 count of less than 200 cells/mm or an opportunistic infection). This patient has both a low CD4 count and symptoms of pneumonia. Patients with a CD4 count less than 200 cells/mm are at increased risk for developing PCP, an infection caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii. This patient's chest x-ray is notable for diffuse bilateral infiltrates with a predilection for the perihilar regions, which is the pattern most fre- quently observed in PCP. Symptoms of PCP may be vague, especially early in the course, so a high in- dex of suspicion should be maintained for this diagnosis. Additionally, LDH is often elevated in these cases, although overall sensitivity and specificity is poor. Additional agents include clindamycin and primaquine phosphate, atovaquone, or pentamidine, if patients have trouble tolerating TMP-SMX. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although A-a gradient is used as a measurement to determine if prednisone should be administered, this patient's A-a gradient of 25 mm Hg is below the thresh- old. The gradient at which prednisone should be added is greater than 35 mm Hg. Respiratory rate and temperature are unrelated to determining when to start steroids on a patient with PCP pneumonia. This patient's respiration and temperature vital signs are immaterial to the physician's decision whether to ad- minister prednisone. This patient's SpO of 93% on room air is too high to warrant the use of prednisone. If a physician is unable to obtain an ABG, it is reasonable to start steroids at an SpO level of less than 92% on room air.

question: A 25-year-old man presents for a psychiatric evaluation after a 2-week history of difficulty sleeping due to recurrent nightmares. His partner mentions that when he is awake, he often seems to be having conversations with people who are not present. The patient was recently diagnosed with HIV and was started on a new medication last month. Which medication is most likely producing these side effects?
englishExplanation: This patient has recurrent nightmares and hallucinations shortly after starting a new medication for HIV. Efavirenz is a nonnucleoside reverse-transcriptase in- hibitor (NNRTI) that is known to cause psychological side effects, includ- ing depression, psychosis, and nightmares. There have been incredible ad- vances made in the treatment of HIV over the past 30 years. The most common classes of antiretrovirals are nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), NNRTIs, protease inhibitors, integrase inhibitors, entry and fusion inhibitors, and CCR5 antagonists. Despite medical advances, many of the medications used can have serious side effects that need to be monitored. Fortunately, given the wide range of available medications to treat HIV, most physicians and patients are able to eventually find a sustainable blend of drugs. Incorrect Answer Explanations Abacavir is an NRTI used to treat HIV. Abacavir's side effects include an in- creased risk of coronary artery disease, hypersensitivity reactions, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Emtricitabine is another NRTI used to treat HIV. Emtricitabine tends to have few side effects, but some rare side effects include skin hyperpigmenta- tion, pancreatitis, and exacerbation of hepatitis in patients with hepatitis B or C and who stop taking emtricitabine. Lamivudine is an NRTI that is commonly used with emtricitabine. Lamivudine has a similar side effect profile, including skin hyperpigmentation and pan- creatitis, which occur rarely. Lamivudine also can cause worsening hepatitis if it is stopped in patients with concurrent hepatitis B or hepatitis C infections.

question: A patient presents with a 2-week history of fever, body aches, malaise, and diar- rhea. The patient has multiple sexual partners and rarely uses protection. A rapid HIV test comes back positive. The patient asks about the prognosis. What is the appropriate counsel?

options.text: Despite medical therapy, the overall life expectancy after an HIV diagnosis is less than 10 years
Maintaining a CD4 count greater than 200 cells/mm<sup>3</sup> will prevent any opportunistic infections
Once on antiretroviral therapy, the risk of HIV transmission to a sexual partner is negligible
With medication compliance and normal CD4 counts, HIV patients have near- normal life spans

correctAnswer: With medication compliance and normal CD4 counts, HIV patients have near- normal life spans
englishExplanation: When HIV was first discovered, treatment options were limited and life expectancy on the first available drugs was about 11 to 12 years. Fortunately, with the discovery of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART), life expectancy is now near nor- mal for those who are compliant with medications, have normal CD4 counts, and have undetectable viral loads. This patient is presenting with symptoms consistent with acute retroviral syn- drome, which often occurs 2 to 4 weeks after the initial infection with HIV. HIV is a retrovirus that causes disease by targeting the host's immune system, specifically CD4 T-cells. This reduces the body's ability to fight infection. Over time, the body becomes susceptible to significant infections and malignancies. Currently, there is no cure for HIV; however, there have been some case reports of people being cured of HIV. The most well known is a patient referred to as the “Berlin patient,” who received two bone marrow transplants in the setting of leukemia. The transplants were from a donor who lacked the T-cell receptor CCR5, which is a coreceptor for HIV entry into the cell. However, mainstream curative ther- apies remain undiscovered. Incorrect Answer Explanations During the initial years of HIV treatment, the life expectancy was about 11 to 12 years. However, with the development of HAART, life expectancy is near normal for pa- tients who comply with medication requirements and who maintain normal CD4 counts and undetectable viral loads. CD4 counts need to be maintained around 500 cells/mm to prevent op- portunistic infections. Unfortunately, even at those levels, opportunistic infec- tions are still possible. It is true that once CD4 counts are normal and the viral load is unde- tectable, the risk of transmitting HIV to a partner is very low. However, it takes time to get to these levels and until that point, there is still a risk of passing HIV on to a partner.

question: Which patient requires immediate postexposure prophylaxis for rabies?

options.text: Farmer who was bitten on the hand by their horse
Teenager who was bitten on the leg by a neighbor's dog
Toddler who woke up in the same room as a bat
Woman who had contact with a raccoon but no injury

correctAnswer: Toddler who woke up in the same room as a bat
englishExplanation: Rabies postexposure prophylaxis (PEP) is indicated for individuals who are bitten by or experience other mucous membrane exposure to a bat. Sometimes, pa- tients are unsure or unaware that they have been bitten by a bat, which might be the case with a small child or with someone who was sleeping at the time. These cases should be considered equivalent to a known exposure. Other high-risk exposures re- quiring immediate PEP include bites or other mucous membrane exposures from rac- coons, skunks, and foxes. If the animal can be captured, PEP can be started on the patient until definitive testing can be obtained on the animal. The PEP process has three steps. First, early and aggressive irrigation of the wound is performed with soap, water, and povidone-iodine solution. Second, human rabies immune glob- ulin (HRIG) is administered surrounding the wound. Third, human diploid cell vaccine is administered away from the HRIG and repeated on days 3, 7, and 14, with a dose at day 28 if the patient is immunocompromised. Incorrect Answer Explanations There has never been a reported case of human rabies as a result of a bite from farm livestock. If there is reasonable doubt, the clinician should contact an infectious disease specialist or the CDC to discuss the case. In the case of a bite from a domestic dog or cat, the animal can be quar- antined and observed for 10 days for behavior suggestive of rabies. If sus- picious behavior is identified, the animal can be killed and tested, and PEP can be ini- tiated pending the results. If the dog or cat cannot be quarantined for 10 days, the clinician should review local public health guidelines and act accordingly; recommen- dations vary among states depending on local prevalence of disease. Rabies is spread through the saliva of an infected animal. A person who has general contact with a rabid animal or a high-risk animal is not considered at risk if they know that there was no animal saliva exposure to mucous membranes. Exposure to animal blood, urine, or feces also does not create risk for contracting rabies. Other insignificant exposures are bites from birds, reptiles, or rodents. Being able to differ- entiate the risk of exposure is crucial for an emergency physician, as it is estimated that 30% to 60% of PEP is avoidable.

question: A 46-year-old man presents with concern for rabies exposure after waking to find a bat in his cabin. A small bite wound is noted on physical examination. He was vaccinated for rabies 3 years ago after a dog bite. What is the correct management?
englishExplanation: Rabies, an extremely rare disease in the United States, results in acute encephalitis and is universally fatal, so both pre- and postexposure prophylaxis are integral in its prevention. After exposure, for a previously vaccinated patient who is otherwise immunocompetent, the rabies vaccine should be given on days 0 and 3 in addition to local wound care. There is no indication for additional ra- bies immune globulin in an already vaccinated patient. The rabies virus is transmit- ted via direct bite and remains close to the site of inoculation for a prolonged incu- bation period (20-90 days). In the United States, bats are the most common vec- tor of rabies exposure, along with skunks, foxes, and raccoons. Worldwide, the vast majority of cases are attributed to dog bites, but domesticated dog bites are gen- erally considered low risk in the United States. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients receiving postexposure prophylaxis for rabies who have not been previously immunized are given immune globulin and are vacci- nated on the initial visit. Repeat vaccination also occurs on days 3, 7, and 14. Repeat administration of immune globulin is not indicated when a patient has al- ready completed a vaccination series. Administration of immune globulin without vaccination is inappropriate for postexposure prophylaxis in patients who have been previously im- munized. These patients need repeat vaccination on days 0 and 3. Wound care is an essential part of management of wounds being evaluated for rabies. However, local wound care alone is insufficient in this case, which requires re- dosing the vaccine for postexposure prophylaxis.

question: A mother brings in her 17-month-old son for a fever of 39.4°C (102.9°F) and a runny nose 4 days ago. The fever resolved on the day of presentation. He has a maculopapular rash on his stomach, back, and neck that the mother says "cropped up" a couple of hours before they came in. The rash is pink and blanchable without involvement of the mucous membranes. He is otherwise healthy and well-appear- ing on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Roseola infantum (or exanthema subitum) is a common acute febrile ill- ness in children 6 months to 3 years old. It is caused by HHV-6. Roseola in- fantum is characterized by a high-spiking fever that lasts 3 to 5 days with addi- tional nonspecific symptoms following defervescence. The sudden-onset rash, which is often described as pink and maculopapular, blanches to touch and is typically located on the neck, trunk, and buttocks and occasionally on the face and extremities. The rash normally fades after 2 days and is treated with sup- portive care alone. Occasionally, roseola infantum can cause febrile seizures due to the rapid and elevated nature of the febrile portion of this disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations Erythema infectiosum (or fifth disease) is a viral exanthem. It is caused by parvovirus B19 and is commonly seen in pediatric patients 5 to 15 years old dur- ing the spring. The rash begins as a diffuse erythema on the cheeks (not on the trunk, as it did in this case) with circumoral pallor and subsequent development of a macu- lopapular rash on the trunk and limbs. The facial rash resolves after 4 to 5 days, but the body rash clears centrally over the course of 1 week, leaving a lacy appearance. Erythema infectiosum is managed with supportive care. Complications include re- currence over the next 3 weeks, arthralgias in teenagers, fetal anomalies in pregnant patients, and aplastic crisis in those with sickle cell anemia. Measles is a highly contagious myxovirus that often presents in the winter or spring months. Although its prevalence has decreased due to vaccinations, measles has had a resurgence in recent years in unvaccinated communities. Measles is charac- terized by a more systemically ill patient with symptoms of cough, coryza, con- junctivitis, and pathognomonic findings of small white to blue spots on a red base seen in the buccal mucosa (known as Koplik spots). The rash begins on the face; the spots rapidly blend into each other then spread down the body with often fine desquamation and resolution into a copper rash. Treatment is supportive, but complications include pneumonia, encephalitis, and years later, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. Rubella (or German measles) is a less commonly seen viral exanthem due to in- creased vaccinations. Rubella is characterized by a prodrome of 1 to 5 days of fever; malaise; sore throat; and suboccipital, posterior auricular, or pos- terior cervical lymphadenopathy. The rash begins as a pink, irregular, macu- lopapular exanthema starting on the face and progressing down the body, eventually reaching the lower extremities and coalescing throughout. Small petechiae on the soft palate (or Forchheimer spots) are occasionally present but can be nonspecific. The treatment is supportive. Key Points Roseola has high-spiking fevers and then a nondescript rash. Rubella has a rash that moves from head to toe with fever and soft palate petechiae. Measles has Koplik spots and spreads head to toe with confluence.

question: A 14-month-old girl presents for evaluation of a rash that started today. She had a high fever of 3 days' duration, but it resolved with acetaminophen administration yesterday. She has been acting normally otherwise, without cough, congestion, or alteration of bowel or bladder habits. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Dina M. Kulik, MD, FRCPC, PEM.
englishExplanation: Roseola infantum (also known as exanthema subitum or sixth disease) is caused by HHV-6 and is a common pediatric infection. It presents as a diffuse maculopapular rash following 3 to 4 days of high fever. The rash often appears as discreet small mac- ules without coalescence that begins centrally and then progresses distally and typi- cally develops after the resolution of the fever. Roseola infantum can be associated with upper respiratory symptoms (lower respiratory symptoms can also be seen), di- minished activity, vomiting, and diarrhea, as well as a bulging fontanelle in infants. Incorrect Answer Explanations Impetigo is caused by either Staphylococcus aureus or group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. The bullous form is almost universally S. aureus, as it can produce ex- foliative toxins that hydrolyze molecules below the stratum corneum. As opposed to staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, the blisters are localized and generally start as small vesicles that become flaccid blisters up to 2 cm in diameter. Impetigo also is commonly found in intertriginous regions. Erythema chronicum migrans is the classic "targetoid" rash associated with Lyme disease. This condition develops 1 to 4 weeks after a tick bite that resulted in trans- mission of Borrelia burgdorferi. Without treatment, the rash clears within 3 to 4 weeks, and only 50% of patients complain of flu-like illness with associated fever, headache, chills, and myalgia. Rubeola, commonly known as measles, has the classic maculopapular rash that starts on the face then spreads down to the trunk and then the extremities. In this case, it is distinguished from roseola because the patient does not have the "three C's" — cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis — that rubeola is known for, which generally start a few days before the rash appears. Key Points Roseola is a common maculopapular rash that often appears after defervescence of a high fever. Roseola is associated with a bulging fontanelle in infants. Rubeola is characterized by the “3 C's” – cough, coryza, conjunctivitis.

question: A 14-month-old boy presents with the rash shown. He had a high fever lasting 4 days that has since resolved without treatment. The rash developed once the fever subsided. He has remained well-appearing throughout this illness without the presence of other symptoms or a source of his fever. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: cha_cha/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: Roseola infantum (exanthem subitum or sixth disease) is a viral illness defined by the appearance of a diffuse, rose-colored rash that develops with defervescence of a fever that has lasted approximately 3 to 5 days. Roseola infantum most commonly occurs in children aged 6 months to 3 years. Although the associated fever can become quite high (up to 40.6°C [105.0°F]), the child usually improves rapidly once the rash appears. There is no specific treat- ment for roseola infantum — only supportive care is indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease, is known to have an abrupt onset of fever and a rash. The “slapped-cheek” rash characterizes this disease. The typical patient is a school-aged child who presents with bright-red cheeks with sparing of the circumoral area, eyelids, and chin. About 1 to 2 days after the appear- ance of the facial rash, an erythematous maculopapular rash appears on the trunk and limbs and can also involve the palms and soles. This patient's rash started after the fever subsided and did not have the fiery cheek rash known to be present in erythema infectiosum. Kawasaki disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syn- drome. The rash of Kawasaki disease is quite variable, but distinguishing features include at least 5 days of fever with concurrent conjunctivitis, erythema of the lips and oral mucosa (commonly known as “strawberry tongue”), and erythema and edema of the extremities. Fever and a rash are most often present concurrently in patients with Kawasaki disease, as opposed to this patient's presentation; notably, this patient also lacks the other characterizing features of Kawasaki disease. Scarlet fever, a rash associated with pharyngitis due to Streptococcus, manifests with fever, sore throat, headache, vomiting, and abdominal pain. This patient had a rash after defervescence of a nonspecific viral fever, whereas scarlet fever is specifically associated with a bacterial cause. The rash in scarlet fever usually occurs 1 to 2 days after the onset of symptoms. It tends to start on the neck, axillae, and groin before spreading to the rest of the body. The rash consists of fine, small (1-2 mm), raised papules that have a characteristic “sandpaper” feel. Linear petechial lines, called pastia lines, can appear in the ante- cubital fossae and axillae.

question: A 3-year-old boy presents with pink spots on his face after an international trip. A blood test confirms the diagnosis of rubella. What additional condition is likely to develop?
englishExplanation: There are two forms of rubella: acquired and congenital. Acquired rubella is a viral illness spread by contact and respiratory droplets. Due to wide-scale immunization, rubella is no longer endemic in the United States. In young children, rubella is typically a mild, self-limited illness characterized by a dif- fuse maculopapular rash, malaise, headache, and polyarticular joint pain. The rash characteristically starts around the head and spreads down to the rest of the body. Rare complications include thrombocytopenia and en- cephalitis. Treatment is supportive and includes diphenhydramine for pruritus and ibuprofen for joint pain. Children should be excused from daycare or school until at least 7 days have passed from the onset of the rash. This mild illness stands in con- trast to the congenital form of rubella that affects fetuses whose mothers contract the illness during pregnancy; it occurs when a newborn has con- tracted rubella during gestation. Congenital rubella syndrome is characterized by se- vere birth defects that can include a purpuric rash described as appear- ing like a blueberry muffin, cataracts, hearing loss, retinopathy, mental impairment, congenital heart defects, and bone diseases. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hearing loss is a complication of congenital rubella, not acquired rubella. Hearing loss could be seen as sequela of treatment with aminoglycoside antibiotics. The blueberry muffin rash also is seen in congenital rubella rather than acquired rubella. It is purpuric and results in blue-purple spots on the skin. In contrast, the rash in postnatally acquired rubella infection is a fine maculopapular rash that spreads from the head downward over the body over time. This description matches that of the patient in this case, whose pink rash was first noticeable on his face. Cataracts are seen in congenital rubella, not in the milder postnatally acquired infections. A 3-year-old would not develop signs or symptoms of congenital rubella.

question: A 5-year-old child presents with a severe measles infection and requires hospital- ization. Which treatment is most appropriate?
englishExplanation: The primary treatment for patients with measles is supportive care; however, supplementation with Vitamin A is indicated for children with severe cases, such as those who require hospitalization. Vitamin A deficiency is a risk factor for de- veloping severe cases of measles, and supplementation, even in children without an underlying deficiency, has been found to reduce mortality. The recommended daily dose for children is 50,000 IU for infants younger than 6 months, 100,000 IU for infants 6 to 11 months, and 200,000 IU for children 12 months and older. The first dose should be administered upon diagnosis, followed by a second dose given the next day. Additional therapeutic measures include administering an- tipyretics, ensuring adequate hydration, and giving targeted antibiotic ther- apy for bacterial complications. Incorrect Answer Explanations Prophylactic treatment with antibiotics such as amoxicillin is not indicated for chil- dren with measles, regardless of the severity of the illness. Measles can, however, be associated with secondary bacterial infections, such as pneumonia and otitis media. When these complications are present, targeted antibiotic therapy should be administered, specific to the causative organism. Since there is no specific antivi- ral agent, the mainstay of treatment for patients with measles includes antipyretics and prevention or correction of dehydration. Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) is not indicated in the acute management of measles infection but can be administered as postexposure prophylaxis (PEP). PEP should be offered to individuals who have been exposed to measles and are un- able to demonstrate evidence of immunity. This evidence can include docu- mentation of adequate vaccinations or laboratory confirmation of immu- nity. PEP can be offered as either a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine administered within 72 hours of exposure or IVIG that is administered within 6 days of exposure. This treatment can prevent or attenuate the measles infection in in- dividuals who are not immune. Diarrhea is one of the most common complications of measles infection; however, routine use of probiotics is not indicated. Despite older clinical trials that offered lim- ited evidence to suggest probiotics shortened the course of diarrhea, newer studies have concluded that probiotics have no benefit in the treatment of infectious diarrhea in children. Instead, the clinician should aim to replace ongoing fluid losses and encourage families to avoid high carbohydrate liquids and dairy-contain- ing foods until symptoms resolve.

question: What is the most common cause of pediatric death in the United States from measles complications?
englishExplanation: The most common cause of death in children with severe measles infec- tion is pneumonia. This pneumonia can either be virally mediated or due to a secondary bacterial infection. Common causative bacterial agents include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Staphylococcus aureus. Coinfection with parainfluenza and adenovirus is also common. Additional potential pulmonary complications associated with measles are croup and bronchiolitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although rare, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is a postinfec- tious autoimmune process that can occur as a complication of measles. Symptoms of this demyelinating disease arise as the initial measles symptoms and rash seem to be resolving. Patients may initially present with fever, nuchal rigidity, headache, nausea, and vomiting. They then rapidly progress to de- velop somnolence, confusion, seizures, ataxia, hemiparesis, and speech impairment. CSF studies in affected patients are often normal but may reveal ele- vated protein and lymphocyte pleocytosis. Brain MRI findings consist of mul- tiple bilateral lesions that are characteristic of demyelination. Treatment is high- dose intravenous steroids. Although diarrhea is one of the most common complications of measles, mortality due to subsequent hypovolemic shock is less common than pneumonia-associated mortality. In addition to fluid loss related to measles-associated diarrhea, measles symptoms of cough and malaise may prevent adequate oral intake in children. The treatment priority in hypovolemic shock is to restore intravascular volume. This should be achieved with rapid administration of 20 ml/kg of isotonic crystalloid fluid. The child's response to the fluid bolus dictates the need for additional boluses and further course of treatment. Although subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is fatal, it is a rare com- plication associated with persistent measles infection in the CNS. Patients do not develop symptoms of SSPE until 7 to 10 years after the initial measles ill- ness. Children may present with changes in behavior and school perfor- mance that can be misdiagnosed as psychiatric illness. As the disease progresses, pa- tients may experience seizures and myoclonus with neurologic decline until they are in a vegetative state. Although there is no cure, antivirals have been shown to slow progression of this disease.

question: A child with fever, cough, and malaise has the following physical examination find- ing. This finding is most consistent with which diagnosis? Credit: CDC/Heinz F. Eichenwald, MD.
englishExplanation: The image displays Koplik spots, which are a pathognomonic feature of measles illness. When present, they typically develop 2-3 days after the initial symptoms begin and appear as white spots on the buccal mucosa, usually op- posite the first and second upper molars. Patients with measles usually follow a typical course. Roughly 7 to 14 days after initial exposure to the virus, patients expe- rience the initial symptoms of fever and general malaise associated with cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. The viral exanthem develops on day 3 to 5 of illness and appears as a maculopapular rash that starts on the head and gradually spreads distally to the trunk and lower extremities. In otherwise healthy in- dividuals, symptoms tend to abate 3 to 4 days after the appearance of the viral exanthem. Incorrect Answer Explanations Parvovirus B19 causes a febrile illness often referred to as fifth disease or ery- thema infectiosum. Patients will have the characteristic erythematous, macular, painless facial rash (often referred to as the “slapped cheek” appearance), but they do not have oral lesions. The generally mild symptoms of fifth disease include fever, headache, and rhinorrhea. Patients may also develop a lacy and reticulated mac- ulopapular rash on their trunk and extremities. Additionally, older children and adults with fifth disease may develop subsequent joint pain and swelling. Treatment of fifth disease is supportive, as symptoms resolve spontaneously. The mucosal findings in Kawasaki disease include dry cracked lips, a deeply red tongue with prominent papillae (also referred to as a “strawberry tongue”), and diffuse oral mucositis. The discrete oral lesions noted in this image are not typical of Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease is a systemic vasculitis that occurs in children. This illness is characterized by the presence of fever for at least 5 days as well as physical examination findings of cervical lymphadenopathy, con- junctival injection, polymorphous rash, and redness and swelling of the hands and feet. Affected children are at increased risk for cardiac complications, such as coronary artery disease. They are treated with IVIG to decrease the risk of developing coronary artery aneurysms and high-dose aspirin to modify inflamma- tion and prevent thrombosis. Contrary to the lesions seen in the image, the oral lesions in Ramsay Hunt syn- drome are clusters of vesicles distributed on the anterior portion of the tongue or the hard palate. Ramsay Hunt syndrome, which is caused by the vari- cella zoster virus, more commonly involves a vesicular rash of the ear and face just anterior to the tragus. Reactivation of varicella zoster virus can affect the fa- cial nerve, resulting in weakness or paralysis of the face ipsilateral to the rash. Other associated symptoms include otalgia, hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo. The mainstay of treatment is antiviral and corticosteroid therapy.

question: A child presents with abdominal tenderness, arthritis, and this skin finding on the lower extremities. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Okwikikim, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
englishExplanation: Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP) is an immune-mediated systemic vas- culitis that is characterized by palpable purpura, abdominal pain, arthri- tis, and renal involvement. HSP occurs most commonly in children and often follows a viral URI. The palpable, nonpruritic rash is seen most often on the but- tocks and lower extremities. Abdominal pain, when present, can be so severe that it is mistaken for an acute abdomen. Additional GI symptoms may include vom- iting, GI bleeding, and, rarely, intussusception. The arthritis symptoms gen- erally involve the knees and ankles. Renal disease tends to occur later in the clini- cal course and can result in nephrotic syndrome, glomerulonephritis, and re- nal failure. Although there is no specific diagnostic test, laboratory tests can aid in distinguishing HSP from other illnesses and identifying potential complications. Despite purpura on examination, the CBC will demonstrate a normal platelet count. Serum elec- trolytes and urinalysis may indicate renal involvement, particularly if the patient has hematuria or proteinuria. Treatment of HSP is guided by the clinical presen- tation. In addition to ensuring proper pain control and hydration, patients with re- nal involvement should be treated with steroids. Incorrect Answer Explanations The skin findings in congenital rubella usually present within the first 24 hours of life and include petechiae, purpura, and blue or purple nodules, giving the “blueberry muffin” appearance. Contrarily, abdominal pain and arthritis are not part of the typical patient presentation. Early maternal infection with rubella results in more severe complications for the infant. Classically, infants will present with deafness, congenital cataracts, and cardiac defects. Other organ systems may be involved, resulting in hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and menin- goencephalitis. Polyarthritis and polyarthralgia are relatively common complications of postnatally acquired rubella infections. Unlike this image, the rash of pityriasis rosea does not appear petechial or pur- puric in nature. Pityriasis rosea is a skin condition that presents with a single, oval- shaped, flesh-colored or pink, scaly lesion called a herald patch. The pa- tient subsequently develops multiple smaller lesions on the trunk and ex- tremities that are similar in appearance. The herald patch and subsequent skin eruption can often be mistaken for tinea corporis or secondary syphilis. Pityriasis of- ten follows a viral illness, and patients may report preceding fever, arthralgia, headache, and cough. This condition is self limited, and patients can be offered symptomatic care with antihistamines, emollients, and topical corticosteroids as needed for pruritus. The prodromal symptoms of rubeola include fever, anorexia, and cough, but arthritis is not a feature of the illness. The classic exanthem associated with rubeola, also referred to as measles, is a blanching, erythematous rash that starts be- hind the ears and on the forehead. The macules and papules subsequently progress caudally to involve the neck, trunk, and upper and lower extremities. The rash appears approximately 14 days after the patient has been exposed to the virus and peaks for 3 to 4 days before it fades in the same order it appeared.

question: During a local measles outbreak, a patient presents with fever, cough, and con- junctivitis but has not yet developed a rash. The diagnosis of measles is confirmed. What is the next best step to mitigate ongoing spread?

options.text: Administer MMR vaccine to the patient's 4-month-old sibling
Administer MMR vaccine to the patient's pregnant nurse
Notify Occupational Health of exposed staff
Place the patient on droplet precautions

correctAnswer: Notify Occupational Health of exposed staff
englishExplanation: Individuals exposed to measles who cannot confirm evidence of immunity should receive postexposure prophylaxis (PEP). In this scenario, Occupational Health and Infection Control should be notified to assist with this process. Evidence of immunity in healthcare workers can be one of the following: documentation of two doses of live measles or measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine administered at least 28 days apart or laboratory con- firmation of immunity or disease. Healthcare workers who have been exposed to measles and cannot confirm immunity should receive two doses of MMR vaccine unless otherwise contraindicated. Measles is a highly contagious virus that was deemed eliminated in the United States in 2000. However, given recent large-scale outbreaks, it is important that clinicians are familiar with appropriate infection control practices. Complications from measles are more likely to occur in young children, pregnant patients, and individuals with compromised immune systems. Incorrect Answer Explanations Infants younger than 12 months are at high risk for developing complications from measles infections and should receive PEP. Infants younger than 6 months, however, should receive intramuscular immune globulin rather than the MMR vaccine. The dose of intramuscular immune globulin is 0.5 mL/kg. This should be ad- ministered in the anterolateral upper thigh, not to exceed 3 mL per injection site. PEP recommendations for infants between 6 and 12 months vary based on the time of their first exposure. MMR vaccine should be administered if they present within 72 hours of exposure; however, if the exposure was greater than 72 hours but within 6 days, they should receive intramuscular immune globulin. Pregnancy is a contraindication to MMR vaccine administration. Additionally, women should be counseled to avoid pregnancy for 4 weeks fol- lowing vaccination. Pregnant patients are at increased risk for a severe course of illness and complications from measles. If they cannot confirm evidence of immunity, they should receive PEP with intravenous immune globulin (IVIG). The dose of IVIG is 400 mg/kg. Measles is transmitted via airborne route, and patients should be placed on air- borne precautions. This includes putting a surgical mask on the patient and placing them in a single patient, negative air pressure room. Additionally, healthcare personnel should wear a fit-tested N95 respirator when entering the rooms of these patients. The measles virus can live for up to 2 hours in the air after an infected person breathes, coughs, or sneezes.

question: An unvaccinated 12-year-old boy presents with fever, headache, left-sided facial pain, swelling near the angle of the jaw, and left-sided testicular pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Patients with mumps often present with viral symptoms such as fever, myalgias, headache, and malaise. Mumps also most often presents with either unilateral or bi- lateral parotitis that often peaks around 1 to 3 days after symptom onset. Patients can also develop orchitis in males (30% in unvaccinated patients) and oophoritis (5%) and mastitis in females. In more severe cases, patients can also develop aseptic meningitis, pancreatitis, and sensorineural hearing loss. Droplet precautions should be utilized with any patient suspected of having mumps. Mumps is caused by a paramyxovirus. The diagnosis is confirmed through PCR and serologic testing. The disease is often self limiting, and there is no antiviral treatment recommended, just supportive care. Otherwise healthy patients with parotitis or or- chitis can be managed as an outpatient. Those with more severe systemic complica- tions should be admitted. Patients who are not vaccinated with the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vac- cine are at higher risk for mumps infection. It is also important to note that vacci- nated individuals can also get mumps, but their presentation is less likely to be se- vere. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are shown to be 88% effective at preventing disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations German measles (rubella) does not present with parotitis and orchitis. It is caused by a rubivirus. Rubella most commonly presents as febrile illness with lymphadenopa- thy and rash. Pregnant patients are at greatest risk because exposure can lead to mis- carriage, stillbirth, and congenital defects, including cardiac abnormalities, cataracts, and hearing loss. Measles (rubeola) does not present with parotitis and orchitis. It is caused by a paramyxovirus. Patients with measles often present with high fever, and the “three C's:” cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. They also may have enanthema or tiny white “Koplik spots” in the oropharynx on examination. An erythematous maculopapular rash commonly develops, starting on the head and spreading to the trunk and limbs. Mononucleosis is most commonly caused by the EBV. In rare cases, mononucleosis can cause orchitis, but it would not be the most likely diagnosis in this case given the described parotiditis. Patients with mononucleosis often present with fatigue, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy. They also may develop hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.

question: For which clinical presentation is empiric corticosteroid treatment recommended in the setting of COVID-19 infection?
englishExplanation: Empiric corticosteroid use in COVID-19 is reserved for patients with hy- poxemia, as evidenced by a low peripheral oxygen saturation, or those requiring supplemental oxygen or ventilatory support. The current corticosteroid of choice is dexamethasone, with a recommended dose of 6 mg daily (0.15 mg/kg up to 6 mg in pediatric patients). Equipotent dosing of alternative corticosteroids, such as prednisone, is also acceptable if dexamethasone is unavailable. At this time, corticosteroids are not recommended for patients without signs of hypoxemia or res- piratory compromise, even for those with otherwise asymptomatic pulmonary infil- trates or those at high risk of developing complications. Incorrect Answer Explanations Altered mental status is commonly reported in critically ill COVID-19 patients. Critically ill COVID-19 patients can be treated with a variety of therapies, mainly the antiviral drug remdesivir. However, empiric corticosteroid treatment is re- served for patients with hypoxemia due to parenchymal lung involvement. Decreased urine output in the setting of COVID-19 can have a variety of causes, such as dehydration, shock, and direct acute kidney injury. Although this finding would certainly prompt intervention and concern for the development of more severe COVID-19 disease, empiric corticosteroid treatment is not indicated. Instead, this therapy is currently reserved for patients with hypoxemia due to parenchymal lung involvement. Increased sputum production is a nonspecific finding in the setting of COVID-19 infection. In the absence of hypoxemia, this finding would not prompt treatment with empiric corticosteroids, even if chest x-ray imaging reveals pulmonary infiltrates. Instead, this therapy is currently reserved for patients with hypox- emia due to parenchymal lung involvement.

question: What is the major etiology of potential drug-drug interactions in the setting of nir- matrelvir-ritonavir treatment for COVID-19?
englishExplanation: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is the first-line oral antiviral medication recom- mended for treating mild to moderate COVID-19 infection. Unfortunately, it carries a significant drug-drug interaction risk, primarily due to major inhibition of CYP3A4, a component of the cytochrome P450 system. This interaction risk can limit the utility of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for treating patients with complex medi- cal histories on multiple medications. The same issue applies to any drug containing ritonavir, which is used in low doses as a “booster,” strongly inhibiting CYP3A4 to in- crease plasma concentrations of the effector drug (nirmatrelvir). The cytochrome P450 system is found primarily in the liver and is responsi- ble for “phase I” metabolism, which ultimately biotransforms xenobiotics to allow for better excretion. CYP3A4 is among the most prominently expressed cytochromes and is responsible for the metabolism of a significant proportion of commonly prescribed medications. Some major drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 that carry risk of dangerous interactions with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir include amiodarone, tacrolimus, and flecainide. Patients should have potential drug-drug interactions checked before starting nirmatrelvir-ritonavir. Incorrect Answer Explanations Mitochondrial cytochromes are found on the inner membrane of mitochondria and are responsible for the electron transport chain, an essential process of oxidative phosphorylation that ultimately allows for cellular respiration and aerobic me- tabolism. Inhibition of mitochondrial cytochromes can lead to severe illness and death by interruption of aerobic metabolism. Examples of mitochondrial cytochrome inhibitors include cyanide, carbon monoxide, azide, hydrogen sulfide, and phosphine. Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir inhibits the cytochromes of the P450 system, not mitochondrial cytochromes, resulting in a high risk of drug-drug interactions. P-glycoprotein is a protein found throughout the body that is responsible for drug efflux from the cell. Inhibition of p-glycoprotein can prevent drug efflux and increase the risk of toxicity; some drugs that carry this risk include colchicine, digoxin, and diltiazem. Although nirmatrelvir-ritonavir does have mild p-glyco- protein–inhibiting properties, inhibition of p-glycoprotein is not a major feature of the drug or mechanism for drug-drug interactions. Instead, inhibition of CYP3A4 is the main source of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir drug-drug interactions and is the limiting factor for its use. Reduction of renal clearance is an important mechanism of potential drug toxic- ity. However, this mechanism is not a major feature of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir–in- duced drug-drug interactions. NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors are known to reduce renal clearance via reduction of glomerular filtration rate. Drugs with exten- sive, unchanged renal excretion are sensitive to changes in renal clearance and can result in toxicity in this setting; digoxin and lithium are major examples. Instead, the main source of nirmatrelvir-ritonavir drug-drug interactions (and the limiting factor for its use) is inhibition of CYP3A4.

question: A 27-year-old patient with no medical history presents after 3 days' of fever and coughing. Their vital signs are within normal limits. The chest x-ray and pul- monary examination results are unremarkable. The SARS-CoV-2 PCR test result is positive. What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Inpatient admission for corticosteroids and remdesivir

englishExplanation: This patient presents with uncomplicated COVID-19 infection without any major risk factors for progression to more severe disease. Per current IDSA and CDC guidelines, this patient should be treated with supportive care without any specific medications. Major risk factors for progression of COVID-19 to severe dis- ease include age greater than 65 years, cancer, diabetes, immunocompro- mised states, asthma or interstitial lung disease (ie, restrictive and ob- structive lung diseases), heart failure, and chronic kidney or liver disease. For patients with mild COVID infection who have major risk factors for severe dis- ease, outpatient management with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is recommended if the pa- tient can tolerate it based on sensitivities and potential medication interactions. Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is the preferred oral agent in the United States at this time. Studies performed generally suggest a moderate efficacy in reducing the risk of hospitalization and death in patients at higher risk of severe disease. Molnupiravir is another available oral agent. However, it is not commonly used be- cause of its limited efficacy. Both oral medications are only available for outpatient treatment. Patients who present with moderate to severe disease, such as those with hypoxemia, are ineligible for treatment with oral agents. Incorrect Answer Explanations Inpatient admission for corticosteroids and the intravenous antiviral agent remdesivir would be the appropriate disposition for a patient with moderate to severe infection who presented with hypoxemia. The corticosteroid of choice at this time is dexamethasone. An otherwise well-appearing patient with a negative workup, normal vital signs, and no risk factor(s) for severe disease is best managed as an outpatient with symptomatic care. Like nirmatrelvir-ritonavir, molnupiravir is an oral treatment that is only available for outpatient management of uncomplicated COVID-19 infec- tion. Thus, observation admission for molnupiravir is unnecessary, and admission for this patient is an inappropriate disposition. An otherwise well-appearing patient with a negative workup, normal vital signs, and no risk factor(s) for severe disease is best managed as an outpatient with supportive care. If this patient had a risk factor(s) for severe disease but is otherwise presenting with normal vital signs and reassuring examination, then they would be treated as an outpatient with nirmatrelvir- ritonavir. Outpatient management with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is appropriate for patients with mild COVID-19 disease but who have major risk factor(s) for severe disease. Because this patient is otherwise healthy, they can be managed with supportive care without prescribing any antiviral medications.

question: An otherwise healthy 65-year-old patient presents with shortness of breath. Their vital signs are BP 122/67, P 102, R 24, and T 38.4°C (101.1°F); SpO is 87% on room air. SpO improves to 96% on 4 L/min of oxygen through a nasal cannula. Pulmonary examination is notable for diffuse crackles. The patient's chest x-ray is shown below; their SARS-CoV-2 test result is positive. Which management plan is the most appropriate? 2 2 Credit: Copyright 2026 Dr. Mohammad Osama Hussein Yonso. Image courtesy of Mohammad Osama Hussein Yonso and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 87971. Used under license.

options.text: Inpatient admission for corticosteroids and remdesivir

correctAnswer: Inpatient admission for corticosteroids and remdesivir
englishExplanation: This patient presents with findings consistent with moderate to severe COVID-19 infection, as evidenced by dyspnea, hypoxemia, and multifocal pneumo- nia. In addition to aggressive oxygenation and ventilatory support as needed, inpa- tient admission for corticosteroids and the intravenous antiviral agent remdesivir is the most appropriate management plan for a patient with moderate to severe infection who presents with hypoxemia. At this time, the corticosteroid of choice is dexamethasone, although alternative corticosteroids can be used if dex- amethasone is unavailable. Unfortunately, no specific guideline recommendations exist at this time for the use of empiric antibiotics. Traditional differentiators, such as procalcitonin, can be el- evated with COVID-19, which limits their value for distinguishing viral from bacterial pneumonia. Local hospital practice guidelines on this subject should be fol- lowed, if available. If local guidelines are unavailable, physician judgment is appro- priate in either direction. Incorrect Answer Explanations Molnupiravir is an oral treatment that is only available for outpatient management of uncomplicated COVID-19 infection, but because of its limited efficacy, it is not commonly used. This patient presents with moderate to severe COVID-19 infection and hypoxia, which mandates admission and treatment with in- travenous antiviral agents and corticosteroids. Observation admission for oral drug therapy would be inappropriate in this case.
