Outpatient management with nirmatrelvir-ritonavir is recommended for patients who present with uncomplicated COVID-19 infection in the set- ting of a major risk factor for the progression to more severe disease, such as asthma; age over 65 years; cancer; diabetes; immunocompromised states; or chronic kidney, lung, heart, or liver disease. Nirmatrelvir-ritonaviris the preferred oral agent in the United States at this time. However, this patient presents with moderate to severe COVID-19 infection and hypoxemia, which mandates admission and treatment with intravenous antiviral agents and corticosteroids. Outpatient man- agement with oral drug therapy would be inappropriate in this case. Outpatient management with supportive care is appropriate for patients with mild COVID-19 disease and no major risk factors. This patient presents with moderate to severe COVID-19 infection and hypoxemia, which mandates ad- mission and treatment with intravenous antiviral agents and corticos- teroids. Outpatient management with supportive care would be inappropriate in this case.

question: You receive a signout on a 68-year-old patient boarding in the emergency depart- ment with moderate COVID-19 infection with mild hypoxia and multifocal pneu- monia. The patient has received two doses of remdesivir and dexamethasone. The patient had normal laboratory test results on arrival. Which finding, if present in the patient's laboratory results today, should prompt discontinuation of remdesivir?
englishExplanation: Remdesivir, an intravenous antiviral medication indicated for the treat- ment of moderate to severe COVID-19 infection, is known to cause hepa- totoxicity. It is recommended to stop remdesivir if the ALT increases beyond 10 times the upper limit of normal because of concern for significant remdesivir-in- duced hepatotoxicity. The normal range of ALT is 0 to 35 U/L. Thus, a new, unex- plained ALT of 1067 U/L should prompt discontinuation. However, most patients with remdesivir-induced hepatotoxicity have a mild, asymptomatic form that is re- versible following discontinuation of the drug; only rarely does ALT exceed 5 times the upper limit of normal. Incorrect Answer Explanations A creatinine of 1.5 mg/dL in the setting of remdesivir use should not prompt discontinuation of its use. Significant renal impairment, manifesting as an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) less than 30 mL/min, should prompt reconsideration of remdesivir use. However, a mild increase in creatinine or acute kidney injury with maintenance of eGFR greater than 30 mL/min does not re- quire dose adjustment or discontinuation consideration. By contrast, elevation of ALT greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal in this setting is concerning for remdesivir-induced liver injury and should prompt discontinuation. Although a D-dimer of 890 ng/mL fibrinogen-equivalent units is high and merits consideration of new venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, or other abnormal coagulation (eg, DIC), it has no known bearing on the use of remdesivir. On the other hand, elevation of ALT to greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal in this setting is concerning for remdesivir-induced liver in- jury and should prompt discontinuation. A procalcitonin of 0.2 ng/mL is within the normal range. Regardless, pro- calcitonin concentration has no known bearing on the use of remdesivir. In general, the use of procalcitonin in COVID-19 infection has not been well estab- lished, and its use is not recommended to distinguish viral from bacterial pneumonia in this setting. By contrast, elevation of ALT to greater than 10 times the upper limit of normal in this setting is concerning for remdesivir-induced liver in- jury and should prompt discontinuation.

question: In the setting of SARS-CoV-2 infection, which aerosol-generating respiratory in- tervention is considered the highest risk of infectious exposure to others?

options.text: HFNC with heated and humidified oxygen

englishExplanation: Endotracheal intubation is considered among the highest-risk aerosol- generating procedures (AGPs) due to open manipulation of the pharyn- geal and laryngeal structures. Other major AGPs of concern include other direct airway manipulations, such as extubation, tracheostomy placement and care, and bronchoscopy. However, mechanical ventilation itself is considered to have a low aerosolization risk. NIPPV, BVM, and nebulizer use are also AGPs of note, although they are lower risk than the aforementioned procedures. AGPs increase dispersal of both droplet and airborne particles. The WHO defines respiratory droplets as particles larger than 5 µm and droplet nuclei (air- borne particles) as particles between 1 and 5 µm. Droplets have an effective range of approximately 1 to 2 meters (3-6 feet), but nuclei can be suspended in ambi- ent air currents and travel much farther. These dispersed particles also carry a risk of surface contamination. Thus, AGPs should ideally only be performed in dedi- cated negative-pressure rooms with proper PPE. Proper removal of PPE after an AGP is also essential. Incorrect Answer Explanations Studies with human mannequin models have shown that increased oxygen flow in- creases aerosol dispersion. However, HFNC with heated and humidified oxy- gen is much less aerosolizing than even low-flow nasal cannula, making it significantly less aerosolizing than intubation; heated and humidified oxygen is thought to reduce aerosol dispersion. NIPPV, which includes CPAP and BiPAP modalities, is an AGP, but it pro- duces fewer aerosols compared with intubation. Since NIPPV has a higher aerosolization risk than HFNC with heated and humidified oxygen, it is best used in situations that are most likely to derive differential benefit, such as acute decompen- sated heart failure or COPD exacerbations. Nonrebreather masks have limited aerosol dispersion, less than other masks. Even so, many published guidelines recommend transitioning to HFNC with heated and humidified oxygen when oxygen requirements exceed low-flow nasal can- nula rather than nonrebreather mask. Regardless, intubation is a much more signifi- cant AGP by comparison.

question: A patient presents for shortness of breath and fever. The patient is noted to be hy- poxic and is intubated. The patient is SARS-CoV-2 positive and unvaccinated. A chest x-ray is obtained and shown below. Which disease process is most consistent with this clinical presentation? Credit: Copyright 2023 Dr. Fabio Macori. Image courtesy of Dr. Fabio Macori and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 74867. Used under license.
englishExplanation: Severe acute hypoxemic respiratory failure seen in COVID-19 mostly closely resembles ARDS, and preexisting ARDS diagnostic and severity criteria apply. Management of ARDS from COVID-19 infection includes antiviral medica- tions; corticosteroids; and general ARDS treatment strategies, such as low tidal- volume ventilation, maintenance of plateau pressures <30 cm HO, and con- servative fluid management. As with other causes of ARDS, prone ventilation and neuromuscular blockade can be beneficial in select cases. Patients who are refractory to aggressive evidence-based ARDS management should be considered for veno-ve- nous ECMO, if available. Incorrect Answer Explanations Unlike ARDS, the presentation of acute decompensated heart failure and the underlying physiology are inconsistent with COVID-19 respiratory failure. Decompensated heart failure is characterized by dyspnea, fatigue, and signs of volume overload, such as increasing body weight, pulmonary edema, and peripheral edema. This differs from the noncardiogenic pulmonary edema as- sociated with ARDS. Whereas COVID-19 infection is necessary to trigger COVID- 19 associated ARDS, heart failure decompensation is commonly due to medication and dietary deviations or cardiac ischemia. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is an uncommon form of interstitial lung disease that is associated with irreversible parenchymal scarring that progressively impairs gas exchange. This differs from ARDS, which is a form of acute noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Risk factors include smoking and occupa- tional exposure to particulates, such as coal and silica. At this time, COVID-19 is not 2 known to be associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, nor is it a cause of acute respiratory failure from COVID-19. Although COVID-19 may trigger a hypercoagulable state and, consequently, a higher risk for pulmonary embolism, the hypoxemic respiratory failure associated with COVID-19 in this circumstance is considered a form of ARDS. Pulmonary em- bolism causes acute hypoxemia due to lost alveolar perfusion, causing ventilation/perfusion mismatch and increased alveolar dead space. This is the inverse physiology of ARDS, which has relatively preserved perfusion but impaired ventilation and gas exchange due to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

question: A patient presents with shortness of breath and fever. The patient is noted to be hypoxic and is intubated. The patient is SARS-CoV-2 positive and has a BMI of 35. A chest x-ray is obtained and shown below. In this situation, which tidal volume is most appropriate? Credit: Copyright 2023 Dr. Fabio Macori. Image courtesy of Dr. Fabio Macori and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 74867. Used under license.
englishExplanation: Low tidal-volume ventilation at 4 to 8 mL/kg ideal body weight (IBW) is recommended for ARDS from COVID-19. IBW should be used to calculate tidal volume, not actual body weight. This management strategy is based on findings from the ARDSNet trial, performed in 2000, and many subsequent validation studies showing significant morbidity and mortality benefit. The ARDSNet trial studied a “lung-protective strategy” using low tidal-volume ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW) and lower plateau pressures (≤30 cm HO) compared with the conventional strategy (12 mL/kg IBW; ≤50 cm HO). This trial demonstrated a number needed to treat (NNT) 2 2 of eleven to prevent one death. Since then, the ARDSNet protocol ventilation has become the standard of care for ARDS and remains so for COVID-19 associated ARDS. IBW is calculated from the patient's height and there are many available calculators. Additional strategies for improving oxygenation in ARDS may include prone venti- lation, neuromuscular blockade (in select cases), and conservative fluid management. Patients who are refractory to aggressive ARDS management should be considered for veno-venous ECMO, if available. Incorrect Answer Explanations A tidal volume of 3 mL/kg actual body weight is inappropriate because it is too little to provide adequate support. Furthermore, the calculation incor- rectly uses actual body weight rather than IBW. Although the difference may be small in some patients, it can be quite dramatic in those who are obese, given that lungs do not enlarge along with the rest of the body. Using IBW prevents the use of tidal volumes that are inappropriate for the patient's lung size, lowering the risk of volutrauma and barotrauma. Although 7 mL/kg is an appropriate amount, actual body weight should not be used in the calculation because it carries the risk of causing volutrauma and barotrauma in patients with a large BMI. Patients with ARDS should always re- ceive tidal volumes based on ideal body weight (IBW). A tidal volume of 12 mL/kg IBW is too high. This tidal volume was used in the control group of the original ARDSNet trial, which showed that patients who received a tidal volume of this amount had a higher mortality rate compared to patients who received 6 mL/kg IBW.

question: A patient presents for shortness of breath and fever. The patient is noted to be hy- poxic and is intubated. The patient is SARS-CoV-2 positive and unvaccinated. A chest x-ray is obtained and shown below. Despite appropriate sedation and venti- lator titration, the patient has persistent hypoxia. Which intervention is the most appropriate next step? Credit: Copyright 2023 Dr. Fabio Macori. Image courtesy of Dr. Fabio Macori and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 74867. Used under license.
englishExplanation: Neuromuscular blockade (NMB) is used to manage moderate-to-severe ARDS as a means of improving ventilatory compliance and mechanics as well as oxy- genation. It is generally reserved for hypoxemia that is refractory to ventila- tor titration and aggressive sedation, especially if plateau pressures limit this titration. Similarly, NMB can be used for persistent ventilator dyssynchrony despite increased sedation; note that regardless of indication, NMB requires continuous deep sedation. NMB can be administered as intermittent boluses of longer-acting NMBs, such as rocuronium, or infusions of short-acting NMBs, such as cisatracurium. Intermittent boluses allow for more frequent reassessment and may limit the risk of postdiscontinuation weakness, which has been seen with infusions. However, there is limited evidence to suggest intermittent boluses should be used instead of an infusion. Hospital NMB protocols should be followed. Incorrect Answer Explanations Diuretic therapy would be most appropriate for treatment of cardiogenic pulmonary edema in the setting of acute decompensated heart failure. This patient has noncardiogenic pulmonary edema from SARS-CoV-2 infection, for which diuretic therapy is inappropriate. NMB is the most appropriate next therapeu- tic choice in this circumstance. Although it is not widely available, ECMO can be used to treat refractory hy- poxemia in the setting of ARDS. However, ECMO is invasive, requiring place- ment of large vascular cannulas, and it carries the risk of line infection, clotting, air embolism, and bleeding. Due to the invasiveness and risks, ECMO is generally re- served for cases that do not respond to less invasive treatments, such as NMB and prone positioning. Consequently, NMB is the most appropriate next therapeutic choice in this circumstance. Prone positioning, rather than supine positioning, is thought to enhance oxygenation by improving compliance and ventilation/perfusion match- ing. Concurrent use of NMB is common. Currently, there are no specific recommen- dations for when to initiate proning in ARDS from COVID-19 patients, and most guidelines mirror proning recommendations for ARDS generally; practice patterns may vary widely by institution. Proning should only be used when the appropriate re- sources and care expertise are available because it is labor-intensive; requires specific nursing expertise; and carries risk of pressure ulcers, tube/line/drain displacement, and clinical decompensation when moving the patient. Since supine positioning offers no therapeutic benefit in this circum- stance, NMB is the most appropriate next therapeutic choice.

question: Which virus most likely caused this rash? Credit: CDC/Dr. Philip S. Brachman.
englishExplanation: "Slapped cheek" is a common description of the malar, papular rash of erythema infectiosum (fifth disease), which is caused by parvovirus B19. The rash is more common in children than in adults and typically subsides in 4 to 5 days. Patients may also develop a second rash on the trunk and limbs; the rash often has a reticulated or lacy, netlike appearance. Associated signs and symptoms of ery- thema infectiosum include fever, malaise, rhinorrhea, sore throat, cough, and headache. Adults are more susceptible to developing arthritis and arthralgias. Although treatment is largely focused on symptomatic care, infection with parvovirus B19 can lead to an aplastic crisis in sickle cell patients and precipitate hydrops fetalis in pregnant patients. Incorrect Answer Explanations Coxsackievirus A16 is associated with hand, foot, and mouth disease. The rash of hand, foot, and mouth disease is characterized by small vesicles on the palms, soles, and buttocks as well as painful intraoral lesions on the soft palate, gingiva, and tongue. HHV-6 causes roseola infantum, a benign illness usually seen in infants 6 to 12 months old. Generally, these children present with a high fever that lasts 3 to 5 days without prodromal symptoms. Then, as the fever abates, a rash charac- terized by small, discrete, rose-colored macules and papules starts on the trunk and subsequently spreads to the rest of the body. "A dewdrop on a rose petal" is a classic description of the vesicular stage of chickenpox, which is caused by the varicella-zoster virus. Lesions first ap- pear on the trunk and then centrifugally spread to the limbs.

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of fever, fatigue, diarrhea, and bleeding gums. She is an international aid worker who returned from West Africa 8 days ago. What is the best initial management?

options.text: Implement standard gloved examination and handwashing and shut down the hospital
Isolate the patient, notify hospital infection control, and don full PPE
Place the patient in a negative pressure room and provide N95 respirators to caregivers
Place the patient in a separate room and ensure she and all caregivers don surgi- cal masks

correctAnswer: Isolate the patient, notify hospital infection control, and don full PPE
englishExplanation: This patient has a history of relevant travel to an area where the Ebola virus is en- demic, and her symptoms suggest hemorrhagic fever secondary to Ebola virus dis- ease (EVD). In the emergency department, the appropriate approach is to iso- late the patient, notify hospital infection control, and don full PPE. The Ebola pathogen is transmitted through contact with infected bodily flu- ids, such as blood, stool, urine, saliva, and semen. Appropriate donning and doffing of PPE are key to protecting caregivers from skin and mucous membrane ex- posures and eliminating cross-contamination. Early notification enables hospital in- fection control to mobilize additional resources required to manage these patients. Signs of EVD can take up to 3 weeks to manifest, but patients often develop a sudden onset of symptoms over the first week. Initial symptoms, which can be vague, include fever, headache, myalgia, minor bleeding, and weakness. Later symptoms include large-volume diarrhea and, in severe cases, diffuse coagu- lopathy leading to multisystem organ failure, massive hemorrhage, and death. Proper management of the disease hinges on identifying persons who are at high risk; the CDC recommends screening all patients for symptoms and travel history. West Africa experienced a significant Ebola virus outbreak in 2014 that resulted in nearly 30,000 cases with a mortality rate of 30% to 40%. Although concerns about a possi- ble pandemic were legitimate, travel restrictions and rapid local infection control mitigated the spread; ultimately, there were only scattered reports of Ebola infections worldwide, including four cases in the United States (two imported and two transmit- ted to local health care workers). Incorrect Answer Explanations Basic infection control, including gloved examinations and handwashing, is inadequate for preventing the transmission of the Ebola virus. According to the CDC, if a diagnosis of EVD is being considered, the patient should be isolated in a single room (with a private bathroom); health care personnel should follow standard, contact, and droplet precautions, including the use of appropriate PPE; and infection control personnel should be contacted immediately. However, it is almost always unnecessary to shut down normal hospital operations if the patient can be isolated effectively. A negative pressure room can be used to isolate patients with suspected Ebola infec- tion. Respiratory isolation alone is appropriate for patients with possible tuberculosis, varicella, or measles; however, N95 respirators do not pre- vent the transmission of Ebola. Although surgical masks meet the standard for droplet precautions, they are insufficient for preventing the transmission of the Ebola virus. Droplet precautions are appropriate for patients with suspected pertussis, meningitis, or influenza.

question: A 19-year-old man presents with a possible spider bite on his thigh, shown below. His doctor prescribed amoxicillin, but the lesion has spread. On examination, it is erythematous, indurated, tender, and warm. There is no clearly localized abscess formation; the patient is otherwise well. Which pharmacotherapy should be administered? Credit: CDC/Bruno Coignard, MD; Jeff Hageman, MHS.
englishExplanation: This patient has a community-acquired MRSA infection. A nonhealing celluli- tis, often with abscess or satellite lesion development, is typical with MRSA. Initial treatment with oral antibiotics can fail, as it did in this case, with ei- ther lack of improvement or progression of cellulitis despite treatment. However, community-acquired MRSA infections are typically sensitive to a wide va- riety of antimicrobial agents, including trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), clindamycin, tetracyclines (doxycycline), and linezolid. Classically, MRSA infections are associated with abscesses due to the presence of the coagulase enzyme that encourages tissue breakdown and pus formation. Local or institutional antibiograms should be consulted to best interpret local popula- tion sensitivities. If the patient is nontoxic and undergoes close follow-up care, outpa- tient therapy is sufficient. Otherwise, a parenteral option (intravenous vancomycin, linezolid, or clindamycin) should be used. Although antimicrobial medications save millions of lives worldwide, antimicrobial resistance — microbes' natural ability to evolve genetically to counter the effect of drugs — is inevitable and a worsening con- cern. Antimicrobial resistance is accelerated by overprescription and improper use of antimicrobials. According to the Infectious Diseases Society of America, about half of antibiotic use is unnecessary or inappropriate, and treating resistant infections costs the US health care system $21 billion to $34 billion annually. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid combines a beta-lactam antibiotic (amoxicillin) with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (clavulanic acid) to enhance bactericidal properties. Although the synergy of combining these medications provides expanded coverage (specifically for anaerobic bacteria), it unfortunately does not provide coverage against MRSA. Bites from spiders of the genus Loxosceles, including the brown recluse spider (found in the south central and midwestern United States), are known to cause large necrotic lesions. Most envenomations cause minimal local or systemic injuries, but 10% of bites can result in subcutaneous tissue destruction, severe pain, and ulcer formation. Most lesions heal naturally within several months; local wound care and debridement surgery can be performed for necrotic lesions. There is no commercial antivenin available for Loxosceles venom. Cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin that is appropriate therapy for simple cellulitis or erysipelas, whether attributed to MSSA or some other typical skin flora, like some Streptococcus species. Cephalexin, however, is an inadequate treatment for MRSA infections because these bacteria have developed resistance to it. Given the patient's history and clinical course, his infection more likely represents MRSA cellulitis that requires appropriate antibiotic coverage. Key Points If a patient with cellulitis fails to improve despite antibiotic therapy, treat it as a pre- sumed MRSA infection. Appropriate antibiotic choices for an MRSA infection when the patient is nontoxic and undergoes close follow-up care include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP- SMX), clindamycin, a tetracycline, or linezolid.

question: A 22-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of worsening left shoulder pain. He denies trauma, fever, chills, and rash. His medical history is significant for sickle cell disease. He is afebrile with normal vital signs. X-rays are obtained and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Copyright 2021 Dr. Maulik S. Patel. Image courtesy of Dr. Maulik S. Patel and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 9287. Used under license.
englishExplanation: This patient has a common complication of sickle cell disease known as avascular necrosis (AVN). The areas of radiolucency alternating with areas of focal sclerosis in the humeral head on this patient's x-ray are a classic appearance of AVN. The most common location for AVN to occur in sickle cell patients is in the femoral head (lifetime prevalence of up to 50%); however, up to 20% of patients also have AVN in the humeral head (as this patient does). The patho- physiology involves a progressive occlusion of microcirculation, which leads to in- creased intraosseous pressure and cell death. Subsequent bone resorption occurs, and collapse of the bone can occur; bone collapse is more common in the femoral head than in the humeral head, likely related to weight-bearing stresses. AVN also occurs in other patient populations. In particular, AVN of the hip has been noted as a post-traumatic complication when the injury disrupts the blood supply to the bone; femoral neck fractures and hip dislocations are common mechanisms of injury that can be complicated by AVN. Other at-risk patients include those on long-term corticosteroid therapy and those with alcohol use disor- der or chronic pancreatitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although AVN puts patients at higher risk for bone collapse, there is no evi- dence of a fracture or dislocation on this x-ray. Additionally, this patient has no his- tory of trauma to suggest traumatic fracture. Patients with osteomyelitis typically present with fever and pain over the affected bone. There can also be skin changes or an obvious portal of entry (eg, ul- ceration or post-surgery). Patients with sickle cell disease are at higher risk for developing osteomyelitis, and the most common causative agents are Staphylococcus aureus and Salmonella species. There is no increased risk of primary bone tumors in the sickle cell pa- tient population. Overall, cancerous bone lesions are still most commonly metastatic lesions, and there are none seen on this patient's x-ray.

question: Which imaging modality is preferred in the diagnosis of avascular necrosis of bone?
englishExplanation: MRI is up to 100% sensitive in the diagnosis of avascular necrosis of bone and is considered the gold standard imaging modality in the diagnosis of this disease process. Avascular necrosis may be associated with trauma and, in that set- ting, is most common in the proximal femur, proximal humerus, scaphoid, or talus. This condition, also known as osteonecrosis, may also be associated with nontrau- matic causes in patients with underlying medical conditions such as sickle cell dis- ease, Gaucher disease, a history of decompression disease or radiation treatments, and glucocorticoid use. Incorrect Answer Explanations MRI is preferred over CT, given the risks of radiation associated with CT and the sensitivity of MRI. However, CT may be used to demonstrate subchon- dral fractures, which can affect the prognosis in the setting of osteonecrosis. Plain x-rays have low sensitivity in the diagnosis of avascular necrosis, es- pecially early in the disease process. However, it is reasonable to begin with x-rays to assess for pathognomonic signs of the disease process or other pathology that could explain the patient's symptoms. Radionuclide bone scanning has low sensitivity in the diagnosis of avas- cular necrosis. This modality may be helpful in patients with contraindications to other imaging types.

question: A fracture of what portion of the scaphoid bone places a patient at the highest risk of avascular necrosis?

options.text: Distal pole because the arterial supply enters the distal scaphoid
Distal pole because the arterial supply enters the proximal scaphoid
Proximal pole because the arterial supply enters the distal scaphoid
Proximal pole because the arterial supply enters the proximal scaphoid

correctAnswer: Proximal pole because the arterial supply enters the distal scaphoid
englishExplanation: Proximal fractures of the scaphoid are at the greatest risk of avascular necrosis and must be referred to an orthopedic surgeon. The vascular supply en- ters the bone distally, and proximal fractures are more likely to isolate the proxi- mal bone fragment from any entering vessels. The more distal the fracture, the less of a chance there is of osteonecrosis. Scaphoid fractures that are treated improperly may result in nonunion and poor outcomes. These injuries, if suspected based on the mechanism of injury and tenderness of the scaphoid, should be immobilized with a thumb spica splint pending further evaluation, even if no fracture is visualized on imaging. Incorrect Answer Explanations The blood supply enters throughout the distal scaphoid, which makes it more likely that a vessel will enter the bone just proximal to a fracture located at the distal pole. This arrangement reduces the likelihood of avascular necrosis of the bone fragment. Fractures of the proximal (rather than distal) scaphoid are more likely to lead to avascular necrosis. The vascular supply enters through the distal scaphoid (not the proximal scaphoid). Fractures of the proximal aspect of the scaphoid are at the highest risk of avascular necrosis. The blood supply, however, enters through the distal pole (not the proximal pole). Key Points The arterial supply to the scaphoid enters through the distal pole. Proximal scaphoid fractures are at high risk of avascular necrosis.

question: A previously healthy 5-year-old presents with progressive right-sided hip pain and a limp. Based on the imaging shown, what is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Bunsinth-Nan-Pua/Shutterstock.com.

options.text: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

correctAnswer: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
englishExplanation: This plain x-ray demonstrates deformity and flattening of the right femoral head, which is suggestive of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. This condition may be idiopathic (eg, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease), ge- netic, or related to glucocorticoid use, autoimmune disease, or sickle cell disease. Children with suspected avascular necrosis should be made non–weight-bearing on the affected extremity and referred for close pediatric orthopedic follow-up care. Plain x-rays may be normal early in the disease course, so MRI may be helpful in diagnosis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ewing sarcoma is a malignant lesion that often involves bone and may present with a limp. The classic description of this tumor is a “moth-eaten” lesion of the diaphysis or metaphysis with an “onion-peel” appearance of the overlying pe- riosteum. Imaging would not demonstrate a deformity of the femoral head, as shown here. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is usually found in early adolescent obese children and may present with sudden hip pain after minor trauma or with in- sidious onset of hip or knee pain. Imaging should demonstrate a displaced femoral epiphysis, rather than flattening of the femoral head. SCFE predis- poses patients to later developing osteonecrosis. Transient synovitis of the hip is a common cause of limping in children, but imaging would not demonstrate a deformity of the femoral head, as shown here. Children with transient synovitis are typically well appearing, but the septic joint must be considered and excluded with a thorough clinical and laboratory evaluation.

question: Which medication commonly prescribed in the emergency department is most likely to predispose a patient to the development of avascular necrosis of bone?
englishExplanation: Glucocorticoids, including prednisone, have been associated with the de- velopment of avascular necrosis of bone, also known as osteonecrosis. Although chronic use of glucocorticoids places patients at higher risk, limited evi- dence suggests that even short courses of glucocorticoids may predispose patients to this condition, and osteonecrosis is more likely to develop after the use of higher doses of glucocorticoids. Other risk factors for osteonecrosis include certain genetic disorders, trauma, and autoimmune disease. Osteonecrosis may be difficult to identify on plain x-rays, but MRI can help confirm the diagnosis when suspected. Incorrect Answer Explanations Clindamycin is not associated with the development of osteonecrosis. Like many antibiotics, however, it is associated with the development of Clostridioides dif- ficile infection and should be prescribed with caution. Furosemide is not associated with osteonecrosis. However, it may cause elec- trolyte imbalances or, less commonly, ototoxicity. Metoprolol is unlikely to cause osteonecrosis. The most commonly discussed side effects of metoprolol include bradycardia, fatigue, bronchospasm, and electrolyte imbalances.

question: In which bony structure does avascular necrosis most commonly occur?
englishExplanation: The precarious vascular supply to the femoral head places it at high risk of avascular necrosis, which may occur in the setting of a fracture, especially of the femoral neck; hip dislocation; glucocorticoid use; heavy alcohol use; or specific predisposing conditions such as sickle cell disease or Gaucher disease. For this rea- son, hip dislocations should be promptly reduced in the emergency department. Avascular necrosis should be suspected in patients with insidious onset of hip pain without infectious symptoms. While late findings can be seen on plain x-rays, outpatient MRI is recommended for a definitive diagnosis. Incorrect Answer Explanations The distal tibia is susceptible to avascular necrosis, as the epiphysis of a long bone. However, this condition is more commonly found in the proximal femur, given its tenuous blood supply. Avascular necrosis is more likely to occur in the proximal femur than in the scaphoid. However, the proximal pole of the scaphoid is at risk of avascular necrosis, particularly with proximal scaphoid fractures, as the blood supply enters distally. Avascular necrosis may occur in the vertebrae, but it is less common than avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Risk factors for vertebral osteonecrosis are similar to those in other areas of the body, but also include vertebral compression fracture.

question: A 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 6 weeks of a painful, non- healing wound to the great toe. Physical examination shows an ulcerated wound with foul-smelling drainage and surrounding erythema and swelling. The distal toe has normal capillary refill, movement, and sensation. An x-ray of the toe is shown below. What is the best next step in management? Credit: Copyright 2024 Dr. Frank Gaillard. Image courtesy of Dr. Frank Gaillard and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 7663. Used under license.

options.text: Admission for IV antibiotics and wound care
Incision and drainage, and discharge home

correctAnswer: Admission for IV antibiotics and wound care
englishExplanation: This patient's x-ray demonstrates cortical erosion of the distal end of the great toe's proximal phalanx, and his clinical presentation is concerning for osteomyeli- tis. Thus, he should be treated with intravenous antibiotics and local wound care. Osteomyelitis is an inflammatory process of the bone secondary to an infectious or- ganism. Radiographic evidence of osteomyelitis is varied. Soft tissue swelling may be the only initial finding, with periosteal elevation occurring at 14 to 21 days. A significant amount of bone loss (40%-50%) is needed to demonstrate bone lucency. Other studies, such as radionuclide bone scanning, MRI, and CT scanning, are more effective in detecting early lesions associated with osteomyelitis. Risk factors for osteomyelitis include diabetes mellitus, intravenous drug abuse, and immune deficiency states, as well as the presence of a pros- thetic device. In diabetics, Staphylococcus aureus is the most commonly iso- lated organism in osteomyelitis, although these infections tend to be polymicro- bial. Patients may complain of fatigue, fever, malaise, nonhealing ulcer, or localized discomfort. The physical examination can demonstrate localized erythema, tender- ness, edema, and fluctuance. Although CBC is often obtained, it may be normal. The ESR and CRP levels are usually elevated. In a case of osteomyelitis, cultures should be obtained, and the patient should be admitted for treatment. Incorrect Answer Explanations In a patient with concerns of osteomyelitis, admission and intravenous antibi- otics as opposed to oral antibiotics is the correct treatment. In a case of simple cellulitis, discharging home with oral antibiotics and close outpatient follow- up may be an appropriate treatment option. In cellulitis, examination may reveal ten- derness, swelling, erythema, and warmth. However, radiography of the affected ex- tremity should not show cortical erosion. If the patient had a fluctuant collection of fluid in the setting of extremity infection, an incision and drainage of this abscess would be an appropri- ate course of treatment. However, this patient has a deep wound with no fluctu- ance noted, so he should be admitted to the hospital and treated with intravenous antibiotics. If this patient had evidence of necrosis, subcutaneous gas, and poor perfusion or neu- rologic function of the toe, then he might be referred for amputation of the digit. However, this patient's x-ray and physical examination are inconsistent with gas gangrene, so amputation would be inappropriate.

question: Which organism most often causes osteomyelitis as a result of a plantar puncture wound to the foot when wearing shoes?
englishExplanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes approximately 90% of cases of osteomyelitis of the foot due to puncture wounds. Patients often sustain plantar puncture injuries through the sole of a shoe; tennis shoes are most frequently known to provide the suitable environment for P. aeruginosa to grow. P. aeruginosa is also seen in os- teomyelitis in injection drug users and postsurgical wounds, such as infected orthopedic joint prostheses. P. aeruginosa osteomyelitis of the foot is treated with in- travenous antipseudomonal antibiotics, such as cephalosporins or fluoroquinolones. Incorrect Answer Explanations Clostridium perfringens infection is a common cause of gas gangrene (or myonecrosis) and food poisoning. C. perfringens infection is not a common cause of osteomyelitis from puncture wounds of the foot when wearing shoes. Staphylococcus aureus is the second most common pathogen in plantar puncture wounds resulting in infection. Staphylococcus is also a common cause of osteomyelitis that does not involve puncture wounds. Notably S. aureus and Staphylococcus epidermidis account for 75% of postsurgical and prosthesis-related causes of osteomyelitis. Streptococcus pyogenes causes pharyngitis, cellulitis, and, in some cases, necrotizing fasciitis. Streptococcus species are another common cause of os- teomyelitis in the general population, excluding patients with puncture wounds to the foot.

question: Which bacteria is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in adults with sickle cell disease?
englishExplanation: Salmonella is a common cause of osteomyelitis in adults with sickle cell disease. Staphylococcus aureus, not Staphylococcus epidermidis, is the most com- mon cause of osteomyelitis from hematogenous spread in all adults, and it is also common in sickle cell patients. Patients with sickle cell disease are at increased risk for hematogenous infection. In patients with sickle cell disease, it may be difficult to differentiate bone infarction from bone infection. Location may be helpful: osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell disease affects the diaphysis of the bone, but osteomyelitis affects the metaphysis in non–sickle-cell patients. Bone infarction and infection look similar on plain x-ray and bone scans, so MRI with contrast is necessary for differentiation. Fever, toxicity, and an elevated ESR support the diagnosis of osteomyelitis but may be absent. Incorrect Answer Explanations Escherichia coli, group B Streptococcus, and S. epidermidis are more common causes of osteomyelitis in neonates. In neonates, this can be a chal- lenging diagnosis, as symptoms are typically mild initially. However, osteomyelitis should be kept in the differential for any infant who presents with sepsis. As the dis- ease progresses, more specific signs may include local swelling, erythema, and focal tenderness. Cutaneous abscesses or skin changes should raise suspicion for os- teomyelitis as well. Risk factors include premature birth, chorioamnionitis, perinatal asphyxia, and prolonged rupture of membranes. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is also an important cause of osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell anemia, but it is not as common as S. aureus or Salmonella. Pseudomonas is a cause of osteomyelitis in puncture wounds on the plantar surface of the foot that can occur while a person is wearing rubber-soled shoes. It is also seen in injection drug users and postsurgical wounds, including in- fected orthopedic joint prostheses. Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common cause of osteomyelitis in neonates. It may also be seen in infected orthopedic joint prostheses. S. au- reus and S. epidermidis account for 75% of postsurgical and prosthesis-related cases of osteomyelitis. X-rays are typically normal but may show signs of bone resorption and loosening of the prosthetic components.

question: What is the most likely etiology of osteomyelitis with isolated Fusobacterium and Eikenella corrodens bacteria?
englishExplanation: The human mouth is a polymicrobial environment that consists of aerobic or- ganisms, oral gram-negative rods (eg, Eikenella), and anaerobes (eg, Fusobacterium). Because of this polymicrobial environment, bone and joint infec- tions caused by a human bite are very difficult to treat. Osteomyelitis from a human bite commonly affects the hands after a fight bite, with contamination of the metacar- pophalangeal joints and metacarpals; this also may be associated with a fracture. In order to prevent the development of osteomyelitis, all human bites should be treated with oral antibiotics (eg, amoxicillin and clavulanic acid) and close follow-up; treatment may also require drainage and debridement. Other bacterial causes of osteomyelitis include Aeromonas hydrophila, which may result from sustaining an open wound near a body of water (eg, stepping on a sharp rock at the beach). Pseudomonas may be present if a patient sustains a plantar puncture wound while wearing rubber-soled shoes. Incorrect Answer Explanations Infections from cat or dog bites are most often caused by Pasteurella multo- cida. These bites typically occur in the hands and feet. Although cat bites only ac- count for 10% of animal bites, significant infection results from 20% to 50% of cat bites versus only 5% of dog bites; this is because of the morphology of cat teeth, which cause deeper puncture wounds. Empiric antibiotics (eg, amoxicillin and clavulanic acid) should be given for any animal bite. X-rays should also be considered to rule out retained teeth and fracture. In intravenous drug users, osteomyelitis is more frequently seen in the axial skeleton than in the extremities, typically causing vertebral osteomyelitis or discitis. Eikenella may be seen if the intravenous drug user licks their needles prior to injection, but typically the bacteria involved is Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas. Roughly 50% of cases involve the vertebra — particularly the lum- bar spine — followed by the sternoclavicular joint, sacroiliac joints, and extremities. Osteomyelitis coexists with spinal epidural abscess in 80% of cases. Postsurgical infections are typically caused by S. aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, and Pseudomonas. Patients with implanted prosthetic devices are more susceptible to infection. The most common form of postsurgical osteomyelitis is infection of a hip prosthesis, which occurs in about 1% to 5% of hip arthroplasties. X- rays are often normal but may show subtle signs of bone resorption and loosening of the prosthetic components. Joint aspiration, synovial fluid analysis, and bone biopsy may be necessary to establish a firm diagnosis.

question: What is the most common source of acute osteomyelitis in children?
englishExplanation: Hematogenous spread of bacteria causes almost all cases of osteomyelitis in children. Pediatric osteomyelitis usually affects the long bones. The focus of in- fection is typically in the metaphysis and leads to cellulitis in the bone marrow. Features that facilitate the pathogenesis of osteomyelitis in children include thin pe- riosteum, low oxygen around the growth plate (which assists in bacterial growth), and transphyseal vessels traversing across the growth plate (which allow bacteria to spread). Treatment is typically 4 to 6 weeks of intravenous antibiotics. Surgery is only indicated if there is an associated abscess or if there is failure of antibiotic treatment. When it comes to neonates (<30 days old), risk factors for hematogenous osteomyeli- tis include complicated delivery, prematurity, skin infection, central venous catheter, urinary tract anomalies, and active maternal infection at time of delivery. Risk factors in older infants and children include sickle cell disease, immunodeficiency disorders, sepsis, and indwelling catheters. Other sources of osteomyelitis include con- tiguous spread from surrounding tissue and joints or direct inoculation of bone from trauma or surgery. In adults, vertebral osteomyelitis is typically caused by hematogenous spread as seen in Intravenous drug users. Most cases of neonatal osteomyelitis are caused by gram-positive bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus and community-acquired MRSA, which is on the rise. Group B Streptococcus causes osteomyelitis in infants younger than 3 months. Streptococcus pneumonia is seen in patients who are at increased risk of invasive pneumococcal disease, such as children with chronic heart disease, diabetes, sickle cell disease, asplenia, splenic dysfunction, and immunodeficiency. Incorrect Answer Explanations Infections from animal bites can lead to osteomyelitis in the hands and feet. Typically, cat bites lead to more significant infections compared with dog bite because of the morphology of feline teeth. Roughly 20% to 50% of cat bites result in significant infection compared to only 5% of dog bites. Thus, antibiotics such as amoxicillin and clavulanic acid should be given prophylactically, if required, and the patient's tetanus status should also be updated. Lacerations may cause osteomyelitis if they are associated with a fracture or serious crush injury or if they communicate with the joint space. It is always important to thoroughly irrigate all lacerations as well as consider joint viola- tion. Most lacerations do not require treatment with antibiotics. Puncture wounds to the feet have a 2% incidence of development of osteomyelitis, typically caused by S. aureus or Streptococcus. Pseudomonas is typically seen after a plantar puncture wound that occurs while a person is wearing rubber- soled shoes. Patients are typically treated with antipseudomonal cephalosporins or fluoroquinolones. For deeper wounds or patients that are contaminated, prophylactic treatment with amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole, or clindamycin with ciprofloxacin should be considered.

question: Which imaging modality has the highest combined sensitivity and specificity for detecting osteomyelitis?
englishExplanation: MRI is far superior to other imaging modalities for detecting early abnor- malities seen in osteomyelitis, including bone marrow involvement and medullary or cortical destruction, periosteal reaction, edema, soft tissue extension, joint effusions, and articular damage. MRI is 95% sensitive in diagnosing os- teomyelitis. Although metal may cause streak artifact, MRI is still the imaging of choice to diagnose osteomyelitis in patients with metal hardware or joint prosthesis. MRI is also useful in differentiating bone infection from bone infarction in patients with sickle cell disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT scan with IV contrast is good for defining bone destruction and the bony cortex. On CT scan, osteomyelitis appears as a lucent area. Gas may be seen in bony abscess cavities. Like x-rays, CT is limited for the early diagnosis of osteomyelitis, and the disease must typically be present for more than 1 week for changes to be apparent. CT may be used as an adjunctive imaging study for surgical planning. X-rays are typically normal early in the course of osteomyelitis but may show bone demineralization, periosteal elevation, and lytic lesions later in the course of osteomyelitis. Lucency is not detected on plain x-rays until about 50% of bone mineral has been lost. Less than one-third of patients with os- teomyelitis will have abnormalities on plain x-rays in the first 7 to 10 days after symp- tom onset. Although it is not as sensitive as MRI, x-ray is a helpful screening tool because it is readily available and can quickly differentiate infection from trauma or malignancy. Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy is more sensitive than plain x-rays in the early diagnosis of osteomyelitis; changes can be detected within 48 to 72 hours after the onset of infection. A radioactive tracer is injected into the bloodstream and areas of increased radioactivity are visualized. Although bone scintigraphy is more sensitive than CT in detecting acute osteomyelitis, it has lower specificity and often requires additional confirmatory imaging. Furthermore, it is less useful in the presence of a fracture. Given the radiation bur- den, technetium-99m bone scintigraphy has been replaced by MRI over the past 2 decades. Although technetium-99m bone scintigraphy has less streak artifact in the presence of metal hardware or prosthetics, MRI is still preferred for its overall in- creased sensitivity and specificity.

question: A patient presents from a nursing home with a foot wound. The patient's vital signs include P 142 and T 40.1°C (104.2°F); blood sugar is 582 mg/dL. An x-ray is obtained and shown below. What is the appropriate antibiotic regimen? Credit: Image courtesy of Dr. Wael Nemattalla and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 8487. Used under license.
englishExplanation: This patient should be treated with vancomycin plus meropenem. This patient has a wound that is suspicious for a diabetic foot ulcer, with x-ray findings that sug- gest osteomyelitis. These infections are typically polymicrobial and require broad- spectrum antibiotics to cover Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, anaerobes, and Pseudomonas. Because this patient is febrile, broad-spectrum antibiotics are warranted. Long-standing diabetes mellitus leads to compromised vascularity, which en- courages the development of osteomyelitis. Once the skin has been violated and infected, it is easy for infection to occur and spread due to the diabetic patient's weakened immune system and compromised vascularity. Hyperglycemia allows bac- teria to proliferate, impairs leukocyte function, and prevents healing, which exacer- bates osteomyelitis. The infection typically starts in the periosteum of the phalanges, spreads to the cortex, and eventually disrupts medullary bone. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that covers gram-positive and gram- negative bacteria. However, it cannot be used as monotherapy for a diabetic foot ul- cer with osteomyelitis. Additional antipseudomonal coverage and anaerobic coverage is needed, in addition to MRSA coverage. Nonpurulent cellulitis can be treated with third-generation cephalosporins if there is no concern for MRSA. Other third-generation cephalosporins include cefotaxime, cefpodoxime, and ceftazidime. Of these, ceftazidime is the only one that has antipseudomonal properties. Ciprofloxacin is often used in the management of uncomplicated osteomyeli- tis, specifically targeting gram-negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas. However, ciprofloxacin does not have adequate coverage against gram-positive bacteria and cannot be used as monotherapy; diabetic wounds are polymicrobial. Patients with osteomyelitis are sometimes discharged on ciprofloxacin, but only after culture data is available. Vancomycin plus ceftriaxone is the antibiotic regimen typically used to treat septic arthritis, where the causative bacteria are S. aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, and MRSA. However, diabetic wounds are polymicrobial, so coverage against Pseudomonas and anaerobes is needed.

question: In the emergency department setting, which imaging modality is most appropriate for the initial evaluation of atraumatic bone pain?
englishExplanation: In any age group, atraumatic bone pain is concerning for disease processes, such as pathologic fracture, bone tumor (eg, osteosarcoma or chon- drosarcoma), or bone metastasis. These processes will often have findings on x- ray, such as particular periosteal reaction types, notable cortical bone ab- normalities, or visible lytic lesions. More benign causes (eg, osteoarthritis or gout) may also have visible (but nonspecific) findings on x-ray. Atraumatic bone pain may also represent bone marrow infiltration by a malignant process. Although this would not be visible on x-ray, x-ray is a reasonable starting point for imaging in the emergency department. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT scan is a useful imaging modality for identifying occult fractures, which are not seen on x-ray; evaluating bone processes for surgical ap- proach and planning; and identifying potential solid primary tumors. However, CT is also more costly and carries a larger radiation burden than x-ray does, so x-ray is the appropriate initial imaging modality for atraumatic bone pain. MRI is a useful imaging modality for identifying occult fractures, evaluat- ing associated soft tissue extension of bony processes, identifying os- teomyelitis, and identifying potential solid primary tumors. However, MRI is a time-consuming test and may not be widely available in smaller emergency de- partments. Thus, x-ray is the appropriate initial imaging modality for atraumatic bone pain. Ultrasound is a useful imaging modality for identifying fractures and evaluating associated soft tissue extensions of bony processes. However, ultrasound quality may be dependent on the technician's skill and radiologist's com- fort with its use for bony processes. X-ray is the appropriate initial imaging modality for atraumatic bone pain.

question: A 25-year-old patient presents with dull, boring pain to the right knee that has grown worse at night over the last several weeks. The patient denies fever or chills, and routine laboratory work is unremarkable. An x-ray of the area is obtained and shown below. What is the next best step in management? Credit: Copyright 2022 Dr. Pir Abdul Ahad Aziz Qureshi. Image courtesy of Dr. Pir Abdul Ahad Aziz Qureshi and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 69332. Used under license.

options.text: Consult orthopedic surgery for expedited follow-up
Obtain CT scan of the right lower extremity
Reassure the patient that their symptoms will resolve

correctAnswer: Consult orthopedic surgery for expedited follow-up
englishExplanation: This patient's x-ray demonstrates a “sunburst” type of periosteal reaction near the metaphysis of the femur. In combination with the clinical presentation of dull, boring pain for weeks and lack of fevers, this is most suggestive of osteosarcoma. An urgent referral to orthopedic surgery is important for tumor biopsy and potential limb-salvage surgery. If necessary, further evaluation of osteosarcoma should be done with MRI, although x-ray is often suggestive enough for a referral to specialty services. An osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone tumor usually seen in the second or third decade of life. Osteosarcoma is most frequently found in the distal femur or the proximal tibia or fibula, and it often arises from bone metaphysis. Dull, bor- ing pain that grows worse at night is a classic presentation for this tumor. Osteosarcoma can be aggressive, and approximately one-fourth of patients will have metastasis at diagnosis. Risk factors for osteosarcoma include prior radiation therapy for other cancers and genetic predisposition. Osteosarcoma classically metastasizes to other long bones, to the same bone as “skip lesions,” or to the lungs. Incorrect Answer Explanations Advanced imaging is not emergent and may be completed as an outpatient. If ad- vanced imaging is warranted, MRI is the test of choice. Although CT in the emer- gency department may further evaluate the area, MRI would better elucidate soft tis- sue extension and other staging concerns. A prescription of outpatient antibiotics would be inappropriate in this case. Although periosteal reactions can represent osteomyelitis, the initial treatment of osteomyelitis should be parenteral antibiotics. Furthermore, lack of fever and normal laboratory work are less suggestive of osteomyelitis in this case. Reassurance that symptoms will resolve would be inappropriate and potentially deadly in this case. The “sunburst” periosteal reaction on x-ray is highly sug- gestive of a bone tumor such as osteosarcoma, which is frequently aggressive in its course.

question: In which decade of life would Ewing sarcoma most likely be diagnosed?
englishExplanation: Ewing sarcoma is a bone tumor that affects adolescents and young adults, with a median age of 15. X-ray classically demonstrates a type of pe- riosteal reaction called an “onion peel.” Clinically, patients present with local- ized pain and swelling for weeks to months, and they may have a tender soft tissue mass in the area. The pain is often worse at night or exacerbated by ex- ercise. Ewing sarcoma is an aggressive tumor that is usually seen in the second or third decade of life. Urgent referral to orthopedic surgery is important for tumor biopsy and potentially limb-salvage surgery. Ewing sarcoma represents a family of tumors described as “peripheral primitive neu- roectodermal tumors” due to their histologic characteristics. Ewing sarcoma usu- ally arises from the diaphysis of long bones, although it may be seen in pelvic bones or the axial skeleton as well. They can be extraskeletal and have an associated soft tissue mass. Like osteosarcomas, a Ewing sarcoma classically metastasizes to other long bones or the lungs. Incorrect Answer Explanations Primary bone tumors are uncommon in the first 10 years of life. Leukemias such as acute myeloid leukemia are much more common at this young age and may also result in bone pain. A bone tumor in the seventh decade of life is more likely to be a sec- ondary metastasis from primary tumors in a lung, breast, or prostate. Central chondrosarcoma is a rare primary bone tumor that may present in patients older than 50 years. A bone tumor in the sixth decade of life is more likely to be a secondary metasta- sis from primary tumors in a lung, breast, or prostate. Central chondrosarcoma is a rare primary bone tumor that may present in patients older than 50 years.

question: A patient with a history of lung cancer presents with the x-ray shown below. Which laboratory abnormality is most likely to be seen? Credit: April stock/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: This x-ray demonstrates an osteolytic lesion that is consistent with probable bone metastasis from lung cancer. Due to dysregulation of the normal bone modeling process, the bone is dissolved by increased osteoclastic activity. As a result, calcium is released into the blood. Hypercalcemia in the cancer patient with bone metastasis should be managed with isotonic saline, bisphosphonates, or monoclonal antibodies directed at inhibiting osteoclast function. Bone metastasis can be osteolytic, as in multiple myeloma; osteoblastic, as in prostate can- cer; or a mixture of both, as in breast cancer. Although osteolytic lesions di- rectly result in hypercalcemia, osteoblastic lesions may also stimulate bone destruction and resultant hypercalcemia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hyperkalemia is unrelated to bone metastasis. Hyperkalemia may be caused by metabolic acidosis, insulin deficiency, acute or chronic kidney disease, or increased tissue breakdown. Hypocalcemia is rarely seen in patients with bone metastasis. Osteoblastic metastasis commonly seen in prostate cancer may cause hypocalcemia, but even in those pa- tients, hypercalcemia is more common due to stimulation of osteoclastic activity from the dysregulation of osteoblasts. Hypocalcemia may be seen in chronic kidney disease, after destruction of the parathyroid glands, or with vitamin D deficiency. Hypokalemia is unrelated to bone metastasis. Hypokalemia may be caused by increased GI losses due to vomiting, diuretic use, or increased potassium entry into cells, such as in the case of increased insulin availability.

question: What is a complication of unicameral bone cysts?

options.text: Pathologic fracture of the bone with minor trauma

correctAnswer: Pathologic fracture of the bone with minor trauma
englishExplanation: Unicameral (simple) bone cysts are benign bone cysts that often occur in the first 20 years of life. Unicameral bone cysts are most commonly seen in the proximal humerus and femur. Pathologic fractures are a common com- plication due to weakening of the structural integrity of the bone. Unicameral bone cysts may be diagnosed on plain x-ray. They may be found as part of an evaluation for bone pain, often contributing to a pathologic fracture, or they may be incidentally found. In the case of incidental findings, activity should be restricted to prevent pathologic fracture, and the patient should be monitored with se- rial x-rays. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bone abscesses are rarely related to bone cysts in the absence of osteomyelitis. Bone abscesses are often insidious in onset and may occur from hematogenous spread, as in the case of the Brodie abscess. Development of chondrosarcoma, a malignant bone tumor found in adults, may be preceded by precursor lesions. Osteochondromas and enchondromas may un- dergo malignant transformation, and any change in size should be investigated in patients with these lesions. Unicameral bone cysts spontaneously resolve and do not undergo malignant transformation. Osteomyelitis has no particular relationship to unicameral bone cysts. Osteomyelitis risk factors include soft tissue wounds with poor healing, internal hardware, peripheral neuropathy, sickle cell disease, intra- venous drug use, or indwelling vascular access devices.

question: A 75-year-old woman with osteoporosis presents with a 2-day history of atrau- matic pain in her right gluteal region that radiates into the pubic area. The pain is difficult to reproduce on examination. She has significant pain with walking that limits her ambulation. A pelvic x-ray is obtained and is read as negative. What is the next best imaging modality to obtain from the emergency department?

options.text: CT scan without contrast of the bony pelvis
MRI with and without contrast of the pelvis
PET scan of the axial skeleton
Ultrasound of the greater trochanteric region

correctAnswer: CT scan without contrast of the bony pelvis
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with nontraumatic pelvic pain that is poorly localized on examination and is most notable with walking. This presentation is quite common for pathology of the pelvic bones. For patients that have a high likelihood of having a pelvic fracture, such as in this patient, a CT scan should be obtained. Patients with osteoporosis are prone to fractures that can occur without trauma or from a minimal traumatic incident. These are often referred to as “atypi- cal” or “fragility” fractures. It is important to note that pelvic x-rays have an inadequate sensitivity (<85%) for identifying pelvic fractures. CT is often helpful to protocolize the scan to optimize bone imaging. Fractures that are diagnosed without a clear mechanism should be suspicious for a pathologic fracture and should trigger further workup, particularly if malignancy is suspected. The most common cause of pathologic fractures is osteoporosis. The bone matrix can become so brittle in osteoporosis that minimal forces can lead to sig- nificant fractures. Metastatic lesions to the bone can cause pathologic fractures and are the second most common cause. Other conditions (eg, vitamin D deficiency, Paget disease, osteogenesis imperfecta, and primary benign and malignant bone tumors) can also lead to pathological fractures. Incorrect Answer Explanations An MRI with and without contrast of the pelvis should not be the next step in this case. Although MRI may have more sensitivity than CT, it is impractical in most emergency departments to obtain an MRI for this reason. Additionally, contrast would not be needed unless there was a high suspicion for infection or tumor. A PET scan of the axial skeleton would not be indicated at this stage. If this patient has a fracture noted on CT imaging, it is likely a fragility fracture from osteo- porosis. However, if additional imaging suggests potentially metastatic disease, then a PET scan would be indicated as part of the patient's workup. This would be done either inpatient or as an outpatient test and is not indicated from the emergency department. Greater trochanteric bursitis and gluteal tendinopathy can be a cause of hip pain in patients. An ultrasound may show an effusion and tendon fraying around the greater trochanter. This usually presents with lateral hip pain and with focal tender- ness around the greater trochanter, which does not describe this case.

question: Which factor confers the highest risk for an osteoporotic fracture?
englishExplanation: Osteoporosis is a condition in which patients have low bone mass and mi- croarchitectural disruption of the bones, resulting in skeletal fragility. In addition to poor bone mineral density, bone fragility is caused by increased rates of bone cell turnover, issues with bone microarchitecture, and abnormal bone geometry. Clinically apparent factors that influence the likelihood of osteo- porotic fracture include advanced age, female sex, low body weight, history of previous fracture, glucocorticoid use, excessive alcohol intake, and to- bacco use. Vertebral compression fractures are the most common manifesta- tion of osteoporosis and are often asymptomatic. Hip fractures and distal radius fractures are also commonly seen. Incorrect Answer Explanations Low BMI, not high BMI, is a risk factor for developing osteoporotic frac- tures. Osteoporosis is, in part, caused by an imbalance of bone resorption and re- modeling, which can lead to decreased skeletal mass. Osteoporosis is more common in women than in men. Up to 38% of women are affected in their lifetimes, compared to only 8% of men. One in three women ver- sus one in five men will have an osteoporotic fracture after age 50. Postmenopausal women are at increased risk. Smoking is associated with increased risk of osteoporotic fractures. The risk is greater in current smokers than in former smokers. Other major risk factors for osteoporotic fractures are corticosteroid use, excessive alcohol use, and history of fractures.

question: What is the most likely location for a fragility fracture?
englishExplanation: Of the sites listed, the forearm is the most common location for fragility fractures. These injuries usually occur from a fall onto an outstretched arm, resulting in a distal radius fracture. Fragility fractures can occur from minimal trauma, such as a fall from standing. These fractures are common in geriatric patients. It is estimated that 10 million Americans older than 50 have osteoporosis, which leads to 1.5 million fragility fractures each year in the United States. The vertebral col- umn, which is not listed, is the most common location for fragility frac- tures overall. Incorrect Answer Explanations In patients with osteoporosis, humeral fractures are less common than distal radius fractures. The ribs, pelvis, and skull are also less likely fracture sites. The most common site for fragility fractures is the vertebral column. Fragility fractures of the pelvis are unlikely. However, the hip (proximal femur) is the second most common site of osteoporotic fragility fractures. In 2000, the hip accounted for 1.6 million fractures worldwide. They always require hospitalization and often result in death (up to 20% of cases) or permanent disability (up to 50% of cases). Only about 30% of patients fully recover. Although traumatic head injuries are common in older adults, intracranial hemor- rhages are more common than skull fractures. The skull is an uncommon loca- tion for a fragility fracture.

question: An 86-year-old woman with osteoporosis presents with severe hip pain after a fall onto her left hip from standing. X-ray is negative for hip fracture, but despite ade- quate pain control, she cannot ambulate. Which imaging study is the best choice?
englishExplanation: This patient is likely to have an occult hip fracture. Given her history of osteo- porosis, a nondisplaced fracture may not be apparent on plain x-ray. In this case, MRI is the test of choice for a suspected occult femoral fracture. Up to 10% of all hip fractures are occult fractures, which are not obvious on plain x- ray. When patients are unable to ambulate despite negative plain x-rays, the suspicion of occult fracture should be high, especially in patients with os- teoporosis. The “road test” is not completely sensitive for occult frac- tures, and many elderly patients can be ambulatory for weeks despite harboring an occult fracture. The T1 weighted MRI can reveal a fracture with reported 100% accu- racy. MRI is more sensitive than CT and remains the “gold standard” for diagnosing occult hip fractures with osteoporosis and minor trauma, although CT can be con- sidered if MRI is unavailable. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT scans are useful to detect hip fractures in the setting of trauma. However, in osteoporotic patients, they lose sensitivity and may not de- tect bone injuries. In low-energy mechanisms of trauma, MRI should be used to detect occult hip fractures. Radionuclide technetium-99m bone scans use technetium methylene diphosphonate to visualize bones. These scans can become positive within 6 hours, but in older or osteopenic patients, positive results can be delayed by 48 to 72 hours. These scans can also have nonspecific results. A radionuclide bone scan should only be used when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated. Although an occult hip fracture can become apparent on x-ray done 1 week following the injury, the delay in diagnosis and definitive care in- creases the risk of avascular necrosis and displacement of the fracture. Failure to detect an occult hip fracture can also increase the patient's risk of death.

question: What is the best diagnostic screening test for osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures?
englishExplanation: Vertebral compression fractures can occur with minimal or no trauma in patients with osteoporosis and are easily diagnosed on x-ray. The radio- graphic diagnostic criteria for a vertebral compression fracture are a 20% loss of vertebral body height or a 4 mm reduction in vertebral body height from baseline. The classic finding is an anterior wedge fracture. Many compres- sion fractures are asymptomatic and are found incidentally on x-ray. X-ray is relatively inexpensive and gives a lower dose of ionizing radiation than CT imaging, making it a suitable screening tool for compression fractures. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT scans are more costly and result in greater exposure to radiation than x-ray. Thus, they should not be used to screen for vertebral compression fractures. CT scans are useful to evaluate for retropulsion and fractures extending into the posterior column. CT can also be considered to further investigate injury in patients who are failing conservative therapy or who have progressively worsening symptoms from a spinal fracture. Dual x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans are used to measure bone min- eral density (BMD). They are useful as an outpatient screening tool to diagnose osteoporosis and may also be used to detect changes in BMD over time. However, DEXA scans are not useful for detection of acute osteoporotic fractures. MRI is useful in determining the age of a fracture based on the degree of edema present. However, it is expensive and time-consuming, which limits its util- ity as a screening tool. MRI is also useful for detecting occult fractures and differenti- ating fractures.

question: An 88-year-old woman with osteoporosis has a sudden onset of severe back pain after bending over. She denies any recent trauma and is neurologically intact. CT is shown below. What is the best initial treatment? Credit: Copyright 2024 Dr. Roberto Schubert. Image courtesy of Dr. Roberto Schubert and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 17333. Used under license.
englishExplanation: This patient sustained a vertebral compression fracture. The goals of treatment for vertebral compression fractures are to relieve pain and restore func- tion. Conservative therapy with pain control and early mobilization is ef- fective in more than 50% of patients at achieving these goals without the risks of more invasive measures. Pain control can be achieved with a wide range of medica- tions but can involve NSAIDs, acetaminophen, opioids, lidocaine patches, and muscle relaxants. These should be used to encourage early mobility, as bed rest can lead to pressure sores, loss of muscle strength, and DVT. Incorrect Answer Explanations With the advent of percutaneous approaches to treat vertebral compres- sion fractures, open procedures are not pursued. Open fixation carries a higher complication risk and a prolonged recovery time as compared to a minimally invasive approach. Due to potential complications, percutaneous kyphoplasty should only be considered if conservative treatment fails. Percutaneous kyphoplasty involves percutaneously injecting a balloon into the vertebral body. The balloon is then in- flated to restore the vertebral height, and cement is injected to reduce pain. Complications include extravasation of the cement, which can cause embolisms, neu- rologic injury, hematomas, bleeding, infection, and iatrogenic vertebral compression fractures at other levels. Although bracing is a common practice, the evidence to support its use is limited. Braces are often prescribed for 6 to 8 weeks for vertebral compression frac- tures. Although some studies find that thoracolumbar bracing improves posture, strength, and quality of life, other studies have found no improvement in disabilities. One benefit to bracing may be reduction in pain; however, this must be balanced against the risk of muscle atrophy and skin pressure ulcers.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with shoulder pain after tripping and hitting the wall. X-ray of the shoulder is shown below. What disorder is this patient most likely to have? Credit: Copyright 2024 Dr. Ian Bickle. Image courtesy of Dr. Ian Bickle and Radiopaedia.org. rID: 83674. Used under license.
englishExplanation: Given his history of minor trauma, a significantly displaced fracture, and osteolytic lesions seen on x-ray, this patient has a pathologic fracture. Pathologic fractures are usually from osteoporosis or metastatic disease. Of the options above, multiple myeloma is the most likely disease that will metastasize to bone and present in a pa- tient of this age. Pathologic fractures are common in multiple myeloma due to the lytic nature of its metastases. It is important to consult orthopedic surgery be- cause pathologic fractures often require surgical stabilization due to poor healing of the natural bone. Lastly, if a patient has a pathologic fracture and no known diagnoses of cancer, further workup and evaluation to diagnose the primary cancer should be strongly considered. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ankylosing spondylitis is an autoimmune disease of the skeletal muscles. It is characteristically diagnosed in men with back pain that is relieved with exercise. X-ray shows a “bamboo spine.” Shoulder involvement and pathologic fractures from ankylosing spondylitis are uncommon. Osteochondromas usually present in the distal femur as a painless mass in adolescent boys. They rarely become malignant or form the type of pathologic frac- ture seen in this patient. Osteosarcoma is a highly aggressive malignant tumor of the bone. Although osteosarcoma can be malignant and cause pathologic fractures, it classically has a sunburst appearance on x-ray and occurs in patients younger than 40 years.

question: A 70-year-old man with stage IV lung cancer presents with shoulder pain after throwing a baseball with his grandson. He is neurovascularly intact. X-ray is shown below. After pain control, what is the next best step in his management? Credit: Copyright 2024 Dr. Ian Bickle. Image courtesy of Dr. Ian Bickle and Radiopaedia.org. rID: 83674. Used under license.

options.text: Sling and discharge with primary care follow-up

englishExplanation: This patient has a pathologic fracture of the humerus. The patient's minor trauma with a significant fracture is a clue that the fracture is pathologic. Additionally, when looking at the x-ray, lytic lesions and an atypical fracture pattern can be seen. Pathologic fractures more commonly come from metastatic disease than primary bone cancer. Lung cancer may metastasize to bone. Although a patient with a regular humerus fracture may do well with a sling or closed reduction, pathologic fractures usually require surgical fixation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Some humerus fractures require hematoma block and closed reduction. However, this patient has a pathologic fracture, likely from bone metastasis, and requires or- thopedic surgery consultation for surgical management. Some humerus fractures can be discharged with a sling and swath. They will self-re- duce with gravity until the patient can have surgery, likely within 14 days. However, this patient has a pathologic fracture, which eliminates him as a good candidate for this management. He requires an orthopedic surgery consultation for surgi- cal management. Although some fractures can cause vascular compromise, this patient is neurovascu- larly intact, so a vascular surgery consultation is unnecessary. This patient has a pathologic fracture, likely from bone metastasis, and requires an orthopedic sur- gery consultation for surgical management.

question: What cancer is least likely to cause a pathologic fracture?
englishExplanation: Pathologic fractures frequently occur in patients with bone metastases. Although liver cancer can metastasize to bone, it commonly metastasizes to the lung and to lymph nodes, and it is less likely to cause pathologic fractures than the other choices. Pathologic fractures occur due to both lytic and cortical destruction of the bone, making the bone susceptible to fracture, even in cases of minor trauma. Breast, lung, and prostate cancer account for most metastatic pathologic fractures from solid tumors. Incorrect Answer Explanations Breast cancer commonly metastasizes to bone. Most pathologic fractures are from solid cancer metastatic disease. Breast, lung, and prostate cancer account for most metastatic pathologic fractures from solid tumors. Lung cancer commonly metastasizes to bone. Most pathologic fractures are from solid cancer metastatic disease. Breast, lung, and prostate cancer account for most metastatic pathologic fractures from solid tumors. Prostate cancer commonly metastasizes to bone.
