Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with acute, nonspecific back pain who are placed on bed rest ac- tually recover more slowly than patients who continue their normal ac- tivity. Early mobility is essential in the acute (<6 weeks) setting. The general consensus for spinal surgery is that it should only be performed when pa- tients meet all three of the following criteria: definitive disc herniation on imag- ing; a clinical picture and neurologic deficits consistent with the imaging findings; and failure to improve with conservative therapy after 4 to 6 weeks. Steroids have not been shown to be effective in treating acute, nonspe- cific back pain and should be avoided. The chronic use of oral steroids is a risk factor for more serious etiologies of back pain.

question: A 45-year-old man presents after an outpatient MRI reveals cauda equina syn- drome. What finding is most likely present?

options.text: More weakness in upper extremities than lower

englishExplanation: Physical examination findings that are consistent with cauda equina syndrome in- clude decreased anal sensation (known as saddle anesthesia), decreased rectal tone, lower extremity weakness, numbness or paresthesias, de- creased or hypoactive lower extremity reflexes, and urinary retention. The most consistent finding in patients with cauda equina syndrome is urinary reten- tion, with a sensitivity of 90%. This can be checked easily in the emergency depart- ment with a postvoid residual. The patient may also complain of urinary or fe- cal incontinence, but urinary retention (which can manifest as overflow incontinence) is more common. Cauda equina syndrome is not a true cord syndrome; it is a syndrome that affects the cluster of lumbar and sacral nerve roots that exist distal to the cord known as the cauda equina (or the "horse's tail"). Patient complaints of low back pain and bilateral motor or sensory findings, especially in the saddle or perineal region, should raise suspicion for this condition. Cauda equina syndrome is a lower motor neuron lesion because it involves only the nerve roots, so hyporeflexia might be seen. An upper motor neuron lesion or a mix of upper and lower neuron lesions can be seen with the pathology of the distal spinal cord; this is known as conus medullaris syndrome. Hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign are upper motor neuron findings. The sensory changes in cauda equina syndrome are dermatomal and correspond to the affected nerve roots. The classic finding in cauda equina syndrome is saddle anes- thesia involving the buttocks, the backs of the thighs, and the perineum. The most common cause of cauda equina syndrome is disc herniation. Other causes include spinal epidural hematoma, epidural abscess, discitis, tumors, trauma, and spinal stenosis. Urinary retention (and postvoid incontinence) and fecal incontinence are signs of sphincter dysfunction that are common in both cauda equina and conus medullaris syndromes. Incorrect Answer Explanations Abnormal Babinski sign occurs when the lateral aspect of the foot is stim- ulated and leads to extension or dorsiflexion of the big toe. This is a patho- logical sign that signals an upper motor neuron problem. Cauda equina syndrome is a lower motor neuron problem, so the Babinski sign should not be abnormal in this syndrome. Upper motor neuron signs indicate a problem in the spinal cord. Increased deep tendon reflexes are suggestive of an upper motor neuron problem arising from the brain, brainstem, or spinal cord. Because cauda equina is a lower motor neuron problem involving the nerve roots distal to the spinal cord, hyporeflexia (or absence of reflexes) would be expected. Upper extremity weakness that is greater than lower extremity weakness is seen often in central cord syndrome, which is a cervical spinal cord condition. Cauda equina syndrome presents with lower extremity weakness that is often bilateral due to compression of the lumbar and sacral nerve roots of the cauda equina. The upper extremities are not involved.

question: What is the most common etiology of cauda equina syndrome?
englishExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) is a relatively rare disorder (1 in 370 patients who present to the emergency department for back pain) that results from compression of nerve roots in the lumbar vertebral canal. Disc herniation is the most com- mon etiology of CES, occurring in up to 45% of cases. Nerve roots involved include lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal levels, with L4 through L5 and L5 through S1 being the most commonly involved. In addition to back pain, symptoms of CES include bladder or bowel dysfunction (ie, incontinence), saddle sensory deficit, and sexual dysfunction. Symptoms may occur acutely or in the setting of chronic back pain, making this a diagnosis that is often missed. Prompt recognition of CES is essential, as delays in treatment may result in permanent neurologic deficits. Regardless of etiology, suspicion for CES should remain high in patients who present with back pain and associated lower- extremity neurologic deficits. Incorrect Answer Explanations Malignancy of the spine, either as a primary lesion or metastasis, may cause nerve root compression in a similar manner as disc herniation. Although relatively com- mon, cord compression due to malignancy occurs less frequently than with disc herniation. Symptoms due to neoplastic compression typically develop more slowly than with disc herniation and are preceded by an extended period of pain. As with malignancy and disc herniation, compression from a spinal abscess may lead to CES. Infectious etiologies — including spinal epidural abscess — com- monly cause neurologic deficits, but development of the clinical signs that define CES occurs less frequently with infection than with disc herniation. Traumatic injury is another cause of CES, although less common than disc hernia- tion. Other potential but less frequent causes of CES include spinal anesthesia, aortic disease, and lumbar spine manipulation. Neurologic deficits and pain caused by these etiologies share a common mechanism with disc herniation: direct compression of the nerve roots that comprise the cauda equina.

question: Which finding is most useful in ruling out cauda equina syndrome?
englishExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) — caused by compression of nerve roots at the lum- bar, sacral, or coccygeal level — manifests as a variety of nonspecific symptoms, in- cluding back pain, urinary incontinence, bowel dysfunction, sexual dys- function, diminished lower-extremity reflexes, and lower-extremity weakness. Of these symptoms, bladder dysfunction is considered most predictive of CES. This dysfunction typically begins as bladder sensory change and incom- plete emptying with progression to urinary retention and overflow incontinence. Measurement of postvoid residual (PVR) volume in the emergency department is a useful tool in evaluating for CES. Although PVR volume cutoffs for diagnosis of CES have yet to be established, both low-volume (rule out) and high volume (rule in) strategies have been utilized. In one study, a PVR volume of <200 mL had a nega- tive predictive value of 97% in the diagnosis of CES. Another study found that PVR volume >500 mL was a reliable predictor of CES. Incorrect Answer Explanations Saddle sensory deficit (saddle anesthesia) has traditionally been associated with CES. Like the loss of sacral reflexes, the presence of saddle sensory deficit is supportive of CES, but its sensitivity and negative predictive value are lower than those of objec- tive measurements of urinary retention. Loss of anal sphincter tone is concerning for CES. However, this physical examina- tion has low inter-rater reliability and low sensitivity in the diagnosis of CES. Although it is classically taught that bilateral sciatica is a red flag for CES, unilateral sciatica is actually more common in confirmed cases. CES should be considered in patients with bilateral sciatica, but the absence of bilateral symptoms does not rule out the diagnosis.

question: What imaging modality is considered the gold standard in evaluation and diagno- sis of cauda equina syndrome?
englishExplanation: MRI remains the gold standard for the evaluation and diagnosis of cauda equina syndrome (CES). Based on American College of Radiology recommendations, MRI without contrast is typically appropriate, although contrast may be useful in set- tings such as suspected malignancy or infection. MRI sequences commonly evaluated are sagittal and axial T1, T2, and STIR of the lumbar spine. Evaluation of the entire spine may be performed if malignancy is suspected, as lesions proximal to the lumbar region may be missed if only localized imaging is performed. CES — caused by compression of nerve roots at the lumbar, sacral, or coccygeal level — manifests as a variety of nonspecific symptoms, including back pain, urinary incontinence, bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, diminished lower- extremity reflexes, and lower-extremity weakness. Of these symptoms, blad- der dysfunction is considered most predictive of CES. This dysfunction typically be- gins as bladder sensory change and incomplete emptying with progression to urinary retention and overflow incontinence. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT, although typically more accessible in the emergency setting than MRI, does not offer sufficient visualization of the spinal cord for diagnosis of CES. The use of CT imaging with contrast is currently being explored for use in patients with con- traindications to MRI (eg, claustrophobia, incompatible metallic implants), but this is not currently in widespread use. POCUS, specifically in the measurement of postvoid residual (PVR) volume, has been used to risk-stratify patients with suspected CES. Although PVR volume cutoffs for diagnosis of CES have yet to be established, both low-volume (rule out) and high- volume (rule in) strategies have been utilized. In one study, a PVR volume of <200 mL had a negative predictive value of 97% in the diagnosis of CES. Another study found that PVR volume >500 mL was a reliable predictor of CES. If CES is sug- gested by ultrasound measurement of PVR volume, further evaluation by MRI is re- quired for definitive diagnosis. X-ray is typically more accessible, faster, and less expensive in the emergency setting than MRI. However, the utility of x-ray in the diagnosis of CES is limited given the lack of visualization of the spinal cord and potential compression.

question: What finding distinguishes cauda equina syndrome from conus medullaris syndrome?

options.text: Absence of upper motor neuron signs

correctAnswer: Absence of upper motor neuron signs
englishExplanation: Absence of upper motor neuron signs can distinguish conus medullaris syndrome (CMS) from cauda equina syndrome (CES). CMS occurs with an incidence of approxi- mately one-third to one-half that of CES. Like CES, CMS is a compression syn- drome, with disc herniation as the most common etiology. CMS results from compression of the distal portion of the spinal cord (conus medullaris), and CES results from compression of nerve roots in the lumbar vertebral canal dis- tal to termination of the cord (cauda equina). Signs and symptoms of these syndromes often overlap, and include back pain, bladder or bowel dysfunction (eg, incontinence), saddle sensory deficit, lower-extremity weakness, and sexual dysfunction. Given the more proximal location of the conus medullaris in relation to the cauda equina, CMS may also result in upper motor neuron signs that are absent in CES. These UMN signs include increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and upgoing plantar response (posi- tive Babinski test). The gold standard for diagnosis of both CES and CMS is by MRI. Prompt treatment by surgical decompression is critical to avoid long-term neurologic sequelae in these syndromes. Incorrect Answer Explanations Back pain, commonly in the lumbar region, is a finding that frequently occurs in both CES and CMS. However, it is important to recognize that back pain may be ab- sent in patients who present with these syndromes. For example, it has been esti- mated that up to 30% of patients with CES present with no complaints of pain. The presence of back pain may be supportive of compression syndromes, but the absence of pain in the presence of concerning neurologic deficits should not exclude the diagnosis. Saddle sensory deficit (saddle anesthesia) commonly occurs in both CES and CMS. Thus, the presence of this finding cannot alone be used to distinguish the syndromes. As described above, CMS may also result in upper motor neuron signs that are absent in CES. Like saddle sensory deficit, urinary incontinence is a finding that commonly occurs in both CES and CMS, so it is of little utility in distinguishing between the disorders. Urinary incontinence in these syndromes typically begins with urinary retention, with progression to overflow incontinence in advanced disease. Other findings common to these syndromes include bowel dysfunction (both incontinence or constipation may be present), sexual dysfunction (eg, erectile dysfunction, pri- apism, dyspareunia, or urination during intercourse), and lower-extremity weakness.

question: What treatment is most essential in the prevention of long-term neurologic seque- lae in cauda equina syndrome caused by a spinal abscess?
englishExplanation: In any patient with cauda equina syndrome (CES), prompt surgical decompression at the site of the offending lesion is the definitive treatment. Although the exact tim- ing of surgery has been debated, decompression within 48 hours of symptom out- set generally leads to more favorable outcomes, including prevention of long-term neurologic sequelae. For patients with advanced symptoms (typically present for >48 hours), surgical decompression may still provide benefit, although surgery may be delayed as full return of function is less likely. If CES is suspected in the emergency department based on clinical history (eg, lum- bar pain, sciatica, bladder or bowel incontinence, or sexual dysfunction), physical examination findings (eg, urinary retention, saddle sensory deficit, lower-extremity weakness, or diminished lower-extremity reflexes) and imaging (MRI), prompt consultation with a spine surgeon is critical in providing the best chance for complete recovery. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although surgical decompression is necessary for the definitive management of CES, symptom relief in the emergency department should not be ignored. Bladder de- compression by Foley catheterization and appropriate analgesia may provide significant patient relief while awaiting imaging and consultation. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics are indicated in patients with CES secondary to spinal abscess, but this treatment does not preclude the need for definitive surgical treatment. Prompt surgical decompression (ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset) remains the gold standard treatment for CES. Dexamethasone IV is often recommended in the emergency department treatment of CES. Dosing is typically in the range of 8 to 10 mg. Although intravenous steroids may improve long-term outcomes in patients with CES secondary to malignancy, their utility in preventing neurologic sequelae in all patients with CES re- mains unknown.

question: Which finding is typically seen early in the course of cauda equina syndrome?
englishExplanation: Urinary retention is one of the most sensitive and specific findings in cauda equina syndrome, and it is typically seen earlier than other symptoms, in- cluding urinary incontinence. Urinary retention is evaluated by obtaining a post void residual (PVR). Normal PVR volumes are less than 30 mL, so PVR volumes greater than 100 cc indicate a denervated bladder and suggest significant neurologic compromise. Cauda equina can be acute in the setting of a large disk herniation, infection, epidural hematoma, and trauma. In patients with a history of low back pain and sciatica, acute bladder dysfunction can also be a present- ing symptom of cauda equina syndrome or a gradual progression of symptoms in pa- tients with chronic back pain and sciatica. Other neurological manifestations of cauda equina syndrome include urinary incontinence, fecal incontinence, erectile dysfunction, decreased rectal tone, progressive and severe leg numbness and weakness, and saddle anesthesia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Decreased rectal tone is often a later clinical examination finding in cauda equina syndrome; it has a sensitivity of 30% and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.90. Bowel incontinence has a sensitivity of 19% and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.97. Both findings have higher specificities, but the rectal examination does not correspond with the severity of cauda equina syndrome on imaging. A history of erectile dysfunction is uncommonly elicited as a symptom of cord compression, not cauda equina syndrome, and is usually noted in more subacute or chronic cases. Parasympathetic fibers arise from S2 to S4 spinal cord seg- ments and exit via the cauda equina to the pelvic plexus. Thus, patients who present with a history of back pain and new neurological symptoms should also be asked about sexual dysfunction. Urinary incontinence is typically caused by urinary retention with subse- quent overflow incontinence, so is not one of the early signs of epidural com- pression. Additionally, patients may report urinary incontinence but actually mean that they cannot make it to the bathroom in time due to pain, so clarification is often needed when a patient reports urinary incontinence.

question: What is the most common symptom in cauda equina syndrome?
englishExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome is a type of epidural compression syndrome simi- lar to spinal cord compression and conus medullaris syndrome. The presentation of each of these syndromes is similar except for the level of neurologic deficit. In a pa- tient with cauda equina syndrome, the most common presenting symptom is urinary retention with or without resultant overflow urinary incontinence. The symptom of urinary retention has a sensitivity of approximately 90% and specificity of 95%. The etiology in cauda equina is usually an intervertebral disc rupture, commonly at level L4-5. Conus medullaris is distinct from cauda equina syn- drome, as the former can have upper motor neuron findings (increased muscle tone) with lower motor neuron findings and is generally bilateral. In contrast, cauda equina syndrome is more likely to occur gradually, often unilaterally, with only lower mo- tor neuron symptoms (incontinence or retention, numbness, or weakness). Incorrect Answer Explanations Sciatica can be a presenting complaint in patients with cauda equina, but it can present either bilaterally or unilaterally. A better predictor for cauda compres- sion is a presentation of bilateral sciatica along with urinary retention. A more com- mon sensory complaint is saddle anesthesia. Lower extremity weakness is another common complaint among patients with cauda equina syndrome, but it is not the most common or consistent finding. It is of- ten described as either a weakness or stiffness. Stool incontinence is another common presentation in cauda equina and is associ- ated with decreased anal sphincter tone. Anal tone is usually decreased in 60% to 80% of cases.

question: Which disease is most commonly associated with inflammation of the sacroiliac joints?
englishExplanation: Ankylosing spondylitis is an inflammatory disorder that is characterized by gradual-onset lower back pain, bilateral sacroiliitis, and limited move- ment of the lumbar spine. The inflammation in this disorder specifically targets where ligaments attach to bones and can ultimately cause new bone formation. This contributes to lumbar stiffness and the appearance of “bamboo spine” on x- rays. Ankylosing spondylitis affects men more than women, and onset of symptoms is before age 45. There is also an association with the development of ankylosing spondylitis and carrying the HLA-B27 gene. Treatment includes administration of NSAIDs and a referral to rheumatology. Complications of this disease include spinal fractures with minimal trauma. Incorrect Answer Explanations Behçet's disease is an inflammatory disease that commonly affects the eyes, skin, GI tract, CNS, and large blood vessels. Bony manifestations like sacroiliitis are unrelated to this disease. Recurrent uveitis and ulcers of the genital and oral mucosa are the most common clinical features. There is a higher prevalence of this disease in people from East Asia, the Mediterranean, and Middle Eastern countries. Treatment includes referral to a rheumatologist for initiation of high- dose steroids and immunosuppressive agents. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is characterized by ossifi- cation of the tendon, ligament, and joint capsule insertions. The spine is most commonly affected by ossification, but involvement of the sacroiliac joints is atypical. Patients with DISH are at increased risk of vertebral fracture and spinal cord injury after minimal trauma. Many patients are asymptomatic. Treatment is usually supportive care. Occasionally, surgery may be needed for severe cases. Psoriatic arthritis is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects some patients with psoriasis. There are multiple subtypes of psoriatic arthritis, but the joints of the hands and feet are often affected. Up to 40% of patients may develop spinal involvement, including sacroiliitis, but less often than in ankylosing spondyli- tis. Other clinical features include dactylitis and enthesitis (inflammation at tendon and ligament insertion sites). Treatment includes NSAIDs and a rheumatology re- ferral for immunomodulator therapy.

question: A patient has disc protrusion at L3 that is causing right-sided lower-extremity neu- rological symptoms. What physical examination finding is most consistent with this diagnosis?

options.text: Decreased sensation over the medial malleolus
Weakness with right great toe extension

englishExplanation: The L3 nerve root provides motor function to the knee extensors and hip adductors and provides sensation to the anteromedial thigh, extending to just below the knee. Thus, weakness with right knee extension would be the most likely physical examination finding in this case. Disc protrusion can be acute or chronic depending on the patient's age and clinical presentation. In younger patients, acute disc herniation or spondylolysis can be caused by trauma, sports, or improper lifting. In older adults, symptoms are typically related to degenerative disc disease or arthritis. Patients will typically present with back pain with or without associ- ated neurological symptoms, depending on the level of injury. Patients who present with sciatica due to a herniated disk generally complain more about the radicular symptoms than about back pain. The majority of disk herniations occur at the L4 to L5 (L5 nerve root) or L5 to S1 (S1 nerve root) level. Understanding der- matomes and myotomes is important in identifying the level of injury and the sever- ity of symptoms. Incorrect Answer Explanations Sensation over the medial malleolus is typically localized to the L4 nerve root. The L4 nerve root provides sensation to the anterolateral thigh, crosses the anterior knee, and wraps around the lower leg to the medial malleolus and the medial aspect of the great toe. The L4 nerve root also assists in knee extension. The ankle jerk reflex is achieved by tapping the Achilles tendon while the foot is slightly dorsiflexed. This reflex is mediated by the S1 spinal nerve root. The patellar reflex or knee jerk reflex is mediated by the L3 and L4 nerve root and may be diminished in a patient with L3 radiculopathy symptoms. Great toe extension, which is controlled by the extensor hallucis longus, is medi- ated by the L5 nerve root. The L5 nerve root is also responsible for sensation over the lateral calf and the dorsum of the foot, including the first and second toe. Sensation for L5 is often checked in between the first and second toes.

question: What is the most common cause of sciatica in nongeriatric adults?
englishExplanation: The most common cause of sciatica is a herniated or bulging disc, espe- cially in younger patients. The sciatic nerve is made up of the L4 through S2 nerve roots and exits the pelvis posteriorly through the sciatic foramen. The sciatic nerve then courses inferior to the piriformis, courses through the gluteal muscle groups, en- ters the posterior thigh, and courses through the hamstrings (biceps femoris) to ter- minate in the popliteal fossa. The sciatic nerve then splits into the tibial and common fibular nerves. Sciatica symptoms can be caused by pathology anywhere along the course of the nerve. The pain is typically unilateral and described as a burning sensation. There may be associated paresthesias. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute trauma is an uncommon cause of back pain with sciatica in young patients. Patients should always be screened for falls or trauma when presenting with back pain. In the elderly, a simple fall can cause a compression fracture that may lead to sciatica symptoms. The back should be fully exposed and in- spected for signs of trauma. Trauma patients should all receive imaging to rule out fracture. Sciatica may result from and be the initial presenting symptom of malig- nancy. The spine is the third most common site for metastatic disease. Other symp- toms that are suspicious for malignancy are pain that is worse at night or with rest, pain in multiple areas of the spine, night sweats, and unexplained weight loss. Atraumatic pain that has been present for over 6 to 8 weeks with no improvement, even in a young person, warrants imaging. Patients with a known history of malig- nancy with new-onset back pain and neurological symptoms should also receive imaging. Spinal stenosis from arthritic degeneration is a more common cause of sciat- ica in the elderly population. Spinal stenosis tends to be progressive and worsens over time. It typically presents as back pain with radiculopathy that worsens with walking, prolonged standing, and back extension. Spinal stenosis improves with for- ward flexion, which increases the spinal canal diameter. The neurological symptoms of spinal stenosis include pain radiating to the buttocks, thighs, and legs; paresthe- sias; weakness; and reflex changes.

question: A patient presents with acute-onset lower back pain and weakness with right big toe extension after lifting heavy weights. Which nerve root is affected by the disc protrusion?
englishExplanation: Disc herniation is most common at the L5 to S1 nerve roots. The L5 nerve root provides motor control for the extensor hallucis longus, which controls great toe extension as well as sensation over the lateral calf and the dor- sum of the foot, including the first and second toe. Sensation for L5 is often checked in between the first and second toes. The L5 nerve root emerges from the L5 to S1 intervertebral or disc space. Paracentral disc herniations tend to affect the nerve root at the level of the disc, whereas lateral disc herniation tends to affect the nerve root below the disc. Incorrect Answer Explanations The L3 nerve root provides motor function to the knee extensors and hip adductors, in addition to providing sensation to the anteromedial thigh ex- tending to just below the knee. The most accurate location to check for sensation corresponding to the L3 nerve root is the medial knee. Disc protrusion is less com- mon at this level. The L4 nerve root provides motor function primarily to the gluteal mus- cles and lower leg muscles that control ankle function. Motor function is tested by checking ankle dorsiflexion. The L4 nerve root also provides sensation to the medial leg below the knee. The most accurate location to check for sensa- tion corresponding to the L4 nerve root is the medial malleolus. The S1 nerve root provides motor function to the gluteal muscles and the muscles of the posterior leg, and it can be tested by checking ankle plan- tarflexion. The S1 nerve root provides sensation to the posterior calf and lat- eral aspect of the foot, including the fourth and fifth toes. The most accurate location to check for sensation corresponding to the S1 nerve root is the lateral heel, just posterior to the lateral malleolus. The S1 nerve root is also responsible for the ankle jerk reflex.

question: Which mechanism is the most likely cause of discitis?
englishExplanation: Hematogenous spread is the most common cause of vertebral osteomyelitis and discitis, with endocarditis being one of the most common sources. A recent study showed that one-third of patients with spinal infections also had endocarditis. The structure of the “corkscrew” nature of the spinal vessels is thought to predispose them to bacterial seeding through hematogenous spread. Discitis is an infection of the vertebral disc space, which can also be associated with vertebral osteomyelitis. Risk factors for discitis include intravenous drug use, history of spinal procedure, diabetes, infective endocarditis, degenera- tive spine disease, immunosuppressive therapy, or immunocompro- mised state. The mechanism of infection is mainly from three potential etiologies: hematogenous spread, contiguous spread from surrounding tissues, or direct inoculation from trauma. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although diverticular abscess can be a source for potential hematogenous or even contiguous spread to the spine, it is not a common source. However, if a patient with an abscess develops worsening back pain or signs concerning for discitis or spinal in- fection, the diagnosis should be considered. Pneumonia is a potential risk for discitis but is not one of the more common causes of spinal infections. However, if there is concern that a patient has midline thoracic spinal back pain with pneumonia, discitis and spinal infection should be considered. Spinal surgery is a risk factor for discitis through direct traumatic inoculation. It is important to identify patients who have had recent trauma, procedures, or surgeries that may put them at risk. However, that risk is not as common as hematologic spread in endocarditis.

question: Which laboratory finding is most likely to be noted in discitis?
englishExplanation: The ESR in discitis is elevated in 90% of cases, and the CRP is also often elevated. Laboratory workup does not often reveal an elevated WBC. Discitis is an infection of the vertebral disc space, which can also be associated with vertebral osteomyelitis. Patients with suspected discitis should undergo a thorough neurologic examination. If the patient has any neurologic deficits, or if imaging reveals cord compression or evidence of an abscess, neurosurgery should be consulted. MRI with contrast is recommended to best identify discitis and other potential associated infections, in- cluding epidural abscess and vertebral osteomyelitis. The majority of infections are caused by Staphylococcus aureus. A biopsy should be conducted, and blood and urine cultures should be obtained. Incorrect Answer Explanations The WBC count is reported to be elevated in <50% of patients presenting with disci- tis. Thus, a normal WBC count is not a sensitive test in the setting of discitis and does not rule out discitis or another vertebral infection. The CRP is often elevated in the setting of discitis and vertebral infection, as is noted with the ESR. However, it is reportedly not as sensitive or specific as the ESR, and an ESR >100 should warrant a high suspicion for infection. The initial biopsy obtained to culture the infectious organism is only positive <50% the time. Thus, it may be necessary to obtain a second biopsy sample. It is also im- portant to obtain urine and blood cultures initially prior to starting antibiotics.

question: Which history and physical examination finding is most common in discitis?

options.text: Symptom onset less than a week

englishExplanation: Spinal pain is one of the most common findings in discitis and is reportedly present in >90% of patients. Pain in discitis is also often localized and reproduced with gentle percussion of the spine on examination. Discitis is an infection of the ver- tebral disc space, which can also be associated with vertebral osteomyelitis. Patients often present with spinal pain that progressively worsens over days to weeks, is not relieved with rest, and often awakens them at night. A little more than half of pa- tients do not have a fever at the time of presentation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Fever has only been reported in about 50% of patients with discitis and is not as com- mon as localized tenderness to spinal percussion. Thus, it is important that the clinician not rely on the absence of fever to exclude a diagnosis of discitis or other vertebral infections. Pain caused by discitis worsens, not eases at night. Patients often awaken from sleep with the pain, and it is often not relieved with rest. It is also important on physical examination for the clinician to look for potential sources for hematogenous etiology of infection, including signs of intravenous drug use or skin infections. Discitis and vertebral infection often have a more insidious progression of symp- toms, averaging around 48 days in duration prior to presentation. The symptoms of- ten slowly worsen over time until the patient seeks medical evaluation.

question: Which antibiotic is most appropriate to utilize for empiric coverage of discitis?
englishExplanation: The majority of discitis and vertebral infections are caused by Staphylococcus au- reus. It is also important to cover for other common pathogens, including Streptococci and gram-negative bacilli. Empiric antibiotic combination therapy with vancomycin to cover for MRSA, in conjunction with either a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin or ciprofloxacin, is recommended. Blood and urine cultures should also be obtained in addition to biopsy. It is also recom- mended that, if possible, antibiotics not be started until a biopsy with culture is performed to isolate the causative organism (except if neurologic compromise or sepsis is present). The course of treatment is for a minimum of 6 weeks, and often longer if the patient has an abscess or drug-resistant organism. Incorrect Answer Explanations Caspofungin is an echinocandin antifungal agent that is not routinely recom- mended as part of empiric antibiotic coverage for discitis, as fungal sources are less common. However, if a fungal source is suspected (Candida) or isolated on biopsy culture, caspofungin is the recommended treatment. Imipenem is a carbapenem that is not routinely recommended for empiric coverage of discitis. It may be utilized for more pathogen specific treatment based on biopsy culture results, especially in the setting of antibiotics resistance. Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole that is not routinely recommended as empiric ther- apy for discitis, as anaerobic organisms are a less common source. However, if there is concern of a potential source of anaerobic organisms (eg, an abdominal ab- scess), metronidazole can be added.

question: What is the imaging modality of choice for discitis?
englishExplanation: MRI with contrast is the diagnostic modality of choice in discitis. Often in vertebral infections, there can be more than one process occurring simultaneously, so it is important to look for and rule out abscess and signs of osteomyelitis as well. MRI with contrast is the most sensitive technique to identify abscess or os- teomyelitis. It is uncommon for osteomyelitis to occur without involvement of the disc. In those cases, sometimes an incorrect diagnosis of fracture or malignancy may occur. Incorrect Answer Explanations CT myelogram is not the ideal imaging technique for discitis and is rarely used. It is more invasive with potential risks for seizure related to intrathecal iodinated con- trast, so patients on medications that lower the threshold for seizures may need to hold medications prior to imaging. Plain CT has a false-negative rate for abscess de- tection that is fairly high. It could, however, be potentially helpful in instances where patients are unable to have an MRI. It is also good at identifying adjacent soft tis- sue abscesses and appropriate biopsy sites. Plain x-rays are not sensitive for vertebral infections and often do not show evidence of osteomyelitis until late in the disease course. Plain x-rays can be helpful if there is suspicion of possible tuberculosis infection as a source. PET is not a common technique used in the diagnosis of discitis. PET-CT is highly sensitive but less specific for discitis and vertebral infections, and it may be limited if the patient has a tumor or hardware in place. Although PET-CT is not as good as MRI with contrast, it can be an alternative option in those who cannot undergo an MRI.

question: A 23-year-old woman presents with wrist, knee, and ankle pain of 4 days' dura- tion. The pain started in her left wrist and ankle, but over the past 24 hours, the pain in her right knee has become progressively worse. Small papules are noted diffusely, including on her palms. She denies trauma. On examination, the right knee is diffusely hot, red, and swollen; no deformities are noted, and other joints appear normal. Arthrocentesis is performed, and the synovial fluid is sent for cul- ture, Gram stain, crystals, and cell count. What additional tests are needed to con- firm the diagnosis?

options.text: Cultures of joint fluid from surgical irrigation
Cultures of the pharynx and vagina

correctAnswer: Cultures of the pharynx and vagina
englishExplanation: Gonococcal septic arthritis is the most common form of septic arthritis in adolescents and young adults, and it has a greater female:male predominance. Because cultures of synovial fluid are positive less than 50% of the time, the physi- cian should obtain specimens for culture from other parts of the body where Neisseria gonorrhoeae may be found (eg, the posterior pharynx, ure- thra or cervix, or rectum). This patient has the typical symptoms of gonococcal septic arthritis: the classic triad of a migratory arthritis in multiple joints, papu- lar or pustular rash, and inflammation of the tendon sheaths. Confirming the diagnosis is important because the treatment of gonococcal septic arthritis is different from that for the nongonococcal type. Gonococcal septic arthritis can be treated with intravenous antibiotics alone (thus avoiding surgical joint irrigation) because it rarely results in the joint destruction that is more typical of nongonococcal septic arthritis. The most effective an- tibiotic for treating gonococcal septic arthritis is a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone, and this approach should continue until all cul- ture results are in. When the diagnosis is unknown initially, many physicians add vancomycin. Vesiculopustular lesions should be looked for on a skin exam- ination, including the classic rash on the palms and soles. This rash is seen in nearly half of patients with this disease, so it can help make the diagnosis. The rash can range from hemorrhagic papules to pustules. Incorrect Answer Explanations Taking a patient to surgery for joint irrigation is usually required in the treatment of nongonococcal septic arthritis, which is highly associated with joint destruction. Joint aspiration is essential to diagnosing septic arthritis, but its sensitivity is poor. Septic arthritis is usually considered with the accepted cutoff of 50,000 cells/mm. Measuring ESR and CRP can also help make the diagnosis, but these are nonspecific indicators. Nongonococcal septic arthritis is usually monoartic- ular; polyarticular involvement is present in less than 20% of adult cases. Lyme arthritis starts with a migratory polyarthritis but typically evolves into a monoarticular process. In contrast to patients with gonococcal arthritis, those with Lyme arthritis typically have brief, recurrent attacks from weeks to months after infection. These attacks cause joint swelling and pain, which progress to chronic arthritis. These patients live in or have traveled to areas known to be associ- ated with Lyme disease, but they may or may not have a history of tick bite or rash. Measuring a patient's serum uric acid level would be reasonable if the suspected diagnosis were gout. However, up to 30% of patients with gout have a normal uric acid level during an acute attack, so a serum uric acid level is not particu- larly helpful in diagnosing gout. Moreover, most patients with gout are older than 40 years and present with symptoms in the great toe or the knee. Gout is usually a 3 monoarthritis and is often preceded by trauma, surgery, a change in medication, or illness.

question: What is the most common etiology of septic arthritis?
englishExplanation: Approximately 70% of septic joints are caused by hematogenous seeding in both children and adults. The synovial membrane lacks a protective basement membrane, so bacteria may enter the joint space. Septic arthritis is usually mo- nomicrobial; Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen overall, but different pathogens can be seen in different age groups and with different mecha- nisms of infection. Risk factors for developing septic arthritis include advanced age, recent joint surgery or trauma, intravenous drug use, immunosuppression, and pre- existing joint disease. The knee is the most commonly affected joint in septic arthri- tis in adults while the hip is the most common in children. The diagnosis of septic arthritis should be based on synovial fluid analysis. If it is possible to obtain synovial fluid in the emergency department, it should be sent for cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis. Patients with septic arthritis should be seen emergently by orthopaedics. Treatment of septic arthritis includes joint drainage (ranging from aspiration to arthrotomy) and antibiotic therapy. Antibiotic choice should be based on the Gram stain of synovial fluid, but the initial empiric choice of antibiotic may be based on the most likely pathogen in the clinical scenario. Incorrect Answer Explanations Septic arthritis due to joint replacement is exceedingly rare, occurring in less than 1% of cases. The risk is higher for knee replacement than for hip replace- ment. Prosthetic joint infections are categorized as early onset (within 3 months of arthroplasty), delayed onset (3-12 months after arthroplasty), and late onset (more than a year after arthroplasty). Septic arthritis due to direct inoculation of bacteria into the joint is less common than septic arthritis due to hematogenous spread. Direct inocula- tion may occur with trauma to the joint, bite wounds, surgical procedures, and intra- articular injections. Septic arthritis may be caused by extension of osteomyelitis into the joint space, but this is less common than hematogenous spread. Rarely, the infection may go through the bone cortex, which then seeds the joint space. This may occur in the shoulder, elbow, knee, or hip since the metaphysis of the long bone is within the joint capsule.

question: Which laboratory test result is the gold standard for diagnosing gout?

options.text: High uric acid levels in serum
WBCs less than 2,000 and PMNs less than 25% on aspirate

englishExplanation: Gout and pseudogout are classified as inflammatory arthritides and are diagnosed by analyzing synovial fluid collected during arthrocentesis. These two can be identified by the level of the cell count along with the presence of crystals, which indicates a crystal-induced synovitis. If the underlying condition is gout, there are negatively birefringent uric acid crystals on aspirate. If it is pseudogout, there is positive birefringence. Patients with gout or pseudo- gout typically present with acute monoarthritis, most commonly seen in either the great toe or the knee, precipitated by factors such as alcohol consumption, noncom- pliance of diet, infection, trauma, or other stressors. The treatment of choice for an acute attack starts with NSAIDs or colchicine only in the absence of re- nal dysfunction. If renal disturbance exists, recent guidelines recommend oral steroids, and a course of narcotic pain medications may be used if necessary. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although the absence of bacteria on joint aspiration can help make the diagnosis of gout, it is not specific for gout itself and is not the gold standard test result. Only in conjunction with the presence of negative birefringent crystals can the absence of bacteria be used to confirm the diagnosis. High levels of uric acid in the serum can be found in patients with gout, but the level can also be normal during an acute gout attack. Thus, this finding should not be used to confirm the diagnosis of gout. A WBC count less than 2,000 and polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) less than 25% on arthrocentesis indicates the presence of a noninflamma- tory arthritis, such as osteoarthritis. Gout is in the category of inflammatory arthritides, which have a WBC count between 2,000 and 100,000 and PMNs greater than 50% with a negative culture on arthrocentesis.

question: An afebrile 67-year-old man who takes hydrochlorothiazide presents with right foot pain, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: tacojim/iStock/Getty Images Plus.
englishExplanation: This afebrile patient has tophi, making a gout flare the most likely diagno- sis. Gout is most common in middle-aged men and postmenopausal women. Additional risk factors for gout include hypertension, obesity, diabetes, a purine-rich diet (eg, meat, seafood, and beer), and the use of cyclosporine, aspirin, or thiazide diuretics. In gout, uric acid builds up in the body, leading to the formation of uric acid (monosodium urate) crystals in the joints. Gout flares oc- cur secondary to WBCs ingesting the crystals, causing cytokine release and inflammation. In 75% to 90% of cases, this occurs in the metatarsophalangeal joint of the great toe (ie, podagra). The gold standard for diagnosing gout is fluid aspiration from the joint, with microscopic analysis showing needle-like and negatively birefrin- gent uric acid crystals. Although laboratory studies such as ESR and CRP can be helpful in ruling out other diagnoses, they can often be elevated in both gout and sep- tic arthritis. Serum uric acid levels are also unhelpful because they can be ele- vated or normal in the setting of a gout flare. Diagnostic x-ray imaging may be helpful in chronic disease, as it may ex- hibit asymmetrical “rat bite” bone erosion that is consistent with gout. Ultrasound may also be helpful because gout crystals may exhibit a “double contour” sign. Gout can be treated in the emergency setting with NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and colchicine. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with significant renal dis- ease, and oral steroids should be used with caution in diabetic patients. Colchicine should be avoided in patients with significant renal or liver disease because it can also cause significant GI side effects. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cutaneous leishmaniasis is an unlikely diagnosis in this case. Cutaneous leishma- niasis is caused by a protozoan parasite that is transmitted through sand fly bites. The bite site, which occurs on exposed areas of the skin, usually develops into a pruritic papule or nodule that progresses to a painless ulcerated lesion. There may be multiple lesions, and they may take months to years to heal. Although gonorrhea is a potential cause of septic arthritis, gonorrhea is unlikely in this case. Patients with disseminated gonorrhea can develop pain and swelling of one or more joints, but it is often polyarticular and asymmet- rical. It most often involves the wrists, knees, and ankles. Patients frequently present with associated tenosynovitis, dermatitis, and polyarthralgia. Patients with disseminated gonococcal infection frequently have systemic signs of infection but may be afebrile on presentation. Joint fluid aspiration is vital if there is any suspi- cion for septic arthritis. Lyme arthritis is unlikely in this case because it rarely involves small joints. Lyme septic arthritis can occur in the setting of both acute and late Lyme in- fection. Lyme septic arthritis often involves the larger joints (most commonly the knees), and it characteristically leads to large joint effusions. Arthropathy from Lyme disease is often polyarticular and asymmetrical. Patients may also present with erythema migrans, the classic “bullseye” rash. Lyme disease is caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is transmitted through the bite of the deer tick.

question: Which synovial fluid finding is most consistent with gouty arthritis?

options.text: 10,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 50% PMNs, positively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and negative Gram stain
15,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 50% PMNs, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and negative Gram stain
75,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 80% PMNs, positively birefringent calcium py- rophosphate crystals, and positive Gram stain
100,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 92% PMNs. negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and negative Gram stain

correctAnswer: 15,000 WBCs/mm<sup>3</sup>, 50% PMNs, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and negative Gram stain
englishExplanation: Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis is key to diagnosing gout. Findings of 15,000 WBCs/mm, 50% polymorphonuclear cells (PMNs), negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and a negative Gram stain are most consistent with gout-induced arthritis. Although the WBC count can be somewhat variable, it should be less than 50,000/mm in the set- ting of a crystal-induced synovitis without septic arthritis; however, septic arthritis can occur when the WBC count is less than 50,000/mm, especially in the setting of immunocompromise, early infection, and certain bacteria (eg, Neisseria and my- coplasma). Consider septic arthritis in conjunction with a gout flare, and administer antibiotics if septic arthritis is a concern. There can be variable percentages of PMNs in gouty arthritis, but arthritis should be suspected if the PMNs are 75% to 90% or greater. Monosodium urate crys- tals are often present in acute gout flares, and they are negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. Joint fluid in the setting of a gout flare should not have a 3 3 3 positive Gram stain. Cellulitis overlying the potential aspiration site and coagulopa- thy are relative contraindications to arthrocentesis. Arthrocentesis of a prosthetic joint should be done in consultation with an orthopedic surgeon and should only be done if necessary to rule out infection. Incorrect Answer Explanations Synovial fluid findings of 10,000 WBCs/mm, 50% PMNs, positively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and a negative Gram stain are not the best choice be- cause uric acid crystals are negatively birefringent. Calcium pyrophosphate crys- tals are positively birefringent and are diagnostic for pseudogout. Synovial fluid findings of 75,000 WBCs/mm, 80% PMNs, positively birefringent cal- cium pyrophosphate crystals, and a positive Gram stain are suggestive of septic arthritis or septic arthritis with pseudogout. WBC count in crystal synovitis can be variable but should be less than 25,000 (with a positive likelihood ratio [+LR] for septic arthritis in this context of 0.32) to 50,000 (+LR of 7.7). There is also a higher percentage of PMNs and a positive Gram stain, which would be concerning for septic arthritis. Synovial fluid findings of 100,000 WBCs/mm, 90% PMNs, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals, and a negative Gram stain are not the best choice. The WBC count is greater than 50,000/mm, and the percentage of PMNs is 92%, making this sample concerning for septic arthritis. Although the Gram stain was negative in this analysis, Gram stain is only 29% to 50% sensitive, so a neg- ative Gram stain does not rule out infection.

question: What is the best oral treatment for acute gout flare in a patient with chronic kidney disease?
englishExplanation: Prednisone is the best oral treatment for acute gout flare in the setting of chronic kidney disease. Courses of prednisone 30 mg to 40 mg PO daily (either in single or divided doses) for 5 days can be effective in treating acute gout flares; ta- pered courses can also be considered. Studies show that steroids can be as effective as NSAIDs in the setting of acute gout flares and may potentially have fewer side effects. However, steroids should be avoided if there is any concern for septic arthritis and in diabetic patients with poor glycemic control. In patients without significant comorbidities, other therapies such as NSAIDs and colchicine may be considered. If there is no concern for a septic joint, glucocorticoid articular injection may also be considered. Incorrect Answer Explanations Allopurinol is a urate-lowering medication used to prevent gout flares. It is not the best initial choice because it may potentially prolong the gout flare. Recent small studies suggest that this may not be the case, but this is still controversial. The me- tabolite of allopurinol remains in the circulation longer in the setting of renal impair- ment and may lead to toxic drug reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. Thus, allopurinol should be used with caution in these patients. Colchicine should be used with extreme caution in patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency. It should also be avoided in any patients taking a P-glyco- protein inhibitor. Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic margin. If it accumulates in the body, colchicine can have potentially serious side effects, including cytope- nias, neuropathy, liver failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Colchicine also can have signifi- cant GI side effects, such as vomiting and diarrhea. Indomethacin is not the best answer choice because NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with renal impairment. NSAIDs should also be avoided in patients with a history of gastric or duodenal ulcers or who are on anticoagulation therapy. NSAIDs are most effective when started at the onset of a gout flare and should be continued for 2 to 3 days after the resolution of symptoms.

question: What crystals are found in the synovial fluid of pseudogout?
englishExplanation: Positively birefringent calcium pyrophosphate crystals are seen on syn- ovial fluid analysis in patients with pseudogout or calcium pyrophos- phate crystal deposition disease (CPPD). Pseudogout is a crystal-induced syn- ovitis that is caused by deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in the joint. These crystals exhibit positive birefringence on microscopy and are rhomboid- shaped. In patients with pseudogout, the most commonly affected joint is the knee. These patients may exhibit findings of white lines of chondrocalcinosis on x-ray imaging of the joint. Treatment of pseudogout is similar to gout flares, with NSAIDs, colchicine, and steroids unless contraindicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Calcium oxalate crystals can be present in synovial fluid but are not are not diagnos- tic for pseudogout. Notably, calcium oxalate crystals can be observed in eth- ylene glycol intoxication as ethylene glycol is broken down into oxalic acid. Subsequently, calcium oxalate precipitates in the kidney. The calcium oxalate crystals can then be identified on urine microscopy. Monosodium urate crystals are present in gout flares, not pseudogout flares. The monosodium urate crystals are negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. Gout most commonly presents with involvement of the first metatarsal pha- langeal joint (podagra), and patients may have tophi, which are nodular deposits of uric acid crystals. Cholesterol crystals can be present in synovial fluid but are not indicative of pseudogout. Cholesterol crystals can be present in states of chronic inflamma- tion, and it is also possible to see lipid droplets on synovial fluid. In that context, the presence of a fracture should be considered.

question: What is most likely to trigger a gout flare?
englishExplanation: Salicylates can increase uric acid levels and have been linked to gout flares. Gout is most common in middle-aged men and post menopausal women. Additional risk factors for gout include hypertension, obesity, diabetes, a purine-rich diet (eg, meat, seafood, and beer), and medications, including cy- closporine, thiazide, diuretics, and aspirin. In gout, uric acid builds up in the body and leads to the formation of uric acid crystals in the joints. Gout flares occur sec- ondary to WBCs ingesting the crystals, causing cytokine release and inflammation. One of the most common locations for this to occur (75%-90%) is in the great toe metatarsophalangeal joint (ie, podagra). The gold standard for diagnosing gout is fluid aspiration from the joint, with microscopic analysis showing needle- shaped and negatively birefringent uric acid crystals. Treatment of gout in the emergency setting involves the use of NSAIDs, corticosteroids, and colchicine. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with sig- nificant renal disease, and oral steroids should be used with caution in diabetic pa- tients. Colchicine should be avoided in patients with significant renal or liver disease because it can cause significant GI side effects. Incorrect Answer Explanations Angiotensin receptor blockers are unlikely to trigger a gout flare. In fact, angiotensin receptor blockers may help lower uric acid levels, based on recent stud- ies. Diuretics such as thiazide, however, do increase urate reabsorption and can trig- ger gout flares. Although more research is needed, several studies have indicated that supple- mentation with ascorbic acid may reduce serum uric acid levels. However, there is no convincing evidence that ascorbic acid supplementation reduces the fre- quency or severity of gout flares. Caffeine is not a likely trigger for gout flares, and it has been shown to potentially decrease uric acid levels. In contrast, alcoholic beverages and bever- ages that are high in sugar or high-fructose corn syrup have been linked to gout flares. Alcohol metabolism blocks excretion of uric acid, leading to increased levels in the body.

question: An otherwise healthy 15-year-old girl presents with 2 months of progressive swelling and pain in the small joints of her hands and feet. She denies any other associated signs or symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), previously known as juvenile rheuma- toid arthritis, is an autoimmune arthritis seen in predominantly female children who are less than 16 years. The diagnosis requires persistent symp- toms for at least 6 weeks without other identifiable causes of arthritis. JIA has multiple subtypes, including the polyarticular form presented in this case. Polyarticular JIA in older children and adolescents typically involves at least five joints and develops rapidly over 2 to 3 months, whereas younger children have more indolent oligoarthritis until the more severe polyarthritis is trig- gered by an underlying infection. The small joints of the hands and feet are of- ten affected in JIA, presenting with symmetric swelling and pain that is usually out of proportion to the visible swelling and inflammation. Rarely, JIA patients present with the systemic form, which is characterized by prolonged fever and rash. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with gonococcal arthritis typically have migratory oligoarthritis or polyarthritis. The arthritis is typically seen in the wrist, ankles, elbows, and knees and is usually asymmetric. The tendons and joints of the hand may be in- volved in the bacteremic form of disseminated gonococcal infections. Disseminated gonococcal infections also typically present with a characteristic pustular rash on the trunk and extremities, including the palms and soles. These patients may also have nonspecific malaise, myalgias, and fevers. This is in contrast to JIA, which is a more persistent arthritis without infectious symptoms or rash. This patient has no associated features to suggest psoriatic arthritis. Psoriatic arthri- tis is one of the categories of JIA, but this patient is presenting with signs and symp- toms most consistent with polyarticular JIA. Beyond oligoarthritis or polyarthritis, psoriatic arthritis is associated with findings such as scaly, erythematous skin plaques, dactylitis, and fingernail pitting. These patients often have a first-degree relative with psoriasis. Reactive arthritis, previously known as Reiter syndrome, is a type of au- toimmune polyarthritis associated with a preceding infection, usually a genitourinary (eg, chlamydia) or GI (eg, Shigella) infection. Reactive arthritis is best remembered by the phrase “can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree,” which alludes to the classic triad of urethritis or cervicitis; conjunc- tivitis or uveitis; and asymmetric, large-joint oligoarthritis. Keratoderma blennorrhagicum — hard nodules on the soles or palms — is pathog- nomonic for reactive arthritis. Reactive arthritis usually develops rapidly over a period of days to weeks as a reaction to an infection and does not constitute systemic dissemination of the triggering infection. It does not require antibiotics unless the triggering infection is still present; in such cases, antibiotics are an appropriate treatment.

question: A 36-year-old woman presents with bilateral ankle pain that has lasted for a week. She also mentions progressively worsening wrist stiffness over the past few months that improves throughout the day with use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic, inflammatory polyarthritis af- fecting the synovial joints. Peripheral joints are usually affected in a symmet- ric pattern, and as the disease progresses, proximal joints may become involved. It is an autoimmune disorder that can lead to joint deformities through cartilage and bone erosion as well as ligament and tendon damage. If untreated, RA may lead to permanent loss of joint function in as little as 10 years from onset. RA is also associ- ated with many extra-articular manifestations, such as heart disease, osteo- porosis, and eye involvement. The onset of RA is insidious, and most patients initially complain of hand or wrist stiffness that improves with use throughout the day. Morning stiffness last- ing more than half an hour after sleep or prolonged inactivity is indicative of an in- flammatory arthropathy. The proximal joints of the fingers, hands, and feet are often the first affected, but patients may experience swelling and pain of more proximal large joints, such as shoulders, elbows, and knees as the disease spreads. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystal deposition in synovial fluid. Gout flares are typically monoarticular with an intense in- flammatory response. Joints in the lower extremities are the most commonly affected. In longstanding disease, gout may present in a polyarticular fashion. Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis associated with the skin disease psoriasis. Joint involvement is often asymmetrical, and distal joints such as the DIPs are affected. The spine may also be involved. In contrast with RA, most patients with psoriatic arthritis are seronegative for rheumatoid factor. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) may present with polyarthritis. It is an autoimmune disease with multisystem involvement. Most patients experience systemic symptoms such as fever, fatigue, weight loss, myalgias, or skin in- volvement in addition to arthritis. SLE is diagnosed based on clinical history and serologic testing.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with complaints of bilateral hand and knee pain. She states her pain is similar to prior rheumatoid arthritis flares. She is currently taking a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) and has an appointment with her rheumatologist in 2 days. What is the best treatment for her present flare?
englishExplanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune systemic inflamma- tory arthritis involving synovial joints. Disease progression includes exacerba- tions of symptoms, known as flares, and spontaneous reductions in disease activity. For acute flares, glucocorticoids are the drug of choice to mediate reduction in inflammation and pain. For mild to moderate disease affecting a few joints, intra-articular injections are helpful. Systemic steroids can be given for pa- tients with more involved disease. Oral medications or long-acting injections are appropriate for this patient. For patients with severe disease with systemic in- volvement, pulse steroids may be used. Outpatient referral to a rheumatologist is recommended, as long-term treatment with and titration of disease-modifying drugs is necessary. Pain relievers are often used as adjuncts for symptomatic control but will not prevent disease progression, so they should not be used alone. Incorrect Answer Explanations Colchicine is a drug that is commonly used in gout, which is an inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystal deposition in synovial fluid. Multiple in- flammatory pathways are affected by colchicine; therefore, it is often used to reduce the severe inflammation associated with an acute gout flare. Ibuprofen is an NSAID that is commonly used to treat pain and minor swelling. It is one of the first-line therapies for osteoarthritis, which is a noninflammatory arthri- tis. In an acute RA flare, ibuprofen is an appropriate drug to help reduce pain but will not modulate the underlying cause as effectively as steroids. Tramadol is an opioid medication that solely provides analgesia. Medications in this class are useful for pain control in end-stage disease or severe acute flares but do not treat the underlying cause. Opioid use in RA has also been associated with increased risk of hospitalization due to serious infection.

question: A 38-year-old woman presents with wrist pain. The joint is tender and warm to the touch. A joint aspiration is performed. Which description of the fluid is most con- sistent with an acute flare of rheumatoid arthritis?

options.text: Cloudy and yellow with 30,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, neutrophilic pre- dominance, and negatively birefringent crystals
Cloudy and yellow with 95,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, neutrophilic pre- dominance, and no crystals
Transparent and yellow with 4,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, without neu- trophilic predominance or crystals
Yellow with 20,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, neutrophilic predominance, and no crystals

correctAnswer: Yellow with 20,000 WBCs per mm<sup>3</sup>, neutrophilic predominance, and no crystals
englishExplanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic inflammatory polyarthritis affect- ing synovial joints. Synovial fluid analysis will show an inflammatory effusion with 1,500 to 25,000 WBCs per mm with a neutrophilic predominance. No crystals will be present as in gout or pseudogout. WBC counts greater than 25,000 per mm should raise suspicion for infection of the joint. All fluid sam- ples should be sent for culture. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cloudy and yellow synovial fluid with 30,000 WBCs per mm with neutrophilic pre- dominance and negatively birefringent crystals is representative of gout. Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystal deposition in syn- ovial fluid. Gout flares are typically monoarticular with an intense inflammatory response, and the most commonly affected joints are the lower extremities. Cloudy and yellow synovial fluid with 95,000 WBCs per mm with neutrophilic pre- dominance and no crystals is indicative of a septic joint. Septic arthritis is a rapidly progressive monocular arthritis due to intra-articular joint infection. Patients may present with systemic symptoms (such as fevers and chills) and hesi- tancy to or inability to range the affected joint due to pain and swelling. Synovial fluid analysis will typically show cloudy fluid with a WBC count greater than 50,000 with a neutrophilic predominance greater than 75%. Transparent and yellow synovial fluid with 4,000 WBCs without neutrophilic pre- dominance or presence of crystals is suggestive of osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis is a chronic polyarticular destructive joint disease, which lacks systemic symp- toms. It is not an inflammatory arthritis. For patients who present with exacerbations of symptoms, analgesics and rest is recommended.

question: Which is the definitive method of diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis?
englishExplanation: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a polyarticular inflammatory arthritis with an autoimmune cause. As with all patients, the initial evaluation of RA should in- clude a history and thorough physical examination. In RA, peripheral joints are initially affected in a symmetric pattern, and as the disease progresses, proxi- mal joints may become involved. Many patients experience morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes as one of their initial symptoms. RA is a chronic condition, and patients who have symptoms for fewer than 6 weeks should have test- ing performed to rule out alternate causes such as viral illness. Definitive diagno- sis of RA is through serologic testing for rheumatoid factor and antibod- ies against cyclic citrullinated peptide. Incorrect Answer Explanations Arthrocentesis is necessary to diagnose septic arthritis, which is a rapidly progressive monocular arthritis due to intra-articular joint infection. Patients may present with systemic symptoms (such as fevers and chills) and hes- itancy to or inability to range the affected joint due to pain and swelling. Synovial fluid analysis will typically show cloudy fluid with a WBC count in excess of 50,000 per mm with a neutrophilic predominance greater than 75%. Although history and physical examination are essential to make a diagnosis of RA, it is not solely a clinical diagnosis. Fibromyalgia, which is a disorder of pain regula- tion characterized by chronic musculoskeletal pain not explained by another systemic disorder, may be diagnosed clinically after other possible causes are ruled out. X-rays of affected joints may help diagnose osteoarthritis, which is the most prevalent arthropathy affecting older adults. Osteoarthritis frequently affects joints in the knees, hips, hands, and spine. It is a chronic, progressive arthropathy char- acterized by degeneration of cartilage and bone. On imaging, there may be non- uniform joint space loss, subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation, or cyst formation.

question: A 6-year-old boy is brought in for evaluation of acute on chronic hip pain. His mother states he has complained of hip and knee pain several times in the past year and he occasionally limps, but today, he is refusing to walk. He has a pink macular rash on his trunk. He has had a fever of 39.2°C (102.6°F) for the past weeks. His mother initially attributed his symptoms to a viral illness, as his younger sibling recently started daycare, but she became concerned when he re- fused to walk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), formerly known as juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, is a rheumatologic disease that causes an oligoarticular arthritis of large joints in children younger than 7. Patients may also present with sys- temic symptoms, such as fever with temperatures greater than 39°C (102.2°F), malaise, weight loss, and rash. Manifestations vary widely and may be severe. Some patients may develop hepatosplenomegaly, pericardial effusion, pleu- ritis, or lymphadenopathy. JIA has no known trigger and is usually not preceded by illness. Although some patients may be positive for rheumatoid factor, there are no specific diagnostic tests for JIA, so other potentially serious conditions such as infection or leukemia must first be ruled out. Treatment is with anti-inflammatories, steroids, physical therapy, and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), if necessary. Patients with suspected JIA must be referred to a specialist for contin- ued care. Incorrect Answer Explanations Legg-Calve-Perthes Disease (LCP) presents with an insidious onset of hip pain in children aged 3 to 12 years. LCP is characterized by an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, which may cause a progressive limp or pain with activity. This pain is not relieved by rest. A high index of suspicion is needed for diagnosis, as initial radiographs may be negative. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) may present with hip, thigh, or knee pain. SCFE is characterized by displacement of the femoral epiphysis from the femoral neck through the growth plate. SCFE most commonly oc- curs in obese adolescents aged 12 to 13, and it is more common in males. Transient synovitis is a relatively common inflammatory condition that causes hip pain and decreased range of motion in children ages 3 to 8. Patients may present with a low-grade fever. Most patients have unilateral symptoms, but bilateral effusions are often detected on imaging. This allows differentiation from septic arthritis, which is usually unilateral.

question: Which finding is most consistent with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis?
englishExplanation: One of the hallmark findings of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) is daily fever. The fever pattern associated with sJIA is described as quotidian, occurring in the late evening and resolving without antipyretics. The diagnostic criteria for sJIA is daily fever for more than 2 weeks, along with arthritis in at least one joint for more than 6 weeks, in a child younger than 16. Additionally, pa- tients must have at least one of the following: lymphadenopathy; splenomegaly; hepatomegaly; serositis; or a migratory, fleeting, pale pink rash. sJIA is a subtype of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). JIA is a broad term that re- places the previous nomenclature of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis and refers to a group of chronic arthritides in children. JIA is a diagnosis of exclusion, as other severe causes of joint inflammation must be excluded prior to confirming the diagno- sis of JIA. The categories of JIA have varying clinical manifestations, including sys- temic arthritis, polyarthritis (RF positive or negative), oligoarthritis (persistent or ex- tended), psoriatic arthritis, and undifferentiated arthritis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dactylitis is a complication of juvenile arthritis that is commonly seen in the psoriatic but not the systemic subtype. Patients with psoriatic arthritis often present with additional findings of fatigue, morning stiffness, and nail abnor- malities, including nail pitting and onycholysis. The presence of dactylitis generally suggests more severe disease. Contrary to arthritis, in which swelling and inflamma- tion is isolated to the joint, dactylitis involves the entire digit. Other potential causes of dactylitis are sickle cell anemia, sarcoidosis, and infection. Treatment is aimed at addressing the underlying cause of the swelling. For patients with psoriatic arthritis, this may include NSAIDs, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), or bio- logic agents. Erythema marginatum is the rash noted in acute rheumatic fever and has a different appearance than the typical rash of sJIA. Both rashes are evanescent in na- ture, but the annular lesions of erythema marginatum have raised edges with central clearing. Acute rheumatic fever is an inflammatory process that results from group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus. Patients present 2 to 6 weeks after a strepto- coccal pharyngitis with fever, polyarticular arthritis, and chorea. Uveitis is a complication of juvenile arthritis that is more often seen in the oligoarticular but not the systemic subtype. Oligoarticular JIA is the most com- mon of the JIA subtypes and involves fewer than four joints, typically the knees and ankles. Uveitis associated with oligoarticular JIA affects the anterior chamber and is often bilateral and painless. Patients with oligoarticular JIA should have regu- lar slit-lamp screening examinations by an ophthalmologist. If uveitis is detected, the first-line treatment is topical corticosteroids.

question: A child presents with daily fevers, rash over the cheeks, joint swelling, and hema- turia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in children is challenging to diagnose since the onset of symptoms is often gradual and can involve all organs. Many systemic symp- toms of SLE, such as fever, fatigue, and lymphadenopathy, can be difficult to distinguish from infectious processes or malignancy. Additionally, hematologic mani- festations such as anemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia can be present. The rash typically associated with SLE is described as malar; however, it may in- volve other areas of the face and appear hypopigmented. Children can experience both arthritis and arthralgias in large and small joints. The kidneys are commonly affected, resulting in both proteinuria and hematuria. Pleuritis and pericarditis are the most common pulmonary and cardiac manifestations, respectively. The diagnosis of SLE should be considered when children present with this constella- tion of findings. Laboratory testing can be guided in consultation with a pediatric rheumatologist. Treatment of SLE can vary depending upon organ involvement and severity of illness; however, hydroxychloroquine is the mainstay of treatment for all patients with systemic disease. Additionally, many children benefit from the use of glucocorticoids. Incorrect Answer Explanations Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is not associated with hematuria. JIA describes a number of inflammatory disorders in children, including systemic, oligoarticular, and polyarticular JIA. In addition to arthritis, patients may have in- volvement of other organs. For example, potential complications of systemic JIA are pericarditis and pleural effusions. A common complication of oligoarticular JIA is uveitis. Renal involvement is rare in patients with JIA. If the patient presents with hematuria, as described in this case, other diagnoses should be considered. Patients with malaria often report symptoms of daily fever, malaise, and arthralgias, but they do not present with rash. Malaria is an infection caused by the parasite Plasmodium, transmitted through the bite of an Anopheles mosquito. Once the parasite enters the bloodstream, it reproduces in the liver and then attacks the RBCs. This results in multiorgan dysfunction. Affected individuals may have splenomegaly and appear jaundiced on examination. Laboratory abnormalities are reflective of hemolysis, coagulopathy, and renal and hepatic failure that can ensue. Pediatric patients with malaria should be hospitalized, and treatment is dependent upon the resistance patterns of the region in which the infection was acquired. Patients with reactive arthritis may experience urethritis but do not have hematuria. Reactive arthritis denotes swelling and joint pain that develops after a preceding infection. The antecedent illnesses are often GI or genitourinary in ori- gin. The most commonly associated bacterial pathogens causing GI illnesses are Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, and Yersinia. Chlamydia, a common STI, may cause arthritis in addition to genitourinary symptoms.
