englishExplanation: Critical care billing includes ventilator management (direct care), but NOT separately billable procedures (intubation, reductions). Trauma team activation = separate code.
arabicExplanation: فوترة الرعاية الحرجة تشمل إدارة المنفسة (رعاية مباشرة)، لكن ليس الإجراءات القابلة للفوترة المنفصلة (تنبيب، إرجاع).

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: In the medical oversight of an EMS system, what is an example of online medical direction?

options.text: Communication of medication orders by radio from an emergency physician to a paramedic
Development of an EMS protocol by a medical director
Implementation of a QI initiative by an EMS medical director
One-on-one retrospective review of a call

correctAnswer: Communication of medication orders by radio from an emergency physician to a paramedic
englishExplanation: Online medical direction (direct/real-time): orders from command physician to paramedic. Offline (indirect): protocol development, QI, education, chart review.
arabicExplanation: التوجيه الطبي المباشر (online): أوامر من الطبيب القائد للمسعف. غير المباشر (offline): تطوير البروتوكولات، QI، التعليم، مراجعة الملفات.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: Under what circumstance may a hospital waive standard staff credentialing procedures?

options.text: Hospital Emergency Operations Plan has been activated

correctAnswer: Hospital Emergency Operations Plan has been activated
englishExplanation: Joint Commission: credentialing waived ONLY when Emergency Operations Plan activated. Hospital bylaws designate who grants privileges. 72-hour oversight required.
arabicExplanation: Joint Commission: إعفاء الاعتماد فقط عند تنشيط خطة عمليات الطوارئ. لوائح المستشفى تحدد من يمنح الامتيازات.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: Which staff members are mostly likely to be victims of workplace violence in the emergency department?
englishExplanation: Workplace violence ED: nurses most common victims, then physicians, then other staff. Reasons: crowding, understaffing, lack of security. Report to police (criminal offense).
arabicExplanation: العنف في مكان العمل في الطوارئ: الممرضون الأكثر ضحية، ثم الأطباء، ثم الطاقم الآخر.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: A 55-year-old man waiting for cough threatens to get a gun and shoot staff. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Call law enforcement to file a police report regarding the threat
Discuss with charge nurse and file incident report

correctAnswer: Call law enforcement to file a police report regarding the threat
englishExplanation: Verbal threats = workplace violence (OSHA) = assault legally. File police report (assess criminal history/firearm status). Also file incident report + notify administration.
arabicExplanation: التهديدات اللفظية = عنف في مكان العمل (OSHA) = اعتداء قانونيًا. ارفع تقرير بوليسي (يقيّم السجل الجنائي/حالة السلاح).

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: During a busy shift, someone walks into the emergency department and starts shooting a rifle. What is the most appropriate response?
englishExplanation: Active shooter: RUN first (as far as possible). Then HIDE (lock/barricade, close shades, quiet, concealed). FIGHT last resort (incapacitate).
arabicExplanation: مطلق نار نشط: اهرب أولًا (بعيدًا قدر الإمكان). ثم اختبئ (اقفل/احجب، أغلق الستائر، صمت). قاتل كملاذ أخير.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: An 89-year-old man with terminal cancer, DNR with comfort care only, presents with severe dyspnea, chest pain, fever, and productive cough. CXR shows lobar pneumonia. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Administer an opioid and a benzodiazepine
Administer supplemental oxygen but withhold antibiotics
Provide aggressive treatment unless signed POLST

correctAnswer: Administer an opioid and a benzodiazepine
englishExplanation: End-of-life care in ED: opioids for pain/dyspnea + benzodiazepines for anxiety/dyspnea. DNR does not mean 'do nothing'. Discuss goals of care. Palliative consult.
arabicExplanation: رعاية نهاية الحياة في الطوارئ: أفيونات للألم/ضيق النفس + بنزوديازيبين للقلق/ضيق النفس. DNR لا يعني 'لا تفعل شيئًا'.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: An 89-year-old man with severe dementia, poor oral intake. Family considering feeding tube. Which specialist would be most helpful?
englishExplanation: Advanced dementia + artificial nutrition question: palliative medicine for goals-of-care discussion. No health benefit from artificial nutrition in advanced dementia. Hand-feeding recommended.
arabicExplanation: الخرف المتقدم + سؤال التغذية الاصطناعية: الطب التلطيفي لمناقشة أهداف الرعاية. لا فائدة صحية من التغذية الاصطناعية.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: An 88-year-old with end-stage COPD intubated by paramedics. POLST indicates no CPR/intubation, comfort-focused. Son agrees. What is the best next step?

options.text: Admit to ICU for terminal extubation
Extubate in the emergency department and provide comfort care

correctAnswer: Extubate in the emergency department and provide comfort care
englishExplanation: POLST valid + son agrees + patient's wishes clear: honor by extubating in ED + comfort care. Use 'liberating from ventilator' language, not 'withdrawing care'. Offer chaplain, family time.
arabicExplanation: POLST ساري + الابن يوافق: احترم رغبات المريض بإزالة الأنبوب في الطوارئ + رعاية مريحة. استخدم لغة 'التحرير من المنفسة'، لا 'سحب الرعاية'.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: A 67-year-old with end-stage pancreatic cancer. Goals: die at home, avoid admission. Worried about pain worsening. Wants something stronger. What is the best approach?

options.text: Admission to hospital with pain consultation

englishExplanation: Terminal cancer + goals: die at home, avoid hospital, symptom control = hospice (Medicare benefit if ≤6 months prognosis). Inpatient hospice for symptom crises.
arabicExplanation: سرطان نهائي + أهداف: الموت في المنزل، تجنب المستشفى، السيطرة على الأعراض = hospice (ميزة Medicare إذا ≤6 أشهر).

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: Which finding suggests that a cancer patient's functional status may be too poor to continue with chemotherapy?

options.text: In bed more than 50% of waking hours
Requires pain medication for activities of daily living

correctAnswer: In bed more than 50% of waking hours
englishExplanation: ECOG ≥3 (>50% in bed) = poor prognosis. ASCO recommends avoiding chemo in solid tumors with ECOG ≥3 + prior non-beneficial treatment. Discuss goals, hospice.
arabicExplanation: ECOG ≥3 (>50% في السرير) = إنذار سيئ. ASCO توصي بتجنب العلاج الكيميائي في الأورام الصلبة مع ECOG ≥3.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: Which criterion is required for a patient to qualify for hospice?

options.text: Patient must stop all current medications
Role of primary care physician must be assumed by hospice medical director

englishExplanation: Hospice Medicare benefit: ≤6 months prognosis. Full code status OK. Patients can continue meds + PCP. Hospice = benefit (home, nursing facility, inpatient).
arabicExplanation: ميزة hospice من Medicare: توقع حياة ≤6 أشهر. حالة الكود الكامل مقبولة. المرضى يمكنهم الاستمرار بالأدوية وطبيبهم.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: According to HIPAA, which circumstance requires written patient authorization for disclosure of protected health information?

options.text: Coordination of health care treatment with medical consultants
Disclosure of psychotherapy notes for use in insurance billing
Release of information for workers' compensation claims

correctAnswer: Disclosure of psychotherapy notes for use in insurance billing
englishExplanation: HIPAA: psychotherapy notes require written authorization (except treatment, specific legal matters, public safety). TPO (Treatment, Payment, Operations) generally no written consent.
arabicExplanation: HIPAA: ملاحظات العلاج النفسي تتطلب إذنًا كتابيًا (باستثناء العلاج، مسائل قانونية محددة، السلامة العامة).

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: A 12-year-old brought by neighbor with severe lawnmower injuries. Tourniquets placed, bleeding difficult. Specialty hospital accepts transfer, but parents don't answer. Regarding consent?

options.text: Parents must be contacted and consent
Patient must agree to be transferred
The patient should be transferred prior to obtaining consent

correctAnswer: The patient should be transferred prior to obtaining consent
englishExplanation: EMTALA: any patient presenting to ED must receive stabilizing treatment. If unable to stabilize, transfer to facility that can (regardless of consent). Life-threatening injury = exception to parental consent.
arabicExplanation: EMTALA: أي مريض يأتي للطوارئ يجب أن يحصل على علاج مثبت. إذا لم يُستطع، يُنقل لمنشأة قادرة (بغض النظر عن الموافقة).

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: A 47-year-old with suicide attempt (wrist cutting), grandiose delusions, flight of ideas, history of bipolar disorder not on meds. Calm, no significant injury, wants discharge. What is the best next step?

options.text: Allow the patient to sign out AMA
Arrange for an emergency psychiatric hold per local state laws
Promise psychiatry will not be involved

correctAnswer: Arrange for an emergency psychiatric hold per local state laws
englishExplanation: Psychiatric hold: gravely disabled (harm to self or inability to self-care) + unable to make informed decisions. Patient lacks capacity to refuse. Involuntary hold.
arabicExplanation: حجز نفسي: عاجز بشكل خطير (إيذاء النفس أو عدم القدرة على الرعاية الذاتية) + غير قادر على اتخاذ قرارات مستنيرة.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: A 58-year-old with head injury. Yelling expletives, slurring, alcohol smell, large scalp hematoma. Refuses care, demands release. What is the best way to proceed?

options.text: Accept refusal, discharge when clinically sober
Involuntarily sedate her to facilitate workup

correctAnswer: Involuntarily sedate her to facilitate workup
englishExplanation: Intoxicated + head injury + lacks capacity to refuse essential evaluation. Sedate/restrain as needed for safety + workup. Determining capacity = any physician.
arabicExplanation: سكر + إصابة رأس + يفقد الأهلية لرفض التقييم الأساسي. هدئه/قيّده حسب الحاجة للسلامة والتقييم.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: Approximately what percentage of emergency department patients leave against medical advice?
englishExplanation: AMA rate: 0.1-2.7% (about 2%). LWBS: ~3%. AMA patients: increased 30-day return + need for emergent hospitalization. Insurance still covers.
arabicExplanation: معدل المغادرة ضد النصيحة الطبية (AMA): 0.1-2.7% (حوالي 2%). LWBS: ~3%.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: How does the 30-day return rate for adult patients discharged against medical advice compare to those discharged per standard processes?
englishExplanation: AMA patients: significantly greater 30-day return rate + need for emergent hospitalization. Myth: insurance won't cover AMA - FALSE.
arabicExplanation: مرضى AMA: معدل عودة 30 يومًا أعلى بشكل ملحوظ + حاجة للاستشفاء الطارئ. خرافة: التأمين لا يغطي AMA - خطأ.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: What is an emergency physician's best defense against liability when managing patients who leave against medical advice?

options.text: Explain risks of refusing care to the patient's family
Have the patient or family sign an AMA form

englishExplanation: AMA defense: thorough documentation in real time (discussion, risks, capacity, patient understanding). AMA forms are supporting, not replacing documentation.
arabicExplanation: دفاع AMA: توثيق شامل في الوقت الفعلي (النقاش، المخاطر، الأهلية، فهم المريض). نماذج AMA دعم وليست بديلًا.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: Hospital gets transfer request for unstable patient with AAA. Normally accepts, but vascular surgeon just started 8-hr case. Can hospital decline and remain EMTALA compliant?

options.text: No, hospitals may not refuse transfers
No, it has a vascular surgeon on staff
Yes, it is illegal to transfer an unstable patient
Yes, because it lacks the capacity to care for the patient

correctAnswer: Yes, because it lacks the capacity to care for the patient
englishExplanation: EMTALA: accepting hospital may decline if no capacity/capability. Surgeon unavailable + no space = lack capacity. Cannot refuse for money/convenience.
arabicExplanation: EMTALA: المستشفى المستقبل قد يرفض إذا انعدمت السعة/القدرة. الجراح غير متوفر + لا مساحة = انعدام السعة.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: What is one responsibility of the critical care transportation team's medical director during hospital-to-hospital transfer?

options.text: Ensuring proper training of transportation teams

correctAnswer: Ensuring proper training of transportation teams
englishExplanation: EMS medical director: training + scope of practice. Transferring physician: mode + monitoring. Accepting physician: bed choice.
arabicExplanation: المدير الطبي لـ EMS: التدريب + نطاق الممارسة. الطبيب المُحوِّل: الوضع + المراقبة. الطبيب المستقبل: اختيار السرير.

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine
question: What types of responders are critical care transportation teams most commonly composed of?
englishExplanation: Critical care transport: nurse-paramedic most common (2 advanced-care clinicians + 3rd non-practitioner). ALS: EMT-paramedic. BLS: 2 EMTs.
arabicExplanation: النقل للرعاية الحرجة: ممرض-مسعف الأكثر شيوعًا (2 أطباء متقدمين + ثالث غير ممارس).

chapterTitle: Other Core Competencies of the Practice of Emergency Medicine

question: A 24-year-old man presents with severe left-sided groin pain of 24 hours' dura- tion after lifting weights. He says that he has a lump in his groin that gets "worse" when he strains or lifts heavy objects but that he has always been able to "push it back in." His vital signs are BP 126/78, P 126, R 25, and T 38.4°C (101.2°F); SpO is 98% on room air. An abdominal examination reveals a 5-cm by 4-cm mass in the left inguinal area. The mass is firm and exquisitely tender to palpation with noted discoloration. What is the best next step in this patient's care?

options.text: Attempt manual reduction of the mass

englishExplanation: This patient's signs and symptoms (including severe pain, skin discoloration, and fever) suggest a strangulated inguinal hernia. This is a true surgical emer- gency, and immediate surgical consultation is warranted. Intravenous fluids, anal- gesia, antibiotics, and preoperative laboratory studies are also indicated. Strangulated hernias typically present with severe, exquisite pain at the hernia site with systemic signs of illness, including a toxic appearance, peritoneal findings, or sepsis. By definition, there is strangulation or vascular compromise of the tissue within the hernia. The history of a recurrent lump in the inguinal area that gets worse with straining or lifting heavy objects is suggestive of an inguinal hernia. Inguinal hernias are the most common type of hernia, occurring in about 75% of all hernias. They tend to be more common in male patients. Hernias can be re- ducible, incarcerated, or strangulated. A hernia is reducible if it is soft and can be 2 easily pushed back into the peritoneal cavity. An incarcerated hernia is firm, painful, and often nonreducible by direct pressure. Reduction of an incarcer- ated hernia should be attempted in the emergency department after ad- equate analgesia is provided; if the attempt is unsuccessful, general sur- gery should be consulted. After reduction of an incarcerated hernia, observation in the emergency department and serial abdominal examinations are reasonable. In contrast, when a patient exhibits signs of hernia strangulation, reduction should not be attempted in the emergency department. If the bowel is necrotic, there is a risk of sepsis; it should not be pushed back into the peritoneum because there is a likelihood of causing perforation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admitting this patient to the hospital for serial examinations without taking any other action is inappropriate because a strangulated hernia is a surgical emergency. This patient requires immediate surgical consultation along with in- travenous fluids, analgesia, antibiotics, and preoperative laboratory studies. When a patient exhibits signs of hernia strangulation, which is an acute surgical emergency, reduction should not be attempted in the emer- gency department. If the bowel is necrotic, there is a risk of sepsis; it should not be pushed back into the peritoneum because there is a likelihood of causing perforation. Imaging, including plain x-rays of the abdomen, is of limited value in the management of a strangulated hernia. It delays definitive management, which is antibiotics and surgical repair, and it provides no information that will not be revealed during surgery.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with acute-onset abdominal pain after coughing. On examination, there is a balloon-like protrusion near the umbilicus that is mini- mally tender without skin changes. What is the best initial management?

options.text: Control pain and attempt manual reduction
Keep NPO and consult surgery immediately
Keep NPO and place nasogastric tube

correctAnswer: Control pain and attempt manual reduction
englishExplanation: This patient has an incarcerated hernia that should be reduced. To prepare for the reduction, the patient should be placed supine in Trendelenburg with an ice pack overlying the hernia. The patient should be given pain medication or procedural sedation to help with abdominal wall muscle relaxation, which will increase success of the reduction and make the patient more comfortable. To reduce the hernia, the outline of the abdominal wall defect should be palpated with the nondominant hand. Gentle, constant, inward pressure should be applied with the dominant hand at the base of the hernia. The smaller the defect, the more difficult the reduction will be and the higher the likelihood of strangula- tion. Reducible abdominal wall hernias without signs of bowel ischemia can be dis- charged with general surgery follow-up for elective surgical repair. Hernias that are unsuccessfully reduced and remain incarcerated require general surgery consultation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although patients with incarcerated or strangulated hernias should receive pain control, intravenous antibiotics are not generally indicated. Occasionally, patients with strangulated hernias may be given empiric antibiotics, but this patient presents with no signs or symptoms consistent with a strangulated hernia. This patient shows no evidence of strangulation and does not require emergent sur- gical consultation. If there is concern for strangulation, bedside reduction is contraindicated, and surgery should be consulted. Patients with strangulated hernias typically appear toxic and have systemic symptoms; the hernia may also have overlying skin changes. A normal lactate level test should not be used to rule out strangulation because it may be falsely normal. This patient has no signs or symptoms of a bowel obstruction, so a nasogastric (NG) tube is unnecessary. The placement of NG tubes is controversial even in pa- tients with bowel obstruction because it is a painful procedure and there is little re- search suggesting benefit of NG tube placement. Key Points Incarcerated hernias differ from strangulated hernias in that the hernia contents are not ischemic. Hernias that are unsuccessfully reduced and remain incarcerated require general surgery consultation. The smaller the fascial defect, the harder it will be to reduce the hernia and the higher risk for strangulation. Incarcerated hernias should be reduced with gentle, constant, inward pressure with the dominant hand placed at the base of the hernia.

question: What is the best management for a reducible umbilical hernia in an infant?
englishExplanation: Umbilical hernias are common in children. The majority of umbilical defects will close spontaneously within 2 years, so surgical repair is usually postponed until age 4 or 5 years. Surgery is indicated earlier for complications (ie, incarceration, strangulation, or rupture). During fetal development, the umbili- cal ring contains umbilical vessels and a loop of midgut. Umbilical hernias result from incomplete closure of the fascia of the umbilical ring. After umbilical cord sep- aration, the ring typically spontaneously closes. Umbilical hernias occur in 10% to 30% of births, with a higher incidence in Black infants. Boys and girls are equally af- fected. Incidence also increases in premature and low-birth-weight babies as well as those with autosomal trisomies and metabolic disorders such as hypothyroidism. Incorrect Answer Explanations Umbilical hernias are typically diagnosed clinically. If it is difficult to dif- ferentiate between an umbilical hernia and a mass, an ultrasound may be obtained. No imaging is required for reducible umbilical hernias. Because most um- bilical hernias resolve spontaneously, expectant management is appropriate. Most umbilical hernias will resolve spontaneously within 2 years and do not require surgical intervention. If there is evidence of incarceration or strangula- tion, then surgery should be consulted.

question: Where do Spigelian hernias occur?

options.text: Anterior abdominal wall, adjacent to the semilunar line
Between the rectus abdominis muscles, at the level of the xiphoid
Between the rectus abdominis muscles, at the linea alba
Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels

correctAnswer: Anterior abdominal wall, adjacent to the semilunar line
englishExplanation: Spigelian hernias are slit-like defects in the anterior abdominal wall ad- jacent to the semilunar line. Most spigelian hernias occur in the lower ab- domen on the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis. They are rare compared to other types of hernia because they do not develop under abdominal layers of fat but be- tween fascia tissue that connects muscles. Because of this, the hernial defects tend to be smaller, which increases the risk of strangulation. Symptoms include abdominal pain, a bulge in the anterior abdominal wall, or symp- toms of incarceration or strangulation. Pain is often aggravated by maneu- vers that increase intra-abdominal pressure, similar to other ventral hernias. These hernias are less apparent on physical examination and are typically diagnosed on radiological studies such as CT scans. Spigelian hernias are surgi- cally repaired because of the high risk of strangulation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Epigastric hernias are typically located between the rectus abdominis at the level of the xiphoid. This type of hernia is caused by a preformed defect in the linea alba between the umbilicus and xiphoid. Most are asymptomatic, but symptoms may include nausea and abdominal pain in the epigastric region. Diastasis recti is located between the rectus abdominis at the linea alba. This is not a hernia, but a separation of the rectus muscles causing an increased dis- tance between the rectus abdominis muscles at the midline. It is common following pregnancy, but obesity and previous abdominal surgeries are also causes. The diag- nosis is made by history and physical examination. A midline abdominal bulge can be seen on abdominal examination, especially with Valsalva maneuvers. Direct inguinal hernias are typically located medial to the inferior epi- gastric vessels, specifically through the Hesselbach triangle. Direct in- guinal hernias are caused by weakness in the muscular layers, which may be due to several contributing factors including older age, smoking, increased intra-abdomi- nal pressure (eg, due to chronic cough or pregnancy), and connective tissue abnormalities.

question: What is the most common type of hernia found in women?
englishExplanation: Inguinal hernias are the most common type of hernia in both men and women, although they are more common in men. Inguinal hernias account for 75% of all abdominal wall hernias. Most inguinal hernias are indirect. Symptoms of an inguinal hernia include groin pain or a bulge in the groin and obstructive symptoms caused by incarceration or strangulation. Physical examination may re- veal a bulge in the groin, which is best visualized when the patient is standing or asked to cough or perform a Valsalva maneuver. Most inguinal hernias are diag- nosed through physical examination, although imaging is sometimes required. Imaging options include ultrasound, CT, and MRI. Surgical repair is the defini- tive treatment for symptomatic patients with an inguinal hernia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Femoral hernias represent 5% to 7% of all hernias. Although they occur pre- dominantly in women, they are less common than inguinal hernias. Femoral her- nias are typically seen in the upper part of the thigh below the inguinal ligament. Spigelian hernias are rare; only 0.12% of all abdominal hernias are spigelian hernias. Most occur in the lower abdomen where the posterior sheath is deficient. Umbilical hernias account for about 6% to 14% of all abdominal hernias. It is the second most common type of hernia in adults, and they are equally common among men and women.

question: What is the most common hernia?
englishExplanation: Indirect inguinal hernias are the most common type of hernia; two-thirds of all inguinal hernias are indirect. They are twice as common as direct inguinal hernias. Indirect hernias more commonly occur on the right, likely because of the slower closure of a patent processus vaginalis on the right side. Indirect inguinal hernias protrude through the internal inguinal ring, lateral to the epigastric vessels. Ultimately, it is not essential to differentiate indirect from direct inguinal hernia on physical examination because both require surgical repair. Incorrect Answer Explanations Direct inguinal hernias are less common than indirect inguinal hernias. Direct inguinal hernias are typically caused by a protrusion of abdominal contents through the transversalis fascia within Hesselbach triangle (the borders being the inferior epigastric vessels superolaterally, the rectus sheath medially, and inguinal ligament inferiorly). They protrude medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Femoral hernias represent 5% to 7% of all hernias. Although they occur pre- dominantly in women, femoral hernias are a less common type of groin hernia than inguinal hernias. They are typically seen in the upper part of the thigh below the in- guinal ligament. Spigelian hernias are rare; only 0.12% of all abdominal hernias are spigelian hernias. Most occur in the lower abdomen where the posterior sheath is deficient.

question: Indirect inguinal hernias occur as a result of incomplete closure of which structure?
englishExplanation: Indirect inguinal hernias are most commonly caused by incomplete clo- sure of the processus vaginalis, an invagination of the parietal peritoneum that precedes testicular descent through the inguinal canal during embryogenesis. Indirect inguinal hernias protrude through the internal inguinal ring lateral to the epigastric vessels. Although most indirect inguinal hernias are congenital, they may also develop after long-term pressure on the processus vaginalis. This can be related to weakening or disruption of the abdominal wall tissues from smoking, old age, increased intraabdominal pressure, and connective tissue disorders. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although indirect inguinal hernias protrude through the internal inguinal ring, they are usually caused by an incomplete closure of the processus vaginalis. The deep (internal) inguinal ring is the entrance to the inguinal canal. It is bounded by the arched lower margin of the transversalis fascia (above and medially) and by the inferior epigastric vessels (below and medially). It contains the spermatic cord in males and the round ligament of the uterus in females. The functioning of the pubic symphysis is unrelated to indirect inguinal hernias. Pubic symphysis is the cartilaginous joint between the superior rami of the left and right pubis of the pelvis. The term sports hernia typically refers to ath- letes who may present with osteitis pubis, or inflammation of the pubic symphysis, which typically occur when athletes suddenly change direction, kick, or pivot. The superficial inguinal ring is uninvolved in indirect inguinal hernias. The superficial inguinal ring is the triangular opening within the aponeurosis of the external oblique that forms the exit of the inguinal canal, and it contains the ilioin- guinal nerve and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. The deep inguinal ring is at the other end of the canal.

question: What is the appropriate technique used to completely reduce an inguinal hernia?

options.text: Place an ice pack on the area of swelling, and reassess after 20 minutes
Place the patient prone in Trendelenburg, and reassess after 20 minutes
Place the patient supine in Trendelenburg, and apply gentle, inward pressure
Place the patient supine in Trendelenburg, and apply intermittent, firm pressure

correctAnswer: Place the patient supine in Trendelenburg, and apply gentle, inward pressure
englishExplanation: Bedside reduction of an inguinal hernia is indicated when there is evi- dence of incarceration but no strangulation. To prepare for the reduction, the patient should be supine in Trendelenburg with an ice pack overlying the area of swelling. Pain control or procedural sedation is typically required to facilitate abdominal wall muscle relaxation. The outline of the abdominal wall de- fect should be palpated with the nondominant hand. Gentle, constant, inward pressure with the dominant hand should be applied. Constant pressure is neces- sary to prevent completely collapsing the lumen of the trapped small bowel, which will cause a ballooning effect. Patients with reducible hernias without signs of bowel ischemia can be discharged with a general surgery follow-up for elective repair. Incorrect Answer Explanations Placing an ice pack on the area of swelling may help reduce swelling. However, in order to fully reduce the hernia, manual pressure is typically required for reduction. The patient needs to be supine, rather than prone, to facilitate manual reduction. Having the patient prone is also an airway risk if any sort of procedural sedation is used to facilitate reduction. Constant and gentle pressure should be applied, instead of intermittent firm pres- sure. Intermittent firm pressure increases the likelihood of collapsing the intestinal lumen and causing strangulation, especially if the defect is small.

question: What is associated with increased incidence of inguinal hernias in infants?
englishExplanation: Preterm birth increases the incidence of inguinal hernias, with the preva- lence being highest during infancy and declining with age. Between 25 and 35 weeks of gestation, each of the testis descends from its retroperitoneal, intra-abdominal lo- cation through the inguinal canal. The processus vaginalis obliterates, leaving no connection between the peritoneal cavity and the inguinal canal and scrotum. This is why 90% of pediatric inguinal hernias are diagnosed in boys. About 3% to 5% of healthy, full-term infants are born with an inguinal hernia, and in prema- ture infants, the incidence is up to 30%. Pediatric inguinal hernias are typically treated with surgery to prevent complications (eg, intestinal perforation, testicular atrophy, and ovarian damage). The contralateral inguinal canal is explored during surgery to detect a concomitant contralateral processus vaginalis defect. Incorrect Answer Explanations Delivery via cesarean section is not associated with an increased inci- dence of inguinal hernias in infants. It does, however, increase the risk of res- piratory distress syndrome. Oligohydramnios has no effect on the incidence of inguinal hernias in infants. Oligohydramnios refers to decreased amniotic fluid volume and is associ- ated with genitourinary tract abnormalities, fetal growth restriction, and chromoso- mal abnormalities. The most common cause of oligohydramnios is rupture of mem- branes, specifically preterm premature rupture of membranes. Increased incidence of inguinal hernias are unrelated to Turner syn- drome. It is the most common sex chromosomal abnormality found in girls, caused by one missing X chromosome, either partially or completely. Infants with Turner syndrome have increased risk of cardiovascular malformations, hearing loss, renal anomalies, ocular abnormalities, and neurocognitive deficits.

question: What is the most common etiology of a ventral hernia?
englishExplanation: The etiology of a ventral hernia can be broken down into two categories, acquired and congenital. Previous surgery is the most common cause of a ventral hernia. Other common causes of acquired ventral hernias include trauma, preg- nancy, and repetitive stress on naturally weakened parts of the abdominal wall. The naturally occurring weak points in the abdominal wall include the umbilicus, semilunar line, ostomy sites, bilateral inguinal regions, and esophageal hiatus. Ventral hernias typically present with abdominal pain and swelling or fullness that changes with position or with Valsalva maneuvers. The her- nia may cause bowel obstructions or become incarcerated or strangulated, requiring emergent surgical correction. Incorrect Answer Explanations Congenital causes of hernias are less common than previous surgery; they include Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and any preformed hernial openings caused by incomplete closure of the abdominal wall, as seen in umbilical and indirect inguinal hernias. Some of these may remain undiag- nosed and may never cause issues during a patient's life. Constipation increases the risk of hernias because of the increased intra-ab- dominal pressure that causes repetitive microtrauma to the muscle and fascia lay- ers, but previous surgery is a more common cause. Other causes of increased intra- abdominal pressure include physical labor, childbirth, excessive coughing, or frequent vomiting. Obesity stretches the fascia of the abdomen causing it to weaken, but obe- sity is less common as a cause of a ventral hernia than previous surgery. Repeat weight gain and loss, as can happen during pregnancy, can also weaken the abdomi- nal fascia. Repetitive stress leads to microscopic tearing of the tissue layers, de- creasing the strength of the fascia and predisposing individuals to hernias. Key Points Previous surgery is the most common cause of a ventral hernia. Congenital causes of ventral hernias are less common than previous surgery and in- clude Ehlers-Danlos and Marfan syndrome. Ventral hernias typically present with abdominal pain and swelling or fullness that changes with position or Valsalva maneuvers. Ventral hernias can cause small bowel obstructions.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with acute-onset abdominal pain and vomiting after coughing. On examination, he appears ill; there is a balloon-like protrusion near the umbilicus that is exquisitely tender and appears purple. What is the best ini- tial management?

options.text: Nasogastric tube and foley catheter placement
NPO status and immediate surgical consultation
Pain control and manual hernia reduction

correctAnswer: NPO status and immediate surgical consultation
englishExplanation: This patient is suffering from a strangulated hernia, which requires immedi- ate surgical consultation. Patients with this condition should be kept NPO as they will likely require emergent operative intervention. A strangulated hernia occurs when the hernia contents become ischemic; it is a surgical emer- gency. The smaller the fascial defect, the higher the risk of strangulation. Femoral hernias are at highest risk for strangulation and are typically surgically repaired when found. When strangulation occurs, the patient presents with symptoms of a bowel obstruction, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and ob- stipation. If the skin appears dusky or erythematous, as in this patient, an emergent surgical consultation should be obtained. A lactic acid level may be helpful when there is concern for ischemia, although it may be falsely nor- mal for up to 8 hours. CT abdomen and pelvis is helpful as well, but in this ill- appearing patient, surgical consultation should be obtained first. The treatment for a strangulated hernia is emergent surgical repair. Incorrect Answer Explanations Placing a nasogastric tube may be appropriate in this patient who presents with symptoms of a bowel obstruction in the setting of a strangulated hernia, but surgical consultation should be done first. A foley catheter may also be placed prior to going to the operating room, but it is a noncritical component of initial manage- ment for a strangulated hernia. Although this patient should be treated with pain medication, intravenous an- tibiotics are unwarranted in initial management. This patient has a strangu- lated hernia, and immediate surgical consultation is needed. Although this patient should be treated with pain medication, manual reduction of the hernia is contraindicated because the patient's presentation is concern- ing for a strangulated bowel. Manual reduction is appropriate when patients present with an incarcerated hernia with no signs of strangulation. Key Points Patients who present with strangulated hernias require immediate surgical consul- tation because the hernia contents are ischemic. Patients with strangulated hernias typically appear ill and present with symptoms of a bowel obstruction, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and obstipation. Manual bedside reduction is contraindicated if there is concern for a strangulated hernia.

question: What is the most appropriate initial test for an otherwise healthy patient who presents with suspected esophageal candidiasis?
englishExplanation: Esophageal candidiasis is considered an AIDS-defining illness and is most commonly found in severely immunocompromised patients (eg, HIV-positive pa- tients, cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, or those with hematologic abnor- malities and malignancies). Given the preponderance of HIV/AIDS–related cases, an otherwise healthy patient with suspected esophageal candidiasis should be ini- tially tested for HIV. After an HIV diagnosis has been ruled out or confirmed, an endoscopy with an esophageal biopsy can confirm the diagnosis of esophageal candidiasis. Esophageal candidiasis is most often caused by a Candida albicans infection of the esophagus and is strongly associated with coincidental thrush. Any patient who presents with thrush and odynophagia should be strongly suspected of hav- ing esophageal involvement. Esophageal candidiasis requires systemic antifun- gal treatment. Treatments, such as oral nystatin, clotrimazole, and miconazole, can be used to treat thrush alone but are ineffective for the treatment of esophageal can- didiasis. A 2- to 3-week course of oral fluconazole is a first-line treatment for esophageal candidiasis; other azoles, amphotericin B, and echinocandins (eg, micafungin) are generally reserved for fluconazole-resistant cases. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although severe retrosternal chest pain can occur with esophageal candidia- sis, a CT of the chest is not the best test to confirm the diagnosis. Suspected esophageal candidiasis is best confirmed by endoscopy with an esophageal biopsy, but this procedure is not required emergently. Although endoscopy with an esophageal biopsy is the gold standard for con- firmation of esophageal candidiasis, it is not required emergently. In fact, those with high clinical suspicion for esophageal candidiasis, such as AIDS pa- tients with odynophagia and coincidental thrush, can be empirically treated without an endoscopic diagnosis. Endoscopy is then reserved for those who do not improve after a few days on empiric antifungal medications. Endoscopy with an esophageal biopsy is the gold-standard test to diagnose esophageal candidiasis because a biopsy can show yeast and pseudohyphae invad- ing mucosal cells. Endoscopy and biopsy, however, are not required ini- tially or emergently.

question: A woman presents with complaints of a large piece of steak stuck in her esopha- gus. She is able to swallow her own secretions but has not attempted to drink or eat. She has had impactions before and episodic symptoms of heartburn despite regular use of a proton pump inhibitor. After a few minutes, her symptoms re- solve, and she can drink water. What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Observe for 6 hours and discharge if she remains asymptomatic

englishExplanation: This patient has the typical symptoms of an esophageal food impaction. Because she could initially swallow her own secretions, watchful waiting is an ap- propriate treatment strategy, with endoscopy within 12 to 24 hours. With acute re- lief, she may be discharged home without further observation. Eosinophilic esophagitis should be considered in patients who present with recurrent esophageal food impaction and symptoms of GERD despite the use of antacid medi- cations. Patients typically are nonresponsive to high-dose proton pump inhibitors. Esophageal strictures are commonly seen in these patients, especially if the un- derlying condition is untreated, and lead to recurrent impactions. Referral for out- patient endoscopy, for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, is the correct disposition. Incorrect Answer Explanations The patient's esophageal food impaction spontaneously passed on its own. Thus, admission is unnecessary if she remains asymptomatic. Although this patient does need to see a gastroenterologist for an endoscopy, biopsy, and further workup and management, she can safely do it as an outpatient. Indications for immediate endoscopy include significant distress, im- pactions that prevent handling of secretions, ingestion of sharp objects or button batteries, and impaction in the esophagus for longer than 24 hours. The food impaction resolved on its own, and the patient was able to drink water with no other symptoms. Thus, observation in the emergency department is unnec- essary. Instead, this patient should be discharged home with an outpatient en- doscopy referral.

question: Which virus is a major cause of odynophagia in AIDS patients?
englishExplanation: Seriously immunocompromised patients — those with severe AIDS, transplant patients, and those on cytotoxic chemotherapy — are at high risk for cytomegalovirus (CMV), an AIDS-defining illness. CMV commonly affects the GI tract and can cause esophagitis, which often presents with odynophagia due to ulcers and erosions in the distal esophagus. CMV esophagitis is less common than candidal esophagitis, so patients with AIDS who present with esophagitis are often empirically treated with oral fluconazole for 2 to 3 weeks. If fluconazole treatment is unsuccessful, an endoscopy and biopsy should be used for definitive diagnosis. CMV is managed with intravenous ganciclovir for 3 to 6 weeks, along with the initi- ation or continuation of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Importantly, CMV retinitis is often present concurrently with CMV infection else- where; thus, screening for CMV retinitis is necessary prior to starting HAART. HAART initiation may cause immune reconstitution inflammatory syn- drome (IRIS) and produce blindness in patients with retinitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations EBV is a type of herpesvirus that is primarily associated with mononu- cleosis and a variety of lymphomas. EBV is a very rare cause of esophagitis, with CMV being more common. In HIV/AIDS patients, EBV is more often associated with oral hairy leukoplakia, which typically manifests as a painless white plaque on the tongue that cannot be scraped off. HHV-8 is associated with the development of Kaposi sarcoma in HIV/AIDS patients and is also considered an AIDS-defining illness. Kaposi sarcoma very rarely manifests in the GI tract and causes ulcera- tion. It is a much less common cause of odynophagia than CMV. HSV, however, is a common cause of esophagitis in HIV patients. HPV infections cause warts in various places on the body, and some strains are associated with cervical cancer. For an HIV patient, invasive cer- vical cancer is considered an AIDS-defining illness. However, HPV is a rare cause of esophagitis in HIV/AIDS patients and is much less common than CMV.

question: What is first-line treatment for gastroesophageal reflux in the third trimester of pregnancy?
englishExplanation: Over-the-counter antacids are the first-line therapy for GERD during preg- nancy. These should be added for patients whose symptoms fail to im- prove with lifestyle modifications (eg, eating small meals, eliminating exacer- bating foods, elevating the head of the bed, and not eating within 3 hours of going to sleep). Antacids often provide immediate relief for patients. GERD is common in pregnancy due to loosening of the lower esophageal sphincter and delayed gastric emptying that result from pregnancy-related hormones. Typical symptoms include burning epigastric pain, which may radiate to the back or neck; pain when lying flat; and pain which is worsened by consuming particular foods (eg, acidic foods). Incorrect Answer Explanations H2-receptor antagonists (eg, cimetidine or ranitidine) are not first-line therapies for GERD during pregnancy. Although they are safe for use in preg- nancy, H2-receptor antagonists should be added after lifestyle modification and antacid use fail to provide relief. Proton pump inhibitors are used for severe, persistent GERD symptoms in pregnancy after H2-receptor antagonists and antacids have failed. Proton pump inhibitors are also safe in pregnancy and have not been shown to be teratogenic. Sucralfate is also not a first-line therapy for GERD during pregnancy. Sucralfate is a therapy used for GI ulcers. It creates a barrier against further damage from secreted gastric acid. Sucralfate is safe for use in pregnancy for patients who have persistent symptoms despite lifestyle modification and use of antacids and H2-re- ceptor antagonists.

question: In an infant with vomiting after feeding and feeding irritability, which sign would support a diagnosis of GERD requiring medication or feeding changes?
englishExplanation: GERD in infants is characterized by frequent vomiting (reflux episodes) associated with complications such as esophagitis or poor weight gain. Feeding refusal and irritability (eg, back arching that occurs with feed- ing) are occasionally seen with GERD in infants. New vomiting beginning after 6 months of life or recurrent pneumonia are infrequently seen with GERD. Apnea or other acute changes in behavior (ie, brief resolved unexplained event [BRUE]) should not be attributed to reflux or GERD. Esophageal pH monitoring is occasionally performed and may assist in the diagnosis and management of GERD in infants. Management may include lifestyle changes or pharmacother- apy with a proton pump inhibitor. Gastroesophageal reflux is a normal physiologic process that affects many infants. It is characterized by frequent episodes of small volume regurgitation that occur after feeding. These patients are often described as “happy spitters.” Notably, other concerning findings that elevate the condition to GERD are absent. Incorrect Answer Explanations Frequent regurgitation is common in infants who are described as “happy spitters.” This is similarly termed gastroesophageal reflux but is consid- ered benign in the absence of symptoms that are concerning for GERD (eg, feed- ing refusal, poor weight gain, and irritability). Projectile vomiting that worsens over several days in the first 2 to 3 months of life should be concerning for pyloric stenosis and is not seen in patients with GERD. Patients with pyloric stenosis present with nonbilious projec- tile vomiting, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances. Rectal bleeding should not be seen in infants with GERD. Blood in the stool of an infant with vomiting and colicky abdominal pain is suggestive of intus- susception, which typically affects children between the ages of 3 and 12 months. Bloody stools can also be seen in food protein-induced proctocolitis.

question: A 60-year-old man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents for epigastric pain that radiates into the chest. Which feature would be most con- sistent with this pain being caused by gastroesophageal reflux?

options.text: Occurs predominantly at night after going to bed
Worsens with exertion and relieved with rest

correctAnswer: Occurs predominantly at night after going to bed
englishExplanation: GERD is a benign noncardiac cause of chest pain. GERD frequently presents with a burning or squeezing retrosternal pain that often occurs after meals and is relieved by antacids. It is common for this condition to present at night after going to bed. When patients lie flat, stomach contents push against the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and can reflux into the esophagus, causing symptoms. Other associated symptoms may include sensa- tion of refluxed stomach contents, sour taste in the mouth, dysphagia, globus sensa- tion, hoarse voice, or chronic cough. Multiple substances are known to relax the LES, worsening reflux symptoms. These include alcohol, nicotine, and caffeine. It is important to evaluate patients for the presence of GI bleeding if a diagnosis of GERD is suspected. This should include asking the patient about the presence of hematemesis, black or tarry stools, or hematochezia. GERD should not cause GI bleeding. If bleeding is noted, this suggests another diagnosis such as peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis or esophageal erosion, Mallory-Weiss tear, esophageal varices, GI arteriovenous malformation, or diverticulosis, among others. It is also important to note that relief of symptoms from a “GI cocktail” in the emergency department is not diagnostic of GERD, and other diag- noses should still be considered as clinically indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients experiencing melena should be evaluated for a more sinister diagnosis than GERD. GERD in and of itself should not cause significant GI bleeding. If there are signs and symptoms of GI bleeding, another diagnosis should be consid- ered, such as peptic ulcer disease, esophagitis or esophageal erosion, tumor, Mallory-Weiss tear, esophageal varices, GI arteriovenous malformation, or diverticulosis. Acid reflux symptoms may be associated with shortness of breath and are known to be a cause of chronic cough. However, epigastric pain radiating into the chest associated with shortness of breath in a patient with known hyper- tension and hyperlipidemia should raise concern that this pain may be cardiorespiratory in etiology. The presence of shortness of breath in this case should not reassure the clinician that the causative diagnosis is GERD. Epigastric pain into the chest that worsens with exertion and is relieved with rest in a patient with underlying hypertension and hyperlipidemia should be considered as cardiac angina until proven otherwise. GERD may worsen with exertion due to increased intra abdominal pressures that can oc- cur with exercise, causing increased pressure on the LES. However, this would be a diagnosis of exclusion after other diagnoses, particularly coronary artery disease, have been evaluated.

question: What may be a complication of GERD?
englishExplanation: Esophageal strictures are a potential complication of GERD, resulting from the healing process related to erosive esophagitis. Esophageal strictures may result in progressive dysphagia to solids and, in some cases, to intermit- tent esophageal obstruction with food (ie, food impaction). Peptic strictures are often located at or near the gastroesophageal junction. Men, older patients, and those with a longer duration of GERD symptoms are all at higher risk for stricture formation. Patients with esophageal strictures may note gradually progressive dys- phagia to solids. This occurs several seconds after the initiation of swallowing, and patients have the sensation that food is stuck in the passage from the esophagus to the stomach. Symptoms usually develop after eating meat. Patients with peptic stricture alone may have a history of only heartburn and regurgitation, while pa- tients with esophageal cancer are likely to be older men who report weight loss. Incorrect Answer Explanations Metabolic acidosis is unassociated with GERD. Metabolic alkalosis may be seen with excessive use of antacids (eg, calcium carbonate) or baking soda (ie, sodium bicarbonate). Hypercalcemia may also be seen in overdoses of calcium carbonate. GERD is not a risk factor for head and neck cancers. Risk factors for head and neck cancers include tobacco and alcohol use, immunodeficiency, radi- ation, occupational exposures, and HPV infections. Chronic GERD in- creases the risk for adenocarcinoma of the esophagus. Water brash or hypersalivation is an uncommon symptom that may be associated with GERD. Dry mouth (ie, xerostomia) is not expected to result from GERD.

question: A patient presents with new-onset burning chest pain that occurs after meals. GERD is suspected. Which additional finding requires close follow-up with upper endoscopy?
englishExplanation: GERD is a diagnosis that may often be made clinically, and it is treated with empiric lifestyle and pharmacologic interventions. A number of risk factors for malignancy, including age older than 60 years, are indications for further workup including endoscopy. Other features suggestive of GI malignancy in- clude weight loss, anorexia, persistent vomiting, iron-deficiency anemia, GI bleeding, dysphagia, odynophagia, and GI cancer in a first-degree relative. GERD patients presenting with these symptoms should be referred to their primary physician or to gastroenterology for further evaluation. Additionally, screening for Barrett esophagus is necessary in patients with a 5- to 10-year his- tory of GERD plus these additional risk factors: age older than 50 years, male sex, white race, hiatal hernia, obesity, nocturnal reflux, tobacco use, and a first-degree relative with Barrett esophagus or adenocarcinoma. Incorrect Answer Explanations Being a member of the male sex, rather than the female sex, is a risk factor for progression to Barrett esophagus in patients with a greater than 5-year history of GERD. These patients require additional evaluation with upper endoscopy. Iron-deficiency anemia may be an early finding in GERD patients with GI malignancy. In the appropriate clinical context, it may prompt additional workup, including upper endoscopy. However, macrocytic anemia would be unex- pected in this context. Microcytic anemia would be an indication for early endoscopy. In a patient with GERD, metabolic alkalosis may result from overuse of antacids, such as calcium carbonate. In this context, hypercalcemia may be observed as well. Metabolic alkalosis is not a risk factor for malignancy and does not warrant close follow-up for endoscopy. A number of risk factors for malignancy (in- cluding age >60 years, not metabolic alkalosis) are indications for further workup including endoscopy.

question: A 22-year-old woman presents with nausea and epigastric abdominal pain after intentionally drinking a bottle of toilet bowl cleaner. Her vital signs are BP 125/85, P 99, R 23, and T 37.3°C (99.1°F); SpO is 98% on room air. Assessment of her oropharynx is unremarkable, and her voice is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Gastric lavage with placement of an Ewald tube

englishExplanation: In the setting of intentional overdose of a large amount of a strongly caustic agent, the appropriate recommendation is admission for close monitoring and serial examinations; endoscopy can be performed to grade the extent of the injury. Serious caustic acid injuries cause coagula- tion necrosis, a process in which hydrogen ions infiltrate tissues, which leads to killing of cells and formation of an eschar. This eschar protects against deeper in- jury, and thus caustic acids typically cause less damage than caustic alka- lis. Despite this, ingestion of strong acids is associated with a higher mortality rate compared to alkali ingestions because of severe gastric damage. An anion gap acidosis (lactic) might result from tissue injury or impending shock. Notably, some acidic agents (eg, hydrochloric acid) might produce a non-gap acidosis, and the acid might be absorbed systemically. Household cleaning agents such as toilet bowl cleaners contain hydrochloric acid. The patient in this question might have 2 some degree of acidosis as indicated by her tachypnea. Psychiatric services are needed, but because she has symptoms of potential gastric injury, she should first be admitted for serial abdominal examinations and monitoring for GI bleeding or perforation. Intentional ingestions are associated with higher grades of GI injury. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient does not show evidence of chemical burn to the oropharynx or swelling of the upper airway, which would necessitate airway protection with emergent intu- bation. However, she does need endoscopy, which should be obtained in a con- trolled setting. Endoscopy should be performed within 12 hours of ingestion and not more than 24 hours afterward to avoid GI perforation during the procedure. Gastric decontamination with activated charcoal is contraindicated in caustic ingestions. Charcoal impairs visualization for endoscopy and does not bind well to most caustic agents. Gastric lavage is not indicated for caustic ingestions. For concern of coingestants, placement of a nasogastric or larger orogastric tube (eg, the Ewald) is contraindicated until an endoscopy has shown that gastric hemorrhage or perfo- ration is not a risk.

question: A 19-year-old man with a history of developmental delay is brought in by his mother after she saw him drink a small amount of household bleach. The patient denies any complaint, and the physical examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
englishExplanation: The appropriate management of asymptomatic accidental ingestion of a small amount of a low-concentration acidic or alkaline substance includes discharge with outpatient follow-up. Household bleach is the most common household al- kali. It has a sodium hypochlorite solution of 3% to 6% and a pH of 11; it is fairly dilute and only minimally corrosive to the esophagus. Household bleach ingestion rarely causes significant injury. Caustic alkali injuries can cause liquefaction necrosis, a process in which the hydroxide ion penetrates deep tis- sues and causes injury secondary to protein denaturation and lipid saponification. However, this is unlikely to occur in this patient, who ingested only a small quantity of household bleach. Incorrect Answer Explanations Certain agents are contraindicated in caustic ingestions. These include neu- tralizing agents, which release heat that can cause additional tissue injury. Ingestion of industrial-strength bleach or powdered hypochlorite solu- tion is much more likely to result in esophageal injury than ingestion of household bleach. Endoscopic evaluation is indicated in patients with these ingestions. Gastric decontamination with activated charcoal is relatively con- traindicated in caustic ingestions. Charcoal does not bind well to most caustics and can impair visualization if endoscopy is warranted.

question: For a patient with dysphagia, which factor is most consistent with distal esophageal spasm?

options.text: Frequent episodes of gagging and coughing when eating
History of food “sticking” and retrosternal fullness with eating solids
Need for repeated swallows to complete swallowing
Needing to lift the neck or throw the shoulders back to complete swallowing

correctAnswer: History of food “sticking” and retrosternal fullness with eating solids
englishExplanation: Distal esophageal spasm (DES) is classically associated with dysphagia, a history of food “sticking,” and retrosternal fullness after eating, but retrosternal chest pain may also be present. Normally, food boluses are transported from the mouth to the stomach by peristaltic waves through the esophageal wall. Patients with DES have abnormal contractions in the distal esophagus that can lead to the improper transfer of a bolus (either solid or liquid) from the esophagus into the stomach, resulting in a characteristic “corkscrew” esophagus on barium esophagram. The underlying cause of this rare esophageal motility disorder is not well understood, but gastric acid exposure is a known secondary risk factor. Incorrect Answer Explanations Frequent episodes of gagging and coughing when eating are associated with oropharyngeal dysphagia. Reported “sticking” and retrosternal discom- fort after eating are much more consistent with distal esophageal spasm. Oropharyngeal dysphagia is characterized by abnormal transfer of a bo- lus from the pharynx to the esophagus. Unlike distal esophageal spasm, oropharyngeal dysphagia is very common and is associated with many different conditions, especially those causing neuromuscular weakness, such as stroke or brain injury. The need for repeated swallows to complete swallowing is more typical of patients with oropharyngeal dysphagia. Oropharyngeal dysphagia generally mani- fests as difficulty initiating a swallow and the sensation of residual food in the pharynx, which requires repeated swallows. These symptoms con- trast with distal esophageal spasm's characteristic “sticking” and retrosternal dis- comfort after eating. Needing to lift the neck or throw the shoulders back to complete swallowing is typi- cal of patients with achalasia. Achalasia is characterized by inadequate re- laxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and lack of peristalsis in the distal esophagus; a “bird beak” sign on barium esophagram demon- strates this pathology clearly. This abnormal relaxation results in solid and liq- uid dysphagia and regurgitation. Notably, these symptoms differ from the “sticking” and retrosternal discomfort after eating that characterize distal esophageal spasm.

question: A 52-year-old man presents with severe chest pain radiating to his neck. It started acutely 2 hours earlier, has been unrelenting, and is worse with deep breathing and swallowing. According to his wife, he regularly smokes marijuana, has been vomiting multiple times today, and "threw up so hard he vomited blood." The patient confirms this, and his voice is notably hoarse. On examina- tion, he appears distressed due to pain, and his skin is sweaty. His vital signs are BP 174/89, P 112, R 24, and T 37.8°C (100°F); SpO is 98% on room air. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation: Boerhaave syndrome is a life-threatening, full-thickness perforation of the esophagus from a rapid rise in esophageal pressure. It can result from any straining valsalva maneuver or weakening of the esophageal mucosa (eg, forceful vomiting, coughing, heavy lifting, childbirth, foreign body or caustic in- gestion, esophagitis, cancer, or trauma). The patient's history of marijuana use with several episodes of vomiting is consistent with cannabinoid hypereme- sis syndrome. Boerhaave syndrome classically results in sudden, severe, and un- relenting chest pain that may radiate to the neck, back, shoulders, and abdomen. Thirty percent of patients develop emphysema in the mediastinal or cervical areas, resulting in crepitus on palpation or a Hamman crunch on auscultation. It is important to note that mediastinal emphysema can take time to develop; its absence does not necessarily rule out perforation. Although Boerhaave syndrome is often the cause of esophageal perforation, it is no longer the most common cause. In this era, iatrogenic causes are more common, resulting from upper endoscopy, esophageal dilatation, TEE, variceal treatment, and a variety of injuries. Incorrect Answer Explanations The presentation of Boerhaave syndrome can be clinically challenging and can mimic other conditions. Although acute myocardial infarction should be con- sidered in a patient who presents with chest pain, it is unlikely given the other as- pects of the complaint, including forceful vomiting and sudden onset of chest pain to the neck. This patient has a trigger for esophageal perforation with powerful emesis and evi- dence for laryngeal involvement. Although peptic ulcer disease can produce vomit- ing with bloody emesis, it usually has a relationship with food and body posi- tion. Perforation can be caused by an ulcer and can produce severe pain, but this would usually not ascend into the neck or shoulders. Pain from spontaneous pneumothorax is not associated with episodes of forceful vomiting. Perforation of the lower esophagus can cause a pneumotho- rax, but this would not be a primary presentation of a spontaneous pneumothorax.

question: What is the most common cause of esophageal perforations?
englishExplanation: Today, esophageal perforations most commonly occur during medical procedures. They have been reported with upper endoscopy (most common), esophageal dilation, TEE, variceal treatment, intraoperative injury, and accidental esophageal intubation. Pain, fever, dyspnea, or crepitus within hours of esophageal instrumentation should be considered a sign of perforation unless proven otherwise. After an esophageal perforation occurs, saliva and gastric contents can enter the mediastinal, pleural, or peritoneal space, triggering a marked infectious and inflammatory response. Depending on the site of perfora- tion, patients may describe severe, unrelenting pain in the neck, chest, or abdomen with radiation to the back or shoulders. Fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea are also common. A Hamman crunch can sometimes be heard on ex- amination. The diagnosis can often be established with CT of the neck and chest with intravenous contrast; if CT is negative but suspicion remains high, patients should undergo video esophagoscopy or esophagography with water-soluble con- trast. Management includes broad-spectrum antibiotics, emergent surgi- cal consultation, and supportive resuscitation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness esophageal rupture that occurs with suddenly elevated intraluminal esophageal pressure; forceful vomiting, cough- ing, heavy lifting, seizures, and childbirth can create sufficiently ele- vated pressure. Most ruptures occur in the distal esophagus. However, Boerhaave syndrome is no longer the most common cause of esophageal perforations. Foreign body ingestion can lead to an esophageal perforation; for example, esophageal perforations can occur secondary to injury caused by a swal- lowed pill, esophageal necrosis from button batteries, or injury caused by a sharp object. Foreign body ingestion, however, is a relatively rare cause of esophageal perforations. Traumatic injury of the esophagus is uncommon, and most cases are as- sociated with penetrating gunshot or stab wounds. Most traumatic esophageal perforations occur in the proximal and middle third of the esophagus; Boerhaave syndrome most commonly occurs in the distal esophagus.

question: A mother brings in her 2-year-old son after she saw him put something in his mouth while he was playing. He has been in no distress since the event and is currently at baseline. X-rays are obtained and shown below. What is the appro- priate disposition? Credit: Copyright 2023 Dr. Yair Glick. Image courtesy of Dr. Yair Glick and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 52187. Used under license.

options.text: Admit him to the hospital for observation
Discharge home with outpatient follow-up in 3 to 5 days
Perform gastric lavage using a nasogastric tube

englishExplanation: The object seen on the x-ray is a button battery in the esophagus, as indi- cated by the radiographic halo or double circle noted on the foreign body. Although coins and other objects are more commonly ingested, they usually require observation and supportive care. An ingested button battery or magnet, in contrast, may need to be removed in the emergency department if it is in the esoph- agus or more proximal; it can cause an external current that can result in hydroly- sis and erosion of the GI tract over time. A button battery that is lodged in the esophagus can cause erosion within a few hours and should be removed as soon as possible. Management otherwise depends on the age of the patient and the size of the button battery. The National Battery Ingestion Hotline can help in the decision- making process, 800-498-8666. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admission for observation is unlikely to be warranted because the child is in no distress. It is also not an appropriate treatment because the battery sim- ply needs to be removed; it can erode the upper GI tract rapidly. Discharge home with follow-up would be inappropriate for a button bat- tery in the esophagus. This needs to be removed to avoid erosion. Observation for 12 to 24 hours would be appropriate for an esophageal foreign body without red flags (eg, airway compromise, inability to swallow secretions, sharp ob- ject, button battery, magnet, or signs of obstruction) and if the ingested object did not have the potential to damage intestinal tissue. This is often the course of treat- ment when a child ingests a coin or dull-edged object. There is no advantage in ex- amining the stool in these cases; instead, close follow-up and immediate re-evalua- tion are indicated for any complaints of abdominal pain or vomiting. Gastric lavage has fallen out of favor with most toxicologists except in some cases of life-threatening toxic ingestions. It is never used in caustics or hydrocarbon ingestions.

question: A 2-year-old girl presents with sudden-onset cough and noisy breathing. Her parents report that she was in her usual state of health 1 hour prior and devel- oped symptoms while playing with an older sibling. She is nontoxic appearing and mildly tachypneic, with faint inspiratory stridor and mild retractions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Young children account for many of the cases of ingested foreign bodies. The diag- nosis can be unclear, however, because the child is unable to provide a history. Patients often present with sudden-onset symptoms, including refusal or in- ability to eat, vomiting, gagging, choking, stridor, neck or throat pain, or drooling. It is important to remember that an esophageal foreign body can cause respiratory symptoms in young children due to compression of the trachea; absence of a foreign body in the airway does not rule out an esophageal foreign body. It is necessary to maintain a high degree of suspicion, especially in sudden-onset symptoms without a suggested infectious etiology, as many ingestions are unwitnessed by the parents. Incorrect Answer Explanations Croup typically presents with gradual onset of a barky cough and inspi- ratory stridor. Patients often have other symptoms of a viral URI, including fever, cough, and rhinorrhea. In an otherwise healthy child with sudden-onset symptoms, an ingested foreign body is more likely. Reactive airway disease typically presents with wheezing and signs of lower-airway obstruction. The presentation is usually gradual in onset and can range from mild to severe with hypoxia and respiratory distress. An ingested foreign body is more likely in an otherwise healthy child with sudden-onset symptoms. Patients with streptococcal pharyngitis typically present with gradual- onset fever and sore throat. Streptococcal pharyngitis is uncommon in children who are younger than 5. On examination, patients have swollen, erythematous ton- sils with exudates, palatal petechiae, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Patients typi- cally lack other signs of a viral URI, like cough and rhinorrhea. This child's sudden- onset respiratory symptoms in the absence of signs of infection strongly suggest an ingested foreign body.

question: Where do most esophageal foreign objects become lodged in pediatric patients?

options.text: Distal esophagus at the level of the gastroesophageal junction
Mid-esophagus at the level of the carina
Mid-esophagus at the level of the great vessels
Proximal esophagus at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle

correctAnswer: Proximal esophagus at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle
englishExplanation: Most pediatric foreign objects become lodged in the proximal esophagus at the level of the cricopharyngeus muscle due to the anatomical narrowing at this site. This is also referred to as the upper esophageal sphincter (UES). In adults, the majority of esophageal foreign bodies are lodged at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). Other major areas of anatomic esophageal narrow- ing include at the intersection with the aortic arch and left mainstem bronchus as well as at the diaphragmatic hiatus that forms the lower esophageal sphincter. Pathologic narrowing, strictures, or other anatomic abnormalities can cause im- pactions at other levels but are much less common. Incorrect Answer Explanations Foreign body impaction can occur in the distal esophagus at the level of the lower esophageal sphincter. However, impaction at the gastroesophageal junction is less common in pediatric patients than in the proximal esophagus. Foreign body impaction can occur in the mid-esophagus at the level of the main- stem bronchi/carina. However, impaction at the mainstem bronchi/carina is less common than in the proximal esophagus. Foreign body impaction can occur in the mid-esophagus at the level of the aortic arch. However, impaction in the proximal esophagus is much more common.

question: An x-ray of a child with a suspected foreign body ingestion reveals a flat, circular object at the level of the thoracic inlet. Which factor can distinguish button bat- tery ingestion from coin ingestion?

options.text: Circular appearance on lateral chest x-ray

englishExplanation: Distinguishing button batteries lodged in the esophagus from coins is crucial. Button batteries are at high risk of causing rapid esophageal perforation, whereas coins are at much lower risk of serious injury. On an anteroposterior (AP) view of the chest, button batteries display the “double ring” sign, which looks like a circular object with a ring along the outer edge. Coins appear as a simple circular object without this ring. On a lateral x-ray, button batteries appear as a stack of two coins on top of each other, whereas a coin ap- pears as a single straight object. Incorrect Answer Explanations Given the anatomy of the tracheal rings, disk-shaped objects lodged in the tra- chea appear flat on AP x-rays and circular on lateral x-rays. Conversely, disk-shaped objects that are lodged in the esophagus appear circular on AP x-rays and flat on lateral x-rays. Given that both button batteries and coins are disk-shaped, orientation cannot distinguish between the two but can strongly suggest the anatomic location. Both button batteries and coins are radiopaque, so this feature cannot dif- ferentiate between the two. Thus, the double ring sign is among the most reliable signs to distinguish between these otherwise similar objects on x-ray. Button batteries and coins both come in a variety of sizes, so size cannot be used to distinguish between the two on x-ray. Instead, the double ring sign is among the most reliable x-ray findings to distinguish between these otherwise simi- lar objects.

question: What is the next best step for managing a confirmed button battery ingestion that is lodged in the proximal esophagus?
englishExplanation: Button batteries lodged in the esophagus require emergent removal be- cause they can cause mucosal injury, necrosis, and perforation within 6 hours of ingestion. If the battery is lodged within the esophagus, emergent con- sultation (and transfer, if necessary) for endoscopy is warranted to prevent serious injury. Other indications for endoscopy in esophageal foreign body management in- clude extremis, signs of esophageal perforation, the inability to handle secretions, or airway compromise. Ingested objects that require endoscopic removal in- clude button batteries, sharp or elongated objects, or multiple objects, especially multiple magnets. Any foreign body that has been present in the esophagus for over 24 hours also warrants endoscopic removal. Incorrect Answer Explanations Administration of intravenous glucagon can be considered for the man- agement of adults with distal esophageal food impaction. Glucagon works by relaxing the lower esophageal sphincter, allowing the object to pass. However, this therapy has a low overall success rate and can also cause vomiting, which can worsen the patient's clinical status. Glucagon is not indicated for pediatric proximal foreign bodies, especially button batteries. Administration of proteolytic enzymes, such as papain, is contraindi- cated in the management of any esophageal foreign body. Proteolytic en- zymes should not be used for button battery ingestions or food impactions because they have the potential to cause severe mucosal damage that can lead to esophageal perforation. Saline or other types of lavage are not indicated in the management of button batteries lodged within the esophagus. Complete esophageal obstruc- tion can lead to pooling of secretions, which can worsen with lavage. Button batter- ies, in particular, require emergent removal due to the high risk of esophageal mu- cosal injury.

question: A 7-year-old child presents with concern for ingestion of a foreign object. A plain x-ray shows a small button battery in the stomach. The child is playing without abdominal tenderness or respiratory distress. What is the next best step in man- agement of the options listed below?

options.text: Endoscopic removal of the foreign body

correctAnswer: Endoscopic removal of the foreign body
englishExplanation: Button batteries can cause severe damage to the GI tract and can cause ulceration or perforation of the esophagus and stomach. Once they have passed into the intestine or distally, though, asymptomatic patients typically can be man- aged expectantly with serial x-rays and monitoring to assess for passage from the stool. Most batteries in the intestine will pass without issues within a week. Although management continues to be controversial, most experts would agree that any esophageal button battery should be emergently removed. Many will also say that stomach button batteries should also be emergently removed; however, some sources recommend that patients with a button battery in the stomach with- out a magnet coningestion can follow-up in 24 hours, with repeat imaging in 24 to 48 hours.
