For batteries in the intestine and distal, management can be expectant if asymptomatic, or it can be managed with GI consultation and possible removal if the patient is younger (<5 years old) or large batteries. For symptomatic patients, emergent GI consultation and endoscopic removal can be considered. For asympto- matic patients with batteries distal to the stomach who are managed expectantly, patients should follow-up to assess for symptoms and undergo repeat ab- dominal x-rays in 10 to 14 days. Symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomit- ing, or signs of peritonitis or obstruction mandate immediate surgical consultation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Intravenous glucagon can be used in the management of distal esophageal food impactions in adults. It decreases the tone of the lower esophageal sphinc- ter. However, its overall success rates are low, and it can lead to nausea and vomit- ing, which is not recommended. Thus, glucagon is not indicated in the man- agement of foreign bodies within the stomach. Repeat abdominal x-rays for button batteries in the stomach should be completed in 24 to 48 hours, with a 24-hour GI follow-up ensured. These bat- teries have been known to cause mucosal damage and even perforation in the stom- ach. Thus, waiting 7 days for repeat testing and follow-up is too long. If the button battery is in the intestine, longer gap time between imaging is acceptable. Whole bowel irrigation can be considered in the management of patients who have ingested multiple small packets of drugs. However, this asymptomatic patient has a button battery in the stomach and can be managed expectantly.

question: A patient presents with hematemesis after binge drinking alcohol. He reports ten episodes of nonbloody emesis prior to noticing “streaks of bright red blood.” He is hemodynamically stable, talking, and not actively vomiting on arrival. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis

englishExplanation: Hematemesis following episodes of forceful vomiting and retching is concerning for Mallory-Weiss syndrome. Correct management for patients with suspected Mallory-Weiss syndrome and ongoing bleeding involves administration of a pro- ton pump inhibitor (PPI) for acid suppression and emergent endoscopy. If the patient is not actively bleeding, an endoscopy is not routinely performed. Mallory-Weiss syndrome results from a longitudinal, partial-thickness tear in the mucosa of the distal esophagus or proximal stomach due to increased intra-abdomi- nal pressure. Development of this syndrome is usually preceded by forceful vomit- ing or retching and is often associated with alcohol use. Most cases are mild, and bleeding spontaneously resolves. These patients are managed with PPI therapy alone following endoscopy. High-risk features for Mallory-Weiss syndrome include active bleeding on endoscopy, severe bleeding with hemodynamic instability or requiring transfusion, advanced age, multiple chronic comorbidities, and active anticoagulation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Mallory-Weiss syndrome is not an infectious process, so use of antibiotics would not be of added value. Management with a proton pump inhibitor is indicated for acid suppression in the setting of GI bleeding. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is unlikely to be of any benefit in the stable pa- tient with a suspected Mallory-Weiss tear. Gastroenterology consultation for endoscopy if actively bleeding is the management of choice, as it allows for di- rect visualization of the gastric mucosa and therapeutic intervention. Critically ill patients with massive GI hemorrhage may require rapid-se- quence intubation for airway protection due to significant risk of aspiration. This patient does not have any signs of massive hemoptysis or airway com- promise, so emergent intubation is not indicated.

question: Shortly after birth, a newborn is found to have a persistent cough, gagging, in- creased oral secretions, and respiratory distress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal connection between the trachea and the esophagus, often causing newborns to aspirate and present clinically with cough, choking, and respiratory distress. There are several types of TEFs. They are characterized by anatomic location of the malformation and the presence or absence of an esophageal atresia (EA). EA prevents oral secretions and food from entering the stomach, so these infants have increased oral secretions and vomiting. The common classification of TEF and EA is as follows: Type A: EA without fistula Type B: EA with proximal TEF Type C: EA with distal TEF Type D: EA with proximal and distal TEF Type E: H-Type Fistula with no EA Incorrect Answer Explanations An esophageal web is a thin tissue that extends into the lumen of the esophagus. This newborn's presentation is inconsistent with an esophageal web because patients are usually asymptomatic. When they do experience symptoms, patients with esophageal webs will commonly present with intermittent dysphagia. Esophageal shortening is most commonly seen as a result of longstanding gastroe- sophageal reflux. Repeated reflux of stomach contents leads to inflammation, edema, and ultimately fibrosis of the esophagus. Congenital short esophagus is a rare condition associated with an intrathoracic stomach and hiatal hernia. These infants usually present with failure to thrive. Both congenital and ac- quired esophageal shortening require surgical repair. Tracheomalacia is a narrowing of the trachea during exhalation result- ing in stridor, cough, and respiratory distress. Although infants with tra- cheomalacia may have feeding difficulty, increased oral secretions are absent. Congenital tracheomalacia is due to cartilaginous defects in the trachea. Acquired tracheomalacia can be caused by inflammation due to recurrent infections, surgical complications, or external compression of the trachea from masses. Key Points Tracheoesophageal fistulas are rare. When present, tracheoesophageal fistulas typically occur with associated esophageal atresia. Newborns present with increased oral secretions, cough, choking, and respi- ratory distress. Congenital tracheomalacia is caused by a cartilaginous defect causing the trachea to partially collapse resulting in stridor, which is often positional. Acquired tracheomalacia can be caused by trauma, prolonged mechanical ventila- tion, or chronic infections and may require surgical repair depending upon the severity of symptoms.

question: Which diagnostic tool is most helpful in diagnosing H-type tracheoesophageal fistulas?

options.text: Chest x-ray following nasogastric tube placement
Upper GI fluoroscopy with water-soluble contrast

correctAnswer: Upper GI fluoroscopy with water-soluble contrast
englishExplanation: An upper GI fluoroscopy utilizes contrast to evaluate the esophagus, stom- ach, and duodenum and is the first-line diagnostic tool to evaluate for H-type tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). An H-type TEF is associated with a patent esophagus; thus, it can be difficult to diagnose in a newborn because the clinical symptoms may be mild. Esophageal endoscopy and bronchoscopy can be instru- mental diagnostic tools when the defect is difficult to visualize. Because TEF and esophageal atresia (EA) are commonly associated with other ab- normalities like CHARGE syndrome (Coloboma, Heart defects, Atresia choanae, Retarded growth and development, Genital anomalies, and Ear anomalies and deafness) and VACTERL association (Vertebral anomalies, Anal atresia, Cardiac anomalies, TracheoEsophageal fistula, Radial or Renal anomalies, and Limb anom- alies), infants diagnosed with TEF and EA should undergo further evaluation in- cluding echocardiography and renal ultrasound. Incorrect Answer Explanations A barium swallow study is a fluoroscopy that can be used to evaluate for pha- ryngeal or esophageal abnormalities. Barium, a radiopaque contrast material, should be avoided when evaluating for TEF because the barium can cause pneu- monitis if aspirated. Barium swallow studies can be particularly useful in evaluating children with dysphagia. If the clinician suspects a TEF, a nasogastric (NG) tube can be inserted in the infant. An H-type TEF is unassociated with EA, and the NG tube will generally pass with ease, limiting its diagnostic utility. However, in patients with TEF asso- ciated with EA, the NG tube will typically stop advancing after 10 to 15 cm into the stomach. The NG tube will subsequently appear curled in the upper esophagus on chest x-ray. TEF can sometimes be visualized on prenatal ultrasound, but this is not a highly sensitive study. Maternal polyhydramnios and a small or absent fetal stomach bubble suggest TEF is present, at which point TEF can be confirmed by a fetal MRI.

question: Which initial task is critical in the preoperative management of infants with tra- cheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia?

options.text: Place the infant in Trendelenburg position

englishExplanation: Patients with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) often have additional con- genital anomalies, including congenital heart defects. Prior to surgery, it is imperative that these malformations are identified because specific anomalies (eg, right-sided aortic arch) may impact the surgical approach and are associated with higher morbidity. Furthermore, it is recommended that infants have laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy prior to surgical repair to further characterize anatomical abnormalities. TEF and esophageal atresia (EA) are often associated with CHARGE syndrome and VACTERL association. Infants with CHARGE syndrome have Colobomas, Heart defects, choanal Atresia, growth Retardation, and Genital and Ear abnormalities. VACTERL association includes Vertebral defects, anal Atresia, Cardiac defects, TEF, Renal abnormalities, and Limb anoma- lies. Infants with confirmed TEF and EA should be screened for these associated conditions. Incorrect Answer Explanations Infants with TEF should remain NPO (nothing by mouth) in preparation for surgical repair. A suction catheter should be placed in the esophageal pouch to con- tinuously clear any pooled secretions. A nasojejunostomy tube may pass into the je- junum in H-type TEF, but it would end in the esophageal pouch if EA is present. Trendelenberg positioning, with the head positioned lower than the feet, is contraindicated in patients with TEF and EA. Prior to surgery, the head of the bed should be elevated 30° to 45° for patients with TEF, which mini- mizes reflux and aspiration events. Because of the high risk for pulmonary aspira- tion, many experts also recommend prophylactic antibiotic treatment with ampi- cillin and gentamicin. Infants with TEF often develop respiratory distress, which requires prompt atten- tion. BVM ventilation should be avoided because it may cause gaseous distention. Alternatively, physicians should intubate patients, taking care to posi- tion the tip of the endotracheal tube distal to the fistula. Bronchoscopy can help with this. Gaseous distention increases the risk of hemodynamic compromise as a result of decreased venous return, and it can also lead to aspiration of stomach contents.

question: A 3-day-old neonate with an unrepaired tracheoesophageal fistula suddenly de- velops cyanosis, hypotension, and shock. Administration of which medication is the next best step?
englishExplanation: This patient is experiencing the hemodynamic compromise associated with closure of the ductus arteriosus, for which prostaglandins are emergently indicated. Infants with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) often have additional congenital anomalies, the most common of which are congenital heart lesions. Neonates with ductal-dependent heart lesions such as tetralogy of Fallot, which is commonly associated with TEF, develop the symptoms of shock as the ductus closes at the 3rd to 5th day of life. These infants require emergent administration of prostaglan- dins to keep the ductus patent and promote the mixing of pulmonary and systemic blood flow. Incorrect Answer Explanations Infants with TEF are at high risk for pulmonary aspiration, and broad- spectrum antibiotics should be considered. However, ceftriaxone is less than ideal due to the risk of hyperbilirubinemia, especially in preterm infants. Ceftriaxone should also be avoided in neonates who are receiving intravenous calcium-containing solutions. Ampicillin and gentamicin would be better choices of prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics for neonates with TEF. The differential diagnosis for this neonate includes septic and hypovolemic shock. One of the primary goals for both these types of shock is to improve circulation by fluid expansion. Epinephrine would only be indicated in fluid-refractory shock. Thus, it is not the next best step in this patient's management. Hydrocortisone would be indicated in neonates if there is a concern for adrenal insufficiency. Infants with adrenal insufficiency usually present between the 10th and 20th day of life. Although the neonatal presentation of adrenal crisis does in- clude hypotension and shock, there is also often a history of atypical genitalia in fe- males as well as electrolyte abnormalities. Additionally, TEF is more closely associ- ated with congenital heart disease than adrenal insufficiency is.

question: Which chronic condition is most likely to develop after tracheoesophageal fistula repair?
englishExplanation: After the repair of a tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), most patients ex- perience esophageal dysmotility and require additional therapy to aid in speech and swallowing. Patients are also at increased risk for GERD and esophagitis, and they should be treated with maximal proton pump inhibitor ther- apy. In adulthood, these patients are at increased risk for developing Barrett esoph- agus and, ultimately, esophageal cancer. Incorrect Answer Explanations Esophageal achalasia is a rare disorder affecting the esophagus in which nerve damage precludes normal peristalsis of the esophagus. The exact cause of achalasia is unknown, and its association with TEF repair is uncommon. Many of the symptoms of achalasia, such as regurgitation of food, heartburn, tran- sient chest pain, and nighttime cough, are similar to those symptoms seen in pa- tients with severe GERD. Patients who have had TEF repair commonly experience esophageal stricture, for which the treatment is esophageal dilatation. These stric- tures can be diagnosed by esophageal contrast studies and endoscopy. Presenting symptoms include recurrent respiratory infections, aspiration, cough, swallowing difficulties, and foreign body impaction. Esophageal varices are not a complication after TEF repair. Esophageal varices are dilated veins in the esophagus that result from portal hypertension. The elevated blood pressure in the portal venous system results in increased blood flow into the thin-walled esophageal vessels, causing swelling and increased risk for rup- ture. Esophageal varices are usually asymptomatic unless they rupture and bleed, at which time patients may present with hematemesis, hematochezia, or melena. Options for the treatment of ruptured varices include endoscopic sclerotherapy and endoscopic ligation of bleeding vessels. There are few case reports describing the rare development of TEF as a complication of these procedures.

question: When a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is used in the management of variceal bleed- ing, which measure is taken to avoid esophageal perforation?

options.text: Decreasing esophageal balloon pressure by 5 mm Hg every 3 hours
Inflating the esophageal balloon before the gastric balloon
Inflating the esophageal balloon to a pressure of 100 mm Hg
Nasogastric suctioning of stomach contents before tube placement

correctAnswer: Decreasing esophageal balloon pressure by 5 mm Hg every 3 hours
englishExplanation: Sengstaken-Blakemore tube insertion can be a lifesaving temporizing procedure for variceal bleeding, but it is performed infrequently be- cause of its associated complications and the development of endo- scopic therapies. One significant complication is esophageal or gastric rupture. When bleeding is controlled, the esophageal balloon pressure should be re- duced by 5 mm Hg every 3 hours down to a pressure of 25 mm Hg to avoid pressure necrosis. The correct placement of the Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is accomplished with the large balloon advanced completely into the stomach. Appropriate positioning can be confirmed with imaging or by auscultating over the stomach while insufflating air into the gastric port. The gastric balloon is initially inflated with about 250 mL of air so that it abuts se- curely against the gastroesophageal junction. Once fixed, the esophageal balloon is inflated if bleeding persists. Notably, the esophageal balloon is inflated to a pressure of no more than 50 mm Hg to control esophageal variceal bleeding. Intragastric bal- loon pressure should be reassessed frequently after placement; increasing pressure may signify esophageal placement or migration. Aspiration and airway compromise are concerns during Sengstaken-Blakemore tube placement, so elevation of the head of the bed and endotracheal intubation should both be strongly considered. Incorrect Answer Explanations The gastric balloon should be inflated first, not the esophageal balloon. Ensure that it is clearly in the stomach before full inflation. This intervention con- trols gastric varices. If bleeding stops after gastric balloon inflation, the esophageal balloon does not have to be inflated. A pressure of 100 mm Hg is too high. The esophageal balloon should be in- flated to a pressure of no more than 50 mm Hg to control esophageal variceal bleeding. Oral or nasogastric suctioning is necessary after the placement of a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube (not before) to decrease the risk of aspiration because secretions collect above the obstructing tube. Nasogastric tube placement before or after Sengstaken-Blakemore tube placement does not affect the risk of rupture.

question: A 54-year-old man presents with frank hematemesis. His vital signs include BP 80/40, P 110, and R 26. He has a history of alcoholic cirrhosis. After initial resus- citation and airway management, what is the most definitive treatment?
englishExplanation: This patient has hemodynamically unstable upper GI bleeding due to esophageal varices. Definitive management includes emergent upper endos- copy because it is the diagnostic study of choice for upper GI bleeding and be- cause treatment options such as band ligation and sclerotherapy can be performed during the endoscopy procedure. Variceal bleeding is a leading cause of death among patients with cirrhosis, although esophageal varices account for only 10% to 20% of all upper GI bleeds. Mortality rates worsen with the severity of cirrhosis. Since the 1980s, survival and rebleeding rates for variceal bleeds have significantly improved due to the introduction of new treatment modalities. In addition to endo- scopic sclerotherapy and band ligation, modalities include splanchnic constrictors, such as somatostatin and octreotide; short-term antibiotic prophylaxis; and early consideration of transjugular intrahepatic por- tosystemic shunt placement. In-hospital mortality rates associated with variceal bleeding are now estimated to be 15% to 20%, compared to 40% to 50% in the 1980s. Incorrect Answer Explanations Administering blood products may stabilize the patient's condition, but it will not definitively treat the underlying cause of the upper GI bleed- ing. A restrictive transfusion strategy (transfusion when the Hgb level falls below 7 g/dL) is associated with reduced morbidity and mortality rates. All patients with significant sources of hemorrhage require adequate intravenous access. Bedside balloon tamponade should be considered for exsanguinating patients with suspected variceal bleeding only if endoscopy is not immediately available. Three balloon tamponade devices are the Sengstaken-Blakemore (or Blakemore) tube, Minnesota tube, and Linton (or Linton-Nachlas) tube. Instructions for use vary by device, but the patient must be intubated before the tube is placed. Vasopressin was commonly used prior to the release of somatostatin and its syn- thetic analogue, octreotide. It is a preferential splanchnic constrictor and re- duces portal hypertension. However, its lack of selectivity at higher doses leads to significant side effects, namely cardiac and mesenteric ischemia. As a result, its use in upper GI bleeding has fallen out of favor.

question: What is the most common site of bleeding from varices in a patient with cirrhosis?
englishExplanation: The most common site of bleeding from varices is the distal esophagus. Whereas varices in the mid esophagus lie deep in the submucosa, varices in the distal esopha- gus near the gastroesophageal junction lie superficial and close to the surface. This superficial location increases the risk for bleeding. Other factors that increase the risk of bleeding include varices that are larger in diameter, certain appearance of varices (red wale marks or red streaks on the varices confer a higher risk), wors- ened liver function, and history of prior variceal bleeding. Incorrect Answer Explanations Varices in the gastric fundus are less common than varices in the distal esoph- agus. When bleeding from gastric varices occurs, it is more severe and has higher transfusion requirements than bleeding from esophageal varices. The proximal esophagus is not a common site of bleeding from varices. However, varices can occur at any point of the GI tract from the esophagus to the rectum. The rectum is not a common site of bleeding from varices. However, varices can occur at any point of the GI tract from the esophagus to the rectum.

question: A patient with a history of cirrhosis and esophageal varices presents with he- matemesis. Which medication will decrease their risk of mortality?
englishExplanation: A meta-analysis of more than 1,200 patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding found that antibiotics (such as ceftriaxone) decrease the risk of mortality, rebleeding, and infections. Without antibiotics, patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding have a 30% to 40% risk of developing infections, most commonly from gram-negative bacteria. Common infections include UTIs, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and aspiration pneumonia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Lactulose is used for hepatic encephalopathy to reduce serum ammonia con- centration by trapping it within the colon. Lactulose has not been shown to reduce mortality in patients with cirrhosis and GI bleeding. Pantoprazole decreases the pH within the stomach and stabilizes clot formation in bleeding from peptic ulcer disease, but it has not been shown to im- prove mortality or help with hemostasis from bleeding varices. Although variceal bleeding is the most common source of bleeding in patients with cirrhosis, bleeding from a nonvariceal source (such as from peptic ulcer disease) can still occur. Thus, pantoprazole can be given to patients with cirrhosis, especially if there is suspicion of nonvariceal bleeding. As of now, more research is needed to determine if tranexamic acid (TXA) improves mortality in patients with upper GI bleeding. There is not a current recommen- dation to use TXA in these patients at this time. Furthermore, it is important to consider that TXA is associated with significant side effects, including development of DVT, pulmonary embolism, and seizures.

question: What is the mechanism of action of octreotide treatment for variceal bleeding?
englishExplanation: In patients with GI bleeding from varices, octreotide decreases portal venous pressures and pressures in varices within seconds of administration. Octreotide has also been shown to achieve earlier hemostasis and decrease rates of rebleeding. However, there is no evidence to show that octreotide decreases mortality. Incorrect Answer Explanations Octreotide does not increase insulin release but rather suppresses it. This is the mechanism that supports its use for patients with hypoglycemia and sul- fonylurea usage. The suppression of insulin and other hormones may contribute to the ability of octreotide to regulate intestinal blood flow, which has been hypothe- sized to help decrease overall variceal pressures. Octreotide does not prevent infection in patients with variceal bleeding. Ceftriaxone is the medication that has been shown to prevent infection, reduce re- bleeding rates, and decrease rates of mortality in patients with variceal bleeding. Pantoprazole, rather than octreotide, is the medication that has been shown to decrease mucosal deterioration, which is one of reasons for its use in patients with GI bleeding from peptic ulcer disease. Pantoprazole also increases gastric pH, stabilizing clots on bleeding ulcers.

question: What is the most lethal complication of placing a Blakemore tube in a patient with bleeding from esophagogastric varices?
englishExplanation: The most lethal complication from Blakemore tube placement is esophageal perforation. This leads to mediastinitis and infection, with mortality rates of up to 50%. Esophageal perforation can occur if the gastric balloon is inflated above the diaphragm. Thus, an x-ray should be obtained prior to fully in- flating the gastric balloon to confirm its placement below the diaphragm. Additionally, esophageal perforation can occur if the esophageal balloon is inflated at exceedingly high pressures. The balloon should be inflated to pressures of 30 to 40 mm Hg. It is important to note that the Blakemore tube is placed as a tem- porizing measure as a bridge to definitive treatment, such as transjugular intrahep- atic portosystemic shunt. Incorrect Answer Explanations Airway obstruction will generally not occur since patients should be intubated prior to insertion of the Blakemore tube, but it can occur and can be substan- tially lethal. The Blakemore tube can be pulled out inadvertently, and the esophageal balloon can migrate into the oropharynx. This is another reason for pa- tients to be intubated prior to Blakemore tube placement. Aspiration pneumonia may occur from GI bleeding or other secretions exit- ing the esophagus and traveling into the tracheobronchial tree. Patients with GI bleeding and cirrhosis are also at increased risk of infections. However, this is not the most lethal complication of Blakemore tube insertion. Gastric perforation is not as likely to occur; the expansion of the gastric bal- loon to 250 mL is not enough to distend the stomach to the point of perforation. Additionally, the Blakemore tube has a rounded rubber tip that is unlikely to punc- ture through the stomach.

question: What procedure is indicated after failed pharmacologic and endoscopic treat- ment of persistent severe bleeding from esophagogastric varices?
englishExplanation: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is a surgical procedure where a shunt is placed between the portal vein and one of the hepatic veins to bypass the liver, thereby decreasing portal venous pressures. TIPS has been shown to increase survival rates of patients with severe variceal bleeding from 10% to 60%. After TIPS placement, over 90% of patients will achieve hemostasis. Since this treatment is invasive, TIPS is indicated after failed pharmacologic and en- doscopic treatment. In a patient with severe bleeding from varices, early consul- tation of gastroenterology will help to expedite both TIPS placement or transfer to a tertiary care center that can perform TIPS, if indicated. Absolute contraindications for TIPS include congestive heart failure, severe tricuspid regurgitation, severe pul- monary hypertension, active systemic infection, several hepatic cysts, and biliary obstruction. Incorrect Answer Explanations Partial esophagectomy is not an indication for variceal bleeding but can be used to treat esophageal cancers, caustic ingestions, esophageal perforation, end- stage achalasia, or strictures that have failed other treatments. Partial gastrectomy is not an indication for variceal bleeding. It can be used to treat gastric cancers, perforation, and bleeding peptic ulcers that fail phar- macologic, endoscopic, and embolization treatment. Liver transplant is an important treatment modality for acute liver failure, of which hepatitis from viruses and drugs are the most common causes. Other candi- dates for liver transplantation include cirrhosis with a Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score of 15 or greater and certain patients with liver neoplasm or metabolic disorders affecting the liver.

question: What is a late complication of esophageal cancer?
englishExplanation: Bronchoesophageal fistulas and tracheoesophageal fistulas result from direct erosion of an esophageal tumor through the esophageal wall into the mainstem bronchus or the trachea. The presentation varies, but it commonly in- volves frequent coughing and recurrent pneumonia. Dysphagia, iron defi- ciency anemia due to microscopic blood loss, weight loss, and retrosternal discom- fort are early complications of esophageal cancer. Esophageal cancer can be either squamous cell carcinoma (most common worldwide) or adenocarcinoma (most common in the United States). Known risk factors for developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma include al- cohol use and smoking. Barrett esophagitis is a risk factor for esophageal adeno- carcinoma; the diagnosis is made by endoscopic biopsy of the esophageal mass. Metastasis of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma is most often to intrathoracic ar- eas, and esophageal adenocarcinoma most commonly metastasizes to intraabdomi- nal sites. GI cancers, such as esophageal cancers, gastric cancer, and pancreatic can- cer, have a high rate of associated clotting disorders. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dysphagia is an early complication of esophageal cancer. Patients may describe their solid food as “sticking.” Dysphagia may progress from solids to liquids over time. Iron deficiency anemia is a common early complication of esophageal cancer. Patients may have microscopic blood loss from the friable tumor site. However, it is rarely sufficient to develop melena or coffee ground emesis. Retrosternal discomfort, often described as burning, is an early complication of esophageal cancer. Because it is also a symptom of gastritis and GERD, patients with isolated retrosternal burning should be referred for outpatient endoscopy for further evaluation.

question: What is the mechanism of lactulose in the management of hepatic encephalopathy?

options.text: Alters urine pH to increase urinary excretion of ammonia
Decreases absorption of ammonia through a laxative effect in the GI tract
Functions as an antibacterial agent in the gut to destroy ammonia-producing bacteria
Increases levels of endogenous zinc to aid in the metabolism of ammonia

correctAnswer: Decreases absorption of ammonia through a laxative effect in the GI tract
englishExplanation: Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide that is a first-line treatment for hepatic en- cephalopathy (HE). It has several proposed mechanisms by which it reduces lev- els of circulating ammonia. First, lactulose acts as a hyperosmolar load in the GI system that is then readily broken down by colonic bacteria, yielding a laxative ef- fect that decreases systemic ammonia absorption. It also decreases the pH level of stool, trapping ammonia in the GI tract as ammonium for fecal ex- cretion. Finally, it is thought that lactulose directly stimulates colonic bacteria to absorb and break down ammonia. HE (also known as portosystemic encephalopathy) is seen in cirrhosis patients with toxin accumulation in the bloodstream due to impaired hepatic clearance. Ammonia is the most well-known toxin and is associated with the neuropsychiatric symptoms seen in HE. Impairments in cognitive and neuromuscular functioning are character- istic of HE and can range from subtle deficits to overt coma. Serum ammonia levels are usually elevated in HE but do not necessarily correlate to the degree of mental status change. Incorrect Answer Explanations Lactulose exhibits its primary effects in the GI tract, not the urinary system. However, lactulose does alter the pH in the intestines to trap ammonia in the form of ammonium in the stool. Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide rather than an antibiotic. Second-line thera- peutics for HE include antibiotics (eg, neomycin, rifaximin, oral vancomycin) that destroy ammonia-producing bacteria in the gut. Zinc replacement is hypothesized to be useful in the management of HE, as zinc is an important nutrient needed in the metabolism of ammonia. However, this is not the mechanism of lactulose.

question: A 45-year-old man presents with multiple episodes of bloody stool over the past 2 hours. His medical history includes hepatitis C with ascites, alcohol cirrhosis, and a recent endoscopy showing peptic ulcers. His vital signs are BP 66/45, P 134, R 24, and T 36.6°C (97.9°F); SpO is 93%. The physical examination is no- table for a nontender, distended, and firm abdomen and melena. After starting resuscitation with intravenous fluids and blood, what pharmacotherapy de- creases mortality?
englishExplanation: Cirrhosis patients who present with upper GI bleeding that is not attributed to varices should receive proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) in addition to prophylactic an- tibiotics. Of the choices available, only antibiotics have been shown to decrease mortality. Cirrhotic patients have a high risk of infection in the setting of GI bleed- ing. For either variceal bleeding or nonvariceal upper GI bleeding, cirrhotic patients should receive prophylactic antibiotics, ideally prior to endoscopy. Antibiotic pro- 2 phylaxis is associated with reduced mortality, decreased risk of bacterial infection, lowered risk of rebleeding, and shorter hospitalization. Standard antibiotic choices are ceftriaxone 1 g IV with transition to ciprofloxacin orally. The PPI of choice is pantoprazole 80-mg bolus IV, sometimes followed by an infusion of 8 mg/hr. Cirrhosis patients have an increased risk of translocation of gut bacteria in the set- ting of acute bleeding. The delivery of a PPI is aimed at increasing gastric pH to al- low for clot formation. It has been shown to reduce the need for surgical interven- tion and hospital length of stay, but has not been shown to decrease mortality. Incorrect Answer Explanations Erythromycin is a prokinetic used in GI bleeding primarily to improve visualization of endoscopy. It has not been shown to decrease mortality. Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue and splanchnic vasoconstrictor, is indicated for patients with variceal bleeding. This patient's recent endoscopy showed peptic ul- cers with no known varices, so splanchnic vasoconstrictors are not indicated. In pa- tients with varices and GI bleeding, octreotide has been shown to decrease rebleed- ing, but not mortality. Vasopressin is another vasoactive medication used to reduce splanchnic blood flow and portal hypertension. However, vasopressin has been largely replaced by octreotide for use in variceal bleeding because of other side ef- fects such as vasoconstriction in other organs (eg, cardiac, cerebral, limb). If any- thing, this may increase mortality in GI bleeding, not decrease it. Tranexamic acid (TXA) is an antifibrinolytic agent that has been used for many other bleeding situations. However, it has been studied for use in GI bleeding, and recent evidence suggests that TXA is not beneficial in GI bleeding, so it is not cur- rently recommended.

question: A 4-week-old Chinese girl presents with jaundice. Laboratory testing reveals a di- rect hyperbilirubinemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Biliary atresia is a disease of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts that leads to obstructive jaundice, cirrhosis, and death, if untreated. Obstructive jaundice causes a relative increase in direct bilirubin that results in di- rect (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia, which is a rare condition that is more common in individuals of Asian descent, particularly Asian females. Biliary atresia presents as new or persistent jaundice after 2 weeks of age, and the bilirubin profile reveals a predominance of direct (conjugated) bilirubin. Failure to thrive, signs of obstructive jaundice (acholic stools and dark brown urine), and hepatosplenomegaly can also be present. Nuclear medicine imaging is used to help determine whether obstruction exists, and percu- taneous transhepatic cholangiography is used to visualize the biliary tree with a con- trast medium and x-rays. Treatment for biliary atresia is surgical — the Kasai proce- dure (hepatoportoenterostomy). Early treatment, ideally before the infant is 2 months old, is the goal in children with biliary atresia. Delay in identification and treatment (after 3 months of age) leads to significantly worse outcomes in terms of both morbidity and mortality. Incorrect Answer Explanations Breast milk jaundice presents after the fifth day of life with indirect (un- conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia. The exact cause is unknown, but elevated bilirubin levels can be seen until the infant is 8 weeks old. The levels decrease with phototherapy and with temporary cessation of breastfeeding, although the latter is generally not recommended. Gilbert syndrome is a genetic defect, a liver dysfunction that results in ineffective processing of bilirubin. It leads to mild, intermittent jaundice and an indirect (un- conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia. Gilbert syndrome typically presents later in childhood or adolescence during periods of stress, fasting, or infection. Physiologic jaundice is due to an immature bilirubin conjugation system in the liver in the early neonatal period. This indirect (unconjugated) hyperbilirubine- mia typically presents before the fifth day of life and improves without treat- ment as the child's liver enzymes mature. Key Points Consider biliary atresia in children older than 2 weeks who present with new or per- sistent jaundice. Biliary atresia presents with a direct hyperbilirubinemia. Other more common forms of neonatal jaundice (eg, physiologic jaundice, breast- feeding jaundice, and breast milk jaundice) present with an indirect hyperbilirubinemia. Early identification and treatment of biliary atresia, ideally before the patient is 2 months old, lead to improved outcomes.

question: What is the most common cause of medication-induced liver injury in the United States?
englishExplanation: Drug-induced liver injury is extremely common and can be caused by a wide variety of prescription and over-the-counter medications as well as herbs and supplements. Acetaminophen is the most common cause in the United States and drug-induced liver injury is the most common underlying cause of acute liver failure. These drug reactions are classified into two distinct groups. One is the predictable reaction, a dose-dependent hepatotoxicity. Acetaminophen is a classic example. The other is the idiosyncratic reaction, which is patient specific and not dose dependent. Isoniazid, amiodarone, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, and phenytoin are major examples. Clinically, drug-induced liver injury ranges from asymptomatic to frank liver failure with jaundice, malaise, vomiting, low grade fever, abdomi- nal pain, and encephalopathy. Laboratory results can show transamini- tis, hyperbilirubinemia, and elevated INR. Severe transaminitis with jaundice portends a poor prognosis. Emergency department management is largely restricted to reversible or treatable causes, such as acetaminophen or val- proic acid toxicity. Regardless of the source, nonessential medications should be held, and the patient should be admitted. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is a major cause of drug-induced liver in- jury; however, acetaminophen is a more common cause. The addition of a beta-lactamase inhibitor to a beta-lactam antibiotic dramatically increases the risk of liver injury. Ibuprofen, along with other NSAIDs, can cause hepatotoxicity but much less com- monly than acetaminophen. NSAIDs are more well known for causing acute kidney injury and peptic ulcers. Isoniazid is a classic example of an idiosyncratic hepatotoxin, and it fre- quently causes liver injury. The risk is higher when combined with rifampin. Although isoniazid is not commonly used in the United States, it is the most frequently used treatment for tuberculosis and, as a result, is a common cause of drug-induced liver injury worldwide.

question: In addition to albumin, which medication is the first-line treatment for sponta- neous bacterial peritonitis for a patient developing hepatorenal syndrome?
englishExplanation: One of the most common risk factors (up to 25%-30% of patients) for de- veloping hepatorenal syndrome is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Cefotaxime is the recommended empiric antibiotic because it covers most of the organisms that cause SBP and has high ascitic fluid concentrations. Correcting the underlying cause of hepatorenal syndrome may reverse the process, but liver transplant is the definitive treatment if no etiology is found or renal function worsens despite therapies. Hepatorenal syndrome can arise spontaneously, but hepatorenal syn- drome associated with cirrhosis has a significant morbidity rate and 2- week mortality rate if left untreated. A paracentesis should be performed to rule this out, and treatment should be started if there is clinical suspicion. Type 1 hepatorenal syndrome, marked by oliguria and rapidly increasing serum creatinine (more than doubling within 2 weeks), is more critical than type 2. Type 2 hepatore- nal syndrome progresses more gradually and may advance less insidiously. Incorrect Answer Explanations Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that can be used along with a third-genera- tion cephalosporin for treatment of pneumonia in patients with hepatorenal failure. Azithromycin is not the first-line treatment for SBP. N-acetylcysteine is usually used to treat acetaminophen overdose. It has been shown to improve renal function, but the mechanism is unclear. N-acetylcys- teine has no role in treatment of liver failure that is not drug related. Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide aid in splanchnic vasocon- striction and are a mainstay for variceal bleeding. There is a potential for benefit in hepatorenal patients due to regulation of splanchnic vasodilation that sec- ondarily causes renal circulatory perfusion problems. However, this possibility has not yet been validated by clinical trials. Key Points Hepatorenal syndrome is highly associated with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Hepatorenal syndrome is marked by acute serum creatinine elevations and oliguria.

question: What laboratory results indicate acute hepatitis B infection? Legend: HBeAg = hepatitis B e-antigen HBsAg = hepatitis B surface antigen Anti-HBc = hepatitis B core antibody Anti-HBe = hepatitis B e-antigen antibody Anti-HBs = hepatitis B surface antibody
englishExplanation: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is the serologic hallmark of hepati- tis B virus (HBV) infection and appears in serum about 1 to 10 weeks after acute exposure. In patients who recover, HBsAg usually becomes undetectable after 4 to 6 months. Persistence of HBsAg may indicate chronic infection. Hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) is the sole marker of HBV infec- tion after HBsAg disappears and is a marker of acute infection until the appear- ance of hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs). During acute infection, antibodies are predominantly of the IgM class. The presence of anti-HBc indicates previ- ous or ongoing infection with HBV. Anti-HBc IgG is produced in response to core antigen later in the course of infection and then persists for life. Anti-HBs is used to detect previous exposure to HBV and indicates immunity to future HBV in- fection. Anti-HBs can be present after HBV vaccination as well. Hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) is a viral protein and an indicator of ac- tive viral replication, making it a marker of infectivity. It is present in acute HBV infection as well as chronic HBV infection with active viral replication. By contrast, hepatitis B e-antigen antibody (anti-HBe) indicates low infectivity and is typically seen in chronic HBV infection with low viral replication or during re- covery from HBV infection. Incorrect Answer Explanations HBsAg +, anti-HBc IgG +, HBeAg + indicates chronic HBV with active viral replica- tion. HBeAg is a marker of infectivity and active viral replication, which distin- guishes chronic HBV with active viral replication from chronic HBV with low viral replication. HBsAg +, anti-HBs –, anti-HBe + indicates chronic HBV infection with low viral replication. Anti-HBc IgG would be positive, and HBeAg would be negative. HBsAg –, anti-HBs+, HBeAg – indicates immunity from HBV, either from illness recovery or previous vaccination. The presence of anti-HBc IgG differentiates recov- ery from infection, rather than immunity.

question: A 47-year-old man is brought in for confusion. His family states that he is a daily drinker. The patient is afebrile and has normal vital signs. An examination re- veals ascites and asterixis. What management is most indicated based on the un- derlying disease?
englishExplanation: Any patient who presents with altered mental status or confusion should have their glucose checked to rule out hypoglycemia as an easily reversible cause. Lactulose is given to treat hepatic encephalopathy in those with cirrhosis, which is most likely what this patient has given the history of daily drinking and the physical examination findings. Additional physical examina- tion findings that may indicate a diagnosis of cirrhosis include jaundice, scleral icterus, asterixis, spider angiomata, caput medusae, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly, among others. The patient's confusion is secondary to hepatic encephalopathy, which causes somnolence and confusion because of elevated ammonia levels. In patients with cirrhosis, liver dysfunction impairs hepatic metabolism of ammo- nia, shunting it into the systemic circulation. Ammonia crosses the blood-brain bar- rier and is metabolized to glutamine, which leads to cerebral dysfunction via multi- ple mechanisms. The treatment of hepatic encephalopathy includes lactu- lose or rifaximin to lower blood ammonia concentrations. Correction of precipitating causes such as GI bleeding, infection, renal failure, electrolyte abnor- malities, hypovolemia, and medication noncompliance is also essential. Incorrect Answer Explanations While this patient is confused, his clinical presentation is most consistent with an underlying diagnosis of cirrhosis and hepatic encephalopathy. Meningitis should be considered if there is no other explanation for the patient's confu- sion; at which point, a head CT and lumbar puncture are appropriate. Intravenous normal saline and lorazepam are used to treat symptoms of acute alcohol withdrawal, which may be seen in someone with cirrhosis from alcohol abuse. This patient, however, has normal vital signs with no other signs of alcohol withdrawal. Intravenous pantoprazole and intravenous octreotide are given to cir- rhotic patients, but typically those presenting with GI bleeding. Intravenous pantoprazole is given to minimize gastric secretion and esophageal complications. Intravenous octreotide reduces splanchnic vasodilation and reduces portal venous pressure, which is important in variceal bleeds. However, neither of these therapies reduces patient mortality.

question: A health care worker who was previously vaccinated against hepatitis B virus is exposed via needlestick to a patient who is HBsAg positive. The health care worker tests negative for HBsAb, his last tetanus vaccination was 4 years ago, and he has been regularly vaccinated. What is the recommended post-exposure prophylaxis?

options.text: Hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccination
Tetanus and hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccination

correctAnswer: Hepatitis B immune globulin and hepatitis B vaccination
englishExplanation: While the health care worker was previously vaccinated, he is no longer immune to hepatitis B because his HBsAb test is negative. Vaccination is required to boost long-term immunity. Hepatitis B immune globulin is also required, as it provides immediate anti-HBs antibodies and protects against infection for 3 to 6 months. Follow-up testing for anti-HBc and HBsAg should be performed 6 months after the exposure if the source patient was HBsAg positive or if their status was unknown. Incorrect Answer Explanations The health care worker was previously vaccinated against hepatitis B but tested neg- ative for HBsAb, which indicates that he is no longer immune. Hepatitis B immune globulin is appropriate for immediate immunity, but the health care worker also re- quires vaccination for long-term immunity, as the immune globulin will only pro- vide antibodies for 3 to 6 months. Although the health care worker was previously vaccinated against hepatitis B, he tested negative for HBsAb, so he is no longer immune. Hepatitis B vaccination is re- quired but will take time to boost immunity. Therefore, immune globulin must also be given to provide immediate immunity. The health care worker does not require administration of tetanus immune globu- lin, which is typically only given if the person has received fewer than three doses of tetanus toxoid. For those who have received more than three doses, and for wounds that are clean and minor, tetanus immune globulin is unnecessary. Tetanus immune globulin is only required for significant wounds, such as those contaminated with dirt, feces or saliva, for puncture wounds, or for someone who has received fewer than three doses of tetanus toxoid.

question: Which hepatitis virus is most commonly transmitted via the fecal-oral route?
englishExplanation: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is transmitted by fecal-oral contamination, usu- ally with improper food handling. It is typically transmitted from asympto- matic children to adults. HAV has an incubation period of 15 to 50 days, followed by a prodromal illness of vomiting, nausea, chills, and fatigue. Patients typically present with dark urine (caused by bilirubinuria), jaundice, clay- colored stool, and elevated AST and ALT levels. Death from hepatic failure is rare. HAV does not lead to chronic disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is typically transmitted sexually, by blood trans- fusion, by contaminated needles, or by perinatal transmission. During acute infection, patients may be asymptomatic or present with acute hepatitis. About 5% to 10% of patients infected with HBV remain chronically in- fected, which can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is typically transmitted via exposure to contam- inated blood or blood products. Around 50% to 80% of patients with HCV de- velop chronic infection. The effects of chronic infection include cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and malignancy. Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is typically seen in patients with preexisting chronic HBV infection and is often associated with intravenous drug use. Hepatitis D replicates independently within hepatocytes but requires hepatitis B surface antigen for propagation. Most patients recover during acute coinfection with HBV and HDV, but about 5% of patients develop chronic infection.

question: A patient presents with right upper quadrant pain and vomiting. The following laboratory results are obtained: AST 300 IU/L, ALT 100 IU/L, normal alkaline phosphatase level, anti-HBs positive, and anti-HBc negative. What is the diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Patients with alcoholic hepatitis typically present with moderate eleva- tions in AST and ALT levels—typically an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2. This patient's hepatitis B virus (HBV) results indicate immunity from previous hep- atitis B vaccination. Patients with alcoholic hepatitis may also have ele- vated serum bilirubin, gamma-glutamyl transferase, and INR levels. Serum AST and ALT levels are typically less than 300 IU/L. Higher transaminase concentrations should raise suspicion for other sources of liver injury, including acute hepatitis infection, drug toxicity, or overdose. Steroid therapy should be considered for patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis, measured as a Maddrey discriminant function (DF) score greater than or equal to 32. This score is based on laboratory values, including PT and total bilirubin. Prednisolone 40 mg for a total of 4 weeks is typically the treatment of choice, as prednisone requires conversion within the liver to its active form. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute calculous cholecystitis may present with elevated liver enzymes, but the AST:ALT ratio of greater than 2 in this scenario is atypical. Usually, AST and ALT levels are more equally elevated in acute calculous cholecystitis. Alkaline phosphatase levels are also typically elevated in acute calculous cholecystitis. Acute HBV infection typically presents with high levels of AST and ALT, typically greater than five times the normal values, and both are usually ele- vated equally, although sometimes ALT is higher. In acute HBV infection, anti-HBs is typically negative, and anti-HBc is positive for IgM antibodies. Chronic hepatitis B infection may present with elevated liver enzymes. In chronic HBV infection, anti-HBs is negative, and anti-HBc is positive for IgG an- tibodies. Patients with chronic HBV infection with active viral replication typically also have a positive HBsAg result.

question: Which liver pathology is most closely associated with future development of hep- atocellular carcinoma?
englishExplanation: Hepatocellular carcinoma is associated with chronic hepatitis C viral (HCV) infection. HCV infection accounts for nearly a third of all hepatocellular carcinoma cases. Hepatitis B infection is similarly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma. It is thought that the higher risk of hepatocellular carcinoma is related to the increased turnover of the hepatocytes due to chronic inflammation in the liver from these viral infections. Hepatocellular carcinoma develops nearly exclusively in patients who have cirrhosis. The risk of hepatocellular carci- noma is estimated to be 1% to 4% per year in patients who have cirrhosis. Hepatitis B and C are both bloodborne pathogens that are transmitted through ex- posure from sexual intercourse, needle sharing, or other blood exposure. Screening should be offered to unvaccinated patients at high risk of exposure as well as any patients, regardless of vaccination status, who are symptomatic or have unexplained liver function test abnormalities. Additionally, screening should occur regardless of vaccination status in pregnant patients, blood donors, and patients who require im- munosuppressive therapy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amoebic liver abscess has no known association with hepatocellular carcinoma. However, it is associated with peritonitis due to rupture of the abscess into the peritoneal cavity. Amoebic liver abscess may also be associated with hepatic vein or IVC thrombosis. Liver hemangiomas have no known association with hepatocellular carcinoma. They are usually asymptomatic but may be associated with bleeding or thrombo- sis of the hemangioma. Traumatic liver laceration has no known association with hepatocellular carci- noma. There is some association between nonoperative embolization of liver lacera- tion and hepatic necrosis, but this can also be seen with operative management.

question: A 56-year-old man presents with lethargy, confusion, and asterixis. His vital signs are normal, but his medical history includes alcoholic cirrhosis. Which medication could worsen his condition?
englishExplanation: Benzodiazepines can precipitate worsening mental status for patients with known hepatic dysfunction and confusion. Most benzodiazepines, in- cluding diazepam, clonazepam, and midazolam, are metabolized by phase I metabo- lism, which is impaired in patients with liver dysfunction. This results in reduced clearance of active metabolites and disproportionate sedation. If a benzodi- azepine must be used in a patient with hepatic encephalopathy to con- trol agitation, for example, lorazepam may be a safer choice; it is metab- olized by phase II metabolism, which is less impaired in liver dysfunc- tion. Hepatic encephalopathy is a common and potentially debilitating manifesta- tion of cirrhosis. Its pathogenesis is complex and poorly understood, but it is likely related to excessive cerebral ammonia elevation. Manifestations occur along a con- tinuum of neurologic and psychiatric abnormalities. In its mildest form, hepatic en- cephalopathy may be detectable only with psychometric testing. As severity in- creases, more clinically obvious symptoms emerge, such as personality changes, sleep disturbances, motor disruption, altered mental status with agitation or som- nolence, and ultimately, stupor and coma. The West Haven Criteria delineate the stages of hepatic encephalopathy from Grade I, in which the person seems to have some trivial cognitive or behavioral decay or euphoria, through Grade IV, coma. Incorrect Answer Explanations Lactulose is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for hepatic en- cephalopathy and does not worsen altered mental status. It is a nonab- sorbable disaccharide that inhibits the proliferation of ammonia-producing gut bac- teria, promotes retention of ammonia in the gut (rather than in the serum), and re- duces colonic bacteria load and ammonia through catharsis. Neomycin was one of the first antibiotics investigated as a potential treatment for hepatic encephalopathy. It is an aminoglycoside that reduces colonic bacteria load, leading to reduced ammonia levels. Its side effects include ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and intestinal malabsorption. In recent years, it has largely been replaced by safer antibiotics, such as rifaximin. However, it is un- likely to worsen this patient's symptoms. Thiamine (vitamin B) is administered to treat Wernicke encephalopa- thy, which is an acute neurologic disorder resulting from thiamine defi- ciency. Clinically, it is characterized by the classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. The safety profile of thiamine is very good, and Wernicke en- cephalopathy is underdiagnosed. It is unlikely that empiric thiamine administration would harm this patient.

question: How is metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis differentiated from metabolic dysfunction–associated fatty liver disease?
englishExplanation: Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a subtype of metabolic dysfunction–associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD). In MASH, hepatic steato- sis is associated with hepatic inflammation that is best detected with a liver biopsy. Liver biopsy can also determine severity of disease, including signs of cirrhosis such as scarring and fibrosis. Liver function tests and ultrasound imaging cannot distinguish between MASH and MAFLD. MASH is thought to represent a progression of MAFLD, with MAFLD being the broader category of steatotic liver disease. These terms have recently changed. The termi- nology previously revolved around the word “nonalcoholic.” Patients di- agnosed with MASH are recommended to abstain from alcohol, obtain vaccinations for infectious hepatitis, pursue weight loss, and attempt cardiovascular risk modifi- cations. To diagnose MAFLD or MASH, exclusion of viral hepatitis and al- cohol use as potential causes is necessary. MAFLD is fairly common in the United States, with an estimated preva- lence of 30% in adults. MAFLD is diagnosed if there is hepatic steatosis in a pa- tient with a BMI >25, type 2 diabetes, or metabolic dysfunction (defined as two or more of the following: hypertension, dyslipidemia, prediabetes, elevated CRP levels, and insulin resistance). Although MAFLD is often an incidental finding on imaging studies, patients may present with abdominal pain and malaise. The pathogenesis of MAFLD seems to be related to insulin resistance, with certain genomic variations increasing the risk of progression from MAFLD to MASH. A subset of patients with MASH may develop cirrhosis and hepatic failure. Incorrect Answer Explanations Liver function test results are similar in both MAFLD and MASH, usu- ally showing a mild elevation in transaminases. Liver function tests can be useful in distinguishing alcoholic liver disease from MAFLD because alcoholic liver disease may demonstrate the classic 2:1 ratio of AST to ALT. Ultrasound appearance is similar in both MAFLD and MASH, revealing fat accumulation. Ultrasound imaging cannot differentiate MAFLD from other causes of fatty liver, such as alcohol use. Viral hepatitis tests are unhelpful in distinguishing between MAFLD and MASH, al- though they help identify other causes of hepatitis. Patients with viral hepatitis are typically symptomatic, with higher elevations in liver function test results than are seen in MAFLD.

question: Which disease process is most commonly related to the development of meta- bolic dysfunction–associated fatty liver disease?
englishExplanation: Insulin resistance is currently thought to be a key mechanism leading to hepatic steatosis. Metabolic dysfunction–associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is increasingly recognized as a multifactorial disease and may have multiple causative factors. Additional research is identifying inflamma- tory factors and other cytokines released from adipose tissue as potentially leading to MAFLD pathology. MAFLD is often found incidentally on imaging or routine laboratory findings with mild transaminitis. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) may develop as a progression of MAFLD, but it requires a liver biopsy to diagnose. MASH can ultimately progress to hepatic carcinoma and cir- rhosis. MASH-cirrhosis is now the second most common cause for liver transplanta- tion, with hepatitis being the most common and alcohol use being the third most common. MAFLD is often identified incidentally on emergency department evaluation from imaging tests or mild elevations in liver function test results. These patients should be counseled on diet modification, exercise, alcohol abstinence, and weight loss. These are the most modifiable factors to reduce hepatic steatosis and prevent fur- ther complications. Incorrect Answer Explanations Adrenal insufficiency is a risk factor for acquired hyperpigmentation of the skin. It is unrelated to increased risk of MAFLD. Biliary dyskinesia and pancreatic sphincter of Oddi dysfunction are associated with recurrent right upper quadrant pain and potentially recurrent pancre- atitis. They do not increase the risk of MAFLD. Renal artery stenosis is a risk factor for hypertension and chronic kidney dis- ease. It is not associated with an increased risk of MAFLD.

question: Steatosis of the liver with visible inflammatory changes but no fibrosis on histopathologic evaluation is consistent with which disease state?
englishExplanation: Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a subtype of metabolic dysfunction–associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD). In MASH, hepatic steato- sis is associated with hepatic inflammation. The hallmark of MASH is steato- sis with inflammatory changes on histopathology. MASH may or may not present with fibrotic changes on histopathology. It can progress to cryptogenic cirrhosis of the liver. MASH-cirrhosis is the preferred terminology for MASH that has pro- gressed to liver cryptogenic cirrhosis. By definition, cirrhosis demonstrates fibrosis on histologic evaluation. Autoimmune hepatitis may demonstrate inflammatory changes but is unlikely to demonstrate steatosis. The differentiation between MASH and MAFLD is made by liver biopsy and the ex- clusion of other causes of hepatitis, such as viral or alcohol-induced. Patients di- agnosed with MASH are recommended to abstain from alcohol, obtain vaccinations for infectious hepatitis, pursue weight loss, improve their diet, and exercise. As noted previously, MASH may progress to MASH-cirrhosis and also increases the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. MASH-cirrhosis is now thought to be the second most common cause of liver failure requiring transplant, with viral hepatitis being the most common and alcohol-associated cirrhosis being the third most common. Incorrect Answer Explanations Autoimmune hepatitis is characterized by inflammation on histopathology but is unlikely to demonstrate steatosis. A variety of histochemical markers can help elucidate the cause of the autoimmune hepatitis. Autoimmune hepatitis may ad- vance to cirrhosis if untreated. Cryptogenic cirrhosis is characterized by fibrosis on histopathology. MASH is a predisposing condition to MASH-cirrhosis. Cirrhosis places patients at higher risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Hemochromatosis is associated with liver failure and certainly with hepatic fi- brosis. This disease in itself does not present with steatosis.

question: A patient presents with right lower quadrant pain and is diagnosed with appen- dicitis on CT scan. The CT scan also shows findings of fatty liver infiltration. What should this patient be counseled to avoid?
englishExplanation: This patient has metabolic dysfunction–associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) and should be counseled to avoid alcohol. MAFLD is a spectrum of disease representing the sequelae of fatty infiltration of the liver. This condition was formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) but has been re- named to better represent the underlying cause of the disease. The pri- mary underlying factor for developing MAFLD is thought to be insulin resistance in association with other metabolic dysfunction comorbidities, such as obesity, dyslipi- demia, hypertension, and genetic factors. Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a subset of MAFLD. MASH is differentiated from MAFLD by signs of inflammation with or without fi- brosis on liver biopsy. Patients who are diagnosed with MAFLD or MASH are recommended to abstain from alcohol, obtain vaccinations for in- fectious hepatitis, pursue weight loss, improve their diet, and exercise. In particular, alcohol may provide a secondary oxidative stressor to the liver and in- crease the likelihood the patient will progress to MASH-cirrhosis. MASH-cirrhosis increases the likelihood of the patient developing hepatocellular carcinoma as well as liver failure that may require a transplant. MAFLD is often an incidental finding from studies obtained in the emergency depart- ment, such as on ultrasound or CT scan. Although they are mostly asymptomatic, these patients should be informed of the finding, coun- seled on the aforementioned recommendations, and encouraged to fol- low-up with their primary care physician. Incorrect Answer Explanations Avoiding carbohydrates in patients with fatty liver disease is unwar- ranted. Although insulin resistance is likely a contributory mechanism to MAFLD, carbohydrate modification as a weight-loss strategy should be explored in depth by patients and their primary care physicians. In particular, complex carbohydrates in moderation are part of a well-balanced diet. Instead of the complete avoidance of carbohydrates, the appropriate types and amounts of carbohydrates should be chosen. Patients with fatty liver disease should not be told to avoid exercise. In fact, the ex- act opposite is true. To prevent progression of fatty liver disease, exercise should be incorporated with diet and other lifestyle changes to improve the patient's overall metabolic function and reduce insulin resistance. Fish oil or other omega-3 fatty acid supplementation does not need to be avoided in the setting of fatty liver disease. In fact, a recent double-blind, randomized, placebo- controlled trial suggested that fish oil supplementation reduced alkaline phos- phatase levels and liver fibrosis in patients with MAFLD.

question: Which comorbid condition is commonly associated with metabolic dysfunction– associated fatty liver disease?
englishExplanation: Insulin resistance, such as in diabetes mellitus, is currently thought to be a key mechanism leading to hepatic steatosis. Metabolic dysfunction–associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) is a spectrum of diseases that represent the sequelae of fatty infiltration of the liver. MAFLD was formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) but has been renamed to better represent the un- derlying cause of the disease. MAFLD is also associated with other metabolic dysfunction comorbidities, such as obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and genetic factors. A subset of MAFLD is metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH). This is differentiated from MAFLD by signs of inflammation with or with- out fibrosis on liver biopsy. Patients diagnosed with MAFLD or MASH are recommended to abstain from alcohol, obtain vaccinations for infec- tious hepatitis, pursue weight loss, improve their diet, and exercise. MAFLD is often an incidental finding from studies obtained in the emer- gency department, such as on ultrasound or CT scan. Although they are mostly asymptomatic, these patients should be informed of the finding, counseled on the aforementioned recommendations, and encouraged to follow-up with their primary care physician. Incorrect Answer Explanations Chronic pancreatitis may be associated with hypertriglyceridemia, pan- creatic sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, or autoimmune disease. However, in itself, chronic pancreatitis is unrelated to MAFLD, which is fatty liver infiltration due to insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction. Congestive heart failure may cause liver congestion and be associated with coronary artery disease, vitamin deficiencies, or other causes. However, it is not associated with the development of MAFLD. Peptic ulcer disease is associated with Helicobacter pylori (or other in- fections), use of certain pharmaceuticals, and Zollinger-Ellison syn- drome (gastrinoma), among other factors. Peptic ulcer disease is not directly causative of or associated with MAFLD.

question: A 69-year-old woman presents with 2 days of right upper quadrant pain. Her vi- tal signs include BP 100/85, P 114, R 22, and T 39.3°C (102.7°F); she has a posi- tive Murphy sign and scleral icterus. Ultrasound reveals a common bile duct di- ameter of 14 mm. Which intervention is the definitive management for this patient's condition?
englishExplanation: This patient has acute ascending cholangitis, which is often accompanied by bacteremia and septic shock. This is a surgical emergency that requires stabilization of hemodynamic abnormalities, initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics, and surgi- cal consultation. Definitive management involves early biliary tract de- compression by ERCP, percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography, or surgery. Studies have shown that the more severe the illness, the more critical the need for urgent biliary decompression using ERCP, which has better results than surgery. Ascending cholangitis is most often caused by blockage of the common bile duct by a gallstone but can also develop secondary to malignancy or be- nign stricture. Ultrasonography can help detect intrahepatic ductal dilation as well as stones in the gallbladder or common bile duct. Patients with cholangitis of- ten develop fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. The Charcot triad of symptoms includes right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice. When these symptoms are also associated with hypotension and altered sensorium due to clinical signs of sepsis, they are described as the Reynolds pentad. Common labo- ratory abnormalities in acute ascending cholangitis include leukocytosis, hyper- bilirubinemia, an elevated alkaline phosphatase level, and increased aminotrans- ferase levels. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although intravenous antibiotics are critical, the definitive manage- ment of ascending cholangitis is decompression of the biliary tract. Broad-spectrum antibiotic choices include piperacillin-tazobactam, imipenem, meropenem, ticarcillin-clavulanate, and ampicillin-sulbactam (with metronidazole). Although this patient likely requires intravenous fluids and perhaps even vasopres- sors for hemodynamic stabilization, intravenous fluids alone are insufficient. If the diagnosis is unclear or there are other competing diagnoses, a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis may be useful; however, cholangitis is the leading diagnosis in this case. Oral antibiotics and outpatient follow-up are inappropriate. This patient re- quires urgent stabilization, intravenous antibiotics, and biliary tract decompression. Key Points Cholangitis is an emergent condition caused by extrahepatic bile duct obstruction and subsequent bacterial infection. Effective initial management of acute cholangitis requires prompt diagnosis, surgi- cal consultation, broad-spectrum antibiotics initiation, and biliary tract decompression. Biliary tract decompression can be accomplished via ERCP or surgery.

question: A 52-year-old man presents with right upper quadrant pain for 24 hours. He un- derwent ERCP 3 days ago. His examination is notable for focal right upper quad- rant abdominal tenderness to palpation; there is no evidence of jaundice. His vi- tal signs include BP 105/60, P 111, R 23, and T 38.4°C (101.1°F). What etiology is this presentation most concerning for?
englishExplanation: This patient's recent ERCP places him at increased risk for acute cholangitis. Acute cholangitis is characterized by Charcot triad, a constella- tion of symptoms including right upper quadrant tenderness, fever, and jaundice. Notably, only 50% to 75% of patients will present with all three findings. Fever is the most common finding, followed by right upper quadrant tender- ness; jaundice is the least common finding, with only around 60% of patients pre- senting with this condition. Alongside gallstones and malignancy, ERCP is one of the most common risk factors for developing acute cholangitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with acute cholecystitis may present with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and fever. However, this patient recently underwent ERCP, which puts him at increased risk for ascending cholangitis. Patients with choledocholithiasis often have evidence of obstruction with- out evidence of infection. These patients often present with jaundice but lack signs of systemic inflammatory response, such as fever or tachycardia. Patients with pancreatitis may present after ERCP (a common cause of pancreatitis), but it is unlikely that they will present with focal right up- per quadrant tenderness. Fever is also less common in pancreatitis as com- pared to ascending cholangitis.

question: What isolated finding is a common presentation of acute cholangitis in elderly patients?
englishExplanation: Elderly patients may lack the common examination findings associated with acute cholangitis: right upper quadrant tenderness, jaundice, and fever (known as Charcot triad). In these patients, signs of systemic inflammation, specifically hypotension, may be the only notable finding. Up to 70% of patients with acute cholangitis have positive blood cultures, indicating systemic infection. Reynolds pentad, which consists of Charcot triad plus altered mental status and hypotension, is very specific for acute cholangitis but is not sensitive. Less than 10% of patients will present with all five findings, and this percentage may be less in elderly patients, who often present atypically. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with acute cholangitis classically present with right upper quadrant tenderness; they rarely present with lower abdominal tenderness. Elderly patients with biliary disease may have minimal or no abdominal symptoms. Pleuritic pain, or pain with inspiration, is a common finding in patients presenting with an abdominal pathology that causes diaphragmatic irritation. However, el- derly patients are less likely to present with pain. Tachypnea is a common vital sign abnormality in patients with systemic inflam- matory response syndrome or sepsis. However, tachypnea is not as associated with acute cholangitis in the elderly.

question: After broad-spectrum antibiotics have been administered, what is the next best step in management for patients with acute cholangitis?
englishExplanation: ERCP is considered the first-line therapy in patients with acute cholangitis af- ter initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Patients with unstable vital signs, evidence of end-organ dysfunction, or septic shock should undergo this pro- cedure emergently, but patients with mild or moderate disease respond to antibi- otics alone in 70% to 80% of cases. Regardless of severity, all patients diagnosed with acute cholangitis should be admitted for administration of intravenous antibiotics and supportive care. Incorrect Answer Explanations Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is considered first-line treatment for pa- tients with cholecystitis. It is not a recommended therapy in those with acute cholangitis. Open biliary decompression is considered second-line therapy for situations in which ERCP is not clinically feasible. However, it is not the first-line therapy for acute cholangitis. Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography is considered a second-line therapy for patients in whom ERCP is not an option. However, it is not the first-line therapy for acute cholangitis.

question: In a 55-year-old patient with right upper quadrant pain, which bedside ultra- sound finding is most specific for a diagnosis of acute cholangitis?

options.text: Common bile duct measurement of 1.0 cm
Gallbladder wall thickening greater than 0.5 cm
Posterior acoustic enhancement of the common bile duct

correctAnswer: Common bile duct measurement of 1.0 cm
englishExplanation: Although bedside ultrasound is classically used in the evaluation of cholecystitis, it can also help evaluate for evidence of biliary obstruction in acute cholangitis. Evidence of cholangitis includes a dilated common bile duct; generally, a di- lated common bile duct diameter is 0.6 cm plus 0.1 cm for every decade of life after age 60. Other signs include evidence of common bile duct wall thickening as well as evidence of biliary stones. Notably, many patients presenting with acute cholangitis may have evidence of cholecystitis present on ultrasound; the four classic find- ings associated with cholecystitis include thickened gallbladder wall, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign, and evidence of stones. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gallbladder wall thickening greater than 0.3 to 0.4 cm is indicative of gall- bladder inflammation, most commonly associated with acute cholecystitis. Common bile duct thickening may be present in those with acute cholangitis, but gallbladder wall thickening alone is not indicative of common bile duct obstruction. The common bile duct may exhibit some posterior acoustic enhancement given the fluid-filled nature of the structure. However, this finding will not help distinguish between acute cholangitis and other etiologies of right upper quadrant pain. Pericholecystic fluid is one of the common ultrasound findings associated with acute cholecystitis. It represents ultrasound evidence of gallbladder inflamma- tion and surrounding fluid.

question: A 72-year-old man presents with severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain ra- diating to his back. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus but no recent illness or sur- gery.
