Physical examination reveals fever and tachycardia with tenderness in the right upper quadrant but no peritoneal signs. There is no jaundice, and the pul- monary examination is unremarkable. Abdominal x-rays are obtained. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Courtesy of David Effron, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: This patient has emphysematous cholecystitis, an acute infection of the gallbladder caused by gas-producing organisms. The abdominal x-ray reveals the classic findings of a fluid-filled gallbladder and gas in the gallbladder wall. Inflammation and gas formation can also extend to involve the pericholecystic tis- sues and perihepatic ducts. Emphysematous cholecystitis frequently affects older men. A significant percentage of patients with this condition have underlying dia- betes mellitus, and 28% to 80% have associated gallstones. Clostridial species, Escherichia coli, and Klebsiella spp. are the most common organisms isolated. Although reports vary in the literature, emphysematous cholecystitis develops in ap- proximately 1% of all patients with acute cholecystitis. Symptoms typically include right upper quadrant pain, fever, tachycardia, and hypotension. Because of the high mortality rate associated with this disease, emergent surgical consultation is indi- cated. Emphysematous cholecystitis is easily seen on CT, which is appro- priate to order if it can be done quickly because it confirms the diagno- sis and assists with surgical planning. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with acute hepatitis generally present with nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. They may be febrile and tachy- cardic and have right upper quadrant tenderness, as in this patient; however, pa- tients usually have jaundice. In acute hepatitis, abdominal x-rays are unremarkable; ultrasound examination of the right upper quadrant would reveal a liver with de- creased echogenicity. Ascending cholangitis classically presents with the Charcot triad: fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice. However, the triad is only present in about half of patients with ascending cholangitis, with jaundice being less com- monly seen than either fever or right upper quadrant pain. The Charcot triad and the additional findings of altered mental status and shock make up the Reynolds pentad. Given the variability of the findings, ascending cholangitis should be con- sidered in this patient, but the x-ray findings suggest emphysematous cholecystitis instead. Ultrasonography and CT are the preferred imaging choices to confirm a di- agnosis of ascending cholangitis in the emergency department. A perforated viscus typically presents with abrupt-onset abdominal pain. Vomiting is common, and fever may develop as a later sign as the patient de- velops sepsis. Abdominal pain is generalized, with diffuse guarding and rebound on examination. In this case, the patient's physical examination findings do not suggest a perforated viscus. Free air is seen under the diaphragm on an upright radiograph in 70% to 80% of cases. Key Points Emphysematous cholecystitis has a high mortality rate and is most commonly seen in elderly patients with diabetes mellitus. Emphysematous cholecystitis patients present with fever, signs of sepsis, and right upper quadrant pain and have evidence of air in the biliary tract. Abdominal x-rays can be diagnostic in some cases of emphysematous cholecystitis, but ultrasonography or CT (or both) also can be performed, according to the clinical presentation and the patient's condition.

question: A 44-year-old woman presents with acute-onset constant right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever for the past 14 hours. Her vital signs include BP 122/76, P 112, R 16, and T 38.8°C (101.8°F). A bedside ultrasound of the right upper quadrant is performed and shown below. What ultrasound find- ing would most strongly support the diagnosis of acute calculous cholecystitis? Credit: Robert Jones, DO, FACEP. Credit: Robert Jones, DO, FACEP.
englishExplanation: The sonographic Murphy sign is considered positive if pressing on the gallbladder while under sonographic visualization maximally repro- duces a patient's abdominal pain but does not do so when performed else- where. In the setting of typical signs and symptoms as well as visualized gallstones, the sonographic Murphy sign is considered highly sensitive for and predictive of acute calculous cholecystitis. The sonographic diagnosis of acute calculous cholecystitis generally re- quires more than just the presence of gallstones and a positive sono- graphic Murphy sign. This is because the sonographic Murphy sign has limited specificity and is operator dependent. Gallbladder wall thickening and peric- holecystic fluid are additional findings that strengthen the sonographic diagnosis of acute calculous cholecystitis. Ultrasound is the recommended initial diagnostic modality for evaluating potential acute cholecystitis due to its high diagnostic accuracy, low cost compared to other modalities, lack of ionizing radiation, wide availability, and ability to per- form provocative testing (sonographic Murphy sign). Once sonographic diagnosis of acute calculous cholecystitis is made, broad-spectrum antibiotics, analgesia, and surgical consultation are indicated. Further imaging (eg, CT, MRI, scintig- raphy) is unnecessary unless the diagnosis is in doubt. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gallbladder wall thickening, not thinning, is one of the sonographic signs of acute cholecystitis and is evident on this patient's sonograms. Although wall thickening is relatively nonspecific for cholecystitis and can occur with multiple other conditions (eg, pancreatitis, ascites, heart failure, or liver disease), it is consid- ered an important finding for the sonographic diagnosis of acute cholecystitis. Wall thickening is defined as a gallbladder wall thicker than 3 mm. In this patient's sonogram, the gallbladder wall measures 13 mm (1.3 cm) in the long axis and 10 mm (1.0 cm) in the short axis. Noncompressibility is a sonographic sign associated with appendicitis, not cholecystitis. Sonographic compressibility is not measured when evaluating the gallbladder. The major sonographic findings associated with acute calculous cholecystitis are the presence of gallstones, a positive sonographic Murphy sign, gallbladder wall thickening, and pericholecystic fluid. Pericholecystic, rather than perihepatic, fluid is a sonographic finding that is strongly associated with acute cholecystitis, although it can be caused by other etiologies such as ascites. Perihepatic fluid, on the other hand, can be caused by a myriad of other conditions (eg, ascites, pancreatitis, and bleed- ing) but is generally not associated with acute cholecystitis. As with the sonographic Murphy sign, the presence of other suggestive findings along with pericholecystic fluid contribute to the sonographic diagnosis of acute calculous cholecystitis.

question: What is the most appropriate management for a patient who presents with inter- mittent right upper quadrant pain and ultrasonographic evidence of chronic cholecystitis?
englishExplanation: Chronic cholecystitis is seen in approximately two-thirds of patients presenting with intermittently symptomatic obstructive biliary disease (biliary colic) and is thought to be caused by inflammation and fibrosis from recurrent biliary obstruction. However, this finding does not change the ultimate disposition for patients presenting with intermittent biliary colic, which is outpatient surgical referral for cholecystectomy. Chronic cholecystitis has some ultrasonographic characteristics of acute cholecystitis, such as gallbladder wall thickening, but lacks other findings of acute cholecysti- tis, such as constant right upper quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Thus, chronic cholecystitis is an imaging diagnosis associated with an otherwise uncom- plicated biliary colic. Incorrect Answer Explanations Admission for intravenous antibiotics alone is a possible management of acute cholecystitis in a medically complex patient that may require optimization before surgery or percutaneous drain placement. Similarly, intravenous antibiotics should be started in any case of acute cholecystitis while awaiting surgical evaluation. Antibiotics with enteric gram-negative and anaerobic coverage should be chosen, such as piperacillin-tazobactam alone or ceftriaxone with metronidazole. However, this disposition is inappropriate for the management of bil- iary colic or chronic cholecystitis because uncomplicated cases can be discharged with surgical follow-up. Gastroenterology consultation for ERCP is a recommended approach for patients with acute common bile duct stones causing choledo- cholithaisis. However, gastroenterology consultation is generally not used in the management of chronic cholecystitis. Surgery consultation for urgent cholecystectomy is most appropriate for acute cholecystitis. Biliary colic and chronic cholecystitis are considered safe to manage as an outpatient if otherwise able.

question: Which condition is associated with a sonographic Murphy sign?
englishExplanation: Acute cholecystitis is inflammation involving the gallbladder. There are many signs and symptoms of acute cholecystitis, but none have a sensitivity or specificity nearing 100%, making the diagnosis challenging at times. It seems the most useful finding is a positive sonographic Murphy sign. This is when tenderness is elicited directly over the gallbladder when pressure is applied with the ultrasound probe during the imaging examination. It is estimated that the positive predictive value of a sonographic Murphy sign in the presence of gallstones for cholecystitis is greater than 90%. Other findings, such as pericholecystic fluid and gallbladder wall thickening, are much less sensitive and specific, as these findings can be present in other conditions or may be absent in the setting of acute cholecystitis. Most commonly, acute cholecystitis is the sequelae of gallbladder stones, or cholelithiasis. When a gallstone becomes lodged in the gallbladder neck, cystic duct, or common bile duct, the gallbladder is unable to empty and becomes in- flamed. As bile and other fluids accumulate in the gallbladder, acute cholecystitis can occur and lead to infection. Although most cases of cholecystitis occur in the setting of gallstones, acalculous cholecystitis can occur and is most of- ten seen in the setting of another acute process, such as in patients with severe sep- sis, trauma, or burns. The initial imaging modality of choice for diagnosing cholecystitis is ul- trasound because it can quickly identify most features associated with cholecysti- tis. An abdominal CT scan can be obtained as well. Data is conflicting on its accuracy, with some data suggesting it to be more sensitive than ultrasound. The most sensitive and specific test for cholecystitis is a hepatobiliary imin- odiacetic acid cholescintigraphy (HIDA) scan. However, this is often not readily available in many settings, particularly from the emergency department. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cholelithiasis is a condition caused by the presence of gallstones in the gallbladder. It is estimated that around 80% of patients with gallstones are asymptomatic. Sonographic Murphy sign is typically negative in the setting of cholelithiasis without cholecystitis. Hepatitis suggests inflammation or infection of the liver that can be related to mul- tiple different etiologies, such as viral infections, substance abuse, and fatty infiltra- tion. Hepatitis typically presents with findings of liver disease and fail- ure. A sonographic Murphy sign would not be expected in this setting. Pancreatitis can occur from multiple different conditions, the most common being alcohol abuse and gallstones. The mechanism of pancreatitis from gallstones involves mechanical obstruction of distal pancreatic ducts, often at the ampulla of Vater, causing fluid to back up into the pancreas. Although there may be concurrent cholecystitis, this is not required, and a sonographic Murphy sign would not suggest pancreatitis.

question: A 56-year-old man presents with vomiting and abdominal pain and is diagnosed with acute cholecystitis. The presence of which finding would suggest that the pa- tient may be developing cholangitis?
englishExplanation: Cholangitis is an infection involving the biliary tree and can be a seque- lae of acute cholecystitis or can occur independently. Patients with cholan- gitis (or infection of the biliary tract) often have additional laboratory findings of cholestasis (eg, elevated bilirubin, AST/ALT, and alkaline phosphatase). It is much less common to see elevated bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase in uncom- plicated acute cholecystitis, so these findings should raise concern about an obstruc- tive process. Both cholangitis and cholecystitis typically present with fever, right up- per quadrant abdominal pain, and leukocytosis. However, the development of jaundice is much more associated with cholangitis than cholecystitis. Cholangitis classically presents with Charcot's triad of fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain, but all three findings are only present in up to 75% of patients with cholangitis. The addition of altered mental status and hypotension define Reynolds' pentad. Cholangitis is treated with aggres- sive hydration; broad-spectrum antibiotic administration; and surgical, gastroen- terology, or interventional radiology consultation for biliary tract decompression. Incorrect Answer Explanations Fever is seen in both cholecystitis and cholangitis and is nonspecific for ei- ther of these conditions. In fact, the presence or absence of fever should not be used to rule in or rule out any infection. Multiple factors including age, individual physi- ology, medications, comorbidities and method of measurement affect body temper- ature readings. Leukocytosis is expected in both cholecystitis and ascending cholangitis and cannot be used to differentiate the conditions. Various infections, physiologic stress, steroid use, and inflammatory conditions can cause leukocytosis as well. Right upper quadrant abdominal pain would be expected in both chole- cystitis and cholangitis. This can also be seen in other conditions (eg, pancreati- tis, biliary colic, pyelonephritis, renal colic, and lower lobe pneumonia) and is not a specific finding to biliary disease.

question: Which initial diagnostic modality is best for evaluating acute cholecystitis in the emergency department?
englishExplanation: Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice for cholecystitis with a sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 78%, as well as being the most easily ac- cessible study in the emergency department. The majority of patients report a his- tory of cholelithiasis, and the finding of gallstones on ultrasound is suggestive of cholecystitis in the setting of pain with fever. Other ultrasound findings include gallbladder wall thickening of more than 3 mm or edema (double wall sign), pericholecystic fluid, and the sonographic Murphy sign, which is identified when compression of the gallbladder causes cessation of inspiration or tenderness, as observed by the ultrasonographer. The complication of emphysema- tous cholecystitis can create the false finding of overlying bowel gas that is actually air within the wall of the gallbladder. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cholescintigraphy (hepatic iminodiacetic acid [HIDA] scan) is often performed when ultrasound has unclear findings. A 99 mTc-HIDA (tech- netium labeled) is injected intravenously and secreted into the bile. A patent, unob- structed cystic duct allows the tracer into the gallbladder, permitting visualization within 30 to 60 minutes. If the gallbladder cannot be visualized at 60 minutes, de- layed images or morphine augmentation is performed. Persistent nonvisualiza- tion of the gallbladder is suggestive of acute cholecystitis. In addition to being a time-consuming imaging modality, it has been found to have many false positives (eg, tumor or stone causing obstruction without cholecystitis, severe liver disease, fasting patients, hyperbilirubinemia, or biliary sphincterotomy). CT is helpful in identifying complications of acute cholecystitis, such as gangrene, perforation, emphysematous cholecystitis, and bowel obstruction from gallstone ileus. CT can evaluate for other etiologies in the undifferentiated abdominal pain patient. CT has a high sensitivity (94%) but low specificity (59%) and may fail to identify gallstones, particularly those with the same density as bile. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is ideal for the evaluation of choledocholithiasis and, on occasion, ascending cholangi- tis. Compared to ultrasound, MRCP performs better at detecting cystic duct stones but worse at gallbladder wall thickening (although sensitivity approaches 100%). Although this technique is noninvasive, it can be time-consuming and expensive.

question: Which antibiotic(s) should be given for acute perforated calculous cholecystitis?
englishExplanation: Acute cholecystitis is initially treated with antibiotics, and this is usually followed by either a cholecystectomy or percutaneous biliary drain placement to decompress the gallbladder, depending on the clinical situa- tion. There are multiple potential antibiotic choices for the treatment of cholecysti- tis, but of the options presented, piperacillin-tazobactam is the most appropriate to treat complicated cholecystitis. When choosing an antibiotic regimen, it is impor- tant to consider the pathogens that are being covered. For cholecystitis, the most common causative bacteria is Escherichia coli, followed by Enterococcus, Klebsiella, and Enterobacter. As a result, treatment needs to be directed primarily at gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria. In complicated cholecystitis, such as with a perforation or abscess, it is important to use a broad-spectrum antibiotic to cover all potential pathogens. In this case, piperacillin-tazobactam provides the best coverage, giving strong gram- negative and anaerobic coverage. Other options include ampicillin-sulbac- tam (although this is usually reserved for uncomplicated cholecystitis) or metron- idazole plus either a third-generation cephalosporin (ie, ceftriaxone or ce- fotaxime) or a fluoroquinolone (ie, ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin). Incorrect Answer Explanations Cefazolin and ciprofloxacin can both be used to treat cholecystitis. However, only one of these agents would be required, and it must in- clude another antibiotic, such as metronidazole, that will cover anaerobes. Ceftriaxone monotherapy will not provide sufficient coverage in compli- cated cholecystitis. Although it will provide strong coverage against gram-nega- tive bacteria, ceftriaxone is weakly anaerobic. Thus, metronidazole should be added to provide additional anaerobic coverage. Levofloxacin monotherapy is insufficient coverage for complicated cholecystitis. Although it provides excellent gram-negative coverage, it has mini- mal activity against the most common anaerobic pathogens seen in cholecystitis. Thus, use of levofloxacin would require the addition of an agent such as metron- idazole in order to cover for anaerobes.

question: A 35-year-old woman with no significant medical history presents with right up- per quadrant pain and vomiting. An ultrasound is obtained, and the patient is di- agnosed with acute uncomplicated calculous cholecystitis. What is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?

options.text: Send the patient for an emergent cholecystectomy

englishExplanation: The next appropriate step in management would be to administer broad-spectrum antibiotics. Acute cholecystitis is inflammation involv- ing the gallbladder that is most commonly the sequelae of gallbladder stones or cholelithiasis. When a gallstone becomes lodged in the gallbladder neck, cystic duct, or common bile duct, the gallbladder is unable to empty and be- comes inflamed. As bile and other fluids accumulate in the gallbladder, acute chole- cystitis can occur and can lead to infection. Treatment of cholecystitis is multifaceted. Definitive treatment is cholecys- tectomy, but this is usually considered on an “early” or “urgent” basis. In otherwise uncomplicated cases, patients are typically admitted, and a cholecystectomy is scheduled within 24 to 48 hours. Until that point, the patient should have supportive care with intravenous fluids and administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Most cases of cholecystitis are inflammatory in nature. However, they are at risk of progressing to infection, particularly with gram-nega- tive and anaerobic bacteria. The 2018 Toyko Guidelines recommend adminis- tration of antibiotics and supportive care preceding the cholecystectomy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Sending the patient for a CT scan is unlikely to be helpful in this case un- less there is another diagnosis being considered. In the appropriate clinical context, positive ultrasound findings for acute cholecystitis have a high sensitivity and are sufficient to establish the diagnosis. Providing intravenous fluids to a patient with acute cholecystitis is appropriate for resuscitation and in consideration that the patient will likely be made NPO (“noth- ing by mouth”) in anticipation of surgery. However, current guidelines recom- mend early administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics in the treatment of acute cholecystitis. Definitive treatment of acute cholecystitis is a cholecystectomy. In most cases of uncomplicated cholecystitis, patients will typically be treated with an- tibiotics, admitted, and have surgery scheduled within 24 to 48 hours. This is termed “early” or “urgent” cholecystectomy. It is rare that uncomplicated cases are taken immediately to the operating room.

question: What factor can predispose individuals to cholelithiasis?
englishExplanation: Cholelithiasis is the main cause of biliary tract disease and results from cholesterol stones or pigmented stones. Sickle cell disease is a risk factor for cholelithiasis. Cholesterol stones form as a result of elevated cholesterol in relation to other components in bile acid. Increased cholesterol becomes insoluble and results in crystal formation within the gallbladder. Black and brown stones are pigmented stones composed of calcium bilirubinate and are associ- ated with intravascular hemolytic diseases and infection, respectively. Intravascular hemolytic diseases, such as sickle cell anemia and hereditary spherocytosis, result in increased bilirubin turnover and repeated episodes of hemolysis. Biliary disease occurs in 30% to 70% of sickle cell anemia patients. Other factors that predispose patients to biliary disease include pregnancy, inflammatory bowel disease, Gilbert disease, obesity, older age, gastric bypass, and certain medications. Incorrect Answer Explanations Moderate alcohol intake, quantified as the consumption of ≤1 drink per day in women and ≤2 drinks per day in men, lowers the risk of gallstones. According to the Nurses' Health Study, women who ingested 2 to 3 drinks per week were 40% less likely to develop symptomatic cholelithiasis than those who abstained from al- cohol. This effect has been observed in men in other studies. Although moderate al- cohol consumption has been linked to lowered risk of symptomatic cholelithiasis, the risk is increased for those with alcoholic cirrhosis. Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome, also known as perihepatitis, is a complication of pelvic inflammatory disease in which fibrinous exudate forms adhesions be- tween the liver capsule and peritoneum. Although Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome can cause similar symptoms to symptomatic cholelithiasis with right upper quadrant pain, it does not increase the risk of cholelithiasis. The most common cause of pancreatitis is obstruction of the ampulla of Vater via the passage of gallstones. Although the association confers a causal link between gallstones and pancreatitis, the risk of cholelithiasis is not increased in those with pancreatitis.

question: A 42-year-old patient presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Which sonographic finding, if measured at 7 mm, would suggest choledocholithiasis?
englishExplanation: Because choledocholithiasis is caused by obstruction of the biliary tract at the level of the common bile duct, the classic ultrasonographic find- ing is an enlarged common bile duct. The size of the common bile duct varies with age; Generally, the duct's diameter is expected to be less than 1 mm per decade of life. For example, a patient younger than 60 would be expected to have a common bile duct diameter of less than 6 mm. Postcholecystectomy patients can have physiologic common bile duct dilation, with diameters up to 10 mm consid- ered within the normal range. Definitive diagnosis is with magnetic reso- nance cholangiopancreatography or ERCP. ERCP also acts as a therapeutic intervention to remove the obstructing stone. Typically, patients with choledocholithiasis also present with right upper quad- rant abdominal pain, elevated transaminases, and alkaline phos- phatase, as well as a direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia. Pain may worsen with eating. Jaundice with lighter stools and dark urine is also a classic finding. Fevers should be absent, and patients with fevers should be ruled out for cholangitis. Vomiting and anorexia may be present. Distal common bile duct obstruction at the level of the ampulla of Vater can also cause obstructive pancreati- tis, which manifests clinically as upper abdominal pain with elevated lipase and amylase levels. Incorrect Answer Explanations Increased gallbladder wall thickness is a typical finding of acute chole- cystitis. A gallbladder wall thicker than 3 mm is considered thickened. However, this finding alone is nondiagnostic for cholecystitis. Other major findings of acute cholecystitis include constant right upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsens with eating, fevers, presence of pericholecystic fluid on ul- trasound, and a positive sonographic Murphy sign. Gallstone size alone is not considered a meaningful measure of biliary pathology. However, it is notable that gallstones larger than the common bile duct diameter are more likely to cause an obstruction. Gallstones smaller than 5 mm may not produce a meaningful acoustic shadow on ultrasound, making them harder to detect. However, these smaller gallstones are also less likely to obstruct; gallstones smaller than the diameter of the common bile duct generally pass without obstructing. A portal vein diameter of 7 mm is within normal limits. The portal vein is not involved in biliary tract obstruction; thus, its size does not directly relate to acute biliary pathology. However, enlargement of the portal vein to greater than 13 mm can suggest nonspecific portal hypertension. Common causes of portal hy- pertension include cirrhosis and congestive heart failure.

question: A patient is undergoing a workup for common bile duct stones. According to the American Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy guidelines, which factor places a patient at intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis and requires magnetic reso- nance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) for further evaluation, not ERCP?

options.text: Dilated common bile duct on transabdominal ultrasound and serum bilirubin >4 mg/dL
Presence of common bile duct stone on transabdominal ultrasound

englishExplanation: A risk stratification scheme proposed by the American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE) for diagnosing common bile duct (CBD) stones places patients into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk categories in order to decrease ERCP utilization. Risk factors that confer an intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis include any of the following: age greater than 55, ab- normal liver function tests, or dilated CBD on abdominal imaging. Patients at intermediate risk for choledocholithiasis (10%-50% probability of CBD stone) require imaging in the form of magnetic resonance cholan- giopancreatography (MRCP) or endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). Patients at high risk for choledocholithiasis (>50% probability of CBD stone) require ERCP or other endoscopic techniques for stone clearance. Risk factors that confer greater than a 50% probability of choledocholithiasis include any of the fol- lowing: the presence of a CBD stone visualized on abdominal imaging, acute cholangitis, or a serum bilirubin greater than 4 mg/dL in addition to a dilated CBD on ultrasound. The risks of undergoing ERCP, including that it is an invasive procedure with complications such as pancreatitis, bleed- ing, and perforation, do not outweigh the benefits in this subgroup of patients. Patients at low risk for choledocholithiasis have none of these risk factors present. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute cholangitis is most commonly caused by gallstones within the common bile duct that result in biliary stasis and infection within the biliary tract. Acute cholangitis should be strongly considered in patients with the Charcot triad of fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, which has a specificity of 93% to 95% for the diagnosis. If this is the most likely diagnosis, then treatment with intravenous antibiotics and ERCP is typical. The diagnosis is typically made with abdominal ul- trasound followed by CT; if both of these are negative, then try MRCP. The presence of a dilated CBD on transabdominal ultrasound in combina- tion with a serum bilirubin greater than 4 mg/dL confers a high risk (speci- ficity of 94%) for the diagnosis of choledocholithiasis. Patients at high risk for choledocholithiasis require ERCP or other methods of endoscopic stone extraction. The presence of a CBD stone on transabdominal ultrasound is diagnostic of choledocholithiasis. CBD stones on transabdominal ultrasound will occur concomitantly with a dilated CBD that typically measures more than 6 mm. CBD stones may not always be observed with transabdominal ultrasound, but CBD dila- tion can be predicted with up to 90% accuracy using ultrasound.

question: Which pain description is most associated with biliary colic?

options.text: Pain episodes usually last 12 to 24 hours

englishExplanation: Typical symptoms of biliary colic include constant right upper quadrant, epi- gastric, or substernal pain that can be associated with nausea and vomiting. Pain is described as dull and can radiate into the right shoulder or right shoulder blade. Precipitating factors can include eating a fatty meal, but pain can also be nocturnal, rather than postprandial, and peak around midnight. The pain can last from 30 minutes to several hours before resolving but does not typically exceed 6 hours. Biliary colic is a manifestation of gallstone disease in which a gallstone or gallblad- der sludge temporarily obstructs the gallbladder neck or cystic duct open- ing when the gallbladder contracts, which leads to pain from increased pressure within the gallbladder. The stone can fall back into the gallbladder with relaxation, resulting in resolution of pain, or can become lodged, leading to complicated gall- stone disease, which includes acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, as- cending cholangitis, or gallstone pancreatitis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pain episodes due to biliary colic typically resolve within 6 hours. If pain per- sists longer than this, other diagnoses should be considered, such as acute cholecys- titis, choledocholithiasis, and ascending cholangitis. Pain may be relieved by food in patients with duodenal ulcers. The converse is true for patients with gallstone disease, whose pain can be exacerbated with food consumption. Although the pain of symptomatic cholelithiasis is termed colic, it is typically steady in nature and is less likely to fluctuate in intensity. Pain due to renal colic or intestinal obstruction can be colicky in nature.

question: Which drug can promote the development of cholelithiasis?
englishExplanation: Estrogen administration for hormone replacement therapy increases the risk of cholesterol gallstone development by increasing biliary cholesterol secretion. According to the Women's Health Initiative and the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study trial, women receiving estrogen therapy had higher rates of gall- bladder disease and cholecystectomy. Other drugs known to increase the risk of gallstone development include fibrates, which reduce bile acid secretion; cef- triaxone, which promotes biliary sludging; and somatostatin analogues, which impair gallbladder emptying. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ampicillin is not known to promote gallstone formation. Ampicillin can cause a rare but serious liver injury complication called vanishing bile duct syndrome. This presents as chronic cholestasis and appears as loss of intrahepatic bile ducts on his- tology. This can result in cholestatic hepatitis. NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen and ketorolac, are frequently used in the treatment of symptomatic cholelithiasis to relieve biliary colic pain. Certain NSAIDs (eg, sulindac and nimesulide) have been linked with drug-induced liver injury through the development of cholestasis, hepatitis, and hepatocellular necrosis. However, NSAIDs have been found to significantly reduce biliary colic pain and decrease the risk of complicated gallstone disease (eg, acute cholecystitis or ascending cholangitis). Moderate and high statin use has been found to reduce the risk of gallstone forma- tion and cholecystectomy. Statins decrease hepatic cholesterol synthesis and, there- fore, reduce cholesterol gallstones through a reduction in cholesterol bile concentration.

question: A 70-year-old woman presents with 2 months of worsening, dull, right upper quadrant pain that has become constant. She also notes pale stools, dark urine, fatigue, itching, and a 9.1-kg (20-pound) weight loss. On examination, she is noted to be markedly jaundiced with right upper quadrant pain and a palpable mass. Which condition is associated with the highest risk of developing this disease?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms of cholangiocarcinoma, which include signs of obstruction (eg, jaundice, pruritus, clay-colored stools, dark urine, and abdominal pain) and, rarely, a palpable gallbladder (also known as Courvoisier sign). Unintentional weight loss, fever, malaise, and night sweats may also be present. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a key risk factor for developing cholangiocarcinoma. Patients with PSC should be regularly screened for development of either cholangiocarcinoma or gallbladder cancer. Other risk factors for cholangiocarcinoma include choledocholithiasis, liver flukes, obesity, chronic biliary tract disease, ulcerative colitis, cirrhosis, and exposure to certain chemicals. Cholangiocarcinoma is a rare but lethal cancer. The prognosis of patients with cholangiocarcinoma is poor because it is usually undetected until late in the disease process. These tumors rarely become symptomatic until they obstruct the biliary drainage system. Laboratory tests will show elevations in bilirubin, AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gallbladder polyps are usually benign and rarely co-occur with stones. Large gallbladder polyps may be associated with an increased risk of gallbladder cancer, but the evidence is unclear. Gallstones in the gallbladder are present in more than 70% of patients with gall- bladder cancer but are not clearly associated with cholangiocarcinoma, and are not an established risk factor. Choledocholithiasis (gallstones in the common bile duct), however, is one of the risk factors for development of cholan- giocarcinoma while gallstones are a strong risk factor for gallbladder cancer. The risk is higher with larger gallstones and longer duration of stones. Obesity is associated with gallbladder cancer as well as other cancers, including en- dometrial, ovarian, breast, pancreatic, colon, and kidney. Although cholangio- carcinoma has been linked to obesity, it does not represent the greatest risk factor.

question: A 34-year-old patient presents in the 3rd trimester of an uncomplicated preg- nancy with 4 hours of severe radiating epigastric pain and nonbilious, nonbloody emesis. The physical examination is notable for a tender upper abdomen with guarding of the right upper quadrant and epigastric and periumbilical areas. A blood sample is drawn and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Rachel Liu, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: The image shows lipemic blood, which is a risk factor for acute pancreatitis. Although alcohol and gallstone obstruction are the most common causes, hy- pertriglyceridemia also results in pancreatitis. Hypertriglyceridemia and gallstone pancreatitis are associated with pregnancy and increase both maternal and fetal mortality rates. This form of pancreatitis correlates with triglyceride levels above 500 mg/dL, with more severe inflammation occurring at 1,000 mg/dL. Treatment for patients with hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancre- atitis focuses on analgesia, antiemetics, intravenous fluid administration, insulin, and lipid-lowering agents. More severe inflammation may require plasmapheresis or surgery if there is evidence of pancreatic necrosis. Antibiotic therapy is not indi- cated unless necrosis, abscess, or infected pseudocyst exists. Pancreatitis can be as- sociated with pleural effusions and hypoxemia. The Ranson criteria are used af- ter 48 hours to determine the severity of disease. Notably, typical emergency de- partment tests do not include the LDH value that is needed for calculating this for- mula. Although these criteria and other prediction rules are unhelpful in the emer- gency department, patients with increased inflammatory markers are generally at an increased risk of death. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cholecystitis should be considered in any patient presenting with upper ab- dominal pain and vomiting. In this case, however, the key is to recognize lipemic blood, as shown in the image, which is associated with acute pancreatitis. Hyperemesis gravidarum presents with profuse vomiting and abdominal pain from gastric irritation. However, it is typically limited to the first trimester, and this patient is in the late second or early third trimester based on physical ex- amination findings. Hyperemesis gravidarum is not associated with the high triglyc- eride level that caused the lipemic blood shown in the image. Placental abruption is a complication of pregnancy that presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. Nausea and profuse vomiting are not usually features of this condition.

question: What is required to diagnose necrotizing pancreatitis?
englishExplanation: Necrotizing pancreatitis is a severe form of pancreatitis that involves necrosis of either the parenchyma or the peripancreatic tissue of the pan- creas. Necrotizing pancreatitis must be diagnosed using either CT with intra- venous contrast or MRI. There are several forms of pancreatitis, divided by severity and type. The Atlanta classification defines pancreatitis as either necrotiz- ing or interstitial edematous. The severity of acute pancreatitis ranges from mild (no organ failure or systemic complications) to moderate (transient organ failure or transient systemic complications) to severe (persistent organ failure). The most common type of acute pancreatitis is acute interstitial edematous pan- creatitis (about 80% of cases). Although approximately 15% to 25% of acute pan- creatitis cases involve necrosis, the interstitial edematous type does not. The mor- tality differs between these groups, with an overall mortality of around 3% in cases of acute interstitial edematous pancreatitis. The case fatality rate of necrotizing pan- creatitis is much higher (17%). The diagnosis of acute pancreatitis in the emergency department is typically clinical, requiring two of the following: acute onset of persistent, severe, epigastric pain often radiating to the back; elevation in serum lipase to three times the upper limit of normal; or characteristic findings on imaging (CT with contrast, MRI, or ultrasound). Imaging is generally reserved only for se- vere cases, for when there is concern for complications such as necrosis, or to ex- clude other possible diagnoses. Most cases of acute pancreatitis will resolve in 3 to 5 days with supportive care, including intravenous fluids, pain control, and nutritional support. About one-third of cases of necrotizing pancreatitis will develop infection, and in those cases, antibiotics are warranted. Severe pan- creatitis should be monitored in the ICU. There are many different scoring systems that can be used to assess the severity of pancreatitis. Known risk factors for severe pancreatitis include older age, obesity, alcoholic etiology, and organ failure upon diagnosis. The Ranson criteria have been used, but it scores six items at admission and six items at 48 hours, making its utility in the emergency department limited. The Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) score and the Bedside Index for Severity in Acute Pancreatitis (BISAP) score can be used in the first 24 hours, and the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE II) score has been used in the ICU setting. None of these scoring systems are perfect, but physicians should evalu- ate the entire clinical picture of patients with acute pancreatitis and consider ICU admission and imaging for those with severe features. Incorrect Answer Explanations Lipase greater than 3 times normal is in the diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis but does not predict its severity or type. Most pancreatitis is of the interstitial edematous type, not the necrotizing type. Imaging is necessary to identify areas of pancreatic necrosis, and CT or MRI are preferred imaging modalities. A Ranson score is used to predict the severity of acute pancreatitis based on multiple factors, with higher scores associated with greater mortality rates. However, the Ranson criteria cannot predict whether pancreatitis is necro- tizing. However, a Ranson score greater than or equal to 3 at admission indicates that severe pancreatitis is likely, and it suggests that ICU admission should be con- sidered. The Ranson criteria are divided into two parts: criteria evaluated on admis- sion and at 48 hours. Necrosis must be identified with imaging; CT and MRI are preferred imaging modalities. An ultrasound of the abdomen can be used in cases of acute pancreatitis to evaluate for gallstones as a cause, and it can also evaluate for pancreatic en- largement or peripancreatic fluid; however, ultrasound is not sensitive for pancre- atic necrosis. A CT scan of the abdomen with intravenous contrast and an MRI of the abdomen are both more sensitive for necrotizing pancreatitis than ultrasound is. To make the diagnosis of necrotizing pancreatitis, parenchymal necrosis or peripan- creatic necrosis must be seen.

question: A 38-year-old patient presents with upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with associated nausea and vomiting. The laboratory evaluation is significant for WBC 9,700/mm, AST 1,246 Units/L, ALT 1,478 Units/L, and lipase 974 Units/L. POCUS of the right upper quadrant reveals a 0.2-cm gallbladder wall thickness, no pericholecystic fluid or visible gallstones, and 1.1-cm common bile duct. Which specialist would be most appropriate to consult at this time?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with choledocholithiasis with gallstone pancreati- tis, all due to distal common bile duct obstruction from a gallstone. The most ap- propriate action is to consult gastroenterology for ERCP, a procedure that can both diagnose and treat this condition. Intravenous fluids, pain control, and ab- staining from oral intake are indicated prior to management with ERCP. Note that ERCP is not recommended for gallstone pancreatitis in the absence of biliary obstruction or cholangitis, especially with mild symptoms. The POCUS reveals an enlarged common bile duct (CBD), which is consistent with this diagnosis. In this age group, a normal CBD measures approximately 0.4 cm, and a CBD greater than 0.7 cm is considered enlarged. Colloquially, this ultra- sound finding is known as a double-barrel shotgun sign, with the enlarged common bile duct and the portal vein forming the two “barrels.” Incorrect Answer Explanations General surgery would be the most appropriate consultant in the setting of acute calculus cholecystitis given the high likelihood of cholecystectomy. However, this patient has no signs of cholecystitis: there is no leukocytosis, and the bedside ultrasound reveals normal gallbladder wall thickness with no visible gallstones or pericholecystic fluid. This patient instead presents with gallstone pancreatitis and choledocholithiasis. This is typically managed non- surgically in the acute setting, although a same-admission cholecystectomy may be recommended. Local protocols may vary, and general surgery may eventually be- come involved. However, without acute cholecystitis, gastroenterology is the most appropriate consultant for this patient at this time. Interventional radiology would be an appropriate consultant if biliary drainage were needed, such as if a patient with acute cholecystitis were too unstable to have surgical resection. In that case, percutaneous cholecys- tostomy with placement of a biliary drain would be performed by interventional ra- diology. However, this patient has no signs of hemodynamic instability or an acute gallbladder emergency. In this case, gallstone pancreatitis and choledocholithiasis are best initially managed nonsurgically with a gastroenterology consultation for ERCP. Vascular surgery would be appropriate if this patient had a vascular emergency, such as an abdominal aortic dissection or aneurysm rup- ture. This patient does present with signs and symptoms that are possibly concern- ing for abdominal aortic pathology, such as acute-onset abdominal pain radiating to the back. However, the diagnostic workup is ultimately most suggestive of gall- stone pancreatitis and choledocholithasis. These are best managed nonsurgi- cally with a gastroenterology consultation for ERCP.

question: A 58-year-old man presents with epigastric discomfort, jaundice, and weight loss for 3 weeks. His medical history is significant for recently diagnosed diabetes and long-term tobacco use. What is the best initial abdominal imaging study to evalu- ate his symptoms?
englishExplanation: This patient's symptoms are highly concerning for a pancreatic malig- nancy, especially given his history of weight loss, tobacco use, and new- onset diabetes. A CT scan with intravenous contrast is easily obtained in the emergency department and can detect pancreatic tumors and assess the extent of disease. Diabetes is a risk factor for many malignancies, including those in the pancreas, liver, colon, and breast. In fact, up to 25% of patients with pancreatic cancer were diagnosed with diabetes within the previous 2 years. Incorrect Answer Explanations MRI is excellent for detecting and characterizing pancreatic tumors, and it provides a sensitivity similar to that of CT. However, it is the less-optimal initial study in this case due to the increased length of time needed to complete the test, the de- creased availability of MRI in the emergency department, and the increased cost. Although abdominal ultrasound can be considered as the initial imaging test to evaluate for biliary dilatation, evidence of cholelithiasis or choledocholithiasis, or large pancreatic or hepatic masses, CT is more sensitive for detecting smaller masses, pancreatitis, and related complications. A CT scan can also provide additional information regarding the etiology of the patient's obstruction and the extent of other intra-abdominal disease. Therefore, abdominal CT is preferred over ultrasound in this case. An abdominal x-ray can be used to detect free air or bowel obstruction, but it provides little information regarding intra-abdominal malignan- cies or biliary obstruction. In this case, CT would provide more information than x-ray.

question: Which is a complication of chronic pancreatitis?
englishExplanation: Chronic pancreatitis results from repeated episodes of acute pancreati- tis. Chronic pancreatitis increases the risk of developing complications, such as pancreatic pseudocysts or pancreatic cancer. A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of fluid that is well circumscribed and is located externally to the pan- creas. Pancreatic pseudocysts are generally a complication of chronic pancreatitis. The proposed pathophysiologic mechanism for the development of pancreatic pseu- docysts is the progressive blockage of pancreatic ducts. This causes a rupture of pancreatic fluids out of the pancreas and leads to the formation of a cystic structure, most often in the peripancreatic space. Patients with pancreatic pseudocysts may be asymptomatic, or they may have GI symptoms, such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and potentially, jaundice if the cyst causes blockage of biliary ducts. The diagnosis is typically made with CT or MRI. If this finding is incidental and unrelated to the patient's emergency depart- ment visit, the patient should be informed of the finding and instructed to follow-up with gastroenterology or general surgery. Depending on the clinical scenario, the patient may need further testing and biopsy of the cyst to rule out a neoplasm. However, the vast majority of pancreatic pseudocysts are benign. Interventional radiology, gastroenterology, or general surgery should be consulted if the cyst is thought to be the cause of a patient's presenting symptoms. In such cases, the patient may need more expedited drainage of the cyst. Incorrect Answer Explanations ARDS is a known complication of acute pancreatitis. It is much less likely to oc- cur from chronic pancreatitis. ARDS is a result of the acute inflammatory cascade that can be triggered in severe cases of acute pancreatitis. DIC is a known complication of acute pancreatitis. It is triggered by a severe in- flammatory cascade that can occur in acute pancreatitis. DIC is far less commonly seen as a complication of chronic pancreatitis. Renal failure is much more likely to occur in the setting of acute pancreatitis. Patients with chronic pancreatitis may slowly develop chronic renal failure. However, there are likely other underlying pathologies contributing to this beyond chronic pancreatitis alone.

question: A patient with a history of alcohol use disorder presents with lower abdominal pain. CT imaging reveals a 4-cm pancreatic pseudocyst. What does this finding most likely represent?

options.text: A benign complication of acute pancreatitis
A benign complication of chronic pancreatitis
A malignant complication of acute pancreatitis
A malignant complication of chronic pancreatitis

correctAnswer: A benign complication of chronic pancreatitis
englishExplanation: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of fluid that is well circum- scribed and is located externally to the pancreas. They are generally a complication of chronic pancreatitis. The proposed pathophysiologic mecha- nism for the development of pancreatic pseudocysts is the progressive blockage of pancreatic ducts. This causes a rupture of pancreatic fluids out of the pancreas and leads to the formation of a cystic structure, most often in the peripancreatic space. Most frequently, pancreatic pseudocysts are benign fluid collections. Patients with pancreatic pseudocysts may be asymptomatic, or they may have GI symptoms, such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and potentially, jaundice if the cyst causes blockage of biliary ducts. The diagnosis is typically made with CT or MRI. If this finding is incidental and unrelated to the patient's emergency depart- ment visit, the patient should be informed of the finding and instructed to follow-up with gastroenterology or general surgery. Depending on the clinical scenario, the patient may need further testing and biopsy of the cyst to rule out a neoplasm. However, the vast majority of pancreatic pseudocysts are benign. Interventional ra- diology, gastroenterology, or general surgery should be consulted if the cyst is thought to be the cause of a patient's presenting symptoms. In such cases, the pa- tient may need more expedited drainage of the cyst. Incorrect Answer Explanations Pancreatic pseudocysts are unlikely to be a benign complication of acute pancreatitis. Pancreatic pseudocysts are most frequently seen as a complication of chronic pancreatitis; they are much less often associated with acute pancreatitis. Pancreatic pseudocysts are unlikely to be a malignant complication of acute pancreatitis. The vast majority of pancreatic pseudocysts are benign and are asso- ciated with chronic pancreatitis. Pancreatic pseudocysts are unlikely to be a malignant complication of chronic pancreatitis. Although pancreatic pseudocysts are associated with chronic pancreatitis, the majority are benign.

question: A patient with a history of alcohol use disorder and chronic pancreatitis presents with jaundice and upper abdominal pain. CT imaging of the abdomen shows an 8-cm pancreatic pseudocyst with biliary tract obstruction. What is the most ap- propriate consultation in this case?

options.text: Interventional gastroenterologist for endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage
Minimally invasive surgical service for laparoscopic management

correctAnswer: Interventional gastroenterologist for endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage
englishExplanation: The most appropriate consultation in this case would be an interventional gastroen- terologist for endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage. A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of fluid that is well circumscribed and is located exter- nally to the pancreas. They are generally a complication of chronic pan- creatitis and are most often benign. Pancreatic pseudocysts may be asympto- matic and an incidental finding, or they may present with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and jaundice. In this case, the cyst is compressing the biliary tract, leading to jaundice. This patient needs management of the cyst to relieve the obstruction. The preferred initial approach is endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage of the cyst. This is most often performed by interventional gastroenterology. This is the least in- vasive option and is often successful in the management of these pseudocysts. Refractory or recurrent cases may require more definitive surgical management. The proposed pathophysiologic mechanism for the development of pancreatic pseu- docysts is the progressive blockage of pancreatic ducts. This causes a rupture of pancreatic fluids out of the pancreas and leads to the formation of a cystic structure, most often in the peripancreatic space. If this finding is incidental and not related to the patient's visit, the patient should be informed of the finding and instructed to follow-up with gastroenterology or general surgery. Depending on the clinical sce- nario, the patient may need further testing and biopsy of the cyst to rule out a neo- plasm. However, the vast majority of these cysts are benign. Incorrect Answer Explanations General gastroenterology for esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) is not the most appropriate consultation for this patient. Drainage of a pseudocyst is not ac- complished with an EGD. General surgery for pancreaticoduodenectomy is not the most appropriate con- sultation for this patient. Pancreaticoduodenectomy, also known as the Whipple procedure, is not the first-line treatment in this case; endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage should be attempted first. Surgery would be reserved for complex or re- fractory cases. Minimally invasive surgical service for laparoscopic management is not the most appropriate consultation for this patient. The first-line treatment for a pancreatic pseudocyst with biliary duct blockage is endoscopic ultrasound-guided drainage. This is most often performed by interventional radiology or gastroenterology. Surgery would be reserved for complex or refractory cases.

question: A patient presents with left lower quadrant abdominal pain and is diagnosed with acute diverticulitis on CT. A pancreatic pseudocyst with findings that sug- gest malignancy is incidentally noted. Which step is most important in choosing a patient-centered approach to communicating these results?

options.text: Include the information about this finding in the patient's discharge instructions
Inform the patient about the concern for possible malignancy and provide fol- low-up details
Send a message to the patient's primary care physician to inform them of the finding
There is no indication to inform the patient because most pancreatic pseudo- cysts are benign

correctAnswer: Inform the patient about the concern for possible malignancy and provide fol- low-up details
englishExplanation: In this case, it is important to inform the patient about the incidental finding, ex- press the concern for possible malignancy, and provide follow-up details. Incidental findings are common in the emergency department setting and are of- ten found with high-resolution imaging. The frequency of incidental findings has in- creased as the number and quality of images obtained have increased; other inci- dental findings can include laboratory abnormalities. Often, these findings, or “inci- dentalomas,” are benign and would be unlikely to cause any significant pathology if they had never been recognized. However, in the emergency department setting, it is often difficult to determine if the findings are benign or require more investiga- tion. Thus, incidental findings must be communicated to the patient. Communication with the patient should be clear and direct. In this case, explain to the patient that the finding might be cancerous. Include specific instructions re- garding when and with whom they should follow-up. To this patient, the physician might say, “You need to follow-up with your primary care physician about this pan- creatic pseudocyst within the next 3 months.” In addition to the discussion, include the information in the patient's written discharge instructions, and document the conversation in their medical record. An emergency physician can also engage the patient's primary care physician to help facilitate follow-up. However, the most im- portant step is direct communication with the patient, including specific fol- low-up instructions. This communication ensures that the patient is aware of the need for appropriate, timely follow-up. Documenting this step protects the physi- cian from the medicolegal risks of missed incidental findings. Pancreatic pseudocysts are collections of fluid that are well circumscribed and are located externally to the pancreas. They are generally a complication of chronic pancreatitis. The proposed pathophysiologic mechanism for the developing pan- creatic pseudocysts is the progressive blockage of pancreatic ducts. This causes a rupture of pancreatic fluids out of the pancreas and leads to the formation of a cys- tic structure, most often in the peripancreatic space. Most frequently, these are be- nign fluid collections. Incorrect Answer Explanations Placing the information about this incidental finding in the patient's discharge in- structions is not the most important step in communicating the finding. Although this step is necessary, it is even more important to communicate the find- ing directly with the patient, including details about when and with whom to follow-up. Not all patients will read and understand written follow-up instructions, so verbal communication of important information is crucial. Sending a message to the patient's primary care physician to inform them of the finding is not the most important step. Communicating concerning findings to the primary care physician can help ensure appropriate follow-up. However, this is not a substitute for direct and clear communication with the patient. Moreover, not all patients have access to primary care. There is certainly an indication to inform the patient of this finding. Although most pancreatic pseudocysts are indeed benign, this patient's CT scan contains find- ings that are concerning for malignancy and should be evaluated further. If the physician fails to inform the patient of this concerning incidental finding, they can be held liable if complications ensue.

question: A patient presents with abdominal pain and is diagnosed with acute diverticuli- tis. A pancreatic pseudocyst is incidentally noted. In the radiology report, the pseudocyst is noted to be indeterminate for malignancy. The patient is directly informed by the physician about this finding and the concern for potential malig- nancy. They are also provided with appropriate follow-up resources. What is the best strategy for medicolegal protection for the physician?

options.text: Document the conversation with the patient in the medical record
Email the patient's primary care physician to inform them of the finding
No further documentation is necessary after informing the patient of the finding
Securely message gastroenterology on-call to help facilitate follow-up

correctAnswer: Document the conversation with the patient in the medical record
englishExplanation: This incidental finding should be communicated to the patient, and the conversation should be documented in the medical record. Documenting this step protects the physician from the medicolegal risks of missed incidental find- ings. Incidental findings are common in the emergency department setting and are often found with high-resolution imaging. The frequency of incidental findings has increased as the number and quality of images obtained have increased. Other inci- dental findings can include laboratory abnormalities. Often, these findings, or “inci- dentalomas,” are benign and would be unlikely to cause any significant pathology if they had never been recognized. However, in the emergency department setting, it is often difficult to determine if the findings are benign or require more investiga- tion. Thus, these incidental findings must be communicated to the patient. Communication to the patient should be clear and direct. In this case, explain to the patient that the finding may be cancerous. Include specific instructions regard- ing when and with whom they should follow-up. To this patient, the physician might say, “You need to follow-up with your primary care physician about this pan- creatic pseudocyst within the next 3 months.” In addition to the verbal discussion, include the information in the patient's written discharge instructions, and docu- ment the conversation in their medical record. An emergency physician can also en- gage the patient's primary care physician to help facilitate follow-up. However, the most important step is direct communication with the patient, including specific follow-up instructions. This communication ensures that the patient is aware of the need for appropriate, timely follow-up. Incorrect Answer Explanations Emailing the patient's primary care physician to inform them of the finding is not the best strategy for medicolegal protection. Although it can be helpful to include the primary care physician in helping facilitate follow-up, it is even more important to properly document the conversation with the patient. It is the Physician's responsibility to inform the patient of the finding and to discuss the need for appro- priate follow-up, and it is the patient's responsibility to follow-up. There is indeed an indication to document further, even though the patient has been informed of the finding. The conversation should be documented. Otherwise, there will be no record to refer to if a medicolegal issue arises in the future. Securely messaging gastroenterology on-call to help facilitate follow-up is not the best strategy for the medicolegal protection of the physician. Although the patient should likely follow-up with gastroenterology, securely messaging on-call gastroen- terology does not ensure follow-up. It also does not provide documentation that the patient was specifically made aware of the finding and the need to follow-up.

question: A 45-year-old patient with alcoholic cirrhosis presents with confusion and in- creasing abdominal pain and pressure over the past week. A paracentesis is per- formed, revealing 520 WBCs with 89% PMNs and 11% lymphocytes. His protein is high, but glucose is normal. What is the best course of treatment?

options.text: Start probiotic therapy and a fluoroquinolone
Withhold antibiotics pending Gram stain and culture

englishExplanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is associated with high mortal- ity rates and should be a consideration in any patient with ascites who presents with fever, chills, malaise, abdominal pain, confusion, hypotension, or general clinical decline. The current treatment of choice for SBP is a third- generation cephalosporin (eg, cefotaxime 2 g every 8 hours). The physical ex- amination findings in patients with SBP are often vague. The definitive diagnosis is made by performing diagnostic paracentesis with collection of ascitic fluid for to- tal leukocyte count, PMN count, lymphocyte count, and fluid culture. Positive fluid culture confirms the diagnosis, but antibiotics should be started before re- sults return. The diagnosis is not always clear, as none of these characteristic fea- tures are consistently present in all patients and some patients are asymptomatic. The definition of SBP includes a PMN count greater than 250 cells/mm; it can be calculated by multiplying the fluid cell count by the percentage of PMNs re- ported. A total leukocyte count greater than 500 to 1,000 cells/mm3 strongly correlates with positive fluid cultures. Symptomatic patients with a PMN count less than 250 cells/mm3 should still be admitted for treatment with antibiotics, with the regimen determined based on cul- ture results. Incorrect Answer Explanations Combination antibiotic therapy with ampicillin and an aminoglycoside is an alter- native to treatment with a third-generation cephalosporin. However, ampicillin has an increased side effect profile with increased risk of nephrotoxic- ity, so it is not the best course of treatment. Probiotic therapies have not been shown to increase antibiotic effects or reduce mortality rates, and they have no role in the treatment of SBP. Fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis for high-risk pa- tients (ie, those who have had SBP before) might prevent future episodes and asso- ciated hepatorenal syndrome. However, these are not primary therapies and lead to drug-resistant peritonitis. Antibiotics should be given based on clinical suspicion and started be- fore culture or Gram stain results are available. Gram stain is not very sen- sitive for visualizing bacteria in early SBP, and culture results can be falsely nega- tive; they do not alter management decisions in the inpatient setting. 3

question: A 27-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, a fever of 2 days' duration, and cloudy dialysate from a peritoneal dialysis treatment. On examination, she appears well but has diffuse abdominal tenderness to palpation with mild re- bound tenderness. Vital signs are normal other than a fever. There are no skin changes. After samples are collected and sent, what is the next step in management?

options.text: Place a Hickman catheter and arrange for emergent hemodialysis
Request a surgery consultation for laparotomy to remove her Tenckhoff catheter
Start intraperitoneal administration of a third-generation cephalosporin or vancomycin
Start intravenous administration of a third-generation cephalosporin or vancomycin

correctAnswer: Start intravenous administration of a third-generation cephalosporin or vancomycin
englishExplanation: The most common complication of peritoneal dialysis is peritonitis. Patients typically present with abdominal pain, fever, and cloudy dialysis fluid that has more than 100 WBCs/mm3 with at least 50% neutrophils. The bacteria most commonly isolated in peritoneal dialysis–related peritonitis are Staphylococcus epidermidis, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus sp., and gram- negative bacteria. In the emergency department, peritoneal dialysis–related peri- tonitis is treated with an intravenous loading dose of a third-generation cephalosporin, such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime. Admission for inpatient care is warranted if the peritonitis is severe, sepsis is suspected, or psychosocial considerations interfere with the patient's self-administration of antibiotics. Incorrect Answer Explanations Emergent hemodialysis is not indicated for the treatment of this patient's condition. If the peritoneal dialysis catheter is patent and functional, use of this dialysis method can continue. However, it may be necessary to change the dialysate formulation or the length of time for infusion. Fortunately, for patients on peritoneal dialysis, peritonitis is rarely cause for removing a Tenckhoff catheter. However, extensive or recurrent exit-site infec- tions can contribute to peritonitis and can be an indication for removal. Intravenous administration of antibiotics is preferred to intraperi- toneal administration for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. In patients with mild, uncomplicated disease and close follow-up, oral fluoroquinolones may be considered.

question: In a cirrhotic patient with ascites, what indicates a diagnosis of spontaneous bac- terial peritonitis?
englishExplanation: A polymorphonuclear leukocyte (PMN) count of 250 cells/mm or higher, along with a positive bacterial culture, is diagnostic of sponta- neous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) and requires prompt initiation of antibiotic therapy to prevent progression to sepsis. Most of these infections are due to single organisms. Escherichia coli is cultured in most cases, but Klebsiella pneumo- niae and Streptococcus pneumoniae are also common. Choices for the treatment 3 of SBP include cefotaxime (or another third-generation cephalosporin). An intravenous fluoroquinolone may also be considered; however, if the patient has received quinolone treatment preventively, it is likely to be ineffective. For a patient with a very mild case, an oral fluoroquinolone may be considered. However, the pa- tient must have good outpatient follow-up, and consideration should be made to co- ordinate with the patient's physician. Patients with SBP can present with a wide range of symptoms, including abdominal discomfort or pain, chills and fever, encephalopathy, and new or worsening renal failure. A physi- cal examination can reveal stigmata of hepatic failure, hypotension, and abdominal tenderness. It is important to note that patients with fever, abdominal tenderness, and a high suspicion for SBP should receive empiric antibiotic therapy immediately following a paracentesis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute renal failure in patients with cirrhosis is known as hepatorenal syndrome and is indicative of high morbidity. It is often seen in patients with SBP; however, its presence does not indicate the diagnosis of SBP. The reason behind the occurrence of hepatorenal syndrome is not well understood. An ascitic WBC count greater than 1,000 cells/mm, not 250 cells/mm, has been used to diagnose SBP in the past; however, most authors currently advocate for the use of PMNs greater than 250 cells/mm. These criteria, and the presence of bacteria on Gram stain, confirm the diagnosis of SBP and require the use of antibiotics. However, if the clinical suspicion for SBP is high, empiric antibi- otics should be started immediately after the collection of ascitic fluid, rather than waiting for fluid analysis. An elevated ammonia level indicates the possibility of hepatic en- cephalopathy but not the presence of SBP. In hepatic encephalopathy, there is an excess of nitrogenous waste that the diseased liver can no longer metabolize. Blood ammonia levels are one way to determine if hepatic encephalopathy is present. Hepatic encephalopathy patients can present with a myriad of symptoms, from lethargy to confusion.

question: A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with fever and abdominal pain. On ex- amination, his abdomen is distended and extremely tender. Which feature of the ascitic fluid confirms the suspected diagnosis in the emergency department?
englishExplanation: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is defined as an infection of as- citic fluid without other identifiable causes of intra-abdominal infec- tion. Paracentesis is the diagnostic procedure of choice, and a PMN count of greater than 250/mm plus positive fluid cultures confirms the diagnosis. SBP's incidence ranges from 7% to 30% of patients with ascites. Bacterial transloca- tion from the bowel is the favored pathogenesis of SBP. In contrast, bacterascites is the colonization of ascitic fluid with bacteria. Fluid cultures will be positive, but the PMN count will be less than 250/mm. Patients may present with symptoms similar to SBP, but repeat paracentesis and cultures are suggested prior to initiation of treatment. Incorrect Answer Explanations A glucose less than 50 mg/dL within ascitic fluid may be associated with SBP or secondary peritonitis, although it is not diagnostic. Secondary peritonitis usually requires surgical treatment and has a mortality rate approaching 100% if treated with antibiotics alone. A high PMN count is often present in sec- ondary peritonitis as well, but cultures will show two or more microorganisms. Gram stain is generally insensitive for detecting SBP and often has a high false-positive rate. Gram stain may be useful in differentiating SBP from secondary peritonitis because multiple bacterial types may be quickly identified in the latter on Gram stain, leading to prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention. A total WBC greater than 500/mm of the ascitic fluid was previously di- agnostic of SBP, but PMN count is now used for diagnosis in the acute setting, followed by cultures. In addition to cultures, ascitic fluid should be sent for evaluation of cell count, albumin, protein, glucose, LDH, amylase, bilirubin, and Gram staining.

question: Which initial antibiotic should be given to a patient with suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
englishExplanation: In patients with suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), ini- tiation of broad-spectrum antibiotics is warranted immediately after collection of peritoneal fluid for laboratory analysis and cultures; antibi- otic therapy should be narrowed once culture results and sensitivities are available. Cefotaxime 2 g every 8 hours is a preferred initial antibiotic choice due to relatively high drug levels in blood and ascitic fluid throughout most of the dosing interval. Fluoroquinolones and other third-generation cephalosporins are also rea- sonable alternatives. In patients who have been on prophylactic antibiotics, the drug class should be changed if SBP is suspected due to the possibility of antibiotic resistance. SBP is believed to be caused by translocation of intestinal bacteria into the peri- toneum. Most cases of SBP are due to Escherichia coli or Klebsiella. However, streptococcal and staphylococcal infections have also been identified, although less commonly. Incorrect Answer Explanations Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that has limited gram-negative coverage. Since most SBP infections are caused by E. coli and Klebsiella, azithromycin would be an inappropriate choice. Cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin with limited gram-negative coverage. Third-generation cephalosporins, such as cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, are recommended due to broader coverage. Vancomycin does not have activity against E. coli. It is not suggested as an initial therapy but can be added if no response to treatment is seen at 48 hours or if MRSA is suspected.

question: Bacterial peritonitis is a dangerous complication that affects patients with as- cites. Which patient population is considered high risk for this condition?
englishExplanation: Peritonitis, both spontaneous and secondary, are common complica- tions in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis. Secondary peritonitis is of- ten caused by urinary tract, lung, or GI disorders. In peritoneal dialysis patients, peritonitis should be suspected when there is abdominal pain or cloudy peritoneal effluent. The dialysate should be collected for analysis, and treatment should be initiated. Diagnosis is presumed if the WBC count exceeds 100 cells/mm, and it is confirmed with cultures. In contrast to usual therapy with in- travenous antibiotics, patients on peritoneal dialysis should receive intraperi- toneal antibiotic administration with vancomycin or cefazolin plus ce- fepime, ceftazidime, or aztreonam. 3 Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a risk for any patient with as- cites. There is an increased risk associated with patients with lower ascitic fluid proteins levels, usually <1 g/dL. Those with serum bilirubin levels >3.2 mg/dL, platelets <98,000/mm, or prior SBP are also at an increased risk. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients who use diuretics have a decreased risk of developing peritoni- tis. Diuretics help decrease the volume of ascites and, more importantly, increase the concentration of the fluid. This increases opsonic activity, which is protective against infection. Patients on hemodialysis may have ascites but are not at as high of a risk for bacte- rial peritonitis as those on peritoneal dialysis are. However, hemodialysis pa- tients are at an increased risk for bacteremia. Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use is discouraged in patients with ascites that is sec- ondary to cirrhosis due to alteration of gut flora and gastric acid secretion, which may increase the risk of bacterial peritonitis. Concomitant use of beta blockers is associated with worse outcomes in patients with SBP; thus, the use of beta blockers is permanently discontinued after an episode of peritonitis.

question: A 56-year-old cirrhotic man presents with ascites and prior spontaneous bacte- rial peritonitis. Due to his history, what is the best choice of prophylactic antibiotic?
englishExplanation: In patients who are identified as high risk for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), prompt initiation of prophylactic antibiotic therapy is recommended if no contraindications exist. Prophylaxis can reduce incidence of SBP by up to 80% in the correct patient population. Treatment options include ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or double strength trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily. Patients that are considered high risk include those who are on peritoneal dialysis or who have prior SBP, variceal or GI hemorrhage, liver failure, serum sodium level <130 mmol/L, ascitic fluid with protein <1.5 g/dL, or renal insufficiency with a creatinine >1.2 mg/dL or a BUN level >25 mg/dL. Incorrect Answer Explanations Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that has limited gram-negative coverage. Since most SBP infections are caused by Escherichia coli and Klebsiella, this would be an inappropriate choice. Azithromycin is commonly used to treat atypical pneumonia and head and neck infections. Cephalexin is a first-generation cephalosporin; third-generation cephalosporins such as cefotaxime or ceftriaxone are recommended for the treatment of acute SBP due to broader coverage. Cephalosporins are not routinely recommended as prophylaxis.
