Parental guidance, dietary changes, and the use of assistive medical therapy, such as stool softeners, can relieve the cycle of chronic constipation. Physical examination of the anal area is necessary to confirm an anal fissure diagnosis, even when the patient provides the typical history of pain with defecation and seeing bright red blood on toilet paper. Separating the patient's buttocks to examine the area often makes the fissure visi- ble; having the patient bear down can also improve visualization. Most patients have only one fissure in the posterior midline; if patients have multiple fissures or fissures in positions other than the midline, causes other than trauma from passing hard stools should be considered. Treatment for anal fissures is usually supportive. Sitz baths, stool softeners, and a high-fiber diet can soothe and prevent further trauma to the area. Topical anesthetics, such as lidocaine gel, can temporarily reduce pain in the area, but they will not directly help healing. Topical nitroglycerin or nifedipine can reduce anal spasms, providing symptomatic relief and promot- ing healing of the torn mucosa. Unfortunately, a recent Cochrane database review concluded that medical therapy provides a cure rate for acute fissures that is only marginally better than a placebo. Surgical treatment options include lateral sphinc- terotomy and anal dilation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dark, tarry, or melenic stools are seen primarily in patients with upper GI bleeding. Blood from sources in the stomach or the small intestine turns dark due to the oxidation of Hgb by intestinal enzymes. By contrast, patients with anal fissures commonly report small amounts of bright red blood on tis- sue paper or in the toilet. Anal fissures can be seen after frequent episodes of diarrhea, but they are most commonly caused by the trauma of passing hard stool. Some pa- tients report a history of neither diarrhea nor trauma from passing hard stool. Inflammatory bowel disease should be considered for patients with recurrent bloody diarrhea and persistent pain. Approximately 90% of anal fissures occur in the posterior midline. The etiology is unclear but may be related to reduced posterior anodermal blood flow compared to the lateral and anterior aspects of the anal canal. Anterior anal fissures are more common in women than in men. Lateral anal fissures or multiple fissures should prompt consideration of a secondary etiology, such as inflammatory bowel disease, granulomatous disease, malignancy, or an STI.

question: A patient presents with prolapsed internal hemorrhoids that cannot be reduced. What is the appropriate management?
englishExplanation: Internal hemorrhoids can be classified based on severity and clinical features (grade I to grade IV, increasing in severity). Grade IV hemorrhoids are nonre- ducible, can become edematous and ischemic, and may require surgical con- sultation for an emergent or urgent hemorrhoidectomy. Grade I hemorrhoids are nonprolapsed. Grade II hemorrhoids are prolapsed (usu- ally prolapsing after a bowel movement) but spontaneously reduce without any in- tervention. Grade III hemorrhoids are prolapsed but can be manually reduced. Hemorrhoids are vascular cushions within the anal canal that can become en- gorged. Since they are supplied by arterial blood, bleeding is typically described as bright red in color. Hemorrhoids that are above the dentate line are con- sidered internal hemorrhoids and are painless. External hemorrhoids occur below the dentate line and can be quite painful, particularly when thrombosed. Internal hemorrhoids may not be apparent on physical examination if they are non- prolapsed. Internal hemorrhoids cannot be readily palpated on digital examination and require anoscopy for visualization. By contrast, external hemorrhoids are easily visible on inspection of the anus. Management of most nonprolapsed internal hem- orrhoids and nonthrombosed external hemorrhoids includes the WASH regime: warm water, analgesics, stool softeners, and a high-fiber diet. Grade III hemor- rhoids require manual reduction in addition to the WASH regimen. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bedside incision and drainage may be indicated for a thrombosed external hemorrhoid. However, a prolapsed, nonreducible (grade IV) internal hemorrhoid requires an emergent surgical evaluation. Sitz baths and stool softeners, along with a high-fiber diet and analgesics, are indi- cated for nonprolapsed internal hemorrhoids and nonthrombosed external hemor- rhoids. This regimen is insufficient for a (grade IV) prolapsed, nonreducible internal hemorrhoid. Topical steroid therapy is often used for external hemorrhoids. However, a (grade IV) prolapsed, nonreducible internal hemorrhoid requires an emergent surgical consultation because of the risk of ischemia.

question: A 68-year-old woman presents with mild abdominal discomfort. She also reports intermittent fecal incontinence and a feeling that she has a "mass" over the past several weeks. Her medical history is significant for chronic constipation, hyper- tension, and osteoporosis. Findings from the physical examination with the pa- tient lying on her stomach are shown. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Lawrence Stacks, MD.
englishExplanation: This patient has rectal procidentia or prolapse. Clues from the history include fecal incontinence, constipation, abdominal discomfort, and a prolapsed anal mass. The diagnosis of rectal prolapse is clinical; visual clues include concentric rings of the rectum protruding through the anus. Concomitant anal sphinc- ter or pelvic floor disorders are not uncommon. Risk factors for rectal prolapse in- clude female sex, multiparity, chronic straining, dementia, stroke, and pelvic floor dysfunction. Medical management includes adequate dietary fiber and fluid intake. The defini- tive management of rectal prolapse is surgery, and incarceration of the prolapsed tissue is a surgical emergency. Other indications for surgery include fecal inconti- nence and presence of a mass, as seen in this patient. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although the patient's description of feeling a mass is concerning, physical exami- nation findings show healthy prolapsed tissue. The diagnosis of rectal prolapse is clinical; visual clues include concentric rings of the rectum protrud- ing through the anus. A prolapsed internal hemorrhoid is generally smaller than the rectum and does not have concentric rings. The diagnosis of rectal prolapse is clinical; visual clues include concentric rings of the rectum protruding through the anus. A prolapsed uterus is generally seen protruding through the vaginal opening. The diagnosis of rectal prolapse is clinical; visual clues include concentric rings of the rectum protruding through the anus.

question: Which condition may lead to splenomegaly?
englishExplanation: Patients with cirrhosis of the liver commonly have associated splenomegaly. Patients with parenchymal liver disease, including those with cir- rhosis or liver fibrosis, develop splenic engorgement and subsequent splenic en- largement. Although the exact mechanism for this is unknown, it is thought to be related to congestion of the red pulp resulting from portal hypertension. Under normal conditions, the spleen is undetectable on physical examination due to its location behind the stomach and under the rib cage in the left upper quadrant. If palpable, it is usually soft and mobile. The spleen may be palpable in some children and adolescents or in thin adults. In rare cases, the spleen can become enlarged such that it reaches the pelvis or right lower quadrant. For this reason, appropriate examination technique when assessing for splenomegaly requires initially palpating the right lower quadrant, traversing the periumbilical region, and terminating in the left upper quadrant. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute chest syndrome is an acute complication of sickle cell disease and leads to significant morbidity and mortality. It is not associated with splenomegaly. However, patients with sickle cell disease are also at risk for splenic sequestration crises, which can manifest with splenic enlargement. Chagas disease is caused by the parasitic infection Trypanosoma cruzi. It does not lead to splenomegaly. However, it is Latin America's most common cause of nonischemic cardiomyopathy. Nonintestinal Entamoeba histolytica infection can lead to amebic liver abscess, but it is not associated with splenomegaly. Although E. histolytica infection is usually asymptomatic, it can also lead to amebic dysentery; brain, lung, and heart involvement is rare.

question: An 18-year-old patient presents with a several day history of fever and fatigue. They also have cervical lymphadenopathy, and tenderness is noted in the left up- per quadrant on abdominal examination. What is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
englishExplanation: The classic presentation of infectious mononucleosis (IM) is fever, lym- phadenopathy, pharyngitis, and fatigue, with a peak incidence in ages 15 to 24. Splenomegaly is seen in 50% to 60% of patients and generally re- solves after about 3 weeks. Malaise and headache are also often reported, and atypical lymphocytosis may be noted on laboratory evaluations. There are many clinical variants of IM, and some patients experience more limited symptomatology. Spontaneous or traumatic splenic rupture is a rare complication of IM. Urticarial, petechial, or maculopapular rash can occur, and various neurologic syn- dromes (including Guillain-Barré syndrome, cranial nerve palsies, meningoen- cephalitis, and transverse myelitis) are occasionally seen. The diagnosis of IM is made by the presence of heterophile antibodies in the ap- propriate clinical context using a mononucleosis spot test. Although heterophile an- tibodies are nonspecific, they are considered diagnostic in a patient with symptoms of IM. There is a 25% false-negative rate in the first week of infection. A patient with a negative mononucleosis spot test early in suspected IM should have repeat testing at a later date. Treatment is supportive with acetaminophen, NSAIDs, and hydration, and patients should be instructed to avoid contact sports or other activities that would put them at risk of splenic rupture. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hematologic malignancies are a cause of splenomegaly, but symptoms would not be expected to develop abruptly over days. IM is a more likely explanation for abrupt-onset viral symptoms associated with fevers. Portal hypertension can result from various processes and can contribute to the de- velopment of splenomegaly. However, causes of portal hypertension are more likely to be chronic in nature (eg, chronic alcohol use or nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) rather than acute, as in this case. The typical presentation of sarcoidosis includes cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath, which can be accompanied by fevers, weight loss, fatigue, and malaise. Symptom onset in sarcoidosis is gradual, and symptoms generally persist for months to a year before diagnosis, unlike IM (which is generally diagnosed within 1- 2 weeks of symptom onset).

question: A 19-year-old man presents with abdominal pain. He was recently diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. His Hgb is 9.6 g/dL. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
englishExplanation: Splenomegaly is commonly seen in the setting of infectious mononucle- osis (IM), and splenic rupture is a complication that is thought to occur in 1 to 2 patients per 1,000 cases of IM. Approximately 50% of splenic rup- tures occur spontaneously, and they are more commonly seen in young men. A patient with splenic rupture would likely present with severe abdominal pain and falling Hgb. Splenic infarction is another rare complication of IM and would also present with abdominal pain. Management of splenic rupture associated with IM is similar to other causes of splenic injury. Conservative and supportive measures and splenic preserva- tion may be preferred when possible, but splenectomy may be required in some cases. Mortality from splenic rupture in IM is exceedingly rare. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute pancreatitis is a potential complication of IM, but it is much less common than splenic rupture. A recent review of the literature from 1966 to 2016 found 14 cases of pancreatitis and 37 cases of acalculous cholecystitis associ- ated with IM. Bleeding from a venous malformation could occur at any time and would not neces- sarily be associated with acute IM. Splenic rupture, however, is a known compli- cation of IM. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage would be an unexpected complication of IM. Subcapsular hemorrhage or capsular rupture and intraperitoneal hemorrhage would be more likely in the setting of IM and splenic rupture.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with several weeks of fatigue, malaise, early satiety, and weight loss. He has tender splenomegaly on examination, and laboratory studies show a WBC count of 80,000 cells/mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient presents with systemic symptoms, tender splenomegaly, and marked leukocytosis. Of the available options, leukemia, specifically chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), is the most likely answer. CML accounts for 15% to 20% of leukemias affecting adults, with a median age at onset of 50 and a slight male predominance. Exposure to ionizing radiation is a known risk factor. CML demonstrates a fluctuating clinical course. Many patients are asympto- matic at the time of diagnosis, with an abnormality incidentally discovered on rou- tine blood testing. Frequent findings at the time of diagnosis include anemia, splenomegaly, thrombocytosis, and a WBC count of 100,000 cells/mm. In general, a leukocytosis greater than 35,000 to 50,000 cells/mm should prompt consideration of hematologic malignancy. Incorrect Answer Explanations DRESS syndrome (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symp- toms) is characterized by a prodromal period (fever and malaise) follow- ing introduction of the causative medication and then a symmetric rash affecting the torso and extremities. Organ dysfunction and splenomegaly can be seen in the setting of DRESS syndrome, but this patient has no reported medication expo- sure or rash. Thus, DRESS syndrome is not the most likely diagnosis. Acute HIV infection generally begins to manifest 2 to 4 weeks after exposure and is characterized by fever, lymphadenopathy, sore throat, rash, myalgias, headache, splenomegaly, diarrhea, and weight loss. Acute HIV infection would not be expected to cause severe leukocytosis on initial laboratory testing. Polycythemia rubra vera is generally found incidentally in routine laboratory test- ing. However, early symptoms can include headache, dizziness, splenomegaly, early satiety, pruritus, and visual disturbance. Laboratory tests generally show elevated Hgb with normal or elevated leukocytes and platelets. By contrast, this patient presents with isolated severe leukocytosis, which is more consistent with a hematologic malignancy.

question: An 18-month-old boy with a history of sickle cell anemia presents with several days of weakness, pallor, and abdominal distension. He is tachycardic, and his abdomen is tender. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Splenic sequestration crisis is a feared complication in a young child with a history of sickle cell anemia (SCA). Crises are thought to result from sickled cells producing vascular congestion and obstruction within the spleen, resulting in sequestration and splenomegaly. This can result in a dangerous drop in circulating blood volume (Hgb), generally of at least 2 g/dL. Minor episodes of acute splenic sequestration can also occur in children with SCA and may resolve on their own. Together, episodes of splenic sequestration and other minor vaso-occlusive episodes contribute to fibrosis and auto-infarction of the spleen over time. Splenic sequestration crises may be the earliest manifestation of SCA in some children, generally occurring between 6 months and 5 years of age, at a median age of 1.4 years. Recurrence rates are higher in patients who have their first splenic sequestration crisis in the first year of life. Patients typically present with abrupt on- set of pallor, weakness, and tachycardia. They will demonstrate tender mas- sive splenomegaly on examination. Patients with SCA typically have spleens en- larged 1 to 2 cm below the costal margin, but during crises, much greater splenomegaly than is typical for them can manifest. Historically, mortality from splenic sequestration crisis was thought to be as high as 12% to 44%; however, more recent evidence suggests mortality is much lower, per- haps less than 1%. Acutely, patients are at risk for severe anemia and cardiovascular collapse. Treatment consists of intravenous fluids and blood transfusions to a goal Hct of about 35%. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute chest syndrome is a life-threatening complication of SCA that can present with fever, cough, tachypnea, chest pain, and wheezing. Patients generally show an abnormal infiltrate on chest x-ray. Acute chest syndrome would not be expected to cause pallor or tender splenomegaly. Aplastic crisis can present with abrupt-onset pallor and fatigue with a low reticulocyte count noted on laboratory evaluation. Unlike splenic sequestra- tion crisis, aplastic crisis would not be expected to present with abdominal fullness or tenderness. Mesenteric ischemia is an uncommon cause of severe abdominal pain in patients with SCA and would not be expected to cause pallor or tender splenomegaly. Splenic sequestration crisis is a more likely explanation for this patient's symptoms.

question: What clinical sign is more consistent with an extraluminal source of bleeding than an intraluminal source of bleeding in a patient who recently underwent bariatric surgery?
englishExplanation: Extraluminal bleeding may occur in bariatric surgery patients with ia- trogenic injury to the spleen, liver, or mesentery, or from bleeding from a trochar site. Surgical injury to these organs can lead to hemoperitoneum and peritonitis. Early intraluminal bleeding may occur at any of the anastomotic sites or staple lines, while late intraluminal bleeding may occur from gastric, duodenal, or stomal ulcers or bleeding from the gastric pouch. Initial resuscitation of either of these subsets of patients should include manage- ment of the ABCs, intravenous fluid administration, blood product transfusion, and correction of possible coagulopathies. Extraluminal bleeding is generally treated with surgery. Intraluminal bleeding may be controlled with endoscopic therapy, if amenable, or surgery if not amenable or hemodynamically unstable. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bariatric patients with blood loss from an extraluminal or intraluminal source can present with hypoperfusion and hypotension. The presence of peritonitis, on the other hand, is indicative of extraluminal bleeding rather than in- traluminal bleeding. Patients with an intraluminal source of postoperative bleeding, such as upper GI bleeds, are more likely to have melena on presentation. Up to 4% of bariatric surgeries are complicated by upper GI bleeds within the first 2 weeks. Tachycardia may be present in patients with either extraluminal or in- traluminal sources of bleeding and therefore does not help distinguish the source of postoperative bleeding. Tachycardia may also be a sign of other complications, such as anastomotic leaks, pain, or pulmonary emboli. The presence of peritonitis, on the other hand, is indicative of extraluminal bleeding rather than intraluminal bleeding.

question: A patient presents with nausea, vomiting, flushing, palpitations, and colicky ab- dominal pain that occur shortly after eating. They underwent a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 2 months ago. The emergency department workup is reassuring. Upon discharge, what dietary modifications should be advised?

options.text: Eat smaller and more frequent meals

correctAnswer: Eat smaller and more frequent meals
englishExplanation: This patient's symptoms are consistent with early dumping syndrome, which results from the rapid emptying of gastric contents into the small bowel and resultant fluid shifts from the hyperosmolar contents. In the emergency department, early dump- ing syndrome is treated with supportive care and may require intravenous fluids, antiemetics, and electrolyte replacement; discharge counseling should focus on dietary modification, including smaller, more frequent meals. Symptoms of early dumping syndrome usually begin within 15 minutes of eating and can include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, colicky abdominal pain, and hypotension. The sympathetic nervous system also may be activated and cause tachycardia, palpitations, dizziness, and flushing. Late dumping syn- drome is a rarer complication of bariatric surgery that occurs 1 to 3 hours after meals. Rapid gastric emptying is thought to cause transient hyperglycemia, leading to increased insulin secretion. Once the intestinal contents are absorbed, this ele- vated insulin secretion causes hypoglycemia and sequelae. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bariatric patients with early dumping syndrome are advised to separate liquids and solids while eating to avoid exacerbating their symptoms. Patients with early dumping syndrome should avoid drinking during meals and up to 2 hours after meals. They should also be counseled to eat smaller, more frequent meals. Bariatric patients with early dumping syndrome should increase their complex carbohydrate intake and decrease their simple sugars and lac- tose. They should also be advised to increase their protein intake. They should be counseled to eat smaller, more frequent meals. Bariatric patients with early dumping syndrome should be advised to increase their dietary fiber intake, as it may delay the absorption of carbohy- drates in the small intestine. They should also be instructed to eat smaller and more frequent meals with more proteins and fewer simple sugars.

question: Three months after receiving Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery, a patient presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confusion as well as a 3-week history of repeated vomiting. Which pharmacotherapy should be administered?
englishExplanation: This patient's symptoms are concerning for Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency, which is a rare but well-known complication of bariatric surgery. Without adequate supply of thiamine from diet or supple- mentation, the body can deplete its thiamine supply in about 20 days. Thiamine de- ficiency is more common in malabsorptive or combination procedures, such as Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, than in purely restrictive procedures, such as laparo- scopic adjustable gastric band. The classic triad of Wernicke encephalopathy symptoms includes eye movement abnormalities, ataxia, and mental status changes, although this is present less than 50% of the time. Additional symptoms may include neuropathies, psychosis, and other neuropsychi- atric manifestations. Treatment of Wernicke encephalopathy should focus on the emergent administration of parenteral thiamine. Wernicke encephalopathy may also be seen in persons with chronic alcohol use dis- order. Symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy may mimic those of hypoglycemia. In persons at risk for Wernicke encephalopathy, thiamine should be adminis- tered prior to administration of glucose in euglycemic patients to avoid pre- cipitation or worsening of Wernicke encephalopathy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although hypocalcemia does occur in bariatric surgery patients, the symptoms are more likely to include tetany, hypotension, ECG changes, seizures, or psychiatric complaints. Ophthalmoplegia and ataxia are not com- monly associated with hypocalcemia and are more suggestive of Wernicke en- cephalopathy, which requires parenteral thiamine administration. Hypoglycemia can occur in bariatric surgery patients, especially if they have poor oral intake. Symptoms of hypoglycemia are nonspecific, including au- tonomic symptoms (eg, palpitations and tremor) and neuroglycopenic symptoms (eg, dizziness, weakness, and mental status changes). Ophthalmoplegia and ataxia are not commonly seen. Additionally, the administration of glucose without thi- amine may worsen the symptoms and prognosis of patients with thiamine deficiency. Bariatric surgery patients can have vitamin D deficiencies. Most patients with mild to moderate vitamin D deficiency are asymptomatic, while those with severe deficiency may have symptoms that are similar to hypocal- cemia. However, this patient's presentation is much more concerning for Wernicke encephalopathy and requires thiamine administration.

question: What is more consistent with gastric band slippage than gastric band overinfla- tion following laparoscopic adjustable gastric banding?

options.text: Failure to improve with band deflation

correctAnswer: Failure to improve with band deflation
englishExplanation: Gastric band slippage is one of the known complications of gastric band- ing that results from downward slippage of the band with resultant gastric pouch enlargement. Since the symptoms are caused by physical slippage of the band and not overinflation, deflating the band usually does not lead to clinical improvement. Symptoms of gastric band slippage include epigastric pain, re- flux, dysphagia, food intolerance, and vomiting. Gastric band slippage can be diagnosed with upper GI imaging, and emergency department management in- cludes intravenous fluid resuscitation and electrolyte replacement as needed. Surgical consultation and intervention are recommended to avoid complications, such as gastric ischemia, necrosis, and perforation. Gastric banding is the third most common bariatric surgery in the United States and involves the placement of an adjustable silicon band at the gas- tric cardia near the gastroesophageal junction. Gastric banding is a purely restric- tive modality that limits the amount of food that is consumed. Although gastric banding has the lowest mortality rate among bariatric procedures, it is associated with several complications, and almost 50% of patients require surgical revision or removal of the band. Gastric pouch dilation occurs in as many as 15% of patients undergoing la- paroscopic gastric banding procedures. Pouch dilation may result from an overly tight or improperly placed band or from excessive food intake. Symptoms of gastric pouch dilation overlap with gastric band slippage but should show improve- ment with deflation of the gastric band, a low-calorie diet, and small portion sizes for 4 to 6 weeks. The band can then be gradually reinflated. If the pouch does not return to its original size, surgical replacement or removal is indicated. Incorrect Answer Explanations Persistent epigastric pain may be experienced by patients with gastric band slippage or gastric pouch dilation. Clinical improvement with band de- flation is more consistent with gastric pouch dilation. Progressive food intolerance and dysphagia may be seen in both gastric pouch dilation and gastric band slippage. However, these symptoms should improve with band deflation if gastric pouch dilation is the underlying etiology. Patients with both gastric band slippage and gastric pouch dilation often present with recurrent reflux and vomiting. As the pouch dilation improves or resolves with band deflation, these symptoms should also improve.

question: Two weeks after a sleeve gastrectomy surgery, a patient presents with redness and warmth overlying the surgical site. What is the most likely organism to be identified from a culture of the surgical wound?
englishExplanation: Surgical site infections occur in roughly 15% of bariatric surgery pa- tients, with a higher incidence in open procedures versus laparoscopic pro- cedures. Although surgical site infections may be polymicrobial, the most com- monly identified organisms are in the staphylococcal family. Surgical site infections most commonly occur within the first 2 to 3 weeks after surgery. The infection may remain superficial and only involve the skin, but it can also in- volve deeper subcutaneous or soft tissues or enter the abdominal cavity itself. Therapeutic interventions should focus on early recognition, antibiotics, and source control. Source control may involve opening the wound to allow drainage, abscess drainage, or further surgical intervention. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although Bacteroides fragilis is a known intra-abdominal pathogen that colonizes almost all human colons, it is much less likely to cause a surgical site infection. The most commonly identified organisms in surgical site infections are in the staphylococcal family. Escherichia coli is a common intra-abdominal pathogen that is known to cause surgical site infections, but E. coli is less common than staphy- lococcal species. Enterococcal species are also known to cause surgical site infections. Streptococcus pyogenes is a common cause of general cellulitis but is not one of the most common bacterial causes of surgical site infections. These infections are more commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase- negative staphylococcal species, Enterococcus species, and E. coli.

question: In the absence of a replacement gastrostomy tube of the same size, what should be placed through the longstanding stoma of a recently dislodged gastrostomy tube to maintain patency?

options.text: Foley catheter of the same French size as the gastrostomy tube
Foley catheter one French unit larger than the gastrostomy tube
Physician should place one finger in the stoma until a gastrostomy tube can be procured
Wire from a central venous catheter kit

correctAnswer: Foley catheter of the same French size as the gastrostomy tube
englishExplanation: In the event that a longstanding gastrostomy tube falls out, it is imperative to maintain patency of the gastrostomy tract so that the tract does not begin to narrow or close. Although an identical gastrostomy tube is a better long-term solution, the correct size may not be readily available. Foley catheters are usually readily available in multiple sizes. A Foley catheter of the same diame- ter may be placed quickly and safely in a mature tract to maintain patency and even provide nutrition when necessary. Gastrostomy tube complications are quite common; they include infection, bleed- ing, fistula formation, necrotizing fasciitis, and inadvertent tube re- moval. Accidental displacement is a very common complication, and if the tract is mature (approximately 4 weeks out from surgery) then replacement with a simi- lar gastrostomy tube or a Foley catheter of the same size is appropriate. If the tract is immature (<4 weeks from surgery), then a replacement tube should not be placed blindly in the emergency department because it may lead to false passage. When appropriate, the process to replace a gastrostomy tube is as follows: lubricate the replacement, place the tip with the ballon into the stoma, apply slow gentle pressure until the tube passes through the stoma, inflate the balloon, pull back gen- tly until there is traction against the skin, and then secure the tube, often using the attached bumper. If a bumper is unavailable, the tube can be taped or bandaged in place. Incorrect Answer Explanations There is no need to upsize the tract with a larger Foley catheter. A larger Foley catheter may be difficult to place, further traumatizing the tract. Instead either a similar gastrostomy tube or a Foley catheter of the same French size can be placed in the mature tract to keep it open. Depending on the size of the patient, the diameter of the gastrostomy tract, and the size of the physician's hands, it may be impossible to pass a finger through the tract. Attempting to force a finger into the tract may further traumatize it and lead to false passage. Moreover, it is unnecessary for a physician to stay in the room and maintain patency because they may need to place the tube itself. The wire from a central venous catheter would not maintain the diame- ter of the tract because the wire is too narrow. Additionally, the sharpness of the wire may lead to further damage or bleeding.

question: A 3-year-old presents with a displaced gastrojejunostomy (GJ) tube. The child's parent has the GJ tube with them; it appears intact. The parent has already placed a Foley catheter of the same diameter in the ostomy. What is the correct next step?

options.text: Consult the service that placed the tube for replacement
Replace Foley catheter with a gastrostomy tube of the same diameter
Replace with a clean GJ tube at bedside
Test the balloon(s) and replace the original GJ tube into the ostomy at bedside

correctAnswer: Consult the service that placed the tube for replacement
englishExplanation: A gastrojejunostomy (GJ) tube cannot be replaced without fluoroscopic or endoscopic guidance. There are multiple types of feeding tubes with which children may present. Because management differs by tube type, always ask the child's parents or try to ascertain which type of tube the patient has. A gastros- tomy tube can be replaced at the bedside if the tract is mature (approximately 4 weeks old), but GJ tubes cannot be replaced at the bedside even when ma- ture. Appropriately, the parents placed a Foley catheter into the gastric tract to maintain patency, but the GJ tube needs to be passed beyond the pylorus, which cannot be done blindly. Children usually have GJ tubes instead of just gastrostomy tubes. One port is used for feeding, and the other port is used for medications or venting. Ascertain why the patient has both ports because critical medications or nutrition may be specific to either. When needed, consider converting medications to intra- venous delivery while waiting for the consulting service to replace the tube. Incorrect Answer Explanations Replacing the Foley catheter with a gastrostomy tube may ultimately be decided as a temporary measure. However, this child had a GJ tube for a spe- cific reason and needs it replaced with a new GJ tube. Thus, consulting the service that placed the GJ tube is the best next step. Procuring an identical replacement is often the best course of action for a displaced gastrostomy tube, if able. However, a GJ tube should not be replaced at the bedside in the emergency department because it is usually impossible to advance the distal end through the pylorus. This should typically be done by the service that placed the tube or by interventional radiology. A GJ tube cannot be replaced correctly without fluoroscopic or endo- scopic guidance. Thus, replacement of even an intact GJ-tube is unlikely to be suc- cessful and should not be attempted.

question: A 58-year-old man with known severe coronary artery disease presents via am- bulance after a witnessed cardiac arrest. He has been intubated by EMS, and CPR is in progress. His end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO) drops from 20 mm Hg to 9 mm Hg during the course of 10 minutes; the waveform maintains a normal mor- phology. Bedside echocardiogram shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the most likely cause of the drop in EtCO?
englishExplanation: Monitoring of end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO) during cardiopulmonary ar- rest has become the standard of care in most emergency departments. EtCO may be used as a marker of perfusion during resuscitation of a patient in cardiac arrest. Near-normal EtCO levels (20 mm Hg) suggest that good chest compres- sions are being provided and that perfusion is adequate. EtCO should ideally be maintained above 10 mm Hg. A gradual decrease in EtCO may indicate that the person giving chest compressions is becoming fatigued and CPR should be provided by a different team member or an automated device. EtCO monitoring provides a real-time assessment of ventilation and perfu- sion in the setting of cardiac arrest, and it may also provide important prognostic information. Changes in EtCO during resuscitation may indicate issues with venti- lation, such as incorrect initial placement of the endotracheal tube or subsequent displacement of the endotracheal tube. Although colorimetric CO detectors may 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 2 change colors early in esophageal intubation, an adequate waveform will not be noted. A sudden decrease in CO with a poor waveform during resuscita- tion likely indicates displacement of the endotracheal tube. A sudden in- crease in EtCO may indicate a ROSC. An EtCO <10 mm Hg at the 20-min mark of resuscitation has been associated with a poor prognosis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Since no cardiac tamponade was noted on bedside echocardiogram, car- diac tamponade is not a likely cause of the gradual decrease of EtCO in this case. Cardiac tamponade can decrease EtCO by decreasing blood flow to the lungs. Displacement of the endotracheal tube would cause a sudden decrease in EtCO with concomitant loss of waveform. A gradual decrease in EtCO may be seen with expanding pneumothorax, which can be a complication of CPR. Significant internal hemorrhage is unlikely to be the cause in this patient with a witnessed cardiac arrest. In trauma, however, ongoing hemorrhage should be considered as a potential cause of decreasing EtCO.

question: A 67-year-old woman presents with chest pain and dyspnea. Soon after arrival, she experiences a witnessed cardiac arrest. The ECG monitor shows the rhythm below. In addition to chest compressions, which resuscitative approach is the best next step? Credit: William J. Brady, MD, FACEP/copyright ACEP.

options.text: Electrical defibrillation and basic airway management
Invasive airway management and cardioactive medications
Invasive airway management and transcutaneous pacing

correctAnswer: Electrical defibrillation and basic airway management
englishExplanation: In cardiac arrest, the initial rhythm provides important information to guide man- agement. This patient's rhythm is ventricular fibrillation, which is a shockable rhythm. Electrical defibrillation is the most appropriate intervention and should be performed as early as possible after resuscitation is initiated. Chest compres- sions are, of course, a priority in early management. Studies have shown that basic airway management (eg, BVM) is appropriate while prioritizing com- pressions and defibrillation. The four cardiac arrest rhythm scenarios are: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT) Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) Asystole Two of the four — VF and pulseless VT — are considered shockable rhythms, meaning that electrical defibrillation is the most appropriate interven- tion and should be provided as early as possible after initiation of resuscitation. In VF and pulseless VT, electrical defibrillation and chest compressions are the priori- ties in early management. The nonshockable rhythms are PEA and asystole; electri- cal defibrillation is not indicated in these two rhythm scenarios. In all four cardiac arrest scenarios, appropriate chest compressions are indicated. Intravenous fluids, cardioactive medications, and airway management are additional priorities. If pos- sible, identification of the underlying or causative issue is important so that addi- tional therapy can be tailored to the situation. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cardioactive medications should become a management priority only after maximizing chest compressions and defibrillation in patients with pulseless VF or VT. Transvenous pacing is unlikely to benefit the patient, is not indicated, and is a laborious procedure that cannot be easily done while chest com- pressions are ongoing. Additional therapies such as definitive airway management with orotracheal intuba- tion are important after the patient is stabilized but must not detract from the first steps in management — chest compressions and electrical defibrillation. Transcutaneous pacing is unlikely to benefit the patient and is not indicated. The priorities should be chest compressions, basic airway management, and debrillation. Key Points High-quality chest compressions and electrical defibrillation are very important in the treatment of cardiac arrest manifesting with pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. Invasive airway management and cardioactive medications can be important inter- ventions in all four cardiac arrest rhythm presentations but should not detract from chest compressions and defibrillation for ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation.

question: What is the appropriate treatment for pseudo–pulseless electrical activity?
englishExplanation: Pseudo-pulseless electrical activity (pseudo-PEA) is a condition of se- vere shock that should be treated with pressor agents and fluid resuscita- tion. A patient may appear to be in PEA with organized electrical activity on the monitor and an impalpable pulse. However, if the patient has a blood pressure so low their pulse is impalpable, they are not truly in cardiac arrest and, thus, not in PEA. Patients in pseudo-PEA must be identified because performing chest com- pressions on them may actually be detrimental. If chest compressions are performed asynchronously with the heart's intrinsic contractions, preload and car- diac output may be reduced. The best way to identify pseudo-PEA is by ultrasound or arterial line. If there are cardiac contractions or pulsations of the femoral artery on bedside ultrasound, chest compressions should not be performed. Instead, care should focus on increas- ing blood pressure with pressor support and fluid resuscitation. Pseudo-PEA may be encountered in any shock state, but it is most likely to be apparent in distributive shock, such as sepsis or anaphylaxis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cardioversion should be used for unstable tachydysrhythmias, such as supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, and ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Intravenous epinephrine is given as bolus dos- ing during ACLS or as an infusion to increase blood pressure. Cardioversion should not be used for pseudo-PEA. Instead, pseudo-PEA should be treated with fluid re- suscitation and continuous infusion pressors. Chest compressions should not be used in pseudo-PEA. Compressions may reduce preload and cardiac output if they are asynchronous with intrinsic cardiac contractions. Pseudo-PEA should be treated with fluid resuscitation and continuous infusion pressors. Defibrillation is not a treatment for pseudo-PEA. Rather, it is reserved for ven- tricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Similarly, amio- darone is indicated for ventricular arrhythmias, not for PEA or pseudo-PEA. Instead, pseudo-PEA should be treated with fluid resuscitation and continuous in- fusion pressors.

question: A 10-kg, 2-year-old patient presents in ventricular fibrillation. A 20 J defibrilla- tion shock is given with no effect. What is the appropriate next defibrillation dose?
englishExplanation: According to PALS, the correct defibrillation dosage is 2 J/kg for the first shock, followed by 4 J/kg for the second shock. This applies to both ventric- ular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and the dosing is independent of biphasic or monophasic defibrillators. The best outcomes are seen with defibrilla- tion as soon as possible once the rhythm is identified. CPR should be resumed for 2 minutes after the shock is given. Then, the rhythm should be reassessed for the need for additional defibrillation or interventions. Incorrect Answer Explanations 10 J would be an appropriate dose for synchronized cardioversion, which is recommended at 0.5 to 1 J/kg. In this case, 10 J would be inadequate because 4 J/kg is recommended for the second defibrillator shock in the setting of pediatric ventricular fibrillation. Although 30 J is an increase from the previous dose, it is less than the recom- mended second dose of 4 J/kg. Since this patient weighs 10 kg, the second defibril- lator shock given should be 40 J. 100 J is the maximum recommended dose if this patient continues to have refractory ventricular fibrillation requiring a third or subsequent defibrillator shock. The PALS guidelines allow third or subsequent shocks to be between 4 and 10 J/kg. In the case of a patient weighing 10 kg, a dose of 100 J is higher than the recommended 4 J/kg for the second shock.

question: Which medication is recommended for managing refractory pediatric cardiac ar- rest due to ventricular fibrillation?
englishExplanation: According to PALS, amiodarone is recommended for use in refractory ven- tricular fibrillation following two unsuccessful defibrillation attempts and administration of epinephrine. The recommended initial dose of amio- darone is 5 mg/kg administered over 20-60 minutes, which can be repeated if needed up to two additional times (maximum dose is 15 mg/kg or 300 mg to- tal). Amiodarone is classified as a Vaughan-Williams class III antiarrhythmic, but in practice, it has broad antiarrhythmic properties, with effects on sodium, potassium, and calcium channels as well as beta blockade. Amiodarone is used for terminating ventricular arrhythmias in children and adults. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bupivacaine is a local anesthetic that is used frequently for nerve blocks due to its long duration of action. Bupivacaine is not routinely used as an antiar- rhythmic, and overdose can actually cause severe cardiotoxicity. It has no recom- mended role in PALS. The local anesthetic lidocaine, on the other hand, is recom- mended as an alternative agent to amiodarone. In this case, amiodarone is the most appropriate medication to treat refractory pediatric ventricular fibrillation. Flecainide is a Vaughan-Williams class Ic antiarrhythmic that is typi- cally used as a controller medication for supraventricular arrhythmias, such as supraventricular tachycardia and atrial fibrillation. Although flecainide is a potent antiarrhythmic, it is only available in oral form and, thus, has no role in the setting of cardiac arrest at any age. In this case, amiodarone is the most appropriate medication to treat refractory pediatric ventricular fibrillation. Procainamide is a Vaughan-Williams class Ia antiarrhythmic that is rec- ommended and used routinely for suppressing stable ventricular ar- rhythmias, such as ventricular tachycardia. However, procainamide does not have a recommended use in the management of pediatric cardiac arrest. In this case, amiodarone is the most appropriate medication to treat refractory pediatric ventricular fibrillation.

question: A 3-year-old child with end-stage renal disease presents in pulseless electrical ac- tivity arrest. Which intervention is most likely to successfully resuscitate the patient? Credit: Copyright ACEP.
englishExplanation: This ECG is representative of the classic “sine wave” pattern of profound hy- perkalemia; in this case, it is severe enough to result in pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest. In addition to standard measures, such as CPR, PEA arrest due to presumed or known hyperkalemia should be treated aggressively with intravenous calcium, either in the gluconate or chloride form. The chloride form is preferred in cardiac arrest situations because it delivers three times the amount of calcium as calcium gluconate for the same volume. Although it carries a risk of ex- travasation injury, this is of lesser concern than controlling the life-threatening ef- fect of hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia causes toxicity by reducing the passive gradient responsible for main- taining normal resting membrane potential, thereby raising the resting membrane potential. At higher potassium levels, this inhibits cardiac sodium channels (which are dependent on resting membrane potential to function properly) and ultimately slows depolarization. This is reflected most severely in the sine wave pattern, al- though it is essential to note that severe hyperkalemia can readily cause ven- tricular fibrillation or asystole and should be considered even in the ab- sence of classic ECG findings. Calcium antagonizes the effects of hyperkalemia by both antagonizing its effect on resting membrane potential and restoring sodium channel function. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amiodarone is appropriate as an adjunctive medication for the manage- ment of refractory pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fib- rillation, but it has no role in the management of PEA arrest with a wide-complex bradycardia. Furthermore, amiodarone use could be dangerous because of its wide receptor-blocking effects. This patient should be treated with empiric calcium chlo- ride because there is significant clinical concern for hyperkalemia-induced PEA arrest. Atropine is appropriate for the initial management of symptomatic bradycardia in children. However, this patient is presenting in PEA arrest with a wide-complex bradycardia, which is highly concerning for hyperkalemia, espe- cially given the patient's history of renal disease. Thus, atropine is not indicated in this situation, and the patient should be treated with calcium chloride. Procainamide is appropriate for managing stable ventricular arrhyth- mias, but it has no role in the management of PEA arrest with a wide-complex bradycardia. Giving procainamide in this circumstance could be dangerous because of its effect on cardiac sodium channels.

question: For which situation is targeted temperature management indicated in children?
englishExplanation: According to PALS guidelines, targeted temperature management (TTM) is indicated for pediatric post–cardiac arrest patients who remain co- matose after successful restoration of spontaneous circulation. The in- tention of TTM is to prevent hyperthermia, which can be deleterious to post–car- diac arrest recovery and neurologic outcomes. Although the ideal target tempera- ture is a matter of debate and investigation, the current guidelines recommend tar- geting a core temperature of either 32°C to 34°C (89.6°F or 93.2°F) for 48 hours, then 36°C to 37.5°C (96.8°F to 99.5°F) for 3 days or 36°C to 37.5°C (96.8°F to 99.5°F) for 5 days. Currently, there is no high-quality evidence to suggest therapeutic hypothermia is superior compared to maintaining normothermia. Additional sedation and shivering control may be needed to achieve adequate temperature. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hypothermia requires rewarming; depending on severity, hypothermia can require passive methods (eg, warm blankets) or active methods (eg, warmed fluids, rewarming blankets, machines, or body cavity lavage). Although the goal of hypothermia management is to ultimately restore normal body temperature, it is not intended to manage the body temperature at a particular tar- get over time, which is the intention of TTM. TTM is a multi-day active cooling process intended to maintain normothermia and prevent hyperthermia in the set- ting of cardiac arrest. It is not indicated for managing hypothermia. Malignant hyperthermia is a life-threatening condition related to expo- sure to a triggering agent (eg, succinylcholine) in the setting of an un- derlying genetic abnormality in the ryanodine receptor. This triggers un- controlled calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to muscle rigidity and, consequently, severe hyperthermia. Relief of this rigidity with dantrolene relieves the hyperthermia; active cooling measures should be used in the meantime to reduce body temperature until the rigidity can be controlled. TTM, on the other hand, is a multi-day active cooling process intended to maintain normoth- ermia and prevent hyperthermia in the setting of cardiac arrest. It is not indicated for the management of malignant hyperthermia. Although patients with sepsis can develop fevers due to the infection, these fevers generally respond to acetaminophen and do not require any active cooling mea- sures. TTM is a multi-day active cooling process intended to maintain normother- mia and prevent hyperthermia in the setting of cardiac arrest. It is not indicated for the management of fever.

question: Which intervention has proven benefit for favorable neurologic outcomes in car- diac arrest?
englishExplanation: Chest compressions are the single most important intervention in car- diac arrest. Chest compressions attempt to provide perfusion to vital organs, in- cluding the brain, to improve neurologic outcomes. Guidelines were changed in 2010 to focus more on chest compressions and shorten the duration to initiation of chest compressions, moving from the ABC (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) model to the CAB (Circulation, Airway, Breathing) model. Chest compressions are so important that lay bystanders are advised to perform chest compressions in pre- sumed cardiac arrest because the benefit outweighs the potential harms, even if the patient is not actually in cardiac arrest. Guidelines recommend chest compressions at a depth of 2 in and a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Incorrect Answer Explanations Amiodarone is an arrhythmic that can be utilized for ventricular tachyarrhyth- mias in cardiac arrest. Studies have shown that amiodarone is associated with in- creased survival to hospital admission but have not shown increased survival to hospital discharge or survival with favorable neurologic outcomes. Amiodarone can be considered for ventricular arrhythmias (pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ven- tricular fibrillation) at a dose of 300 mg IV. Epinephrine is one of the hallmarks of ACLS, although the evidence supporting im- proved neurologic outcomes is severely limited. Epinephrine is recommended by the American Heart Association at 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes. Some studies have shown increased rates of ROSC, survival to hospital admission, and hospital discharge. However, they have failed to show any improvement in neuro- logic outcomes. Intubation or advanced airway management is oftentimes pursued during cardiac arrest to prevent orogastric aspiration and improve ventilation. However, endotra- cheal intubation can be particularly difficult with ongoing CPR, which can lead to tube malposition. Furthermore, advanced airway management may interrupt valu- able chest compressions. Studies have not shown any survival benefit with favorable neurologic outcomes, and some nonrandomized studies have shown worse out- comes. If intubation occurs, continuous chest compressions should be done at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute without pauses for ventilation, while breaths should be delivered at 10 per minute or one every 6 seconds.

question: A patient presents in cardiac arrest, and CPR is initiated. The initial rhythm is ventricular fibrillation. Defibrillation is attempted, and CPR is resumed. What is the best next step?
englishExplanation: The American Heart Association (AHA) currently recommends epi- nephrine 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes for adult patients during cardiac ar- rest. Epinephrine has been shown to increase the probability of ROSC, hospital ad- mission, and hospital discharge. However, it has failed to demonstrate dis- charge with favorable neurologic outcomes. Despite this, the AHA continues to recommend epinephrine for cardiac arrest because it is believed to increase coro- nary perfusion. High-dose epinephrine (0.1-0.2 mg/kg) theoretically can increase coronary artery perfusion pressure and potentially increase the chance of ROSC. However, studies comparing high doses to standard doses of epinephrine have shown no benefit re- garding survival to admission, survival to discharge, or discharge with favorable neurologic outcome. There are some studies that show short-term improvement in ROSC, but studies have not shown benefit with respect to more meaningful long- term outcomes. The AHA currently does not recommend the use of high-dose epinephrine. Incorrect Answer Explanations Calcium chloride can be considered in cases of suspected hyperkalemia. However, it is not recommended as part of the standard treatment for patients with ventricular fibrillation. Sodium bicarbonate can be considered in cases of severe metabolic acidosis, al- though its role in cardiac arrest remains nebulous. Sodium bicarbonate is not rec- ommended as part of the standard treatment for patients with ventricular fibrillation. Vasopressin is a peripheral vasoconstrictor. It was previously recommended in the ACLS algorithm to replace a round of epinephrine. However, vasopressin failed to show improved outcomes when it replaces or is added to epinephrine. As a result, it was removed from the AHA guidelines in 2015. Current recommendations say that vasopressin may be considered, but it has no advantage as a substitute for epinephrine. The current AHA recommendation is to give epinephrine.

question: A 22-year-old man visiting the hospital suddenly collapses in the cafeteria. CPR is started immediately. An AED is applied, and a shock is delivered. The patient is in ventricular fibrillation on arrival to the emergency department. He is defib- rillated again, given epinephrine and amiodarone, and intubated. ACLS care is continued for another two rounds of CPR, defibrillation, and additional epineph- rine and amiodarone administration. The patient remains in ventricular fibrilla- tion. What should be done next?

options.text: Administer an additional 300 mg of amiodarone and prepare to give lidocaine
Change the vector orientation of the defibrillation pads and defibrillate again
Infuse 4 g of calcium gluconate intravenously over 15 minutes
Terminate resuscitative efforts because the patient is unlikely to survive

correctAnswer: Change the vector orientation of the defibrillation pads and defibrillate again
englishExplanation: This patient presents in refractory ventricular fibrillation (VF), or VF that is unresponsive to traditional ACLS care. Refractory VF can occur for multiple rea- sons, including coronary artery disease, ACS, and undiagnosed cardiac abnormali- ties, such as long QT syndrome and electrolyte abnormalities. Multiple strategies have been proposed to treat refractory VF and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT). One of the most discussed strategies is to change the way defibrillation is performed, such as changing the vector of the defibrillation. If the patient was initially defibrillated with pads in an anterior-posterior position, the position- ing may be changed to an anterior-lateral position and defibrillation tried again, or vice versa. Double sequential defibrillation, also known as dual sequential defibril- lation, has also shown benefit in refractory VT and VF. To perform double sequential defibrillation, place two sets of pads on the patient: one in an anterior- posterior position, and the second in an anterior-lateral position; ensure the pads are not touching one another. A variation of double sequential defibrillation in- volves placing both sets of pads next to each other in anterior-lateral positions. Some studies suggest using both defibrillators simultaneously; others suggest a short delay (<1 second) between defibrillation with each machine. Other treatments have also been proposed to treat refractory VT and VF. These treatments include magnesium when refractory arrhythmia is caused by prolonged QT and calcium in the setting of suspected hyperkalemia. Esmolol, a beta-blocker, has been shown to help terminate refractory VT and VF in small stud- ies. One study used a loading dose of 500 µg/kg of esmolol, followed by an infusion of up to 100 µg/kg/min. It has been suggested that esmolol confers benefit by block- ing the adrenergic or catecholamine storm produced in refractory VT and VF. There are also some data to support trying lidocaine if amiodarone has been ineffective. Incorrect Answer Explanations At this point, the patient has received two doses of amiodarone per the ACLS guide- lines. Giving an additional bolus of 300 mg is unlikely to have any effect. Administering a different antiarrhythmic such as lidocaine may have some benefit, but the recommendation is to change the vector orientation of the defibrillator pads first. Calcium should be administered in the setting of cardiac arrest if severe hypocalcemia or hyperkalemia is considered as a cause. In cardiac arrest, cal- cium is typically administered through bolus dosing of calcium chloride rather than slow infusion of calcium gluconate. Terminating resuscitation at this time is premature. This young patient had a witnessed in-hospital cardiac arrest and could still have a meaningful neurologic outcome. Additional treatment modalities should be tried first, such as changing the vector orientation of the defibrillator pads.

question: Which cardiac arrhythmia should prompt consideration of double sequential defibrillation?
englishExplanation: Double sequential defibrillation (also known as dual sequential defibrillation) has been studied for the treatment of refractory ventricular fibrillation (VF) and refractory pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT). Refractory VF can occur for multiple reasons, including coronary artery disease, ACS, and undiagnosed cardiac abnormalities, such as long QT syndrome and electrolyte abnormalities. There is a modest amount of evidence suggesting that double sequential defibrillation may be more successful at restoring a perfusing cardiac rhythm than continued attempts at single-set biphasic defibrillation. To perform double sequential defibrillation, place two sets of pads on the pa- tient: one in an anterior-posterior position, and the second in an anterior- lateral position; ensure the pads are not touching one another. A variation of double sequential defibrillation involves placing both sets of pads next to each other in anterior-lateral positions. Some studies suggest defibrillating with both defibril- lators simultaneously; others suggest a short delay (<1 second) between defibrilla- tion with each machine. Another treatment option for refractory VF or VT is to change the vector of the defibrillation. If the patient was initially being defibrillated with pads in an anterior- posterior position, this can be changed to pads in an anterior-lateral position and defibrillation tried again, or vice versa. Other treatments have also been proposed to treat refractory VT and VF. These treatments include magnesium (when refractory arrhythmia is caused by prolonged QT) and calcium (in the setting of suspected hy- perkalemia). Esmolol, a beta-blocker, has been shown to help terminate refractory VT and VF in small studies. One study used a loading dose of 500 µg/kg of esmolol, followed by an infusion of up to 100 µg/kg/min. It has been suggested that esmolol confers benefit by blocking the adrenergic or catecholamine storm produced in re- fractory VT and VF. There are also some data to support trying lidocaine if amio- darone has been ineffective. Incorrect Answer Explanations Defibrillation should not be used to treat supraventricular tachycardia (SVT). If SVT is unstable, synchronized cardioversion should be performed. If SVT is defibrillated instead of cardioverted, there is a risk of causing an R-on-T phenom- enon and inducing VF. Patients with unstable atrial fibrillation should have synchronized car- dioversion performed, not defibrillation. Defibrillation is reserved for VF and pulseless VT. VT with a pulse should be treated with synchronized cardioversion. This prevents an R-on-T phenomenon that may lead to VF. However, if a patient is in cardiac arrest and showing VT, defibrillation should be used. Refractory pulseless VT may be treated with double sequential defibrillation.

question: A 25-year-old man presents to a level 1 trauma center in cardiac arrest after sus- taining a gunshot wound to the chest. He lost pulses immediately prior to enter- ing the trauma bay. What should be performed next?
englishExplanation: Resuscitative thoracotomy (or an emergency department thoracotomy) is indicated for a patient with penetrating trauma who loses pulses either in the emergency department or immediately prior to arrival. The procedure involves making a large anterolateral incision starting at the sternum of the 4th/5th intercostal space extending the incision to the midaxillary line. Cut through subcu- taneous tissue and muscle until the pleura is entered; then, use rib spreaders to en- ter the chest. If any blood is encountered, evacuate the blood and then identify and enter the pericardium. Next, cross-clamp the aorta and provide direct cardiac massage. The goal of a resuscitative thoracotomy is to address immediately re- versible causes of the arrest (eg, tension pneumothorax or cardiac tamponade), address any immediate penetrating injuries to thoracic organs, and tempo- rize lower bleeding with cross-clamping of the aorta. The neurologically intact survival rate of resuscitative thoracotomy is low, but it is highest in patients with penetrating chest trauma. Follow local guide- lines, but know that many institutions will not initiate a resuscitative thoracotomy after blunt trauma that arrests prior to arrival. The Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma (EAST) guidelines are helpful. For this specific patient (ie, pene- trating chest trauma with no signs of life), EAST conditionally recommends a resus- citative thoracotomy. Incorrect Answer Explanations This young patient who arrested immediately prior to arrival may have immediately reversible causes of death that can be fixed with interventions, specifically a resusci- tative thoracotomy. Calling time of death for a patient may be appropriate after a resuscitative thoracotomy, for a patient with prolonged down time, or in blunt trauma, but it is not immediately warranted in this case. The eFAST examination uses ultrasound to identify blood in the peri- toneum, blood around the pericardium, and lack of lung sliding (indicating pneu- mothorax). However, treatment for reversible causes of trauma should not be de- layed for — sometimes — timely diagnostic studies, such as ultrasound or x-ray. A resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) can be used in unstable patients with suspected hemorrhagic shock. REBOA is placed in the femoral artery and occludes the aorta, thereby temporizing hemorrhage and prioritizing flow to the brain and coronaries. Its use has come un- der some question with the recent UK-REBOA trial, but it can still be considered. REBOA is not indicated in patients who are pulseless from penetrating chest trauma.

question: A mother brings in her 30-day-old daughter for difficulty breathing. The baby was born at home at 37 weeks' gestation. The mother received normal prenatal care, and there were no complications during the pregnancy or delivery. The baby only recently returned to her birth weight of 6 pounds. She is formula fed 3 ounces every 2 to 3 hours and is noted to fall asleep during most feeds. The baby is awake and responsive on examination, with a palpable liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin. A 3/4 harsh, holosystolic murmur is noted at the left lower sternal border. Upper and lower extremity blood pressures are symmetric. What is the likely underlying cause of her symptoms?
englishExplanation: In this case, the initial clinical clues to an underlying congenital cardiac disease in- clude poor weight gain (weight loss in some infants), tiring while feeding (sweating in some cases), and signs of congestive heart failure ("trouble breathing"). Because this patient does not have signs of cyanosis or a ductal-depen- dent lesion, other types of congenital cardiac disease should be considered. Ventricular septal defect is the most common congenital cardiac lesion, and the degree of disease is dependent on the size of the defect. This can range from no issues to signs of congestive heart failure, such as enlarged liver, which happens as the disease progresses. Incorrect Answer Explanations Coarctation of the aorta would likely show a differential between the upper and lower extremity blood pressures. Given this patient's presentation, ven- tricular septal defect is more likely. Total anomalous pulmonary venous return is a cyanotic congenital cardiac dis- ease that would likely present with some degree of cyanosis or alteration in pulse oximetry. Ventricular septal defect is more likely in this case. Transposition of the great arteries is a cyanotic congenital cardiac disease, and it would likely present with some degree of cyanosis or alteration in pulse oximetry. Because this patient does not have signs of cyanosis or a ductal-depen- dent lesion, other types of congenital cardiac disease, such as ventricular septal de- fect, are more likely and should be considered.

question: A 2-week-old girl presents via ambulance in shock. Which sign is most suggestive of a ductal dependent lesion from congenital heart disease?
englishExplanation: Shock or cyanosis occurring in the first 2 weeks of life is very alarming, and an undiagnosed congenital heart disease (CHD) should be strongly considered given that the ductus arteriosus is closing. Treatment with prostaglandins can be lifesaving. Other more common diseases such as septic shock must also be considered and treated as required in the critically ill neonate. With advances in imaging technology, CHD can be diagnosed in utero or in the newborn nursery. However, some disorders are not diagnosed until several weeks of life when the ductus arteriosus closes, and even then, the signs are subtle and easily missed. Common indicators of CHD are poor feeding with or without sweating, irritability, unexplained hypertension, hepatomegaly, and a pathologic murmur. On presentation, neonates with undiagnosed CHD often have mottled skin, cyanosis, and shock. If this is the case, especially if the in- fant is younger than 1 month of age, treatment with prostaglandins should be con- sidered as the culprit is likely a ductal dependent congenital heart lesion. Incorrect Answer Explanations Peripheral edema as a manifestation of heart failure is rare in infants. More common indicators of CHD are poor feeding with or without sweating, irritability, unexplained hypertension, hepatomegaly, and a pathologic murmur. The presentation described above with shock and central cyanosis is more consistent with a diagnosis of CHD. Murmurs are common in pediatric patients, present in more than 50% of newborns. Most of these patients have structurally normal hearts and have an "innocent" murmur, such as a grade 1 to 2 soft with normal split and normal periph- eral pulses. Two of the most common murmurs are: Peripheral pulmonary stenosis: a midsystolic high-pitched ejection murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border of the pulmonary area. The Still murmur: a low-pitched systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border and often described as musical. Stridor is audible breath sounds that typically originate from the ex- trathoracic airways. The presence of stridor indicates turbulent flow from a par- tial obstruction of the upper airways, glottis, or trachea. Congenital stridor presents at birth or within the first few weeks of life and is rarely life threatening. The most common causes include laryngomalacia, subglottic stenosis, bron- chogenic cysts, tracheomalacia, gastroesophageal reflux, and foreign body. Key Points Subtle indicators of congenital heart disease in neonates include poor feeding with or without sweating, unexplained hypertension, hepatomegaly, and a new patho- logic murmur. Signs of heart failure, such as edema, are uncommon in neonates. Shock and cyanosis in the first weeks of life strongly suggests a congenital heart dis- ease, and treatment with prostaglandins can be lifesaving.

question: A mother brings in her newborn son because she noticed he was working harder to breathe and the skin around his mouth looked blue. The baby was born 2 days earlier at home. On examination, he is awake and responsive but cyanotic. An ECG is obtained and shows a loss of right-sided forces and borderline left-axis deviation. What is the best choice for immediate pharmacotherapy?
englishExplanation: This baby has signs of cardiac failure with resultant pulmonary edema, and the ECG shows a loss of right-sided forces and borderline left-axis devia- tion, which suggests tricuspid atresia as a cause of the cyanosis. Prostaglandin E (PGE) is a life-saving medication in this ductal-dependent cyanotic sce- nario and must be started as soon as possible. Dosing of the infusion is 0.05 mcg/kg per minute. Side effects of PGE1 include apnea, bradycardia, and hypoten- sion. Beyond initial care, the patient requires ICU admission and a cardiology con- 1 1 sultation. Treatment decisions are then made depending on the degree of cardiac defect and patient stability. Definitive repair with cardiothoracic surgery may be de- layed until the child grows and matures so that he is better prepared for the surgery. Incorrect Answer Explanations Atropine is used in pediatric resuscitation for bradycardia related to a vagal cause or as an antisialagogue. Prostaglandin, not atropine, is not used to keep the ductus arteriosus patent in ductal-dependent lesions, such as tricuspid atresia. Epinephrine, a staple medication in the resuscitation of critically ill patients, is not warranted in this case. This patient has clinical and ECG signs of a cyanotic car- diac defect, so the addition of epinephrine may cause cardiac instability and prompt worsening shunting of deoxygenated blood. A fluid bolus using normal saline is contraindicated in this clinical sce- nario. The child has signs of cardiac dysfunction and pulmonary edema, and adding fluid could worsen his condition.

question: Which symptom is most commonly seen in infants with congestive heart failure?
englishExplanation: Infants and older adults differ in the presenting signs, symptoms, and complaints associated with congestive heart failure. Although older adults with congestive heart failure typically present with jugular venous distention, weight gain, bi- lateral pitting edema, and rales on examination, infants experiencing con- gestive heart failure typically present with prolonged poor feedings accompa- nied by sweating, poor growth, poor weight gain, weak cry, coughing, and at times, wheezing. Congestive heart failure in infants is usually congenital. Conditions that result in left-to-right shunting (eg, ventricular septal de- fects, patent ductus arteriosus, and atrioventricular canal defects) are 1 commonly identified as the etiology in infants younger than 6 months. Other condi- tions, such as aortic coarctation and aortic stenosis, that present the develop- ing myocardium with a left-sided obstruction can also result in infantile conges- tive heart failure. Less commonly, acquired disorders such as myocarditis can cause congestive heart failure. Treatment goals for children with congestive heart failure include relieving pul- monary and systemic venous congestion, improving myocardial performance, and reversing the underlying process. Key interventions in the management of an in- fant with congestive heart failure include providing supplemental oxygen; ele- vating the head and shoulders 45 degrees; administering furosemide, ni- troglycerin, and digoxin; and administering an inotropic agent to im- prove cardiac contractility. Incorrect Answer Explanations Peripheral edema can be seen in infants with congestive heart failure but is not as common as sweating with eating. Peripheral edema is more commonly seen in adults with congestive heart failure. Peripheral pulses in children who are experiencing congestive heart failure are typically weak. Children with aortic coarctation present with diminished femoral pulses whether or not they have congestive heart failure. Jugular venous distention is commonly seen in adults with congestive heart failure. It is often difficult to appreciate in infants and is not often seen.

question: A 4-day-old girl, born at home, presents with progressively worsening lethargy, pallor, diaphoresis, dyspnea, and discoloration of the legs that started 30 min- utes before presentation. She was previously noted to be acting normally and feeding well. Femoral pulses are absent. The right arm is pink and well perfused with palpable pulses. Telemetry monitoring shows sinus tachycardia. What is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to treat this condition?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms consistent with a critical coarctation of the aorta dependent on the ductus arteriosus to maintain adequate systemic blood flow. Administration of alprostadil, a synthetic pros- taglandin E1, prevents closure of the ductus arteriosus and is necessary to stabilize patients in this situation prior to definitive procedural management. Other major “ductal-dependent lesions'' include hypoplastic left heart syndrome, pulmonary atresia with intact interventricular septum, transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch, and criti- cal aortic and pulmonary stenosis. As the ductus arteriosus begins to close (usually within the first few days of life but up to 2 weeks after birth), perfusion through it becomes compromised, and the ductal-dependent abnormality rapidly becomes symptomatic. Unfortunately, presentation will vary between these pathologies, and most patients presenting to emergency departments in this situation will not have established diagnoses at the time of presentation. Any early newborn presenting with acute-onset respira- tory distress, difficulty or sweating with feeding, signs of shock (“grey baby”), or cyanosis (“blue baby”) without an identifiable alternative cause should be considered to have a possible ductal-dependent lesion. Differential blood pressure and pulse oximetry between “preductal” and “postductal” limbs is also strongly suggestive; the right arm is reliably “preductal,” whereas the legs are reliably “postductal.” Incorrect Answer Explanations Indomethacin is an NSAID that is classically used to close a patent duc- tus arteriosus. Consequently, use would close the ductus arteriosus faster rather than maintain it open. Administration of alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) is the cor- rect intervention in this case because it prevents the ductus arteriosus from closing. Milrinone is an inhibitor of phosphodiesterase-3 and is used as a positive in- otropic agent for patients with severe ventricular cardiac failure. Although a critically ill patient with congenital heart disease may also require this form of inotropic support, in this case, it is the sudden closure of the ductus arterio- sus that led to the patient's precipitous presentation. Consequently, administration of alprostadil (prostaglandin E1) is the correct intervention in this case because it prevents the ductus arteriosus from closing. Phenylephrine is given to increase systemic vascular resistance during an episode of shunting associated with tetralogy of Fallot, or a tet spell. It can diminish the right-to-left shunting and improve overall circulation. Phenylephrine has no role in the management of a closing ductus arteriosus di- rectly, although other vasopressors with inotropic activity, such as epinephrine, can be used as adjunctive therapy in certain circumstances. Administration of al- prostadil (prostaglandin E1) is the correct intervention in this case as it prevents the ductus arteriosus from closing.

question: What is the most likely cause of a single second heart sound with a harsh systolic ejection murmur in an infant?
