In cases of orthodromic WPW, adenosine is a first-line agent, with calcium-channel blockers and beta-blockers as second line. For antidromic AVRT (wide), it is important to avoid typical AV nodal–blocking agents for supraventricular tachycardia (eg, adenosine, calcium-channel blockers, and beta- blockers). Additionally, in WPW syndrome that presents with atrial fibrilla- tion, AV nodal blockers like adenosine, digoxin, calcium-channel blockers, and beta-blockers should be avoided. Incorrect Answer Explanations Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside with AV nodal–blocking properties. Digoxin can de- crease the refractory period of the accessory pathway, increasing acces- sory pathway conduction and the risk of degeneration to ventricular ar- rhythmias. Additionally, digoxin does not treat ventricular arrhythmias. Because procainamide can both block the accessory pathway and treat ventricular arrhyth- mias, it is the preferred medical treatment for presumed antidromic AVRT. Diltiazem is a calcium-channel blocker that causes longer duration of AV nodal blockade. Although AV nodal blockade can technically disrupt antidromic AVRT, this blockade can also preferentially shunt conduc- tion through the accessory pathway, causing extreme ventricular con- duction and degeneration to ventricular arrhythmias. Additionally, diltiazem does not treat ventricular arrhythmias. Because procainamide can both block the acces- sory pathway and treat ventricular arrhythmias, it is the preferred medical treat- ment for presumed antidromic AVRT. Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective beta-blocker. Like diltiazem, metoprolol can put the patient at risk of ventricular arrhythmia from prolonged AV nodal blockade, resulting in preferential conduction via the accessory pathway. Also, metoprolol generally does not treat ventricular arrhythmias. Because procainamide can both block the accessory pathway and treat ventricular arrhythmias, it is the preferred medical treatment for presumed antidromic AVRT.

question: The below rhythm is from a patient currently in cardiac arrest. Which condition is most likely associated with this cardiac arrest patient's rhythm? Credit: Mary Jo Wagner, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: This rhythm shows a patient with narrow-complex pulseless electrical activ- ity (PEA). Given the scenarios presented, this is most likely COPD re- lated to a pneumothorax from a ruptured bleb. Narrow-complex PEA gener- ally results from mechanical obstruction, coronary ischemia, or hypov- olemia, including hemorrhage. Mechanical obstruction can be caused by a tension pneumothorax, which is associated with COPD and trauma. Other causes of me- chanical obstruction include pulmonary embolism (associated with findings of right-heart strain) and cardiac tamponade (associated with low voltage and electri- cal alternans). Incorrect Answer Explanations Diabetic ketoacidosis is most likely to cause cardiac arrest due to acidosis or electrolyte derangements such as hyper- or hypokalemia, which are not evident on this patient's rhythm strip. Instead, hyperkalemia is associated with peaked T waves, prolonged PR and QRS complex intervals, and in severe cases, a wide-complex bradycardia with a sinusoidal pattern. By contrast, hypokalemia is associated with a U wave and flattening of the T wave in its mild form and dysrhythmias when severe. Cardiac arrest due to acidosis is likely to present with a bradyarrhythmia, particularly if concomitant hyperkalemia is present. Physicians should consider the use of bicarbonate to treat bradycardic PEA if severe acidosis is considered a possible etiology. Cardiac arrest in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) is most com- monly associated with cardiovascular disease (eg, coronary ischemia or ventricular dysrhythmias) or hyperkalemia (ie, peaked T waves, prolonged PR and QRS complex intervals, and in severe cases, a wide-complex bradycardia with a sinusoidal pattern) — neither of which are apparent on this patient's rhythm strip. Hyperkalemia can also cause cardiac arrest in this population, but again, find- ings of hyperkalemia are absent. Finally, although cardiac tamponade can occur in patients with ESRD, causing PEA with a narrow complex, the classic findings for cardiac tamponade include low voltage and electrical alternans. PEA from a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose is most likely to have a wide QRS complex, which is not evident on this patient's rhythm strip. A wide QRS complex is associated with the inhibitory effect of TCAs on the recovery of car- diac sodium channels. Although the anticholinergic effects of TCAs can cause nar- row-complex tachycardia in lower doses, this effect would not be associated with cardiac arrest.

question: A 73-year-old man presents with fever, chest pain, and a cough 1 week following mitral valve repair. He denies syncope or shortness of breath. His vital signs in- clude BP 136/56, P 80, and T 38.8°C (101.8°F); SpO is 98% on room air. The physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds in the right posterior lung fields with inspiratory wheezes and rales. His rhythm strip is shown below. What is the best initial management? Credit: William J. Brady, MD, FACEP.

options.text: Chest x-ray and infectious disease workup
Stat electrolytes, cardiac markers, ABG, and lactate
Transcutaneous pacing with admission for permanent pacemaker 2

correctAnswer: Chest x-ray and infectious disease workup
englishExplanation: Although this patient recently underwent cardiac surgery, he does not have any spe- cific cardiac symptoms, such as shortness of breath or syncope. His symptoms more likely have an infectious etiology such as pneumonia, so a chest x- ray and infectious disease workup are indicated. His ECG demonstrates a second-degree type I (Mobitz) heart block (Wenckebach), which is typi- cally transient and does not require intervention. If the ventricular rate is very slow, leading to hypoperfusion, then atropine may be given. Second-degree type I block can be seen after an acute inferior myocardial infarction, digoxin toxicity, myocarditis, or cardiac surgery. It can also oc- cur after the AV node is subject to rapid atrial rates. Second-degree type I block may also be seen as a normal variant in endurance athletes, such as marathon runners. In second-degree heart block, atrioventricular (AV) conduction is inter- mittent; some atrial impulses reach the ventricles, but others are blocked. Second- degree type I (Mobitz) block occurs when successive depolarizations produce a pro- longation of the refractory period at the AV node. Subsequent depolarizations arrive at the AV node during a refractory period, and conduction is thus slower through the AV node. Eventually, an atrial impulse attempts to conduct during an absolute refractory period; conduction is blocked completely, and a nonconducted or “dropped” beat occurs. The PR interval prolongs un- til a dropped QRS complex, the dropped beat, occurs. Generally, the P wave to P wave interval is constant, and the R wave to R wave interval shortens. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient's rhythm strip and symptoms do not indicate any signs of is- chemia that require cardiac catheterization. Second-degree type I heart block often occurs following cardiac surgery and is most often a benign rhythm. The patient's rhythm strip demonstrates second-degree type I block, which often oc- curs following cardiac surgery and is not due to an electrolyte abnormality. This form of AV block is rarely compromising and does not require further interven- tion unless due to inferior myocardial ischemia. Typically, second-degree type I (Mobitz) blocks do not require interven- tion if the patient is asymptomatic. Hemodynamic instability is not usually encoun- tered, and permanent pacing is rarely required.

question: A 70-year-old woman presents after suddenly fainting in a grocery store. She de- nies being dizzy or nauseated before she lost consciousness but says she has been getting "winded" lately around the house. Her vital signs include BP 120/80 and P 40; SpO is 98% on room air. She is asymptomatic now. The rhythm strip is shown below. What is the correct initial management? Credit: William J. Brady, MD, FACEP.

options.text: Atropine 1 mg IV push and discharge if the dysrhythmia resolves
Monitor for 4 hours, and discharge with cardiology follow-up if she remains stable
Place transcutaneous pacer pads, and admit to cardiac telemetry unit

correctAnswer: Place transcutaneous pacer pads, and admit to cardiac telemetry unit
englishExplanation: Third-degree heart block, or complete heart block, is characterized by the absence of AV conduction because all atrial impulses to the ventricles are blocked. 2 The diagnosis is made by recognizing the characteristic ECG features — no associa- tion of P wave with QRS complexes, an atrial rate greater than the ventricular rate (which is regular), wide QRS complexes (usually), and narrow QRS complexes (oc- casionally) — and relating them to the patient presentation. In this case, the patient's syncopal episode and dyspnea and bradycardia on presentation are consis- tent with the diagnosis. Definitive management is placement of an implanted pacemaker. Correct initial emergency department management of this patient involves placing transcuta- neous pacer pads and turning them on if needed, close cardiac monitoring, ruling out correctable causes such as electrolyte abnormality, monitoring her condition closely, and admitting her to a cardiac unit where she can undergo cardiac monitor- ing. Typically an escape pacemaker paces the ventricles at a rate that is slower than the atrial rate. The QRS interval is either narrow or wide, depending on whether the escape pacemaker is at the AV node or infranodal, respectively. Complete heart block is associated with acute ischemia (inferior and anterior STEMI) leading to structural heart disease, medication adverse effects (digitalis, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers), and other conditions such as Lyme disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations Administration of atropine in this setting is unlikely to produce benefit. Additionally, the rhythm diagnosis is third-degree heart block; this presentation requires admission to the hospital for monitoring and further management. Discharge from the hospital is inappropriate for the vast majority of pa- tients with third-degree heart block, even after a period of observation. Admission for further evaluation and management is correct, especially since this patient had an associated syncopal episode with her dysrhythmia. The initial evaluation and management of this patient might include the placement of transcutaneous pacing pads in case she has another episode of syncope. However, transcutaneous pacing does not need to be started immediately because she is cur- rently asymptomatic with normal blood pressure.

question: What is the best description of the following ECG performed on a patient with chest pain? Credit: Harrigan RA. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with left bundle-branch block
Normal sinus rhythm, first-degree AV block, left anterior fascicular block
Normal sinus rhythm, first-degree AV block, left posterior fascicular block
Third-degree AV block, left anterior fascicular block

correctAnswer: Normal sinus rhythm, first-degree AV block, left posterior fascicular block
englishExplanation: This ECG demonstrates a normal sinus rhythm (P wave is present before each QRS complex). The PR interval is prolonged >200 ms, indicating a first-degree atrioventricular (AV) block. There is a right axis deviation (QRS in lead I is net negative while the QRS in lead aVF is oriented positively) with a normal duration QRS complex. There are small R waves with deep S waves in leads I and aVL. These findings are consistent with a left poste- rior fascicular block. The left bundle of the cardiac electrical conduction system separates into the left an- terior fascicle and the left posterior fascicle (with a small septal fascicle branch). Blocks in these fascicles will present with characteristic ECG changes. Notably, it is important to ensure there is not another reason for a right axis deviation in this case, such as right ventricular strain. In contrast, a left anterior fascicular block will present with a left axis deviation and a normal duration QRS complex. Typically, there will be small R waves with deep S waves in leads II, III, and aVF. There also are no ST-seg- ment or T-wave changes associated with either left anterior or posterior fascicular blocks. Incorrect Answer Explanations The QRS complexes occur at a regular rhythm on this ECG. This is not consistent with atrial fibrillation, as the rhythm will be irregular. The QRS is normal duration and is not consistent with a right or left bundle-branch block, which will present with a QRS complex >120 ms. This ECG is consistent with a left posterior fascicular block. A left anterior fascic- ular block will present with a left axis deviation (positive QRS in lead I and negative QRS in lead aVF) with small R waves and deep S waves in leads II, III, and aVF. The P wave and QRS rates are the same on this ECG, with each QRS being preceded by a P wave. A third-degree AV block would present with a P wave rate dissociated from the QRS rate, with the P wave rate being faster than the QRS rate. The PR interval is >200 ms, making this a first-degree AV block. Furthermore, this ECG is consistent with a left posterior fascicular block, not a left anterior fascic- ular block.

question: What is the best interpretation of this ECG? Credit: Harrigan RA. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay
Atrial flutter with left bundle-branch block
Normal sinus rhythm with left bundle-branch block
Normal sinus rhythm with right bundle-branch block

correctAnswer: Normal sinus rhythm with right bundle-branch block
englishExplanation: This ECG is consistent with a normal sinus rhythm with a right bundle- branch block (RBBB). There is a P wave clearly before each QRS, and each QRS is associated with a P wave. There are no extra P waves, and the P wave and QRS rate is the same, indicating a normal sinus rhythm and not a third-degree atrioven- tricular (AV) block. The QRS complex is widened (>120 ms), which is con- sistent with an intraventricular conduction block; RBBBs and left bun- dle-branch blocks (LBBBs) are the most common cause of a widened QRS. Based on the pattern seen here, there is an RSR' configuration of the QRS complex in leads V1 to V2 with associated ST depression and T-wave inversions. This is coupled with reciprocal changes (deep S waves with upright T waves) in leads I and aVL. This pattern is consistent with a RBBB. A RBBB occurs when there is a block in the conduction down the right bundle-branch. Recall that normal cardiac conduction begins with an impulse in the sinoatrial node to the AV node. This signal extends down the bundle of His where the conduction breaks off into the right and left bundle-branches. These then have Purkinje fibers extending from them that leads to cardiac muscle depolarization. When the right bundle-branch is blocked, the depolarization travels down the left bun- dle-branch and then to the right bundle-branch, causing a delay in ven- tricular polarization denoted by a prolonged QRS interval. The R prime (R') part of the QRS complex seen in a RBBB represents the current moving to the right side of the heart after the left side has depolarized and is paired with deep late S waves in the reciprocal leads (I, aVL, V5, and V6). Bundle-branch blocks (both left and right) can occur for many reasons, including ischemia, scar tissue formation, ventricular hypertrophy, cardiomyopathies, valvular abnormalities, and pulmonary disease, among others. Incorrect Answer Explanations This ECG shows a normal rate of both P waves and QRS complexes, and each QRS complex has a preceding P wave. The rhythm is regular. In atrial fibrillation, the rhythm would be irregular, and P waves would not be seen. Additionally, this block pattern is consistent with a RBBB. “Nonspecific intraventricular conduc- tion delay” is a term used to refer to a prolonged or wide QRS that is not consistent with either a RBBB or a LBBB. Atrial flutter will present with either a regular rate of QRS complexes in a fixed block pattern or an irregular rate with a variable block pattern. Atrial flutter will also present with flutter type repeating P waves in between QRS com- plexes, which is not seen here. Additionally, this pattern is consistent with a RBBB. A LBBB will present with wide notched R waves in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6 with as- sociated T-wave inversions and deep S waves in leads V1 and V2. This ECG is consistent with a normal sinus rhythm, given that each QRS complex is preceded by a P wave at a fixed interval with both the P waves and QRS complexes having the same rate. Additionally, the ECG here shows a RBBB pattern, not a LBBB pattern.

question: Which ECG characteristics are associated with a left bundle-branch block?

options.text: QRS duration of 105 ms, right axis deviation, and normal T waves
QRS duration of 110 ms, left axis deviation, and normal ST segments
QRS duration of 130 ms; broad notched R waves in leads I, aVL, and V5 to V6; and late deep S wave in lead V1
QRS duration of 135 ms, RSR' configuration in leads V1 to V2, and late deep S waves in leads I and aVL

correctAnswer: QRS duration of 130 ms; broad notched R waves in leads I, aVL, and V5 to V6; and late deep S wave in lead V1
englishExplanation: A left bundle-branch block (LBBB) occurs when the left bundle-branch in the ven- tricular cardiac conduction pathway is delayed or blocked. This causes the conduc- tion to proceed down the right bundle-branch first and then swing to the left side of the heart. The result is a wide QRS complex (>120 ms) due to delayed ven- tricular depolarization. The R waves in the leads over the left ventricle (I, aVL, and V5 to V6) will be broad due to slowed depolarization of the left ventricle. These leads will discordant ST and T-wave changes relative to the QRS complex. Reciprocal changes will be seen in V1 and often V2, being late deep S waves, as these leads lie over the right ventricle. Bundle-branch blocks, both left and right, can occur for many reasons, including ischemia, scar tissue formation, ventricular hypertrophy, cardiomyopathies, valvular abnormalities, and pulmonary disease, among others. Incorrect Answer Explanations A QRS duration of 105 ms is normal and is not consistent with a LBBB. These ECG findings, with a right axis deviation, may represent a left posterior fascicu- lar block. A QRS duration of 110 ms is normal and is not consistent with a LBBB. These ECG findings, with a left axis deviation, may represent a left anterior fascicular block. RSR' configuration of V1 to V2 with a wide QRS complex is consistent with a right bundle-branch block. This will present with reciprocal changes in leads I and aVL, being deep S waves.

question: A patient with chest pain presents with the following ECG. What is the best inter- pretation of this ECG? Credit: Harrigan RA. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation with a left bundle-branch block
Atrial flutter with a right bundle-branch block and left posterior fascicular block
Normal sinus rhythm with left posterior fascicular block
Normal sinus rhythm with right bundle-branch block and left anterior fascicular block

correctAnswer: Normal sinus rhythm with right bundle-branch block and left anterior fascicular block
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with active chest pain and an abnormal ECG showing a right bundle-branch block (RBBB) and a left anterior fascicular block (LAFB), also called a bifascicular block. The rate of this ECG is regular, and there are P waves be- fore each QRS complex, which rules out atrial fibrillation. There are no clear flutter waves on this ECG, making atrial flutter unlikely. The QRS complex is wide, sug- gesting either a RBBB or left bundle-branch block (LBBB). The RSR' pattern seen in this ECG in leads V1 to V2 with T-wave inversions and ST depres- sions indicate the presence of a RBBB. Additionally, this ECG shows small R waves with deep S waves in the inferior leads with a left axis deviation (positive QRS in lead I and negative QRS in lead aVF). These findings are consistent with a LAFB. The pattern of a new RBBB with a LAFB is associated with left main or left anterior descending coronary artery disease that may lead to com- plete occlusion. This finding is at risk of degenerating into ventricular tachycar- dia or complete heart block. As with any noted ECG changes, comparison with a prior ECG should be performed to assess for the chronicity of the findings. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient's ECG is consistent with normal sinus rhythm, not atrial fibrilla- tion. The rate is regular, with P waves before each QRS. The block pattern is consis- tent with an RBBB, not a LBBB. LBBB classically has a broad, notched R wave in leads I, aVL, and V5 to V6 with reciprocal changes in leads V1 to V2. The ECG in this case is consistent with a RBBB. There are no flutter waves, and there is a P wave before each QRS, denoting this to be normal sinus rhythm. A left posterior fascicular block will show small R waves with deep S waves in leads I and aVL. This ECG is normal sinus rhythm. However, there is a bundle-branch block, given the QRS duration of >120 ms. Additionally, a left posterior fascicular block will show small R waves with deep S waves in leads I and aVL, which is not seen in this ECG.

question: A 32-year-old man presents after passing out in his living room. His vital signs are stable, and he is asymptomatic. The physical examination is unremarkable. An ECG is obtained and shown below. What is the underlying diagnosis? Credit: Christopher Amato, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: Brugada syndrome is a genetic disorder that causes abnormal sodium channel function and is associated with a high risk of death. The classic ECG findings with Brugada syndrome, which appear on this patient's ECG, include an incomplete RBBB pattern and ST-segment elevations in leads V1 and V2. Death resulting from Brugada syndrome is related to subsequent polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. Patients commonly have a family history of sudden death or cardiac syncope without structural heart dis- ease. Management in the emergency department includes cardiac monitoring with admission for further monitoring and cardiology consultation. The ultimate treat- ment includes placement of an automatic implanted cardiac cardioverter- defibrillator. The ECG findings can often be normal at the time of evaluation in the emergency department, so any patient with a family history of sudden death should be referred for further evaluation and provocative testing. Incorrect Answer Explanations The ECG findings in prolonged QT syndrome are notable for significant prolon- gation of the QT interval. The syndrome causes increased susceptibility to polymor- phic ventricular tachycardia. However, the QT interval in this patient's ECG is normal. Third-degree AV block (complete heart block) is noted with dissociation of P waves from QRS complexes. A ventricular rate of less than 60 is noted; the specific rate and QRS complex morphologies are dependent on the level of the block (nodal versus infranodal). The PR intervals are normal and regular on this ECG and show no evidence of heart block. Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome can also lead to syncope and, extremely rarely, sudden cardiac death. The associated ECG changes (while the patient is in normal sinus rhythm) are shortened PR interval, delta wave, and minimally widened QRS complex — which are absent in this patient.

question: A 75-year-old woman presents with a decreased level of consciousness. Her vital signs are BP 70/40, P 40, R 12, and T 36.5°C (97.7°F); her bedside blood glucose level is 114 mg/dL. Her rhythm strip is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: alfa md/iStock/Getty Images Plus.

options.text: Mobitz second-degree heart block, type I (Wenckebach)
Mobitz second-degree heart block, type II
Sinus bradycardia with premature ventricular contractions

correctAnswer: Mobitz second-degree heart block, type II
englishExplanation: In Mobitz second-degree heart block, type II, the PR interval is constant (although sometimes prolonged) until there is a dropped beat. This patient is con- ducting only some beats, with the P waves after the premature ventricular com- plexes (PVCs) blocked, which is consistent with Mobitz second-degree heart block, type II. This rhythm strip also demonstrates a bradycardic rhythm. Further analy- sis involves identifying all the P waves and the relationship of each to the following QRS complex. A P wave precedes each normal QRS complex with a relatively nor- mal and nonvarying PR interval. There are some P waves (seen best im- mediately following the QRS complex of the PVC) that are not conducted and have no QRS complex following them. Mobitz type II heart blocks are often seen in an anterior wall myocardial in- farction (MI), whereas type I blocks are more often associated with an increased vagal tone accompanying an inferior wall MI. Distinguishing type II blocks is important because they are more likely to progress to complete heart blocks and have a higher mortality rate. Incorrect Answer Explanations In a complete heart block, there is no association between the P waves and the QRS complexes (complete atrioventricular dissociation). In this case, there is an association between some of the P waves and the QRS complexes. A Mobitz second-degree heart block, type I, referred to as Wenckebach, is associated with progressive PR interval prolongation from beat to beat until there is a dropped beat (or nonconducted P wave). The cycle is then reset. In this case, the PR interval is constant. In sinus bradycardia, although the heart rate is slow, each P wave is followed by a QRS complex. In this patient, some of the P waves are not being conducted, which indicates some type of heart block.

question: Which drug can be used to treat a patient with known Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome who presents with the rhythm shown below? Credit: Garmel Gm. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady w, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.
englishExplanation: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is a condition of abnormal conduction between the atrium and ventricle that is characterized by an accessory pathway to the normal atrioventricular (AV) node. WPW is often accompanied by wide-complex tachycardias (as seen in the figure above) and is best treated with procainamide. In this situation, all drugs that slow or block AV con- duction are contraindicated because of the risk for increased conduc- tion across the accessory pathway that might produce ventricular fibrillation. Synchronized cardioversion is also a therapeutic option to terminate the dysrhythmia. In patients with WPW, the ECG may exhibit a delta wave or slurring of the upstroke of the QRS complex, with a shortened PR interval during sinus rhythm. The accessory pathway can contribute to reentrant tachycardia. When this tachycardia occurs with a wide QRS interval, the accessory pathway is used for ante- grade conduction between the atrium and ventricle, and the AV node conducts in a retrograde direction (antidromic conduction). Incorrect Answer Explanations Adenosine also inhibits sinus and AV nodal function; use of this drug has previously been advocated as a diagnostic and therapeutic means of evaluating wide-complex tachycardias of uncertain etiology. More recently, this use has not been encouraged because adenosine can theoretically increase the conduc- tion rate, and the rhythm could degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Adenosine can be used in orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia. Calcium channel blockers (such as diltiazem) slow AV conduction and are contraindicated with antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia because of the risk for increased conduction across the accessory pathway that might produce ventricular fibrillation. Calcium channel blockers can be used in orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia. Beta-blockers (such as metoprolol) also slow AV conduction and are contraindicated in antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia because it may re- sult in ventricular fibrillation. Beta-blockers can be used in orthodromic AV reen- trant tachycardia.

question: A 74-year-old woman presents after she passed out. She is currently awake and alert but says she feels dizzy. Her vital signs include BP 80/50, P 47, and T 36.8°C (98.2°F); SpO is 99% on 3 L of oxygen by nasal cannula. Cardiac moni- toring reveals the rhythm shown below. Administration of atropine 1 mg IV has no effect on her blood pressure or heart rate. What is the next step in management? Credit: Mary Jo Wagner, MD, FACEP. 2
englishExplanation: A patient who is lightheaded with a low blood pressure and heart rate would be considered to have symptomatic bradycardia, a condition that is usually treatable with atropine. However, this patient's rhythm strip shows a complete heart block, which is often unresponsive to atropine and re- quires cardiac pacing due to the slower ventricular response. Complete heart block on this rhythm strip is noted with constant P-P and R-R intervals, but the P complexes and the QRS interval do not have an obvious relationship to each other. When initiating cardiac pacing, transcutaneous placement of external pads and pacemaker is preferred as the initial modality because it is minimally invasive and can be initiated faster than transvenous pacing. Incorrect Answer Explanations Another dose of atropine can be considered in patients with symptomatic bradycar- dia, but it would not be expected to help those with a high-grade heart block. Given that this patient's blood pressure is low, a dopamine or epinephrine infusion could be considered as a temporizing measure while pace-maker placement is being arranged. A fluid bolus may help with hypotension caused by decreased fluid sta- tus, but the hypotension in this case is likely from the bradycardia and subsequent low perfusion. The heart rate must be corrected to fix the blood pressure. Transvenous cardiac pacing may eventually be required for long-term pacing, but it requires more time to initiate and a greater level of skill and experience. Although this patient may eventually require transvenous pacing, a temporary transcutaneous pacemaker can be started sooner and can provide a bridge to improvement in cardiac output and blood pressure, allowing more time to convert to transvenous pacing. Key Points Atropine does not help with complete heart block; start emergent transcutaneous pacing instead. Complete heart block can be identified by constant P-P intervals and R-R intervals but shows no association between the P waves and QRS complexes.

question: Which finding is an indication for placement of a pacemaker?

options.text: New right bundle branch and left anterior fascicular block
Sinus bradycardia with a heart rate of 50 bpm

correctAnswer: New right bundle branch and left anterior fascicular block
englishExplanation: In the presence of a new right bundle-branch block with a left anterior fascicular block, placement of a temporary pacemaker can prevent com- plete heart block and reduce bradycardia. Because both the left anterior fas- cicle and the right bundle branch of the conducting system receive their blood sup- ply from the proximal LAD artery, findings of new bundle-branch blocks suggest oc- clusion of that vessel. PR prolongation and the finding of a new or alternating bun- dle-branch block further increase the likelihood that a complete heart block will de- velop, indicating the need for temporary pacing. In an anterior wall myocardial infarction (MI), necrosis of the septum from occlusion of the left ante- rior descending (LAD) artery, which supplies blood to the left anterior fascicle and the right bundle branch, has a poor prognosis and can progress to complete heart block. Incorrect Answer Explanations First-degree AV block does not need treatment. Higher grade AV blocks in anterior and lateral MIs should have transcutaneous pacing applied, but in infe- rior and posterior MIs, this is typically transient and conservative management is indicated. Bradycardia alone is not an indication for pacing, unless it does not cor- rect with pharmacologic intervention and the patient is unstable. Bradycardia may also result from therapy with beta-blockers and is reversible with discontinuation of these medications. Second-degree heart block, type I (also known as the Wenckebach type) is a much more stable block that rarely needs treatment. Higher grade blocks than Wenckebach are more ominous in anterior/lateral STEMIs, and pro- phylactic placement of a transcutaneous pacemaker is recommended. In inferior/posterior STEMIs, they are usually temporary and can be managed conservatively. Key Points Anterior myocardial infarctions indicate a left anterior descending artery occlusion and can cause necrosis of the septum, leading to arrhythmias. A new right bundle-branch block with a left anterior fascicular block may develop into a complete heart block and thus require pacing.

question: In children, which condition is most strongly associated with congenital pro- longed QT interval on ECG?
englishExplanation: A family history of exercise-induced syncope is associated with pro- longed QT syndrome. Prolonged QT syndrome is a serious cause of cardiac syn- cope and sudden death in children that can be congenital or acquired. The congeni- tal forms include Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome, which is characterized by re- current exercise- or stress-induced syncope, sudden death, and deafness, and Romano-Ward syndrome, which is similar to Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome but is not associated with deafness. A corrected QT interval longer than 0.44 seconds is considered abnormal, but a corrected QT interval longer than 0.55 seconds is strongly associated with sudden cardiac death. Incorrect Answer Explanations Congenital bicuspid aortic valve is a relatively common cardiac defect, seen in approximately 1% of the population. It can also be seen in patients with Marfan syn- drome, polycystic kidney disease, and other connective tissue disorders. Congenital bicuspid aortic valve can be associated with aortic dissection and aortic aneurysms. By itself, a bicuspid aortic valve does not lead to prolonged QT interval, but there are case reports of the syndromes, such as Marfan syndrome, leading to longer QT interval. Profound bradycardia on prenatal ultrasonography is a nonspecific find- ing. It does not have a known association with prolonged QT syndrome; however, it is associated with fetal loss. Multiple medications are associated with prolonged QT syndrome, but these cases are acquired and not congenital. Thus, syncope after initiating antifungal therapy with drugs such as fluconazole or ketoconazole may be due to ac- quired QT prolongation, but it is not a congenital disorder. Key Points Congenital prolonged QT syndrome is associated with a family history of exercise- induced syncope. A corrected QT interval longer than 0.44 seconds is abnormal but is associated with sudden death if it is longer than 0.55 seconds.

question: A patient presents from urgent care for an “abnormal ECG.” The following ECG is obtained. What block pattern does this ECG demonstrate? Credit: Harrigan RA. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.
englishExplanation: This patient's ECG demonstrates a left axis deviation (positive QRS orientation in lead I and negative QRS orientation in lead aVF), but the QRS is not widened past 120 ms, signifying that the patient does not have a full bundle-branch block on ECG. The left bundle of the cardiac electrical conduction system separates into the left an- terior fascicle and the left posterior fascicle (with a small septal fascicle branch). A block in the left anterior fascicle will cause a delay in conduction down that pathway, leading to conduction primarily down the posterior fasci- cle and then retrograde to the anterior fascicle. This will cause a left axis de- viation. However, the delay is not sufficient enough to cause a widened QRS as it would be in the setting of a full bundle-branch block. It is also typical to see small R waves with deep S waves in the inferior leads II, III, and aVF. In contrast, a left posterior fascicular block will present with a right axis deviation and a normal duration QRS complex. Typically, there will be small R waves with deep S waves in leads I and aVL. Importantly, for this criteria, there cannot be another cause of a right axis deviation, such as an RV-strain pattern. There also are no ST-segment or T-wave changes associated with either left anterior or posterior fascicular blocks. Incorrect Answer Explanations A left bundle-branch block will present with a widened QRS complex >120 ms. There tends to also be tall wide R waves in leads I, aVL, and V5 to V6 with ST de- pressions and T-wave inversions. These findings are not seen in this ECG. A left posterior fascicular block will present with a right axis deviation (nega- tively oriented QRS in lead I and positively oriented QRS in lead aVF). This is the opposite of what is seen in this ECG. Typically, there will be small R waves with deep S waves in leads I and aVL. A right bundle-branch block will present with a widened QRS complex to >120 ms. There is typically an RSR' pattern seen in leads V1 to V2, with ST depression and T-wave inversions. These findings are not seen in this ECG.

question: An otherwise healthy young adult presents after an episode of palpitations. The initial ECG is shown below. Which tachyarrhythmia is most commonly associ- ated with the major pathologic finding on this ECG? Credit: Liang SY, Farzad A. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady WJ, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.
englishExplanation: This patient's ECG shows a shortened PR interval associated with delta waves, which is consistent with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome (WPW). In patients with WPW, atrioventricular reentry tachycardia (AVRT) is the most common tachyarrhythmia, with over 90% of cases being classi- fied as orthodromic (ie, anterograde conduction through the AV node and retro- grade conduction via the accessory path). The opposite direction of conduction, known as antidromic, accounts for the remaining cases of AVRT in WPW patients. Other arrhythmias seen less commonly in WPW include atrial fibrillation (which can cause a serious tachyarrhythmia if involving the accessory pathway) and ventricular arrhythmias. WPW is caused by abnormal conduction through an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent), which allows abnormal, uncontrolled electrical conduction. When a reentry circuit is formed between the normal conduction system and the accessory pathway, supraventricular tachycardia can occur; the direction of this reentrant circuit, as noted above, determines orthodromic or antidromic AVRT. Orthodromic con- duction causes a narrow-complex tachycardia, while antidromic con- duction causes a wide-complex tachycardia that may be difficult to differen- tiate superficially from ventricular tachycardia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Antidromic atrioventricular reentry tachycardia (AVRT) occurs when a reentry circuit is formed and the anterograde conduction moves through the accessory path and the retrograde conduction via the AV node. This results in a wide-complex tachycardia that may appear similar to ventricular tachycardia. Although antidromic AVRT is certainly possible in patients with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, it is much less common than orthodromic AVRT. Atrioventricular nodal reentry tachycardia (AVNRT) is the most com- mon type of supraventricular tachycardia that occurs when a functional reentry circuit occurs within the AV node itself and not through an anatomic ac- cessory pathway. It may be difficult to distinguish AVNRT from orthodromic AVRT. This patient has baseline Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, so ortho- dromic AVRT is most likely. Sinus node reentrant tachycardia (SNRT) is related to a reentry circuit within or near the sinus node. This tachyarrhythmia will have P waves and appear similar to sinus rhythm; SNRT should be considered in any abrupt onset or termination tachycardia that appears to be sinus in nature. This patient's ECG is consistent with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, so the most likely tachyarrhyth- mia is orthodromic AVRT.

question: A 75-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease presents with a 2-hr history of palpitations; he is otherwise asymptomatic. His vital signs include BP 150/84, P 146, and R 13; SpO is 99% on room air. An ECG is obtained and shown below. What is the preferred initial treatment? 2 Credit: alfa md/iStock/Getty Images Plus.
englishExplanation: This ECG shows monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) in a patient who is currently hemodynamically stable. The initial treatment for stable sustained monomorphic VT is generally intravenous administration of antiarrhythmic agents (including procainamide, amiodarone, sotalol, or lidocaine) or synchronized car- dioversion. Procainamide and amiodarone are considered the first-line antiarrhythmic agents in stable VT. Procainamide is a Class Ia antiarrhythmic agent administered at a rate of 25 to 50 mg/min IV with a maximum dose of 17 mg/kg. It should not be used in patients with acute myocardial infarction (MI), long QT interval, or significant left ventricular dysfunction. Amiodarone is the antiar- rhythmic agent of choice in stable monomorphic VT when the patient has an acute MI or severe left ventricular dysfunction. Sotalol is a nonselective beta-blocker with Class III antiarrhythmic properties that is also used in stable VT but should not be given in patients with a long QT interval. Lidocaine is a second-line therapy in sta- ble VT. Synchronized cardioversion may be considered in any patient with sustained VT and is the treatment of choice in unstable VT. Incorrect Answer Explanations Calcium-channel blockers such as diltiazem and verapamil are not rec- ommended in the acute treatment of stable or unstable VT or to aid in the diagnosis of a wide-complex tachycardia. Although they can be effective in rhythm conversion, these medications can cause serious adverse events, such as severe hypotension. Magnesium is the initial treatment of choice in the polymorphic VT tor- sades de pointes. However, it is unlikely to be of use in a patient with monomor- phic VT with a normal QT interval. Unsynchronized cardioversion, or defibrillation, is used in pulseless VT or ventricu- lar fibrillation arrest or where the defibrillator is unable to synch in an unstable pa- tient. Electrical cardioversion in stable patients should be synchronized. Key Points Treat stable VT with intravenous antiarrhythmic agents or synchronized cardiover- sion, and consider the need for procedural sedation. First-line antiarrhythmic agents for stable VT include amiodarone and procainamide. Don't use procainamide and sotalol in patients with a prolonged QT interval.

question: In which condition is a decreased BNP concentration most likely to be found?
englishExplanation: BNP is a counterregulatory neurohormone produced by cardiac my- ocytes in response to the stretching of ventricles and to high end-dias- tolic pressures. For unclear reasons, obese patients produce less BNP than nor- mal, even in those with high left-ventricular end-diastolic pressures. BNP is re- leased into circulation, where it is cleaved into an active BNP and an inactive NT- proBNP. The half-life of BNP is 20 minutes. BNP promotes vasodilation, diuresis, and sodium elimination; suppresses the renin-angiotensin system; and correlates with the presence and severity of heart failure. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cor pulmonale, or sustained right-sided heart failure from pulmonary arteries, will cause BNP elevation from right-sided ventricular dysfunction. Thus, a BNP level may be diagnostically helpful in such patients. A pulmonary embolism causing ventricular dysfunction can elevate BNP con- centrations, typically from right-sided heart failure. For this reason, BNP is often used in risk stratification for patients with pulmonary embolisms. In patients with renal insufficiency, there is a small increase in BNP (due to vol- ume overload and decreased ability to clear metabolites). This is one reason that an elevated BNP is just one piece of information that should be taken in the overall clinical context of the patient when making a diagnosis of heart failure.

question: Which intervention is most appropriate for hemodynamic support of a patient in medication-refractory cardiogenic shock?

options.text: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA)

englishExplanation: Patients who present with cardiogenic shock refractory to medical management should be considered for circulatory support with ECMO. Specifically, venoarterial (VA) ECMO is intended to be a temporary hemodynamic support system to allow for recovery and/or deployment of more definitive therapies. Note that local institutional policies will vary as to which patients are candidates for VA ECMO. Not all patients with refractory cardiogenic shock are appropriate candidates. VA ECMO functions by augmenting or replacing (in the event of cardiac ar- rest) cardiac output. The venous circuit is the afferent limb, which feeds into a system that pumps blood into the arterial system directly via an efferent limb. Oxygenation and removal of carbon dioxide also occur during system transit. VA ECMO in the emergency department generally requires placement of two cannulas. These include a venous cannula that drains from either the IVC (femoral approach) or the right atrium (internal jugular approach) and an arterial catheter, most com- monly placed in the right femoral artery. A small catheter is often used to provide arterial perfusion to the right leg. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hemoperfusion is a form of extracorporeal blood purification in which anticoag- ulated blood is filtered through an adsorbent material, usually activated charcoal. It can be paired with hemodialysis and is run similarly. Hemoperfusion was classically used for removal of toxic substances from the blood, but for this role, it has been supplanted by high-flux hemodialysis in most places. It has no direct role in hemodynamic support for medication-refractory cardiogenic shock. Instead, ECMO is the most appropriate choice for hemodynamic support in this setting. The molecular adsorbent recirculating system (MARS) is a form of hemodialysis intended to act as an extracorporeal liver support. It uses a charcoal filter and dialysate augmented with albumin to remove albumin-bound toxins. MARS is primarily for patients with severe hepatic failure. It has no direct role in hemody- namic support for medication-refractory cardiogenic shock. Instead, ECMO is the most appropriate choice for hemodynamic support in this setting. Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is a temporary endovascular aortic occlusion procedure used to stop life-threatening bleeding distal to the carotid arteries. Depending on the location of balloon placement, it can be used to halt aortic flow from the left subclavian artery and dis- tal (zone I) and more selectively from the pelvis and lower extremities (zone III). It has no direct role in hemodynamic support for medication-refractory cardiogenic shock. Instead, ECMO is the most appropriate choice for hemodynamic support in this setting.

question: A man presents via EMS after a witnessed cardiac arrest. He has Factor V Leiden and is not on anticoagulants. His presenting rhythm shows pulseless electrical activity. Prior to becoming unresponsive, he complained of acute-onset shortness of breath and chest pain. His baseline echocardiogram, which was obtained 1 week earlier, and a bedside echocardiogram are shown. Based on his new echocardiogram, which medication should preferably be administered? Baseline echocardiogram. Credit: Cassandra Mackey, MD. Bedside echocardiogram. Credit: Cassandra Mackey, MD.
englishExplanation: This patient's bedside echocardiogram demonstrates new severe right ventricu- lar dilatation; this finding, coupled with the patient's baseline hyperco- agulable state and prearrest complaint of sudden-onset chest pain and shortness of breath, is concerning for acute pulmonary embolism leading to cardiac arrest. Use of a tPA (or thrombolytic) such as alteplase is indi- cated to reverse the obstructive shock caused by a massive pulmonary embolism. tPAs are medications that accelerate thrombolysis by catalyzing con- version of plasminogen to plasmin. Two common types of tPAs used in the United States are alteplase and tenecteplase. However, thrombolytic medica- tions should only be used if the benefit outweighs the risk of potential uncontrolled bleeding; patients should be screened for high-risk conditions, such as severe active bleeding or recent neurosurgery, before use. Incorrect Answer Explanations Calcium chloride is frequently used as part of empiric medications for undifferentiated pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest to stabilize cardiac membrane conduction in the setting of fatal hyperkalemia. In this case, calcium chloride could be given empirically, but the patient is presenting with signs, symptoms, and echocardiogram findings most suggestive of a massive pulmonary embolism, causing the PEA arrest. Thus, alteplase is more appropriate. Enoxaparin is indicated in many cases of stable pulmonary embolism; however, in this case, it is less preferred. This patient has likely arrested due to a massive pulmonary embolism, which requires immediate thrombolysis. Although there is some controversy about whether and when to anticoagulate patients receiv- ing thrombolysis for a massive pulmonary embolism, most experts prefer heparin over enoxaparin in a situation where the patient is unstable, as you can turn off the heparin. Patients are usually started on heparin following thrombolytic infusion, but anticoagulation is generally held during thrombolysis to reduce the bleeding risk. If a patient is already anticoagulated and requires thrombolysis, thrombolysis should be performed with careful attention to the added bleeding risk. Normal saline would be indicated if this patient arrested due to hypov- olemia. However, there is no evidence of this being the case; this patient's signs, symptoms, and echocardiogram findings are most suggestive of a massive pul- monary embolism, causing the PEA arrest. Although empiric intravenous fluids would be reasonable, alteplase is the most appropriate treatment for the underlying cause.

question: Which condition is most likely to result in cor pulmonale?
englishExplanation: Cor pulmonale, a term that means “pulmonary heart,” is characterized by hypertrophy of the right ventricle or alteration of right ventricular function as a result of pulmonary hypertension or chronic lung disease. The most common underlying condition that causes cor pulmonale is COPD because it frequently results in pulmonary hypertension, which is defined as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure greater than 20 mm Hg. Pulmonary hyperten- sion is divided into classifications based on the cause. Other causes of pul- monary hypertension include left heart disease, pulmonary arterial hy- pertension or obstructions, and mixed mechanisms. The pathophysiology of cor pulmonale results from the increased filling pressure in the right ventricle, which often occurs in patients with lung disease. Cor pulmonale, by definition, alters the function of the right ventricle due to a pul- monary process, and even though left heart failure can lead to right heart failure, left heart failure is not considered cor pulmonale. The most common symptom at presentation is dyspnea on exertion, but cor pulmonale patients may also present with jugular venous distention, peripheral leg edema, loud or split second heart sound, and even hepatomegaly or ascites. In addition to COPD, other primary lung disorders that can ultimately result in cor pulmonale include massive pul- monary embolism, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, connec- tive tissue disease, and pneumoconiosis; several different pathophysiologic mechanisms can lead to pulmonary hypertension and, subsequently, to cor pul- monale. Diagnostic modalities, such as laboratory and radiographic studies, should aim to determine and treat the underlying disease causing cor pulmonale. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dilated cardiomyopathy is primarily an enlargement of the left ventricle that causes left ventricular heart failure, which can lead to right heart failure. However, by itself, dilated cardiomyopathy due to left ventricular heart failure is not considered the cause of the right ventricular structural changes that characterize cor pulmonale. Essential hypertension can cause dysfunction of the myocardium (eg, cardiomyopathy, myocardial hypertrophy), which is a disease process of the left ventricle. Any primary abnormality of the left side of the heart or congen- ital heart disease that causes right-sided ventricular disease is not considered cor pulmonale. Remember, cor pulmonale is a term that means “pulmonary heart.” Left-sided heart failure is not a primary disorder of the lung, which is why it is not considered to be cor pulmonale. Cor pulmonale stems from pri- mary lung disorders that result in pulmonary hypertension and impaired function of the right ventricle, either due to dilation or hypertrophy.

question: A patient presents with chest pain and shortness of breath. The following ECG is obtained. What pattern is present on this ECG? Credit: Reproduced with permission from: Amal Mattu, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with multiple ECG abnormalities, including T-wave inver- sions to III and aVF accompanied by T-wave inversions and ST depressions in the anterior precordial leads. Additionally, there is a right axis deviation (net negative QRS in lead I and positive QRS in lead aVF). This constellation of findings is consistent with right heart strain. This patient has an acute pulmonary em- bolism, leading to these findings on ECG. Additional findings associated with right heart strain include ST elevation to leads III, aVR, and V1 and an incomplete right bundle-branch block (RBBB). Multiple factors can lead to right heart strain. Right heart strain can be acute due to a pulmonary embolism or can be more chronic, as seen in pa- tients with pulmonary hypertension, interstitial lung disease, COPD, and mitral valve stenosis. Identification of this ECG pattern, particularly if these findings are new compared to prior, should prompt investigation into these potential diagnoses. Incorrect Answer Explanations Brugada syndrome is due to a hereditary defect in cardiac sodium channels that puts patients at risk for sudden cardiac death. The ECG of patients with Brugada most often show ST elevation in leads V1 to V3 with a sharp downslope into a T- wave inversion. De Winter T waves are hyperacute T waves to the precordial leads with upslop- ing ST depressions. These are indicative of severe LAD stenosis and impending total occlusion. There are no significant ST elevations on this ECG. The ECG criteria for STEMI in an ECG without a bundle-branch block are ST elevation of ≥1 mm in two or more contiguous leads with reciprocal changes in other leads.

question: High-output heart failure is defined by which physiologic pattern?

options.text: Decreased cardiac output with high systemic vascular resistance
Decreased cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance
Elevated cardiac output with high systemic vascular resistance
Elevated cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance

correctAnswer: Elevated cardiac output with low systemic vascular resistance
englishExplanation: High-output heart failure is an uncommon condition defined by ele- vated cardiac output (CO) in the setting of low systemic vascular resis- tance (SVR). This elevated CO is pathologic because it exceeds physiologic de- mands, resulting in its clinical manifestations. There are a large number of possible causes of high-output heart failure, but many fit into several broad categories: Hypermetabolic states, such as hyperthyroidism and hyperproliferation states (eg, leukemia, lymphoma), are among the best understood. Hyperthyroidism directly stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, resulting in an otherwise unnecessary sympathetically driven hyperme- tabolic state, which explains why beta blockade is an effective treatment for hyperthyroidism. Predominantly peripheral vascular causes, such as acquired (eg, surgi- cal, traumatic) or congenital arteriovenous (AV) fistulas, AV shunts as- sociated with cirrhosis, and Paget disease of the bone, can result in high volumes of blood bypassing intervening capillary beds, which can cause a compen- satory increase in CO to accommodate the reduced SVR associated with the loss of capillary bed circulation. Morbid obesity can cause high-output heart fail- ure by what is thought to be a predominantly peripheral vascular mechanism, but this is not well understood. Pregnancy is also a rare cause. Mixed cardiogenic and vascular causes, including sepsis, can manifest in a variety of ways. It is primarily a distributive process with low SVR that can result in excessive compensatory CO (although ejection fraction may ultimately be depressed) that leads to high-output heart failure. Rarer mixed causes include acromegaly and thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi). Causes with unclear mechanisms include severe, chronic anemia and COPD. Definitive diagnosis of high-output heart failure is largely beyond the capabilities of the emergency department; however, it is important to recognize the signs and symptoms of high-output heart failure and screen for clear, possible underlying causes. High-output heart failure presents similarly as other decompen- sated heart failure states but is much more hyperdynamic and well per- fused. Widened pulse pressure, warm extremities, and tachycardic, bounding pulses are among the more common findings, along with the classic findings of volume overload. Other findings are often specific to the underlying cause. Emergency department management of high-output heart failure in- volves screening for and administering specific treatment for underly- ing conditions such as hyperthyroidism, hyperproliferative hematologic abnor- malities, anemia, sepsis, and traumatic AV fistulas, when applicable. High-output heart failure by other causes, including from a surgical AV fistula, does not usually require immediate, direct intervention, with the exception of thiamine supplemen- tation if wet beriberi is suspected. Instead, if a clear, intervenable cause like sepsis, severe anemia, or hyperthyroidism cannot be appreciated, general management is similar to other decompensated heart failure states: salt and fluid re- striction, gentle diuresis, and admission. Patients who present in shock can be managed similarly with vasopressors. If symptoms persist, more aggressive man- agement should be considered outside of the emergency department. Incorrect Answer Explanations Decreased CO with high SVR is characteristic of a severe hypovolemic state or cardiogenic shock. In severe hypovolemia, the low preload state causes decreased CO and triggers vasoconstriction, resulting in an increased SVR. In car- diogenic shock, the directly decreased CO due to pump failure causes a relative hy- poperfusion, triggering a rise in SVR by the same mechanisms. Decreased CO with low SVR is characteristic of neurogenic shock. Neurogenic shock is due to the loss of sympathetic tone, most often seen in spinal cord injury above the T6 level. This sympatholysis results in a signif- icant decrease in peripheral vascular tone as well as a diminished ability to augment CO, often presenting with hypotension and bradycardia. Acute fluid resuscitation and vasopressors (preferentially norepinephrine) should be used to maintain a MAP of 85 mm Hg to 90 mm Hg to enhance spinal cord perfusion. Elevated CO with high SVR is seen with milder sympathetic activation states, such as acute stress or sympathomimetic drug use. Extreme sym- pathetic activation, such as in hyperthyroidism, can result in high-output heart fail- ure with different hemodynamic characteristics.

question: Which laboratory finding is an independent predictor of an adverse event in acute heart failure?
englishExplanation: Patients with acute heart failure (AHF) can have a variety of abnormal laboratory test results. Renal function can worsen in up to 25% of patients with heart failure, and an elevation of serum creatinine or BUN is a strong predic- tor of adverse outcomes, including death and extended hospital stay, with a 7% increase in mortality rate for every 10 mL/min decrease in glomerular fil- tration rate. Other abnormalities can include elevation in troponin or lactate, which is associated with worse outcomes. In patients with troponin elevation alone and no ischemic ECG findings, troponin elevation is not necessarily diagnostic for myocardial infarction. Abnormalities in liver function can occur in up to 75% of patients due to systemic congestion and increased portal pressures. Incorrect Answer Explanations Thrombocytopenia can be caused by another hematologic abnormality and is not directly related to adverse events in heart failure. Chronic ane- mia, however, can lead to heart failure due to decreased oxygen delivery to the tissues. A serum sodium level of 136 mEq/L does not meet the definition of hyponatremia. The trials note that a chronic hyponatremia (serum sodium level of ≤134 mEq/L) is associated with worse outcomes in AHF. Elevated WBC counts can be related to many etiologies, such as an infection that can lead to worsening heart failure. The elevated WBC count is not an independent variable.

question: A 70-year-old woman with severe pulmonary hypertension presents with dysp- nea and lightheadedness. Her vital signs include BP 95/58 (MAP 70), P 112, and R 26; SpO is 82% on 4-L nasal cannula. On examination, she is cool to the touch with noticeable jugular vein distention. POCUS shows a dilated right ventricle. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
englishExplanation: This patient is experiencing decompensated right ventricular (RV) failure. In chronic pulmonary hypertension, the RV becomes thin-walled, dilated, and highly afterload-sensitive. HFNC is the ideal intervention because it pro- vides a high FiO without the significant increase in intrathoracic pressure associ- ated with positive-pressure ventilation. The primary management priorities are to maintain RV coronary perfu- sion pressure, ensure adequate oxygenation, and minimize further in- creases in pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR). Preventing the RV death spiral is critical. In this spiral, hypoxia triggers pulmonary vasoconstriction, which increases RV afterload and leads to further RV dilation. This dila- tion causes the RV to compress the left ventricle, while systemic hypotension simul- taneously reduces right coronary artery perfusion, causing worsening myocardial is- chemia. Maintaining a systemic MAP that exceeds pulmonary pressures is vital. Furthermore, any intervention that increases intrathoracic pressure, such as NIPPV or intubation, will further increase RV afterload and decrease venous return, often precipitating immediate hemodynamic collapse. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although the RV is traditionally considered "preload dependent," it is extremely easy to overload a failing, chronically dilated RV. Administering 2 L of lactated Ringer solution to a patient who already has evidence of right-sided overload (eg, jugular vein distention) increases RV end-diastolic pres- sure, which pushes the interventricular septum into the left ventricle and worsening RV dynamics. Although NIPPV is a mainstay for left-sided heart failure (to reduce preload and af- terload), it is often harmful in severe RV failure since it increases right- sided afterload and reduces right-sided preload. Similar to intubation, NIPPV can cause hemodynamic collapse. Intubation is one of the most dangerous procedures in a patient with RV failure because the transition to positive-pressure ventilation and the sympatholytic effects of induction agents often lead to immediate car- diovascular collapse and cardiac arrest. The sudden increase in intrathoracic 2 pressure decreases venous return (preload) and increases PVR (afterload), which a failing RV cannot overcome.

question: Which type of cardiomyopathy is best described as a long-term condition charac- terized by impaired ventricular filling, nondilated ventricles, and normal systolic function early in the disease?
englishExplanation: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricles that are not dilated but have impaired ventricular filling. Biatrial enlargement is seen on echocardiogram. Usually, there is no ventricular hypertrophy unless an infiltrative disease (eg, amyloidosis) causes an increase in left ventricular thickness. Early in the disease, the systolic function is normal. Plain two-dimensional echocar- diography may not catch the impaired ventricular filling — Doppler echocardiogra- phy is an effective tool for diagnosis. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient has ventricles that are not dilated. Dilation of the ventricles is pathognomonic for dilated cardiomyopathy, as is suggested by the name. The dilation becomes severe over time, and patients have impaired systolic function and clinical symptoms of heart failure. On echocardiogram, the left ventricle may appear more spherical due to dilation. Left atrial enlargement can also often be seen in conjunction with the other findings described. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), the left ventricular volume is normal or reduced, and diastolic dysfunction is generally present. Technically, HCM includes a variety of conditions characterized by increased ven- tricular wall thickness or mass that are not caused by cardiovascular pathologies, such as hypertension or valve disease. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is also known as apical ballooning syndrome or broken heart syndrome. It is considered a stress-induced cardiomyopathy, character- ized by transient systolic dysfunction of the apical and/or middle segments of the left ventricle.

question: What is a causative agent for myocarditis (inflammatory cardiomyopathy)?
englishExplanation: Commonly known as myocarditis, inflammatory cardiomyopathy is acquired. Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle and is pathologically characterized by focal infiltration of the myocardium by inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes). Episodes are often mild, so they do not always come to medical attention. Coxsackie B is one example of a viral agent that can cause myocarditis. Others are listed below. Bacterial: Beta-hemolytic streptococci (rheumatic fever) Corynebacterium diphtheriae Lyme disease Mycoplasma pneumoniae Neisseria meningitidis Viral: Coxsackie B virus Echovirus EBV Hepatitis B virus HIV Influenza virus Parainfluenza virus Incorrect Answer Explanations Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is a heart muscle disorder, not a func- tion of an inflammatory condition. It is caused by structural abnormalities of the myocardium and causes arrhythmia that is not explained by ischemia, hyper- tension, or valve disease. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), the left ventricular volume is normal or reduced, and diastolic dysfunction is generally present. Technically, HCM includes a variety of conditions characterized by increased ven- tricular wall thickness or mass that are not caused by cardiovascular pathologies, such as hypertension or valve disease. It should not cause a sudden inflammation of the heart. Left ventricular noncompaction is very rare and is a childhood/developmental disorder. Left ventricular noncompaction is an un- classified cardiomyopathy due to an altered myocardial wall. The left ventricle does not develop correctly, and the cardiac muscle in this area is thick and appears spongy. Consequently, there is continuity between the left ventricular cavity and in- tertrabecular recesses. When severe, left ventricular noncompaction can be associ- ated with heart failure and arrhythmias. Left ventricular noncompaction is a slow progression of symptoms and disease that can later require heart transplant, but it should not cause myocarditis.

question: In patients with heart failure and dilated cardiomyopathy, which pharmacologic treatment has been proven to improve survival rates?
englishExplanation: Beta-blockers, specifically carvedilol and metoprolol, have been shown to improve survival in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure. Notably, ACE inhibitors have also been shown to decrease mortality in these patients. Patients should be started on 12.5 mg to 25 mg of metoprolol succi- nate CR/XL daily, with a later goal of 200 mg daily. Incorrect Answer Explanations Chronic therapy for patients with heart failure and dilated cardiomy- opathy may include digoxin, but it does not seem to improve survival rates. Digoxin may be added as part of the treatment regimen for adult patients with mild to moderate heart failure. Its secondary benefit is that it may control ven- tricular rate in patients with atrial fibrillation. Chronic therapy for patients with heart failure and dilated cardiomy- opathy often involves diuretics, such as furosemide, bumetanide, or torsemide. Diuretics allow for patient comfort and treatment of fluid overload sec- ondary to heart failure. However, they do not improve survival rates. Morphine has historically been used in the treatment of congestive heart failure. However, there is no evidence of a mortality benefit, and in fact, some evi- dence of harm. It may be used in a palliative capacity for patients with end-stage heart failure.

question: What is the gold standard for diagnosing myocarditis (inflammatory cardiomyopathy)?
englishExplanation: Technically, an endocardial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing my- ocarditis, but it is rarely used because of its invasiveness. Instead, a review of clinical symptoms and supportive testing can be used. An ECG, echocardiogram, and chest x-ray may be beneficial as supporting tests to reach this diagnosis. Other helpful studies may include a troponin or BNP level (which may be elevated), PET scan, or cardiac MRI. Fever, myalgias, headache, and tachycardia are common signs and symp- toms of myocarditis. Heart failure can develop in severe cases. Chest pain may occur when pericardial inflammation is also present (myopericarditis). Incorrect Answer Explanations A chest x-ray is usually normal or nondiagnostic in myocarditis. In severe cases in which heart failure is present, cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion/pulmonary edema may also be present. Despite this, a chest x-ray is an adjunct that should be added to the overall workup when considering myocarditis as a potential diagnosis. ECG changes will generally be nonspecific in myocarditis. Examples of what may be seen include nonspecific ST-T–wave changes, ST-segment elevation or PR depression from associated pericarditis, atrioventricular block, and QRS interval prolongation. Echocardiography can help to support the diagnosis of myocarditis, but it can be nonspecific and is not the gold standard. In severe cases, symp- toms of heart failure such as myocardial depression and wall motion abnormalities may be seen. If there is concomitant pericarditis, an effusion may be seen. Newer imaging modalities like nuclear imaging with PET and cardiac MRI may be useful to add.

question: A 65-year-old woman with well-controlled hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents with 5 days of chest pain and dyspnea after the death of her husband. She has normal vital signs. Her ECG demonstrates T-wave inversions in the pre- cordial leads and QT prolongation. Apical ballooning and decreased systolic function are seen on bedside ultrasound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: The most common form of stress cardiomyopathy is Takotsubo syn- drome, which is characterized by acute and transient left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction following an emotionally or physically stressful event. Symptoms typically occur within 48 hours of the event, and significant emotional stress is causative in 90% of cases in postmenopausal women. In men, a more com- mon trigger is physical stress. In cases of Takotsubo syndrome, transient dys- function and ballooning of the left ventricle of the heart can be seen (also known as apical ballooning). These regional left ventricular wall motion abnormalities generally resolve within 2 to 3 weeks. The most common ECG findings in Takotsubo cardiomyopathy are deep symmet- ric T-wave inversion in the precordial leads and QT prolongation. In up to 40% of cases, precordial ST-segment elevation is reported. A definitive di- agnosis of Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is based on history, ECG findings, elevated troponin levels, echocardiography showing transient or re- versible left ventricular dysfunction, and the absence of a lesion on coronary angiography. Incorrect Answer Explanations In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), the left ventricular volume is normal or reduced, and diastolic dysfunction is generally present. Technically, HCM includes a variety of conditions characterized by increased ven- tricular wall thickness or mass that are not caused by cardiovascular pathologies, such as hypertension or valve disease. This patient's sudden onset of symptoms are unlikely to be caused by HCM; she has well-controlled hypertension and is noted to be normotensive despite her medical issues. This patient is more likely to have stress cardiomyopathy. Fever, myalgias, headache, and tachycardia are common signs and symptoms of myocarditis. Heart failure can develop in severe cases. Chest pain may occur when pericardial inflam- mation is also present (myopericarditis). Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricles that are not dilated but have impaired ventricular filling. On echocardiogram, there will be biatrial enlargement. The apical ballooning seen in this case is more con- sistent with stress cardiomyopathy. With restrictive cardiomyopathy, there is usually no ventricular hypertrophy unless an infiltrative disease such as amyloidosis causes an increase in left ventricular thickness.

question: A 20-year-old man presents after an urgent care visit where he was told he had an “abnormal ECG.” The ECG is repeated and shown below. What is the diagnosis? Credit: Abella BS, Chelluri J. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with an ECG that is consistent with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC). The three primary findings of ARVC on ECG are prolonged S-wave upstroke; Epsilon wave (extra small wave right after the QRS complex); and T-wave inversions to V1 to V3. ARVC is a genetic cause of heart disease, leading to right-sided heart failure and predispos- ing to ventricular arrhythmias. ARVC predisposes patients to sudden cardiac death. It is particularly important to assess for these findings on screening ECGs in athletes during preparticipation physicals; identification of these findings may prompt referrals to the emergency department. Medications are typically not useful to prevent arrhythmias, and most often, these patients will have an AICD implanted by cardiology. Incorrect Answer Explanations Atrial fibrillation will present with an irregular heart rate and the absence of P waves. This ECG demonstrates a regular rate, and there are P waves present consis- tently throughout. Hyperkalemia will present with multiple ECG findings including peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, and progressive widening of the QRS complex. This ECG is not consistent with these findings and is more consistent with ARVC. Pericarditis most often presents with diffuse ST elevations without reciprocal de- pressions. This ECG does not demonstrate these findings.

question: A 31-year-old man presents after he fainted while mowing his lawn. He remem- bers feeling short of breath before he fainted but is now asymptomatic. A physi- cal examination reveals a healthy-appearing man with a harsh crescendo-de- crescendo midsystolic murmur that increases with a Valsalva maneuver. An ECG is obtained and shown below. Assuming basic laboratory test results are normal, which diagnostic study should be ordered? Credit: William J. Brady, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: The ECG demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy, and Q waves in leads I and aVL are all characteristic and highly suggestive of hypertrophic car- diomyopathy. Such findings should prompt ordering of transthoracic echocardiography to confirm the diagnosis; furthermore, exercise restriction and cardiology referral should also be considered. Hypertrophic cardiomyopa- thy is an autosomal-dominant disease characterized by disorganized cardiac cell ar- rangement, asymmetric hypertrophy of the ventricular septum, and malformations of the mitral valve leaflets. These structural abnormalities can lead to fatal tach- yarrhythmias and ventricular outflow obstruction. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the single most common cardiac cause of death in young athletes. Patients might present with activity-induced shortness of breath, near-syncope, syncope, chest pain, palpitations, and even sudden death. In addition to strenuous activity or exer- tion, other “hyperadrenergic” states can precipitate arrhythmia, including extreme emotions (anger, fright). Thus, the consideration of adrenergically related syncope is a more appropriate screening process than simply exertional syncope. The most specific ECG findings in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are deep, narrow Q waves in the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6). The most common, however, are large-amplitude QRS complexes consistent with left ventricular hypertrophy and associated ST-seg- ment and T-segment changes in the precordial leads. Other ECG findings might in- clude high-voltage R waves in V1 and V2 and deep narrow Q waves in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). In the 12-lead ECG from this case, note the presence of promi- nent R waves and ST-segment elevation in the right to mid precordial leads and Q waves in the lateral leads. The lateral Q waves are very specific in the correct clinical setting for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Beta-blockers, which are the mainstay of therapy, decrease the effect of catecholamines on the outflow gradient.
