Incorrect Answer Explanations Chest x-ray has limited value for stable patients who had a syncopal episode without any respiratory abnormalities. A transthoracic echocardiogram would be a more helpful test in this situation. Coronary CT angiography is useful in some chest pain patients suspected of coronary abnormalities, but it has no value in the initial evaluation of the syncope patient. A transthoracic echocardiogram would be a more helpful test in this situation. Head CT scans have limited utility in the syncope patient who has no neurologic concerns. A transthoracic echocardiogram would be a more helpful test in this situation.

question: A 19-year-old man presents after a syncopal event that occurred while he was ex- ercising. What is the diagnostic test of choice to evaluate for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
englishExplanation: Transthoracic echocardiography is the diagnostic test of choice to as- sess for suspected hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). It can demon- strate the hypertrophic segment, cardiac function, left ventricular outflow gradient, and any associated valvular abnormalities. Cardiac MRI is generally used as a second-line imaging alternative if the echocardiogram provides inadequate views. Although physical examination and ECG can demonstrate characteristic find- ings, these are considered more appropriate for screening than diagnosis. Physical examination may reveal a crescendo-decrescendo midsystolic murmur that decreases in intensity when the patient is squatting. ECG may reveal classic inferior and lateral “dagger” Q waves. This case is a classic presentation of symptomatic HCM: a young adult patient who develops syncope associated with exertion. Symptoms can range from vague fatigue, dyspnea, chest pain, and palpitations to exertional presyncope and syncope. In some patients, the initial presenting event is sudden death, whereas others may remain asymptomatic. Beta-blockers are first-line treat- ments for HCM. They decrease myocardial contractility and heart rate, thereby increasing the diastolic filling period. The pathophysiology of symptomatic HCM is complex. Classically, symptoms are thought to be due to left ventricular outflow obstruction caused by abnormal left ventricular hypertrophy. Increases in heart rate, such as from exertion in this case, decrease the diastolic filling period, thereby compromising left ventricular fill- ing and worsening function. However, the hypertrophy can occur in different loca- tions and have different levels of severity, leading to heterogeneous presentations. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although a CT scan of the chest can theoretically visualize an abnormally enlarged section of the heart, it has no established role in the evaluation of HCM specifically. In this setting, it would be more valuable for ruling out other dan- gerous causes of syncope, such as a large pulmonary embolism. CT coronary angiog- raphy is also sometimes used to evaluate the coronary arteries in the setting of HCM, but this is generally done only after diagnosis. An echocardiogram is the test of choice to diagnose HCM in this patient. The classic ECG findings associated with HCM include left axis devia- tion, left atrial enlargement, and deep and narrow inferior (II,III, aVF) and lateral (I, aVL, V4 to V6) Q waves, known as dagger Q waves. However, these features are neither universally present nor diagnostic of HCM alone; ECG findings are normal in a small percentage of patients with HCM. Although ECG is an essential part of the diagnostic evaluation for this patient, it is not the best diagnostic test for HCM. This patient should receive a echocardiogram to definitively diagnose HCM. Exercise stress testing may be used following diagnosis of HCM for additional risk- stratification purposes, but it is generally not used as an initial diagnostic test. Instead, this patient should receive a echocardiogram to definitively diagnose HCM.

question: A pregnant patient presents with shortness of breath. Which finding is most con- sistent with a diagnosis of peripartum cardiomyopathy?
englishExplanation: The most widely accepted definition of peripartum cardiomyopathy man- dates left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of less than 45%. A variety of terms and definitions have been used to characterize peripartum cardiomyopathy, including toxic postpartum heart failure, Meadows syndrome, Zaria syndrome, and postpartum myocardiosis. However, the definition developed by the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) in 2010 (which was included in the 2018 ESC guidelines) is the most widely used and has been incorporated in position statements and management guidelines. The ESC defines peripartum cardiomyopathy as an idiopathic process with the fol- lowing characteristics: Heart failure at the end of pregnancy or in the 5 months following delivery; Absence of another identifiable cause; and Left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of less than 45%. Incorrect Answer Explanations The working definition of peripartum cardiomyopathy precludes an identifiable cause of heart failure, such as cocaine abuse. Several factors are associated with an increased risk of peripartum cardiomyopathy, including preeclampsia or eclampsia, pregnancy-induced hypertension, cocaine cardiomyopathy, and hypertension disorder. Because the etiology of peripartum cardiomyopathy is idiopathic, identifiable causes (eg, cocaine abuse) are excluded. Peripartum cardiomyopathy typically results in systolic dysfunction rather than diastolic dysfunction. Left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of less than 45% is included in the working definition. Although re- strictive cardiomyopathies (eg, amyloidosis or endomyocardial fibrosis) can result in diastolic dysfunction, peripartum cardiomyopathy is associated with systolic dysfunction. Peripartum cardiomyopathy is rarely seen prior to 36 weeks of gesta- tion; most cases present in the 1st month postpartum. Pregnant patients with un- derlying cardiac disease may present with heart failure earlier in the second trimester; however, first-trimester presentations are extremely unlikely.

question: Which test has the greatest diagnostic value when evaluating a 1-week postpar- tum patient with symptoms of heart failure?
englishExplanation: Echocardiogram should be performed in pregnant and postpartum pa- tients who are clinically suspected of having peripartum cardiomyopa- thy. It usually reveals a dilated left ventricle with reduced left ventricular systolic function and an ejection fraction less than 45%. Other findings may include a dilated left atrium, a left atrial or ventricular thrombus, dilated right ventricle with hypokinesis, mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, or a pericardial effusion. Besides an echocardiogram, the other test that is highly recommended in heart fail- ure and peripartum cardiomyopathy is an ECG. ECG is helpful in identifying car- diac ischemia. Cardiac MRI, cardiac catheterization, and endomyocardial biopsy have limited utility, except in special cases. Incorrect Answer Explanations A measurement of plasma BNP or NT-proBNP may be useful if the diagnosis of heart failure is uncertain. However, it will not provide as much diagnostic in- formation as an echocardiogram and is not as helpful and a good history and physical examination. It is worth noting that elevated BNP levels should be inter- preted with caution because an acute large pulmonary embolism may cause similar elevations of the peptide. Although it is not as useful as an echocardiogram and good history and physical ex- amination in making a diagnosis of heart failure, a chest x-ray may be a useful an- cillary test in select cases. A chest x-ray will typically show an enlarged heart with evidence of congestion and interstitial edema, but an echocardiogram will provide more useful diagnostic information. Elevated D-dimers are generally used to rule-out pulmonary embolism in non- pregnant patients, but they are of less diagnostic utility in pregnant or postpartum patients for whom D-dimers tend to be elevated. An echocardiogram is generally more useful to diagnose heart failure in peripartum cardiomyopathy.

question: Which ultrasound finding is expected in a patient with decompensated peripar- tum cardiomyopathy?

options.text: B-lines in more than two rib spaces limited to the right thorax
E-point septal separation of more than 10 mm
IVC collapsibility index of more than 50%
Tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion of more than 17 mm

correctAnswer: E-point septal separation of more than 10 mm
englishExplanation: The E-point septal separation (EPSS) is a surrogate measurement of left ventricular function. Performed in M-mode, the EPSS measures the minimum distance between the interventricular septum and the anterior leaflet of the mitral valve at its maximum excursion in the ventricular diastole. A value of less than 7 mm is considered normal, and a value of more than 10 mm is suggestive of heart failure. The utilization of POCUS in pregnancy has become increasingly popular because it can be done at the bedside, has minimal radiation exposure to the fetus, and is highly sensitive and specific when performed by a trained operator. In heart failure, performance of the “triple scan” (POCUS of the heart, lungs, and IVC) reveals a specific pattern of abnormalities: reduced left ven- tricular function (<45%), diffuse bilateral B-lines, and a plethoric IVC. Overall, POCUS provides a reasonable, quick bedside screening of a suspected peripartum cardiomyopathy, with the potential of minimizing radiation exposure typical of other imaging modalities. Incorrect Answer Explanations B-lines are hyperechoic lines perpendicular to the pleural margin. They move with respiration and erase the normal A-lines. In acute decompensated heart failure, POCUS of the lungs will depict three or more B-lines per rib space in two or more rib spaces bilaterally across the thorax, a pattern indicative of an acute inter- stitial syndrome due to increased fluid in the lungs. Focal B-lines in a single area or in one lung suggest some other lung pathology (eg, pneumonia or pulmonary embolism). In fluid-overload states (eg, acute decompensated heart failure), the POCUS of the IVC typically reveals a plethoric vessel with a very low collapsibility index. An IVC collapsibility index of more than 50% is typically seen in volume-contracted states (eg, dehydration or sepsis). The tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE) is a validated parameter of global right ventricular function. A normally functioning right ventricle would demonstrate a TAPSE of more than 17 mm. This test is typically per- formed to assess right ventricular strain (eg, pulmonary embolism) rather than acute decompensated heart failure. In peripartum cardiomyopathy, the primary deficit is reduced systolic function of the left ventricle.

question: Which medication is contraindicated in the treatment of peripartum cardiomyopathy?
englishExplanation: Angiotensin II receptor blockers, as well as ACE inhibitors and an- giotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors, pose a high risk of adverse ef- fects to a fetus in every trimester. Although these medications both alleviate symptoms and prolong survival, they are contraindicated in pregnancy. These drugs are part of the standard long-term therapeutic regimen in nonpregnant pa- tients with heart failure, but in a pregnant patient, they could have serious conse- quences to the fetus, including renal failure and death. These drugs should be dis- continued if a patient is attempting conception and for the full term of pregnancy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Beta-blockers are generally considered safe and effective during preg- nancy. Beta-1 selective agents are preferred because they are less likely to interfere with beta-2 mediated uterine relaxation and peripheral vasodilation. There have been concerns with fetal growth restriction, so fetal growth should be monitored. In patients with acute decompensated heart failure, beta-blockers are not initiated. Digoxin is considered generally safe in all trimesters of pregnancy. It can be particularly useful in pregnancy due to increased metabolic demands that exacer- bate heart failure symptoms and because several first-line heart failure therapies are contraindicated in pregnancy. Digoxin dosing may need to be increased to achieve therapeutic levels. Diuretics for the management of pulmonary congestion are safe in preg- nancy. Loop diuretics are preferred over thiazide and potassium-sparing diuretics. Potential maternal complications include volume contraction and hypokalemia.

question: Which medication regimen has been shown to prolong survival and is the treat- ment of choice in a 36-week pregnant patient with peripartum cardiomyopathy?
englishExplanation: Evidence points to the combination of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate as the vasodilator-combination therapy of choice in pregnant patients with hypertension, severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and de- compensated heart failure. Hydralazine and nitrates are both safe for mother and fetus. Although ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers have stronger evidence for clinical efficacy in heart failure, these drugs are contraindi- cated in pregnancy because they are teratogenic. Other drugs utilized in the treat- ment of peripartum cardiomyopathy that are considered safe in pregnancy include diuretics, beta-blockers, and digoxin. Incorrect Answer Explanations Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor that is contraindicated in pregnancy. These drugs pose a high risk of adverse effects to the fetus in every trimester and may have serious consequences, including renal failure and fetal death. The role of aspirin in cardiomyopathy is not as clear as it is in coronary artery disease, and aspirin is not included in standard heart-failure regimens. Ivabradine is a selective sinus node inhibitor that has been shown to reduce the risk of hospital admission and death in heart failure. However, due to the lack of a safety profile in pregnancy, ivabradine is not currently recommended. Metoprolol, a beta-1 selective blocker, is generally safe in pregnancy, and it is less likely to interfere with beta-2 mediated uterine relaxation and vasodilation. However, there is a slight risk of fetal growth restriction, so fetal growth should be monitored by ultrasound if metoprolol is administered. Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist that has been shown to prolong sur- vival in selected patients with heart failure. However, animal studies have shown male fetus feminization. Since data is limited on the safety profile of spironolactone in pregnancy, this drug is best avoided. Digoxin is considered safe in pregnancy. Although it is not a first-line agent, digoxin is particularly use- ful in pregnant patients in whom conventional therapies, such as ACE inhibitors, are contraindicated (due to teratogenicity). Indications for digoxin use include per- sistent symptoms despite treatment and rate control in atrial fibrillation.

question: Which test is most specific for diagnosing takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
englishExplanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, also known as stress-induced cardiomyopa- thy or broken heart syndrome, occurs when the heart experiences a usually transient wall motion abnormality. This mimics a myocardial infarction in the absence of any coronary culprit, pheochromocytoma, or myocarditis. The wall motion abnormalities usually extend beyond the distribution of one coronary artery and classically has apical ballooning that resembles an octopus trap, hence the name “takotsubo.” Of the tests listed, cardiac angiography is most specific for the diagno- sis. Approximately 2% to 6% of all suspected cases of ACS are misdiag- nosed cases of stress-induced cardiomyopathy. Often, takotsubo cardiomy- opathy will present with clinical presentations similar to ACS, such as chest pain and dyspnea. Cardiac angiography is needed to rule out ACS and acute plaque rup- ture as the cause of the patient's signs and symptoms. In the catheterization labora- tory, the classic apical ballooning of takotsubo cardiomyopathy is often seen. Patients have positive troponins and ECG changes, but cardiac catheterization is clear of any culprit lesion. Incorrect Answer Explanations BNP is usually elevated in patients with takotsubo cardiomyopathy. However, this elevation is nonspecific and can be seen in many other disease processes, such as heart failure and other cardiomyopathies. Although 90% of patients with takotsubo cardiomyopathy have abnormal ECG findings, this test alone is not specific enough to make the diagnosis. ST elevations in precordial leads occur in 40% of cases; this mimics an anterior STEMI. Other common ECG changes include deep symmetrical T-wave inversions in the precordial leads, which can mimic ACS. However, QT prolongation, T-wave inver- sions, and ST depressions are also possible. In any patient with chest pain and possible cardiogenic shock, troponin should be obtained. Patients with takotsubo cardiomyopathy often have elevated cardiac en- zymes, but this is nonspecific; elevated troponins can also be seen in ACS and myocarditis.

question: What is the best first-line treatment for a hemodynamically unstable patient with takotsubo cardiomyopathy?
englishExplanation: The best first-line treatment for a hemodynamically unstable patient with takotsubo cardiomyopathy is phenylephrine. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is a stress-induced cardiomyopathy. The apical sparing nature of this disease causes the left ventricle to resemble an octopus trap (takotsubo) used in Japan, which has a circular bottom with a narrow neck. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is often caused by emotional stress (more common in postmenopausal women) or physical stress (more common in men). It is often misdiagnosed as ACS. The pathophysiology of the disease is thought to be related to an acute release of catecholamines, which causes endothe- lial and myocyte dysfunction. This results in a transient and reversible left ventricu- lar dysfunction and myocardial inflammation. Although there is a paucity of evidence regarding which vasopressor or inotropic medications work best for hemodynamic support in takotsubo, a few recommenda- tions are agreed upon. The greatest question for cardiogenic shock associated with takotsubo is related to left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. This is sim- ilar to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, in which there is systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. This occurs in 10% to 25% of patients. This is often worsened by agents with inotropic effects, which lead to further hypotension. Emergent echocar- diography should be pursued to evaluate for LVOT obstruction. Until LVOT ob- struction is ruled out, alpha agonists (phenylephrine), which increase vasoconstric- tion without an increase in inotropy, should be used. For patients with persistent shock, mechanical support (eg, balloon pumps, percutaneous heart pumps, or ECMO) should be considered. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dobutamine is an inotropic agent. Until LVOT obstruction is ruled out, alpha ago- nists (phenylephrine) that increase vasoconstriction without an increase in inotropy should be used, rather than agents with inotropic effects, which will lead to further hypotension. Dopamine has both inotropic and vasoconstrictive effects that are dose dependent. Inotropic agents should be initially avoided in takotsubo because they can worsen LVOT obstruction. In some studies, dopamine was associated with higher mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock; thus, dopamine should be avoided in this population. Epinephrine has both beta and alpha agonist activity, giving it both inotropic and vasoconstrictive abilities. Inotropes should be initially avoided until LVOT obstruc- tion has been ruled out with echocardiography. This is because inotropes can worsen the LVOT obstruction and the hypotension. Additionally, the pathophysiol- ogy of takotsubo is related to a catecholamine excess, and the effects of adding other sympathomimetics such as epinephrine have not been fully established in the literature.

question: Which condition can falsely lower a BNP level?
englishExplanation: BNP is a counterregulatory hormone produced by cardiac myocytes in response to increased end-diastolic pressure and volume, as occurs in the setting of heart fail- ure. ProBNP is released into the circulation and cleaved into biologically active BNP and an inactive N-terminal fragment (NT-proBNP), which has a half-life up to six times that of BNP. Patients with a high BMI tend to have lower levels of BNP and NT-proBNP. Plasma levels of BNP and NT-proBNP correlate with the degree of left ventricular overload, severity of clinical heart failure, and both short-term and long-term cardiovascular mortality rates. Acutely dyspneic patients with BNP lower than 100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP levels lower than 300 pg/mL are very unlikely to have acute decompensated heart failure, whereas those with BNP levels higher than 500 pg/mL or NT-proBNP levels higher than 1,000 pg/mL are very likely to have it. Intermediate levels must be in- terpreted in the clinical context. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients of advanced age tend to have higher levels of BNP and NT- proBNP than younger patients. Patients with a high BMI tend to have lower levels of BNP and NT-proBNP. Patients with pulmonary disease resulting in cor pulmonale and pa- tients with right heart stretch from pulmonary embolism have slightly elevated BNP levels. Neither condition causes a falsely low BNP. As with advanced age, renal insufficiency can falsely elevate BNP slightly. Significant increases in BNP are the result of heart disease.

question: Which medication when used in the out-of-hospital setting has been shown to cause harm in acute heart failure?
englishExplanation: Out-of-hospital use of morphine sulfate for presumed pulmonary edema has been associated with a higher rate of endotracheal intubation, particularly in patients whose conditions turn out to have been misdiagnosed in the field. It is also associ- ated with a longer stay in the hospital, a higher rate of ICU admission, and a greater risk of death. Clinical evaluation and empiric therapy often occur simultaneously in acute heart failure (AHF). Initial management consists of supplemental oxygen, car- diac monitoring, pulse oximetry, and intravenous access. Patients with clinical signs of exhaustion or hypoxia despite supplemental oxygen require respiratory support via either invasive or noninvasive means. Pooled data from several randomized, controlled clinical trials suggest that the use of CPAP (at 5-10 mm Hg) improves hemodynamics by reducing preload and afterload, thereby enhancing left ventricu- lar performance in patients with respiratory distress caused by AHF. Ultimately, CPAP has been shown to reduce the need for endotracheal intubation and is associ- ated with a lower mortality rate. Nitroglycerin is another measure to improve pul- monary edema and the work of breathing. Early administration of furosemide in acute pulmonary edema appears to have very little benefit and might result in short- term complications because many patients with AHF are intravascularly volume de- pleted (the volume has been redistributed to the wrong area, such as the lungs). Incorrect Answer Explanations Aspirin has not been found to be harmful in heart failure and should be provided if ischemia is suspected. Other NSAIDs should be avoided due to the risk of renal in- jury and further salt and water retention through their effects on prostaglandin synthesis. A small number of trials have demonstrated rapid improvement in dyspnea after a single dose of sublingual captopril. Significant reduction in blood pressure after in- travenous administration of enalaprilat has also been seen. Nitroglycerin has been proved to be the safest and most effective therapy for pre- sumed pulmonary edema. Compared with placebo therapy in the Vasodilation in the Management of Acute Congestive Heart Failure (VMAC) trial, intravenous ni- troglycerin resulted in marked improvement in dyspnea. The ability of nitroglycerin to decrease preload and produce cardiac vessel vasodilation ultimately reduces my- ocardial effort.

question: A patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction presents with dyspnea, respiratory distress, and hypoxia. Bedside lung ultrasound is shown below. Which respiratory intervention decreases the risk of intubation? Credit: Frances Russell, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: Symptomatic acute decompensated systolic heart failure with pul- monary edema (as evidenced by B lines on bedside ultrasound) and hy- poxia is best treated with NIPPV in addition to standard medical therapy, such as nitrates and diuretics. A 2019 Cochrane Review noted this combination signifi- cantly decreases endotracheal intubation rates and in-hospital mortality com- pared with standard medical therapy alone. BiPAP or CPAP can be used; as of this writing, there is no evidence to suggest one method is superior to the other — both provide ventilatory and oxygenation sup- port. CPAP works by providing constant pressure throughout the respi- ratory cycle, decreasing the work of the inspiratory musculature and in- 0:00/ 0:05 creasing tidal volume by reducing dead space and increasing alveolar ventilation. Additionally, the increased intrathoracic pressure reduces preload and afterload. Unlike CPAP, BiPAP pressures are different between expiration and in- halation. BiPAP has two elements, the inspiratory positive airway pressure (IPAP) and the expiratory positive airway pressure (EPAP), which is conceptually similar to CPAP. The IPAP is always higher than the EPAP. The difference between IPAP and EPAP is known as the delta pressure and is the measure of the ventilatory support the BiPAP is providing. This allows for active augmentation of ventilation with further decreased respiratory muscle workload while also maintaining the ben- efits attributed to CPAP. Patients with coincidental acute hypercarbia may benefit from this additional ventilatory support. Endotracheal intubation is indicated in settings where NIPPV would be contraindicated, such as depressed or altered men- tal status, apnea, and cardiac arrest. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although this patient should be provided oxygen support, high-flow oxygen, such as with nonrebreather mask or HFNC, has no additional value in this circumstance over other forms of oxygen delivery. When given the choice between high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask and NIPPV, NIPPV is the superior choice because it provides oxygen and ventilatory support and can improve outcomes in this setting. Inhaled nitric oxide is a potent, selective pulmonary vasodilator used to treat a variety of right heart and pulmonary vascular conditions, such as pulmonary hypertension. Its mechanism of action is local vasodilation of venti- lated lung, which reduces pulmonary vascular resistance. This improves both V/Q matching and pulmonary arterial forward flow. Although the effect of inhaled nitric oxide on the pulmonary vasculature is similar to that of systemic nitrates, it does not affect systemic preload or afterload. As the left heart is distant from these local pulmonary vascular effects, inhaled nitric oxide is unlikely to provide mean- ingful benefit for acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Instead, NIPPV has several beneficial effects in this setting and should be used early and aggressively. Nebulized bronchodilators are valuable in the setting of bronchospasm, such as with asthma or COPD. However, bronchodilators have no estab- lished role in the treatment of acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Additionally, use of beta agonists such as albuterol would increase cardiac work by beta-1 receptor stimulation, potentially worsening the patient's clinical condition. Instead, NIPPV has several beneficial effects in this setting and should be used early and aggressively.

question: A 60-year-old man presents with chest discomfort. His history is moderately concerning for ACS. His vital signs are normal. The ECG demonstrates normal si- nus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave abnormalities. Initial therapy is started, and laboratory tests are ordered. The patient remains stable, and the ini- tial troponin level is normal. What is the correct approach to treatment, observa- tion, and reassessment?

options.text: Intravenous heparin, oral clopidogrel, and oral aspirin with immediate exercise stress testing
Intravenous heparin, oral clopidogrel, and oral aspirin with serial troponin and 12-lead ECG sampling
Oral aspirin therapy with immediate exercise stress testing, with or without nu- clear imaging
Oral aspirin therapy with serial troponin measurement and 12-lead ECG sampling

correctAnswer: Oral aspirin therapy with serial troponin measurement and 12-lead ECG sampling
englishExplanation: Hemodynamically stable patients with suspected ACS and entirely normal ECG results have a very low rate (1%-3%) of acute myocardial infarction (MI). Thus, management decisions should be based on the total presentation, con- sidering all the features of the patient's data, observing the patient's response to treatment, and reassessing the clinical picture and risk factors. This patient's HEART score is 2, based on one point for age and one point for moderately suspi- cious history. This has an associated 0.9% to 1.7% 30-day risk of major adverse car- diovascular events. A patient who is stable, does not develop concerning issues dur- ing the emergency department stay, has a negative workup with normal serial tro- ponins and ECGs, and does not exhibit signs of worrisome alternative diagnoses can be safely discharged and referred to either a primary care physician or cardiologist for further evaluation. In this setting (ie, stable patient with initially negative evalu- ation), oral aspirin is the most appropriate therapy. Incorrect Answer Explanations In a stable patient with an initially negative evaluation who has remained hemodynamically stable during a period of observation and reassessment, adminis- tering antiplatelet and anticoagulant agents in the emergency department is exces- sive. Of course, this statement does not apply to oral aspirin therapy. The early use of exercise stress testing (emphasis on “early”) is likely not the most appropriate evaluation strategy in a patient with a concerning but stable ACS presentation. Heparin and clopidogrel are unnecessary since the patient is stable. However, monitoring with serial troponin measurements and 12-lead ECG sam- pling is appropriate for this nondiagnostic chest pain presentation. Aspirin is one of the most appropriate initial therapies in suspected ACS; it has a significant ability to favorably affect mortality rates. Without serial troponin measurements and 12-lead ECG sampling, early exercise stress testing at this point in the patient's care is not the most appropriate evaluation strategy for a concerning but stable ACS presentation.

question: Which finding has the highest positive-likelihood ratio for a diagnosis of ACS?

options.text: Radiation of pain to both arms

correctAnswer: Radiation of pain to both arms
englishExplanation: Although it is not diagnostic of ACS, the presence of radiation of chest pain to both arms is strongly suggestive of ACS and presents a high like- lihood for it. A JAMA Rational Clinical Examination Systematic Review found this feature to increase the risk of ACS 2.6x (positive LR 1.8-3.7). In the approach to a patient with suspected acute coronary ischemia, the emergency physician has to consider many factors of the history and examination, such as how the patient de- scribes their symptoms, the patient's medical history, whether there is a family his- tory of cardiovascular disease, what clues the ECG provides, and what abnormalities are noted in cardiac markers. In addition to pain radiation to both arms, other high-likelihood features of ACS include chest pain that is similar to the patient's prior anginal chest pain, change in pattern of pain over 24 hours, diaphoresis, known coronary artery disease (CAD), history of pe- ripheral arterial disease, abnormal prior stress test result, a history of myocardial infarction (MI), hypotension, pulmonary edema, ischemic ECG changes, ST depressions, and elevated HEART score. Incorrect Answer Explanations If a patient presents with classic risk factors for CAD (eg, a medical history of hyper- tension, diabetes mellitus, or hyperlipidemia; a family history of MI before age 50; and smoking), the emergency physician should consider ACS. However, these features are not the most suggestive of acute coronary ischemia, and are not even high-likelihood features for ACS. At most, these features represent inter- mediate-likelihood features. Recent cocaine use is a low-likelihood finding for acute MI. More important acute factors are an abnormal prior stress test result, known CAD, peripheral arterial dis- ease, pain radiating to both arms, and pain similar to prior ischemia. Although T-wave flattening is an abnormal ECG finding, it has a low likelihood for ACS. More important markers are pain radiating to both arms, previous abnormal stress test result, and known CAD, among others. ECG findings with the highest likelihood ratios for ACS include ST depression or ischemic-looking ECG. Key Points Radiation of pain to both arms is strongly suggestive of ACS. Clinical features associated with a high likelihood for ACS include pain radiating to both arms, pain similar to prior ischemia, change in pattern of symptoms over 24 hours, diaphoresis, hypotension, and elevated HEART score. The ECG features on the ACS high likelihood list include new ischemic ECG findings or ST depressions. High likelihood features of ACS from a patient's history include known coronary artery disease, peripheral arterial disease, an abnormal previous stress test, or pre- vious myocardial infarction.

question: What is the most appropriate disposition for patients who are being evaluated for ACS based on their HEART score in the emergency department?

options.text: Admit a patient with a HEART score ≤3 for observation and noninvasive cardiac testing
Admit every patient with chest pain for cardiac testing regardless of the HEART score
Discharge a patient with a HEART score of ≤3 with two negative troponins
Discharge a patient with a HEART score of 4 to 6 and a negative initial troponin

correctAnswer: Discharge a patient with a HEART score of ≤3 with two negative troponins
englishExplanation: Patients with a HEART (History, ECG findings, Age, Risk factors, and Troponin) score of 0 to 3 and two negative high-sensitivity troponins (taken 3 hours apart within 6 hours of onset symptoms) have a <0.4% chance of cardiac-related mortal- ity or myocardial infarction (ie, a Major Adverse Cardiovascular Event [MACE]) and can be safely discharged. The HEART score tool has been validated to predict 30- day adverse events in patients with suspected ACS in the emergency department. However, validation studies of the HEART score revealed the need to add a 3-hr repeat troponin for patients with risk score of 0 to 3 who presented within 6 hours of symptoms onset. This is what is considered a HEART pathway. Multiple studies have shown more than 99% sensitivity of the HEART pathway; a randomized clinical trial has validated the HEART pathway, and no patients had ad- verse cardiac events at 30 days. As in any clinical presentation, it is important to consider all potential diagnoses of chest pain. The HEART score specifically applies to ACS. However, there are multi- ple other causes of chest pain that must be considered and that can be life-threaten- ing if undiagnosed, such as pulmonary embolism or pneumothorax. Incorrect Answer Explanations Most patients with a HEART score of ≤3 do not need to be admitted for further test- ing (eg, noninvasive cardiac testing) to rule out ACS. Patients with a HEART score of ≤3 after two sets of negative troponins can be safely discharged and do not require admission for further evaluation. Not all patients presenting with a history of chest pain need to be admitted, and it is no longer required to admit all patients with a history of chest pain for cardiac test- ing. The addition of the HEART score has helped decrease some of these admis- sions. Multiple studies have shown that low-risk HEART score patients can be safely discharged. Also, there are many causes of chest pain that are not cardiac in nature, some of which do not require hospital admission. Patients with a moderate-risk HEART score (4-6) are at higher risk for adverse car- diac events, and many of these patients should be admitted. If there is clinical con- cern for ACS, a moderate-risk HEART score confers a risk of MACE of >12%. Thus, these patients should be admitted for further cardiac testing. If the patient's troponin is significantly elevated, cardiology should be consulted.

question: A 70-year-old man presents for evaluation of intermittent chest pain episodes over the past month. He is currently pain free, and his last pain episode occurred yesterday while mowing the grass. The following ECG is obtained. What is the best next step in management? Credit: Glass G. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady w, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.

options.text: Perform a CT chest pulmonary angiography

englishExplanation: The next best step in management would be to obtain a troponin level. This ECG demonstrates biphasic T waves to the precordial leads. Deep T-wave inversions or biphasic T waves, particularly in leads V2 to V3, are referred to as Wellens syndrome. This finding in the context of a patient having angina symptoms is concerning for critical left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery stenosis. This finding is associated with a high proba- bility of progression to an acute myocardial infarction within the next month. When this finding is seen, the next best step is to evaluate the patient for acute myocardial ischemia with a troponin level. In patients who have this ECG finding and are not actively experiencing chest pain, the troponin level will often be negative or minimally elevated. If the patient has Wellens syndrome with active chest pain and a positive troponin, cardiology should be consulted emergently as this is more suggestive of active ongo- ing cardiac ischemia. If the troponin is negative and the patient is pain free, cardiology should be consulted and the patient should be started on as- pirin if there are no other contraindications. These patients should be ad- mitted for cardiac monitoring and cardiology evaluation for further workup, includ- ing cardiac catheterization. Serial ECGs should be performed, particularly if the pa- tient develops pain again or if troponin levels are rising. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient is currently pain free. Wellens syndrome is concerning for critical LAD stenosis but is not an STEMI equivalent. In this case, it is best to obtain a troponin level and proceed with cardiology consultation. Ibuprofen would be an appropriate therapy to initiate in the setting of pericardi- tis. Pericarditis on ECG will often appear with diffuse ST elevations without recip- rocal changes. Additionally, the symptoms of pericarditis will trend toward being constant and not episodic over a prolonged period of time. This ECG, as well as the periodic nature of the chest pain with exertion, is con- cerning for coronary artery disease (CAD). In this case, evaluating for CAD with a troponin is the best next step. It is less likely that a CT to evaluate for pulmonary embolism would be positive.

question: What is an absolute contraindication to beta blocker administration within 24 hours of an acute STEMI?
englishExplanation: Absolute contraindications to beta-blockers include hemodynamic in- stability, cardiogenic shock, acute bronchospasm, severe bradycardia, heart block greater than first degree, and overt heart failure. This patient is hemodynamically unstable; in this setting, beta-blockers should be avoided be- cause they may further reduce blood pressure. In hemodynamically stable patients, beta-blockers decrease myocardial oxy- gen demand by reducing heart rate, blood pressure, ventricular fibrilla- tion, and myocardial contractility. They also improve coronary diastolic perfu- sion by decreasing automaticity and slowing conduction, which causes modest bradycardia and prolongs diastole. The American Heart Association has placed a class A recommendation for oral beta-blockers within a 24-hr window of acute myocardial infarction (MI) if no contraindications are present. In patients with additional signs of heart failure, oral beta-blockers should be initiated after stabilization; intravenous beta-blockers have shown no benefit in ACS management. Incorrect Answer Explanations A patient with COPD without wheezing should be given oral beta-blockers within 24 hours. Acute bronchospasm is considered a contraindication for beta- blocker therapy, but this patient has clear lungs and should be given treatment. Patients with first-degree heart block should be given oral beta-blockers within 24 hours if their ejection fraction is preserved and vital signs are stable. Second- and third-degree heart blocks are considered contraindications to therapy, but treatment with oral beta-blockers is considered safe in first-degree blocks. Patients with stable vital signs should be given oral beta-blockers within 24 hours of an acute STEMI. Absolute contraindications to beta-blockers include hemodynamic instability, cardiogenic shock, acute bronchospasm, se- vere bradycardia, heart block greater than first degree, and overt heart failure.

question: A 56-year-old diabetic man with a history of tobacco use presents with chest pain that does not improve with rest. His troponin is negative at 0 hours and 6 hours. An ECG is obtained and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.
englishExplanation: The clinical presentations of ACS range from unstable angina to STEMI. Unstable angina is the presence of symptoms that are concerning for ACS without troponin elevation. Patients with unstable angina may have varying presenta- tions and ECG changes including ST depression, new T-wave inversion, or even transient ST elevation. Distinguishing types of unstable angina. Credit: Infographic: David Yamane, MD; photo: Kiwis/iStock/Getty Images Plus. Incorrect Answer Explanations NSTEMI is characterized by clinical symptoms of myocardial ischemia with an elevated troponin level and no ECG changes characteristic of STEMI. The ECG in NSTEMI may still have ischemic-appearing changes (eg, ST- segment depression, T-wave inversions) or it may appear normal. STEMI is characterized by clinical symptoms of myocardial ischemia with characteristic ECG changes (ie, elevation of the ST segment), which must be in two contiguous anatomical leads. Although the diagnosis of my- ocardial ischemia requires elevation in biomarkers (such as troponin), the initial troponin levels may be nondiagnostic if the patient presents early in the disease course. Stable angina is defined as the clinical characteristics suggestive of ACS (ie, chest pain), that are relieved or resolved by rest. Stable angina will not have an elevation in biomarkers such as troponin.

question: A 50-year-old man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes presents with chest pain. An ECG is obtained and is shown below. Which coro- nary artery is the cause of this patient's symptoms? Credit: David Yamane, MD.
englishExplanation: This patient is having an inferior STEMI, as seen in the ECG with ST eleva- tions in leads II, III, and aVF; this is characteristic of a right coronary artery (RCA) occlusion. Another indicator is that this patient is in a junctional rhythm, indicating atrioventricular (AV) nodal dysfunction. The AV node is sup- plied by the RCA. Other possible complications of inferior wall STEMI include right ventricular infarction and hypotension. Incorrect Answer Explanations This ECG demonstrates inferior wall ischemia, which is inconsistent with circumflex artery occlusion. Occlusions of the circumflex artery will typically cause a lateral STEMI with elevations of leads V5 through V6, I, and aVL. These can also present with reciprocal changes of the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF). This ECG demonstrates inferior wall ischemia, which is inconsistent with left ante- rior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion. Occlusion of the LAD causes an anterior wall STEMI. ST elevation is seen in the precordial leads (V1 through V4) with reciprocal changes in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF). This ECG demonstrates inferior wall ischemia, which is inconsistent with a left main coronary artery occlusion. The left main coronary artery gives rise to both the LAD artery and the circumflex artery. A left main coronary artery occlusion can present with both anterior and lateral STEMI, which cause eleva- tions in the anterior leads (V1 through V4) and the lateral leads (V5 through V6, I, and aVL).

question: Which biomarker is the most specific for an acute myocardial infarction?
englishExplanation: Cardiac troponin is both sensitive and specific for myocardial injury, commonly caused by ischemia. An acute myocardial infarction (MI) is the clinical consequence of myocardial injury from cardiac ischemia. Ischemic injury to cardiac myocytes causes the breakdown of myocyte membranes and the subsequent release of intracellular contents, including troponin, into the bloodstream. Because serum troponin does not begin to rise until 2 to 3 hours postinfarction, multiple measurements may be necessary to determine the presence of an acute MI. The di- agnosis of an acute MI requires both biochemical evidence of myocardial injury and clinical symptoms (ie, chest pain). Biochemically, an acute MI is defined as a tro- ponin level above the 99th percentile of the upper reference limit. Incorrect Answer Explanations CK and CK-MB were the most commonly used diagnostic biomarker tests prior to the use of troponin. However, CK and CK-MB are less specific and sensitive than troponin for the detection of myocardial injury. CK is an isoenzyme present in many muscle tissues, including skeletal muscle. Muscle breakdown can lead to increases in serum CK, making it less specific than other biochemical mark- ers of ischemia. The diagnosis of an acute MI requires a two-fold increase in the concentration of CK. However, older individuals with lower muscle mass may not reach the required rise in total CK, making it less sensitive as well. Although CK-MB is more specific than CK for myocardial injury, it is less specific than troponin. The CK-MB fraction is a combination of the dimers of M and B chains of the CK isoenzyme. CK-MB has a high concentration in heart muscle, making it more specific than overall CK. However, CK-MB can be ele- vated in chronic skeletal muscle injury, such as in dermatomyositis or polymyositis, lowering its specificity for the detection of an acute MI. Highly sensitive troponin, as its name suggests, has higher sensitivity but lower specificity than standard troponin testing. The highly sensitive troponin tests were first approved in the United States in 2017. They have improved early detection of cardiac ischemia and increased the negative predictive value for acute MI. However, the 99% percentile criteria of the upper reference limit for highly sensitive troponins may vary with age, renal function, and sex of the patient, making the optimal cutoff for this test unclear.

question: A 40-year-old man with a history of hypertension and tobacco use presents with substernal nonexertional sharp chest pain without radiation. He has no family history of cardiac disease. His troponin is negative at 0 hours and 3 hours. An ECG is obtained and shown below. According to the HEART pathway, what is the next best course of action? Credit: Mattu A, Tabas JA, Brady WJ, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.
englishExplanation: This patient qualifies for an early discharge with outpatient follow-up. The original HEART (History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, and Troponin) score is a five-ques- tion scoring system, with each question scoring 0,1, or 2 points. This patient scores 0 points for history, 0 points for ECG, 0 points for age, 1 point for risk factors, and 0 points for troponin. With negative troponins at 0 hours and 3 hours, his risk of an adverse cardiac event is low, and he qualifies under the HEART pathway for early discharge. The risk factors included in the HEART score are hypertension, hyperc- holesterolemia, diabetes, obesity, smoking, family history, and atherosclerotic disease. In the original derivation study, a score of 0 to 3 (low risk) was associated with a 2.5% chance of acute myocardial infarction, percuta- neous coronary intervention, coronary artery bypass graft, or death; based on this, discharge of low-risk patients was supported. A score of 4 to 6 points had a 20.3% risk of adverse cardiac events, and a score of 7 or greater had a risk of 72.7%. The HEART score was subsequently validated in several other studies. The HEART pathway combined the HEART score of 0 to 3 (low risk) and a negative troponin at 0 hours and 3 hours to identify low risk patients who were suitable for early discharge. This study found a decrease in length of stay by 12 hours, decreased cardiac testing by 12%, and increased early discharges by 21%. There were no major adverse cardiac events seen within 30 days in those patients identified for early discharge. HEART score calculation. Credit: Infographic: Yanina Purim-Shem-Tov, MD, FACEP; illustration: peterschreiber.media/iStock/Getty Images Plus. Incorrect Answer Explanations Based on the HEART score of 1 and negative troponin tests, this patient has a low probability of an adverse cardiac event within the next 30 days, so hospitalization for coronary angiography is unwarranted. Given this patient's history, ECG, and troponin, his risk for an adverse cardiac event is no more than 2.5%. Since this patient is low risk per the HEART pathway, he does not require admis- sion for stress testing. A select group of low-risk patients with chest pain can be safely discharged early with a reduction in objective cardiac test- ing. This patient's HEART score of 1 and negative troponin testing places him in this low-risk group. The HEART pathway in low-risk patients recommends discharge without further objective testing. Coronary CT evaluates the presence and extent of coronary artery disease using contrast as a means of angiography. This technique has a high accu- racy for detecting obstructive coronary artery disease (>50% luminal narrowing) with high sensitivity and a low rate of false negatives.

question: A 65-year-old man with a history of hyperlipidemia, stroke, and hypertension presents with chest pain. An ECG is obtained and shown below. What medication is most likely to improve the outcome for this patient? Credit: David Yamane, MD; copyright ACEP.
englishExplanation: Of the medications listed, tenecteplase is the most likely to improve this patient's outcome. This patient is having an STEMI, as evidenced by the tombstone-shaped ST-segment elevations in the precordial leads (V1, V2, and V3) in addition to recip- rocal changes in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF). For acute STEMI, reperfu- sion is the most important intervention in the patient's care. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is the recommended choice of the American College of Cardiology, American Heart Association, and the European Society of Cardiology for reperfusion therapy in an acute STEMI. However, if acute PCI is impossible within the optimal “door-to- balloon time” of less than 90 minutes, a fibrinolytic such as tenecteplase should be considered for reperfusion. Fibrinolytics are capable of restoring blood flow in 75% of patients and have been shown to reduce mortality up to 30%. They are most effective within 3 hours of symptom onset but may be used up to 12 hours after symptom onset. Fibrinolytic therapy should not be delayed for the results of cardiac biomarkers. The first fibrinolytic agent was streptokinase; however, newer fibrinolytic options such as tenecteplase or reteplase are preferred for their side effect profile. High-risk pa- tients should still undergo diagnostic coronary angiography and PCI, which may re- quire transfer to a PCI-capable facility. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although aspirin is an important treatment for STEMI, reperfusion therapy more dramatically improves outcomes. Aspirin is an antiplatelet therapy that inhibits platelet adhesion and aggregation, which are early steps in the formation of a coro- nary artery thrombus. Patients with an STEMI should be given 162 to 325 mg of aspirin as well as another agent for dual-antiplatelet therapy. Clopidogrel is a P2Y12 receptor antiplatelet agent. Although dual-antiplatelet ther- apy is an important treatment, reperfusion is more vital to managing an STEMI. Clopidogrel is a commonly used second antiplatelet agent used for dual- antiplatelet therapy in conjunction with aspirin. Platelet adhesion and ag- gregation are responsible for early thrombus formation, so antiplatelet agents are crucial in the prevention of thrombus formation. Other newer generation an- tiplatelet agents (such as ticagrelor and prasugrel) are also used for dual-antiplatelet therapy. Heparin is an anticoagulant used to treat intraluminal thrombosis from the rup- tured atherosclerotic plaque causing STEMI, but it is not the medication most likely to improve this patient's outcome. Anticoagulants are recommended for all STEMIs because they reduce the risk of acute vessel closure due to thrombosis. Heparin is recommended as a part of STEMI treatment as an adjunct to reperfusion. Other common anticoagulant therapies are low-molecular-weight heparin, bivalirudin, and fondaparinux.

question: A 58-year-old patient presents with chest pain. ECG shows 1-mm ST depression to the inferior leads without ST elevations. A high-sensitivity troponin results as 900 ng/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with chest pain and ECG changes that are concerning for ischemia (ie, ST depressions with an elevated troponin). There are no ST eleva- tions, so this is not diagnostic of an STEMI and, instead, would be con- sidered a NSTEMI. There are multiple ECG changes that are associated with my- ocardial ischemia, including ST elevations, ST depressions, T-wave inversions, biphasic T waves, and hyperacute T waves. Conduction and rhythm disturbances may also occur in myocardial ischemia, including new onset of bundle-branch blocks, atrioventricular (AV) nodal conduction blocks, bradycardia, atrial fibrilla- tion, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation. NSTEMIs should be managed similarly to STEMIs. Cardiology should be emergently consulted, and the patient should be treated with antiplatelet agents and heparin, depending on the clinical situation and the recommendations of cardiol- ogy. These patients are likely to go for cardiac catheterization as well, but the time- line will be determined by cardiology. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with stable angina present with anginal symptoms that are stable over time. Typically, this is chest pain or other symptoms that occur with exertion and are predictably relieved with rest. In these cases, the ECG should be normal, and the troponin will be negative. In patients with a STEMI, ST elevations are seen on ECG in addition to elevated troponins. There are no ST elevations in this case, making it more consistent with NSTEMI. Unstable angina suggests that the patient with angina symptoms is having a change in their symptoms or is developing symptoms at rest. The ECG may show nonspecific changes, but the troponin will be negative.

question: A 60-year-old woman presents with severe chest pain. The following ECG is ob- tained. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: copyright ACEP.
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with chest pain and an ECG that shows hyperacute T waves to the precordial leads with upsloping ST depressions, and there may be re- ciprocal subtle ST elevation in aVR. These findings are consistent with De Winter T waves. These are considered an STEMI equivalent and should prompt emergent cardiology consultation and treatment of myocardial infarction. De Winter T waves are concerning for acute left anterior descending (LAD) coro- nary artery occlusion. Most often, these patients will be taken emergently to the catheterization laboratory by cardiology. Additional care should be provided, in- cluding troponin levels and antiplatelet medications per hospital protocol. De Winter T waves are also suggestive of an evolving STEMI, and serial ECGs should be performed for close monitoring. De Winter T waves are considered “hypera- cute T waves,” which refers to T-wave changes associated with acute car- diac pathology. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cerebrovascular accident (CVA) (also known as stroke) is well known to present with ECG changes in some cases. This will typically be deep T-wave in- versions diffusely but can also present with ST elevations. However, this patient has severe chest pain and no noted neurological symptoms, making this diagnosis less likely. Pulmonary emboli will often present with chest pain. ECG findings in acute pul- monary emboli range from normal to sinus tachycardia to signs of right heart strain, such as ischemic changes to the inferior leads and right axis deviation. This patient has De Winter waves to the precordium, which is associated with acute my- ocardial ischemia. Patients with an aortic dissection will typically present with chest pain. Type B aortic dissections predominantly involve the descending aorta and are much less likely to cause ECG changes. Type A dissections may dissect down to the coronary arteries and can cause ECG changes.

question: A 52-year-old man presents with 20 minutes of crushing substernal chest pres- sure and diaphoresis. His vital signs are BP 88/60, P 85, R 18, and T 36.4°C (97.5°F); SpO is 100% on room air. An ECG is obtained and shown below. After providing aspirin and activating the STEMI alert protocol, what is the most ap- propriate next step in management? Credit: William J. Brady, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: 2 Approximately 30% to 50% of inferior STEMIs are associated with right ventricular infarction. This patient is experiencing an inferior STEMI with right ventricular infarction, and signs of acute right heart failure include hypotension, jugular venous distention, and clear lung sounds. Given that the patient is already hypotensive and preload dependent, the correct management is to administer a normal saline fluid bolus to increase preload and improve blood pressure. The patient's history and ECG findings match the diagnostic criteria for STEMI, includ- ing two contiguous leads with ST-segment elevation of more than 2 mm in leads V2 and V3 or more than 1 mm in all other leads. In this case, the inferior STEMI is indicated by the ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. Extension of the infarction into the right ventricle would be indicated by ST-segment eleva- tion in right-sided leads V3R-V6R. There is also evidence of respectively greater ST-segment elevation in lead III compared to lead II, which suggests RV in- farct. These ECG changes require immediate evaluation by a cardiologist for poten- tial percutaneous coronary intervention. Incorrect Answer Explanations Morphine, oxygen, nitroglycerin, and aspirin (MONA) administration with STEMI protocols are appropriate for patients with STEMI who are not preload dependent. However, patients with right ventricular infarction are preload dependent with regard to maintaining adequate blood pressure. Medications such as nitroglycerin and opioids are contraindicated because they can lower preload and subsequently result in worsening hypotension and perfusion. Oxygen is not needed in this case because no respiratory distress is noted and hypoxia is not present. Hyperoxia produced by supplemental oxygen therapy can be detrimental in an STEMI patient. Both can lower preload, re- sulting in worsening heart failure, hypotension, and coronary perfusion. Oral beta-blockers are indicated in STEMI within the first 24 hours of symptoms. However, beta-blockers are not indicated for STEMI patients if they demonstrate signs of cardiogenic shock or heart failure. This patient is hypoten- sive and has signs of right-sided heart failure with distended neck veins. Vasopressor therapy as the initial choice for resuscitation of a hypotensive MI is rarely correct. In this particular situation, the patient is experiencing an inferior STEMI with right ventricular infarction. In such settings, the patient is preload dependent and requires initial intravenous fluid for initial resuscitation. Key Points Patients with right ventricular infarctions are preload dependent and susceptible to worsening hypotension via nitrates and opioids. The diagnostic criteria for STEMI are two contiguous leads with ST-segment eleva- tion of more than 2 mm in leads V2-V3 or more than 1 mm in all other leads. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in STEMI patients with hypotension or heart failure.

question: In addition to aspirin and heparinization, what is the most appropriate interven- tion for a patient with an acute STEMI pending imminent percutaneous coronary intervention?
englishExplanation: Before the patient undergoes percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for an acute STEMI, oral antiplatelet agents and anticoagulant therapy should be administered. The preferred oral antiplatelet agents are tica- grelor and prasugrel, which both show superiority to clopidogrel in head- to-head clinical trials. Ticagrelor and prasugrel both antagonize P2Y12 adenosine diphosphate receptors on platelets, preventing platelet aggregation. Oral an- tiplatelet agents are better studied and much longer lasting compared to intra- venous agents, such as cangrelor. Consequently, oral antiplatelet agents are preferred under routine conditions. Incorrect Answer Explanations Alteplase is a recombinant tPA that acts as a fibrinolytic agent; other fibrinolytic agents include tenecteplase and streptokinase. Fibrinolysis is appropriate for treating an acute STEMI, but only in the context of significant delay (>120 minutes from arrival) to undergoing PCI. In this case, imminent PCI is pending, making fibrinolysis unnecessary. This patient should receive ticagrelor to complete antiplatelet initiation prior to PCI. Cangrelor is an intravenous P2Y12 receptor antagonist with a similar mechanism of action to ticagrelor. Cangrelor is rarely used because it has a short duration of ac- tion, and no study has yet shown it to be superior to oral antiplatelet agents. Reasons to consider intravenous cangrelor include a need for rapid-onset antiplatelet effects, an inability to tolerate oral administration, shock (due to de- creased GI absorption), and a desire for a short-acting antiplatelet agent. Alternatively, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors such as tirofiban can be considered, but these agents are even less commonly used outside of the cardiac catheterization laboratory. Any decision to deviate from oral antiplatelet therapy should be directed by the consulting cardiologist and established hospital protocols. In this circum- stance, this patient should be given ticagrelor to complete antiplatelet initiation prior to PCI. Rivaroxaban is an oral Xa inhibitor used as a long-term anticoagulant. Initiation of oral anticoagulants can have long-term benefits for patients with ACS not undergo- ing PCI. However, it is inappropriate to initiate rivaroxaban in the setting of an acute STEMI. As noted, heparinization was already initiated for this pa- tient, and heparin is the preferred anticoagulant; additional oral anticoagulation is unnecessary. This patient should be given ticagrelor to complete antiplatelet initia- tion prior to PCI.

question: What is the most appropriate disposition plan for an alert 75-year-old patient with chest pain and stable vital signs who presents with the following ECG? Credit: alfa md/iStock/Getty Images Plus.
englishExplanation: This patient is having an acute STEMI. ST-elevations can be seen in the infe- rior leads, with reciprocal changes also present. This patient needs emergent percu- taneous coronary intervention (PCI). Aspirin should be given, along with pain con- trol. Unfractionated heparin can be administered prior to PCI but should not delay sending the patient to the catheterization laboratory. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient is having an acute STEMI and should be sent for emergent PCI. It would be inappropriate to admit them for an inpatient consultation. This patient is having an acute STEMI and should be sent for emergent PCI. The ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without evidence of heart block and arrhyth- mia; an electrophysiology consultation is not indicated. This patient is having an acute STEMI and should be sent for emergent PCI. They are stable and do not have any immediate ICU needs. Their immediate desti- nation should be the catheterization laboratory.

question: A 60-year-old patient presents with chest pain and diaphoresis. What abnormal finding is seen on their ECG? Credit: copyright ACEP.
englishExplanation: This ECG is consistent with De Winter T waves, which are described as upsloping ST depressions in the precordial leads associated with tall, upright T waves. De Winter T waves are concerning for left anterior descending (LAD) coro- nary artery occlusion. This is considered a “STEMI equivalent.” As with any case, this ECG finding should be interpreted in the clinical context of the patient. Comparison to a prior ECG, if available, is important as are any abnormal findings found on a presenting ECG. This patient is presenting with symptoms con- cerning for myocardial ischemia. Those symptoms accompanied by their ECG show- ing De Winter T waves are concerning for an STEMI, and cardiology should be emergently consulted. In addition to noting the De Winter T wave pattern, there may be reciprocal ST ele- vation to aVR. This may be subtle and is noted on this patient's presenting ECG. De Winter T waves are considered “hyperacute T waves,” which refers to T- wave changes associated with acute cardiac pathology. Incorrect Answer Explanations An inferior STEMI will present with ST elevation to the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). ST elevation is not present in the precordial leads on this patient. Left bundle-branch block (LBBB) is associated with a QRS duration of 120 ms or greater, deep S wave in V1, and a broad notched or slurred R wave in V6. This ECG has normal QRS duration and is inconsistent with a LBBB. Wellens syndrome is characterized by biphasic or deeply inverted T waves to V2 to V3. This is concerning for a developing myocardial infarction.

question: A 70-year-old man presents with chest pain. He has a history of hypertension and coronary artery disease, and he has been having exertional chest pain for the past 2 days associated with diaphoresis. An ECG is obtained and is concerning for STEMI. How would this myocardial infarction (MI) best be characterized? Credit: Levis JT, Garmel GM. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with ST elevation in leads I and aVL with reciprocal ST depression and T-wave inversion in lead III. This is characteristic of a “high lateral” myocardial infarction (MI). High lateral MIs typically present with ST elevation in leads I, aVL, and possibly, V2. Typically, there will be reciprocal changes (ie, ST depression and T-wave inversions) to inferior leads, par- ticularly lead III. High lateral MIs usually suggest occlusion of the first di- agonal branch (D1) of the left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery. This may also be seen in occlusion within the left circumflex artery. It is im- portant to interpret any ECG in the clinical context of the presenting patient, includ- ing presenting symptoms; prior ECGs should also be compared, if available. Incorrect Answer Explanations Anterior MIs will most often present with ST elevation in the precordial leads. Anterior MIs are most commonly associated with occlusion of the LAD coronary artery. Inferior MIs will present with ST elevation in the inferior leads, particularly leads II, III, and aVF. The most commonly involved artery in inferior MIs is the right coronary artery (RCA). Posterior MIs will have elevation on posteriorly placed leads (referred to as V7, V8, and V9). These leads should be obtained when a standard 12-lead ECG shows ST depression or hyperacute T waves in leads V1 to V3 without ST elevation in other leads. The most commonly involved artery is the posterior descending artery branch of the RCA.

question: A patient presents with severe chest pain. An ECG shows a left bundle-branch block. Which ECG criteria would be concerning for an acute myocardial infarc- tion when applying the modified Sgarbossa criteria?

options.text: Concordant ST depression of ≥1 mm in lead III
Discordant ST depression in leads V2 and V3
Discordant ST elevation of ≥1 mm that is 10% the amplitude of the preceding S wave
Discordant ST elevation of ≥1 mm that is 30% the amplitude of the preceding S wave

correctAnswer: Discordant ST elevation of ≥1 mm that is 30% the amplitude of the preceding S wave
englishExplanation: The Sgarbossa criteria were initially designed to assist in identifying pa- tients having an acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in the setting of a left bundle-branch block (LBBB). The original criteria were specific for AMI but were not sensitive. Those original criteria were concordant ST elevation >1 mm in leads with a positive QRS, concordant ST depression in leads V1 to V3, and exces- sively discordant ST elevation of >5 mm in leads with a negative QRS. The criteria were further adjusted into the Smith-Modified Sgarbossa criteria to improve sensi- tivity of the criteria. The modified Sgarbossa criteria are: Concordant ST elevation of ≥1 mm in any lead with a positive QRS complex Concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in leads V1 to V3 Discordant ST elevation of ≥1 mm in any lead with the ST elevation being at least 25% of the amplitude of the preceding S wave (ST:S ratio of ≥0.25) Meeting any of the modified criteria is considered positive and should be considered concerning for an AMI in the appropriate setting. The third modified criterion has a sensitivity reported of 91% compared to the previous defi- nition in the original Sgarbossa criteria that had a sensitivity of 50% to 60%. Incorrect Answer Explanations Concordant ST depression is a criterion in the modified Sgarbossa criteria. However, this is only applicable to leads V1 to V3, not to lead III. Discordant ST depression does not factor into the modified Sgarbossa criteria. The only ST depression criterion in the modified set of criteria is ST depression ≥1 mm in leads V1 to V3. Discordant ST elevation of ≥1 mm that is 10% the amplitude of the preceding S wave does not meet the threshold of at least 25%. The third criteria of the modi- fied Sgarbossa criteria requires the ST elevation be at least 25% of the amplitude of the preceding S wave.

question: What decision rule should be utilized when assessing an ECG for signs of an acute myocardial infarction in the setting of a left bundle-branch block?
englishExplanation: The Smith-modified Sgarbossa criteria were developed to improve the sensitivity of detecting acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in the setting of a left bundle-branch block (LBBB). These criteria are: Concordant ST elevation of ≥1 mm in any lead with a positive QRS complex Concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in leads V1 to V3 Discordant ST elevation of ≥1 mm in any lead with the ST elevation being at least 25% of the amplitude of the preceding S wave (ST:S ratio of ≥0.25) It is challenging to identify AMI in the setting of LBBB, as multiple leads will demonstrate ST elevations and reciprocal changes can be difficult to identify. The original rule developed was the Sgarbossa criteria. Although this rule is specific, it lacks sensitivity. The modified Sgarbossa criteria are much more sensitive when used to evaluate for AMI. Incorrect Answer Explanations The Duke criteria are used to diagnose infective endocarditis. These are made up of major and minor criteria. The major criteria are blood cultures positive for an organism associated with infective endocarditis and echocardiographic findings consistent with endocarditis. The PERC rule is used to rule out low-risk patients for pulmonary embolism (PE). Any positive answer to the rule out criteria indicates the possibility of PE, and further testing is required. As a reminder, the PERC criteria are age ≥50, heart rate ≥100, SpO <95% on room air, unilateral leg swelling, hemoptysis, recent surgery or trauma, history of venous thromboembolism, and hormone use. S1Q3T3 is an ECG finding that has been associated with pulmonary embolism. This refers to the presence of an S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III, and a T-wave inversion in lead III.

question: A 56-year-old man presents with severe chest pain of 6 hours' duration. His vital signs include BP 68/38 and SpO 92%. An ECG is obtained and shown below. Transfer to another hospital where cardiac catheterization is available has a door-to-balloon time of 90 minutes. Concurrent with blood pressure stabiliza- tion, which intervention is the best next step? Credit: Heather Rozzi, MD, FACEP.

options.text: Coronary artery bypass grafting as soon as possible
Fibrinolytic therapy now with admission to the ICU
Fibrinolytic therapy with immediate transfer for percutaneous coronary intervention
Immediate transfer for primary percutaneous coronary intervention

correctAnswer: Immediate transfer for primary percutaneous coronary intervention
englishExplanation: Patients with STEMI and cardiogenic shock or severe heart failure initially seen at hospitals without percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) capabilities should be transferred for cardiac catheterization and revascularization as soon as possible, regardless of time delay from STEMI onset. This patient is hy- potensive, thus in cardiogenic shock. His ECG shows significant anterolateral ST- segment elevation and inferior reciprocal change. Transfer for PCI can be achieved in less than 120 minutes, so he should be transferred immedi- ately without fibrinolytics. Immediate transfer to a PCI center is also recommended for patients without shock if the symptoms have been present for less than 12 hours and the first physician contact-to-balloon time is expected to be less than 120 minutes. Generally, transfer for primary PCI (the preferred strategy in STEMI) is indicated in STEMI patients but is related to the total STEMI duration. Early in STEMI, the recommended time to reperfusion therapy is quite short — if the dura- tion of the STEMI is less than 2 hours, PCI should be initiated in 60 min- utes or less, and if the duration of the STEMI is 2 to 3 hours, PCI should be initi- ated within 120 minutes. Later in the STEMI time course, longer time periods are allowed: after 3 hours of STEMI, PCI should be initiated within 120 minutes. Incorrect Answer Explanations Emergency coronary artery bypass grafting within 6 hours of symptom onset may be considered in patients with STEMI who do not have car- diogenic shock and are not candidates for PCI or fibrinolytic therapy. This pa- tient is demonstrating signs of cardiogenic shock and can be transferred for PCI within 120 minutes, so he should be transferred for primary PCI. Because this patient in cardiogenic shock can undergo PCI within 120 minutes, fibrinolytic therapy is not indicated. In the absence of contraindi- cations, fibrinolytic therapy should be started for patients with STEMI and onset of ischemic symptoms within the previous 12 hours when it is anticipated that primary PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes. In the absence of contraindica- tions (eg, prior intracranial hemorrhage, known malignant intracranial neoplasm, or suspected aortic dissection) and when PCI is unavailable, fib- rinolytic therapy is reasonable for patients with STEMI if there is clinical or ECG evidence of ongoing ischemia within 12 to 24 hours of symptom onset and a large area of myocardium at risk or hemodynamic instability. Multiple studies have investigated the role of facilitated PCI (full-dose or par- tial-dose fibrinolysis followed by immediate transfer to a PCI-capable facility for PCI) in the management of STEMI. Generally, this reperfusion strategy has failed to show a benefit when giving full-dose or partial-dose fib- rinolytic agents with planned PCI within 90 to 120 minutes as compared to PCI alone, so it is not recommended.

question: What ECG change occurs in posterior wall infarctions?

options.text: Biphasic T waves or deep T-wave inversions in V2
J-point depression with prominent T waves in V2 to V3
ST-segment depression in V1 to V3
ST-segment elevation in V1 to V3

correctAnswer: ST-segment depression in V1 to V3
englishExplanation: A posterior wall infarction occurs in conjunction with inferior or lateral wall myocardial infarction (MI) and is seen in 15% to 20% of all infarctions. Lead V1 is opposite the posterior wall, resulting in acute ST-segment depression in V1, rather than ST-segment elevation when the posterior wall experiences acute is- chemia. Similarly, the normally inverted T wave seen in lead V1 “inverts” and appears as a tall upright T wave. ST-segment depression in V2 to V3 may also be seen. Other ECG findings in posterior wall MI include an RS ratio >1 in V1, V2, and V3, so prominent R waves are often noted. If additional ECG leads V8 and V9, which “look” at the posterior wall, are recorded, then ST-segment elevations will be seen. Posterior wall MI results from occlusion of the right coro- nary artery or its posterior descending branch, or blockage of the left circumflex artery. Treatment of a posterior wall infarction should be similar to treatment of an inferior wall MI. These patients can present with atypical symptoms of nausea and vomiting rather than chest pain. Incorrect Answer Explanations Biphasic T waves or deep T-wave inversions in V2 are seen in Wellens syndrome. These changes are usually seen in the anterior precordial leads, which are indicative of left anterior descending artery stenosis. These ECG changes would not be found in a posterior wall infarction. J-point depression with prominent T waves in V2 to V3, coupled with ST-elevation in aVR, refers to de Winter presentation and is indicative of left anterior descending artery stenosis. These changes would not be found in a posterior wall infarction. ST-segment elevation in V1 to V3 is seen in an anterior wall STEMI and not a posterior wall infarction. Instead, ST-segment depression in V1 is more likely to be seen. Key Points ST-segment depression in V1 to V3 may indicate a posterior wall infarction.
