Posterior wall infarctions often accompany inferior myocardial infarctions and should be treated similarly. If a posterior myocardial infarction is suspected, leads V8 and V9 should be ob- tained via ECG.

question: A 54-year-old man presents with chest heaviness, nausea, and vomiting. His vital signs include BP 90/60 and P 58; SpO is 99% on room air. His lungs are clear. The patient is given aspirin. An ECG reveals a 2-mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF, with reciprocal ST depressions and inverted T waves in aVL, V2, and V3. Which pharmacotherapy should be initiated?
englishExplanation: This patient has ECG findings that indicate an inferior wall myocardial infarc- tion (MI). In the absence of congestive heart failure (CHF), the first step in man- agement should be to administer an adequate fluid bolus to raise and maintain the patient's blood pressure; repeated small boluses of normal saline may be needed. Once blood pressure is increased, small doses of nitrates or opiates may be 2 administered to alleviate chest pain, with careful continued monitoring of blood pressure. Patients who are unresponsive to a fluid bolus or who are hy- potensive with signs of CHF (cardiogenic shock) may require pressor support. In the setting of inferior wall MI, right ventricular ischemia and dys- function are possible. Bradycardia can also be associated with an MI due to in- volvement of the right coronary artery, which provides perfusion to the sinoatrial (SA) node. Incorrect Answer Explanations The use of dopamine is likely to increase the patient's heart rate and in- crease the work of the infarcting heart. The initial management for this patient's hypotension is intravenous fluids. Morphine is effective at reducing chest pain but can cause vasodilation, which can further reduce preload and likely worsen hypotension. This ef- fect is thought to be due to histamine and direct effect on vascular smooth muscle. Additionally the dose of 10 mg is too high to start in a patient with hypotension. It should be avoided in this hypotensive patient. Instead, intravenous fluids should be started using normal saline. Nitroglycerin, which is commonly used to reduce chest pain, causes va- sodilation that will reduce preload and worsen hypotension. It should be avoided in this hypotensive patient. Instead, intravenous fluids should be started using normal saline.

question: A 68-year-old man presents with left-sided chest pain and shortness of breath at rest that started 5 hours ago. His vital signs include BP 110/68, P 100, and R 18; SpO is 100% on room air. Physical examination is unremarkable. An ECG is no- table for a left bundle-branch block. Which additional ECG criteria would suggest an acute myocardial infarction?

options.text: Concordant ST depression of 2 mm in lead aVR
Concordant ST depression of 3 mm in leads V1 to V3
Discordant ST elevation in positive QRS leads of 2 mm
Discordant ST elevation of 2 mm with negative preceding 12 mm S wave

correctAnswer: Concordant ST depression of 3 mm in leads V1 to V3
englishExplanation: Diagnosing acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in patients with a left bundle-branch block (LBBB) remains challenging. The Sgarbossa criteria were developed to define ECG criteria that are specific to AMI in the setting of a LBBB. The three original criteria that are part of the Sgarbossa rule are: ST-segment elevation of >1 mm concordant with the QRS complex in at least one lead (5 points) Concordant ST-segment depression of >1 mm in lead V1, V2, or V3 (3 points) Discordant ST-segment elevation >5 mm in at least one lead with a negative QRS (2 points) These rules were modified to improve accuracy, and they are now called the “Smith-modified Sgarbossa criteria.” In the Smith-modified version, the first two criteria change to be “≥1 mm.” The last criteria changed to “Discordant ST- segment elevation of ≥1 mm in at least one lead where the ST elevation is at least 25% of the amplitude of the preceding negative S-wave (2 points).” For example, it would be a positive finding if lead III showed a negative S wave of 8 mm and ST ele- vation of 3 mm. An accurate diagnosis of ischemia requires a minimum score of 3. To interpret the Sgarbossa criteria, it is important to understand the meaning of “concordant” and “discordant.” “Concordant” refers to the ST segment going in the same di- rection as the QRS complex (ie, ST elevation in a lead with a positive QRS). “Discordant” is the opposite, referring to the ST segment going in the opposite direction of the QRS complex (ie, ST depression in a lead with a positive QRS). The best strategy for detecting acute MI includes comparing old ECGs, examining serial ECGs, and understanding the ST-segment changes of LBBB; if the patient has a history or presentation that suggests ACS, consider a cardiology consultation. The ECG criteria for LBBB are: QRS complex longer than 0.12 second; abnormal QRS morphology in the left precordial leads (V5 and V6) and left limb leads (I, aVL); and QS or rS pattern in the right precordial leads (V1 and V2). Incorrect Answer Explanations For Sgarbossa criteria, concordant ST-depression evaluation is only applied to leads V1, V2, or V3. This finding in aVR would not be suggestive of AMI be- cause it does not fit into the Sgarbossa rule. There cannot be “discordant” ST elevation when the QRS is positive. Definitionally, ST elevation with a positive QRS would be termed “concordant,” given both the ST segment and QRS complex are oriented in the same direction. In leads with a negative QRS, there must be “excessive” discordant ST elevation to satisfy the modified Sgarbossa criteria. This means the ST elevation must be at least 25% of the preceding negative S wave. In this case, the ST elevation would have to be at least 3 mm to satisfy the rule.

question: An otherwise healthy 37-year-old woman presents 4 days after a vaginal birth with chest pain that has been present for 3 hours. She describes sudden-onset, pressure-like chest pain radiating to the left arm, which has been associated with dyspnea, nausea, and vomiting since it began. She is diaphoretic and is clutching her chest. Her cardiopulmonary and vascular examination findings are unre- markable. Her ECG is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: copyright ACEP.
englishExplanation: This patient presents with signs and symptoms concerning for spontaneous coro- nary artery dissection (SCAD). SCAD is a form of ACS caused by an acute, atraumatic local dissection resulting in the obstruction of a coronary artery by formation of a false lumen and intramural hematoma. Consequently, SCAD generally presents like other forms of ACS, with anginal chest pain, dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, and diaphoresis, among other find- ings. As with other forms of ACS, more severe manifestations can occur, such as ventricular arrhythmias and cardiogenic shock. SCAD is the most common cause of myocardial infarction in pregnant patients and especially in recently postpartum patients (>70%). SCAD is also a major cause of myocardial infarction in women with limited risk factors for atherosclerotic heart disease; SCAD is thought to be responsible for up to 35% of all ACS in women aged 50 years or younger. The left anterior descending artery is most commonly involved. However, SCAD can involve any coronary artery. Major risk factors for SCAD include fibromuscular dysplasia, advanced pregnancy and the recently postpartum period, connective tissue dis- eases, and systemic inflammatory diseases. There is concern for exogenous hormone use as a risk factor as well. Potentially triggering events have been re- ported in a large percentage of cases, such as significant physical exertion (eg, exer- cise or labor, as in this case), cocaine use, or emotional stress. Initial evaluation and management of SCAD is the same as for any patient who presents with symptoms consistent with an ACS. The ECG and troponin level are likely to be abnormal. ECG commonly demonstrates an STEMI, as in this case. Coronary angiography is the diagnostic test of choice, so the diagnosis in most cases is uncertain in the emergency department. Thus, initiation of standard treatments for ACS in the emergency department — such as anticoagulation, an- tiplatelet agents, and antianginals — is reasonable. If the SCAD diagnosis is known (eg, because of positive CT coronary angiography results), anticoagulation may be held because of the theoretical risk of enlarging the intramural hematoma. Early cardiology consultation is strongly recommended. Incorrect Answer Explanations Esophageal rupture is classically associated with heavy retching or vom- iting (Boerhaave syndrome). It presents with acute-onset midsternal chest pain and dysphagia. A chest x-ray will show free mediastinal air, and the diagno- sis is generally made with a contrast esophagogram using water-soluble contrast. Although this patient is vomiting, her symptoms are more consistent with angina than other forms of chest pain. Thus, she is less likely to be experiencing an esophageal rupture than an ACS. Given her risk factors, SCAD is the most likely diagnosis. Perimyocarditis is a potentially life-threatening inflammatory condition involving the pericardium and myocardium. It has a wide variety of in- fectious and noninfectious causes and can result in severely reduced cardiac function. Classically, patients with perimyocarditis present with chest pain, dysp- nea, and fatigue after a preceding viral illness. The ECG can show concave ST el- evations that may mimic the ST elevations from an STEMI but do not involve the coronary arteries. Troponin measurements may be elevated as well. This patient presents with acute-onset, anginal chest pain with no viral symptoms or preceding medical history other than recent delivery, making SCAD a more likely diagnosis than perimyocarditis. Patients in the later stages of pregnancy are at higher risk of pulmonary em- bolism, which should be considered in this setting. However, this patient presents with classic, acute-onset anginal symptoms: pressure-like chest pain radiating to the left arm, diaphoresis, nausea, vomiting, and ST elevations on ECG. Pulmonary embolism is expected to cause pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia rather than these symptoms. Thus, she is less likely to be experiencing a pulmonary em- bolism than an ACS such as SCAD. Given her risk factors, SCAD is the most likely diagnosis.

question: A 40-year-old man presents with cough, low-grade fever, and myalgias that have been present for the past 3 or 4 days. Today, he has experienced severe, sharp, pleuritic chest pain radiating to the left shoulder that is worse when he is supine and is improved when upright. He smokes one pack of cigarettes per day. His vi- tal signs are BP 160/95, P 110, R 18, and T 37.2°C (99°F); SpO is 98% on room air. A 12-lead ECG is shown below. What are appropriate next steps in management? Credit: Bond MC, Alblaihed L. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. Dallas, TX: American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.

options.text: Administer enoxaparin subcutaneously and admit to the hospital 2
Administer nitroglycerin IV infusion titrated to pain and request a cardiology consultation
Start acetylsalicylic acid, nitroglycerin, and heparin, and activate the cardiac catheterization team
Start ketorolac IV followed by ibuprofen and colchicine for outpatient care

correctAnswer: Start ketorolac IV followed by ibuprofen and colchicine for outpatient care
englishExplanation: This patient's clinical presentation and ECG are characteristic of acute pericarditis. NSAIDs and colchicine are the recommended treatments for acute pericarditis. Typical ECG findings of pericarditis in stage I include dif- fuse ST-segment elevation with a “concave up” pattern (except in lead aVR) and PR-interval depression. In stage II, ST segments begin to normalize, and T waves flatten. Finally, in stage III, ST segments have returned to normal, but T- wave inversions are present and may become permanent. Symptoms of pericarditis can mimic acute myocardial infarction (MI) and may include pleuritic pain that is often positional and improved by sitting up. Although symptoms usually resolve with NSAID therapy alone, the addition of colchicine is recommended to re- duce the rate of recurrent pericarditis. NSAIDs are typically given for 1 to 2 weeks, whereas colchicine is given for 3 months. Incorrect Answer Explanations Subcutaneous enoxaparin would be used to treat a pulmonary embolism and should be considered in patients with tachycardia and pleuritic pain. However, this patient's lack of hypoxia and tachypnea, as well as the ST-elevations seen on the ECG, are not suggestive of a pulmonary embolism. Nitroglycerin is used to reduce blood pressure and myocardial oxygen demand in the setting of acute cardiac ischemia, barring instances of contraindication. However, nitroglycerin is unwarranted for treating pain in the setting of pericarditis. Although acetylsalicylic acid can be an effective treatment for the pain of pericarditis, there is no indication for nitrates, anticoagulation, or admission to a monitored setting. The tachycardia and hypertension seen in this case are most likely the result of pain, and both should improve with analgesia.

question: A 34-year-old man presents with generalized fatigue, chest pain, and exertional dyspnea that have worsened over the past 5 days. He had a URI about 2 weeks ago. His vital signs are BP 70/30, P 130, R 32, and T 37.6°C (99.7°F); SpO is 91% on room air. An ECG is obtained and shown below. Which diagnostic study will definitively identify this patient's underlying condition? 2 Credit: Copyright ACEP.
englishExplanation: This patient has myocarditis. Although most cases are presumptively diagnosed based on clinical presentation, endocardial biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis. Myocarditis is an inflammation of the myocardium, which can be due to a number of infections and noninfectious causes. Many cases of myocarditis are preceded by a viral illness. Parvovirus B19 is a frequently recognized pathogen in myocarditis: it has been identified in 11% to 56% of patients with my- ocarditis and in 10% to 51% of patients with diastolic cardiomyopathy. Presentations of myocarditis are variable, ranging from chest pain to congestive heart failure, arrhythmias, and even sudden cardiac death. Approximately 10% of patients with myocarditis display fulminant myocarditis at the time of presentation. This condition is characterized by an abrupt-onset of myocarditis with development of overt heart failure within days to weeks of a viral illness such as COVID-19. The ECG may be abnormal. Findings are typically nonspecific and may include tachycar- dia or diffuse ST- segment elevation with PR-interval depression; they may also mimic STEMI. The troponin level is typically elevated. Imaging modalities for myocarditis include echocardiogram — which may demonstrate impaired ventricular function — and cardiac MRI. Cardiac MRI may show myocardial edema, myocyte necrosis and scarring, ventricular dysfunction, and pericardial effusion. MRI findings are nonspecific but may support the diagno- sis of myocarditis. Although it is frequently unnecessary, the definitive diagnosis of my- ocarditis is based on endocardial biopsy. Characteristic findings on histology and immunohistochemical staining provide a definitive diagnosis of myocarditis if there is diagnostic uncertainty following laboratory studies and cardiac imaging. The decision to proceed with biopsy is made on a case-by-case basis by weighing the risks and benefits of the procedure; this decision does not need to be made in the emergency department. All patients with myocarditis should be admitted. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cardiac CT imaging is not used for the diagnosis of myocarditis. It is increasingly commonly used in the form of contrast-enhanced coronary CT angiography (CTA) to evaluate for coronary artery disease. Coronary CTA is highly sensi- tive in the detection of obstructive coronary artery disease. In patients with myocarditis, echocardiography reveals diffuse global hy- pokinesis, normal or small ventricular size, and ventricular wall thick- ening, which is likely due to myocardial inflammation and edema. Decreased left ventricular ejection fraction is often seen, but none of these findings is definitive for the diagnosis of myocarditis. Positive viral titers might support the presumption of a viral cause for the myositis that is causing the patient's symptoms. However, positive viral titers alone do not provide a definitive diagnostic finding. There are many causes of myocarditis that are not viral in nature.

question: Which finding is most suggestive of myocarditis?
englishExplanation: Myocarditis is an inflammatory condition that causes myocardial dam- age, usually as a result of infectious, immunologic, or toxin-mediated conditions. It can manifest as mild constitutional symptoms, moderate cardiopul- monary symptoms, or fulminant cardiopulmonary decompensation leading to death. The notable physical examination findings are low-grade fever, tachypnea, and tachycardia. Classically, the tachycardia is out of pro- portion to the fever. In most adult cases, the myocardial damage is thought to be autoimmune and triggered by a virus (most commonly Coxsackievirus) or other in- fections. In neonates and infants, injury to myocytes is believed to occur more often because of direct injury by the pathogen itself. The clinical manifestations of myocarditis usually begin days to weeks after the acute infection, especially when viruses are implicated as the cause. Only 50% of pa- tients report a recent upper respiratory or GI viral type of infection. The initial symptoms are nonspecific and constitutional, such as low fever, fatigue, malaise, myalgia, and arthralgia. These mild symptoms are often the reason for initial misdiagnosis or delays in proper diagnosis of this condition. Cardiopulmonary symptoms such as chest pain and dyspnea are also commonly seen. The most common abnormalities on ECG are sinus tachycardia and nonspecific ST-segment or T-wave changes. Chest x-rays may reveal signs of congestive heart failure (cardiomegaly, pulmonary vascular re- distribution, interstitial edema, frank pulmonary edema). Close attention should be paid to the ABCs of resuscitation because patients with fulminant myocarditis can decompensate rapidly. The mainstay of treatment of myocarditis is primarily supportive with a focus on hemodynamic sup- port and management of complications. Incorrect Answer Explanations A low-grade fever can be seen in patients who develop myocarditis, but it is not the most suggestive or classic finding of the disease. Fever with night sweats is characteristic of tuberculosis. In fact, only 50% of patients report a recent vi- ral-type upper respiratory or GI infection. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea is a symptom seen in patients with de- compensating heart failure; they wake from sleep to sit upright due to sudden increasing shortness of breath. Although patients with myocarditis can have parox- ysmal nocturnal dyspnea with heart failure, it is not the most suggestive symptom of myocarditis. Pleuritic chest pain is a common symptom of acute pericarditis but is less commonly associated with myocarditis. The progression of myocarditis involves necrosis of the myocardial cells with inflammatory cells leading to fibrosis. This does not lead to the irritation or pleuritic pain associated with pericarditis.

question: A 14-year-old patient presents with 3 days' of fever, chest pain, and worsening shortness of breath. The patient reports viral URI symptoms for several days prior. The patient's vital signs are BP 76/56, P 122, R 24, and T 38.4°C (101.1°F); SpO is 94% on room air. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia with low voltage and diffuse, concave ST elevations. A chest x-ray reveals an enlarged cardiac silhou- ette and mild bilateral pulmonary edema. A high-sensitivity test reveals a tro- ponin level of 1,267 ng/L.What is the most appropriate next step?
englishExplanation: This patient's signs and symptoms are concerning for pericarditis compli- cated by myocarditis and pericardial tamponade, given the low-voltage ECG with diffuse ST elevations, hypotension with tachycardia, and severely elevated tro- ponin level. A bedside echocardiogram is the essential next step to evalu- ate for presence of a pericardial effusion and echocardiographic signs of peri- cardial tamponade. The bedside echocardiogram can also evaluate for functional ab- normalities consistent with myocarditis to assist with preliminary diagnosis. Pericardial tamponade due to a pericardial effusion has several notable echocar- diographic findings, including right atrial and right ventricular diastolic collapse as well as a plethoric IVC. Focal or global systolic dysfunction is suggestive of my- ocarditis. Pericarditis with associated troponin elevation and systolic 2 dysfunction is termed “perimyocarditis,” whereas “myopericarditis” de- scribes the same circumstances with preserved systolic function. Ultimately, definitive diagnosis and management of (peri)myocarditis occurs mostly outside of the emergency department. Emergency department laboratory tests and bedside echocardiographic evaluation are intended to guide acute stabilization, which may include emergent relief of pericardial tamponade with pericardiocentesis and hemodynamic and circulatory support as needed. Admission with cardiol- ogy consultation and continuous telemetry monitoring is recommended. Incorrect Answer Explanations Coronary angiography would be appropriate in the setting of acute STEMI. Although this patient presents with ST elevations, they are diffuse, rather than territorial, as would be seen with an STEMI. Additionally, this pediatric patient is much less likely to have an obstructive coronary lesion than an adult. The overall clinical picture in this case is more consistent with perimyocarditis complicated by pericardial tamponade. A bedside echocardiogram is the most appropriate next step. Endotracheal intubation is potentially dangerous given this patient's hemodynamics and clinical concern for pericardial tamponade. Intubation and initiation of positive-pressure ventilation could rapidly and precipi- tously further decrease cardiac preload, resulting in hemodynamic collapse. Because this patient is not clearly demonstrating an airway emergency, diagnosis of the pericardial tamponade with a bedside echocardiogram is the most appropriate next step. An acute thoracentesis would be appropriate if the patient's symptoms were caused by a pleural effusion large enough to cause mediastinal compression, termed “tension hydrothorax.” However, the chest x-ray demonstrates no pleural effusions, so thoracentesis is not indicated. The overall clinical picture in this case is more consistent with perimyocarditis complicated by pericardial tamponade. A bedside echocardiogram is the most appropriate next step.

question: A 78-year-old man presents with shortness of breath that has worsened over the past 2 weeks. He has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia and is not compliant with treatment. He has no chest pain. An ECG is obtained and shown below. What is the most likely cause of this patient's primary ECG abnormalities? Credit: In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019.
englishExplanation: A left ventricular (LV) aneurysm is a focal area of infarcted myocardium that bulges outward during both systole and diastole. The ECG changes associated with LV aneurysm, as seen in this case, are typically ST-segment elevation in the an- terior leads (V1-V5) with accompanying Q waves. It can be difficult to distin- guish LV aneurysm from anterior myocardial infarction (MI); however, the pres- ence of Q waves typically reveals a completed anterior infarction. Approximately 10% to 30% of patients who survive an acute MI develop a left ventricular aneu- rysm. Patients with large LV aneurysms can present with dyspnea that often has persisted from the time of infarction. The prevalence of LV aneurysm appears to have declined with the improved reperfusion treatment of acute MI. Patients who experience acute MI without prompt or appropriate therapy can have a completed infarction with a large amount of infarcted myocardium; these patients can then de- velop a ventricular aneurysm. Most LV aneurysms are anterolateral near the apex of the heart and are the result of complete occlusion of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. Small and moderate-sized aneurysms are often associated with no symptoms, although the patient might experience angina in other portions of adja- cent myocardium. Incorrect Answer Explanations Late post-MI myopericarditis, often referred to as Dressler syndrome, typi- cally presents with pleuritic chest pain, fever, leukocytosis, and pericardial friction rub. It usually occurs a few weeks after large acute MI. Typical ECG find- ings are similar to pericarditis with diffuse ST-segment elevation and PR segment depression without reciprocal change of both the PR and ST segments. Of course, not all cases of myopericarditis demonstrate these classic ECG abnormalities. The electrocardiographic pattern of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) fre- quently has repolarization abnormalities, which include ST-segment elevation and depression as well as T-wave abnormalities. Approximately 75% to 80% of patients with electrocardiographic LVH have these ST-segment and T-wave ab- normalities, termed the strain pattern. Electrocardiographic LVH should be consid- ered if the sum of the S wave in lead V1 or V2 and the R wave in lead V5 or V6 is greater than 35 mm in a patient older than 35 years. In this patient, ST-segment elevation MI (STEMI) is less likely both clinically and electrocardiographically. He has had persistent dyspnea for 2 weeks without appar- ent change in the pattern; thus, no new major event appears to be occurring. Regarding the ECG, the prominent Q waves with ST-segment elevation sug- gest possible aneurysm. Also, a comparison of the height of the T wave to that of the QRS complex can also assist in this distinction. With LV aneurysm, the T wave is of- ten small or flattened compared to a prominent QRS complex in the configuration of a Q wave. With STEMI, the T wave is often quite prominent and near-equal to equal in amplitude to the accompanying QRS complex.

question: A 35-year-old woman on daily prednisone for systemic lupus erythematosus presents with 2 days of shortness of breath. Her vital signs include BP 68/51 and P 122; SpO is 98% on room air. Bedside echocardiography is performed and shown below. What is the most appropriate next step in management? 2 Credit: William J. Brady, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: Pericardial effusion is an abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pericar- dial space, and it is evident on this patient's echocardiogram. This patient has hy- potension with a large, circumferential pericardial effusion — a presentation most consistent with pericardial tamponade. Pericardiocentesis is indicated in the emergency department to remove the fluid in this unstable patient. The pericardial space has a limited volume. With the accumulation of fluid, in- trapericardial pressure increases and can negatively impact cardiac function, ulti- mately reducing cardiac output and producing systemic hypoperfusion. Slowly ac- cumulating pericardial effusions cause hemodynamic compromise less often than those that develop more rapidly. Several diseases can produce pericardial effu- sions, such as rheumatologic disorders, chest malignancies, atypical infectious dis- orders such as tuberculosis, perforation of cardiac chambers, and proximal aortic dissection, among others. Echocardiography is usually very helpful in establish- ing the diagnosis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although this patient is hypotensive, there is no clear indication that she is bleeding and requires a transfusion. Rather, she is hypotensive due to pericardial tam- ponade and requires an emergent pericardiocentesis. Although chest tube placement is a very reasonable intervention in pneumotho- rax and hemothorax, it has no utility in the resolution of a pericardial effusion. A pericardiocentesis would be appropriate in this case. Needle thoracostomy should be reserved for patients with tension pneu- mothorax. This patient has signs of pericardial tamponade and requires an emer- gent pericardiocentesis or pericardial window.

question: A 51-year-old man with hypertension and end-stage renal disease presents with chest heaviness and shortness of breath. His vital signs include BP 85/70, P 135, R 18, and T 36.7°C (98.1°F). A physical examination reveals jugular venous dis- tention, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, distant heart sounds, and pitting periph- eral edema. Portable chest x-ray demonstrates cardiomegaly with mild bilateral pulmonary vascular congestion. The rhythm strip is shown below. What is the most appropriate therapy? Credit: Mary Jo Wagner, MD, FACEP.

options.text: Calcium gluconate IV, insulin 10 units IV, and dextrose 50 g IV
Diltiazem 20 mg IV bolus, followed by infusion of 5 mg/hr
Heparin 5,000 units IV bolus, followed by synchronized cardioversion at 75 J
Normal saline 500 mL IV bolus and emergent pericardiocentesis

correctAnswer: Normal saline 500 mL IV bolus and emergent pericardiocentesis
englishExplanation: Patients with renal failure are at risk for developing pericardial effusion and tamponade as well as uremic pericarditis. Treatment includes increas- ing right heart filling/cardiac output by fluid loading and emergent pericardio- centesis to drain the accumulated pericardial fluid. Fluid in the pericardial space interferes with ventricular filling and can produce hypotension with narrow pulse pressure, jugular venous distention, and muffled heart sounds. The ECG finding of electrical alternans is a beat-to-beat variation in the amplitude of P and R waves caused by movement of the heart within the fluid-filled pericardium. Incorrect Answer Explanations Administration of calcium gluconate, insulin, dextrose, and dialysis would treat hyperkalemia, a condition often seen in patients with renal failure who are noncompliant with dialysis. However, this approach is not indicated for this patient because the ECG findings include widening of the QRS complex, peaked T waves, and QT prolongation, which are not present on this patient's ECG. Electrical alternans is not a finding associated with hyperkalemia. Fluid overload in these patients may cause symptomatic hypotension due to the direct effect on the myocardium causing heart failure. Diltiazem is useful for rate control in rapid atrial fibrillation; however, this patient's tachycardia is likely compensatory for the hypotension, and the ECG is indicative of electrical alternans. Use of diltiazem in this patient might lower the blood pressure even more and is, therefore, contraindicated. Rapid atrial fibrillation may cause a drop in blood pressure, but this is typically seen with higher heart rates. Electrical alternans are a beat-to-beat variation of the amplitude of the P and R waves as a result of the heart moving in the fluid-filled pericar- dial sac. Cardioversion of this will not treat the life-threatening cardiac tamponade. There is no indication that electricity is of benefit in the case of elec- trical alternans. Instead, the underlying pericardial effusion must be addressed. Heparin may be considered for the treatment of a patient with atrial fibrillation; however, it would be contraindicated for a patient with cardiac tamponade requir- ing an emergent procedure. Key Points Tachycardia, hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and ECG evidence of electrical al- ternans point to pericardial effusion and tamponade, making pericardiocentesis an emergent treatment priority. Electrical alternans is a beat-to-beat variation of P and R waves signifying the heart moving within the fluid-filled pericardial sac. In cardiac tamponade, a fluid load may temporize the patient by increasing the car- diac output, while pericardiocentesis is the definitive treatment.

question: A patient with a history of lung cancer presents with dyspnea and lightheaded- ness. Their vital signs are notable for BP 88/52 and P 127. A large pericardial ef- fusion and right ventricular end-diastolic collapse are noted on bedside ultra- sound. While arranging for definitive management, what is the most appropriate intervention?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with an atraumatic pericardial tamponade, likely due to malignancy. While awaiting definitive management (ie, decompression of the peri- cardial effusion with pericardiocentesis [bedside or otherwise]), intravenous flu- ids should be administered. Cardiac preload is reduced in the setting of in- creased pericardial pressure; intravenous fluids increase cardiac preload and re- verse this process temporarily, but definitive treatment is still required. Most re- sources advocate a small bolus (generally 500 mL) in euvolemic patients to achieve adequate preload augmentation without triggering additional complica- tions, such as pulmonary edema and worsening hemodynamic instability. Characteristic findings of pericardial tamponade include hypotension, tachycar- dia, jugular venous distention, pulsus paradoxus (ie, systolic BP de- crease >10 mm Hg with inspiration), and electrical alternans on ECG. Along with the culprit pericardial effusion, echocardiogram may reveal systolic right atrial or diastolic right ventricular collapse as well as plethoric IVC. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bedside thoracotomy in the setting of pericardial tamponade is indi- cated only following cardiac arrest from penetrating chest trauma. Even if this patient were in cardiac arrest, bedside thoracotomy is not indicated; rather, an emergent bedside pericardiocentesis should be performed. In this scenario, in- travenous fluids are the most appropriate pending definitive decompression with pericardiocentesis. Diuretics can be used in certain circumstances to reduce the size of a small pericar- dial effusion without tamponade physiology. However, in the setting of pericardial tamponade, diuretics would be counterproductive since they reduce preload and can precipitate or worsen hemodynamic instability. Thus, intravenous fluids are more appropriate pending definitive decompression with pericardiocentesis. Although vasopressors may improve blood pressure and stimulate inotropy, they do not directly address the physiology underlying pericardial tamponade–induced ob- structive shock. The impact of reduced preload on cardiac output can only be addressed with increasing preload via volume resuscitation; no amount of vasopressor use will address the fall in stroke volume. Thus, intravenous fluids are the most appropriate intervention pending definitive decompression with pericardiocentesis.

question: A patient with lung cancer presents with mild dyspnea. A large pericardial effu- sion is noted on beside echocardiogram. Their vital signs are BP 120/72, P 82, R 14, and T 36.6°C (97.9°F), SpO is 97% on room air. The patient is currently pending pericardial drain placement. Which finding, if newly present on re- assessment, would be concerning for development of pericardial tamponade?
englishExplanation: Patients with large pericardial effusions may develop pericardial tampon- ade at any time, making urgent drainage necessary; close observation and careful reassessment of these patients prior to drainage may detect signs of tampon- ade as they develop. Right ventricular diastolic collapse on echocardiogram is considered diag- nostic for pericardial tamponade. Other major ultrasound findings include right atrial systolic collapse and plethoric IVC. Clinical findings include tachycardia, hypotension, jugular venous distention, and pulsus para- 2 doxus (ie, decrease in the systolic BP during inspiration exceeding 10 mm Hg). Typically, the ECG will show sinus tachycardia with low voltage. “Electrical alternans” is a classic pattern of undulating QRS voltage present in 10% to 30% of patients with large pericardial effusions. This classic pattern is thought to be caused by the "swinging" or changing position of the heart in the peri- cardial fluid relative to the electrodes on the chest wall. Incorrect Answer Explanations Central venous pressure increases due to increased pressure within the peri- cardial space preventing right heart filling. This results in both jugular venous distention and a plethoric IVC. A collapsable IVC would be suggestive of the opposite process, such as hypovolemia. Pulsus tardus et parvus is a weak peripheral pulse that is notably de- layed from the central cardiac pulse. This is a classic physical examination fea- ture associated with severe aortic stenosis. Pulsus paradoxus (a major [>10 mm Hg] decrease in systolic BP with inspiration) is associated with pericardial tam- ponade. The mechanism of tamponade-induced pulsus paradoxus is complex. It is a result of the complex interplay between thoracic negative pressure, impaired right ventricular filling, ventricular interdependence, and increased blood flow to the pulmonary vasculature – all of which contribute to a drop in stroke volume and, therefore, cardiac output and systolic BP. Second-degree type II atrioventricular block, otherwise known as a Mobitz II, is a pathologic cardiac conduction block that signals significant malfunction of the His-Purkinje system. Although it is associated with a wide range of cardiac dis- orders, (eg, myocardial infarction amyloidosis), it is not a major feature of pericar- dial tamponade specifically. Major ECG findings associated with pericardial tam- ponade include sinus tachycardia, low-voltage QRS, or “electrical alternans.”

question: What feature is most specific for cardiac tamponade?
englishExplanation: Tamponade develops when intrapericardial fluid produces pressure sufficient to compress the cardiac chambers, which subsequently impairs ventricular diastolic filling and stroke volume. The pericardium is capable of stretching and can accommodate several liters of fluid when the fluid accumulates slowly. However, if the fluid accumulates rapidly, as in trauma, the intrapericardial pressure is changed all at once, and pericardial tamponade can ensue. Compensatory mechanisms such as tachycardia can temporarily sustain blood pressure, but as the pericardial fluid continues to increase, the compensatory mech- anisms begin to fail, which results in diminished cardiac output, hypoten- sion, and full cardiovascular collapse. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although beat-to-beat swinging of the heart indicates a large effusion causing electrical alternans, this alone does not suggest impending cardiovascu- lar collapse, especially if the fluid has accumulated gradually. With pericardial tamponade, pericardial effusion is present on echocardiog- raphy with a dilated IVC without inspiratory collapse. Other findings on echocardiography that are diagnostic of pericardial tamponade include early dias- tolic right ventricular collapse, systolic right atrial collapse, and hemodynamic derangements. Pulsus paradoxus (drop in systolic blood pressure >10 mm Hg during normal inspiration) can be seen in tamponade; however, its presence has limited specificity. Several other conditions that are associated with hy- potension or dyspnea can also produce pulsus paradoxus, including massive pul- monary embolism, hemorrhagic shock, and obstructive lung disease.

question: A 47-year-old man presents with chest pain and dyspnea that started while he was lying on the couch. An ECG is obtained and shown below. What is the appro- priate management? Credit: Bon MC, Alblaihed L. In: Mattu A, Tabas J, Brady W, eds. Electrocardiography in Emergency, Acute, and Critical Care. 2nd ed. American College of Emergency Physicians; 2019. Reproduced with permission from Amal Mattu, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: Pericarditis is inflammation within the pericardial space involving the pericardial surfaces that generally presents with sharp pleuritic chest pain. The mainstay of treatment is NSAIDs. The pain classically is pleuritic, radiates to the back, and tends to improve when the patient is sitting up. The diagnosis in this case is supported by the ECG findings of normal sinus rhythm, diffuse ST-seg- ment elevation, and diffuse PR segment depression. Leads I and aVR can show reciprocal ST-segment depression in acute pericarditis. Uncomplicated cases of pericarditis can be treated with NSAIDs in the outpatient setting. Glucocorticoids were previously recommended but should only be used if the patient cannot tolerate NSAIDs because they can increase the risk of recurrence. Colchicine can be used as an adjunct to NSAIDS or glucocorticoids, but it should be avoided if bacterial pericarditis is suspected. Pericarditis is often idiopathic or related to a viral infection, but it can be caused by various underlying disease states. There is often a prodromal period of low- grade fever, malaise, or flu-like symptoms. On examination, a pericardial friction rub can sometimes be appreciated. A bedside echocardiogram can be ob- tained to evaluate for an associated pericardial effusion. Patients with large effu- sions or pericardial tamponade benefit from inpatient evaluation and management. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although they were previously commonly recommended for the treatment of peri- carditis, glucocorticoids have been shown to be associated with recur- rence of pericarditis and should generally be avoided. Glucocorticoids should only be considered in rare cases in which the patient cannot tolerate NSAIDs. This presentation is most consistent with acute pericarditis because of the diffuse ST changes seen in essentially all leads. This is not a typical pattern indicating cardiac ischemia, which might have ST changes in contiguous leads consistent with specific cardiac vessels (inferior ischemia seen in leads II, III, and aVF). Thus, ni- trates would likely be of no benefit to this patient. Heparin is indicated in suspected pulmonary embolism or in certain ACS presenta- tions. Although pulmonary embolI can cause ECG changes, most commonly tachy- cardia and classically S1Q3T3, they are not expected to cause diffuse ST-segment el- evation, as is seen on this patient's ECG. Heparin should not be given to pa- tients with pericarditis. Pericarditis is often associated with pericardial effu- sion, which may be worsened by heparin.

question: What treatment option is recommended to prevent recurrences of pericarditis?
englishExplanation: Pericarditis is diagnosed in about 5% of emergency department presentations for chest pain that is not related to myocardial infarction; for the vast majority of these patients, the underlying cause cannot be identified. First-line treatment includes as- pirin and other NSAIDs; ibuprofen is effective in most cases and has fewer side ef- fects. Evidence now suggests that the addition of colchicine (1-2 mg for the first day and then 0.5-1 mg/day for 3 months) to the standard regimen is effective in hasten- ing the resolution of acute symptoms and also preventing recurrence rates, regard- less of the cause of the pericarditis. Colchicine is also effective in cases of recurrent pericarditis. Incorrect Answer Explanations Anti-inflammatory agents are the first-line therapy for pericarditis. The pain usually improves significantly within days of ibuprofen therapy. If symptoms persist, an al- ternative NSAID is indicated. Indomethacin is often used for severe cases because of its stronger anti-inflammatory effect, but it should be avoided in patients with a his- tory of ischemic heart disease because it can decrease coronary blood flow. However, anti-inflammatory medications have not been shown to change the recur- rence rate. Narcotic medications provide pain relief for patients with pericarditis but do not change the course of the disease or reduce the likelihood of recurrence. The use of corticosteroids is generally reserved for recurrent pericarditis or for the treatment of pericarditis that is unresponsive to aspirin or NSAIDs plus colchicine. Initiation of steroids early in the course of first-time pericarditis might actually be an independent risk factor for recurrence.

question: What is a criterion for hospital admission in a young, otherwise healthy person with newly diagnosed pericarditis?
englishExplanation: Patients with acute pericarditis (inflammation of the pericardium) present with sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal chest pain that radiates to the trapezius ridges and changes with body position (worse when lying down). The physical examination might reveal a pericardial friction rub. It can be an isolated condition or it can suggest underlying disease. Hospital admission is warranted for patients who also present with fever in order to actively investigate the etiology of the pericarditis and to closely monitor the patient's condi- tion. The hallmark of the early stage of disease is diffuse ST-segment elevation noted on an ECG; PR-segment depression can also occur but is not specific for pericarditis. The etiologies of pericarditis are vast and include infection (viral, bac- terial, fungal, parasitic), malignancy, medications, renal disease, connective tissue disease, myocardial infarction, trauma, and surgery. Reasonable indications for ad- mission include, again, fever or suspicion of a bacterial cause, as well as immuno- suppression, associated trauma, elevated biomarkers (myopericarditis), and hemo- dynamic instability. An effusion larger than 2 cm warrants admission to the hospital due to the risk of additional increase in size and the potential for cardiac tampon- ade. A history of active anticoagulant use is generally considered a poor prognostic factor and warrants hospital admission as well. In most patients, outpatient man- agement is appropriate, and symptoms resolve in days to weeks. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute onset is not a criterion for admission. Most patients with pericarditis present in the acute stage of symptoms. Subacute course is an indication for admis- sion, not acute onset. Elevation of CRP, along with other inflammatory markers, is one of the diagnostic markers for pericarditis, but it does not predict increased severity of the dis- ease. An elevated WBC count can also be used to track the course of the disease. Any hemodynamic instability or hypotension — not hypertension — indicates the need for admission. Tachycardia out of proportion to pain or fever indicates my- ocarditis or myopericarditis.

question: What is a classic ECG finding associated with pericarditis?
englishExplanation: Pericarditis is a condition whereby the pericardium becomes inflamed for a wide variety of reasons. Pericarditis causes ECG changes, such as PR-interval de- pression with diffuse ST elevations once the pericardial inflammation reaches the epicardium. Classically, the expected ECG changes associated with pericarditis progress through four stages: Stage one occurs within hours to days and is the classic “pericarditis” pattern, with diffuse PR depressions and ST elevations. The ST elevations may be difficult to separate from STEMI. Distinguishing features include small, upsloping ST eleva- tions that are generalized, have a diffuse distribution, do not have additional recip- rocal ST depressions aside from aVR and V1, and lack other ischemic changes (eg, T-wave inversions, Q waves, hyperacute T waves, etc.). Stage two occurs within 1 week and shows that the ST and PR segments have normalized. Stage three has no well-defined time frame, but it occurs after normalization of the ST and PR segments and shows diffuse T-wave inversions. Unlike with is- chemia, T-wave inversions and ST elevations that are associated with pericarditis usually do not exist simultaneously. Stage four also has no well-defined time frame but shows normalization of the ECG. Note that it is unnecessary for patients to progress through all four stages of classic ECG changes, and some may show rapid transition from stage one to stage four in mild cases. Changes like PR depressions and ST elevations may be tran- sient. Also, some patients will not follow this classic pattern and may demonstrate different morphologies. This can complicate the diagnosis of pericarditis, often making it a diagnosis of exclusion once ischemia has been ruled out. Incorrect Answer Explanations Coved ST-segment elevation is associated with Brugada syndrome, which is a congenital abnormality in cardiac sodium channels, not pericarditis. Pericarditis is strongly associated with diffuse PR depression and concave-upward ST elevation. Diffuse ST-segment depressions are associated with diffuse subendocar- dial ischemia or proximal left main coronary artery occlusion. ST eleva- tion in aVR is a common finding in this scenario as well. Pericarditis, however, is strongly associated with diffuse PR depression and ST elevation, with reciprocal ST depression in aVR and V1. Enlarged R wave in aVL is associated with left ventricular hypertrophy, which is most commonly caused by hypertension. Pericarditis, on the other hand, is strongly associated with diffuse PR depression and ST elevation.

question: What best distinguishes myopericarditis from pericarditis?
englishExplanation: Pericarditis is a condition wherein the pericardium becomes inflamed for a wide variety of reasons; this inflammation can also involve the myocardium, causing myopericarditis (alternatively, perimyocarditis). Unlike pericarditis, myopericarditis is associated with elevated cardiac biomarkers, such as troponin, as well as left ventricular dysfunction noted on echocardiogram. Unclear cases can also be distinguished with cardiac MRI, which will show focal myocardial inflammation. Patients with myopericarditis have a wide range of dis- ease severity; some present similarly to pericarditis — with positional chest pain and ECG changes — and others present as critically ill with florid cardiogenic shock. Due to this risk of severe decompensation, any patient with clinical findings concerning for myopericarditis should be admitted. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although myopericarditis can manifest different ECG findings than peri- carditis, ECG changes do not reliably distinguish pericarditis and my- opericarditis to the extent that cardiac biomarkers do. Pericarditis and myoperi- carditis may show similar ECG changes, but myopericarditis may also show territorial ECG changes that are not typically associated with pericarditis due to localized myocardial inflammation. Unlike pericarditis, myopericarditis is also asso- ciated with arrhythmias. The epicardium is the outermost layer of the visceral heart and is, more specifically, the visceral pericardium. Extension of pericarditis from the pari- etal pericardium to the visceral pericardium/epicardium is what results in the char- acteristic ECG changes associated with pericarditis. Generally, this is a benign process that does not result in severe illness. Only involvement of the my- ocardium results in biomarker elevation and ventricular dysfunction, leading to the diagnosis of the more dangerous myopericarditis. Positional chest pain is a classic finding for both pericarditis and my- opericarditis, so it does not help distinguish them. Patients with isolated my- ocarditis without pericardial inflammation may complain of a different type of chest pain that is constant, not positional, and more akin to ischemic chest pain. However, when the pericardium is involved, positional chest pain is an unreliable differentiator.

question: A patient with end-stage renal disease presents with hypotension and altered mental status. The family noted the patient had been complaining of vague chest pain for the past week and has missed dialysis. What bedside echocardiogram finding should prompt emergent intervention?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with a pericardial effusion that is presumptively causing cardiac tamponade, which requires emergent pericardiocentesis. Based on the history, this patient likely has preceding uremic pericarditis that resulted in missed hemodialysis sessions and, consequently, worsening uremia, en- cephalopathy, and fluid accumulation. Patients presenting with uremic pericarditis and pericardial effusions without tamponade physiology should undergo urgent hemodialysis; dialysis alone resolves symptoms and pericardial effusions in most cases. Uremic pericarditis causes vague, usually positional chest pain, and it frequently causes pericardial effusions in patients with end-stage kidney disease; upwards of 50% of patients with uremic pericarditis have an associated pericardial effusion. Although any type of pericarditis can cause a pericardial effusion, uremic pericarditis is known for causing large effusions to form, likely due to the accumula- tion of metabolic wastes and fluid. Recurrent pericardial inflammation also results in a thickening of the pericardium, causing a restrictive pericarditis as well. Incorrect Answer Explanations End-point septal separation (EPSS) is a method of estimating left ven- tricular ejection fraction based on the movement of the mitral valve rel- ative to the interventricular septum. An EPSS of less than 5 mm is considered normal, whereas an EPSS greater than 7 mm is considered sensitive for a reduced ejection fraction of less than 50%. Although a mildly reduced ejection fraction war- rants consideration given the patient's hypotension, the presence of a large peri- cardial effusion and hypotension prompts greater concern for pericar- dial tamponade and the need for emergent pericardiocentesis. Pericardial fibrinous stranding is a classic echocardiographic finding associated with uremic pericarditis. These strands form due to chronic peri- cardial inflammation and scarring. The pericardium may also appear thickened. These fibrinous strands alone do not require any specific acute interven- tion, unlike a large effusion in the setting of likely cardiac tamponade. Regional wall-motion abnormalities would certainly be concerning findings in a pa- tient with a week of chest pain symptoms and hypotension. However, in this cir- cumstance, the presence of a large pericardial effusion and hypotension prompts greater concern for pericardial tamponade and the need for emergent pericardiocentesis.

question: What is the first-line medication for managing acute viral pericarditis?
englishExplanation: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, indomethacin, or aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) are first- line treatments for acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis; other causes, such as uremic pericarditis, are less common but may have their own specific treat- ments. Patients should be treated with full doses (eg, 600-800 mg of ibuprofen three times daily) for 2 to 4 weeks. The addition of colchicine can improve pain control and reduce recurrence rates. Incorrect Answer Explanations Acetaminophen is a reasonable adjunctive pain-control medication for patients with acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis but should not take the place of NSAIDs. NSAIDs and other anti-inflammatories have strong evidence supporting their effectiveness in the management of acute pericarditis. Methyl salicylate (otherwise known as oil of wintergreen) is a type of salicylate that is generally used as a topical pain reliever and, in very small quantities, a flavoring agent. Although aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is indicated for the manage- ment of acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis, methyl salicylate should not be used for this purpose. Steroids like prednisone are considered second-line agents and are only used for patients who are unable to take NSAIDs or whose symptoms are refrac- tory to NSAIDs. This is due to steroids' lower efficacy and side effect profile given duration of treatment (2-4 weeks).

question: According to the American College of Cardiology guidelines, what should prompt consideration of hospital admission for a patient with clinical pericarditis?

options.text: Pain refractory to NSAID dose in ED

englishExplanation: The disposition of acute pericarditis is split between low-risk and high-risk groups. A majority of pericarditis patients are low risk and can be safely dis- charged with outpatient follow-up. Patients who meet high-risk criteria (eg, fever) mandate admission for expedited evaluation of the underlying cause. Although this list is not exhaustive, several well-accepted high-risk criteria include: Signs of myocarditis (eg, elevated troponin) Non-acute-onset symptoms Fever greater than 38°C (100.4°F) Large pericardial effusion (>2 cm) or signs of cardiac tamponade Anticoagulation Immunosuppression Failure of initial course of NSAIDs and colchicine use History of acute trauma Incorrect Answer Explanations Acute-onset chest pain is typical of acute pericarditis and does not mandate admission. Patients with indolent courses should prompt more concern because the underlying cause is more likely to be pathologic. Pain refractory to an NSAID dose in the emergency department is not considered high risk. On the other hand, patients without relief after 1 week of consis- tent NSAID therapy should be considered for admission and further workup because their pain is less likely to be from benign acute pericarditis. Pericarditis frequently causes a mild pericardial effusion. A 0.5-cm pericardial effusion is small and would not be a reason to admit a patient with pericarditis unless the effusion showed signs of cardiac tamponade. By size of pericardial effu- sion alone, a large pericardial effusion exceeding 2 cm is considered high risk and should prompt admission.

question: A 56-year-old man presents with a severe headache, nausea with vomiting, and confusion. His vital signs include BP 201/135, P 102, and T 37°C (98.6°F); SpO is 99% on room air. A CT scan of the brain reveals bilateral white matter hypo- densities in the occipital and parietal regions consistent with vasogenic edema. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Hydralazine titrated to a target BP of 140/80
Metoprolol titrated to a target P of 60
Nicardipine titrated to a MAP of 126
Nitroprusside titrated to a diastolic BP less than 100

correctAnswer: Nicardipine titrated to a MAP of 126
englishExplanation: This patient's history, presentation, and CT findings are consistent with hypertensive encephalopathy, which is a true hypertensive emergency. Nicardipine, a peripherally acting calcium channel blocker given intra- venously, has consistent effects on dilating vascular beds and is considered first-line therapy for hypertensive encephalopathy. Therapy goals include lowering the MAP back into a range where cerebral autoregulation can occur. Generally, the MAP should be lowered by 20% in the first hour but by no 2 more than 25% in the first day. This formula can be used to estimate MAP: MAP = Diastolic BP + 1/3(Systolic – Diastolic pressure). Lowering the blood pressure too rapidly can provoke cerebral ischemia in a brain that is accus- tomed to higher blood pressures. These findings on CT, in combination with the hy- pertension, headache and confusion, are consistent with posterior reversible en- cephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Incorrect Answer Explanations Hydralazine is not considered first-line therapy for hypertensive en- cephalopathy. It can unpredictably lower cerebral perfusion pressure, precipitat- ing ischemia in the brain. Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective adrenergic receptor blocker. It primarily affects the heart rate with no vasodilatory properties. Although metoprolol can lower blood pressure, direct-acting vasodilator agents are considered better options. Additionally, therapy for hypertensive encephalopathy does not normally focus on heart rate. Nitroprusside, like hydralazine, can unpredictably lower cerebral perfu- sion pressure and paradoxically elevate intracranial pressure. It can be considered as second-line or third-line therapy but should not be used as a first-line agent.

question: In which condition is more rapid blood pressure control (ie, more than the stan- dard reduction of MAP by 25% over 1 to 2 hours) required?
englishExplanation: For most patients with a hypertensive emergency, the goal of medical management is to reduce MAP by approximately 20% to 25% over the first 1 to 2 hours. In aortic dissection, however, both blood pressure and heart rate must be lowered rapidly to prevent aortic shearing forces and further propagation of the intimal flap, which can result in imminent death. According to the Joint National Committee on Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Pressure (the JNC7), a patient has a hy- pertensive emergency when their blood pressure is severely elevated (>180/120) and complicated by evidence of impending or progressive target organ dysfunction. This critical condition requires immediate reduction of the blood pressure (although not necessarily to normal). Examples include hypertensive encephalopathy, intrac- erebral hemorrhage, acute myocardial infarction, acute left ventricular failure with pulmonary edema, unstable angina pectoris, dissecting aortic aneurysm, or eclampsia. Hypertension injures the arterioles and leads to ischemic damage or hemorrhage. The brain, heart, blood vessels, and kidneys are most commonly affected; persis- tently elevated blood pressure can trigger or exacerbate crises in these target or- gans. In the treatment of hypertensive emergencies, a drug that is easily titratable with rapid onset, rapid maximal effect, and rapid offset is ideal; the optimal thera- peutic agent is dependent on which type of hypertensive crisis is being treated. For example, in aortic dissection, the recommended sequence is as follows: first, decrease intimal shear forces through reduction in heart rate and stroke volume; then, decrease systolic BP. Reduction in heart rate can be achieved with a medication such as esmolol, targeting a goal heart rate of less than 60 bpm; reduction of systolic BP can be achieved with a vasodilator (eg, nicardipine, clevidipine, or sodium nitroprusside) tar- geting a goal systolic blood pressure of less than 110 mm Hg. In aortic dis- section, a faster decrease in blood pressure is essential to reduce further injury and perioperative adverse events. Incorrect Answer Explanations In ACS, significantly elevated blood pressure and increased afterload lead to decreased coronary artery perfusion and increased cardiac work. Although it is important to reduce blood pressure, this decrease can occur within 1 to 2 hours. Other interventions, such as antiplatelet and an- ticoagulant medications with reperfusion therapy, take precedence. Nitroglycerin causes coronary vessel dilation, which leads to a decrease in vascular resistance that is dose dependent. Hypertensive encephalopathy is the result of vasogenic cerebral edema and the failure of CNS autoregulation. In hypertensive encephalopathy, a decrease in blood pressure should occur within 1 to 2 hours. Patients of- ten present with headache, vomiting, and altered mental status; focal neurologic deficits might be present but not follow a specific anatomic pattern. Treatment with antihypertensive medications such as labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine can re- verse the effects and symptoms. Nitroprusside is not recommended. Renal injury is defined by an increase in serum creatinine of 0.3 mg/dL in 48 hours, or 1.5 or more times the baseline value in 7 days, or urine volume less than 0.5 mL/kg/hr in 6 hours. As with treatment in myocardial infarction and hy- pertensive encephalopathy, blood pressure reduction in renal injury is needed within 1 to 2 hours but not as emergently as it is in aortic dissection. Fenoldopam is a first-line agent in this setting; its use can lead to improved renal perfusion, and it is associated with reduction in in-hospital death and need for dialysis.

question: Which drug is safe for patients taking MAOIs?
englishExplanation: Monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors are used in the treatment of some patients with depression but can cause complications, such as serotonin syndrome and hypertensive crises, when taken in conjunction with other medications. Morphine is the only opioid that is safe for patients taking MAO in- hibitors. Patients who take MAO inhibitors are also at risk of developing severe hypertension if they ingest foods that contain large quantities of tyramine (eg, beer, cheese, bananas, processed foods, or soy products). Incorrect Answer Explanations Taking MAO inhibitors with amphetamines can potentiate the effects of amphetamines and cause a hypertensive crisis. Taking amphetamines with MAO inhibitors is contraindicated. When given to a patient taking an MAO inhibitor, meperidine can cause excita- tion, agitation, severe hypertension, and hyperthermia. However, seizures, coma, and even death can also result. A number of other over-the-counter and prescription drugs can cause severe inter- actions in patients taking MAO inhibitors. Tricyclic antidepressants, for instance, stimulate a release of norepinephrine and inhibit reuptake. Patients should be instructed to check with a pharmacist or physician before taking any new medication.

question: A previously healthy 40-year-old man presents with isolated lumbar back pain after lifting a heavy object. His vital signs include BP 180/100. Laboratory tests reveal a creatinine level of 0.8 mg/dL; his electrolyte levels, ECG, and an x-ray of the lumbar spine are normal. What is the most appropriate medication to give in the emergency department?
englishExplanation: NSAIDs are the first-line therapy for back pain and are a reasonable first step in this case. This patient has asymptomatic hypertension with nothing to suggest end-organ dysfunction. Laboratory testing has been done in this case; however, ACEP's 2023 clinical policy on asymptomatic elevated blood pressure suggests that routine screening for target organ injury is not required for patients with asymptomatic hypertension in the emer- gency department. Screening can be considered in select patients, such as those with poor access to timely follow-up (level C recommendation). Furthermore, treat- ment to emergently lower the blood pressure is not required. Incorrect Answer Explanations The first-line medication for hypertension in many patients is amlodipine. However, without signs of end-organ damage, emergent treatment of asymptomatic hypertension is not required in the emergency department. In select patients (eg, those without access to timely follow-up), initiation of long-term antihypertensive therapy can be considered. Metoprolol is a good first-line therapy for certain patients and may be beneficial in patients experiencing signs of end-organ damage related to hypertension. However, without signs of end-organ damage, emergent treatment of asympto- matic hypertension is not required in the emergency department. In select pa- tients (eg, those without access to timely follow-up), initiation of long-term antihy- pertensive therapy can be considered. Opioids are not a first-line therapy for musculoskeletal back pain and should be avoided when possible. NSAIDs are a more appropriate first step in this case.

question: A patient with hypertension and severe asthma presents with acute chest pain ra- diating to the back. Their vital signs include BP 210/140 in the right arm, BP 170/100 in the left, and P 110. There is moderate diffuse wheezing. A chest x-ray was performed and is shown below. What is the most appropriate pharmacologic intervention? Credit: Copyright 2024 Dr. Craig Hacking. Image courtesy of Dr. Craig Hacking and Radiopaedia.org, rID: 73356. Used under license.
englishExplanation: The most appropriate pharmacologic intervention is diltiazem. This patient has a wide mediastinum, and their presentation is concerning for aortic dissection. The first-line impulse-control therapy for aortic dissection is a beta-blocker, such as esmolol or labetalol. However, in patients with a history of asthma, respiratory status must be closely monitored; beta-blockade can worsen asthma. In this case, the shear forces on the aorta must be reduced with intravenous antihypertensives with an alternate agent, targeting a systolic blood pressure of 100 to 120 mm Hg. Remember that the Stanford classification categorizes aortic dissections as either Type A or Type B. Type A can involve the ascending aorta, the arch, and thoracoabdominal aorta. Type B involves the descending thoracic aorta distal to the left subclavian artery without involvement of ascending aorta. The other common classification is the DeBakey system. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient has findings concerning for an aortic dissection. Although la- betalol would help lower the blood pressure and heart rate, it could worsen the patient's asthma and respiratory status. Thus, an alternative agent, such as a cal- cium-channel blocker, is more appropriate. Nitroglycerin is the first-line therapy for flash pulmonary edema because it is pri- marily a venous dilator. It is only effective on arterial circulation at very high doses. There is no pulmonary edema noted on the x-ray in this case. This patient has findings concerning for an aortic dissection, and an alternative antihy- pertensive agent, such as a calcium-channel blocker, is more appropriate. This patient has findings concerning for an aortic dissection. Phentolamine is an alpha-1 and alpha-2 blocker, and its primary uses are in sympath- omimetic hypertension and hypertension secondary to pheochromocy- toma. It is rarely used in the emergency department and is not a recommended therapy for aortic dissection.

question: A patient in the third trimester of pregnancy presents with headaches and leg swelling. Her vital signs include BP 170/130 and no fever. Her urine dipstick test result is positive for 3+ protein. Which medication is indicated?
englishExplanation: The patient's presentation is concerning for preeclampsia. It is important to rec- ognize preeclampsia, which affects 5% to 7% of all pregnant patients and is respon- sible for more than 70,000 maternal deaths and 500,000 fetal deaths worldwide every year. The presenting symptoms include new-onset hyper- tension and proteinuria during the third trimester, which can progress rapidly to serious complications. The first step is to reduce the systolic blood pressure to <140. There are three first-line medications for this condition: hydralazine IV, labetalol IV, and nifedipine PO. These medications are necessary to reduce blood pressure and en- sure maternal and fetal health. Magnesium is also added for preeclampsia with se- vere features. Incorrect Answer Explanations ACE inhibitors, such as enalapril, are contraindicated in pregnant pa- tients. ACE inhibitors have resulted in fetal malformations including renal failure, bony malformations, and pulmonary hypoplasia. Nitroprusside, in combination with esmolol or a beta-blocker, has historically been used in acute aortic dissection. Nitroprusside is contraindicated in pregnant patients because of potential cyanide toxicity. Valsartan is an angiotensin-receptor blocker and would not be used in the acute set- ting of preeclampsia. Valsartan's use in pregnant patients is also contraindicated be- cause it has been shown to be harmful to the fetus in the second and third trimesters.

question: What is a first-line medication for nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage?
englishExplanation: Nicardipine is an effective treatment for hypertension associated with intracerebral hemorrhage. This drug acts by blocking the influx of calcium into vascular smooth muscle and cardiac cells. The inhibition of calcium flux leads to va- sodilation. It is typically given as an infusion and can be titrated to achieve the de- sired effect. Incorrect Answer Explanations Nitroglycerin is not indicated in intracerebral hemorrhage. It is a first- line therapy in acute pulmonary edema and for anginal chest pain. It can be used in refractory hypertension particularly in those settings. Its mode of action is primarily on the venous system. With regard to the intracerebral vascular system in particular, nitroglycerin causes vasodilation of the basal intracranial arteries. Phentolamine is an alpha-1 and alpha-2 blocker. Its primary use is in sympath- omimetic hypertension and hypertension secondary to pheochromocytoma. Phentolamine is rarely used in the emergency department and is not part of the rec- ommended therapies for intracranial hemorrhage. Verapamil is not indicated. Medications for intracerebral hemorrhage due to hypertension include nicardipine, labetalol, and esmolol. Verapamil is not a first-line therapy for this condition.

question: A 50-year-old asthmatic patient presents with an isolated dry cough for the last week. Their vital signs are BP 170/100, P 75, R 18, and T 38.0°C (100.4°F); SpO is 98% on room air. Laboratory findings, including the results of a comprehen- sive metabolic panel, are within normal limits. Auscultation of heart and lungs reveals no abnormalities. A chest x-ray is shown below. What is the best next step in management? 2 Credit: WILLSIE/iStock/Getty Images Plus.
englishExplanation: At this time, there is no indication for further or acute management of this patient. The chest x-ray is normal. Although the patient's blood pressure is ele- vated, there are no signs of end-organ damage, which would require fur- ther evaluation and management in the emergency department if present. In the setting of a singular reading of hypertension, the diagnosis can be confirmed and treated if necessary in a primary care setting. Communication and patient education are important to help the patient understand why their cough and high blood pressure reading are not emergent conditions at this time. It is also im- portant to ensure that the patient has access to outpatient follow-up. Incorrect Answer Explanations Antibiotics are not indicated at this time. The patient's chest x-ray does not show evidence of pneumonia, and no abnormalities were heard on auscultation. This presentation is unlikely to be a bacterial infection. Thus, the patient can be dis- charged home with supportive care. Although the patient is hypertensive in the emergency department, there are no signs of acute end-organ damage. At this time, the emergency physician does not need to reduce the patient's blood pressure because there are no signs or symp- toms attributable to hypertension. However, it is important to help ensure that the patient has access to outpatient follow-up. A needle thoracostomy would be indicated in the setting of a tension pneumotho- rax. However, this patient has a normal chest x-ray and nothing else suggestive of a pneumothorax.

question: A healthy 34-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of fever and fatigue. She denies any other symptoms. Laboratory workup is reassuring, and a bedside cardiac ultrasound is performed and shown below. What is the diagnosis? Credit: Courtesy of JETem.org.
englishExplanation: 0:00/ 0:06 Atrial myxomas are the most common primary cardiac tumor. They vary in size, ranging from 1 to 15 cm in diameter. Larger tumors have a smooth surface and may be associated with constitutional symptoms, embolic events, ar- rhythmias, or symptoms of valvular obstruction. They are typically identified on bedside ultrasound or TEE as isolated hyperechoic masses, usually in the left atrium (~75%). Most myxomas are benign and either are found incidentally or present with consti- tutional symptoms. Most originate in the left atrium. Myxomas are more common in women. Myxomas are treated with resection of the tumor, with usually low re- currence rates. Incorrect Answer Explanations Apical thrombi are typically found after myocardial infarction (MI), par- ticularly anterior STEMI. These can lead to arterial embolic events such as stroke. Risk can be mitigated with at least 3 months of anticoagulation. With the in- creasing frequency of reperfusion therapy, apical thrombi are now less common. On ultrasound, they appear as echogenic material within the apex of the ventricle. Papillary muscle rupture is a life-threatening complication after STEMI and non-STEMI, occurring about 2 to 7 days later. The most common type is pos- teromedial papillary muscle rupture. Clinically, patients will be hypotensive with pulmonary edema. A holosystolic murmur may be heard as well. On ultrasound or echocardiography, a flail segment of the mitral valve will be appreciated with the free segment moving in the left ventricle. Valvular vegetations are typically seen in patients with endocarditis. Risk factors for development include existing valvular conditions, indwelling catheters, recent dental or surgical procedures, and intravenous drug use. Most patients present with fever, anorexia, weight loss, and bacteremia on laboratory tests. These patients require intravenous antibiotics. Uncommon ex- amination findings include Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, and splinter hemorrhages. They can be visualized on ultrasound as vegetation(s) on the valve and may move with valve movement. Transesophageal echocardiogra- phy is more sensitive than transthoracic echocardiography for vegetations.

question: A patient arrives septic, and native valve infective endocarditis is suspected. Which antibiotic is the most appropriate initial choice for empiric treatment in the emergency department?
englishExplanation: Vancomycin is the most appropriate initial antibiotic choice for the emergency department treatment of suspected infective endocarditis. Definitive therapy should be tailored to blood culture results, and it may be appro- priate to obtain three sets of blood cultures and admit the patient pending results. In a patient who is septic, it is important to start empiric antibiotic therapy, and this should cover Staphylococcal, Streptococcal, and Enterococcal species. These are the most common causative pathogens in all types of infective endocarditis worldwide, and in the United States, Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism. Vancomycin provides excellent antibiotic coverage and is a good initial choice for most patients. It also is the drug of choice for MRSA infections. Use of combination antibiotic therapy with regimens such as vancomycin and gentamicin is generally recommended for endocarditis, but vancomycin is the most appropriate first-line antibiotic for an emergency physician to start while considering the possible etiol- ogy and assistance from infectious disease consultation. Note that native valve en- docarditis and prosthetic valve endocarditis are treated differently depending on the culture results, but initial regimens include vancomycin, gentamicin, and rifampin. Most patients with endocarditis have either predisposing cardiac abnormalities (eg, prosthetic valve, mitral valve prolapse, bicuspid aortic valve, or calcific aortic stenosis) or risk factors for disease (eg, injected drug use, indwelling catheters, poor dental hygiene, or HIV). A history of intravenous drug abuse puts a patient at even higher risk of S. aureus infection (>50% cases). The diagnosis of infective endocarditis can be made using the modified Duke Criteria (sensitivity >90%), which involves the identification of: two major criteria; one major and three minor criteria; or five minor criteria.
