Nonsevere infection is the “typical” presentation of watery diarrhea, crampy abdominal pain and tenderness, and fever, but otherwise normal laboratory work and vital signs. Severe and nonsevere cases can be treated with low-dose oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Severe cases should be imaged to rule out ful- minant findings such as toxic megacolon. Major risk factors for developing a C. difficile infection include recent antibiotic use, age over 65 years, use of acid-suppressing medications, obesity, im- munosuppression, a history of inflammatory bowel disease, and ad- vanced liver disease. Older age, in particular, is associated with a more than 10 times higher rate of C. difficile infection as well as more severe and fulminant pre- sentations that carry with them greater morbidity and mortality. Historically, clin- damycin use was thought to be high risk for developing a C. difficile infection; how- ever, any antibiotic use can actually increase the risk. Risk increases with the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics, use of multiple antibiotics simultaneously, and with longer treatment courses. C. difficile can be acquired both in health care and community settings. Incorrect Answer Explanations Intravenous ceftriaxone is used for the treatment of spontaneous bacte- rial peritonitis. It has no role in the management of fulminant C. difficile infection. Intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam are commonly used broad-spectrum antibiotics in the setting of undifferentiated sepsis or septic shock. However, this patient's history and evaluation are highly concerning for fulminant C. difficile infection; therefore, targeted treatment is most appropriate. Rifaximin is an oral antibiotic primarily used for the treatment of he- patic encephalopathy and traveler's diarrhea. Although multiple studies have shown it to have efficacy against C. difficile, the current Infectious Diseases Society of America treatment guidelines only recommend it as a second-line agent for recurrent C. difficile infection. It does not have an established role in the treatment of fulminant C. difficile colitis at this time.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with diarrhea and flatulence for 1 month. She also has a burning pruritic rash on her knees, shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Credit: Mendes FBR, Hissa-Elian A, Abreu MAMM, Gonçalves VS.
englishExplanation: The rash above is dermatitis herpetiformis, and the patient likely has celiac dis- ease, which is also known as gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Dermatitis herpetiformis is a burning, pruritic rash that is associated with celiac disease and can last weeks to months. Celiac disease is an immune-me- diated disorder of the small intestine that is triggered by ingested gluten. The protein gliadin, found in gluten, triggers an immune response that leads to villous atrophy and inflammation of the lamina propria. Celiac disease is more common in women than men, and there is a genetic compo- nent to the disease, with first- and second-degree relatives of patients with celiac disease being at higher risk. Additionally, people with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroiditis, pulmonary hemosiderosis, Down syndrome, and Turner syndrome are at increased risk of developing celiac disease. Patients with celiac disease often present with bulky, foul-smelling, floating diarrhea (steatorrhea) and flatulence, as well as signs and symptoms of malabsorption, such as fatigue, weight loss, and smaller stature in children. They may also report abdominal distention and pain. Patients can develop atrophic glossitis, aphthous stomatitis, and dermatologic manifesta- tions, such as dermatitis herpetiformis. Some patients also develop iron-defi- ciency anemia, bone loss, and neurologic symptoms related to nutritional malab- sorption. Celiac disease patients often have ineffective absorption of their medica- tions as well. They are considered to have hyposplenism and may, therefore, benefit from pneumococcal vaccination. Patients with recurrent diarrhea should be evaluated by a gastroenterologist and tested to rule out celiac disease and other bowel disorders. The preferred sero- logic test for celiac disease is tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) antibody. Patients should also undergo an upper endoscopy with biopsy of the small bowel. There are many additional antibody assays that can be used in conjunction with tTG-IgA antibody and upper endoscopy to determine if a patient has celiac disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations Colon cancer would be an unlikely cause of this patient's diarrhea. Although pa- tients with colon cancer can develop skin metastases, this is extremely rare. Dermatitis herpetiformis is not associated with Crohn disease. However, Crohn disease can present with skin lesions, such as pyoderma gangrenosum (which manifests as a painful ulcer that often enlarges rapidly) as well as erythema nodosum (which are tender red nodules of the skin). Crohn disease is an inflammatory bowel disease that is often associated with diarrhea and abdominal pain. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is a tickborne illness caused by the bac- teria Rickettsia rickettsii. Patients with RMSF can have GI symptoms, but the rash often starts on the wrists and palms, spreading up the limbs and trunk. The rash begins as macules that progress to petechiae.

question: A 20-year-old man with Down syndrome presents with 1 month of foul-smelling, floating diarrhea; flatulence; fatigue; and weight loss. He also has painful ulcers in his mouth, as shown below. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms? Credit: blanscape/iStock/Getty Images Plus.
englishExplanation: This patient likely has celiac disease (also known as gluten-sensitive enteropathy). He is experiencing weight loss, steatorrhea, and aphthous stomatitis. Celiac dis- ease is an immune-mediated disorder of the small intestine that is trig- gered by ingesting gluten. The protein gliadin, found in gluten, triggers an im- mune response that leads to villous atrophy and inflammation of the lamina pro- pria. Patients with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroiditis, pulmonary hemosiderosis, Down syndrome, and Turner syndrome are at increased risk of developing celiac disease. Patients with celiac disease often present with bulky, foul-smelling, floating diarrhea (steatorrhea) and flatulence, as well as signs and symptoms of malabsorption (eg, fatigue, weight loss, and smaller stature in children). They may also report abdominal distention and pain. Patients can develop atrophic glossitis, aphthous stomatitis, and dermatologic manifesta- tions, such as dermatitis herpetiformis. Some patients also develop iron-defi- ciency anemia, bone loss, and neurologic symptoms related to nutritional malab- sorption. Celiac disease patients often have ineffective absorption of their medica- tions. They are considered to have hyposplenism and may, therefore, benefit from pneumococcal vaccination. Patients with recurrent diarrhea should be evaluated by a gastroenterologist and tested to rule out celiac disease and other bowel disorders. The preferred sero- logic test for celiac disease is tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) antibody. Patients should also undergo an upper endoscopy with biopsy of the small bowel. There are many additional antibody assays that can be used in conjunction with tTG-IgA antibody and upper endoscopy to determine if a patient has celiac disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cholera is an unlikely diagnosis in this patient. Cholera is a waterborne diar- rheal illness caused by the bacteria Vibrio cholerae, and it is very rare in places with adequate sewage and water treatment infrastructure. In severe forms of this illness, patients often present with watery diarrhea (“rice water stools”) and dehydration. Cholera is treated with rehydration and antibiotics, such as doxycycline and ciprofloxacin. Colon cancer would be an unlikely cause of this patient's diarrhea. Although pa- tients with colon cancer can present with weight loss and diarrhea (and the inci- dence of early-onset colorectal cancer is increasing), it would be improbable in this young patient. Patients with Down syndrome and Turner syndrome have a higher risk of celiac disease. They also have increased risk of leukemias, liver cancer, and testicular cancer. Syphilis is not a likely cause of this patient's diarrhea, and the oral le- sions (chancres) in primary syphilis are often painless. However, patients with other STIs can develop various intestinal infections, including cryptosporid- ium, and can exhibit aphthous stomatitis on examination, so it is important to rule out other potential causes of diarrhea.

question: Patients with which modifying factor have an increased risk of developing celiac disease?
englishExplanation: Patients with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroiditis, pulmonary hemosiderosis, Down syndrome, and Turner syndrome are at increased risk of developing celiac disease. Celiac disease is also more common in women, and there is a genetic component to the disease, with first- and second-de- gree relatives of patients with celiac disease being at higher risk. Celiac disease is an immune-mediated disorder of the small intestine that is triggered by ingesting gluten. The protein gliadin found in gluten triggers an immune response that leads to villous atrophy and inflammation of the lamina propria. Patients with celiac often present with bulky, foul-smelling, floating di- arrhea (steatorrhea) and flatulence, as well as signs and symptoms of malabsorption, such as fatigue, weight loss, and smaller stature in children. They may also report abdominal distention and pain. Patients with recurrent diar- rhea should be evaluated by a gastroenterologist and tested to rule out celiac disease and other bowel disorders. The preferred serologic test for celiac disease is tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) antibody. Patients should also undergo an upper endoscopy with biopsy of the small bowel. There are many additional antibody assays that can be used in conjunction with tTG-IgA anti- body and upper endoscopy to determine if a patient has celiac disease. Treatment for celiac disease primarily involves removing gluten from the diet. If symptoms are unimproved after removal of gluten, prednisone or budesonide is recommended. In rare cases, children and adults with celiac disease can also present with celiac crisis (gliadin shock), which is often triggered by an im- mune stimulus (eg, infection, pregnancy, or surgery). In celiac crisis, patients develop severe diarrhea, which can be life-threatening. Patients with celiac crisis require hospitalization, intravenous fluids, electrolyte re- placement, and further workup to rule out other potential causes of diarrhea. Incorrect Answer Explanations HLA B27 is a human leukocyte antigen linked to spondyloarthritis and other autoimmune disorders, but not to celiac disease. There is thought to be a clinical link between HLA-DR3, DQ2, DQ8, and celiac disease. Celiac disease is also associated with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune thyroiditis. Patients who smoke cigarettes appear to have a lower risk of celiac dis- ease. The association is unclear, but it is believed to be related to effects of smoking on the immune system and gut permeability. However, smoking increases the risk of other inflammatory bowel diseases, such as Crohn disease. Patients with type 2 diabetes do not appear to have an increased risk of developing celiac disease. Patients with type 1 diabetes, however, have a greater risk of developing celiac disease. This is likely related to HLA factors DR3, DQ2, and DQ8, which are associated with both type 1 diabetes and celiac disease.

question: What is the best test to diagnose celiac disease?
englishExplanation: Patients with celiac disease often present with steatorrhea and flatulence, as well as signs and symptoms of malabsorption. Patients with recurrent diarrhea should be evaluated by a gastroenterologist and tested to rule out celiac disease and other bowel disorders. The preferred serologic test for celiac disease is tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) antibody. The tTG-IgA test is 90% to 98% sensitive and 95% to 97% specific for celiac disease. Patients should also undergo an upper endoscopy with biopsy of the small bowel. There are many additional antibody assays that can be used in conjunction with tTG-IgA to determine if a patient has celiac disease. Treatment for celiac disease primarily involves removing gluten from the diet. If symptoms are unimproved after removal of gluten, prednisone or budesonide is recommended. In rare cases, children and adults with celiac disease can also present with celiac crisis (gliadin shock), which is often triggered by an im- mune stimulus (eg, infection, pregnancy, or surgery). In celiac crisis, patients develop severe diarrhea, which can be life-threatening. Incorrect Answer Explanations Anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA) are not associated with celiac disease, but they are associated with Crohn disease. ASCA are specific but not sensitive for diagnosing Crohn disease. HLA B27 is a human leukocyte antigen linked to spondyloarthritis and other autoimmune disorders, but not to celiac disease. There is thought to be a clinical link between HLA-DR3, DQ2, DQ8, and celiac disease. Perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA) are not as- sociated with celiac disease, but they are associated with ulcerative coli- tis (UC). pANCA are specific but not sensitive for diagnosing UC.

question: What is the best medication to treat celiac disease?
englishExplanation: The best intervention for patients with celiac disease is removal of gluten from the diet and vitamin supplementation to help replete any vita- min deficiencies that have occurred as a result of malabsorption. The best pharma- cologic intervention in a patient whose condition is unimproved after removing gluten is a steroid, such as prednisone or budesonide, to reduce intesti- nal inflammation. Celiac disease is an immune-mediated disorder of the small intestine, triggered by ingested gluten. The protein gliadin, found in gluten, triggers an immune response that leads to villous atrophy and inflammation of the lamina pro- pria. Celiac disease is more common in women, and there is a genetic component to the disease, with first- and second-degree relatives of patients with celiac disease being at higher risk. Patients with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroiditis, pulmonary hemosiderosis, Down syndrome, and Turner syndrome are also at increased risk of developing celiac disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations Azathioprine is a purine analog and an immunosuppressive medication. Although it is not recommended to treat celiac disease, it is used to treat Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Azathioprine has a slow onset of action and might require several months of treatment to see an effect. Mercaptopurine is an antimetabolite antineoplastic drug and is not rec- ommended to treat celiac disease. However, it is used to treat Crohn dis- ease and ulcerative colitis. Mercaptopurine can cause bone marrow toxicity, so patients on this medication should routinely have blood counts monitored. Mesalamine is an aminosalicylate immunosuppressive medication. It is not recommended for celiac disease. Mesalamine is used to treat Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Because it can cause bone marrow toxicity, pa- tients on this medication require routine monitoring of blood counts.

question: What is one of the criteria used to diagnose celiac crisis?

options.text: Elevated tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody titers

englishExplanation: The criteria for diagnosing celiac crisis are acute onset of rapidly progress- ing GI symptoms related to celiac disease that require hospitalization or par- enteral nutrition along with two of the following: Signs of severe dehydration, including hemodynamic instability or orthostatic changes Neurologic dysfunction Renal dysfunction: creatinine greater than 2 g/dL Metabolic acidosis: pH less than 7.35 Hypoproteinemia: albumin less than 3 g/dL Abnormal electrolytes including hypernatremia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hy- pokalemia, or hypomagnesemia Weight loss greater than 4.5 kg (10 lb) Patients with celiac crisis (also known as gliadin shock) require hospi- talization, intravenous fluids, electrolyte replacement, and workup to rule out other potential causes. Celiac crisis is often triggered by an im- mune stimulus, such as infection, pregnancy, or surgery. In celiac crisis, patients develop severe diarrhea, which can be life-threatening. Incorrect Answer Explanations Tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A (tTG-IgA) antibody titers are the best serologic test to diagnose celiac disease. However, they are not among the criteria to diagnose celiac crisis, and results are unlikely to be obtained rapidly. The tTG-IgA test is 90% to 98% percent sensitive and 95% to 97% percent specific for celiac disease. Hemoccult-positive stools are not part of the criteria to diagnose celiac crisis. Bleeding does often occur chronically in celiac disease, which is likely a contributor (alongside decreased iron absorption) to the iron deficiency these patients often de- velop. Thus, patients with celiac disease will often have hemoccult-posi- tive stools. Anemia is not among the criteria for diagnosing celiac crisis. Patients with celiac disease will often be anemic as a result of decreased iron absorption and chronic small bowel bleeding; thus, they may have anemia and a de- creased mean corpuscular volume until gluten is removed from the diet, malabsorp- tion improves, and nutrients (including iron) are replenished.

question: Which medication should be administered to a patient presenting with dysmenorrhea?
englishExplanation: Patients with dysmenorrhea have recurrent abdominal or pelvic pain during menses. NSAIDs are the first-line pharmacologic treatment for dysmenorrhea be- cause they reduce prostaglandin levels, acting as an effective anti-inflammatory and helping with the pelvic pain. Typically, these patients present with an unremarkable examination, including pelvic examination findings, vital signs, and laboratory find- ings. If pursued, they will also have an unremarkable or noncontributory pelvic ul- trasound. The first steps in treating dysmenorrhea include educating patients, en- couraging exercise, using heat packs, and likely referring to gynecology. Incorrect Answer Explanations Estrogen alone is not indicated in the treatment of dysmenorrhea. However, certain hormonal contraceptives, such as mixed estrogen-progestin oral contraceptives or progestin-only contraceptives, can be included in the management of dys- menorrhea for some patients. These medications reduce prostaglandin in the uterus, reducing both flow and cramps for patients. NSAIDs are the first line of pharmacologic treatment for dysmenorrhea. Leuprolide may be considered in refractory dysmenorrhea, usually in conjunction with the patient's gynecologist. Leuprolide suppresses the menstrual cycle, is expensive, and includes significant side effects. Thus, leuprolide is not a first-line treatment but can be considered for persistently symptomatic patients. NSAIDs are the first line of pharmacologic treatment for dysmenorrhea. Methotrexate is not used in the treatment of dysmenorrhea. However, it is sometimes used in conjunction with OB/GYN consultation as an abortifacient, particularly when opting for medical management of an ectopic pregnancy. NSAIDs are the first line of pharmacologic treatment for dysmenorrhea.

question: A 73-year-old man presents with tightness in his chest after eating a pulled pork sandwich. He is unable to tolerate liquid by mouth; anything ingested is almost immediately regurgitated. An ECG is normal. What is the most effective manage- ment for this condition?
englishExplanation: This patient has food impaction, which most often occurs in the distal esophagus. The best management for food impaction is esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and manual retrieval or advancement of the food bolus. Medical ap- proaches to encourage esophageal relaxation are unlikely to be successful, and feed- ing agents to dissolve the food can be harmful. Esophageal food impaction may de- velop for multiple reasons, aside from simply trying to swallow a mouthful that is too large. Patients might have structural abnormalities (eg, strictures, a Schatzki ring, esophageal webs, or a Zenker diverticulum). The narrowest point in the esophagus is the cricopharyngeus muscle or upper esophageal sphincter. Children account for 80% of cases of swallowed foreign bodies, and they tend to get objects trapped in the upper esophagus. Adults, especially prisoners and psychiatry patients, who ingest foreign bodies most often get theirs stuck at the lower esophageal sphincter. Anything that passes through the pylorus is likely to complete transit of the GI tract. Although expectant management is reasonable for a patient who is tolerating the obstruction, food impactions should not be allowed to persist for more than 24 hours because they can lead to esophageal perforation. Dangerous objects, such as sharp objects or button batteries, need to be re- moved immediately. Incorrect Answer Explanations Glucagon has been widely advocated for use in food bolus impaction to relax the esophageal smooth muscle and allow passage of the material. However, glucagon was shown to be ineffective when studied against a control and may be associated with vomiting. Although glucagon is likely nonharmful and could be offered while awaiting the availability of an EGD, it is not the most effective treatment ap- proach in this case. Effervescent beverages (ie, sodium bicarbonate plus a mild acid such as lemon juice or a brand-name cola) can dislodge food impactions by generating carbon dioxide in the esophagus to push the food bolus along, and there are case reports of this ap- proach occasionally being effective. However, effervescent beverages are difficult to administer and prone to induce aspiration in patients with complete obstruc- tions, as in this case. Papain, a trypsin-like enzyme, is used as a meat tenderizer. Although it has previ- ously been suggested as an option for dissolving food boluses, it can dissolve the esophagus itself, leading to perforation. Papain has been associated with fa- tal outcomes and should never be considered as a potential therapy for food impaction.

question: A 27-year-old man presents with dysuria and urethral discharge. What is the most appropriate test to determine the etiology of this patient's condition?

options.text: Insert a swab into the urethra and send the sample for culture and blood agar plating
Obtain a pharyngeal swab and test for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Send a urine sample for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae PCR assay
Send a urine sample for urinalysis, microscopic examination, and bacterial culture

correctAnswer: Send a urine sample for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae PCR assay
englishExplanation: Among patients in the United States, urethritis is most commonly caused by infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. The most sensitive and specific test for C. trachomatis is a nucleic acid amplification technique (NAAT), such as the PCR assay. Because infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae often accompa- nies infection with C. trachomatis, if one is suspected, the other must be considered as well. The NAAT is not quite as sensitive for gonorrhea as it is for chlamydia, but the yield is still vastly improved over the traditional chocolate agar or Thayer- Martin culture medium. Most chlamydial infections are asymptomatic: in men, up to 70% of chlamydia cases are asymptomatic, and the symptoms — dysuria with urethritis or epididymitis — appear 1 to 3 weeks after exposure. In women, chlamy- dia is asymptomatic in up to 90% of cases, so the CDC recommends the screening of asymptomatic women as a public health measure. Samples may be obtained from the urethra in women, but endocervical samples have a higher yield. Treatment recommendations have recently changed; CDC guidelines were updated in 2021. A single dose of Azithromycin 1 g PO is no longer recommended as the first-line treatment for chlamydia. Current guidelines recommend Doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 1 week for chlamydia and Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM for gonor- rhea. In N. gonorrhoeae, options for oral therapy are severely limited by wide- spread resistance to quinolones and other agents. In addition to urethritis, gonor- rhea can cause pharyngitis or proctitis. When they are present, symptoms of gono- coccal and chlamydial infections are generally indistinguishable. Coinfection is common. Incorrect Answer Explanations Due to the availability of NAAT for testing patients' urine, it is unneces- sary to obtain samples from men from inside the urethra. Swabbing in- side the urethra is also very painful. Furthermore, cell cultures for C. tra- chomatis are difficult to perform and are unreliable. Also, the proper medium for N. gonorrhoeae is the chocolate agar or Thayer-Martin agar, not the standard blood agar. Detection via latex agglutination testing of C. trachomatis and N. gonor- rhoeae in the pharynx is possible for patients who have engaged in oral- genital contact. If they have not, the best test is PCR assay and urinalysis. A urinalysis with microscopic examination and culture is appropriate for patients with dysuria when a UTI is suspected. That is a reasonable initial step in this patient's evaluation, but the presence of urethral discharge (“drip”) is strongly suspicious for urethritis caused by C. trachomatis or N. gonor- rhoeae. A standard urine culture does not grow either of these organisms.

question: A 9-year-old boy presents with progressive facial swelling. His features are dis- torted from swollen eyelids and generalized edema. Examination of his abdomen is consistent with mild ascites. He has not had any recent infections. Urinalysis reveals 4+ protein and no hematuria. What is the physiologic cause of this patient's edema?

options.text: Decreased excretion of free water due to decreased glomerular filtration in the kidney
Decreased production of albumin and other proteins in the liver
Release of nitric oxide, histamine, and other inflammatory mediators from mast cells
Urinary excretion of protein leading to decreased oncotic pressure in the plasma

correctAnswer: Urinary excretion of protein leading to decreased oncotic pressure in the plasma
englishExplanation: This boy is presenting with a nephrotic syndrome, which could be induced by a number of different pathological changes in the glomerulus. These processes lead to increased permeability of the glomerulus to proteins and the excretion of proteins in the urine, hence the large amount of protein detected on urinalysis. This leads to de- creased serum albumin and hypoproteinemia, with a loss of oncotic pressure in the plasma and resulting generalized edema. The kidney also retains salt and water in response to increased aldosterone secretion, and the edema worsens. The liver attempts to counter the loss of albumin by increasing protein production of all kinds, including lipoproteins, leading to hyperlipidemia and hypercoagulabil- ity. In this patient, the most likely renal pathology is minimal change disease. It is the most common primary glomerulonephritis in children and one of the few that is unlikely to have concomitant hematuria. A similar complaint with a recent URI is a typical presentation for post-Streptococcus glomerulonephritis. Other causes of glomerulonephritis include IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), focal segmental glomerulonephritis, and membranous glomeru- lonephritis (as seen in systemic lupus erythematosus). Incorrect Answer Explanations When faced with decreased blood flow to the glomerulus, the kidney re- sponds appropriately by decreasing filtration and retaining sodium and free water as much as possible. This decreased filtration leads to the uremia seen in acute kidney injury from shock or severe dehydration. This patient has increased fil- tration, leading to increased permeability of the glomerulus to proteins; the loss of these in the urine is consistent with nephrotic syndrome. Decreased production of albumin and other proteins in the liver may cause edema in the setting of liver failure. However, this patient's symptoms are more consistent with nephrotic syndrome with increased permeability of the glomerulus to proteins and the loss of these in the urine. In nephrotic syndrome, the liver in- creases production of albumin and other proteins to compensate for the loss in the urine. This results in hyperlipidemia and hypercoagulability. Anaphylaxis is the result of sudden degranulation of mast cells in response to an antigen. These granules contain preformed vasoactive substances, including his- tamine and nitric oxide that lead to increased vascular permeability and edema. This patient is suffering from the gradual onset of nephrotic syndrome with in- creased permeability of the glomerulus to proteins and the loss of these in the urine. Key Points Minimal change disease is the most common cause of the nephrotic syndrome in children. Characteristics of nephrotic syndrome include loss of protein in the urine leading to generalized edema, increased risk of infections, hyperlipidemia, and increased risk of thromboembolic disease. The presence of protein and blood in the urine is consistent with nephritis.

question: A 3-month-old girl born at full term presents with failure to thrive, with a growth rate consistently falling below the second percentile. On presentation, she is afebrile with normal vital signs but appears lethargic. During the examination, she has a seizure. What is the most likely cause of the seizure?
englishExplanation: The most common cause of poor growth in infants is inadequate dietary intake. Overdilution of infant formula with water can cause significant hypona- tremia, particularly in infants with vomiting and diarrhea, which can cause altered mental status and seizures. A detailed history and physical examination can often indicate other causes of failure to thrive; for example, respiratory distress or cyanosis while feeding may indicate congenital heart disease. Other causes of failure to thrive include diseases that cause inadequate nutrient absorption (eg, GERD, protein allergies, inflammatory bowel disease) or increased me- tabolism (eg, infection, congenital syndromes). Additionally, neglect and in- gestions must always be considered in the differential diagnosis of poor growth. Incorrect Answer Explanations Although biliary atresia can cause poor growth in infants, patients with biliary atresia typically present with jaundice between the 3rd and 6th weeks of life. Caregivers may describe acholic stools and dark urine. Physical findings of bil- iary atresia may include ascites. The most common cause of poor growth in infants is inadequate dietary intake. Overdilution of infant formula with water can cause significant hyponatremia, leading to seizures. Hyperthyroidism is another possible cause of poor growth in infants, but it typically presents within the first 2 weeks of life as irritability. Examination findings, including hypertension, tachycardia, exophthalmos, and goi- ter, may also be present. The most common cause of poor growth in infants is inadequate dietary intake. Overdilution of infant formula with water can cause significant hyponatremia, leading to seizures. Maple syrup urine disease is an autosomal recessive disorder that can cause poor growth in infants. However, it typically becomes apparent soon after birth due to the characteristically sweet odor of the infant's urine. Other symptoms of maple syrup urine disease include poor feeding and lethargy. The most common cause of poor growth in infants is inadequate dietary intake. Overdilution of infant formula with water can cause significant hyponatremia, leading to seizures.

question: A 2-week-old boy is brought in by his mother, who is concerned that he has been sleepier than usual for the past 2 days. The child has been eating 2 oz of pow- dered formula every 2 hours without issue. His vital signs are BP 72/55, P 148, R 47, and T 37°C (98.6°F). The patient is awake and responsive with abnormal skin turgor. Laboratory results include Na 123, K 3.4, Cl 99, HCO 20, BUN 10, Creatinine 0.9, and Glucose 70. What should the initial treatment be?
englishExplanation: This infant has hyponatremia. The initial treatment in a responsive child is 0.9% saline. This infant is likely water intoxicated, stemming from improper mixing of the powdered formula. Treatment of this disorder should include a slow return back to normal sodium level, preferably no more than 12 mEq/L in 24 hours or 0.5 mEq/L/hr. A 10-mL/kg bolus of saline in a 5-kg infant (50 mL) will provide ~8 mEq of Na, which should then increase the serum sodium by 1.5 mEq. Because nor- mal saline has 154 mEq of Na/L, the calculation is 0.154 x 50-mL 0.9 bolus = 7.7 mEq Na, which is then divided by the infant's weight (7.7 mEq Na/5 kg = 1.5 mEq Na serum). Other causes of hyponatremia include: low total body sodium (loss from vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding, a mineralocorticoid deficiency, severe sweating, or renal dis- ease), normal total body sodium (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion [SIADH], adrenal disease, or water intoxication), and high total body sodium (congestive heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, liver failure, or other organ dysfunction). Incorrect Answer Explanations 3 In emergency settings (altered neurologic state or seizure), hypertonic 3% saline may be used, even in pediatrics (2-3 mL/kg = 2-3 mEq of Na increase in serum). However, as this infant is responsive, the appropriate initial therapy would be 0.9% saline. Intravenous dextrose would be indicated if hypoglycemia was the cause of the patient's presentation. However, in this case, the patient has a normal glucose level. Prostaglandin E1 should be considered in a cyanotic infant when sur- vival is dependent on patency of ductus arteriosus. Early infusion with Prostaglandin E should be considered when congenital cardiac disease is a concern.

question: A 46-year-old man presents with 2 hours of hematemesis. He has a history of cir- rhosis and states that the episode was sudden in onset and is not associated with any pain. Which medication is the correct choice to prevent infection and mortal- ity in this patient?
englishExplanation: In the setting of known cirrhosis, painless hematemesis is most con- cerning for variceal bleeding. In patients with upper GI bleeding and known varices or cirrhosis, antibiotic prophylaxis has been demon- strated to prevent infection and mortality. Although there is no clearly supe- rior antibiotic, the 2018 American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases guide- lines recommend agents with broad-spectrum, gram-negative coverage, such as third-generation cephalosporins (eg, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime). These recom- mendations are consistent with most other available guidelines. Incorrect Answer Explanations Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, is recommended in patients with variceal bleeding to slow the hemorrhage by reducing splanchnic and portal blood flow. Octreotide is associated with improved hemostasis and lower rates of rebleeding; however, unlike ceftriaxone, octreotide has not been shown to reduce mortality. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as pantoprazole and omeprazole are frequently given to reduce the effects of acid on bleeding gastric ulcers and have been found to reduce the rate of postendoscopy rebleeding for variceal bleeding; however, like octreotide and unlike ceftriaxone, PPIs do not reduce mortality. The role of PPIs is unclear in nonulcer upper GI bleeding, but they should be given if the source of upper GI bleeding is undifferentiated (or if requested by the consulting gastroenterologist). Although antifibrinolytic tranexamic acid (TXA) seems like a logical choice for uncontrolled bleeding, it has failed to show a meaningful mortality benefit for GI bleeding of any source. The HALT-IT trial compared high-dose TXA to a placebo in patients with upper or lower GI bleeding, but it failed to demonstrate any improvement in mortality and found that the TXA group had higher rates of venous thromboembolism following treatment. Although TXA has demonstrated mortality benefits in other contexts, such as trauma, this benefit has yet to translate to GI bleeding. As a result, TXA does not have a meaningful role in the management of variceal bleeding at this time.

question: A 73-year-old man presents with painless intermittent gross hematuria. He smokes cigarettes daily and frequently uses ibuprofen for back pain. Urinalysis reveals 3+ blood and 1+ protein with 30 RBCs/hpf and no WBCs on microscopic examination. Which disposition plan is most appropriate?

options.text: CT scanning of the abdomen and pelvis followed by urgent urology follow-up
Manual irrigation of the bladder by catheter until the urine is clear and then admission
Reassurance and consideration of prostate hypertrophy therapy
Urine culture and empiric antibiotic coverage for Escherichia coli

correctAnswer: CT scanning of the abdomen and pelvis followed by urgent urology follow-up
englishExplanation: The presentation of an older patient with painless intermittent hematuria should prompt suspicion for a urinary tract carcinoma, most often bladder or renal cell cancer. Patients with this complaint should undergo CT imaging of the ab- domen and pelvis, which is likely to reveal a complex mass in the kidneys if the pa- tient has renal cell cancer. Bladder cancer, however, may not be detectable on CT in its early stages. Therefore, regardless of the imaging results, the patient should be urgently referred to a urologist for appropriate screening by cystoscopy and, if necessary, biopsy. Risk factors for bladder cancer include tobacco use, exces- sive analgesic use, radiation to the pelvis, exposure to cyclophosphamide, and occu- pational exposure to aromatic amines or benzenes. For patients in tropical areas, es- pecially Africa, infection with Schistosoma haematobium is associated with an in- creased rate of bladder cancer. The strongest risk factors for renal cell cancer are to- bacco use, obesity, and hypertension. Incorrect Answer Explanations Patients with large amounts of gross hematuria with visible clots are prone to de- velop a urinary obstruction from a blood clot in the urethra and may re- quire bladder irrigation. Typically, a patient with a urinary tract structural ab- normality or surgery who is taking anticoagulants can develop this complication. The intermittent, mild (only 30 RBCs/hpf) bleeding of the patient in this case is un- likely to cause an acute obstruction or necessitate bladder irrigation or admission. Painless intermittent hematuria with blood appearing at the conclusion of the stream can be caused by benign prostate hypertrophy. Although initiating ther- apy for prostate enlargement can be reasonable, patients with this complaint and multiple risk factors for neoplastic disease should undergo imaging and then be re- ferred. Reassurance alone is not the ideal management. Older men with prostate enlargement and incomplete bladder emptying can de- velop UTIs, which present with hematuria and dysuria. They do not typi- cally complain of painless, intermittent bleeding. Initiating antibiotic therapy and sending a urine culture may be reasonable for this patient, but he should undergo advanced imaging first because of the high risk of cancer.

question: A 63-year-old man with a history of tobacco use and DVT on warfarin presents with intermittent, painless passage of bloody urine of 2 weeks' duration. His physical examination is unremarkable. A urinalysis reveals TNTC (too numerous to count) RBCs/hpf, 5 WBCs/hpf, negative nitrites, negative protein, and no bac- teria. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, WBC count 5.4 x 109/L, Hgb 13.8 g/dL, and INR 2.9. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis is normal. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Administer 10 mg of intravenous vitamin K to reverse anticoagulation
Prescribe a 7-day course of oral ciprofloxacin
Refer the patient to a urologist for cystoscopy
Tell the patient he has passed a stone and needs no treatment

correctAnswer: Refer the patient to a urologist for cystoscopy
englishExplanation: It is tempting to dismiss this patient's hematuria simply because he takes warfarin, but 80% of patients who have hematuria while taking anticoagulant drugs have some underlying pathology. This patient should be referred to urology for cystoscopy to evaluate for cancer of the urinary tract. Although the CT scan was normal, bladder cancer can be missed on CT, and the patient should have a cystoscopy. As little as 1 mL of blood in 1 L of urine can cause noticeable gross hematuria. More than 5 RBCs/hpf is considered significant and is an indication for further investigation. The most common causes of hematuria are kidney stones, carcinoma of the bladder or kidney, trauma, UTI, prostatic hypertro- phy, and glomerulonephritis. In men older than 40 years, carcinomas, espe- cially of the bladder, are the most common cause of hematuria. Risk factors for hematuria include smoking, workplace exposure, race (white), and family history. Incorrect Answer Explanations This patient is not suffering from life-threatening hemorrhage or anemia, so immediate warfarin reversal with intravenous vitamin K is unneces- sary. Withholding warfarin temporarily, however, can be considered. An immunocompetent patient with a UTI would be expected to have dysuria, uri- nary urgency, or suprapubic abdominal discomfort. Additionally, a urinalysis would reveal the presence of WBCs, nitrites, or bacteria. This patient's presentation and workup are inconsistent with infection, so initiating antibiotics is inappropriate. Because this patient's hematuria is painless, urolithiasis is less likely. Given his age and medical history, carcinoma of the bladder is more likely and should be investigated.

question: Which risk factor warrants urgent follow-up in a patient who presents with asymptomatic microscopic hematuria without an obvious life-threatening cause?
englishExplanation: In patients who present with hematuria without an obvious life-threatening cause, outpatient follow-up is appropriate. The urgency of follow-up depends on the pres- ence of gross hematuria or any risk factors for significant disease, including malig- nancy. In patients with microscopic hematuria, these risk factors include male sex, age older than 50, smoking history, occupational exposure to chem- icals or dyes (benzene or aromatic amines), renal insufficiency, history of radiation, and known malignancy. Smoking triples the risk of bladder can- cer compared to nonsmokers. Patients with significant risk factors like these should follow-up with urology for repeat analysis and consideration of further diagnostic testing, ideally within 2 weeks. Microscopic hematuria is a laboratory diagnosis defined as 3 or more RBCs/hpf on a centrifuged urinary specimen. Gross hematuria is diagnosed clinically when there is visible blood in the urine. Microscopic hematuria is a com- mon incidental or pathological diagnosis in the emergency department. The most common causes of hematuria are UTI, nephrolithiasis, and neoplasms. Incorrect Answer Explanations Age older than 30 is not an indication for urgent follow-up or a predictor of signifi- cant disease in patients with microscopic hematuria. However, age older than 50 significantly increases the risk of neoplasm. Some institutions suggest all patients older than 35 with microscopic hematuria and no identifiable benign cause should follow-up within 1 month for continued evaluation. Female sex is not a risk factor for significant disease with microscopic hematuria. Male sex, however, is a risk factor for bladder cancer. Men with microscopic hema- turia should be referred to urology for follow-up. A history of nephrolithiasis is not an indication for urgent outpatient follow-up in a patient who presents with microscopic hematuria without an obvious cause. Microscopic hematuria is very common in patients with nephrolithiasis, which com- monly presents with nausea, vomiting, and unilateral flank pain radiating toward the groin. Hematuria is present in 85% of patients with renal colic.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with gross hematuria, abdominal pain, and urinary retention. A postvoid residual bladder scan shows 850 mL of urine. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Triple-lumen urinary catheter placement with irrigation

correctAnswer: Triple-lumen urinary catheter placement with irrigation
englishExplanation: The next best step in management is to place a triple-lumen urinary catheter to al- low for irrigation. Acute urinary retention is the sudden inability to urinate vol- untarily from the bladder. The initial emergency department management of uri- nary retention includes decompression of the bladder with insertion of a urethral catheter. Although the most common cause of urinary retention is benign prostatic hypertrophy, gross hematuria can lead to clot formation and obstruc- tion in the bladder. This is particularly common in patients who take a blood-thin- ning medication. In these patients, a 20 to 24 Fr triple-lumen catheter should be inserted into the bladder to allow for irrigation. One port is used for balloon in- flation, one is used for urinary drainage, and the other is used for continuous or in- termittent bladder irrigation. To ensure clot evacuation, irrigation should continue until clear urine is produced. Patients with persistent clot burden may require ad- mission and cystoscopy. Incorrect Answer Explanations A single-lumen catheter is used in cases of uncomplicated urinary retention. In cases of urinary retention caused by gross hematuria and clot formation, irrigation must be performed to ensure adequate drainage, and a three-way Foley catheter should be used. Suprapubic catheter insertion can be used in patients with urinary re- tention if urethral catheterization fails. However, this should not be the first step in patients with urinary retention and gross hematuria. Cystoscopy is not the initial treatment for patients with urinary retention caused by gross hematuria with clot formation. Treatment should instead focus on bladder decompression and irrigation using a three-way catheter.

question: A 72-year-old man presents with gross hematuria. He has a history of atrial fib- rillation and is currently on warfarin. What is the most likely cause of hematuria?
englishExplanation: UTI is the most common cause of hematuria and can occur at any age. Hematuria in the anticoagulated patient should not be assumed to be caused directly by chronic anticoagulation. Instead, it should be evaluated similarly to hematuria in patients who are not anticoagulated. In studies of patients on chronic anticoagulation who present with hematuria, the vast majority (>80%) are found to have genitourinary pathology. Infection is the most common cause, fol- lowed by papillary necrosis, bladder malignancy, and renal cysts. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bladder malignancy is a common cause of both microscopic and gross hematuria, especially in patients older than 50 and in those with other risk factors. However, UTI remains the most common cause of hematuria, even in anticoagu- lated patients. Supratherapeutic INR can cause hematuria in a patient anticoagulated with war- farin, but it is not the most likely cause. Most patients on chronic anticoagulation who present with hematuria have an underlying genitourinary cause unrelated to their anticoagulation. Trauma can be a cause of gross hematuria, especially in a chronically anticoagulated patient. Traumatic injuries (eg, renal laceration, bladder contusion, ureteral injury, and urethral injury) can cause gross hematuria. However, UTI remains the most common cause of hematuria, even in this patient population.

question: A 25-year-old woman presents with painless hematuria shortly after running a marathon. She denies any other symptoms. Urinalysis shows 20 to 50 RBCs/hpf without any other abnormality. A BMP is unremarkable. What is the next best step in evaluating this patient's hematuria?

options.text: Abdominal and pelvic CT with IV contrast
Abdominal and pelvic CT without contrast

englishExplanation: Exercise-induced hematuria is a diagnosis of exclusion and should be differentiated from rhabdomyolysis. In rhabdomyolysis, dipstick urinalysis is positive for blood due to the presence of myoglobinuria, but microscopic urinalysis does not show hematuria. In exercise-induced hematuria, urine should return to normal within 7 days, so follow-up is indicated with a repeat urinalysis in 4 to 6 weeks to ensure that microscopic hematuria has resolved. Exercise-induced hematuria is a benign, painless gross or microscopic hematuria that occurs after vigorous exercise. Exercise-induced hematuria resolves with rest and has no apparent underlying urinary tract or renal pathology. There are many hypothesized explanations for transient hematuria after exercise, including increased glomerular permeability and transient renal ischemia. Studies suggest that up to 25% of long-distance runners experience hematuria after running. Incorrect Answer Explanations Abdominal and pelvic CT with intravenous contrast is typically used to evaluate gross hematuria in the setting of trauma to assess for renal laceration, bladder injury, or ureteral injury. Because this patient has a benign workup and no trauma, a CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast is not indicated. Abdominal and pelvic CT without contrast can be used to evaluate for nephrolithiasis in patients who present with hematuria, flank pain, and a classic re- nal colic syndrome. This patient does not have any signs or symptoms other than hematuria. Thus, a CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast is not indicated. Serum CK should be obtained if there is concern for rhabdomyolysis. A five-fold increase above the normal threshold is needed for diagnosis. Rhabdomyolysis typically presents with weakness, fatigue, and muscle aches, which are not present in this patient. Rhabdomyolysis also causes dark or brown urine due to the presence of myoglobinuria. Myoglobinuria results in a positive dipstick uri- nalysis result for blood, but it does not cause microscopic hematuria. Thus, no fur- ther workup for rhabdomyolysis is indicated in this patient.

question: A 33-year-old man presents with gross hematuria after a motor vehicle collision. On examination, he has no blood at the urethral meatus and no genitourinary ab- normality. What is the next best step for diagnosis?

options.text: Abdominal and pelvic CT with IV contrast

correctAnswer: Abdominal and pelvic CT with IV contrast
englishExplanation: Abdominal and pelvic CT with intravenous contrast is the appropriate initial imaging test to evaluate gross hematuria in the setting of blunt or penetrating trauma. CT with intravenous contrast has a high sensitivity and specificity for traumatic renal, bladder, and ureteral injury. The degree of hematuria that should prompt a CT is unknown, but patients without gross hematuria or other pelvic injuries are less likely to have significant injuries found on CT. Similarly, there is no direct correlation between the degree of microscopic hematuria and the severity of injury. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cystoscopy is not the best initial test to assess gross hematuria in the setting of trauma. Cystoscopy can be used to evaluate for bladder malignancy or urethral pathology in the setting of gross hematuria, but CT of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast is the preferred initial imaging modality in trauma. A pelvic x-ray is often included in the initial evaluation of pelvic trauma. Pelvic frac- tures are associated with an increased risk of ureteral injury, but the evaluation of gross hematuria warrants an abdominal and pelvic CT with intravenous contrast. Retrograde urethrogram is the initial test of choice if there is concern for urethral injury in trauma. However, the absence of blood at the urethral meatus, perineal ecchymosis, or genitourinary abnormality significantly decreases the likelihood of urethral injury.

question: A 54-year-old man presents with massive repeated hemoptysis. He produces 500 mL of bright red blood within 20 minutes of arrival. He has an irregular heart rate of 135; BP is 92/45. A stat portable chest x-ray is obtained and shown below. His wife says that he has atrial fibrillation and takes "something that starts with an 'X.'" In addition to considering reversal agents, what is the most appropriate next step in this patient's management? Credit: Timothy H. Kaufman, MD.

options.text: Immediately transfer to the operating room for emergent open thoracotomy
Intubate with a large endotracheal tube into the right mainstem bronchus
Position the patient on his right side with his head elevated

correctAnswer: Intubate with a large endotracheal tube into the right mainstem bronchus
englishExplanation: The acute management of life-threatening pulmonary hemorrhage follows the same principle as any other resuscitation: airway, breathing, and circulation. This patient needs a definitive airway, and it should be established in a way that protects the remaining functional lung; the right lung can still ventilate and should be protected from blood pooling from the left lung hemorrhage. In this case, the best approach is a standard intubation, but the endotracheal (ET) tube should be pushed in deeply until it meets resistance. A single-lung intuba- tion of the right lung (the unaffected side in this case) is fairly easy to achieve with- out special equipment. Selectively intubating the left lung requires finesse and expe- rience and is made easier with the use of bronchoscopy. Without a bronchoscope, it is possible to maneuver the ET tube into the left mainstem bronchus by turning the tube 90 degrees to the left after passing the cords. Regardless, a large ET tube should be used in a patient with pulmonary hemorrhage so that a bronchoscope can be passed through it later for closer examination of the lung injury and possible sclerotic therapy of the bleeding vessel. Based on the history, the patient is most likely taking rivaroxaban, one of the novel anticoagulants. These medications do not require the frequent monitoring and adjustment necessary with warfarin use, but their function is not easily reversed; vitamin K has no role in their reversal. In addition to recently approved specific fab-fragment antidotes, there are some gen- eral therapies that can help the severely bleeding patient. Dabigatran has low pro- tein binding and can be removed via dialysis, or an activated prothrombin complex concentrate (factor VIII inhibitor bypass activity [FEIBA]) might help. The antico- agulation effect of rivaroxaban and apixaban can be lessened by the use of a pro- thrombin complex concentrate. Incorrect Answer Explanations An immediate, emergent open thoracotomy is an extreme measure with a high risk of death. Localized treatment of the bleeding vessel with a broncho- scope is a preferred approach. Regardless, the patient's airway must be secured and the anticoagulation reversed before a thoracotomy is possible. In theory, a patient with pulmonary hemorrhage should be placed with the bleeding side down (left in this case, not right) so that the blood pools in the “bad” lung and the “good” lung can continue to ventilate. This practice has not been validated by scientific study and might increase ventilation-perfusion mismatching. Intubation with a large endotracheal tube into the right mainstem bronchus is a bet- ter definitive management of the airway. CPAP is very effective in patients with ventilator failure such as those with COPD and congestive heart failure. However, it would be disastrous to attempt in a patient who is struggling to clear the blood from his airway. Intubation with a large endotracheal tube into the right mainstem bronchus is a better defini- tive management of the airway.

question: What is the most common etiology of massive hemoptysis in the developing world?
englishExplanation: Tuberculosis (TB) is the most common cause of massive hemoptysis in the developing world. In South Africa, up to 73% of massive hemoptysis cases are caused by TB. There are multiple mechanisms of bleeding with TB, in- cluding ulceration into a bronchial artery, rupture of a pseudoaneurysm of the pulmonary artery, and erosion of a calcified lymph node. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bronchiectasis, an inflammatory process of the lungs, is the most com- mon cause of life-threatening hemoptysis in the developed world, but not the developing world. In bronchiectasis, rupture of a capillary plexus or bronchial arteries causes massive hemoptysis into the airways. When associated with cystic fibrosis, it can account for 40% of all massive hemoptysis cases. Lung cancer accounts for up to 30% of massive hemoptysis. These bleeds can often be heralded by a smaller sentinel bleed weeks prior. However, in the de- veloping world, lung cancer is a less common cause of massive hemoptysis than TB. Although pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common diagnosis, it is an uncommon cause of hemoptysis. PE can be associated with hemoptysis, but this is rare; it is even rarer as a cause of massive hemoptysis. The mechanism of hemoptysis is usu- ally pulmonary infarction, and it usually occurs with small, distal thromboembolisms.

question: What is the best initial diagnostic test for undifferentiated hemoptysis?
englishExplanation: Chest x-rays are good initial screening tools in patients with undifferen- tiated hemoptysis. They can locate the cause of hemorrhage in as many as 46% to 80% of cases. Chest x-rays should be the first diagnostic test along with laboratory studies (CBC, PT/INR, and type and screen). In young, healthy patients with nor- mal chest x-rays and a likely viral cause of hemoptysis, the diagnostic workup can stop there with close follow-up. Those with normal chest x-rays and more concerning history will need further diagnostic workup, potentially in- cluding CT scans and/or bronchoscopy. Incorrect Answer Explanations Angiography is not the first-line diagnostic test for hemoptysis. Angiography is often used as a therapeutic option once the source of bleeding has been identified using other techniques (eg, chest x-ray followed by CT scan or bron- choscopy). Although angiography is relatively minimally invasive, it is still more in- vasive than other diagnostic tools and requires the use of intravenous contrast. Because bronchoscopy is relatively invasive, it is not the initial diagnos- tic test for hemoptysis. However, it is a useful tool in hemoptysis because it can be diagnostic as well as therapeutic. Bronchoscopy can be used to locate sources of bleeding and remove blood from the airways. Often, bronchoscopy is synergistic with CT imaging in the diagnosis and treatment of hemoptysis. CT imaging can lo- cate peripheral bleeding that is unreachable by flexible bronchoscopes. A CT scan is often useful as a second step in the diagnosis of hemoptysis in patients with normal chest x-rays. Because most sources of bleeding can be identified on a chest x-ray with far less radiation exposure, a chest x-ray is the pre- ferred initial diagnostic test.

question: Which clinical finding in patients with hemoptysis is most reliably predictive of mortality?
englishExplanation: The most common cause of mortality in hemoptysis is asphyxiation from blood in the airway. Hypoxia is a sign that the patient's airways are filling with blood, so they are at high risk of death. Patients with impaired alveolar gas ex- change have mortality rates of up to 80%. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hypotension is a sign that the patient may be undergoing hemodynamic collapse from acute blood loss and hemorrhagic shock. Although this is a life-threatening event, impaired gas exchange and hypoxia from blood in the airways is even deadlier. Tachycardia can be a sign that the patient has lost a significant amount of blood and may herald potential circulatory collapse from acute blood loss. However, pa- tients with hemoptysis are more likely to die from impaired gas ex- change and hypoxia from blood in the airways than from hemodynamic collapse. Although massive hemoptysis is a life-threatening event, it is less deadly than hy- poxia caused by blood in the airway. When based on blood volume, massive hemoptysis has variable definitions ranging from ≥100 to ≥1,000 mL of blood loss in 24 hours. These “amount of blood” criteria for massive hemoptysis have been shown to be unreliable because patients cannot reliably determine the amount of blood lost.

question: A 74-year-old man with a history of lung cancer presents with massive hemopty- sis. Despite intubation, he is persistently hypoxic. His chest x-ray is shown below. Which positioning maneuvers should be undertaken? Credit: David Yamane, MD.
englishExplanation: In patients with massive hemoptysis, the most common cause of mortal- ity is asphyxiation from airway obstruction. In these cases, contamination of blood into the good lung should be minimized. To prevent involvement of the unaf- fected lung, the bleeding lung should be kept down. This patient is bleeding from the left lung, so he should be put in the left lateral decubitus position. Incorrect Answer Explanations Prone positioning has been shown to reduce mortality and improve hypoxia in se- vere ARDS. The benefits are thought to be due to the mechanisms of lung recruit- ment and changing compliance of the lungs. However, in massive hemoptysis, the goal should be to avoid further contamination of blood into the un- affected lungs. Prone positioning does not prevent bleeding into the unaffected lung. In some asymmetric lung conditions, oftentimes the “good” lung is placed down to improve ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch. When placed down, the unaffected lung will have increased blood flow and thus improved perfusion to the lung with better ventilation. However, in cases of massive hemoptysis, bleeding will contaminate the unaffected lung, preventing gas exchange in both lungs. Thus, the affected lung should be placed down to prevent bleeding into the unaffected lung. This patient is bleeding from the left lung, so the left lung should face down. Supine positioning is not preferred in cases of hypoxia in which one lung is causing massive hemoptysis. Instead, the bleeding lung should be kept down (in this case of left lung bleeding, using the left lateral decubitus position) so that blood does not drain towards the unaffected side.

question: What is the most appropriate consultation for massive hemoptysis?

options.text: Anesthesia consultation for dual-lumen endotracheal tube placement
Interventional radiology consultation for emergent embolization

correctAnswer: Interventional radiology consultation for emergent embolization
englishExplanation: Massive hemoptysis has multiple definitions ranging from ≥100 to ≥1,000 mL in the first 24 hours. However, acute blood loss is difficult to quan- tify. Although the majority of the blood supply to the lungs is supplied by the pul- monary arteries (90%), it is a low-pressure system, so it rarely accounts for massive hemoptysis. Conversely, the bronchial arteries account for only 10% of the blood supply but are a high-pressure system, so they account for the ma- jority of massive hemoptysis. Bronchial artery embolization was first introduced in 1972 and is currently the most effective method to obtain definitive hemostatic control. Bronchial artery embolization is highly effective at controlling hemoptysis while being mini- mally invasive. A percutaneous arteriogram of the bronchial arteries, which origi- nate at the level of T5 to T6 from the thoracic aorta, allows for direct embolization with success rates of up to 70% to 95%. The most morbid complication of this pro- cedure is spinal cord ischemia from accidental embolization of the spinal arteries, occurring in 1.4% to 6.5% of cases. Incorrect Answer Explanations Dual-lumen tubes were previously used for massive hemoptysis to isolate each lung and prevent contamination of blood from the unaffected lung. However, their use has diminished due to their narrow individual lumens, which do not permit efficient evacuation of the clots or use of standard flexible bron- choscopes. Dual-lumen tubes are commonly placed by anesthesia to isolate each lung for single-lung ventilation during thoracic surgery. They should be placed un- der direct visualization using a fiberoptic scope. Flexible bronchoscopy is useful to find the location and cause of the le- sion for diagnostic purposes. It is also useful for extraction of the ob- structing blood clots. However, it is less effective than bronchial artery embolization in controlling massive bleeding. Bronchoscopy can also be used to isolate bleeding by placing bronchial blockers. One benefit of this procedure is that it can be performed at the bedside in unstable patients. Bronchoscopy can also be used to inject iced saline and epinephrine to help control bleeding, although these techniques do not have a robust evidence base to support their use. Although surgery was once the first-line therapy for massive hemoptysis, the advent of less invasive techniques has limited its role. Emergent thoracotomy remains the first-line treatment for iatrogenic pulmonary artery (PA) rupture (from PA catheter placement), complex arteriovenous malformation, and chest trauma. Emergent surgery for hemoptysis had a mortality rate of up to 34%. Given the high risk of surgery, less invasive approaches (eg, bronchial artery emboliza- tion) are preferred.

question: A 67-year-old woman presents with hiccups lasting 3 days after receiving a pace- maker placement 1 week ago. What is the best initial diagnostic study?
englishExplanation: An ECG is the best initial diagnostic study to evaluate for possible car- diac pacemaker lead displacement, which is a rare cause of persistent hiccups. Loss of pacemaker capture on ECG in the setting of hiccups strongly suggests lead dislodgement. A chest x-ray can then be used to visualize the placement of the suspected dislodged lead. Pacemaker leads are more likely to become displaced within the first 3 months of placement, but late dis- placements are also possible. Hiccups can be defined as benign (present for <48 hours) or persistent (present for >48 hours); intractable hiccups can last for more than a month. Persistent hiccups are often secondary to vagal or phrenic nerve injury or inflammation, but extracardiac pacing can also cause hiccups. Incorrect Answer Explanations Chest CT can aid in the diagnosis of persistent hiccups with an unknown etiology, but it is not the best initial test in this case. A CT scan can aid in an alternative diagnosis or show a lead displacement, specifically a perforation, but would not be used as the initial test for someone who presents with hiccups. A chest x-ray, together with an ECG, typically leads to the diagnosis of lead displacement quicker and may aid in the avoidance of advanced imaging and radiation. Although pacemaker interrogation is useful in the workup of lead migration, it is not the best initial study in this case. On pacemaker interrogation, low im- pedance and a high capture threshold are suggestive of a displaced lead. An upper GI series is rarely useful in determining the etiology of hic- cups and is never the best initial test. Fluoroscopy can be used to evaluate di- aphragmatic movement but would not be done in the emergency department.

question: A newborn baby presents with jaundice after being born at home 17 hours ago by spontaneous vaginal delivery at 37 weeks' gestation; the mother received no pre- natal care. The baby's vital signs include P 178, R 66, and T 37°C (98.6°F); SpO is 97% on room air. What is the most concerning potential cause?
englishExplanation: When considering the possible causes of jaundice, time of onset is a cru- cial branch point that provides clues to the underlying cause and its severity. Jaundice in the first 24 hours of life is an ominous finding because these patients are more likely to develop severe jaundice that could progress to ker- nicterus (hyperbilirubinemia-induced encephalitis). The factors that place a patient at high risk include a total bilirubin at discharge in a high-risk zone, gesta- tional age of 35 to 36 weeks, jaundice in the first 24 hours, a sibling who required 2 phototherapy, ABO incompatibility or hemolytic disease, breastfeeding but poor growth or feeding, and East Asian or Mediterranean ancestry. Hemolytic disease can lead to not only jaundice but also anemia, which can affect the patient's hemo- dynamic stability. A Coombs test can detect maternal IgG antibodies on the baby's RBCs; it should be included in the evaluation of this patient, as should testing for Hgb, liver function, total and fractionated bilirubin, and, possibly, blood typing for the neonate and birthing parent if this information is unknown. Incorrect Answer Explanations Jaundice develops in 30% of healthy breastfed infants and is 3 to 6 times more likely in a breastfed child than in one who is bottle fed. Breast milk jaundice has two stages: early (starting within the first week of life) and late (start- ing in the first week, peaking by 2 weeks, and then resolving by 3 months). Early breast milk jaundice is likely related to the decreased volume or frequency of feeds. This can lead to dehydration and delayed meconium passage. Early breast milk jaundice may also be related to the decreased enterohepatic recirculation and im- maturity of the liver in these children. Treatment for early breast milk jaundice is geared toward improving hydration (eg, increase to more than 10 feeds per day and possibly supplement with formula [not water or dextrose/HO]) while continuing to breastfeed. Late breast milk jaundice is believed to be caused by properties of the breast milk (eg, beta-glucuronidase and nonesterified fatty acids), which seem to decrease bilirubin metabolism. Treatment for late breast milk jaundice is to tempo- rarily withhold breastfeeding, although the mother is advised to continue to pump. The bilirubin level should decline rapidly in 48 hours with this approach. Bilirubin levels generally peak on days 6 to 14. Phototherapy is used to decrease the rise of total bilirubin in any neonate of any gestational age. Phototherapy should be used when the rate of rise is greater than 5 mg/dL per 24-hr period or when advised to do so using either the bilirubin nomogram or bilirubin calculator. Familial nonhemolytic jaundice, also known as Gilbert disease, is a hereditary disorder that leads to decreased bilirubin metabolism. It is uncommon in neonates but is often found in older children and adults. Physiologic jaundice is related to polycythemia of newborns as well as the immatu- rity of the liver, which leads to an elevated unconjugated bilirubinemia. This peaks between days 3 and 5 and resolves spontaneously by 14 days of life. 2

question: What is the most likely cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in school-aged children?
englishExplanation: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is an alarming laboratory finding that is pathologic in patients of any age. In the neonatal period, etiologies include bil- iary atresia, genetic disorders such as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and sepsis. Beyond the neonatal period, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia is caused by either bil- iary obstruction or hepatocellular injury, which can be caused by hepatitis A. Interestingly, symptom manifestation in hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection de- pends on age. In children younger than 6 years, 70% of HAV infections are asymp- tomatic and often develop without jaundice. Older children and adults, however, are frequently symptomatic, with jaundice occurring in more than 70% of patients. Additional symptoms include fever, malaise, abdominal discomfort, nausea, and dark urine. Treatment is typically supportive, and most cases resolve within 2 months. The virus is spread via a fecal-oral route, with transmission occurring among close contacts. Common-source outbreaks can also occur from food or water con- taminated with feces. In the United States, the number of children vaccinated against HAV since 1996 has increased, resulting in a precipitous decline in infection rates, which are at the lowest rates ever recorded according to the CDC. However, hepatitis A is still one of the most frequently reported vaccine-preventable diseases in the United States, and outbreaks still occur. Between 2016 and 2017, there was an outbreak of 251 cases of hepatitis A with five deaths reported in San Diego, largely affecting the vulnerable homeless population. Infection rates among Hispanic per- sons remain higher than among non-Hispanic persons. The highest rates of disease have been reported among children aged 5 to 14 years; approximately 25% of re- ported cases are in persons younger than 20 years. Incorrect Answer Explanations Biliary atresia, which develops due to obliteration of the extrahepatic biliary system, is a concerning cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with high associated morbidity rates; however, it does not occur in school-aged children. Jaundice manifests in infants aged 2 to 3 weeks, along with other signs of cholestasis, such as pale stools and dark urine. Treatment re- quires surgical intervention. If diagnosis is delayed, infants inevitably develop liver failure. Gilbert syndrome (also known as familial nonhemolytic jaundice) is common in the general population, but it causes unconjugated hyper- bilirubinemia, not conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Patients can develop self-resolving jaundice during mild illnesses. Sepsis from serious bacterial infections can trigger jaundice in newborn infants, but it typically causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Neonatal jaundice is also associated with UTIs and TORCH infections (toxoplasmo- sis, other/syphilis, rubella, cytomegalovirus, and HSV).

question: A 56-year-old man presents with severe right shoulder pain, a swollen and warm shoulder joint, and fever to 39.1°C (102.4°F). His range of motion is severely lim- ited by pain. Arthrocentesis is performed, and 30 mL of fluid is obtained and shown below. What is most likely to be found in the fluid under microscopic examination? Credit: Hans R. House, MD, FACEP.
englishExplanation: Considering the patient's fever and the pus-like appearance of the shoulder synovial fluid, it is likely the patient has septic arthritis. The most common cause of sep- tic arthritis is Staphylococcus aureus, which typically appears as a gram-positive cocci collecting in grape-like clusters. Other bacteria that can be found in septic arthritis include Group A Streptococcus, Streptococcus pneumo- niae, and, rarely, Neisseria gonorrhoeae (a gram-negative diplococci). Patients with septic arthritis typically present with fever, joint swelling and pain, and limited range of motion in the affected joint, which is almost always monoarticular. Elevated ESR and CRP levels are suggestive of infection. Septic arthritis, especially in children, is not an obvious diagnosis, and clinicians must be cautious about performing arthrocentesis. One set of clinical criteria is the Kocher criteria, which were developed retrospectively to estimate the risk for septic arthritis of the hip in children. But a definitive clinical diagnosis can be made only from a synovial culture, which must be obtained by arthrocentesis. A Gram stain of the synovial fluid might reveal the causal bacteria but is more likely to show only WBCs. The synovial fluid drawn from the septic shoulder is turbid and purulent and has a low viscosity, low glucose, and 30,000 or more WBCs/cm, most of which is polynu- cleated cells. Incorrect Answer Explanations Gram-negative diplococci are the typical appearance of Neisseria species. N. gonor- rhoeae can cause a migratory polyarthritis associated with a vesicular or pustular rash. It can also, rarely, cause a septic monoarthritis, usually in the knee, wrist, or ankle. The most common cause of septic arthritis is S. aureus, which typ- ically appears as a gram-positive cocci collecting in grape-like clusters. Needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals are caused by the precipitation of monosodium urate in the synovial fluid. This is the cause of gout and typically af- fects the first metatarsal phalangeal joint but can occur as a monoarthritis in other joints, including the ankle, knee, and elbow. Although gout can lead to low-grade fevers and slightly cloudy synovial fluid, the high fever and turbid appearing puru- lent synovial fluid in this case is most consistent with septic arthritis. The most common cause of septic arthritis is S. aureus, which typically appears as a gram-positive cocci collecting in grape-like clusters. 3 Rhomboid-shaped positively birefringent crystals are caused by the precipitation of calcium pyrophosphate crystals and are seen in pseudogout. Although pseudogout can lead to low-grade fevers and slightly cloudy synovial fluid, the high fever and turbid appearing purulent synovial fluid in this case is most consistent with septic arthritis. The most common cause of septic arthritis is S. aureus, which typically appears as a gram-positive cocci collecting in grape-like clusters.

question: A 55-year-old woman presents with light-headedness and generalized weakness. Her medical history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and diabetes mellitus. She reports that she started taking trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI 4 days ago. Her vital signs are BP 138/72, P 112, R 18, and T 36.6°C (97.9°F); SpO is 98% on room air. Her ECG shown below reveals a QRS width of 174 ms at a rate of 119 bpm. What is the correct next step in management? 2 Credit: Mattu A. Amal Mattu's ECG case of the week – January 13, 2020. ECG Weekly. https://ecgweekly.com/2020/01/amal-mattus-ecg-case-of-the-week- january-13-2020/
englishExplanation: The ECG is significant for a very wide QRS complex (>170 ms) at a rate less than 120 bpm, which is consistent with hyperkalemia; thus, calcium glu- conate would stabilize the myocardium and is the correct next intervention. Ventricular tachycardia and hyperkalemia can be easily mistaken for one another. Traditionally, the QRS complex in hyperkalemia is greater than 170 ms but can be slower than the typical ventricular tachycardia rate of greater than 120 to 130 bpm. Normally, ventricular tachycardia does not exceed 200 ms in QRS width. Both hy- perkalemia and ventricular tachycardia can present with a QRS complex between 170 ms and 200 ms, so look toward the heart rate, medical history, and pre- sentation to help differentiate between the two conditions. The ECG shown has multiple QRS complexes greater than 200 ms, a heart rate less than 120 bpm, and a presentation that is more suggestive of hyperkalemia than ventricular tachycardia. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can lead to hyperkalemia in patients with renal impairment, or in patients taking any medications that affect the potassium levels within the body, such as ACE inhibitors (ACE-I), even with base- line normal renal function.
