The relationship between trimethoprim-sulfamethoxa- zole and potassium stems from the trimethoprim component. Trimethoprim has a similar molecular structure to amiloride, which restricts sodium channel excretion by competitive inhibition and impairs potassium excretion within the kidney; when coupled with the addition of another component (eg, ACE-I, renal dysfunction), an additive effect leads to hyperkalemia. In this patient, the recent initiation of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole pushed her into hyperkalemia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Adenosine is an atrioventricular (AV) nodal-blocking agent that is tradi- tionally used to treat certain tachyarrhythmias, including supraventric- ular tachycardia (SVT), AV reentrant tachycardia (AVRT), AV nodal reen- try tachycardia (AVNRT), and even certain atrial tachycardias. Adenosine is con- traindicated in this case; if any concern for an accessory pathway is present, adeno- sine may cause deterioration into an unstable tachyarrhythmia (ie, ventricular fibrillation). Procainamide is a sodium channel–blocking antiarrhythmic tradition- ally used to treat stable ventricular tachycardia or tachyarrhythmias due to Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. In this scenario, the significant widening of the QRS complex makes a metabolic (ie, hyperkalemia) or toxicologic (eg, sodium channel blockade) cause more likely. In either case, procainamide ad- ministration could worsen the patient's clinical status and is not treating the hyperkalemia. Synchronized cardioversion is indicated for any unstable tachyarrhyth- mia; however, because this patient has a stable blood pressure and is conversant, pharmacotherapies are indicated as the first step in inter- vention. Specifically, treating hyperkalemia with calcium. When synchronized car- dioversion is necessary, the traditional starting energy level is between 150 and 200 joules.

question: A 61-year-old woman presents with vertigo that starts every time she moves her head. She has no hearing changes, tinnitus, or significant medical history. Her blood pressure is 178/85; there are no neurologic deficits. Bedside positional testing demonstrates nystagmus with a long latency and transient duration; it is suppressible with repeated testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is suggested by the onset of vertigo with changes in head position and by the age of the patient. More importantly, the physical examination confirms that this patient has peripheral vertigo; the nystagmus has a long latency, has a transient duration, and is fatigable with provocative testing (the Dix-Hallpike ma- neuver). Furthermore, it is not associated with any other neurologic deficits. This is distinct from central vertigo, such as that caused by strokes and tumors. Central vertigo tends to have nystagmus with a short latency and a sustained duration, is not fatigable, and tends to be accompanied by other cranial and peripheral nerve deficits. BPPV is the most common cause of vertigo overall, accounting for approxi- mately 40% of vertigo diagnoses and affecting roughly 10% of all adults by age 80. The incidence of BPPV increases with age, with peak onset between age 50 and 60. Women are more commonly affected than men, with almost a 3-to-1 female-to-male ratio. Osteoporosis, vitamin D deficiency, and a history of prior head trauma have all been associated with the development of BPPV. BPPV is believed to be caused by loose calcium carbonate otoliths moving aberrantly within the semicircular canals of the inner ear, ultimately resulting in the false sensation of rotation. The posterior semicircular canal is most commonly affected and accounts for approximately 60% to 90% of all cases of BPPV. Patients usually present with brief episodes of vertigo, typically lasting less than 1 minute, that are provoked by head position changes (eg, rolling over in bed, getting out of bed, tilting the head upward to reach objects on high shelves, or tilting the head downward to tie shoes). BPPV can be diagnosed with a series of bed- side maneuvers known as the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, which provokes di- rectional and torsional nystagmus depending on the involved semicircular canal. If a Dix-Hallpike test result is negative, a supine roll test may be performed to evalu- ate for lateral semicircular canal BPPV. The first-line treatment for BPPV is an at- tempt at repositioning the misplaced otolith with a procedure known as the Epley maneuver. This is effective in approximately 90% of cases. Pharmacologic treat- ments such as meclizine, ondansetron, and diazepam may be used to temper nausea and emesis in patients with BPPV but are not as effective as the Epley maneuver. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ménière disease is unlikely because this patient lacks the typical aural symptoms. The classic triad for Ménière disease is intermittent episodes of ear full- ness, tinnitus, and vertigo. In BPPV, the nystagmus has a long latency, has a transient duration, and is fatigable with provocative testing. A transient ischemic attack is an important consideration but is unlikely because of the lack of central signs on physical examination, including ataxia. In BPPV, the nystagmus has a long latency, has a transient duration, and is fatigable with provocative testing. Vertebral basilar artery insufficiency is an important consideration in the differen- tial diagnosis, but this condition is unlikely because of the lack of central signs on physical examination. Vertebral basilar artery insufficiency should always be considered in patients with vertigo that occurs when they look up (when raising the head compresses the vertebral artery). In BPPV, the nystagmus has a long latency, has a transient duration, and is fatigable with provocative testing.

question: A 65-year-old woman presents with recent-onset vertigo and difficulty with her balance for the past few days. Her symptoms are not worsened by any particular position and are occasionally associated with nausea. Her medical history is sig- nificant for hypertension. The physical examination reveals normal hearing, ver- tical nystagmus, abnormal Romberg testing, and ataxia. What is the most likely etiology for these symptoms?
englishExplanation: This patient's recent onset of vertigo and ataxia with several signs of central vertigo (no change in symptoms with head movement and verti- cal nystagmus) suggests a cerebellar infarct. Differentiating between periph- eral and central vertigo is an important distinction for diagnostic and therapeutic reasons, and careful physical examination is critical. Central vertigo is caused by ab- normalities of the brainstem or cerebellum, including hemorrhage or infarct, verte- brobasilar insufficiency, multiple sclerosis, neoplasms, and migraine-related ver- tigo. The onset of symptoms for central vertigo can be gradual or abrupt, and the severity of vertigo is often less intense and defined compared with that of peripheral vertigo disease. Additionally, central symptoms are usually present, including motor weakness, ataxia, difficulty speaking, or vertical nystagmus. Hearing loss and tinni- tus are absent. Posterior circulation ischemia accounts for approximately 20% of ischemic events in the brain. Ischemia can be caused by occlusion, dissection, or embolism. Cerebellar infarcts account for 1% to 4% of all strokes and can be caused by is- chemia to the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), or vertebral arteries. Full PICA territory strokes can lead to a syn- drome known as pseudotumoral cerebellar infarction, which results in headache, vomiting, and decreased consciousness, followed by stupor and deep coma. Pseudotumoral cerebellar infarction is caused by edema. Incorrect Answer Explanations Peripheral vertigo symptoms usually occur more acutely and are aggravated by po- sition and movement. They frequently have associated nausea and vomiting, com- pared to central vertigo. Examples of peripheral vertigo include benign positional vertigo, Ménière disease, perilymph fistula, vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, ototox- icity, and eighth nerve lesions. Recent onset of vertigo and ataxia with sev- eral signs of central vertigo (eg, no change in symptoms with head movement and vertical nystagmus) suggests a cerebellar infarct. Vestibular nerve schwannomas, when large, compress the cerebellopontine angle and can be considered a central cause of vertigo. Because the symptoms in this case have a relatively acute onset and are not associated with any disorders of hearing (eg, hearing loss or tinnitus), a cerebellopontine angle tumor is unlikely. Recent onset of vertigo and ataxia with several signs of central vertigo (eg, no change in symptoms with head movement and vertical nystagmus) sug- gests a cerebellar infarct. Ménière disease is associated with increased endolymph within the cochlea and labyrinth. It is characterized by intermittent episodes of unilateral tinnitus, hearing loss, and ear pressure, along with vertigo. Antihistamines are the initial choice for symptom control for patients with Ménière disease. The definitive diagnosis of Ménière disease is generally not made in the emergency department. If it is sus- pected, patients should be referred to an otolaryngologist for further evaluation. Recent onset of vertigo and ataxia with several signs of central vertigo (eg, no change in symptoms with head movement and vertical nystag- mus) suggests a cerebellar infarct.

question: A 14-month-old boy presents because he hurt his leg and will not walk. The par- ent says the boy was playing on the stair landing and got his left foot tangled in a bannister. The child is calm and playful on examination but cries when his left leg and ankle are manipulated. An x-ray of the lower leg is obtained and shown below. What is the most appropriate management? Credit: Hans R. House, MD, FACEP.

options.text: Apply a long-leg splint to the left leg and arrange follow-up care
Consult orthopedics for percutaneous pinning of the growth plate
Obtain urgent orthopedic consultation for open reduction and internal fixation
Report suspected child abuse and immobilize the left leg

correctAnswer: Apply a long-leg splint to the left leg and arrange follow-up care
englishExplanation: Toddler fracture is a very common injury in toddlers who recently began to walk. Toddler fracture is a fracture of the tibia diaphysis and usually occurs in the distal third but can extend into the midshaft. Emergency department treatment is largely supportive, usually placement of a long-leg splint. The mecha- nism of injury in this case is consistent with findings on the x-ray, so there is no spe- cific reason to suspect child abuse. This type of fracture, considered to be a subset of childhood accidental spiral tibia (CAST) fractures, occurs in young children from those just beginning to walk to those older than 7 years. The mean age for it is 50 months, just over 4 years. Spiral fractures of the proximal third of the tibia or of the femur are less likely to be accidental and should prompt consideration of abuse. A toddler fracture can be ra- diographically obscure at initial presentation. If this fracture is suspected because the patient is not walking but x-rays are negative, repeat the x-rays in 7 to 10 days: the fracture might be more evident then. The patient might benefit from splinting of the extremity in the interim. Incorrect Answer Explanations Percutaneous pins are used to secure the epiphyseal (growth) plate to the diaphysis in unstable Salter-Harris fractures. This patient's injury is limited to the diaphysis; the epiphyseal plate is not involved. Toddler fractures are generally benign and may be treated conservatively with long leg splint and outpatient follow-up. The higher types of Salter-Harris fractures carry a worse prognosis for normal bone development and might need more aggressive treatment. Also, supracondylar frac- tures require immediate operative management. However, toddler fractures are generally benign and may be treated conservatively. However, toddler fractures are generally benign and may be treated conservatively with long leg splint and outpatient follow-up. Spiral fractures can result from child abuse, from a perpetrator twisting the victim's arm or leg. Spiral fractures of the tibia in a toddler, given the appropriate context, are very common and do not always warrant suspicion of abuse. They may be treated conservatively with long leg splint and out- patient follow-up. Spiral fractures of the proximal third of the tibia or of the fe- mur are more likely the result of abuse.

question: An adolescent with persistent lymphadenopathy, unresponsive to antibiotics, presents after his first seizure. Which initial diagnostic study is the most appropriate?
englishExplanation: The most appropriate initial study in this case is serum electrolytes. Persistent lymphadenopathy associated with systemic symptoms should raise clin- ical suspicion for malignancy in this patient. Evaluating for life-threatening metabolic derangements is critical in patients with suspected malignancy, as tumor lysis syndrome can occur spontaneously. Tumor lysis syndrome results in hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia, and hyperuricemia. The subsequent symptoms are related to electrolyte derangement and can include seizure, tetany, lethargy, muscle cramps, weakness, and cardiac dysrhythmias. The initial diagnostic evaluation for patients with suspected malignancy should also include a CBC with differential, blood group type and antibody screen, coagulation studies, and a chest x-ray to evaluate for a mediastinal mass. In addition to tumor lysis syndrome, emergent complications include heart failure from profound ane- mia, cerebrovascular accident related to hyperleukocytosis, hemorrhage due to co- agulopathy or thrombocytopenia, and superior vena cava syndrome associated with mediastinal masses. Incorrect Answer Explanations Bone marrow aspirate analysis, while potentially diagnostic, would not be the best initial study to obtain. The first priority in this patient would be to evaluate for any emergent, life-threatening complications of a suspected malig- nancy, including electrolyte abnormalities. Additionally, one should evaluate for profound thrombocytopenia and DIC prior to performing the procedure. The emergency department setting is not ideal for bone marrow aspiration, as this pro- cedure requires preparation of specialized materials and laboratory protocols. CSF studies would not be indicated emergently unless the patient demonstrates additional history and physical examination findings sug- gestive of meningitis. This patient's clinical presentation could represent CNS invasion of leukemic cells, in which case diagnostic CSF can be obtained for analysis once more immediate complications have been addressed. CSF analysis can subse- quently serve to direct intrathecal chemotherapy. Lymph node culture will not yield results that will aid patient manage- ment in the immediate setting, making it less useful as the initial diagnostic study. In patients with persistent lymphadenopathy, culture can help distinguish in- fected lymph nodes from lymphoma. It can also identify the specific microorgan- isms causing lymph node infections and guide subsequent therapy.

question: A child presents with fever, malaise, cervical lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
englishExplanation: Infectious mononucleosis is most commonly caused by EBV and classi- cally presents as fever, fatigue, exudative tonsillopharyngitis, and adenopathy. Many infectious mononucleosis patients will also have splenomegaly and are, subsequently, at risk for splenic rupture. The lymphadenopathy is typi- cally in the posterior cervical nodes, although patients may develop diffuse lym- phadenopathy. The exudative pharyngitis associated with infectious mononucleosis is often initially mistaken for streptococcal pharyngitis. When treated with amoxi- cillin, the sore throat will persist, and patients often develop a maculopapular rash. Laboratory findings in infectious mononucleosis include an atypical lymphocytosis as well as an elevated AST and ALT. Diagnosis can be made with the heterophil antibody test, but this test is less accurate in children younger than 4. Confirmatory testing can be done with EBV serologies or PCR. Treatment of infectious mononucleosis is supportive, and the majority of symp- toms resolve within 2 weeks. Patients should be advised that fatigue can be pro- longed, and athletes should avoid strenuous and high-contact sports for at least 4 weeks. Incorrect Answer Explanations Splenomegaly is a rare clinical manifestation of cat scratch disease (CSD). CSD is caused by a bite or scratch from a young cat infected with Bartonella henselae. Typically, younger patients will develop a skin lesion, followed by regional lymphadenopathy that develops close to the site of the initial exposure. These ten- der, erythematous lymph nodes may become fluctuant. Disseminated disease is rare but can involve both the liver and spleen and cause encephalitis, neuroretinitis, and arthritis. Patients with uncomplicated CSD can be treated with a 5-day course of azithromycin. Patients with Kawasaki disease (KD) have fever and cervical lymphadenopathy, but splenomegaly is not a typical feature of their initial presentation. KD is an immune-mediated vasculitis characterized by fever lasting longer than 5 days plus at least four additional signs of mucocutaneous inflammation (eg, limbic spar- ing, nonexudative conjunctivitis, oral mucositis, cervical lymphadenopathy, rash, or redness or swelling of hands and feet). Laboratory findings that support the diagno- sis include elevated inflammatory markers, sterile pyuria, hypoalbuminemia, and elevated transaminases. Treatment with intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) and aspirin aims to minimize the risk for cardiac complications, such as coronary artery aneurysm formation. Although patients with mycobacterial infections can develop splenomegaly, splenic enlargement is more commonly noted in patients with infectious mononucleosis. Tuberculous lymphadenitis is an extrapulmonary manifestation of tuberculosis (TB) and is most often caused by reactivation of latent TB. The cervi- cal lymph nodes are most commonly affected and present as unilateral, nontender masses. Definitive diagnosis requires identification of the mycobacteria organism from lymph node culture. Multidrug antituberculosis therapy should be adminis- tered based on drug susceptibilities.

question: A 34-year-old man is transferred from a long-term care facility shortly after inad- vertently pulling out his gastrostomy tube. A review of his records shows that it was surgically placed 6 days earlier without complication. He has mild abdomi- nal tenderness and is otherwise well appearing with stable vital signs. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a sterile occlusive dressing to the opening and arrange follow-up care
Obtain surgical consultation while considering imaging and intravenous antibiotics
Replace it with a similarly sized gastrostomy tube or Foley catheter to maintain tract patency
Use a wire and Seldinger technique to replace it with a similarly sized gastros- tomy tube

correctAnswer: Obtain surgical consultation while considering imaging and intravenous antibiotics
englishExplanation: Most gastrostomy tube (G-tube) tracts mature after 2 to 3 weeks, and dis- lodgement of the G-tube puts patients at risk for intestinal content leakage and peri- tonitis. Imaging, antibiotics, and surgical consultation are typically recom- mended. Attempting to replace a G-tube or Foley catheter into the tract before the tract matures can create a false lumen or worsen intraperitoneal leakage. In distinction, if the G-tube had been in place long enough for the tract to mature (2 to 3 weeks), emergent replacement with another G-tube is in- dicated to maintain tract patency. Maintaining temporary patency with a Foley catheter (typically 16 Fr or 18 Fr) is an acceptable alternative. To confirm that the tube has been replaced correctly, about 25 mL of a water-soluble contrast material should be injected through the tube then checked with a supine abdominal x-ray. Incorrect Answer Explanations Conservative wound management by applying an occlusive dressing may be appro- priate after surgical consultation. However, this patient likely requires observa- tion and potentially alternative parenteral access, while awaiting a replace- ment of the G tube by a consulting service. Inserting a replacement G-tube or temporary Foley catheter to maintain tract patency is the appropriate intervention only after the tract has ma- tured, which takes about 2 to 3 weeks. If replacement is attempted before the tract matures, it can create a false lumen or worsen intraperitoneal leakage. If the G-tube had been in place long enough for the tract to mature (2 to 3 weeks), then emergent replacement with another G-tube is indicated to maintain tract pa- tency. Using a wire to insert a similarly sized G-tube carries the risk of creating a false lumen, but this procedure may be performed by a consultant with sufficient experience.

question: In young infants who present with vomiting, which finding is most likely to dif- ferentiate acute malrotation with midgut volvulus from pyloric stenosis?
englishExplanation: The color of the vomitus in acute malrotation with midgut volvulus is the feature that best differentiates it from pyloric stenosis. Acute malrotation with midgut volvulus involves locations of the GI tract more distal than the pylorus, resulting in hallmark bilious vomiting. Conversely, pyloric stenosis is an obstruction at the level of the distal stomach, so bilious vomitus is unex- pected. Vomiting in pyloric stenosis is typically described as forceful, projectile, and with large amounts of breast milk or formula. Patients with midgut volvulus present with bilious vomiting, sudden onset of severe abdominal pain, irritability, and ill appearance. Midgut volvulus is a surgical emergency that can result in is- chemia of the intestine if not treated urgently. The confirmatory imaging study of choice is a limited upper GI series showing a characteristic “corkscrew” ap- pearance of the duodenum. Incorrect Answer Explanations Abdominal distention can be seen in both of these conditions because they lead to an obstructive picture. In pyloric stenosis, a progressive gastric outlet ob- struction results from a growing pylorus. In the late stages of this condition, a distended pylorus and body of the stomach can be seen as a result. In malrota- tion with midgut volvulus, an obstruction of the distal duodenum leads to sudden onset of vomiting and abdominal distention. However, it is im- portant to note that abdominal distention may not be seen in either of these diag- noses, so this is an unreliable diagnostic clue. Pneumatosis seen on abdominal x-ray is not a characteristic of either pyloric stenosis or malrotation with midgut volvulus. Rather, this finding is characteris- tic and pathognomonic of infants with necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). NEC occurs most commonly in premature infants, and they present with either bil- ious or nonbilious vomiting and feeding intolerance. A high fever is not a characteristic finding in acute malrotation with midgut volvulus or pyloric stenosis. Neither of these conditions is from a pri- marily infectious cause. Rather, the inciting cause of both is mechanical.

question: A 3-year-old boy fell from a shopping cart, hitting his head. There was no loss of consciousness, and his GCS score is 15. He has normal mental status and behav- ior and no signs of a basilar skull fracture. If the patient presents with vomiting, what is the recommended diagnostic approach according to the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Pediatric Head Injury Prediction Rule?

options.text: No diagnostics required; the patient may be discharged
Observation or head CT are acceptable approaches

correctAnswer: Observation or head CT are acceptable approaches
englishExplanation: The Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Pediatric Head Injury Prediction Rule is an externally validated clinical decision tool that enables physicians to identify children at very low risk of clini- cally-important traumatic brain injuries (ciTBI) to avoid head CT. This patient is deemed moderate risk using this criteria based on the presentation of vomiting. Moderate risk patients may either undergo head CT or observation. There are two rules (one for age <2 and the other for ages 2-18) each utilizing six predictors to determine risk of a ciTBI. High-risk predictors are: GCS score ≤14, signs of basilar skull fracture or palpable skull fracture, or signs of altered mental status (eg, agitation, somnolence, repetitive questioning, or slow response to verbal communication). Moderate-risk predictors for children ages 2 to 18 are loss of consciousness, severe headache, vomiting, or severe mechanism (eg, rollover motor vehicle collision, patient ejection, death of another passenger, pedestrian or nonhelmeted bicyclist struck by a vehicle, fall >3 ft for chil- dren <2 y old or >5 ft for children ≥2 y old, or head struck with a high-impact ob- ject). For children <2 years old, occipital, parietal, or temporal scalp hematomas are included and vomiting is excluded as moderate-risk predictor variables. Patients with any high-risk predictors should undergo head CT. Those with no risk factors present do not need a head CT or period of observation. Those with moderate-risk findings, as in this case, may either undergo CT or a 4 to 6 hour period of observation. A several hour observation period is preferred, but the clinician may consider personal experience, parent preference, worsening signs or symptoms during observation period, age <3 months, and the presence of multiple versus isolated findings when deciding between observation and head CT in this circumstance. Incorrect Answer Explanations Head CT is recommended when any one of the high-risk predictors is present: GCS score<15, altered mental status, or signs of a basilar skull fracture. In the PECARN study, these were associated with a 4.3% incidence of clinically impor- tant TBI. Although subspecialty consultation should always be a viable option when expert advice is needed, neurosurgical consultation is not part of the PECARN de- cision rule. The PECARN rule is utilized to predict ciTBI, of which neurosurgical intervention is one. Other ciTBIs included in the rule are death, intubation, and hospital admission. Patients can be safely discharged if none of the PECARN risk predictors are present. If no predictors are present, the risk of ciTBI is <0.02% for age <2 and <0.05% for ages 2 to 18. This patient presented with vomiting, which is a mod- erate risk factor.

question: A natural gas worker presents with headache, nasal irritation, skin irritation, and eye watering after exposure to a substance that smelled like “rotten eggs.” What is the most appropriate management of this exposure?
englishExplanation: This patient was exposed to hydrogen sulfide (HS), which is a toxic, color- less gas with a characteristic rotten egg smell. This patient had a mild expo- sure that requires decontamination by clothing removal followed by skin and eye ir- rigation with normal saline. Relatively minor exposures to HS primarily cause mucous membrane irritation and can lead to bronchitis, pul- monary edema, and keratoconjunctivitis. Severe exposures demonstrate HS's cyanide-like toxicity against cytochrome oxidase and present with severe lac- tic acidosis, kidney injury, CNS abnormalities (eg, stimulation or de- pression, dizziness, headache, seizures, disorientation, coma), and car- diac symptoms (eg, chest pain, abnormal conduction). The most severe ex- posures can cause immediate incapacitation and death within a few breaths. Direct exposure to liquid HS can cause rapid skin injury and frostbite. Management varies by level of exposure. All patients should have their cloth- ing removed and any exposed surfaces (including eyes, unless frostbitten) should be irrigated with copious normal saline or clean water. Supplemental oxygen, bronchodilators, and racemic epinephrine can be used for respiratory symptoms, and in severe cases, intubation may be necessary. Skin injuries should be treated with appropriate wound and frostbite care. Those with more severe exposures showing signs of CNS or cardiac abnormalities should be managed sup- portively. Nitrite rescue therapy can be used but may be effective only if adminis- tered soon after exposure. However, it should be considered in severe cases. Hyperbaric oxygen has been used but is not currently recommended over high-flow oxygen therapy. Hydroxocobalamin, used in cyanide toxicity, is currently being studied as a rescue therapy. Most exposed patients are admitted for contin- ued supportive care and observation for delayed symptoms. Incorrect Answer Explanations 2 2 2 2 Hydroxocobalamin is used as a treatment for cyanide poisoning. At this time, there is ongoing research for its use in hydrogen sulfide exposure, but it is not currently recommended. It can be considered in severe cases in conjunction with a toxicology consultation, but its utility in mild exposures is especially unclear. Hyperbaric oxygen has been used for treatment of hydrogen sulfide poi- soning, but there is no clear benefit. It is not recommended for mild expo- sures to HS, as in this case, but it can be considered in severe cases in conjunction with toxicology consultation. Current recommendations are for high-flow oxygen therapy. N-acetylcysteine is used as a treatment for acetaminophen overdose. It has no known role in hydrogen sulfide exposure.

question: An 8-year-old boy with no significant medical history presents with palpitations. An ECG shows a wide-complex regular tachycardia at a rate of 290. Which thera- peutic option should be avoided in this patient?
englishExplanation: The differential diagnosis of regular, wide-complex tachycardia includes ven- tricular tachycardia and supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction. In a pediatric patient with no previous cardiac history, the latter is more likely. Because of the patient's age, wide QRS, and ventricular rate, an- tidromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT) in the setting of Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is a concern. AV nodal blocking agents such as adenosine should be avoided in antidromic AVRT. Incorrect Answer Explanations Electrical cardioversion is the indicated treatment if the patient is hemodynami- cally unstable and should not be avoided. The vignette does not give us much in- formation about his other vital signs, so depending on the individual case character- istics, electrical cardioversion might be indicated. The drug of choice for acute termination of suspected antidromic AVRT is intra- venous procainamide. Procainamide can be used safely in WPW and does not have the risk of increasing accessory pathway conduction. Vagal maneuvers should be attempted in stable patients with potential supraven- tricular tachycardias, including AVRT. Placing a bag of ice water over the nose and forehead of a patient for 15 to 20 seconds at a time, or having the patient blow into an occluded straw or syringe, are options in pediatric patients. Key Points Avoid AV nodal-blocking agents such as adenosine, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers in antidromic antidromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT). When unsure of the underlying rhythm in a patient with wide-complex tachycardia, treat it as ventricular tachycardia.

question: Which presentation is most consistent with classic botulism?

options.text: GI illness followed by descending symmetrical flaccid paralysis with the cranial nerves often being affected first
Ocular muscle weakness causing diplopia, blurred vision, or ptosis that is often worse at the end of the day
Progressive proximal muscle weakness and hyporeflexia that improves with brief, vigorous exercise
Viral illness followed by ascending symmetrical paralysis and loss of deep ten- don reflexes

correctAnswer: GI illness followed by descending symmetrical flaccid paralysis with the cranial nerves often being affected first
englishExplanation: Classic botulism, also known as foodborne botulism, is characterized by initial GI symptoms of nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea after eating food that is contaminated with preformed botulinum toxin. The onset of neurologic symptoms typically occurs within 24 hours (al- though it can be delayed) and most commonly starts with bilateral cranial nerve abnormalities (ie, ocular or bulbar symptoms), such as diplopia, blurry vision, facial muscle weakness, and difficulty speaking and swal- lowing. There may also be symptoms similar to an anticholinergic toxidrome (eg, constipation, urinary retention, dry mouth, mydriasis). Botulism can be differ- entiated from an anticholinergic toxidrome by the absence of altered mental status and tachycardia. Treatment of botulism involves monitoring for signs of impending respiratory fail- ure, intubation if respiratory failure ensues, administration of antitoxin, and sup- portive care. Once botulism is suspected, clinicians should administer botulism antitoxin as soon as possible. In the US, clinicians need to contact the state health department to obtain the antitoxin. Most of these patients require ICU admission. Incorrect Answer Explanations The worsening of symptoms throughout the day suggests myasthenia gravis. The edrophonium challenge test used to be a common maneuver in which acetylcholinesterase inhibitor edrophonium was administered to see if an improve- ment in ocular weakness occurred. However, this test is not performed anymore largely due to a lack of availability of the drug. Currently, the diagnosis of myasthe- nia relies on physical examination with assistance of serologic testing. One interest- ing bedside test involves briefly placing an ice pack over a ptotic eyelid (for about 5 minutes). Improvement of ptosis by greater than or equal to 2 mm is considered positive, with reportedly over 98% specificity for myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia crisis can be severe and lead to respiratory failure. Common causes of crisis include medication, infection, pregnancy, and surgery. Progressive muscle weakness and hyporeflexia that improves with vig- orous exercise is the classic description of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). Additionally, LEMS is different from the other options in its more common proximal muscle weakness. LEMS is associated with small-cell carcinoma of the lung. Treatment of LEMS focuses both on primary treatment of the malignancy and symptom management. This is a classic description of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS). Although GBS has many variations with different clinical presentations, the description of ascending symmetrical paralysis and loss of deep tendon reflexes should raise sus- picion for GBS, particularly in the setting of a recent viral illness. Other features that suggest GBS include the presence of mild sensory symptoms, absence of a fever, autonomic dysfunction, and albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with normal WBCs) in the CSF.

question: What electrolyte abnormality presents with circumoral and digital paresthesias?
englishExplanation: Although many electrolyte abnormalities present with paresthesias, hypocalcemia and hypophosphatemia both present with paresthesias that are local- ized to the circumoral region. Other symptoms of hypocalcemia include muscle spasms, cramps, tetany, and seizures. Hypocalcemia causes pares- thesias due to increased neuromuscular excitability. Calcium is essential for cell function, nerve transmission, bone structure, intracellular signaling, and coagula- tion. Calcium levels are regulated by Vitamin D, parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, and FGF23. Causes of hypocalcemia include kidney disease, alcohol abuse, medica- tion side effects, recent head and neck surgery, and other electrolyte abnormalities, among many others. Treatment typically includes calcium repletion (IV or PO, depending on severity) as well as correction of the underlying cause and any other electrolyte abnormalities. Incorrect Answer Explanations Hypermagnesemia rarely produces symptoms. Mg2+ decreases the trans- mission of neuromuscular messages, acts as a CNS depressant, and decreases neu- romuscular activity. CNS depression symptoms progress with the degree of magnesium elevation and include nausea, somnolence, loss of deep ten- don reflexes, respiratory depression, hypotension, heart block, and car- diac arrest. Symptoms of hypernatremia depend on the type and may include nau- sea and vomiting, lethargy, weakness, increased thirst, low water in- take, salt intake, and polyuria. Hypernatremia is primarily seen in infants and the elderly. In infants, their smaller mass to surface area ratio as well as their de- pendency on a caretaker put them at higher risk of hypernatremia. In the elderly, impaired thirst mechanism, immobility, neurologic impairment, and reliance on a caregiver may lead to hypernatremia. Hyponatremia symptoms are influenced by the rapidity of onset. Moderately severe symptoms may include headache, nausea, disorien- tation, confusion, agitation, ataxia, and areflexia. Moderate symptoms typi- cally occur with a Na+ <130 mEq/L. If Na+ is <120 mEq/L, severe symptoms may develop, including intractable vomiting, seizures, coma, and ultimately, respiratory arrest due to brainstem herniation.

question: A patient presents with paresthesias as well as twitching of the upper lip with tapping on the cheek. What ECG finding is most commonly associated with this condition?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms of hypocalcemia. The classic findings on ECG in a patient with hypocalcemia are QT interval prolongation due to prolonged ST segment from increased duration of phase two of the action po- tential of cardiac muscle. QT interval prolongation is proportional to the degree of hypocalcemia and can lead to torsades de pointes, which can be fatal. Other elec- trolyte abnormalities may be present as well. Hypocalcemia presents with digital and circumoral paresthesias as well as seizures, fatigue, depression, and anxiety. Heightened neuromuscu- lar excitability may cause twitching of the upper lip with tapping on the cheek (known as Chvostek sign) and carpopedal spasm observed follow- ing application of an inflated blood pressure cuff over systolic pressure (known as Trousseau sign). Treatment includes calcium repletion as well as in- vestigation into the underlying cause, such as parathyroid hormone disorders, low vitamin D levels, and hyperphosphatemia, among others. Incorrect Answer Explanations Peaked T waves are typically associated with hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia is a life-threatening electrolyte abnormality that can cause fatal dysrhythmias. Patients with hyperkalemia who have peaked T waves, bradycardia, wide QRS com- plexes, or other ECG findings should be treated with calcium for cardiac membrane stabilization. The U wave is a small deflection immediately following the T wave, usu- ally in the same direction as the T wave, and is best seen in leads V2 and V3. Prominent U waves are typically >1 to 2 mm or 25% of the height of the T wave. U waves are most commonly seen in patients with severe hypokalemia. Although U waves may be present in patients with hypocalcemia, QT interval prolongation is more commonly seen. A wide QRS complex refers to a QRS complex duration >120 ms and is related to slower spread of ventricular depolarization. Causes may include right or left bun- dle-branch blocks, pacemaker, hyperkalemia, ventricular preexcitation (as is seen in Wolf-Parkinson-White pattern), and a ventricular rhythm (eg, ventricular tachycardia).

question: A patient presents with paresthesias of the hand, localized to the volar surface of the first through third digits. What are the associated ultrasound findings?

options.text: Fluid around the flexor tendon sheaths
Median nerve cross sectional area greater than 10 mm<sup>2</sup>
Median nerve with lower intraneural vascularity on color Doppler
Ulnar nerve measuring greater than 5 mm<sup>2</sup>

correctAnswer: Median nerve cross sectional area greater than 10 mm<sup>2</sup>
englishExplanation: This patient presents with signs and symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, which is compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel of the wrist. Diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome via ultrasound is becoming more common because it is more comfortable and less time consuming than electrodiag- nostic testing. The most important parameter of median nerve ultrasonography is cross sectional area. For the median nerve at the level of the carpal tunnel, a cross sectional area greater than 10 mm is considered abnormal. Other important ultrasonographic parameters include the longitudinal appear- ance of the nerve as notched, waistline with compression under the flexor retinaculum, or higher intraneural vascularity on color Doppler. 2 Treatment options for carpal tunnel syndrome include activity modification, NSAIDs, bracing, injections, and surgery. Incorrect Answer Explanations Fluid around the flexor tendon sheaths is typically seen in tenosynovi- tis. Although the flexor tendons are also part of the carpal tunnel along with the median nerve, fluid around the flexor tendon sheaths is not commonly seen with carpal tunnel syndrome. Tenosynovitis can be caused by trauma, mechanical irrita- tion, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, diabetes, infection, and compartment syndrome, among others. One of the ultrasound findings associated with carpal tunnel syndrome is high, not low, intraneural vascularity of the median nerve on color Doppler. This phenomenon is thought to be secondary to venous congestion, nerve edema, and impairment of the arterio-venous supply as a result of entrapment. Patients without carpal tunnel syndromes show no intraneural blood flow on ultrasound. Ulnar nerve measuring greater than 5 mm may be seen in a patient pre- senting with symptoms of distal ulnar neuropathy or Guyon canal syn- drome. This syndrome is caused by swelling or compression of the nerve in Guyon canal between the pisiform and hook of hamate. It typically presents with symptoms in the fourth and fifth digits, such as tingling, weakness, or paralysis of the intrinsic muscles of the hand, which may present as a weakened hand grip or clawing of the fourth and fifth digits.

question: A patient presents with ascending paresthesias in the bilateral lower extremities 1 week after a diarrheal illness. What other findings are associated with this syndrome?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms that are concerning for Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), which results in autoimmune destruction of the nerves in the peripheral nervous system. GBS patients classically present with ascending flaccid paralysis, which can be preceded by paresthesias. Areflexia or hyporeflexia is usually present. Respiratory failure can oc- cur in up to 30% of patients, leading to prolonged hospitalization and recovery. Other symptoms include facial muscle weakness (due to involvement of facial cra- nial nerves), dysautonomia, neck flexion weakness, and dysphagia. There are other GBS variants that may have slightly different presentations. GBS is most commonly seen after an infection, usually a diarrheal ill- ness such as Campylobacter jejuni. Up to 70% of GBS patients report some sort of preceding infection within 1 to 6 weeks of their illness. GBS has also been seen 1 to 3 weeks after receiving a vaccination. Although GBS is primarily a clinical diagnosis, evaluation includes nerve conduction studies, head imaging, and lumbar puncture (CSF typically shows elevated protein level) in addition to other laboratory testing. Treatment of GBS include IVIG, plasma exchange, and supportive care. Respiratory assistance should be provided for patients who are unable to perform a negative inspiratory force (NIF) of -20 to -30 cm H0. Incorrect Answer Explanations Diplopia and color vision changes may be seen in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). Although these patients may present with paresthesias, they are typically more diffuse, episodic, and not ascending, as in GBS. MS patients may have a delay in their diagnosis given the episodic nature of their paresthesias sec- ondary to lesions in the CNS occurring at different times and at different locations. Excessive salivation and hydrophobia are symptoms that are more char- acteristic of rabies. Rabies is one of the oldest known diseases in history and causes viral encephalitis, typically as a result of an animal bite. Following viral transmission from infected animal saliva, the virus travels through the peripheral nervous system. In humans, the first symptoms seem like a viral syn- drome, but then, they progress to anxiety; agitation; delirium; hyper- salivation; and pharyngeal muscle spasm at the sight, sound, or taste of water (known as hydrophobia). Eventually, the virus progresses to death. The diagnosis is typically made based on history but also with CSF, blood, saliva, or tis- sue testing. There is no effective treatment for rabies, so any bites from a bat, skunk, raccoon or fox are treated with rabies vaccine and immune globulin. Slurred speech with hemiplegia are symptoms of an acute ischemic stroke. Although some strokes can present with paresthesias, symptoms are 2 typically unilateral and not ascending. Middle cerebral artery strokes com- monly present with unilateral weakness as well as speech deficits. Neurological deficits are graded based on the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS). Treatment of an acute stroke depends on the time from symptom onset; options include intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy for patients who qualify.

question: Where are paresthesias associated with disc herniation at the L4 level located?
englishExplanation: Lumbar disc herniations may present with radicular pain that can assist with local- izing the lesion. In this case, a disc herniation at L4 may cause radiating pain or paresthesias in the anterior thigh, medial aspect of the leg, and medial ankle. The most sensitive place to check for sensation within the L4 der- matome is the medial ankle, according to the ASIA examination. The L4 nerve root exits the L4 to L5 foramina. It can be assessed with the patellar reflex. Ankle dorsi- flexion may be affected as well. Disc herniations are common and may be acute or chronic as a result of disc degeneration. Incorrect Answer Explanations Paresthesias in the anterolateral leg correlate with symptoms at the L5 level. Depending on the severity of the herniation or degeneration, a patient may present with symptoms at multiple levels. The L5 to S1 level is the most common lo- cation for a lumbar disc herniation. This typically presents with back pain that radi- ates to the buttock, lateral thigh, lateral calf, and the dorsum of the foot. The key sensory point for the L5 dermatome is the first webspace on the dorsum of the foot. Great toe extension is typically used to assess for motor involvement. Paresthesias in the inguinal region correlate with symptoms at the L1 level. The L1 nerve root exits at the L1 to L2 foramina. This nerve root is responsi- ble for the cremasteric reflex in men. There is rarely motor involvement with com- pression at this level, although hip flexion may be slightly affected. Paresthesias in the posterior calf correlate with symptoms at the L5 and S1 levels. The S1 nerve root can be assessed with the Achilles reflex. S1 nerve root compression will present with sacral or buttock pain that radiates into the postero- lateral thigh, calf, and lateral foot. There may be weakness with ankle plantar flex- ion, making it challenging for a patient to walk on their toes. Other symptoms in- clude urinary or fecal incontinence and sexual dysfunction.

question: A patient presents with paresthesias of the left arm, face, and leg without motor involvement. What is the location of their acute ischemic stroke?
englishExplanation: This patient is presenting with symptoms of an acute ischemic stroke of the right thalamus. A pure sensory stroke involving face, arm, leg, and trunk usu- ally localizes to the thalamus. The thalamus is located in the dorsal midbrain and has several functions, such as relaying sensory and motor signals to the cerebral cortex, sleep regulation, consciousness, and alertness. The ventral posterolateral nucleus is specifically one of the parts of the thalamus that projects sensory infor- mation to the somatosensory cortex of the brain. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ischemic strokes of the cerebellum are most commonly caused by ob- struction of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Patients typ- ically present with symptoms of headache, vertigo, horizontal ipsilateral nystagmus, and truncal ataxia. Obstruction of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) and the superior cerebellar artery (SCA) can also lead to cerebellar strokes. Symptoms may be subtle, and strokes of the posterior circulation are most often missed. Approximately 75% of patients report “dizziness” of some sort, al- though this is a nonspecific symptom. Strokes in the internal capsule are typically pure motor strokes, and dif- ferent areas of the internal capsule (anterior limb, genu, posterior limb, sub- lentiform part, and retrolentiform part) are supplied by different arteries. Symptoms typically include contralateral pure motor hemiparesis af- fecting the face, arm, and leg. Mild dysarthria may be present, specifically with the stroke syndrome known as dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome, which is rare. Cortical signs such as aphasia, visual disturbances, or cognitive deficits are absent. Strokes of the occipital lobe result from obstruction of the superficial posterior cerebral artery (PCA). The occipital lobe is essential for vision and is where sensory input from the eyes is interpreted. Patients will present with oc- ular findings such as homonymous hemianopsia (ie, visual field deficits in half the visual field) as well as impairment of tactile sensation and proprioception.

question: A 35-year-old man presents with significant agitation, confusion, dilated pupils, and dry, flushed skin. His vital signs are BP 160/90, P 140, R 20, and T 40°C (104°F). Administration of which medication would be detrimental to this patient's condition?
englishExplanation: This patient is suffering from anticholinergic toxicity. Of the answer choices provided, diphenhydramine is most likely to be harmful, as it is an antihis- tamine that possesses anticholinergic properties and could potentially has- ten an anticholinergic toxidrome. Patients who present with an anticholinergic tox- idrome should be screened for potential diphenhydramine or other antihistamine ingestion, since this is a common culprit in the development of this toxidrome. Classically, anticholinergic overdose should be suspected in patients with an agi- tated delirium; mydriasis; dry, flushed skin or mucous membranes; hy- pertension; tachycardia; urinary retention; hypoactive bowel sounds; and hyperthermia. This toxidrome is often remembered by the memory aid “hot as a hare, red as a beet, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, mad as a hatter, full as a flask, and ‘tachy' as a pink flamingo.” This toxidrome must be differen- tiated from a sympathomimetic toxidrome, which can present similarly. A key differentiating factor is the skin: Anticholinergic toxicity presents with dry skin, whereas sympathomimetic toxicity presents with diaphoretic skin. Many common medications, such as antihistamines, antipsychotics, antidepressants, my- driatics, atropine, and muscle relaxants, can lead to an anticholinergic toxidrome when taken in excess. Natural substances, such as plants (eg, Jimson weed) and mushrooms in the genus Amanita should also be suspected. The antidote to an- ticholinergic toxicity is physostigmine. It is a cholinergic agent that should only be used in a closely monitored setting because there is risk of precipitation of cholinergic toxidromes, seizures, and severe bradydysrhythmias. Incorrect Answer Explanations Ketamine, an N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist, is often used dur- ing procedural sedation and in the treatment of agitated delirium. It does not have anticholinergic properties and would not be expected to harm this patient. If ad- ministered, the patient should be monitored, since he is already tachycardic. Midazolam, a benzodiazepine, would not be expected to harm this patient. Although it is not an antidote to this syndrome, it is the preferred treatment for sedation of patients with anticholinergic toxicity. Physostigmine, a cholinergic agent, is the preferred antidote to anti- cholinergic poisoning. It should be used judiciously due to its risk of precipitat- ing cholinergic toxidromes, seizures, and severe bradydysrhythmias culminating in asystole.

question: Which intervention is most appropriate for a patient who has overdosed on an extended-release formulation medication?
englishExplanation: Whole-bowel irrigation (WBI) is a technique used primarily to treat oral overdoses of medications or other substances that would make expe- dited GI transit beneficial. In particular, WBI is commonly used following large ingestions of extended-release, long-acting, or enteric-coated formula- tions of dangerous medications to limit the risk of severe, prolonged toxicity. Other indications include toxic ingestions that are not well adsorbed by activated charcoal — such as metals — and removal of ingested drug packets. WBI uses the same electrolyte-balanced polyethylene glycol solution used to pre- pare the bowel for colonoscopies. However, WBI is performed at a much higher volume and rate than colonoscopy preparation, approximately 1.5 to 2 L/hr in an adult. Consequently, it is commonly performed with a nasogastric tube because oral ingestion of such a large volume is extremely difficult. WBI is generally well toler- ated, and complications most commonly include GI upset and discomfort. However, for patients with depressed levels of consciousness, it is prudent to con- sider intubation for airway protection prior to starting any oral or enteric treatment, including WBI. WBI is discontinued once the patient has clear rectal ef- fluent. Contraindications include active GI tract pathology, such as ileus or bowel obstruction, and anatomic variation, such as prior bariatric surgery or stricture. Although WBI uses electrolyte-balanced solutions, it is prudent to ensure euvolemia, normal serum electrolyte levels, and hemodynamic stability before starting. Although WBI is thought to be beneficial for the aforementioned indications, its ef- ficacy is not well established. Currently, WBI is not considered to be the stan- dard of care for the management of any oral ingestion, and recommendations for its use are largely on a case-by-case basis. There is also some controversy as to whether WBI should be used concurrently with activated charcoal, but there is cur- rently little evidence to suggest a negative interaction. Incorrect Answer Explanations Endoscopic retrieval is not routinely performed after extended-release drug ingestion; WBI would generally be initiated first in this circumstance. Endoscopic retrieval can be performed in certain circumstances following ingestion of a potentially toxic object or packet. Most commonly, endoscopic retrieval is con- sidered following failure of WBI to clear the target from the GI tract if the target is located in an accessible location. Gastric lavage is an older method of gastric decontamination whereby a large-bore tube is placed into the stomach; the stomach is lavaged with fluid, then aspirated. This method is now rarely used and has mostly fallen out of favor because of poor tolerance, efficacy, and risk-benefit profile. Additionally, the value of gastric lavage is even further limited for later-presenting ingestion by its inability to reach pills that have passed out of the stomach. Whole-bowel irriga- tion would be indicated over gastric lavage in this circumstance because it is better tolerated, safer, and more likely to address an ingestion of extended-release medications. Surgical resection, like endoscopic retrieval, can be performed in certain circumstances in which a potentially toxic object or packet is present but cannot be removed by other, less invasive methods. Surgery is not the first-line treat- ment of an overdose with an extended-release formulation. Thus, whole- bowel irrigation would be indicated over surgical resection in this circumstance.

question: A patient presents comatose after a presumed metformin overdose. Laboratory studies are notable for a pH level of 6.9, a pCO of 35 mm Hg, a creatinine level of 1.71 mg/dL, a glucose level of 56 mg/dL, and a lactate level of 21 mmol/L. What is the most critical intervention?
englishExplanation: This patient is critically ill after a metformin overdose. Patients who present with significantly elevated lactate levels (>20 mmol/L), severe acidosis (pH level <7.0), altered mental status, renal dysfunction, and shock in the setting of metformin overdose should receive hemodialysis per the Extracorporeal Treatments in Poisoning Workgroup (EXTRIP) guidelines. Metformin is a biguanide antidiabetic agent that is used to treat type II diabetes mellitus. It acts by several mechanisms, perhaps the most important of which (in the setting of poisoning) is mitochondrial inhibition. Additionally, inhibition of hepatic gluconeogenesis from pyruvate leads to decreased lactate consumption (and therefore lactate accumulation). Inhibition of aerobic metabolism also contributes to acidosis and increased lactic acid production — the entity referred to as met- 2 formin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA). Metformin is renally cleared and may accumulate in the setting of kidney dysfunction, inducing toxicity with acidosis and lactate accumulation. Additionally, massive ingestions of metformin (>20-50 g) may result in severe toxicity (GI upset, delirium, coma, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, shock, acidosis, hepatotoxicity, renal failure, and elevated lactate), which generally occurs within 6 to 12 hours of ingestion. Outside of MALA, death after metformin overdose is exceedingly rare, and ingestions up to 5 g are generally well tolerated. Treatment of massive metformin ingestion is generally supportive, although hemodialysis may be indicated, as described below. Appropriate patients (who present within 4 hours with airway controlled) should receive activated charcoal. Hypoglycemia should be corrected with intravenous dextrose. Altered mentation and coma may require mechanical ventilation. Shock can be treated initially with in- travenous fluids and then with vasopressors as needed. Severe acidosis can be tem- porized with sodium bicarbonate. However, definitive management of severe MALA is with hemodialysis. Metformin is small and has limited protein binding, but it has a large volume of distribution; thus, it is moderately dialyzable. Severe acidosis (pH level <7.0), elevated lactic acid (>20 mmol/L), renal fail- ure, liver failure, decreased level of consciousness, shock, and failure of supportive measures are indications to perform hemodialysis in the set- ting of metformin overdose per EXTRIP guidelines. Incorrect Answer Explanations ECMO can be considered in patients severely poisoned by metformin overdose, but it is not the first-line or primary therapy. There are case reports of metformin overdose treated with ECMO. ECMO may be indicated for patients with metformin overdose as a bridge therapy in the setting of shock during hemodialysis or continu- ous renal replacement therapy. Sodium bicarbonate can be administered in the setting of severe acidosis after toxic ingestion, including after metformin overdose. However, in the setting of metformin overdose, it is a temporizing measure only — not definitive management. One possible approach to the use of sodium bicarbonate in this setting might be a bolus of 100 mEq NaHCO followed by an infusion at a rate of 200 to 250 mL/hr. Hemodialysis is the definitive management of severe metformin poisoning. Vasopressor infusion may be needed in patients with shock after a metformin overdose, but there is no indication that this patient is experiencing shock. A trial of 3 supportive care with intravenous fluids would generally precede administration of vasopressor agents in the setting of metformin overdose.

question: Which finding distinguishes poison ivy dermatitis from phytophotodermatitis?
englishExplanation: Poison ivy dermatitis is characterized by intense pruritus. Phytophotodermatitis can be intensely painful, but is not pruritic. Poison ivy dermatitis is a type IV hypersen- sitivity reaction to the protein urushiol, which is present in poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac. Approximately 70% of people are sensitized to these plants. Dermatitis occurs after direct exposure to the protein, which is released by damaged plants. Treatment includes supportive care, topical corticosteroids for mild reac- tions, and oral corticosteroids for severe reactions. Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic reaction that occurs after topical exposures to certain plant-derived substances, including celery, parsnip, parsley, lemons, and limes. This condition is frequently seen in gardeners, children, and food-industry workers. Skin manifestations are similar to those of poison ivy dermatitis, with the exception of being isolated to sun-exposed areas. Treatment includes sun avoid- ance, broad-spectrum sunscreen, supportive measures, and topical or oral steroids for more severe reactions. When compared to poison ivy dermatitis, phytophotoder- matitis carries an increased risk of prolonged hyperpigmentation (months to years) of affected areas. Incorrect Answer Explanations Both conditions manifest multiple hours after exposure, so the delay would not dif- ferentiate between the two. Because it is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction, poison ivy dermatitis generally manifests 4 to 96 hours after exposure. Phytophotodermatitis generally manifests 24 hours after sun exposure. Both poison ivy dermatitis and phytophotodermatitis manifest as papules, plaques, or bullae in a linear, patterned distribution. One distinguishing factor in appearance is that phytophotodermatitis should only manifest on sun-exposed regions of the skin. Poison ivy dermatitis will occur on the areas of the skin that were exposed to the plant, or more specifically, the urushiol. Both conditions are caused by exposures to plants. Poison ivy dermatitis is caused by exposure to poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac, as urushiol protein in all three cross-reacts. Phytophotodermatitis can be caused by fig, St. John's wort, and many herbs and vegetables.

question: Which disease has a rash that spares the patient's palms and soles?
englishExplanation: The characteristic rash associated with Lyme disease occurs a few days to a month after the initial tick bite occurring wherever a tick might attach, but it notably spares the soles and palms. Often unnoticed when the disease first starts, a small erythematous region immediately surrounding the tick bite can be seen called erythema migrans. This can then expand into an erythematous lesion that can be as large as 30 cm in diameter. Classically, as this initial lesion grows, the center clears, resulting in the classic “target” pattern. However, not all cases involve central clearing, and many patients with Lyme do not recall a tick bite. If the disease pro- gresses without treatment, other target lesions will appear. Other systemic symp- toms of Lyme disease include fever, aches, and joint pain; neurologic and cardiac symptoms may appear later in the course of the disease. Incorrect Answer Explanations Disseminated gonorrhea presents with a rash that is generally an erythema- tous base with either macular, papular, or petechial rash on most skin surfaces, including the palms and soles but sparing the face. Other associ- ated symptoms include fever, joint pain, and genital discharge. Another STI that has a characteristic rash on the palms and soles is secondary syphilis. The Rocky Mountain spotted fever rash is seen a few days after the typical symptoms of high fever, myalgias, and headache. The initial macular rash starts on the hands, wrists, feet, and ankles; then, it extends centrally. After several days, the rash develops into the more classic diffuse petechial lesions, in- cluding the palms and soles. Petechiae are a sign of severe, possibly life-threatening disease progression. Scabies is a skin rash caused by a mite (Sarcoptes scabiei). The immune reaction to the mite causes the severely pruritic rash that presents with papules, bur- rows, and vesicopustules. A classic presentation on the palms and soles is often seen as a vesiculopapular outbreak. Scabies is more commonly seen in less devel- oped countries, and patients with an infestation will present with thousands of crusted lesions.

question: An 8-month-old girl presents for evaluation of a rash overlying her trunk and ex- tremities that started this morning. Two days ago, she had a high fever, but she is now awake and alert, is in no distress, has age-appropriate vital signs, and is afebrile. The rash is blanchable without petechiae or mucous membrane involve- ment. What is the most likely etiology? Credit: phadungsak sawasdee/Shutterstock.com.
englishExplanation: Roseola infantum, also known as exanthem subitum, typically occurs in children from 6 to 15 months of age and is characterized by upper respi- ratory symptoms with a preceding high fever (which may lead to febrile seizures) followed by a diffuse body rash. Human herpesvirus 6 is the most common cause of this infection. The rash typically starts on the trunk and may extend to the extremities, neck, and face, but it lacks apparent discom- fort or itch. There are rarely any major sequelae from this infection, and complete resolution is the norm. Incorrect Answer Explanations Erythema chronicum migrans (ECM) is associated with Lyme disease and is characterized by an erythematous rash with a target-like appear- ance. There are many different iterations of ECM, which may also include a bluish hue. Purpura fulminans is associated with severe meningococcal infection and is characterized by a diffuse purpuric rash related to DIC issues. This rash heralds a life-threatening infection and should be treated rapidly with an- tibiotics and blood products to counteract the bleeding diathesis inherent in this disorder. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is associated with a reaction to medications or may be caused by certain viral or bacterial infections (eg, herpes and hepatitis A as typical viral causes or mycoplasma pneumonia as a bacte- rial cause). The rash is characterized by the development of blisters or bullae and involves the mucous membranes. The Nikolsky sign, where the skin denudes from deeper tissue with simple manipulation of the bullae, is common in this condition. These patients may be best treated at a burn center to support the injury to the integument.

question: A 22-year-old man presents with months of intermittent lower abdominal cramping and bloody diarrhea that has worsened over the past week. He passed gross red blood this morning, has been dizzy, and "almost passed out twice." Abdominal examination is diffusely tender. Rectal examination reveals gross red blood on the examination glove, but no hemorrhoids were seen and the rectum was nontender. What is the most likely cause of the bleeding?
englishExplanation: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is the most likely cause of this patient's symp- toms. Classic presenting symptoms of IBD are abdominal pain, diarrhea, tenesmus, and bloody stools. IBD usually refers to two major disorders, Crohn disease and ul- cerative colitis. The crampy abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea are also consistent with the diagnosis of IBD, as would be tenesmus (feelings of cramping like having to defecate). Peak incidence of IBD is between the ages of 15 to 30, with another bimodal age of diagnosis around 50 to 80. There is a slight male preponder- ance for ulcerative colitis as well as a strong familial association with Crohn disease. Smoking is a risk factor for Crohn disease, but not for ulcerative colitis. Bleeding from IBD can be intermittent, and the symptoms can last for weeks prior to presen- tation. The diagnosis of IBD is generally confirmed with endoscopic evaluation. When clinically indicated, CT is the most useful imaging modality to evaluate for ex- traluminal complications in the emergency department. Incorrect Answer Explanations Colonic angiodysplasia is an acquired lesion, usually of the ascending colon and cecum, affecting patients older than 60 years. Although patients infrequently present with massive blood loss, they most often present with signs and symptoms of anemia and syncope due to intermittent episodes of bleeding. Bleeding from diverticula is unusual in this age group and is generally painless. Bleeding can be significant and is thought to be due to an erosion in the penetrating artery of the diverticulum. Hemorrhoids are the most commonly identified source of lower GI bleeding. Internal hemorrhoidal bleeding is usually associated with in- termittent, painless bleeding and can be found in patients of all ages. External hemorrhoids are usually painful and apparent on physical examination. Bleeding associated with hemorrhoids typically results in brown stool mixed with streaks of blood and blood after wiping, not the bloody diarrhea described by this patient. Furthermore, hemorrhoids generally do not cause abdominal pain, only localized rectal pain.

question: A 2-year-old child presents with intermittent abdominal pain and hematochezia. An ileocolic intussusception is diagnosed and is successfully reduced with an air enema. On re-evaluation 2 hours later, the child is well appearing, nontoxic, tol- erating oral fluids, and has normal vital signs. What is the correct disposition?

options.text: Endoscopy suite for endoscopic bowel evaluation

englishExplanation: This patient presented with an uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception, which was appropriately reduced using an air enema. Following a short period of postprocedural observation, discharge home is appropriate if the patient is well appearing and tolerating oral intake. A vast majority of intussusception patients are stable and have an uncomplicated clinical course, making them eligible for discharge. Enema-based reduction of ileocolic intussusception carries a very small (<1%) risk of perforation. It is prudent to give return precautions related to the development of new abdominal pain and fever along with obstructive and recurrent intussusception symptoms. Recurrence can occur in up to 20% of cases, usually within the first 72 hours. Notably, 95% of pediatric intussusceptions are ileocolic, 90% occur before 2 years of age, and 75% in the common age group (3 months to 3 years) are idiopathic/primary and do not have a pathological lead point. Very young or older children with intussusception are at higher risk for a pathological lead point. Incorrect Answer Explanations Endoscopic bowel evaluation is more appropriate for other causes of hematochezia, such as inflammatory bowel disease. It is generally unneces- sary following reduction of an uncomplicated ileocolic intussusception and is cur- rently not utilized in the management of active intussusception. For this patient, discharge home with return precautions is the most appropriate disposition. Observation admission for bowel rest is appropriate for patients with a small bowel obstruction, often in conjunction with nasogastric suction. However, no additional interventions are required following successful reduction of an uncomplicated ileo- colic intussusception. Operating room for laparoscopic surgery would be appropriate in only a few circum- stances. An intussusception that does not respond to nonoperative reduc- tion, or is complicated (eg, peritonitis, perforation, hemodynamic insta- bility), should receive emergent surgical evaluation. Complicated patients should also receive aggressive resuscitation and empiric antibiotics. Surgical evalua- tion is appropriate if a mass is noted on imaging. This patient does not meet any surgical indications, so discharge home with return precautions is the most appro- priate disposition.

question: A 70-kg, 52-year-old man presents via ambulance after 24 hours of right lower quadrant abdominal pain and fever. His vital signs include BP 85/45 (MAP 58), P 135, R 27, and T 38.5°C (101.3°F). Resuscitation is initiated while pursuing fur- ther diagnostic evaluation, treatment, and surgical evaluation for appendicitis and appropriate antibiotics are given. His blood pressure does not significantly improve with an additional 2 L of normal saline, lactate remains elevated at 4.6 mg/dL, and urine output is negligible. What is the best next step in management?

options.text: Administer stress-dose intravenous steroids and continue aggressive fluid resuscitation
Continue aggressive fluid resuscitation with repeat boluses

englishExplanation: This patient is presenting in septic shock with evidence of organ hypoperfusion and dysfunction. Septic shock is defined as MAP is <65 mm Hg despite adequate [30 mL/kg] isotonic crystalloid resuscitation or who have lactate >2 mmol/L. At this time, it is most reasonable to initiate vasopressor medications. Norepinephrine is preferable because dopamine has a higher rate of mortality and arrhythmias in sepsis patients. In the emergency department, there are several possible methods of assessing re- sponse to fluid resuscitation in septic shock. These include lactic acid clearance, urine output, central venous pressures, or central venous oxyhemoglobin saturation (via a central venous catheter). Per the 2021 Surviving Sepsis guidelines, “Dynamic parameters include response to a passive leg raise or a fluid bolus, using stroke vol- ume (SV), stroke volume variation (SVV), pulse pressure variation (PPV), or echocardiography, where available.” A recently used alternative assessment of ade- quate resuscitation in patients without known cardiac dysfunction is the use of ul- trasound assessment of IVC collapse to guide fluid resuscitation therapy. However, this methodology continues to have some limitations in the general population and is currently not incorporated into the 2021 Surviving Sepsis guidelines. Incorrect Answer Explanations The use of stress-dose intravenous steroids in septic shock is controversial, with conflicting study results. Stress-dose intravenous steroids are only recommended in septic shock refractory to multiple vasopressors. At this time, it is most reason- able to initiate vasopressor medications, specifically norepinephrine. Initiating dopamine could be considered for this patient. However, norepineph- rine is the preferred agent in septic shock because dopamine has been linked to a higher mortality rate and arrhythmias. Fluid resuscitation should be continued to achieve ventricular filling, and additional fluid may be indicated. However, this patient remains hypotensive with evi- dence of organ hypoperfusion, so vasopressors, specifically norepineph- rine, should be initiated.

question: A 19-year-old man presents via ambulance with chest and abdominal pain fol- lowing a single-car crash. He was an unrestrained driver and was ejected from the car. On arrival, he is amnestic to the event. His neck veins are flat, and there is an odor of alcohol on his breath. His vital signs include BP 78/55, P 122, and R 16. What is the most likely cause of his hypotension?
englishExplanation: This patient's hypotension and tachycardia indicate uncompensated shock. The additional physical examination finding of flat neck veins completes the classic constellation of signs for hypovolemic shock but not of the other condi- tions listed. Hypovolemic shock can be classified as either hemorrhagic or non- hemorrhagic. Hemorrhagic shock should be assumed to be present in any hypotensive trauma patient until proven otherwise. It is important to note that multiple types of shock may be present simulta- neously in a trauma patient. For example, a severely injured patient might have life-threatening hemorrhage, a tension pneumothorax, and a spinal cord injury. Nonetheless, hypovolemic shock is the most appropriate answer in this scenario. Incorrect Answer Explanations Cardiac tamponade presents with distended neck veins, not flat neck veins, unless the patient has profound concomitant hypovolemia. The classic triad of car- diac tamponade (Beck triad) involves distended neck veins, hypotension, and muffled heart sounds. Thus, tamponade is unlikely in this case. Neurogenic shock can lead to hypotension, bradycardia, paralysis, and urinary retention, among other signs. Spinal shock occurs in trauma patients after a spinal cord injury and can lead to a temporary loss of reflexes and mo- tor function. This patient is not bradycardic, so hypovolemic shock is more likely. Tension pneumothorax can present with distended neck veins and tra- cheal deviation. It also can present with hypotension, tachypnea, and de- creased breath sounds on the side of the pneumothorax. This patient has flat neck veins, making tension pneumothorax less likely. However, if tension pneu- mothorax is suspected, the emergency physician should have a low threshold to in- tervene, and they should be prepared to perform needle decompression or tube tho- racostomy, if needed.

question: A 19-year-old man presents after a diving injury in a swimming pool. On physical examination, his vital signs are BP 76/44, P 59, R 12, and T 36°C (98.6°F); SpO is 94% on room air. He has 2/5 strength in the upper extremities bilaterally and 1/5 strength in the lower extremities bilaterally. Which agent is the best option to manage this patient's hemodynamic instability?
englishExplanation: There are no strict guidelines on vasopressor use in neurogenic shock, but the Consortium for Spinal Cord Medicine recommends the use of norepinephrine for hypotension in cervical or upper thoracic regions related to the loss of sympathetic tone. Dopamine is also mentioned as an alternative treatment, but systematic reviews have demonstrated that there are some advantages to utiliz- ing norepinephrine. Small studies have demonstrated an increase in MAPs and fewer complications (eg, arrhythmias and troponin elevations). 2 Norepinephrine also utilizes both alpha- and beta-receptor activation. The alpha-re- ceptor activation will increase peripheral vascular tone, which will help raise the blood pressure; however, the beta-receptor activation will also prevent any reflex bradycardia. Incorrect Answer Explanations Atropine should always be considered for bradycardia causing significant hypoten- sion; however, in patients with neurogenic shock, the primary mechanism of hy- potension is the vasodilation from lack of sympathetic tone. The bradycar- dia is often relative to the hypotension, rather than the direct cause of it.
